I've pledged this Kickstarter, I was following this since the beggining. The game I've receive is not what was promised, it's just an lazy animated book, filled with meaningless text 80% of the time. What's the point of interact with a blue floating orb that emits light, if the only thing I'm presented is a text saying "it's a blue floating orb with light pouring from it"? Yes, I can see that, are you just trying to increase ingame word-count? You can't take pride of 3+ milion word-count if almost all of those words are just wasted text.
It's  just a little bit of Numenera (the world), if you already read the Ninth World Guidebook you'll be disapointed because this game can't make justice to this amazing world.
It's not Cypher System, in the worst way, as the developer just got a system that made a paradigm shift in RPGs and returned it to the status quo. The system uses your stat pools as "HP", the developer just ignored this and created out of thin air a HP stat. There are just 3 foci, instead of dozens that you have in the original Cypher System. And even with all those changes, if you make a Nano and go full INT, the game turns so easy that's almost like you're cheating. Just to show how poorly implemented the system is: you can 90% of time use your companions stat pools in your personal checks. It doesn't make any sense. You're not that good at lying? No problem at all, because this other nano is a lying machine and will make sure you deceive everyone around you with his talking skills, even while he is not taking any part in the talk!
Very lazy texts, unpolished UI that screams "CONSOLE GAME", forgettable NPCs, boring combat system. It's an abomination to call this a "spiritual successor" of Planescape: Torment. It isn't, and by far.
Stick to Pillars of Eternity if you're dying for a CRPG, it's a better product than this mess.

So as the thumb shows. I don't recommend this and just to point this out. I did not back this on kickstarter and bought this purely on an "looks like a neat RPG" motive. I don't know Torment Planescape or have played it. I'm essentially new to this kind of "world" or... whatever it is people are comparing this to.
So why do I not recommend Tides of Numenera?
It's not a simple, short answer. I wish it was. It'd make it easier.
Unlike other people who don't recommend this on the basis of "can't create your character appearance" I don't really mind it very much, but I will admit whoever drew the male and female 'main character' avatar pictures... should be fired. They're horrible, I've seen better ones in far worse games.
It would have been nice if there was a place in-game where you could 'edit' your avatar's appearance (and that horrible picture), but like I said I don't find it too big of a problem. I pester npc's no matter my appearance. This is simply a QoL (Quality of Life) thing that 'would' have been nice to have, but does nothing to impact my opinion on the game as a whole.
Now the 1st third of the game is in Sagus Cliffs is great. It's fun, it's interesting. Once you leave Sagus Cliff's to continue the story... it slowly, very slowly but surely gets worse.
Adding onto the fact that if you do not have 3 companions with you after leaving Sagus, you're screwed as you'll never get another companion afterward. Why? No idea a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ design decision I figure, and you CAN lose your companions so if you lose them, you don't get a replacement as you'll never return to the first city to grab another one, which in turn makes combat (if you get into it) annoyingly hard.
EDIT: Thank to a few people who commented on my review. I've discovered you 'can' swap companions, but somehow in my playthrough I was never able to. Why? Apparently an item that allows you to swap them, was in all likelihood bugged for me and prevented this. Given you can't access the companions in later areas, it seems this bug I had with swapping them should have been dealt with 'before' release given it is particularly critical. (If albeit rare as I seem to be the lucky minority)
And combat as it is in-game is like putting your hand in an active garbage disposal. Painful. Combat isn't fun, it isn't "intuitive" It's annoying, it's painful... it's tormenting. The game calls battles a "crisis" and it is one, for you because you're going to go through your own crisis trying to "win" these battles in a horribly made combat mechanic. So if you DO buy the game... avoid combat like you'd avoid getting the plague. You'll save yourself a lot of headaches.
The 2nd part of the game (before getting to the end-game city) is strange, and not in the 'oh this is neat' strange. It's a "What is this?" kind of strange, with admittedly bits of the first kind. The 2nd part is mostly there so the dev's can say "Hey, look at these names. They backed us." Beyond that, it really serves no purpose in the game.
The last part of the game is... almost as awesome as the first, but it wears off quickly and it gets replaced with annoyance. The third part of the game feels rushed, like some invisible force is whipping your character to do things right away and while you don't have to (and if you buy the game anyways) you should go slowly. Makes it a bit more enjoyable.
But therein lies the problem. The first part of the game will take you 10 hours to get through it. The rest of the game... 8 hours and that is doing "ALL" of the side quests as well, exploring the cities, talking to npc's, etc.
And it's not even worth replaying the game in a different way. It'll all lead down the same path no matter what. (Yay for youtube)
Nothing changes very much beyond how much your companions "like" you, and how other npc's might, and it takes a lot to get them to dislike you. (All npc's generally dislike you to start with, so your screwed there either way)
The companions, they aren't very... interesting. Actually no, I'm lying. Only 1 companion is interesting, and this is "AFTER" they cut 3 other companions to 'expand/flesh out' the six they kept. Apparently they didn't put much effort into five of these companions, so they probably should have just kept the other 3 anyways.
The rest don't have this kind of impact. The rest are screwed up beyond any measure of saving or bothering to learn about.
Playing it, it feels like the dev's were doing good in the first part, but then said "screw it" and rushed up the rest just to shove it out the proverbial door and if the steam forums show anything.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off almost everyone who have backed the game because of cut content, changed goals, etc.
Which even though I didn't back this. I feel it's a horrible move by the dev's given that while they have the choice. They should have brought it up to those who backed the game, the people who PAID them to create this game and paid for the "cut content" that isn't in the game. (Especially when people paid the 'stretch goals' for specific content and the dev's just told them it won't be there. (That's downright lying)
Sure there are "creative problems" and issues they have to be worked through or past but they aren't allowed to make those kind of choices when the people who paid money for specific content are told "Yeah, you paid for it to be in game but... we feel it's not a good choice to put it in. Sorry."
In business, this causes a business to go OUT of business as the investors abandon it for another business that'll do as it promises.
Speaking of cut content... I'd say this decision was a bad move given how short the game is past the first part of the game, but chances are it was "cut" so it will be later added as paid dlc.
If it doesn't I would be surprised.
In the end, with the bad business practices, relatively short gameplay (with it's price as it is at the time of this review), no replayability, downright abusive combat mechanics, I can't recommend this game to anyone until it's priced around $20 (or regional equivelant)
I'd give this game a 5 out of 10. It's average, in the end that's all it is. Instead of buying this, go watch a let's play on youtube. You'll find it more enjoyable and if combat happens. At least you won't be the one harmed by it.

Let's start off by stating this game doesn't succeed Arkham City in the way I hoped. It does however entertain for what it's worth. The game is set 5 years before Arkham Asylum, where you play a less refined and experienced Batman. Black Mask places a bounty on your head which 8 of the world's greatest assassins heed the call to. The Gotham City Police Department aren't fond of Batman, and the tactical team, lead by Branden, attempt to take Batman down themselves to earn the bounty. At this point James Gordon isn't the commissioner yet, as he is the Captain, and he and Detective Harvey Bullock are trying to take down the Batman.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I was never too fond of Arkham Asylum, giving it an average rating, however I loved Arkham City, and it remains to be one of the very fews games I've ever given a 10/10 for. Regardless of whatever issues that game had, I enjoyed it far too much to deny it of that rating. Sadly to say Arkham Origins didn't entertain me as much as Arkham City did, but it did (in my opinion) stay true to the franchise. I would've loved to see Mark Hamill and Kevin Conroy reprise their roles as Joker and Batman, however I enjoyed the new voice actors as they really did sound like the characters they were portraying. That being Troy Baker as Joker, and Roger Craig Smith as Batman.
One disappointing factor about this game is that you don't see much of the assassins, when that was one of the high points of this game,
The DLCs released for the game haven't been too impressive, I always like the extra skins for my character as they are always really good adaptations of the DCU comics, however aside from that the Initiation DLC was a huge let down in my opinion, as it was just a challenge campaign and not a real story. The new DLC just announced (I'm speculating to be a Mr. Freeze DLC, based on the picture alone which is an award for the "Wayne Foundation Humanitarian of the Year" where a sculpture of a woman holding a huge heart shaped diamond over her head, with shards of ice all around her) seems to be promising as it will carry on where the game left off, and I hope will provide that same story telling that was so greatly successful in Arkham City.
Overall I love the Batman series, from comics, to movies, to games, so my review may be a little biased and skewed to give this game a victory it may not completely deserve, I still recommend it to anyone who likes Batman, wants to get into the series, or just wants an exciting open world superhero game to play in.
WB Montreal played it on the safe side and didn't change too many things. They added many new features, but all of which are on a small scale, so if you liked Arkham City, or even Asylum, as far as their game play went, there should be no reason for you to not like the game play of Arkham Origins.
Rating the three games in order I would say Arkham City wins, followed by Arkham Origins, and Arkham Asylum. I would recommend this game to be played from beginning to end, from the main story, to the side stories, and even those annoying Enigma challenges.

Star Wars: Jedi Knight - Jedi Academy, oh boy, where do I start? I started playing this game at such a young age, probably 4-5, but the only reason I knew this game is because I played the one that came before this, Jedi Outcast, which is actually the first video game I ever played. Anyways, enough with my backstory and nostalgia, let's get to the actual review. The game was released in 2003 and the graphics are pretty good for it's time, but if you're a modern gamer who only cares about graphics, there are tons of mods. Continueing on, the game is very fun and has an interesting story. You are a person who wants to become a Jedi so they go to the Jedi academy to learn the ways of the force. As you progress through the game your force abilites get stronger and so does your lightsaber skills. There are also certian force abilites that you can choose to unlock and upgrade yourself, theese include force abilites from the light and dark side. The multiplayer is a hell of fun, the lightsaber combat is good/okay, but maybe a few problems here and there. This game also has one of the least toxic communities ever. But if this game doesn't offer you too much, it has lots of mods, the best one being Movie Battles II. Cook noodles according to package directions; drain. Meanwhile, in a Dutch oven, cook sausage, beef and onion over medium heat 8-10 minutes or until meat is no longer pink, breaking up meat into crumbles. Add garlic; cook 1 minute. Drain.
Stir in tomatoes, tomato paste, water, sugar, 3 tablespoons parsley, basil, fennel, 1/2 teaspoon salt and pepper; bring to a boil. Reduce heat; simmer, uncovered, 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
In a small bowl, mix egg, ricotta cheese, and remaining parsley and salt.
Preheat oven to 375°. Spread 2 cups meat sauce into an ungreased 13x9-in. baking dish. Layer with three noodles and a third of the ricotta mixture. Sprinkle with 1 cup mozzarella cheese and 2 tablespoons Parmesan cheese. Repeat layers twice. Top with remaining meat sauce and cheeses (dish will be full).
Bake, covered, 25 minutes. Bake, uncovered, 25 minutes longer or until bubbly. Let stand 15 minutes before serving. Yield: 12 servings.

of Heavy Bullets are really, really positive. The first thing that sets it apart from other ego shooter are the visuals. Everything is made of simple shapes and high contrast colours and shadows, combined with a sightly glitchy image filter layer over it.
The levels are short, the tempo and difficulty are high. You don’t have that much health and ammo and every corner bares the risk of dying. It’s fast and thrilling. The levels are randomly generated with every new play through. There are a couple of enemies and different items, which can be found in levels or bought at vending machines. I haven’t played it long enough, but there seems to be quite some depth buried behind the simple mechanics.
Heavy Bullets reminded me of Superhot or Eldritch in a lot of ways. Glitchy or retro graphics, fast gameplay, short levels, high stakes, many deaths. There seems to be a trend in indie games for highly polished shooters that take lots of inspiration from classic skill based shooters combined with a polished gameplay and unique visuals. And it’s starting to make me like shooters again.

It's repetitive. I know this isn't a unique thing to say about it, but if you are the person checking the negative reviews for more depth and not just constant praise then you are in the same boat I was in a few days ago.
It isn't just combat, while it's literally click. click. click. right click. click. click. over and over again, this wouldn't bother me. And I told myself it wouldn't bother me when I decided to take a chance with the game anyway.
You have no tactical approach to ANYTHING, I know ammo is scarce, but your only gun is a shotgun that you will likely only have a shell or two for most of the time. You don't get any of the other guns you saw in the movies. The problem with this is that if we had more guns in the game with specific uses then combat would actually have a bit of variety with it. I heard people compare the combat to the batman games but those games have far more layers of depth that Mad Max doesn't even come close to having, the entire stealth elements are gone, the various gadgets and combos just don't exist. Every fight will be the same.
The world is not good, I know it's a big♥♥♥♥♥desert, but look what Fallout 3 and Borderlands 1 have. This game copy pastes a lot of locations, and once you've played the first 2 hours you have seen everything unique about the game. It's after you start exploring where you realize this game has about as much depth to /anything/ as a puddle. You won't find unique NPCs or locations and you don't have random encounters. It just feels stale, like the world was generated by a computer and untouched by humans. You aren't ever going to find anything, it's always going to be scrap. Not unlike other games where you could find all sorts of loot, lore or interesting sights and characters. Nope just scrap.
This adds to the repetitive nature, I can handle barebones combat, but if the environment and enemies are all the same, it's basically replaying a level over and over again for hours at that point, and that would drag on for anyone. Except those that have hundreds of hours somehow.
You might think the car stuff is the bees knees and the rest pales in comparison, but car combat is pretty meh at best, I like traveling in a car I slowly upgrade overtime, I like hookshotting parts of other cars or people in the car and ripping them off. But you won't find the combat anything like it is in fury road, it usually dwells into driving in a circle around the other trying to nitro boost ram them over and over until they blow up. It just isn't enough.
You can assault locations like oil rigs, and the game implies some form of tactics here in its tutorial, destroying perimeter defenses and eventually the gate. But it's always the same damn defenses so what is the point?! And you take out all 3 of them (Sniper tower, fire tower, and gate) by just driving past it and using the hookshot to knock them over. Torment: Tides of Numenera is an experience. It is a vast, sprawling world of strange and bizarre sensations. Filled with wonder and horror.
It is a very wide and deep world that allows you to dig into all kinds of strange backstory and really learn the setting and the people and creatures inhabiting it.
Frankly it is a very good argument to try out Monte Cook`s tabletop version. It is also a rather poor game, unfortunately.
As i mentioned, the world, the canvas on which this game is painted can be explored, poked and prodded like no other game i can remember in at least the last ten years. That part is exceptional and memorable. The story itself is...good. Not great or amazing but good.
But everything else from the graphics to the UI to the combat to the utilization of the PnP ruleset is lacklustre and uninspired and/or cut. I have seen the Devs argue about making the cuts for the benefit of the story, that they had to do it this way to make it fit properly. And i dont believe them. I would like to do so but the state of the game would be obvious, should have been obvious at least a year back and yet they said nothing. A month ago they did tell us some content was cut but did not mention all the other cuts that happened. Lies by omission may not strictly be lies but they certainly dont engender trust.
Torment: Tides of Numenera is an elegy to halfassed shoddy work in almost every aspect but the world and story, which admittedly are the two most important parts of a RPG but that cant make up for all the other failings.
Do i regret Kickstarting this game?
...No, i dont.
Would i have Kickstarted it even knowing what i do now?
...Yes.
But that is because this is exactly the kind of experience that i love. And even then i have to think it through before i answer in the positive.
In the end Torment behaves like a game that was made by people that would rather write a visual novel. Four years and millions of dollars was spent on Torment and the game part of it show no evidence of that at all.
To sum it up: Do you love Planescape: Torment`s story and weird worldscape? Then you might like Torment: Tides of Numenera too.
Do you want to play a RPG game? Then i cant recommend Torment: Tides of Numenera.
And ultimately i believe most people want to play a RPG game.

It's a very tough one to review in a short space so I will keep it brief. ToN preserves the sense of alien-ness you got with the original Torment without trying to link itself TOO directly. To me this is a smart move because to do so would only invite all the nerd-ranger (rager?) fans from crucifying it for minor reasons. I like that this game also adds a much needed extra element to conversation options because although there is no way out of the basic mechanic of that it was becoming very stale and, whilst not everyone will appreciate the change, I find the solution quite elegant as well as more realistic. It's not for anyone who isnt into descriptive text and is even more of a slow starter than others of its kind but that is because it builds atmosphere through that text so well that I would venture to suggest no other game handles that side of things better. Much like Tyranny it offers subtle but important innovations in the genre and is a brilliant and utterly absorbing game that wont be for everyone due to some significant flaws. If it's straight combat action you are looking for then don't even think about it. It has actually been made with those fussy purists in mind - how else CAN you follow a legend? I just feel the low combat model is a mistake.
*edit*
I have noticed that a lot of people are randomly downvoting this game across the board as well as randomly downvoting all positive reviews. Bare in mind that the achievements show that less than 15% of all players have even looked at the game in any sufficient depth. I am in that 15% and yet after 24 hrs play I have barely scratched the surface. You may be asking "but WHY have so few played it more extensively?". The answer to this is simply the way the game starts out. As I already mentioned, it's a very slow starter in terms of actual action. Expect to play for a good 10 hours and more before any meaningful combat. There ARE encounters you can enforce but there doesn't seem to be any benifit to doing so.

I adored Planescape: Torment (PT) and Torment: Tides of Numenera (TTN) is exactly like it.
When you compare the Torment games to the Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights games, then NWN are the most combat heavy and the Torment games are the most dialogue heavy, with BG being in between.
I usually dislike dialogue heavy games, because many games have♥♥♥♥♥♥dialogue, but the Torment games had great writers working on them and I haven't met a single boring NPC in the 5 hours of play time.
The type of storytelling that games excell at, is where you get to explore a world. Many wannabe movie directors make games nowadays (esp. AAA games), but the linear stories are anathema to the interactive medium of games.
The Torment games are not linear.
In the storytelling aspect, TTN is a lot like Witcher 3 with more dialogue.
If you like dialogue heavy games, you can't go wrong with TTN.
If you dislike dialogue in games (because it's usually badly written), then I suggest you give the much cheaper PT a try first.
Edit:
Many reviews are mad about cut content etc.
I didn't follow the development the last 4 years and didn't play any alpha versions.
I don't even remember the promises made for the game; all I expected was another PT.
Thing is, PT was mostly an interactive novel with very basic RPG elements.
TTN is the same thing. Shocker! I know.
I got what I expected, which is the first time on Kickstarter for me.
So to make it clear: TTN is mostly reading, not combat.

Edit: I've now finished the game and I should edit this review. The original post is at the bottom. Also, I was a backer on kickstarter for the game.
Since my original review was more a warning about bugs, I can say all totaled I ran into six bugs that caused either a freeze, a crash or logic bug that hurt gameplay. The last being a shop bug where I managed to lose all my money. There are other bugs, including pathing issues, but they were easy to work around. In fact, I managed a work around on all the issues I found.
I'm a fan of this genre of computer game and I was really anticipating this title based on the talent involved and the description of the product. As an exploration game, it's very interesting and I did get lost in the world at times. By the time of release, I knew what I was getting in terms of art and music and I found it appealing.
I wish there was more to do with the companions as I didn't feel a particularly strong connection with most of them. And for a story that explored so many ideas, it feels like the ending could have been stronger.
Ultimately, the gameplay is weak. I played the pen and paper Numenera rpg over the course of a year and I don't think any of the strengths of that game made it into the computer game. The whole purpose of the multiple stat pools is to make encounters were each character has different responsibilites, and each action has consequences for the characters performing that duty and the overall encounter.
Instead, the crisis feel like your standard crpg encounter but hobbled by a thin out-of-place conflict resolution system. It's great that almost every problem can be solved without combat but why are all the advancement options centered on combat? Why not give the characters spells and abilites to improve their non-combat interactions and then make the social encounter more complex and interesting?
And if you're not going to make social, mental or dexterity encounters more complex, why use the Numenera system over something like the Pillars of Eternity combat system? It would have been better to stick to what works in the genre until someone really wanted to make a Numenera computer game. You don't need Numenera to tell a science fantasy story and, here, the story is underserved by the mechanics.
I'm sure there's good answers to all these questions but I cannot divine them. In terms of a recommendation, I would say that if you like the graphic novel style of storytelling, this has a lot of good moments. In terms of style and imagination, it's a good vision of the science fantasy setting of Numenera. It is not, however, a good interpretation of Numenera mechanically nor is it strong as a modern crpg.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a rather unusual one for its genre. It is a game as much (if not more so) about the world as it is about the characters and delving into that lore tends to offer up a far juicier experience than running from fight to fight and quest point to quest point. It encourages curiousity and dialog with other characters and that is a feeling I've not gotten to savor in a game for a long time.
The game does have some pitfalls of course. The combat mechanics are a bit simplistic when placed alongside comparable games (though I stress that this is not a game about combat!) And while it seems like every character has a story (a good thing) it can often feel like the personalities lack depth. The world itself is bountiful in both depth and story and it is worth going around looking at things and really getting a feel for it.
I backed both this game and the Numenera Tabletop game on which this is based. Though I've run RPGs before I found that I lacked the wild imagination to run a really good Numenera game. In contrast inXile has made a game that is a wonder to explore and interact with and I hope that they might continue to create and refine these tales for years to come.
Oh, and for those that attended or viewed the crowdfunding completion party - Yellow Shirt Guy totally did make it into game!

Torment: Tides of Numenera nails the old Fallout 1&2 / Baldurs Gate / Planescape Torment CRPG format.
It's what I hoped Pillars of Eternity would be.

But then you are able to set in and understand that this world is strange and complex and you are supposed to feel overwhelmed by all the quirky weird billion years old tech gadgets and multidimensional hivemind wizards. The quality of writing is magnificent and the quantity of it is simply immense (as can be expected for a Planescape Torment "sequel").
While the engine is dated, and graphics are not the focal point of a game that is so rich in story, the graphical design is really beautiful.
The Numenera ruleset is quirky and different from what Im used to but I think that sits well with the quirky and different from what Im used to world that the game takes place in.
Combat so far has been a bit boring, but that part honestly is the least of my worries in a story driven game like this.
I made a promise to my self to never pre-order / kickstart / indiegogo another product if this one falls flat on its face, but it doesnt. It delivers on what I wanted and more. Now I gotta get back to playing the damn thing.

Torment is a niche game for a niche category of gamers. And in this niche it does very well: story and dialogs are great, the world is interesting to explore, failure does not mean autoload of a previous save, etc. If you knew what you are getting, it hits the spot.
Most of negative reviews either mention dialog focus or limited combat (not a lot of encounters and combat system being pretty rudimentary). While both of those are true, this is exactly what the game was offering and joke is on the people who expected anything else. I like good combat and would like to see it improved a bit in Torment, but the game does not deserve a negative review because of it.
There are also complaints about cut content - I am a day 1 backer and I was backing the core of the game, which I am satisfied with, not the extras. I believe the game was made with a lot of care and attention to detail and I do not think Inxile just drank the extra money away (not all of it, at least). This is an issue with too many promisses which inxile didnt manage to keep fully and too much emotion from the backers who seemingly would not back the game if they knew from the start it is going to be turn-based or have only 6 companions.
In conclusion, it is a fun game unless you had some unreasonable expectations or not a fan of reading alot.

Original Review: First off I'd like to say that I am a fan of the series and was really excited for this game.  I don't like how they took the episodic approach here. Apparently there was a lot of behind the scenes drama on this game and that ultimately shaped its release strategy but personally, I feel the episodic thing should be left to Telltale and more story centered games.  But thats just my own preference.  Anyway,  ignoring the frequent server drops and other little issues,  I actually quite enjoyed Episode 1: Paris.  It felt like a great open, pick how you want to kill level. Now cue the wait for the second episode....  When I turned on the game yesterday to get started on the second episode, imagine my surprise to see that the game was broken. Not just Episode 2, but the first as well, which ran fine before. Audio issues and video settings not working, on top of gameplay bugs which dont allow for my preferred style of play, I couldn't understand what had happened. Well today a patch was released that did fix the audio and graphical issues for the most part (but not completely), but did not address gameplay problems.  I cannot recommend this game in this state and based on the issues since launch so far,  and I'd say it's most likely only going to continue.  Steer clear of this one for a while and whatever you do dont pay full price for it... this is at best a sale pick up. Hopefully a developer will once again do right by Agent 47, but this attempt so far has come up short for me...

A joyful and funny 3d platformer collectathon. Yooka-Laylee has some smart and fun puzzles, and exploring the worlds is often rewarded. I'm excited to play more!
At first the amount of collectables seems excessive, like Riddler Trophies in Arkham City, but the Quills for example are a currency as well as markers to areas you've been before. With each area having unique puzzles and POIs, you'll collect the majority of them with ease as you progress.
Being made by previous Banjo Kazooie devs, this was a labor of love, and with Grant Kirkhope music as well!
Top-notch.

I really loved this game - that it held my attention for the 19 hours it took to finish (not 100% completion - i'm not crazy!) is a testament to some great character work and interesting challenges.  It's not perfect of course - The first world is definitely one of the strongest, and the second probably the weakest so it does have a few issues with pacing, and some of the challenges are definitely more interesting than others, but there are enough that you can pick and choose and still get through the game.  I also found the final boss fight kind of swerved into frustrating territory, but that might just be my experience.  I think its a great revival of the Banjo Kazooie style platformer, and on PC, which is great!  We've been missing these kind of games on this platform for too long!
As an aside, given the number of reviews now spruiking it, while A Hat in Time is a very good game, its worth noting its quite different than Yooka-Laylee - its more Mario 64, Mario Galaxy than Banjo Kazooie.  Its also a significantly shorter experience (my non-rushed completion time for it was about 5 hours).  In the end, I like Banjo Kazooie more than Mario and I like Yooka Laylee more than aHiT.  Though they are, imo, both very good platformers.  Not particularly innovative, but also not just an exercise in nostalgia - they stand up quite well against the older games they seek to emulate.

A solid and pun filled platformer that unfortunately falls flat of its predecessor Banjo-Kazooie. It was not as interesting, well designed, humorous or inventive as BK.
There's 5 worlds and a hubworld. The hub is awful. A dull large mess to connect so few actual things connected by randomish shortcuts.  They also felt a need to bring back the annoying quiz hallway (more than once too) because apparently a slow trivia section before exploring a new world makes a you enjoy the platforming more? (No, JK they suck.)
The tropics is ok but does not feel coherent, more like they made the center and added a bunch of connecting pieces like separate but somewhat similar lego pieces.
The glacier world is ok but feels generic.
Moodymaze marsh is dull. It's a dark mess that feels smacked together like the tropics and bunch of the pagies require annoying swimming puzzles.
The casino sucks. The only boring piece of music in the game, annoying minigame style BS slot machines and puzzles everywhere and you don't even get pagies directly you get bunch of coins from doin stuff and finding them around and turn them at a kiosk.
The galaxy world is the best by far (once you expand it anyway). The music is lively, there's all crazy kinds of colors a bunch of different puzzles and characters, a memorable boss fight and the most useful transformation in the game.
If they had made more worlds instead of adding "meh" expansions to each world it probably would've felt more fleshed out. If they had more unique characters and puzzles for pagies it would've been more entertaining.
There's some other glaring design issues/decisions that break the game in my opinion. First the stamina bar is lame. Sitting there for a bar to refill in an adventure platformer is DULL AS HELL. And almost all your moves use it so you regularly have to wait, never use the fast roll move, or constantly look out for butterflies.
Speaking of butterflies second issue - grabbing butterflies feel inconsistent. Touch them to get energy or eat them to get a bar. Except the hit box can be oddly precise and it's very easy to miss a butterfly mid-challenge, run out of stamina and have to restart. Or you have to flick your tongue out like 5 times to eat one for.
Three is Kartos. Referring to the lack of diversity in pagie puzzles he's a great and annoying example. He does DK country style minecart tracks where you have to collect gems. But again its not consistent and he may not jump when you tell him to or you might slow or speed up in the exact same spot on your last attempt only to have it not work the same way. Don't forget the camera doesn't show a lot so its easy to have no idea whats coming up reducing them down to an annoying trial and error process. They even the gall to make a boss fight using him and it was by far my least favorite part of the game.
Four is Rextro. Again referring to the lack of diversity in pagie challenges and characters. I like his character design but you find a coin for him in every world and play a boring minigame TWICE in each one. He's supposed to be about OG arcade games but its just crappy minigames - even though its supposed to be retro style its just the same 3d assets as the world you find the machine in. It might be more fun of the games were at least a recreation or homage to well known classic arcade games like bubble bobble, raiden, double dragon, or dig dug.
Fifth and last design issue is with special moves. Eating berries to shoot is the only ranged attack other than your sonar stun. The fire berry doesnt hit consistently, the hit box on the ice is so small unless you stop and first person aim it you'll probably get whacked by a minion (same with the sonar stun but with an even shorter range, I largely stopped trying to use it other than the big pulse).
But the biggest issue if when you unlock flying. Even though it controls like your flying through syrup it breaks the game. You largely ignore warps and paths in world and straight up skip portions if not entire puzzles for a huge amount of pagies. It is stupidly broken especially considering how long you can fly on one charge of energy once you have all the energy increases.
It's got problems but I still enjoyed it enough to 100% it. The character designs are fun (especially Trowzer), the music is great (other than the boring casino theme), its got some decent humor and some clever ideas, but fell short of all the classic rare N64 adventures.

Max Payne is the first game in the Max Payne trilogy developed by Remedy Entertainment, the same people behind the Alan Wake game and Quantum Break, produced by 3D Realms, makers of such classics as the Duke Nukem series and Commander Keen and published by none other than Rockstar Games, makers of such games as Bully, Manhunt, L.A. Noire and the Grand Theft Auto series
You play Max Payne, a police officer who experiences the death of his wife and new born daughter and is framed and under constant lookout by the New York Police Department (NYPD). Max Payne wants to seek revenge on the people who murdered his wife and daughter and bring them to justice
This game is old, it came out in 2001 and it shows. Firstly, you will need a mod that fixes some compatibility issues and makes the game run on modern systems, so much so, you also need a mod that makes the game widescreen which makes it playable on widescreen monitors, however, you make experience graphical issues which thankfully I overlooked
The graphics, for what they were at the time have aged pretty well. The environments are well designed and the attention to detail is really there, however the character models such as Max Payne and other characters have aged horribly from other games released at the time
The music and sound effects are good and the voice acting is good too. However, the game does suffer with volume level issues, sometimes the voice actors sound loud then at some points they sound low. Sometimes the cutscenes volume is good and at some points I can't hear a thing and have to riase the volume from my speakers to hear what they are saying, this is due to it being an old game so I don't blame the game per sei
The cutscenes are told through a form of a graphic novel and although I don't mind this, the graphic novel models such as the person playing Max Payne and other characters did not look authentic to the characters they are portraying and looked like they just went into a green screen room and took pictures just for fun
The gameplay is a mixed bag. The famous bullet time is fun and will save you a lot of health as Max Payne dies easily, even on medium and easy difficulty. And the game is hard, you will die constantly, so much so, that I had to replay the game from medium difficulty to easy difficulty and still the game was hard
You will die constantly, and this is where my main complaint comes in. There is no auto save! If you get shot and die, you will reset to the latest save you or the game has done which is normally in the beginning of a chapter, so if you did not save manually (either by pressing F5 or by saving in the main menu), then expect to be teleported back to the latest save either you or the game did for you. This can be extremely annoying!
However, Max Payne is a fantastic start to the trilogy and I can't wait to play Remedy's sequel; Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne and Rockstar's take in; Max Payne 3
Max Payne runs pretty well on modern systems, just be sure to download a mod that fixes the compatibility issues and makes the game playable on widescreen monitors and you should be fine! Just be wary of the game's difficulty at some points...

** GETTING THE GAME TO WORK **
There are guides for running bat files, etc.
However, I found a simpler solution that worked for me (eliminates the need to manually run a bat file from the root directory or a shortcut everytime--my way allows me to launch from library).
I don't know if it's a universal fix, so if this doesn't work for you, then I apologize -- just google guides for 'Max Payne Windows 10 fix'; you will get a resolution if mine won't help.
Here's how I got it to run on Windows 10:
1. ------> go to ../steamapps/common/Max Payne/
----> find "maxpayne.exe"
---> right click on "maxpayne.exe"
--> click on "compatibility" pane (no pun intended ;])
-> look for the area that says "compatibility mode"
> Enable 'Run this program in compatibility mode for:' and set the option to either Windows 95 or Windows 98 in                      the drop down menu (find which one works for you).
2. ----> Go to:

---> Select "Download" from the first widget box. This is for Max Payne 1. The second widget box is for MP2.
--> Follow the instructions from the website and extract the contents of the zip into the root Max Payne dir.
-> Launch the launcher -- the zip file we extracted in the previous step contains the Direct X 8 library necessary to play the game and scale the graphics to newer aspect ratios.
> Put in your 16:9 or 16:10 settings, upgrade the graphics options, etc. and press play!
3.-> Whenever you see a cutscene in game, or one of those comic-esque interludes pops up, press the "E" key. It will start the cutscene over but play it with sound this time.
> If this doesn't work, just google the sound fix.
10/10

Heavy Bullets is great as both a roguelike and an FPS. The main concept is that you can only have six bullets in your gun at a time, so you have to pick up bullets and reload them. This means that you have to have decent aim. There are quite a few different enemy types, and each one requires precise shooting in order to survive. Luckily, every enemy (except the dreaded one) type emits some kind of warning sound, so if you're careful you can spot them. It ends up becoming fairly tense, and you might find yourself creeping around with one sliver of life left trying to avoid getting hit, and those playthroughs are awesome. As a roguelike, it works well because there are ways for you to save cash and items, and there are quite a few different items that can help you in the game. Despite being Early Access, it's a full game and I've not encountered any bugs in over a dozen runs.

Torment: Tides of Numernera is a unique, enjoyable RPG experience and a step up in storytelling, lore and creative quest design from previous crowdfunded CRPG efforts such as Wasteland 2 and Pillars of Eternity. The same traits that made Planescape Torment such an unforgettable experience are in full force here- bizarre worlds to explore that ride the line between sci fi and fantasy, difficult moral choices, and and the ability to persuade/manipulate your way out of practically every confronation in the game. Without spoiling too much of the story, your character- the Last Castoff- is a relic of a mad shapeshifting immortal who also has the ability to seemingly cheat death time and time again. The Castoff goes on a long quest to piece together their memory while discovering their role in a grand scheme that could shape the fate of the worlds forever.
Much of the player's interaction with the world comes through the stat system, which is simplified in a way that is both clever and functional. Alll of your character's abilities are reduced to into three stat pools- Might, Speed and Intellect. These act as as resources that can be used in both combat and practically every conversation/quest interaction option where a typical RPG might require a charisma/dexterity checks. The only way to recover these stat pools without using items is by resting, which typically costs a good chunk of money and eats up valuable time (which directly impacts certain quests). What this means is that the player needs to ration out these stats carefully, forcing players to consider other creative ways to solve problems if their party's stats look tight. While these stat checks being odds based does tend to encourage save scumming I feel like this isn't much of an issue because the game tends to give interesting results for
as well as succeeding in them.
One example of the care and detail that went into Torment is with the Heretic's Fork, an obscure, expensive piece of equipment that takes up a valuable artifact slot and comes with no useful combat bonuses, but grants you the ability to "scan the surface thoughts of most people or creatures you speak with". Just to see what would happen, I bought this item and stuck it on my protagonist for the rest of the game, and was pleasantly surprised to find that all of my companions and practically every NPC I met from that point on had unique dialogue lines of dialogue (some of which directly influenced conversations). This is a lot of effort for one seemingly gimmicky item that the majority of players will probably never use.
Combat is simple to learn but tricky to master, and there is plenty of room to creative clever character builds in the three unique classes and the variety of obtainable items. My personal protagonist was a Light Armor/Weapons using Jack with a focus on building up a massive Speed stat, raising her Evasion to such a high degree by the end of the game that she was effectively immune to all basic weapon attacks. Cyphers are monstrously powerful consumable items which you can purchase and find throughout the game, and intelligent use of them can allow you to overcome overwhelming odds even with a character build not focused on combat. Fettles such as flanking and spells which buff multiple characters encourage intelligent positioning and teamwork. I often found myself deliberately taking the violent path to resolve quests towards the end of the game, simply because I enjoyed seeing all the abilities and powerful gear I was collecting go to good use.
The major complaint I see from some other Steam Reviews is that either combat is too difficult, or that enemies tend to mob and kill off the main character before you even have a chance to react. While enemies do tend to focus fire on targets- you know, like any compentent AI enemies should- the Stealth mechanic greatly increases the survivability of your members, and getting quality armor and artifacts helps your characters survive some pretty serious beatings. I am convinced that these players either are unable or unwilling to build effective characters or try to hoard/sell all of their Cyphers instead of using them in combat.
If there's any legitimate issues to be had with Torment, it would be with the length of the game- even if you complete all the sidequests you're likely to finish in around 25 hours. The game comes rolling to a seemingly abrupt end and you don't have a chance to revisit any of the past locations you've been to to see more of the consequences of your actions. Another small issue I had was that the conclusion for Erritis's storyline was pretty weak for otherwise very likable companion. Also, the game hypes you up the entirety of the story for a big final boss fight against the giant eldritch abomination terrorizing your mindspace, but this simply never happens no matter what story path you pick, which is a bit of a letdown.
These flaws do little to diminish what's so great about to what the game offers as a whole- a spectacularly original and detailed world to explore filled with interesting lore and memorable characters. Torment kept me hooked from start to finish with its compelling story, rich writing, and difficult storyline choices. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who played through Pillars of Eternity or the old Infinity Engine games, as well as any CRPG fans in general.

I don't write reviews usually, but this one deserves it.
I'm a huge fan of Planescape: Torment. It's a masterpiece, the best CRPG I've ever played. It becomes a cult game for me and friends of mine. We spent not a single evening discussing our experiences in that world. And, to be honest, I didn't expect that a "sequel" will match his predecessor. I totally understand that my expectations are too high. Still, I expected significant satisfying experience from Torment: Tides of Numenara. To enjoy it, I've even taken a several days vacation, settled things with my wife and turned off all communication channels. And I dive into the world of Numenara.
And found it extremely satisfying. New Torment over-performed all my expectations. The story is excellent. Every single bit of it. The Ninth World is intriguing. It constantly reminds me "Roadside Picnic", short science fiction novel written by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky.  I enjoy exploration. Integration with various pieces of Numenara. I care about every single choice.  I feel sympathy for characters. And, of course, a strong sense of nostalgia. This game feels exactly as I expect new Torment title should.
Of course, this game is not perfect. I didn't expect it to be.
There are minor UI glitches. But nothing fatal. I expected some rare crashes at least (like in Tyranny) - but none found so far. The game runs flawlessly on my Mac. A close friend of mine was not so lucky - he encountered significant "Visual Upside down" issue. Maybe, I simply have a good Karma.
The role-playing system looks simplified at first glance. But it's deep enough. Not so big amount of choices like in old-school AD&D, but now every single choice matters. I'm more than happy to accept that.
Cutting content is unpleasant, of course. But in this exact case, I totally support developers decision. I strongly prefer a smaller amount of well-polished content over a bigger amount of mediocre one. Every single flaw may easily break well-crafted atmosphere. So far I didn't found any. Of course, developers should've communicated this changes to the community earlier. But nobody's perfect. I can live with that.
Can't say anything about the combat system. For now, I've spent over 16  hours in the game. And fought only two battles for now. First one was an introduction, the tutorial one. Not sure even should I count it or not. The second one was a result of a choice I don't really want to make, just because I wanted to take a look at combat. Let's face it - battles was not a strong side of Planescape also. Combat there was repetitive and often boring. If I wanted a good fight - there are a lot of titles to satisfy my desire. From what I've seen, battles are mostly optional in Tides of Numenara, so I'm extremely glad that I can recommend this game to my wife. She hates complicated battles and, hopefully, will enjoy brilliant storytelling.
This game is a masterpiece. If, by any chance, developer will read my review - I want to say "thank you". You did perfectly. I can't imagine better.

This recommendation has a very large asterisk next to it. So I've put a few questions together on whether or not you'll like this game. First: Did you like the two other Batman games? Second: Can you forgive Call of Duty style recycling for gameplay features? Third: Can you tolerate the new voice over for Batman? Fourth: Do you mind bugs? If you answered no for any of them, please avoid this game.
It's pretty much Arkham City with a clean up and two new enemy types. Of course there are 'new' gadgets, but they are technically reskins of previous ones or they are just a single feature of old gadgets. So yeah, if you liked Arkham City and want more Arkham City, this game is for you.
As for the Call of Duty reference, this game is just like Call of Duty: It takes stuff from the previous installment and shuffles them. I didn't think it was that bad UNTIL I played Arkham City again. A little more than half of what is in Arkham Origins is a slightly reskin or reworking of gameplay scenarios from Arkham City.
The new voice actor for the Joker, Troy Baker, is perfect. He sounds different enough for a younger joker and sounds like the Joker. Batman, however, does not sound like Batman. Roger Smith is NOT a replacement for Kevin Conroy. Even if this Batman is supposed to be younger, the voice actor just doesn't seem right at all.
And last: Bugs. A lot of them are fixed, just like Arkham City's PC bugs were fixed, but they are still here. Most of the bugs are timing issues during combat. I've resorted to NEVER using the 'stun nade' gadget because it always resets the combo meter. There are also times when you SWEAR you hit the button... but it just doesn't register or somehow resets the counter.
Oh and the multiplayer sucks because it lags to high hell. When it doesn't lag, ooo that's fun! But the chances of you finding a match and people staying aren't worthy of any price tag.

Secara gameplay, Batman™: Arkham Origins tidak berbeda dengan Arkham city, memiliki sistem pertarungan yang sama persis dengan pendahulunya, flow animasi yang sangat bagus serta combo yang dapat di hubungkan tanpa terputus memberikan tantangan tersendiri. Terdapat fitur baru yang diberikan adalah kemampuan merekonstruksi ulang tempat kejadian pada mode detektif yang memungkinkan untuk mengumpulkan beberapa bukti untuk mendapatkan petunjuk.
Cerita yang disuguhkan sedikit menarik dengan setting cerita sebelum cerita pada arkham asylum, karakter yang diberikan sangat menarik dengan voice acting yang sangat bagus. Pemain disuguhkan dengan banyaknya misi sampingan yang dapat mengalihkan perhatian dari misi utama, tetapi semakin lama terasa membosankan dengan misi - misi yang mirip. Loved the Hitman games, but this episodic release pattern totally kills it for me. I beat the bejesus out of the first "episode" (and myriad Vampire Magician options). Having no other missions to complete, I basically revisited Paris a dozen or so times until I was thoroughly sick of it. Now, fatigued by Paris, I go into Sapienza and I can't even be bothered. I basically ran around stabbing everyone with a screwdriver just to see how many people I could kill before a guard finally shot me (the guards are quite forgiving as you can literally bludgeon someone right before their eyes and they'll just yell at you).
The problem with this episodic release for me is that I like to get immersed in a game and play it through to completion. It's that initial rush that fuels me to keep going. Having a single mission and being forced to play it over and over again until the next release weeks/months later puts all of Hitman's glaring weaknesses (horrible AI!! Still somewhat on rails despite "sandbox" claims) under a microscope.

Season 1 is done, time to update my review.
Old Blood Money fan here, didn't much like Absolution. This game on a scale:
Blood Money ||----O---------------------|| Absolution
Overall it's a true sandbox assassination game like Blood Money. Not limited small levels, bad disguise system and point shooting like Absolution. It's basically the Blood Money 2 you've been waiting for, with some small caveats.
There is no fixed difficulty modes. The game allows enabling/disabling different HUD helps freely. They are all ENABLED BY DEFAULT, essentially "Very easy" mode. Make sure to turn it off right away, unless you want a very casual experience.
I REALLY recommend turning at least "Opportunites" and "Challenges" helps off. They are basically an in-built spoiler system.
Personally I've disabled the Minimap and Instinct too, to get more challenge.
Sapienza is best Hitman mission ever, surpassing classics like A New Life or Curtains Down. It's simply magnificient location. It really feels like Italian coastal town.
People criticize the lack of levels, but they are HUGE. One map in this game has more to do than 2-3 missions in Blood Money.
Loadout selection is back. No gun customization, but there is a ton of weapon variants. You can smuggle items in and start the game undercover (as house staff etc) once you unlock these options.
More stealthy gadgets like Emetic poison, Audio distraction device, breaching charge and explosive cell phone (Taking one phonecall may change your life ;). People whining about lack of gun customization, tend to forget Blood Money had none of these things. This is not essentially a shooter, but a stealth game in shooter disguise (pun intended) so this kind of gear makes IMO more sense.
Instinct is in the game, but it's truly optional (unlike in Absolution), can be disabled completely. I never used it after the tutorial, no problems. There is no stupid "blending" associated with it like in Absolution, it's more like just 3D navigation tool. You can easily play without
Best disguise system in Hitman game ever. It's almost like Blood Money, with a clever twist. Some people are more observant (marked with a white sphere), so you are always a bit on your toes. 90% of time you can hide in plain sight, just like in Blood Money, just avoid the few enforcers, or switch costume to fool them too. In Blood Money the disguises were a bit too powerful, and in Absolution they were too weak. Now there's a perfect balance, leaning towards Blood Money style though.
Ability to climb walls and windows more freely, more ways to tamper with environment and with different gas and electrical systems, overflowing sinks, poisoning nearly anything and many more...
...but saldy also slight downgrades from Blood Money.
No human shield. Being able to fake surrender feels half-pointless because of it.
Keyhole peeking being gone I can understand, since modern keyholes aren't really big enough to see through. But light switches in rooms cannot be turned off like in BM, these people must have huge electrical bills.
NPCs don't care about blood stains on floors (might be strawberry juice, right?), and civilian NPCs never pick up weapons from the ground to fight back. Both were features in Blood Money, why remove it?
Online only DRM. In a single player game doesn't make much sense, but I don't care that much since my connection is stable and I have it all the time anyway. The game does have some online elements like Leaderboards, Elusive Targets, Contracts mode and other live content.
No sniper suitcase. There is the same sniper rifle in final mission unlocks, but without case.
My main complaint about this game: Player proximity triggered events. Key conversations or events don't happen, unless you are in the room. "Oh the bald guy showed up, let's  talk about that thing we weren't supposed to talk about" It feels fake, the more you play the more you notice it. Not like this ruins the game, scripted events are quite rare, and repeat only once per mission.
Voice acting. Every French, Italian, African and Thai person speaks flawless English without local accent. You stop caring about it after a while, but a clear downside. There is some effort for the main targets, but not for other NPCs. However, NPCs do have more dynamic dialogue and react a lot into what you do, carry and wear, which wasn't a feature in past games.
No newspaper rating system from Blood Money, I kinda liked tha. But people don't read printed newspaper that much anymore. They could have replaced it with some online news article.
Music isn't by Jesper Kyd. For me not a huge deal, the music is fine and reacts dynamically to the action, without getting annoying. But for some people might be a con.
Optimization isn't that great, even now after the game is finished, and multiple patches delpoyed.
Latest three episodes (Bangkok, Colorado and Hokkaido) run better, problem is mainly the two largest levels with lot of NPCs. WIth 980 ti and i7, I was able to mostly run Ultra settings with 60 fps, but in these certain areas the framerate tanks a bit.
Devs added recently a Professional Mode into all of the story missions. The base game can get quite easy after you learn the levels and unlock all gear.
Pro is a lot tougher, you can save only 1 time per mission. Guards are more alert, gunfights more lethal and security is tighter. Some items aren't in the same place anymore. And if you spill blood on a disguise (gunshot, stabbing) you can't use it. Pro mode provides extra replay value and challenge, great addition from developers.
The game is based on replaying the levels a lot, killing the targets in different ways and unlocking stuff each time, to allow new approaches.
If you're in for the story, and just complete missions once and move on, this is maybe not for you. The story is quite vague, when it finally starts to get interesting, Season 1 ends.
But for hours and hours of murderous shenanigans, it's very good and content-rich game. It's probably closest to Blood Money 2 we're ever going to get. Just remember that it's more of a stealth puzzle with some shooting, than actual shooter.
Strongly recommended, and can't wait for Season 2.

IDK, Helk seems to have taken Rust in a not-fun direction.
I tried to hold out. It all started in July of 2016, when the developers removed the blueprint system. Under the BP (Blueprint) system, you would collect fragments to piece together blueprints which you would consume to unlock the ability to craft a specific item. The better the item, the more blueprints it required. They replaced the BP system with the XP system. Under the XP system, you would receieve experience for completing tasks (basically just grinding, you would get xp for hitting nodes, chopping trees, picking up crates, and whacking barrels) and you would then consume the points to unlock the ability to make a specific item.
So, XP was a mess for a lot of months. Mostly because Helk decided he didn't like XP, and wanted to overhaul again, but it took 4 months for them to come up with a new system. So for 4 months, from July 2016 through November 2016, Rust was very grind and in a state of Flux.
The new system that replaced XP in November of 2016, which is still in use to this day, is what's known as the component system. Under the component system, you are able to craft everything right from the start. If you have the apropriate "components" you can craft the item.
This component system has a lot of drawbacks.
1) It made an already grindy game, even grindier.
- Instead of having to collect Wood, Stone, Sulfur, Metal, High Quality Metal, and BP frags, you have to collect Wood, Stone, Sulfur, Metal, High Quality Metal, + Rope, blades, Semi-Auto Body, Rifle-Body, springs, gears, SMG Body, pipes, sewing kits, etc.
2) It causes servers to die in 2-3 days
-No progression system tieing players to servers. If you get raided, there's no reason to stick around on a server anymore. Wipe these days go like this: Wipe day - Servers are full pop. Next day - Servers are half pop. Day after that - Servers are 10-20 pop. Back during blueprints, and even XP, servers never used to die like this. You could make it a full 5 days with max pop, and even longer with 2 week/monthly servers.
-Community is also gone. Severs used to have a distinct identity. You got to know the people on your server, because they played there every wipe. Now? people switch servers too frequently. Everyone is a stranger.
3) Being 1-2 hours late to a wipe is disasterous.
- With high-tier weaponry being available within the first half-hour of a wipe, if you happen to have a job and you don't get off work until 5 on thursdays, you're going to have to compete against full-geared players with the nerf-to♥♥♥♥♥♥bow/xbow/and pipes.
So like I said, these changes were made in November of 2016, and the system hasn't been tweeked at all. The only changes have been to HQM costs on auto-turrets, and gear costs on a few items. 8 months is a long time to have to watch a game that was once amazing, turn into a heaping pile of grindy♥♥♥♥♥♥
To amplify Rust's problems even worse, gunplay has now devolved into this terrible system where the guns don't really shoot where you're aiming. I cannot describe the feelings associated with wasting your time grinding for weapons and armor, just to be able to PVP, and then you end up losing all of your gear because your gun doesn't shoot where you tell it to. (This isn't even taking into account the horrible lag spikes that preceed any gunplay. Rust is not optimized. If you have a low-end graphics card you will not be able to achieve more than 20 fps, and if you have a good one you will sit at 100 until any sort of action happens, and you'll spike to 5-10 until you die or you happen to be blessed by lag-jesus.)
Due to all of the reasons outlined above I cannot support anyone purchasing this game. There are better uses of $5 at this point. Had you asked me a year ago, I would have raved about Rust. I would have told you to buy it and if you were hesistant I would have bought it for you just so that I knew you got to experience it. Now, the devs just don't give a ♥♥♥♥, and it really shows.

The epitome of a story-driven RPG. Lives up to the original Torment in many ways and will likely surpass it if the developers continue polishing and adding to the game.
It boasts a STAGGERING - 1.2 million words of text. Surpassing the original Torment's 800k by 50%. It crushes Dragon Age: Origins and Pillars of Eternity and their ~700k words. It even surpasses Baldurs Gate II with its 1 million words.
Tides of Numenera is the ultimate story driven RPG with more text than every book of the Harry Potter series combined.
I played the Beta in early access and then started a new game after full release. Every time I've opened the game I've played for 12 hours straight. The world draws you in and keeps begging you to stay.
This is a game with endless story potential and mind numbing amounts of information to take in. This is Earth 1 billion years in the future. One can barely begin to imagine what that vast history could entail. And you get to explore it as much as you can. You'll only scratch the surface, but what you find will give you many many hours of entertainment.
The combat is - as far as I can tell - completely optional. And while you will probably want to dabble in multiple combat events, you can further reduce actual combat by simply using stealth, diplomacy or the environment to solve the problem. Being attacked by a swarm of bloodthirsty drones? Sneak past them to disable their AI core. Attacked by nightmares? Paralyze them with nearby technical equipment. There are many options.
To keep the exploration interactive and engaging without using constant heavy combat, your existing ability stats can be used as a depleting resource which can be restored by rest or items. So for example if you need to dig up some treasures under a pile of rocks, you may have to expand some of your "Might" stats, reducing the available resource. Deplete the resource too low and you may find that you'll lack it when you need it next. And you can never be sure when another need arises, and many of the resource checks can only be done once. So if you mess up, the story can change.
Luckily, your companions can also help in many situations - though not in all. So hang around with the right people and you can have all the muscle, speed or intelligence you may require. But just like you, their resources will deplete and they will eventually run out.
While resting is the obvious way to restore said resources, it often costs a fair bit of money, and furthermore - rest too often and you may find that the story of the game world passes you by and events can spiral out of control. Events that could have been solved one way, may eventually end in a completely different way because you tarried too long. Yet you never feel pressured for time since nobody really keeps track, you just have to trust your gut instincts.
The companions are well written and have deep, complicated personalities. They will interject themselves into events and discussions, share information, gear and abilities. They each have their personal agendas with which you can help with or not. And many of the choices you make can have unpredictable outcomes.
---
All in all, Torment: Tides of Numenera is an excellent game as long as you have no illusions about what you're getting yourself into. It's not a combat heavy game like Pillars of Eternity, or any of the old Infinity Engine games or later series like Neverwinter nights - though it's story depth could certainly be compared to that. No, Torment is all about the story and the setting.
Torment is a massive 1.2 million word "Hands on" Novel that you can experience. And it draws you in like any great sci-fi or fantasy book (or series of books) should.
You're an immortal being with fading memories of a thousand lifetimes, walking the Earth 1 billion years in the future, trying to figure out who or what you really are and how you fit into the events unfolding around you.
Every inch of this game is endlessly fascinating.

It is amazing how a game like this can see the light of day when most major releases are the same chewed-out spoonfed concepts and gigantic overhyped disappointments full of repetitive elements such as leveled loot and fetch quests. Games which are usually filled with bloatware and microtransactions. I don't need to name any examples. You know what I am talking about.
This game is a big '♥♥♥♥ you' to that. It is also a big '♥♥♥♥ you' to the culture of fast, flashy graphics, "carrot on a stick" playstyles, and excessive player guidance.
Is it an archaic game? Sure. That's the whole point - the entire world of Numenera is archaic. It solely exists as parts of an infinity of other worlds, so it cannot be anything other than archaic. That is one of its strong suits - it does not simplify the complexities of an infinite world.
Is this a game with poor combat? No. If you think so, you are missing the entire point of the game. Visit the Fifth Eye in Cliff's Edge and talk to the veterans. The world of Numenera is largely beyond simple combat. It is so vast and complex that wars are fought as folds between time, as complexities in a universe that is perceived entirely differently by its inhabitants - many of whom you'll meet in the game. The combat in this game is interwoven in its story.
But are the actual combat mechanics poor? Not at all. They are not on par with Shadowrun, but Shadowrun's immersion pales in comparison to what this game has on offer. The combat in this game is about as good as the stories of Shadowrun.
But is the game an interactive book, then? This term has a negative connotation that is not necessary. The world is incredibly rich, so rich that it would simply be impossible to animate everything. By relying on intricate conversations that are highly interwoven, a level of complexity is achieved that would normally not be possible. Granted, if you do not enjoy reading, you should not play this game. You should also stop reading my review, and install Call of Duty.

Out of all the games that came out in 2013, Arkham Origins arguably had the most potential to fail. A new studio working on their first full game, A complete recasting of the iconic voice actors, and making it a prequel story, were all very risky things for this game. Initially I was worried that this game simply wouldnt be able to live up to the expectations set by it's predecessors. I am SO happy that I was wrong.
Somehow, despite all the factors working against it, this game manages to perform on a level that sometimes matches that of Arkham city. While the world is not nearly as interesting as City (even though it is bigger) and some of the assassins and villains not getting as much of the spotlight deserved, Arkham Orgins makes up for it with an engrossing and captivating story that addresses batman's obsession with working alone, his brash and violent approach and his stubborness with the justice system, and through the new yet familiar game mechanics.
I was pleasently surprised witht he performance of the new voive actors. Rodger Craig-Smith broings a completly new angle to the Dark Knight, with his voice highlighting the impatiant and angry attitude of this younger batman that simply wasn't there in Kevin Smith's approach. The biggest surprise was Troy Baker's Joker, which astounded me beyond all others. the realisation that the same voice of Booker (Bioshock Infinite), Joel (The Last of Us), and Delsin (Infamous Second Son) made a Joker that on multiple times made me mistake him for Mark Hamill (The original Joker in the Arkham Series)
To put it short, if you are an Arkham fan, or even a batman fan in general,
You'll get a much greater kick out of it if you have played past installments (Batman Arkham Asylum, Batman Arkham City) becuase of the prequel approach and the references, but all can get a lot of great hours from this game.
Even though Arkham Origins is obviously a filler game to appease fans while Rocksteady works on thier 'next-gen' Arkham installment, it is still very much worthy of the Arkham title.

The first thing you'll notice when you look at the game trailer for Heavy Bullets are the vivid neon colors that the game uses. The art direction for this game is without a doubt pretty unique to this era, it's something we've really not seen a lot of sine the early 90's.
The gameplay is to be expected from a first person shooter, it's fast, precise and simple without any unecessary features or buttons. The reload and ammo feature in this game must be its strongest feature by far, as it stops you from conserving or scavenging for ammo. The vendor machines that are scattered around also contain some nifty perks, upgrades and items for you to use and they will save your life when you're in dire need.
The roguelike elements compliment the game nicely, it keeps it all fresh and exciting so that you won't get burnt out by it. It has more or less everything you're looking for in a roguelike inspired game; permanent death, procedurally generated content, randomized monsters and items, high difficulty and so on.
The only negative I personally can say about this game so far is that it needs more content. It's currently an Early Access Game so hopefully the developer takes this to mind while working on it. More weapons, perks monsters, traps, items and rooms/areas would certainly help the longevity of the game.
If you're into roguelike inspired games, just want something new and unique or if you're into games like: Tower of Guns, Rogue Shooter, Black Ice, Paranautical Activity, Fancy Skulls, Eldritch or Delver then I'd highly recommend Heavy Bullets. It's a fun little indie game with a lot of charm and I'm really looking forward to see where the developer takes it further down the road.

Count your shots and steady your aim.
That is what you are going to be repeating to yourself in this frantic 1st person rouge like shooter that has the movement of a quake or unreal tournament game but with half the health and way less ammo.
The game has an interesting presentation which is of that of a PS One era game with polygons as its main focus. It is nice to see this in an indie game since the indie scene has been oversaturated with 2d pixel animated side scrollers. It is a good change of pace and makes me think of LSD dream emulator. One game i kept thinking of when i was playing this game was Receiver. Receiver is another game that does many things this one does. They are both 1st person roguelike games, they both have a polygon style and both force the player to manually reload.
This is where counting your shots comes in. You have an indicator in the bottom right corner of your screen that shows you how many bullets you have in the gun as opposed to just a number. This is important since the game only starts you out with six bullets. When you get into a fight you better be ready because they can be fast and only last a matter of seconds and if you miss your shots you better be ready to run, but with no ammo you're not completely out of luck though. The game allows you to pick up all bullets you have shot.This means unless you have a melee weapon you are going to have to dodge and weave past turrets and other enemies to get to the bullets you fired.
Time to talk about the roguelike aspect of the game.Ugh, is it just me or am I tired of hearing roguelike lately. It has become a real selling point for games lately. Just slap on the roguelike sticker on it and its guaranteed to sell a few copies. Some do the roguelike better than others, so how does this game fair. Actually pretty good. Its nowhere near the best but it feels good and not just a way to give permadeath and have it lengthen the game. I mean it does lengthen the game but the challenge is good and the randomly generated items each time you play add quite the variation. It has a banking system that allows you to save money and items across playthroughs.
So you have only half a heart left and 100 coins, go put that money in the bank and make the next run easier. Storing items is also extremely useful to make it even easier.
I actually want to take the time to talk about the Items. In the game you can only carry one item at a time, some have active effects such as the rocket and others have passive abilities such as the silver heat that allows one hit of damage without you getting hurt. It also breaks in half and falls to the ground after you get hit, no my broken heart. There are also items that you can sell at the bank and get even more coins. Some items are potions that will give you special powers such as a few seconds of bullet time or just heal you.There are also melee weapons you can get such as the knife and the pickaxe with will let you break rocks to get ore which you can sell.
My personal favorite item is the teleporter. It allows you to set a portal in a spot and at any time jump back to it instantly.
This game is a fun waste of time and for 10$ is well worth the price. I can’t wait till the game goes full release. I give it a 7.5 out of 10.
