I have very mixed opions on this game. Part of me really wants to love it, but there's also the more practical side that says it's perhaps the worst game in my steam collection. I am a huge sports management sim enthusiast, and as such I picked this game up a long time ago expecting a game on the level of front office football, but not quite as polished as OOTP Baseball. I was disappointed to find that the game simply doesn't work. As such I moved on rather quickly from it. I have since came back to it and I have been able to get it working enough to give it a throrough review.
PROS
- Recruiting, gameplanning, setting schedules, and the simulation engine itself are all very good.
- The UI is solid in terms of its looks, but could use polish.
I'll be honest with you, the first point above is the big one. without those things being accurate the game would be bad whether it worked or not. Now on to the elephant in the room.....
GAMEBREAKING CONS
- Frequent crashes that REQUIRE a computer restart to play the game again
- Multiple errors, including one where I had to start a new save file after 30 seasons at my school
- Extremely small text (on my display I had to change the resolution down to be able to read it)
MINOR CONS (Could easily be overlooked)
- Offensive styles are outdated and do not include the spread offense
- Coach hiring is frustrating. If you do not get the guy you target you automatically receive a heap of trash to replace him.
- Some of the conferences don't schedule rivalries correctly (Purdue doesn't play IU every year, but they DO face Notre Dame yearly)
FINAL THOUGHTS
The game simply doesn't work. In my experience, every 2 hours this game crashes like clockwork. It happened even more frequently until I realized running as an administrator would help.  It wouldn't be as bad if you didn't have to restart your computer every time this thing crashed. Imagine if you bought a bike, and every time you drove any distance greater than 10 miles all the tires fell off. You would have to stop, put them back on, and then proceed to ride.But that isn't enough! In order to get the tires back on again you MUST walk back to where you started and then you can ride again. Pretty annoying right? My point exactly.
I want this game to be good, and I hope that the developer will listen to the concerns myself and many, many others have raised. The combination of it being out of date, and quite unstable makes it hard to reccomend to anybody. Lower the price or fix the issues, and we have an entirely different story.

The game was able to simulate each week but never actually simulated my games.
Now if you do want to play this game, be prepared to save after you advance the game each time.  I have been the victim of many crashes which has set back tons of progress I've made in some of my saves.  I have tried multiples fixes including: uninstalling and re-installing, launching as Administrator from the Local Steam Folder, verifying the integrity of the game cache, etc.  Nothing has resolved the issue of constant crashes, generally in the offseason, which is when you will constantly be needing to save as there are many weeks in the offseason.
The game itself is fun and has the a decent simulation engine that produces good stats and scores.  However, the technical issues have made this game unplayable for me and I cannot recommend anyone purchase this unless you like to take chances.

One of the games that introduced me to online multiplayer- STAR WARS Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy is by far a well polished gem, holding up even today. The game allows you to create your own character, even your own lightsaber, straight from scratch, bringing you on a decently well-paced action-filled singleplayer that has an interesting take on the post-Empire Star Wars universe.
Starting off: You are a Padawan named Jaden Korr, sent to a Jedi Training ground deep on the moon of Yavin 4, you meet a fellow Jedi-in-training Rosh Penin, and for some reason immediately become friends, despite Rosh clearly having some form of mental issue. Your ship is attacked, and you are sent careening towards the surface below, and forced to make your way towards the temple that is not too far off in the distance. There, you find the sith draining the Dark Side aura that remained on the temple ground for years with some sort of staff, and thus, you are thrust directly into the story's narrative.
The way this game's levels work is fantastic- offering you a chance to pick your own mission and force abilities at the beginning of said mission. Want to be a sith? A Jedi? A well balanced Jedi with all the abilities evened out? You can do that. This game offers many of opportunities to change your playstyle and try new things. If a level isn't working out, you can always leave, and return later once you've picked up a new force power you like.
The physics in this game don't support ragdoll physics by any means; but certain force powers let you pick up and swing enemies into walls like it does, and it's great.
The multiplayer for me is where this game really shines: A skill based Lightsaber and Blaster dueling arena filled with mayhem and carnage, truly showing who is the best fighter at the end of the day. Sadly, one of the servers that got me into the realm of online gaming, the Purple Clan, is no longer around. But the game's community still lives on strong. This and Republic Commando are one of THE best, if not THE best Star Wars games ever.
It even has the best (in my opinion at least) lightsaber physics of any game, scraping and sizzling through walls and insta-killing your enemies with a single swing.
The only negative thing I can say, however, is that the Vehicle physics (like the Swoop/Speederbikes) are garbage. They bounce all over the place.
Get this game if you can, it's definitely worth the money.

I reviewed this game once before, when I was about 25% of the way through it's contents. I realized later, after fully dating all the dads (all endings, including the bad ones) that it wasn't quite fair to rate it so hastily.
Pros:
- Sprites for the Dads and other characters in the game are really clean and well done. Their expression are always really readable, and the colors are super pleasing and clean.
- Several dads have very heartwarming and sincere stories that I would play through again because they were so interesting and well written. (Looking at you Robert/Craig/Damien)
- Interactions with you daughter Amanda are really cute.
- Some minigames were actually really fun, even if they were just filler or reskins of previous games (I particularly like Brian's fishing minigame on his second date. It's basically just a less readable Bejewled, but I love Bejeweled, so it was fine with me.)
- Robert
- The ending is well constructed as a narrative device, a good way to bring back all the dads in one place after you've dated all of them (to at least 2, which I've found gives the meatiest ending).
Cons:
- Musical score is boring. Even scenes where it really could have used some kind of emotional or moving score, it just feels really generic or entirely lacking.
- Some of the backgrounds are just laughably bad. They seem like hastily scribbled drawings with some quick coloring overlayed on them (Looking at you bayfront/yacht scenes)
- Some dads have really unfulfilling or even confusing (Brians don't even feel like dates. Just you being a♥♥♥♥♥♥to him for no reason and then kiss.) stories. Joseph and Brian in particular are probably the worst.
- Joseph's storyline in general is its own issue that needs its own bullet. If you're going to have him as a datable dad, and make TWO achievements concerning him, don't try and shame your fans as "homewreckers" for trying to date him. Give him a good ending that rewards work into getting SSS ranked dates. Especially when you establish Joseph's marriage as an unhappy and mutually unfulfilling affair.
- Hugo is boring. The end. And his "See you at school.......♥♥♥♥♥." Voiceline literally made me cringe. Who wrote this?
- On release, apparently they didn't even have one of the minigames playable. I hear it's been fixed since patch, but it's still a note.
- It's very obvious they intended for the "Secret Ending" to be a more integral part of the game, and the removal of it has left the overarching story confused. Robert's hand tattoo (that you can even ask about), the matching symbol on Joseph's clock/cross/map, the mysterious necklace in his living room, Robert's appearence before Joseph's 3rd date, the "Walk Mary Home" section, the elusive Crish. It all feels excessive and confusing when it has no pay off.
- Speaking of "Walk Mary Home." They seem adament on not fixing the glitch where it triggers twice, with the second triggering after a date with Joseph after dates with Robert/Damien, which cancels out the events of the first. There's rumors that this is because the positive outcome is considered necessary to unlock the now unplayable cult ending.
- I get tired of Amanda's storyline after exactly one playthrough. That skip button gets a lot of use once I've played through it once.
Overall, had a good time, but I would recommend it on sale. The games story is just too confusing for a game based ENTIRELY on its store as an interactive visual novel. There's just not currently enough in it to justify the price tag, when the cons easily outway the pros and I have more to say negatively than positively.

I cannot recommend this game as it is right now and I wish there's a middle option like "Maybe". As an avid visual novel reader, there are just some basic things that makes this an annoying experience for me.
Here are some of the biggest caveats if you want to give this a try:
1.) The save system is terrible. It creates a new file every time you save so you'll end up with a huge list. And deleting the en masse of files is a chore because of how "slow" deleting something is (where it shows the choices after some animation and having 15+ files to delete gets to you really quickly). It's also really buggy as the choices would restart an initial choice if you decided to load a save file after seeing the outcome of that one choice you are curious about. An example of this is in the chapter cook out or graphics randomly missing. You also won't remember which save file contains a chapter of your character so you might end up starting a new game.
2.) There's no way to change the speed of the text display and from what I can remember, there's no auto function.
3.) The skip feature is not fast enough. Because of issue #1, you have to recreate a character, do the same choices, go to cookout again and then start on dadbook. I probably should've made everyone at 2 hearts but by the time I finished Robert's route and going to a new one I was exhausted. It is not fun going through the same scenarios and waiting for the scenario to go to the first dadbook scenario.
I also don't know what it means to 2 hearts everyone in one run (like will Amanda graduate if I do x amounts of hearts?) and I probably should've done that first before I 3 hearted Robert, but man. I don't know.
A lot of my issues are technical and less about the writing of the game itself which is fine for the most part. But repetitiveness is a huge turn off for me but not necessarily yours.
I will update this review if the UI updates to something where it's easier to go back to certain scenarios like what most Visual Novels do. But for now, I just have to say no.

Before I go into my issues with the game, I will start off by saying that the game is acceptable on sale for $20 or less. If you think you may enjoy the game and it's on sale it's worth a look, but unfortunately Yooka-Laylee isn't $20. And also keep in mind, A Hat in Time is better in pretty much every single way, so get that before you buy this.
The collect-athon genre is bad and outdated. Banjo-Kazooie has not aged well without the nostalgia factor. This game absolutely delivers on being a collect-athon but people realized that's not what they wanted only after this game was delivered.
You run around levels picking up trash in order to expand levels and get abilities to pick up new trash. The game is almost never challenging at least not in fair ways. If you ever do fail it's because you either didn't know how to do something properly or because the game's camera just doesn't do its job properly. And the levels are just damn boring. Collectables are too spread out and just placed randomly throughout the world. Most aren't visually pleasant to look at and just feel lazy with their design.
The dialogue is one of the worst parts of the game by far. Everything about the writing is completely awful. Nevermind that breaking the 4th wall every five minutes with your characters is annoying. Nevermind that the characters make you want to scrape your ears off with sandpaper. Nevermind that the game literally can't have a single dialogue without a joke. The worst crime is every single character in the game is unlikeable and annoying.
Nearly every dialogue plays out like the following
Yooka: "Hello friend!"
NPC: "Hello, can you go do x for me?"
Laylee: -throws random insult at NPC-
Yooka: "LAYLEEEEEEE" -shakes head at camera while sitcom laugh plays-
It's incredibly cringey and I dreaded talking to every single NPC in the game because of it. Yooka is boring and has no personality. Laylee is just a♥♥♥♥♥♥for usually no reason. Top this off with half of the insults or "jokes" being gross out humor (Using a fart bubble to swim underwater or laylee threatening to poop on someone) and you have a script that should be burned.
There's basically nothing here of value besides it being somewhat competent (beyond the camera) as a 3d platformer. It can invoke some nostalgia for sure, but since A Hat in Time released and is cheaper, this game is really not worth buying unless you've already played Hat in Time and want more. Just don't expect much.

Pros:
* The Developers heard complaints about the game on launch and fixed a lot of the problems: making the camera less wonky, making cutscenes skippable, adding signs in the overworld so levels are easier to find, etc.
* Hilarious writing and charming characters.
* Impressive music and good overall sound design.
* Good looking graphics and appealing visual design.
* Very well optimized, almost all loading screens take under three seconds to finish.
* Uses a rechargable power meter instead of abilities which require ammo, so reaching an area but being unable to complete it since you lack the resources is very rare.
Cons:

This game is one of my favorite games to play. I've been playing it since around Alpha 18 (maybe?) and have greatly enjoyed seeing the monthly updates come out.
The game comes with three gamemodes to choose from:
The bulk of the game is in the prison management portions of it. In this mode, you build a prison from the ground up (and eventually back into the ground if it collapses). It's incredibly immense and complex, which is why they added the campaign mode in the latest version, which is essentially a story-based tutorial. While the tutorial seemed somewhat repetitive to me, as I'd been playing the game for quite a while, it was nice to see Edward's connection with the rest of the story.
The campaign mode comes with five story-based chapters. They're pretty much just a tutorial for new players, but I enjoyed them as well.
The third mode is escape mode. In this mode, you play as a prisoner and attempt to escape from the prison while causing as many causulties as possible (this is the best way to get points). Although fairly barebones right now, this mode is still fun to play. Hopefully it'll be updated in a future update. It comes with a way to attempt an escape from a random Workshop prison.
There's also an extensive Workshop-based community that creates prisons and mods for the game. Modding is Lua-based and quite powerful. However, there are still quite a few things that cannot be done that the modding community would like to be able to do.
Overall, this game is quite a lot of fun and still has not managed to bore me out of it. It's extremely polished in addition to being extremely complex.

IDK, Helk seems to have taken Rust in a not-fun direction.
I tried to hold out. It all started in July of 2016, when the developers removed the blueprint system. Under the BP (Blueprint) system, you would collect fragments to piece together blueprints which you would consume to unlock the ability to craft a specific item. The better the item, the more blueprints it required. They replaced the BP system with the XP system. Under the XP system, you would receieve experience for completing tasks (basically just grinding, you would get xp for hitting nodes, chopping trees, picking up crates, and whacking barrels) and you would then consume the points to unlock the ability to make a specific item.
So, XP was a mess for a lot of months. Mostly because Helk decided he didn't like XP, and wanted to overhaul again, but it took 4 months for them to come up with a new system. So for 4 months, from July 2016 through November 2016, Rust was very grind and in a state of Flux.
The new system that replaced XP in November of 2016, which is still in use to this day, is what's known as the component system. Under the component system, you are able to craft everything right from the start. If you have the apropriate "components" you can craft the item.
This component system has a lot of drawbacks.
1) It made an already grindy game, even grindier.
- Instead of having to collect Wood, Stone, Sulfur, Metal, High Quality Metal, and BP frags, you have to collect Wood, Stone, Sulfur, Metal, High Quality Metal, + Rope, blades, Semi-Auto Body, Rifle-Body, springs, gears, SMG Body, pipes, sewing kits, etc.
2) It causes servers to die in 2-3 days
-No progression system tieing players to servers. If you get raided, there's no reason to stick around on a server anymore. Wipe these days go like this: Wipe day - Servers are full pop. Next day - Servers are half pop. Day after that - Servers are 10-20 pop. Back during blueprints, and even XP, servers never used to die like this. You could make it a full 5 days with max pop, and even longer with 2 week/monthly servers.
-Community is also gone. Severs used to have a distinct identity. You got to know the people on your server, because they played there every wipe. Now? people switch servers too frequently. Everyone is a stranger.
3) Being 1-2 hours late to a wipe is disasterous.
- With high-tier weaponry being available within the first half-hour of a wipe, if you happen to have a job and you don't get off work until 5 on thursdays, you're going to have to compete against full-geared players with the nerf-to♥♥♥♥♥♥bow/xbow/and pipes.
So like I said, these changes were made in November of 2016, and the system hasn't been tweeked at all. The only changes have been to HQM costs on auto-turrets, and gear costs on a few items. 8 months is a long time to have to watch a game that was once amazing, turn into a heaping pile of grindy♥♥♥♥♥♥
To amplify Rust's problems even worse, gunplay has now devolved into this terrible system where the guns don't really shoot where you're aiming. I cannot describe the feelings associated with wasting your time grinding for weapons and armor, just to be able to PVP, and then you end up losing all of your gear because your gun doesn't shoot where you tell it to. (This isn't even taking into account the horrible lag spikes that preceed any gunplay. Rust is not optimized. If you have a low-end graphics card you will not be able to achieve more than 20 fps, and if you have a good one you will sit at 100 until any sort of action happens, and you'll spike to 5-10 until you die or you happen to be blessed by lag-jesus.)
Due to all of the reasons outlined above I cannot support anyone purchasing this game. There are better uses of $5 at this point. Had you asked me a year ago, I would have raved about Rust. I would have told you to buy it and if you were hesistant I would have bought it for you just so that I knew you got to experience it. Now, the devs just don't give a ♥♥♥♥, and it really shows.

The September 11 attacks (also referred to as 9/11)[a] were a series of four coordinated terrorist attacks by the Islamic terrorist group al-Qaeda on the United States on the morning of Tuesday, September 11, 2001. The attacks killed 2,996 people, injured over 6,000 others, and caused at least $10 billion in infrastructure and property damage.[2][3]
Four passenger airliners operated by two major U.S. passenger air carriers (United Airlines and American Airlines) — all of which departed from airports in the northeastern United States bound for California — were hijacked by 19 al-Qaeda terrorists. Two of the planes, American Airlines Flight 11 and United Airlines Flight 175, were crashed into the North and South towers, respectively, of the World Trade Center complex in New York City. Within an hour and 42 minutes, both 110-story towers collapsed, with debris and the resulting fires causing partial or complete collapse of all other buildings in the World Trade Center complex, including the 47-story 7 World Trade Center tower, as well as significant damage to ten other large surrounding structures. A third plane, American Airlines Flight 77, was crashed into the Pentagon (the headquarters of the United States Department of Defense) in Arlington County, Virginia, leading to a partial collapse of the building's western side. The fourth plane, United Airlines Flight 93, was initially steered toward Washington, D.C., but crashed into a field in Stonycreek Township near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after its passengers tried to overcome the hijackers. 9/11 was the single deadliest incident for firefighters and law enforcement officers[4] in the history of the United States, with 343 and 72 killed respectively.
Suspicion quickly fell on al-Qaeda. The United States responded by launching the War on Terror and invading Afghanistan to depose the Taliban, which had harbored al-Qaeda. Many countries strengthened their anti-terrorism legislation and expanded the powers of law enforcement and intelligence agencies to prevent terrorist attacks. Although al-Qaeda's leader, Osama bin Laden, initially denied any involvement, in 2004 he claimed responsibility for the attacks.[1] Al-Qaeda and bin Laden cited U.S. support of Israel, the presence of U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia, and sanctions against Iraq as motives. After evading capture for almost a decade, Osama bin Laden was located and killed by SEAL Team Six of the U.S. Navy in May 2011.
The destruction of the World Trade Center and nearby infrastructure caused serious damage to the economy of Lower Manhattan and had a significant effect on global markets, resulting in the closing of Wall Street until September 17 and the civilian airspace in the U.S. and Canada until September 13. Many closings, evacuations, and cancellations followed, out of respect or fear of further attacks. Cleanup of the World Trade Center site was completed in May 2002, and the Pentagon was repaired within a year. On November 18, 2006, construction of One World Trade Center began at the World Trade Center site. The building was officially opened on November 3, 2014.[5][6] Numerous memorials have been constructed, including the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York City, the Pentagon Memorial in Arlington County, Virginia, and the Flight 93 National Memorial in a field in Stonycreek Township near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

The Cold War was a state of geopolitical tension after World War II between powers in the Eastern Bloc (the Soviet Union and its satellite states) and powers in the Western Bloc (the United States, its NATO allies and others). Historians do not fully agree on the dates, but a common timeframe is the period between 1947, the year the Truman Doctrine, a U.S. foreign policy pledging to aid nations threatened by Soviet expansionism, was announced, and either 1989, when communism fell in Eastern Europe, or 1991, when the Soviet Union collapsed. The term "cold" is used because there was no large-scale fighting directly between the two sides, but they each supported major regional wars known as proxy wars.
The Cold War split the temporary wartime alliance against Nazi Germany, leaving the Soviet Union and the United States as two superpowers with profound economic and political differences. The USSR was a Marxist–Leninist state led by its Communist Party of the Soviet Union, which in turn was dominated by a leader with different titles over time, and a small committee called the Politburo. The Party controlled the press, the military, the economy and many organizations. It also controlled the other states in the Eastern Bloc, and funded Communist parties around the world, sometimes in competition with Communist China, particularly following the Sino-Soviet split of the 1960s. In opposition stood the capitalist West, led by the United States, a federal republic with a two-party presidential system. The First World nations of the Western Bloc were generally liberal democratic with a free press and independent organizations, but were economically and politically entwined with a network of banana republics and other authoritarian regimes throughout the Third World, most of which were the Western Bloc's former colonies.[1][2] Some major Cold War frontlines such as Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Congo were still Western colonies in 1947.
A small neutral bloc arose with the Non-Aligned Movement; it sought good relations with both sides. The two superpowers never engaged directly in full-scale armed combat, but they were heavily armed in preparation for a possible all-out nuclear world war. Each side had a nuclear strategy that discouraged an attack by the other side, on the basis that such an attack would lead to the total destruction of the attacker—the doctrine of mutually assured destruction (MAD). Aside from the development of the two sides' nuclear arsenals, and their deployment of conventional military forces, the struggle for dominance was expressed via proxy wars around the globe, psychological warfare, massive propaganda campaigns and espionage, rivalry at sports events, and technological competitions such as the Space Race.
The first phase of the Cold War began in the first two years after the end of the Second World War in 1945. The USSR consolidated its control over the states of the Eastern Bloc, while the United States began a strategy of global containment to challenge Soviet power, extending military and financial aid to the countries of Western Europe (for example, supporting the anti-communist side in the Greek Civil War) and creating the NATO alliance. The Berlin Blockade (1948–49) was the first major crisis of the Cold War. With the victory of the communist side in the Chinese Civil War and the outbreak of the Korean War (1950–53), the conflict expanded. The USSR and USA competed for influence in Latin America and the decolonizing states of Africa and Asia. Meanwhile, the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was stopped by the Soviets. The expansion and escalation sparked more crises, such as the Suez Crisis (1956), the Berlin Crisis of 1961, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. Following the Cuban Missile Crisis, a new phase began that saw the Sino-Soviet split complicate relations within the communist sphere, while US allies, particularly France, demonstrated greater independence of action. The USSR crushed the 1968 Prague Spring liberalization program in Czechoslovakia, and the Vietnam War (1955–75) ended with the defeat of the US-backed Republic of Vietnam, prompting further adjustments.
By the 1970s, both sides had become interested in making allowances in order to create a more stable and predictable international system, ushering in a period of détente that saw Strategic Arms Limitation Talks and the US opening relations with the People's Republic of China as a strategic counterweight to the Soviet Union. Détente collapsed at the end of the decade with the beginning of the Soviet–Afghan War in 1979. The early 1980s were another period of elevated tension, with the Soviet downing of Korean Air Lines Flight 007 (1983), and the "Able Archer" NATO military exercises (1983). The United States increased diplomatic, military, and economic pressures on the Soviet Union, at a time when the communist state was already suffering from economic stagnation. In the mid-1980s, the new Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev introduced the liberalizing reforms of perestroika ("reorganization", 1987) and glasnost ("openness", c. 1985) and ended Soviet involvement in Afghanistan. Pressures for national independence grew stronger in Eastern Europe, especially Poland. Gorbachev meanwhile refused to use Soviet troops to bolster the faltering Warsaw Pact regimes as had occurred in the past. The result in 1989 was a wave of revolutions that peacefully (with the exception of the Romanian Revolution) overthrew all of the communist regimes of Central and Eastern Europe. The Communist Party of the Soviet Union itself lost control and was banned following an abortive coup attempt in August 1991. This in turn led to the formal dissolution of the USSR in December 1991 and the collapse of communist regimes in other countries such as Mongolia, Cambodia and South Yemen. The United States remained as the world's only superpower.
The Cold War and its events have left a significant legacy. It is often referred to in popular culture, especially in media featuring themes of espionage (e.g., the internationally successful James Bond movie franchise) and the threat of nuclear warfare.

This review is just after the release of Sapienza.  At first I was skeptical of this game, but went ahead and bought it anyway since I'm a big fan of the series (wasn't impressed with Absolution, but it was an okay game...it just wasn't a good Hitman game).  This, I have to say, is a Hitman game.  I love that they got back to the Sandbox style, and Sapienze is BIG with tons of options.  My first play through I went through it with reckless abandon, exploring and killing like a maniac.  My second playthrough I was able to obtain the sniper rifle and start in the safe house.  I then waited outside for one of my targets to appear and shot her dead right at the very beginning.  This is what I was hoping for, but it is still a bit sad that they decided to release it like it's being released, and there are still some bugs to work out.  One is the V-sync problem.  I get 60fps, but I see a slight tearing effect so obviously something is broken or I'm missing something.  Other people are reporting the same problem.  But, the bottom line is this:  if you are a fan of the Hitman series (the real one where you play on a map and figure out different ways of killing the target(s), and loved how replayable the games were in the past, then I recommend this game.   As of this review, I have 14 hours on an intro and two maps, and I still haven't explored everything on both maps.   They are definately making this worth the money, IMO.

Because the game is fun and entertaining, I cannot give this a negative review. The game itself is very well done and there are many replayable options (this is both good and bad). I just wish games these days would stop replacing storyline and gameplay time with replayable maps. Although it is fun to replay a map now and then, it should not be the main attraction! If you just played through this game one level at a time without going back to try it another way, then you would finish it in about an hour, tops.
If you are going to buy this game, you might as well buy the "Full Experience"; otherwise you are wasting your money. The fact that there is even an option to buy this game in sections, is just stupid! Why release an unfinished game? Why not label this as "Early Access"? It would have made MORE sense to either just wait until all of the content was finished or just NOT release it at all (if they didn't want an early access that is).
I absolutely hate that we have to buy this game in segments! I wish, If I could, I would rate the publishers with a 4/10 (with this game alone) Why? Because, cash cow, that's why. I get that they want to make more money, but to nickel and dime us like this; I will run out of money to buy games. So, if you DO NOT buy the full version from the start, then you are left with paying more than you should. At least the first episode was only ten bucks. Let's just hope they stay cheap! Although, I would rather it be that they did not release games in segments, to begin with.

First - the 2015 release date on the Store page is when it was released on Steam. The game is actually much, much older. Sure, it had a small udpate where the developer added the college playoff framework, but the when they made that update, they didn't address a number of others, to include technical issues.
Now, some folks may not have any issues. Others (you can see in their reviews, forum posts, online searches) experience a crash after playing it for a bit. I'm one of those who seems to get about 2-3 hours of play before it crashes. And by crash I mean freeze, unresponsive with it apparently sucking the life out of the computer so you have to kill it manually. Not the end of the world in some cases, however, some folks when this happens, finds that even after the game is closed, that their operating system begins acting strangely, with odd errors. I'm also one of those, adn the odd errors are things like Windows Explorer failing when I right click on an object, and somethings refusing to launch without a restart of the computer (to include the game itself).
I first thought it was a simple memory leak, but my RAM tools tend to show nothing wrong. Even worse, I enjoyed it enough that I figured I'd just deal with restarting my computer every few hours. Now, after the last crash, restarting my computer isn't getting rid of the oddities at all. The only thing that has triggered this behavior is this game. My only guess is it's a game that the method in which it was written, doesn't run well on current computers, although it could have been like this for years, as I've found others, with no solid fixes, who have mentioned the same issue and who've sought and seem to not have found an adequate resolution.
So, it's fun if you like simulators. It's not the most accurate, and parts of it are both vague and seemingly broken, but it was really scratching my itch for what I was looking for. I just can't recommend it though, as if you're really jonesing for it, you'll likely buy it anyway, but if you're semi-interested for a time killer - don't do it, as you could be making headaches for your computer.
As it is, it has gotten bad enough for me that I've uninstalled it. So, buyer beware if you decide to go for it.

I remember this game when it came out in early 2000-something. Specifically, I remember the PC game magazine reviews of the time loved the "bullet time" effect, letting you slo-mo gunfight like a scene from The Matrix. The only exposure I got first-hand was playing a demo on a store computer at a Costco electronics section. However, the thing that stuck out most to me at the time was Max Payne's goofy-looking grimace during cutscenes. And having played the whole thing now? The grimaces are REALLY goofy looking. Obviously the graphics have aged but that only serves to underscore how wonky these pasted on faces seem when the rest of the character model is more pixelated.
Overall, I didn't really like it too much. The gunplay mechanics are rudimentary. There's no cover really, besides standing behind boxes or around corners. And this doesn't really help that much because enemies have lightning reflexes. When you strafe out of cover they fire IMMEDIATELY. The only way to avoid getting shot is to use some bullet-time every time you come out of cover. There is no stealth. Even melee kills aren't "silent" because no enemy can be killed in one hit, even from behind, and this triggers the alert. The lack of any stealth counts as a big negative for me. Furthermore, enemies react instantaneously when they spot you. They go from having a casual conversation to firing at you immediately. There's no surprise or shock when you run around a corner. Seems like a small thing but it really made me feel like this game lacks polish.
Speaking of lack of polish, other little things just pile on to bring down the experience as a whole. When you stand in front of cabinets and open them the doors swing outward but get jammed on your character model. You have to step back to allow the doors to open all the way.
Story-wise, I enjoyed the comic-panel style of the cutscenes and the noir-esque monologues. Speaking of which, it annoys me that Max's in-game model looks very different from the Max Payne in the cutscenes. As far as depth and richness, this game is basically an interactive shoot 'em up action movie with all the flaws that entails. The ending doesn't really bring a lot of closure but honestly I didn't care, for better or worse.

If you've played Max Payne before, you already know what made it such a great game back in 2001. If you haven't played it yet, I highly recommend you pick it up here or for an old console at a used games shop. If you do decide to purchase it on Steam there's a few things you should know:
Max Payne is a classic and, like a lot of classics, it did not age well. It’s been 15 years since Max Payne was first released and things have gotten a lot nicer for us in that time. If you’re expecting HD graphics and flawless gameplay you will be disappointed, instead I would suggest that you pick up
for a much more updated take on the series or Remedy’s awesome thriller
. If you’re willing to do a bit of work for a great game experience, you should be happy with your purchase. To get up and running as quickly as possible, you can follow
which will make the game playable for Windows 10 users. If you’re more comfortable tinkering with game files there are plenty of mods and unofficial fixes that can be found online to improve your experience. Each system can encounter different bugs so I suggest playing the game for a few minutes and searching out fixes for any bugs you find.
Despite having a good time overall with the PC version of the game there were a few bugs still present that I wasn’t able to fix on my system. I’d like to list them here with my workarounds so you can see for yourself any deal-breaking bugs that you’re likely to encounter:
- As with a lot of old games, the higher you set your graphics, the more likely it is you’ll run into trouble. Increasing the resolution to fit your monitor will stretch the image while decreasing it will leave you with black bars.
aims to fix that. I could not get the game to start unless anti-aliasing was disabled.
- You may come across some issues with your character or the enemy AI getting stuck on stairs or small obstacles typically jumping will fix the problem but sometimes you may have to roll backward and jump over the obstacle completely to move forward. You may also find that sometimes you get stuck in walls and are unable to back away from them. Moving forward will usually release you once you get to the next room or you can try rolling backward as soon as you realize you’re stuck. I wouldn’t consider it a game breaking problem but it does affect your ability to “shoot dodge.” You’ll complete this playthrough with a lot more combat while running - you’ll frequently dodge from behind a corner only to become stuck on that corner. This bug also made it difficult to jump over gaps as your character seems to want to stick to the floor at ledges, but these were really only a problem for me during the dream sequences.
- Yes, they’re in the game. No, they aren’t any more fun than the last time you played them. (Sorry, Remedy. Loved the break in action to explore Max’s psyche, hated the weird platforming exercise.) If you have difficulty jumping between the blood trails due to the collisions glitch, try running and jumping sideways. Diving sideways seems to clear the gap easily but make sure you direct the following roll so that you don’t accidentally roll off the path. If you find yourself stuck on a wall you can jump over the nearest doorway and you’ll be free when you land on the ground, for this reason it’s best to stay in the middle of the hall during the extended hallway sequences.
- In several of the cutscenes, the characters may get stuck on a small obstacle they were intended to move over. As soon as you notice a character get stuck, pause and resume the game to free them. In one particular instance (
) the actors in the cutscene were able to open fire and kill the player character before the cutscene was over. To keep Max alive I had to move the player character backwards without being able to see him until the camera returned to normal.
I fully enjoyed Max Payne back in 2001 and I’m glad I had the opportunity to sit down and play it again on my PC today, even if the experience was quite different. Quicksaving is going to be your best friend and the initial setup may not be as easy as you’re used to, but it was well worth it to me to be able to return to New York for some good old fashioned revenge.

Anyone who appreciates a time-attack platformer will want to check out Super Meat Boy. The game may have a reputation for being overwhelmingly difficult, but it does a good job of easing in different elements to prepare you for the hard worlds, so the difficulty is not unfair. The later levels do however become increasingly unforgiving and can require near perfect jumps and timing, meaning anyone easily frustrated may give up. The environments and music are very well polished, which lends character to a game like this with its simple mechanics. Retro warp zones, hidden bandages, boss battles, and unlockable characters all provide a break from the normal speedy gameplay. Unfortunately there are some occasional crashes, and the global leaderboards have been hacked to bits which is disappointing. Despite a few problems, Super Meat Boy's excellent gameplay outshines any of its flaws.

I love the Mad Max franchise, I enjoyed all the films, and I revere Mad Max for its influence on pop-culture (post-apo / diesel punk).
This game is a real tribute to what Mad Max is. It really catches what makes Mad Max great.
In this game you will find:
- 30h+ of gameplay (if you're a completionist or just like to explore, you can expect about 50 hours). It's well worth the money.
- Superb and detailed graphics.
- Splendid environments. The Wasteland is varied and beautiful, even though it's hard to make a "wasteland" a thing of beauty, but this game nails it. Oh, and not to mention that the sky is amazing.
- Awsome cars. They feel powerful, fast, and they're very well-made. Max's car is absolutely gorgeous and you'll love her more than your GF.
- Car chases, car combat. They're well-made, filled with tension and adrenaline.
- Foot exploration  and combat (but let's face it, driving in the car is much better, VROOOOOOOOOM). Thumbs up for Max's shotgun though, this thing feels devastating, it's definitely not a toy gun. It spits fire.
- A very large sandbox map, you can go pretty much anywhere you want and when you want (need to progress through the story a bit to unlock some parts, obviously).
There are a few drawbacks  you need to be aware of, though:
- The game is varied, but once you tried everything, it feels kinda repetitive. Drive there, do that, break this, kill these guys, wreak havoc there, get chased... It's basically all the same activities throughout the game, but it's a sandbox game after all and no game is perfect. The car stuff is very pleasant, but foot combat, even though it's efficient (it's Batman Arkhams style, but dumbed-down), is a bit boring. It just gets the job done (in this case, breaking bones and jaws, and shanking crazy wastelanders).
- The story is meh for the most part except the end which is awsome. It's got a slow pace, no ups and downs (sandbox game).
All in all, this game is absolutely gorgeous, fantastic if you love Mad Max, cars, and the post apocalyptic stuff (if you liked RAGE for example), and it's still good even if you're not particularly into these things. The game has got the normal drawbacks that go with this game style, and you need to be aware of that.
It's a very good game and you should buy it, whatever the price.

---It perfectly captures the feel of my university days spent playing NCAA '09 on my PS2 with two lukewarm 40s of King Cobra on either side and a backup controller for when I smash the one in my hands against my apartment's concrete walls. Except without the trips to Gamestop for new controllers.
---Playcalling during games is easy. The recommended plays also seem to adapt to those that have been effective against the current team, which can lead to big gains.
---It's a college football game on PC...or even a college football game at all, which apparently isn't even a thing any longer.
---The management aspect straddles the line between user-friendly and 6deep9me very well, which allows it to be accessible for everyone while supplying tons of data for those of us who are stats ♥♥♥♥♥s. (I mean, I used to keep a notepad file of my completed seasons in NCAA '09. How obsessive is that? Here you can export things to Excel spreadsheets extremely easily.)
---The game trusts you to be an adult; there is a player and coach editor built in that allows you to do whatever you want to the stats. Sadly, it doesn't allow changes to appearance. Playing with linemen who look like yetis never felt better. On the flip side, adding your favorite IRL player is easy, as long as you don't mind him looking like an anthropomorphic♥♥♥♥♥♥
---Installing the mod for real teams takes about five seconds,
---Besides the real teams mod, user support for the game is nonexistent. It looks like there might have been mod support five or ten years ago, but certainly not any more.
---No sound effects, music, or fullscreen. None of that bothered me, as I listen to my own music while playing most games. And the fullscreen wasn't a problem for me; I just kept a chat window open or watched hentai or /wildcrazy or whatever off to the side.
---More drops than Sprint. Seriously, you thought dropped passes were a problem in action football games? This is a whole new level.
---Extremely cheap match engine cheeses you hardcore in the fourth quarter, no matter what the score or how good your players are (more on this below).
---Match engine hangs momentarily after plays. It's not a problem if you only play one game per session, but if you play for several hours at a time, it's incredibly frustrating.
---Award watch list throughout the season is useless. The player who will actually win any given award is never actually on the list, or at least never near the top. Confirmed this through simulating further seasons. What's the point of the list, then?
---Rankings system throughout the season is useless. I was unranked as Western Kentucky until the bowl season, then shot to #2 in the computer and #10 in the main poll after one week (then #1 in the postseason). True to form, I got a worthless matchup against a 6-6 Cincinnati, so at least that's realistic. But all season and even in the final rankings, .500 and even sub-.500 teams were routinely in the top-25, which is obviously ludicrous. Also, in no reality ever would a C-USA team be ranked in the top five, particularly when any other team in the top-25 refuses to schedule a match against me. (As a sub-remark, Brandon Doughty and/or a C-USA QB would never win the Heisman. Sorry.)
---The game is clearly out-of-date. For example, there are still five-yard facemask penalties, the extra points are still from the 2.5 yard line, and there is absolutely no evolution of the spread offense. Running a pass-heavy offense is possible (more below), but trying to role-play it isn't very fun because 80% of your plays are going to be from single back or I-set formations. As a sub-remark, it should be noted that the dev did patch in CFB playoffs. Why he left all the other outdated stuff in is another example of no TLC.
---There are no AI sliders, and exploiting the AI in the first three quarters is easy with a competent quarterback and at least one receiver who graduated to the Verizon School.
---There is also no record-keeping, so when you BTFO an NCAA record, there are no congratulations. I know the game doesn't come with the NCAA license, duh, but I'm sure there was a way to get something like this in there somehow.
---There is hardly anything to do during the season besides play the games.
---The official forums are a laugh. Unless I'm a complete idiot (possible; I did go to a Big Ten school), you can only see threads from the last thirty days. So what if I want to find tips, tricks, or any other information on a ten-year old game? Too bad. And good luck getting any answers from the Steam community, that place is drier than my post-grad sex life.
---I played one entire season without a single crash--16 hours of gameplay. This was pleasing, as many people in the reviews complained about the instability. Then I spent two hours recruiting in the offseason, advanced to the final week, and the game handed me an APPCRASH. Not only that, but opening any other program in Windows supplied me with a strange "out of RAM" error that I've never seen before, even though Task Manager showed I had over seven gigs free. My PC takes about 10-15 minutes to fully recover from a reset (don't I ♥♥♥♥ing know it), so this was a massive rage moment. Two hours lost + the reset time.
---Absurd, entry-level typos/grammatical errors in the play-by-play text and in the game. Most people probably won't notice them, but it's a prime example of the lack of TLC that I mentioned above. (EX: "QB's" instead of "QBs")
Even after all the hate, I'll still give it a reluctant 4/10. I doubt I'll play for hundreds of hours like other people on Steam have, but I've already gotten 18 hours out of it (though two were completely wasted). It's college football, and it's a sports management game. It's not going to compete with FM, but it will occupy you for a few hours. Definitely get it on sale. It's not worth twenty, it's barely worth ten unless you're a sports management nut or are really looking for some football on the PC. $7.50 or under is the sweet spot.
Once the clock strikes midnight on the third quarter, the game engages Maximum Cheddar Mode. In fourteen games, my quarterbacks threw fourteen interceptions. All fourteen came in the fourth quarter. My players lost sixteen fumbles. Twelve came in the fourth quarter. In one game I held the opposing QB to 37 yards passing through three. He ended the game with 411. In the entire season, my team allowed 137 points, good for second in the nation. 105 came in the fourth quarter. I've tried manually subbing players, letting the AI sub players, and leaving my tip-top-tier starters in the whole game. It absolutely does not matter: fourth quarter AI will destroy you with its cheese.
In another game, Brandon Doughty was 45-49 for 441 yards with 5 TDs through three. I really wanted to win the Heisman, so I left him in to run up the stats and the score. He finished 47-71 for 470 with 5 TDs and 2 INTs. Yeah, that's fair. Good job, game. Joke's on them, I guess, since he finished the year 510-750 for 6543 yards with 57 TDs and 11 INTs...along with the Heisman and the Davey O'Brien.
As I said before: once you figure out how to exploit the AI, it's simple to run up the score [in the first three quarters]. This game desperately needs sliders to adjust the difficulty. Sure, I was playing the C-USA with a good quarterback, but my starting running back shouldn't catch 106 screen passes for 1167 yards out of the shotgun. Maybe if this was online Madden on the Xbox against a 12-year old that would work, but not in a supposedly-realistic simulator.
Game crashes, don't waste your money

Wow. So, as is usual with things like this, it seems people went into the game with vastly different expectations than what was being developed. If you look at the majority of negative reviews, you will noticed two things: First, an average time played of 1-2 hours which makes any opinions they have on it laughable. Second, the most frequent complaint seems to whining about the combat system. The game isn't about combat, in fact every single combat situation in the game can be resolved in an alternate way.
Anyway, enough about Steam reviews being mindless dogpiling. How is the game itself?
It's a worthy successor to Planescape: Torment I feel. There are lengthy conversations with interesting characters to be had, nearly all of the companions have their own quirks and peculiar 'things' about them, and the world itself is based on the setting of one of the best Tabletop RPGs in the past few years. Seriously, I can't really explain just how much the world itself is a character in this game, full of weird, mysterious and wonderful things.
I'm also not sure what people are talking about when they're complaining about the game being too short, I'm still in the first city, am 7-8 or so hours in, and still haven't explored two entire districts of the city. I feel the people complaining about there only being a few areas must have rushed through the game and completed zero sidequests, talked to people, or explored.
So yeah. If you're a fan of old school CRPGs, if you enjoy reading, and you're interested in one of the most unique game worlds in recent memory, you should pick this up.

I played Planescape: Torment up to the release of Torment: Tides of Numenera. It felt like a fluent transition. Besides the 90's feel of planescape, they feel like brother, made from the same mind. I was a bit surprised at how similar they felt. Very surprised.
Maybe its the way I'm looking at it, as these people are looking at it as a game, I'm looking at it as a planescape torment in a new setting.
And to be fair, planescape torment was not a criticaly sucessful game, many hated it, many felt it was boring. It was only with those who admired and loved what it was made for that allowed it to be seen as a classic. As such I have a feeling the game will be the same way, not loved by every person, but with the crowd it intends to reach it will succeed.
If you currently fire up planescape: torment and like it, you WILL like this game. I am sure of that.

*Introduces one of the wildest, most creative settings in recent memory, filled with insane possibilities and prospects.
*As the hours go by, a sense of incompleteness slowly begins to pull you away from TToN’s immersion.
*While the foundation for an interesting system was indeed laid, it’s like it was left unfinished, sadly not reaching its full potential
*Takes us back to the old Baldur’s Age technique of marvelous paintings that are meticulously drawn, but are sadly void of life.
*Depending on your playstyle, you should estimate that about 70-80 per cent of the content is spent in dialogue trees, reading.
*Not a combat-based game, but a series of dialogue-checks that after you expand the basic Might/Speed/Intelligence pools, are not even that challenging.
*Despite the shortcomings it’s very easy to fall in love with TToN’s setting and its enthralling penmanship.
*It’s sad to see a very passionate community of gamers being divided and polarized. Maybe expectations were set too high, maybe there’s a lesson for all of us in this bizarre tale.
*Definitely a niche game, Torment: Tides of Numenera is under no circumstances easy to recommend to an impatient low/med level gamer

I started playing this game without any knowledge of it 3 days ago.  I played the original Planescape years ago and loved it so I thought I would try this out.  I have to say that overall I love it.  I started streaming my reactions to it live and will continue to do so.  Here are parts 1 and 2 of my first look.
Part 1
Part 2
Update 3/02/2017
After a few days of playing (and restarting) I have figured out the most optimal way to start playing.  There are some very crucial decisions that you will lose out on if you select the wrong options.  I created another video of the first few levels and quests with key decision points that you should select.
Part 3
Update 3/05/2017
Good
•	Deep story with many choices.  Often times choices can cut off entire quests or rewards.
•	Interesting familiar but different mechanics
•	Locations - Great location design and artwork.  Each location looks hand drawn and painted.  Modern, futuristic, and fantasy at the same time.  A real unique blend of styles.
•	Advancement system - There is a traditional leveling system called Tiers.  When you get enough XP you can level up and choose certain things to advance.  BUT in addition to that, there are my NPCs or items or locations or quests in the game that will ALSO bestow on you new skills or stats or abilities, etc.  There are even some unique abilities you unlock throughout the game this way as well.  This is very cool.  It makes you want to talk to everyone.  Check every nook and cranny.  Scour everything.
•	Graphics – The graphics are good.  I enjoy playing all zoomed in.  There is a good amount of detail and your character changes appearance depending on what he/she is wearing.
•	Items – there are so many crazy items in the game.  For instance, I have an artifact that looks like a slug.  The description says something to the effect of when worn it burrows in the skin and strengthens the muscles that affect hand to hand combat.  There are tons of items in the game just like this.  Strange, creepy, fantastical items that you have never seen in a game before.
Bad
•	Bugs – I’ve run into a few bugs where I was unable to continue.  I needed to load an earlier save and revisit specific area to get past it.  While annoying, saving my game often is something I do anyway so no big deal.  If you are the type to save once or infrequently, this could be a bigger deal.
•	LOTS of text reading.  I am not a huge fan of reading walls of text and this games has gobs of it.  I generally read the responses and can get the gist of what is going on.  I miss out on some of the story doing this for sure but if you like knowing every detail about everything and reading walls of text is your thing, this may be a good point for you.
•	Time based quests - there are a number of time based quests which aren't my favorite.  For instance, right in the beginning of the game there is a quest that will disappear after 3 different days of sleeping.  It vanishes forever with no way to get it back.
•	Gear – I have yet to find armor for any of my companions.  They always look the same.  I doubt I will find any which is a bit of a bummer.  Weapons and accessories are shareable.
•	Traveling – There is a great overhead map that you can open that shows all of the major points of interest.  But you CANNOT click on it and have your characters move to that location?!?!!  It’s such a handy little feature that I am surprised it never made it in.  Like I mentioned above, I like to stay zoomed in and without this I have to constantly zoom out and back in which is annoying.  Just let me click on the map and travel to that location.
•	Character advancement – There is NO documentation on what skills or abilities your chosen character/class will get.  This is super frustrating.  For instance, I got a unique item that confers a permanent +1 bonus to my concentration skill.  I was just about to use this on my main character but decided to use it on one of my followers instead.  Soon after, I leveled to the next tier and got a +1 bonus to my concentration skill for free as part of the Nano class.  Had I used this item on my main it would have been a total waste because the free +1 skill point maxed me out.  Knowing that skills and abilities you get will help you plan your character immensely and will prevent you from making stupid mistakes like wasting a single use unique item in the game.  I got lucky this time but may not be so lucky next time.
•	Spells – I haven’t played Planescape for many years but I do remember that the spells were massive.  You got the sense that you were this massively powerful being that could affect things on a galactic level.  The spells in this game are meh.  Different but nothing special or not very different than any other magic using type class in similar games.
Overall
If you love CRPGs in the style of Baldur’s Gate or Icewind Dale or Pillars of Eternity you will like this.  That is assuming you are not expecting a pure fantasy experience.  While I would have loved to hear more voice acting and less reading of text, the story is very deep and the writing is good…albeit really crazy.  I still look forward to playing this game daily and will hop at the chance to buy some good DLC if/when it is available.

This is the first Steam review I've ever re-written after finishing the game. My original review was extremely positive, focusing on the varied writing and dismissing the lacklustre combat. This review, having finished the game (with positive ending results) must now be rewritten.
Torment Numenera is a game looking for a subject. I won't be talking about its much superior predecessor (Planescape Torment) except to say that everything bad in Numenera was also bad in PS:T, but everything good in PS:T is missing in this one.
There is no plot structure whatsoever in this game. The main character is formless and shapeless, and for a million words in the game text, scant few are dedicated to the plot itself. The companion characters are woefully underwritten. PS:T had companions with detailed storylines all relating back to you and your meaning on the world / to them; hell, 10 years since I played P:ST I can still recall many of the details of the companion storylines.
I completed Numenera 5 minutes ago and I cannot remember the name of one of my companions. That's not a joke.
This extends in all directions. The game is littered with interesting NPCs that serve absolutely no purpose and could be moved from one area of the game to another with absolutely no impact on the greater story or even the micro-stories of the NPCs. The world (The Ninth World) is supposed to be a universe with untold civilizations' detritus scattered around. In reality it means a game with terrible random floating pyramids and uninteresting set design for no reason. There is no rhyme or reason to the setting, the characters, the storyline, or the final confrontation. The mechanism by which the final confrontation is achieved actually made me laugh out loud at how improbable it was. It is poorly written, though and through.
This is a game that didn't need to be made and should not have been made, at least not as it is. The story of the original was "What can change the nature of a man?". This game's story was, apparently, "What does one life matter?" but, had they not said that in the closing dialogue, it just as easily could have been ten other things. Torment Numenera is a staggering example of hubris and failing to understand what made the original great -- not fantastical worlds, not strange achitecture, but a human storyline with compelling characters. This game has neither.

I backed this game on Kickstarter, so it's been a couple years coming. Unfortunately the finished product isn't anything more than an excellent argument for why crowdsourced games can be a bad idea.
This game doesn't stand on its own merits and, really, was never intended to. From the beginning it was pitched as a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment, which was a well-written novel expressed through a bad (by today's standards) game engine. Much of the appeal of PS:T came from exploring the incredibly cool and weird D&D setting of Planescape where it all went down, and the equally cool and weird setting of Numenera is a good fit for an unofficial sequel. So that's all well and good. The other main part of PS:T's greatness was its cast of characters.
Tides does an uneven job of bringing the Numenera setting to the computer screen. There's a lot of awkward callbacks to Planescape that feel fairly out of place in the Ninth World, like the "Endless War" made up for Tides for no apparent reason other than because Planescape: Torment featured the Blood War, but that can probably get away with being called fanservice. The deliberate references and callbacks to Planescape: Torment make this game weaker, but they're obligatory since the only reason anyone funded this project was out of nostalgia.
The developers clearly lacked a strong understanding of how Numenera plays, or at least were shaky on how to best translate the feel of the tabletop into video game form. Cyphers, which are supposed to be the star of the setting, are reduced to a series of bland grenades and healing potions that are just sold by vendors on the street. Since the game actively punishes getting into fights, both because enemies tend to be stronger and more numerous than you and because the "Crisis" combat system is tedious and awful, the vast majority of items and abilities are useless garbage which you nevertheless must manage at least a little because they kept the Cypher Sickness mechanic.
It's difficult for me to find things worth writing about this game. Wherever there are game mechanics you're much better off avoiding them--fighting is boring at best, frustratingly unfair at worst. Approaching the game as a piece of interactive fiction, something has to be said about the Tides: they're a really bizarre morality concept which the game makes a big deal about but which are way too vague and unintuitive to actually become meaningful. Basically, depending on your words and actions your levels in the five Tides go up and down. There is text to indicate what the Tides are supposed to be about but there's a complete disconnect between your choices and the fluctuations of the Tides. If you're compassionate it's a toss-up between Gold and Indigo, if you're brash it's a toss-up between Red and Silver. Oftentimes they'll mix and on rare oddball occasions you'll lose out on Tides, even though most of the time even if you go completely against what a particular Tide is supposed to be about it doesn't drop. You're likely to gain a lot of Blue just because they hand out Blue for exhausting dialogue options and asking a lot of questions--which is standard operating procedure for these games so that you don't miss out on content. I have no idea what the point is. The Last Castoff is an aggressively blank brick of a character and most of your dialogue is gormlessly asking questions and whining that you have no idea what is going on. It's a pretty big letdown compared to the Nameless One from Planescape, or the main characters of the Dragon Age series, or the Exile from Knights of the Old Republic II. Even the utterly generic PCs of Icewind Dale II had more character, and they were solely defined by their class, alignment, and who was speaking to the NPCs at the time.
Since the main character is a blank slate, it falls to the NPC companions to carry the weight of the storytelling, which they don't. This is an area where the developers constantly inviting comparisons to Planescape: Torment hurts them hardest. The party members here aren't exactly on the level of Dak'kon or Fall-From-Grace or Morte. Most have no compelling connection or tie to the Last Castoff, which already is a problem, and they don't really do much to endear themselves to the player either. The developers chose to make them all very optional, which also means that they can't develop as a team, as was done in Dragon Age or KotOR. They feel like hirelings with short stories attached that they can spew out if you bother to ask them.
Look, if you really want Planescape: Torment, just (re)play that game. Tides is boring. Tides is awkward. It very painfully wants to be something that it very clearly lacks the creativity to be. There's lots of little design decisions that add up to big frustrations and immersion-breaking laughs at just how pretentious and absurd this game can be. For example: the lengthy sidequest where if you rest an arbitrary number of times the quest-giver literally falls off a cliff off-screen for no reason. Or how about the numerous (optional, to be fair(?)) fights where if you do choose to [Attack] your enemies all get to go first, with no possibility of you getting the drop on them (of course you can't position your party or do anything to prepare before the fight, I guess because someone decided that would make it too easy). This is a pretty bad RPG by today's standards (even PS:T handled combat better), and it's not great interactive fiction either.
It fills you with determination.

Max Payne is a third-person shooter released back in 2001. It was the first video game to feature bullet-time (slow motion gameplay). The gameplay is inspired by John Woo action movies. There's a lot of shooting while leaping, jumping and running in slow motion. Bullet time turns you into a badass but that's not all.
The game gives you a wide arsenal of weapons: Bats, pistols, shotguns, grenades, a sniper rifle, an assault rifle and uzis. You can of course dual wield pistols and uzis and don't worry about having to pick between dual pistols or an assault rifle. You can carry the entire arsenal with you at all times. Slow motion dual wielding renegade cop with no thoughts of his own safety.
The game uses comic book panels with voice overs to tell you the story. The story itself is presented to you through the eyes of our hero, Max Payne. He is narrating throughout the game.
I can't really tell you much about the story without spoiling it. The front cover of the game should give you all the information you need:
Why? A dark neo-noir story combined with a very unique bullet time gameplay.
It took me only 7 hours to beat the game but it's worth every single penny. Just trust me. The gameplay still holds up.

If you had asked me in 2001 what I thought of Max Payne, you would have gotten an incredibly enthusiastic, positive answer. I freakin loved Max Payne, everything about it at the time was mindblowing, it was the first game to have competently done slo-mo, the storyline (at the time) was not only fairly dark and compelling, but also funny and self-aware, in a way much more subtle and enjoyable than something like Duke Nukem 3D. Visually mindblowing, with intensely cool effects like bullets being modelled, shell casings being modelled (dropping to the floor as you filled enemies with lead) and real world locations with explosive set-pieces and action.
At the time, it was absolutely mindblowing.
But now, it is pap. It is infuriatingly dated, it's like your grandpa who won't shut up about Vietnam or the Korean War or whatever and at first it was cool when you're a kid but now you're just depressed at his psychological devesation at the death of his friends, what? Nothing, nevermind.
Anyway, the root of the problem is that Max Payne's level design is absolutely donkey dongs, the AI behavior is entirely scripted so basically every moment of the game can be memorized, and you'll HAVE to memorize the more difficult segments, as they are difficult for exclusively arbitrary and crap reasons.
Since Max takes locational damage like any other enemies, your dives should almost exclusively be backwards with his feet facing forward, since diving forward is welcoming Max's instantaneous, welcomed release from his hellish torment of a life as bullets pile-drive his face and you get to watch in glee like you're some kind of kid from a special needs program who absolutely loves WWE.
But this mechanic is the biggest reason why this game is so frustrating, an enemy sprays you in the chest? Fine, you'll like lose most of your healthbar, but you'll live, a single shot in the head? Instadead. Max lies down with a look like his bunger screamed flaming diarrheatic doodoo in his moment of death.
Now this wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for a few things, one, this game loves deathtraps, and they aren't just environmental hazards like a door exploding or whatever, they'll be enemies that are scripted to run around a corner immediately, throwing a grenade down stairs (which there is only ever one correct direction to run away from, anything else gets you killed) and since the enemies' reactions are absolutely pearl beyond belief, you end up getting a face full of buckshot while they mug at you goofily with their weird rictus grins of stupidity.
So you basically quick-save nonstop, running into an area, hoping you don't get riddled with really slow moving bullets (the physics in this game are weird) try to kill the enemies through a combination of manual bullet-time and shoot dodges (by the way, manual bullet-time is not set by default, make sure to go into the key bindings and set a key for it) without having a stray bullet slap you in the noggin.
If you die, quick load, if you don't, move to the next door, quick-save, then repeat endlessly until the end of the game.
Mooks also take about a dozen bullets to kill, and since weapons spray in indiscernible trajectories most of the time, you can't consistently land headshots, even with the most accurate weapons in the game, like the Desert Eagle or Colt Commando, the only gun that always lands its shot is the Sniper Rifle, and that gun sucks crap in most of the game's areas and prevents you from shoot dodging.
Oh, and speaking of shoot dodging, it's almost always a bad idea, it looks cool, but you're pretty much better off only using manual bullet-time, running around, instead of shoot dodge, since shoot dodge only allows you a very limited amount of shots before you're prevented from firing anymore as you lie on the ground, giving enemies plenty of time to kill you murderously or run over and pee in your mouth or a host of other possibilities.
It's just annoying constantly hearing "HEYA" and having your brain squished out of your skull. Enemies will literally wait around corners and without hesitation pound you to death as soon as you turn the corner, even shoot-dodging won't save you most of the time.
There's also just a ton of annoying segments in the game that force you to do platforming or climb up pillars or etc. and Max's movement is so stiff and unnatural, his jump so iffy and weird, that oftentimes you'll fall to your death or stumble around like a drunken ape as you shuffle on pipes and other pieces of junk.
At least the level design is straight forward enough that you never get lost, which is saying something for a game from this era, old school shooters used to think sending you into a monochromatic labyrinth of banality was amazing level design (see Unreal/Daikatana/etc.)
I still love the story, it's unapolagetically ridiculous and the writing has a lot of character and personality to it, Max's character arch is interesting and well developed, and there's a lot of funny dialogue between idling enemies. The comic book segments are well done and feature a lot of beautiful to look at grimaces and weird faces from Sam Lake.
Ambient sound is great, the music is fantastic, the guns sound wonderful, basically, the production values of this game have held up well, they're not stunning like they used to be, but for the most part the presentation of this game is acceptable and doesn't hold the game back by modern standards.
But it's just such a frustrating slog to play, there's very little rhyme or reason to it, you can be a great FPS gamer and yet most of your encounters are just down to luck, like that idiot Leprechaun from those crap Leprechaun movies, where he's murdering people in really dumb ways and saying completely stupid crap, I hate those movies and I hate that idiot Leprechaun. Just like I hate the encounter design of this game.
Hell, even Max says it himself at one point, as you assault a mob boss's mansion, it has nothing to do with skill, or playing your cards right, it's all chaos and luck.
That's a very apt thing to say Max, you sexy boy.
Max Payne 2 and 3 are fortunately, much much better games, and I highly recommend them, but I can't really recommend MP1 as its gameplay design is archaic and frustrating. It's a shame, and I haven't even said anything about the dead baby dungeon and Twizzler tight ropes and Max's wife screaming at him because she burnt the roast or something.
Anyway, I wish I could still like Max Payne 1 like I did back in the day, but unfortunately I have to sensually whip off my rose-colored glasses and call it as it is. This game is straight doodie.

Anyone who appreciates a time-attack platformer will want to check out Super Meat Boy. The later levels do however become increasingly unforgiving and can require near perfect jumps and timing, meaning anyone easily frustrated may give up. Retro warp zones, hidden bandages, boss battles, and unlockable characters all provide a break from the normal speedy gameplay. Supet Meat Boy is the best platforming game ever made. Hell, it's one of the best *games* ever made, period. You'll replay the earlier levels later on, and you'll wonder how you ever thought they were hard, because you've gotten so good at the game - "Super Meat Boy" is a skill you can learn and improve on over time.
I used to say that the SNES platformers were the peak of the genre - the likes of Donkey Kong Country 2 or Yoshi's Island. But no, Super Meat Boy is the absolute pinnacle of platforming perfection. If you enjoy platforming games at all, you *must* play this game.
