This is my first review so bear with me pls c:
This installment of the Arkham series was actually my personal least favorite… but do not misunderstand me, this game (and series) is an amazing and, in my opinion, the only right way to present a videogame centered on The Dark Knight himself.  The reason I say that this is my least favorite installment is because little was added to the original Arkham Asylum story, and I really set my hopes to high with wanting an epic, almost cinematic Deathstroke battle sequence. (sorry if I just popped your balloon. Part of me thinks that the story writers were just like “eh, we dunno what to do after Arkham City yet so let’s just put this together”, at the end of the day, they did a pretty damn good job.
First of all, and the thing that’s kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone off including myself, is the fact the they put time into making multiplayer for the game rather than adding more unique gadgets or some crap like that. I guess if you’re in to that sorta thing go for it, but apparently a lot of us wanted more story or gameplay or really anything but that. SplashDamage made it though, so it’s probably great for people that like that kind of stuff, but I don’t really think it NEEDED to be there.
The gameplay is awesome. I could make a nice, fancy long sentence about the overall gameplay, but that’s gonna sum it up. The Predator gameplay and challenges absolutely put you in Batman’s cowl as you pick off armed thugs one… by one… by one… until that last guy remains. The dialogue between the henchmen and their boss also adds a realistic and sometimes humorous mood to the gameplay.  The Freeflow hand-to-hand combat also gives you that awesome feeling of kicking♥♥♥♥♥as you break bones, call on bats, and utilize Batman’s arsenal of gadgets.
Sort of going back to the story element of the game, the most pleasurable thing about it is seeing Batman going from thinking he’s a one man army (even though he kinda is) to humbling himself a bit to forge an early bond with Gordon, Barbra, and the Joker. As for the Joker, the story does a great job of explaining his unexplainable madness and connection to Batman. Like I mentioned earlier, Batman eventually humbles himself, but in that part of the story were he doesn’t he shows a different character than the Batman in the previous games. You’ll discover a young, unrelenting, borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Batman that destroys cops and thugs alike and even makes a mistake or two (can you believe that?) but it makes this particular game pretty enjoyable.
Overall this game gets an 8/10 from me which is a little humbling compared to Arkham City’s 15/10.

The third installment (or is this Batman Arkham 2.5?) is not as polished as the sublime Arkham Asylum or the engrossing Arkham City. Arkham Origins is in fact quite buggy.  The combat slightly more frustrating. The gliding and grapplehook mechanics not quite as smooth. The loading breaks up the gameplay - I've noticed usually when I'm gliding between areas.
But the voice acting is fantastic, especially for the Joker as I'm sure you've heard.  When the controls don't hinder your experience the Boss fights are challenging  and enjoyable - save for one Boss battle which seems to attempt to copy The Scarecrow from the original but only lets down this sequel and make it seem like a poor copy.
Arkham Origins also offers new features and Easter Eggs, like visiting the Batman Cave - which help seperate Origins from the other games. The Proto-Riddler mission is more of the same, but feels quite organic. this is not just the Origins for Batman but also the villains. You will obsessively hunt the  Datapacks in the attempt to 100% the game and more importantly bring Enigma to justice.
In the end I would recommend Batman: Arkham Origins - providing you're lucky with the bugs you will find this an enjoyable addition to the Batman: Arkham brand. Some larger reviews have been harsher on this game, giving it average ratings and calling it "more of the same". Although many of this reviews also hand out top scores to COD and FIFA sequels far too freely so do be careful whose advice you go for. As I write this there is still DLC due to be released, and the GOTY version quite some way off - and I have not touched the multiplayer. So I'm not quite reviewing the full game here. But if you've played the previous games and loved the characters and the story then Batman: Arkham Origins really is more of the same, and it doesn't let the franchise down. The best game in the franchise is still the first, Batman: Arkham Asylum, but if you wanted more story after beating Arkham City then this game does deliver.

Calling Yooka-Laylee a spiritual sequel to Banjo-Kazooie is like calling a skirt a kilt. Same thing. Buy pants.
Yooka-Laylee misses the mark in a few ways. Quills are supposed to replace musical notes but they do not function the same. Instead of being navigational points for determining if the player cleared a section they act as collectibles making it a task on par with finding an elderly man's keys when you're left with one quill to find in some dank crevice. Swore I saw them here somewhere. The camera can be jittery and wonky at times. Outright rebellious even. But these plague every 3D indie title anyways and I know some games are outright broken by it. This one isn't and that's just good enough. Worlds are large but mostly empty. Would prefer smaller and more numerous, diverse worlds packed with things to do but these worlds look gorgeous at least. And we get a Halloween marsh world with pumpkins. The retro-minigames are a hassle but at least there's only one each world.
The platforming and puzzle-solving is where the game shines the most. If you played Banjo-Kazooie, this will feel familiar and outright addictive. It feels rewarding and came be a bit of a challenge at times. Unfortunately due to the size of the world, finding these can be a pain. One thing missing is a jig reminiscent of Banjo's for getting the golden collectible. The NPCs are also charming and mostly adorable in design. Unfortunately, they exist solely for exposition so I guess they'd need charm to have a reason for existing. The music was definitely good but certainly not a selling point.
Overall, solid platformer. Maybe advanced for very young beginners but platforming fanatics and Banjo fans will enjoy this and hopefully Playtonic makes a sequel full of improvements addressing the criticisms fans have been making towards it. Because I do really want this game to continue but it does have to evolve.

Yooka-Laylee the crowd funded revival of Banzo Kazooie...  Well I've finally played it, and this is yet again a borderline game.
If I wanted to I could easily write this review and give it a positive spin.  This is a 3d Platformer on the PC and that's a rare breed.
But I just as easily could just rip the game to shreds.  The game is often frustrating and sometimes just very frustrating to the point of making my quit, the world 4 boss stops being fun, and the way to get to him is just annoying.
In fact if I took my first 6 hours where I spent it mostly in the first world, I would definitely have landed in the positive category, but I pushed on and eventually after about 12 hours, I started to see the problems.   Still, it's really both opinions, and once again, I wish Steam offered a "push" option.
That's the thing, ultimately Yooka-Laylee is not bad enough to be awful, but it's not good enough to warrant the "successor to Banjo Kazooie."  In fact that comparison I feel is one of the big issues I really disliked about the game.  There's an insufferable quiz that appears in the game, and the only reason the game has that is because people really loved the finale of Banjo Kazooie.  Similar to most of these callbacks, it's done because Banjo liked it.   But people enjoyed it in Banjo because it was different novel and unique.   Now it's just there because Banjo had it.
Why do animals make grunting noises?  Because Banjo.  Why collect thousands of Quills and hundreds of Pagies, because Banjo...  This entire game is because of Banjo, and yes it's a "sequel" to that game, but people enjoyed Banjo (and conker's bad fur day) because it was novel unique and brilliant games that people hadn't experienced before.  When playing Yooka Laylee, that novel aspect is completely missing because it's just like Banjo, wink wink.
That's the other thing, much of this game decides to wink at the audience, and tell you X is done because of reasons that amount to "It's a game".  Ok, but you're using a satirical look at something... and then doing the exact same thing.  If you died 5 times, and it said "Game over."  Then played a quick skit that said Game overs are stupid.  and then continued playing.  That'd be satire.  When you look at the camera and say "I can't open the door because we have to find the key because otherwise the game would be too simple."  and then make me go find the key anyways.  That's not a joke.  That's just giving a BS reason for BS.
There's a great deal of other "modern gaming" jokes.  DLC and similar are referenced, even a microtransaction... And yes it all kind of is there because the big boss is "Corporations" or probably Microsoft directly.... but it gets stale.  Hardy Har Har, This is an old school game.   There was points where I eventually thought "Well, I'd rather have X feature" because...that would make the game more fun.
I think of how the main Mario games continued to release games, and never felt like they were standing on the previous game (with the exception of Mario Galaxy 2).  If you think about it, Super Mario, Super Mario 3, World, 64, Sunshine, Galaxy, and Odyssey each are different and unique games.  Yooka Laylee should have linked to Banjo Kazooie similarly.  It should have been the same (type of) character and an all new adventure.  Instead Yooka Laylee sticks to the formula a bit too hard.
At the same time, that's a lot of complaints, but there's a lot of good parts of the game.   The levels are unique, and while I could see some themes not working as well, There is a great diversity for the game.  Much of the game is hunting and exploring for secrets and challenges.
Every world is chock full of things to do, and while there's only 5 worlds, they grow from a smaller world to a huge world.  They might be too big, but if you want to explore, you're definitely able to.  In fact you won't be able to complete the worlds until you come back with abilities you get later.
The game is a bit too much like Banjo, but it's like Banjo and that's something PC games really don't have in any abundance.  There's Hat in Time and that's about it (maybe the sonic games, but less said about that, the better).
The enemies can be annoying (especially the flying "bees" ) but most of them are great, in fact the bosses are hard and enjoyable, though I hate the world 4 boss, the rest are good and unique.
The gameplay is excellent about 90 percent of the time.  There's a few frustrations and I absolutely hate doing a long section only to realize I have to go back to the top of a slide that is one way.  A problem that is solved by an ability in World 5 that wasn't even hinted at, but also breaks most puzzles in the game.    But there's still some annoying platforming too.
So ultimately it comes down to this.  I like the game, but I get incredibly frustrated by the game.  I feel this game is lacking in a lot of ways, but  I also think it's a great return to the 3d platformer.  I started writing this review fully sure I would not recommend this game, but at the same time, some of my frustration with the levels and such are because it's a 3d platformer made for an explorer.
My final verdict comes down to this.  If you have a switch, you can go get Mario odyssey and that's going to beat this game.  If you can't get that game or a console platformer, you can pick up this game and experience what a platformer is supposed to be like.  I just think that in the overall tier of games, this is more of a relic from an old age, than the amazing platformer that was promised.  I hope we see another game, I hope it goes for more world and maybe a little smaller worlds.   I also hope it brings the 3d platformer to the modern Era, Mario proves you could, but at the same time, This is a good game.  I might not pay 40 bucks for it, but I am getting more hours out of it than expecting.  I just wish it rose to the levels it wanted to hit, rather than the end result we actually got.

First things first, if you did not like Banjo-Kazooie or Banjo-Tooie, or even thought they were meh, this isn't the game for you. You will not enjoy it.
Positives: It is Banjo-Threeie. You could swap out Yooka and Laylee for the bear and bird and nothing would seem out of place. It has the gameplay, it has the humor, and it has the overall charm. The idea of unlocking levels and the expanding them later to open up more pagies to get is fun. The characters are varied and strange and fun.
Negatives. The worlds are too big. It's easy to get lost when there's so much verticality and when various segments don't look much different. The energy bar by itself is fine, but it didn't need to be used for basic things like the rolling movement to get up slopes. There are too many collectibles per world, 200 quills is too many. It wouldn't be as bad if quills were like Banjo-Tooie's note baskets.
As a huge BK/BT fan, I think Yooka-Laylee is worth playing, and I'm hoping they make a second game that improves on it.

[Edit: Finished game twice. Extra thoughts at end of Review]
7 hours in to my first Post-release play through.
I have only had one combat, but felt that it was avoidable, and that I may have narrowly missed getting in to a few scraps. The turn based combat is good; an 'all at once brawl like other games would not have allowed the Numenera rules to translate well.
It cleaves closely to the source material put out  by Monte Cook games, so if you are looking for a good adaptation of the RPG you will find it here. I am unsure if I found the game easy to get into because it was well designed and the tutorial was clear, or if it was just that I have had experience running the table top version of this.
It is early in the release, but I have encounter only a few glitches. Nothing game breaking. And ultimately very minor that I expect will be cleaned up in the weeks to come. No crashes, no Framerate issues, runs like a charm.
The game has a great deal of depth. Lives up to the promise of many options and solutions to different problems. I have not felt forced in to a course of action - and if anything - was a bit overwhelmed by the freedom I have had in it.
I am a huge fan of the Planescape setting, and of the forebearer to this game. The game took no time in bringing back the old feelings of the origional. Where I feel I need to search out every corner, carefully read clues, and am worried about even tossing away Oddities, incase they are useful later on.
If you are a fan of Pillars of Eternity, Tyranny, or the original Planescape: Torment you will enjoy this. Things are well written, characters are interesting, Numenera captures that sense of bizzare and wonder that players had the first time stepping in to Sigil. I imagine I will have a great deal of fun exploring the Cliffs and other regions for some time, and I expect fans of CRPG's will feel the same.
Highly recommended.

Max Payne is one of those classic games that's really hard to forget because of the unique experience that it delivers. The cinematic gameplay, the gritty story, the noir-inspired aestethics - the game has a timeless quality to it that you rarely find in old titles. There's something about playing as a rogue cop who guns his way through crazy mobsters and corrupt government agents that I can't quite put my finger on which makes it so memorable. Maybe its Max's inner monologues about his sense of right and wrong. Perhaps it's the difficult gameplay and the "shoot first or get shot" attitude of the combat which really brings out the rush in the player. Whatever it is, there's no denying that Max Payne is still fun to play, years after its release and still holds up pretty well on all aspects.
You play as the titular Max Payne, an appropriately named cop turned undercover DEA agent who lost his wife and daughter to drug-crazed addicts. The events of the game starts three years after his family died, at a time when Max is deep inside the Punchinello crime family, one of New York's biggest mafia organizations and a major distributor in the drug trade. On a snowy night, he recieves a call from one of his partners telling him to meet up at a train station and from there starts the ball rolling into the world of crime and corruption.
Now, why in the world would you want to spend both your $$$ and time on this really old game? First of all, it's literally a John Woo action flick in video game form. The game features Bullet Time, slow-mo mechanics, and chaotic gunplay that Remedy, the developers, have admitted to having been inspired by the acclaimed director's movies. If you want to play a difficult action game without the constant hand-holding and the hassles of modern game mechanics, then this game is for you. Second, it has a mature noir story that's full of twists and turns. The game shows Max as an anti-hero, a man with nothing to lose who will go to great lengths to bring the people who killed his family to justice. He spends a night in New York getting tangled with the city's most ruthless individuals who plays each other for their own ends.
An interesting detail with the game is how involved the world around Max Payne is. TV and radio shows report about the people of New York's overwhelming support for Max's vendetta against the mafia. The police are constantly on his tail as they try to stop him from causing further damage. As Max moves up the food chain, so does word of his presence. Small details here and there but it improves the immersion of the player in the story in a huge way. To top it all off, story segments and cutscenes are presented like a graphic novel starring the people who made the game. A tight budget forced Remedy to be as creative as possible and made the game stand out as a result. Sam Lake, head writer for Remedy Entertainment acts as the face and body of Max Payne with James McCaffrey serving as the memorable monotome voice.
How about downsides? Well, as stated above, there are issues with the sound on modern operating systems which can easily be fixed. Other than that, I haven't experienced any performance issue or game-breaking bugs. There's also the fact that this is an old game, meaning that your tolerance will be tested if you're accustomed to modern titles. No health regen, no cover, an easy mode that kills Max in 2 hits - It's going to take a very patient player to finish the game.
And there you have it.
Max Payne, right in the feels.

If the two KOTORs are praised as one of the best, if not the best games in the Star Wars universe thanks to their well-written and entertaining story, Jedi Academy deserves the same recognition for its perfectly designed combat mechanics. The JKA singleplayer offers  an  intriguing lightsaber combat featuring 5 different techniques, including a staff and dual sabers, and accompanied by both light and dark side force powers. As such, the game will test your combat abilities and put you against stormtroopers, proper Dark Jedies, and other enemies, letting you enjoy all the perks of being a Jedi. Trust me, there is no better feeling than force gripping a defenceless stormtrooper, choking him while he levitates above a botomless abyss, only to release him the second before he dies to watch his body fall into the darkness and oblivion (dark side forces are always so entertaining!).
When finally bored with the singleplayer (replayability confirmed, only the story is a bit dull), I recommend installing Movie Battles II, a multiplayer mode for JKA that features a complete lightsaber combat overhaul, focusing on blocking mechanics and different fighting styles from the SW universe. With this mod, the game changes into an incredibly challenging beast, able both to entertain you for hundreds of hours before you finally master it's combat system, and drive you completely nuts by being defeated and humiliated again and again by duelists better than you. What is more, besides waving with a pointy lightstick, you can take on the role of other professions from the Star Wars universe and play in an open mod with objectives as a stormtrooper, bounty hunter, wookie or various types of droids, all with their own special abilities.
Playing MBII is sometimes like being in an abusive relationship. It beats the sh*t out of you in such a manner that you feel like having been an*ly r*ped by a particularly large exemplar of a rancor, but somewhere deep inside you know that you want more. And that you seem to enjoy it.

STAR WARS™ Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy allows the player to control a character named Jaden Korr, a student who is brought to the academy from Coruscant, after he/she managed to create his/her own lightsaber without any previous Jedi training or experience.
Jaden is customizable by the player, with options like different races, different genders, different lightsabers and more.
The game takes place after the events of Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast.
At the start of the game, the Jedi Academy is attacked by Imperial Remnant forces, as well as by unknown Sith.
They manage to steal some information that is critical to the Jedi Academy and the Jedi Order.
Jaden then gets dispatched after completing the training at the Academy, and he/she is tasked with keeping the peace across the galaxy.
Along Jaden's journey, he/she meets a variety of legendary Star Wars characters like Luke Skywalker and Chewbacca, as well as the iconic Jedi Master Kyle Katarn.
Jaden also meets new enemies like Tavion and her Disciples of Ragnos.
Besides this, Jaden visits various iconic places like Yavin IV, Tatooine, Hoth & many more.
The game features a RPG-like system which allows the player to distribute certain points on certain force abilities (the previous instalment, Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast, did not feature this feature).
Besides this, the game also allows the player to partially customize their characters, with options to choose things like the race and the clothes, as well as the lightsaber style and colour.
The game feels very similar to Jedi Outcast, with many of the controls as well as the hud elements being identical.
The combat is very similar to the previous instalments in the series, but the lightsaber combat in particular feels much better than  the previous game. I found the lightsaber to be a much more viable option than the blasters, which were the way to go in Jedi Outcast.
In the end, I managed to finish the entire game with only the lightsaber.
For the first time ever in the Jedi Knight series, the game allows the player to choose from a number of different missions, which will lead the player to different planets and it ultimately allows them to meet different legendary characters.
Before you start any mission, you get to choose what force abilities, weapons and utilitarian items you want to bring, which is a very neat feature in my opinion.
The game features some very unique and dynamic levels that can be very overwhelming at times, but they are ultimately a joy to play through.
Halfway through the game, you get to make a choice between the light and the dark side, with either option giving you a different path to follow for the rest of the game.
The only issue that I have with this game is its length.
I managed to finish the game in less than 8 hours, while I managed to finish Jedi Outcast in 12 hours.
Nonetheless, I felt like the story and the gameplay made up for this issue, and because you get a choice between the light and the dark side halfway through the campaign, the game is highly replayable.
This game did not have any issues on my end, with no crashes, freezes or any major lag spikes.
The game felt very optimized in my opinion.
The only reasonable issue that one could have is the lack of modern resolutions for the game, meaning that the game is only playable with black bars if you play on a monitor with a 16:9 aspect ratio.
Anyone that has played any of the previous instalments in the Jedi Knight series should not have any issues with this, newer players however might need to adjust to this.
The game once again features the brilliant quick save and quick load system from Jedi Outcast, allowing you to quickly save and load at any moment during the game (except the cutscenes, obviously).
Lastly, the controls are once again completely customizable, with the ability to rebind every single function at will.

All in all, Jedi Academy is a worthy ending to the Jedi Knight series.
Its core gameplay feels very similar to previous instalments, but its story is completely fresh and memorable.
If you have played any of the previous Jedi Knight games, or even if you are a fan of older games with some great gameplay and a good story, then you should definitely add this game to your collection.

-Episodes: I am not a fan of episodes either, I've played a few episode games so far, and the waiting really does get boring. However, unlike other reviewers I'm willing to take HITMAN episodes with a grain of salt. Especially in light of what the game makers are working to achieve.
-For those who may not know:
-This is one of the first games to support Dx12
-The episodes / levels on this HITMAN are larger then ever before
Level Rant:
I'll admit, I didn't like the idea of only one level at the begining, but as I challenged myself to complete more tasks available in the game. I saw more and more details that the game developers added. Things I missed if I were elsewhere in the level, and what could easily be described as repeating events, in watching (while try to silently kill) my targets i saw little changes constantly in the main targets behavior. This is something new the game developers are trying and I applude them for their efforts. Also I would trigger different events at different times, and yet the targets responded predictibly (which is a nessacary evil if were going to set them up for a silent kill) without breaking their "routine"...they would finish their current thing and then proceed to my trigger, so far i've yet to see a trigger fail...I did see a trigger not fire once, but I was far away from the target...it then triggered on the next run. Maybe this was a bug, maybe this was on purpose.
Okay so I maybe rambling at this point, but my point is that the details the developers are adding considering the larger size of the levels is exteremly ambitious, and I support the month to month releases.
I didn't like the fact that the April release was delayed until the near end of April, but we do have the after launch patches to compensate for that. There is nothing saying that the May release will be early, ontime, or late. Honestly I've always been in favor of supporting the developers, especially if there is evidence of them working to improving the game. So even if May's level released in June, but it was obvious that the developers did it for a reason...I as a gamer who enjoys well developed games would appreciate it. Even if the waiting was killer.
Sum up:
Pros:
-Level design is done very well
-Details in levels are good
-# of props, areas to achieve creative kills are higher than any other game
-Levels are huge
-ways to trick / distract AI are better than ever.
-Gameplay allows for good difficultly, yet hitman's abilties allow for creative ways around guards etc.
-DirectX 12 imbeded (more on this below)
Cons:
-Developers didn't stress to gamers the graphical achievements of the game (game runs slow, except on med-high+ systems)  [Yet I was able to run this on my gaming laptop with a 2yr old GPU]
-The always online DRM is a mistake, no way around this but again my score won't reflect this, as I care about the gameplay
-DirectX 12 imbeded (pro and con)
DirectX 12: The Dx12 API is to Dx11 what Dx10 was to Dx9...That is the programing allows for better graphics, with smoother gameplay. Now anyone with a win10 system and a newer card  will easily see that in comparing Dx11 to Dx12 on Hitman there is only a 10-15% bump...not nearly as much as desired or as much as Dx12 should do. This is because you can overlay Dx12 on top of Dx11, but it doesn't allow for as great a proformance boost as creating a game from scratch with Dx12.
If anyone is still reading this, I am sorry this isn't a very good review, more of a rant...but hopefully it helped someone.
I as a fan of hitman, but also a gamer expecting much of the series really enjoy the new Hitman, and am looking forward to the new level coming soon.

Campaign
-----------
Although I have not actually finished the campaign of this game, I played nearly all of it. The Campaign is good to play when you're bored, but don't expect for it to blow your socks off.
Multiplayer
------------
Personally, I think the multiplayer in this game is one of the best Call of Duty has seen! It's fast timing is great, and the colourful graphics is even better, but the best thing about Multiplayer, is that it is great for casual and competitive player of COD! If you just want to hop on and have a bit of fun with your friends, all you have to do is join a party with them. If you want to play competitively get on to Ranked Play, which is like a gigantic eSports with thousands of people in it. I should also mention the "Pick 10" class creation style. With the pick 10 system, you have 10 slots for your class. That includes; guns, attachments, perks, wildcards, lethals and tacticals! This makes classes more realistic than all the other games.
Zombies
---------
Zombies is a different story though. Don't get me wrong, zombies and a fantastic and fun gamemode, but if you want to have the most fun, you will have to buy the DLC packs, otherwise you are stuck with some boring maps. The free maps you get are; Dus Depot (TranZit), Town and Farm. The only fun map for playing with friends out of those is Town, and the only good one for Solo is Farm! When you buy a DLC you get some of the best maps in the entire Call of Duty franchisel, such as Mob of the Dead and Origins!
Overall
--------
Overall this is a fantastic game! The multiplayer is great for just hopping on or playing competitively, the campaign isn't that bad and the zombies is amazing if you want to buy DLC Packs.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys FPS games.

Unlike most RPG's character creation is limited. You don't get to name your character or customize their appearance. You're either a man or a woman with "smooth, light brown skin" and "good muscles - strong, but not bulky - and slim hips." The games stats, skills and abilities are not exactly the same as those found in Planescape: Torment nor do they have the breadth of a hardcore D&D ruleset but there is enough to be found to create a unique build. The game will add much more depth as you begin leveling up. Your character will be named The Last Castoff for the entirety of the game.
The game has elements of time travel, segments that take place within your own mind (The Calm), and often pivots around interactive memories. At first the game is more than a little overwhelming with all the strange naming conventions and world building elements. It takes some time to get your footing.
If you don't like reading this game is not for you. It's basically one huge choose your own adventure novel. You'll spend 90% of your time reading.
The writing is superb throughout, with just enough humour and wonder to keep the games dark tone from becoming suffocating. The writing can feel a bit disjointed at first. However that disjointed feeling is INTENTIONAL. Every strange, semi-nonsensical conversation is a layer to the story. The more layers you add, the more the story grows and the deeper, more understandable narrative emerges.
The brilliance of Torment: Tides of Numenera's writing really hits home during the games final hours when a whole host of smaller story threads, characters and decisions finally bare fruit. It took me 47 hours to complete my first playthrough. That is reading everything, thoroughly searching every area and completing every side quest (which are all great and interesting). Things do play out differently depending on the choices you make so there is incentive to replay the game again.
Torment: Tides of Numenera put together a solid group of companions to explore the Ninth World with and I know I will think about Tybir and Rhin in particular for years to come.
What will put some people off is the combat. There just is not very much of it to speak of. I had played for almost 8 hours before I had a single fight. Every fight is a set piece that affects the story. All told I probably had to fight less than 20 times in the entire game. Now that number will vary a lot player to player because you can talk your way out of (or into) a lot of the fights. Even so I doubt there is even 50 fights to be had even if you went looking for them. It would have been nice to have some more combat to help break up the extraordinary amount of text you'll read during the course of completing the game.
Because you so rarely fight it can be hard to really get a handle on the games combat system. With Torment: Tides of Numenera you don't really feel like you have a firm grasp on everything until the end of the game. Not that the combat is all that tough even when you take inexperience into account. Other than the first few fights most of the difficulty during combat comes from the unique elements of that set piece encounter. Are you trying to escape? Are you trying to interact with objects? Are you trying to just stay alive against waves of enemies? From the mid-point onward your party is pretty damn powerful.
When you are fighting you'll often also be given the option to speak with enemies, convincing them to flee, change sides and more. If you do die, most of the time, you won't have to reload a save. That's because death is a core gameplay and story mechanic in Torment: Tides of Numenera. When you die you'll awaken in The Calm, the labyrinth within your own mind. There may be times when you'll find it expedient to die on purpose. Once you are done you simply enter a portal and awaken again in the real world.
Which could leave you feeling like the game is now too easy or has no consequence but Torment: Tides of Numenera still finds ways to make you fight hard to live most of the time.
The game is beautiful to look at. Equal parts gorgeous and horrifying (in a good way). Assets are not reused and each location is unique. The game is only semi-open, meaning once you leave a major location you cannot backtrack. However the games two main hubs (the rustic but also futuristic Sagus Cliffs and the monstrous, nightmarish Bloom) are vast and full of characters to interact with and quests to complete. It's unfortunate the fast travel system in Sagus Cliffs is poorly implemented and there isn't one at all in The Bloom.
The music is great but not as memorable as that found in some other recent RPGs. There is very little voice work.
There are relatively few bugs though I did have the game freeze on me once, and I encountered a few instances where I had to reload a save when NPC's, companions or the main character got stuck in an animation or failed to move like they should, preventing the game from progressing. There were also a few instances where dialogue referenced the wrong gender for my main character. I must point out I completed my first playthrough on a review build I received on February 9th so it is likely patches and changes will be present in the final build players will experience.

Backed this game. Was REALLY excited for it. I kept my spoilers to a minimum...and in doing so apparently missed my chance at getting a refund. Which, to be clear, I would have certainly done had I realized how bad of a shape this game was in.

Cuts to the fundemental rules set the game is built upon (aka, if you're familiar with how the PnP Numenera game works, there are MASSIVE cuts to that rule set).
Further, there are other major issues with the game. These include truly ugly character models/animations (although the rest of the game looks quite nice), an extreme imblance in the importance of different skills/abilities/classes/companions/etc (saying much more than that would be super spoilery, but, simply put, if you choose X, Y, and Z there can be no need to replay the game, as you'll have seen basically everything in a single playthrough, where as if you choose A, B, and C instead, you'll see about a 4th of the game's content, max, even if you're SUPER dilligent), unnanounced timed quests (aka quests you can fail by taking too long IRL to do them, with no indication that you need to do them in a timely manner), and relatively short playtime for a RPG of this price.
Finally, some other things to note, smaller, less important things, but bothersome things nonetheless include but are not limited to voice acting for the female player character that is probably the worst I've heard from any game in years, certain static images (like loading screen images and such) being the wrong resolution regardless of the resolution you set (resulting in things like "loading tips" being off screen), the inability to lock the mouse cursor to a single monitor in multimonitor setups (even in fullscreen), the lack of a boarderless window mode, the fact that you can die in the text-only intro of the game and get a game over screen, and many, many other small problems (including performance issues...which this game should have even a little).
Combine all this with what I feel are many poor design decisions that happened in the middle of development and had I know what was coming, I certainly would have asked for a refund back when I had the chance. Sadly, as this was a Kickstarter game for me (aka I got a CD key) I cannot get a refund through Steam, even though I've barely used it at all.
To be clear: If you are looking for an in-depth CRPG with heavy RPG elements, a complete Numenera experince, or a mixture of both, you will likely be dissatisfied with your purchase. If, on the other hand, you're here EXCLUSIVELY for the story and want a Planescape: Torment like story experience, this IS the game for you, and you'll likely be VERY satisfied with your purchase. But I fall into the first camp, not the second camp. It should also be noted that if you want the game promised in the Kickstarter this is NOT going to live up to your expectations.
All in all, this is not the game promised, it's a shell. It's not a CRPG, it's an incredibly detailed and intricate Choose Your Own Adventure visual novel with EXTREMELY light turn based combat on rare occasions. The broad strokes of the original premise are still there, but compared to other recent CRPGs (Pillars of Eternity, Divinity: Original Sin), the RPG elements are EXTREMELY lacking.
So, should you buy it? Well, that's up to you. Some people WILL be VERY satisfied with this purchase. As for me, I wanted a complete Numenera CRPG. This is not that game. So I can't recommend it.

Plot[edit]
Breakin' 2 features three characters from Breakin' – Kelly (Lucinda Dickey), Ozone (Adolfo Quinones), and Turbo (Michael Chambers) – who struggle to stop the demolition of a community recreation center by a developer who wants to build a shopping mall. Viktor Manoel, Ice-T, and Martika (who was little known then) also appear as dancers.

Critical reception[edit]
Though most critics rated the film poorly,[3][4] New York Press film critic Armond White considered it to be "superb"[5] and Roger Ebert gave the film a three-star rating.[6]
Soundtrack[edit]
Like its predecessor, much of the film's soundtrack was provided by Ollie & Jerry, comprising the duo Ollie E. Brown and Jerry Knight. The title track, "Electric Boogaloo", reached number 45 on the R&B charts.[7]

Home video releases[edit]
On April 15, 2003, MGM Home Entertainment released Breakin' 2: Electric Boogaloo as a bare-bones DVD. On April 21, 2015, Shout! Factory released the film, along with Breakin', as a double feature Blu-ray.
Legacy[edit]
The subtitle "Electric Boogaloo", originally a reference to a funk-oriented dance style of the same name, has entered the pop-culture lexicon as a snowclone pejorative nickname to denote an archetypical sequel.[8] The usual connotation is of either a ridiculous sequel title, or of the follow-up to an obscure or eclectic movie (or other work).[9][10] It was used by Wil Wheaton as a subtitle as a plug for his radio show. The band Five Iron Frenzy titled one of their albums Five Iron Frenzy 2: Electric Boogaloo.[11] An episode of the television show It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia was titled "Chardee MacDennis 2: Electric Boogaloo".[12] Other news articles and media have used the Electric Boogaloo subtitle, and it has also become an Internet meme.[11]
A documentary about the Cannon Group was released in 2014 called Electric Boogaloo: The Wild, Untold Story of Cannon Films of which Breakin' and Breakin' 2 were featured.[13]

I don't have too many hours in this game yet, however I would like to give people who are about to buy this game some insight on my first look into the game.
I restarted the world seed about 8~9 times and failed multiple times just so I could learn the game.
In order to understand the game, it will take multiple trial and error. Failing after two hours of hardwork and gameplay will happen more often then some might like. However, once you do understand build paths (varies depends on the resources you are given around the starting area), and what the priorities at each stage of the game is, the game becomes this massive online puzzle. It will NEED you to problem solve. It will also need you to think and plan ahead, predict problems that will happen and balance your colony so you have an equalibrium.
Patience is also another key for this game, trying not to do things as soon as possible, instead, do them at the right pace and right time to yield best result.
This game does hurt the brain, because there are 10 diiferent layers that must be taken care off, from power generation, to stress levels of your duplicants( the workers of the colony). Problems rises and sometimes there just is no right answer, thus you would have to find the best solution. There are also tons of different items to remember, what do the do, how do you make them work, what do you need so that they actually does their job, how to balance all of the items in the colony so you don't have too much of one thing and not enough of the other.
To conclude, this game isn't just material gathering game. It involves many different aspects that are quite realistic, even thought the art style may look very cartoonish. I very much enjoy this game and will continuing learning. Once I have a better understanding, I may come back and write a more indepth review.

When it comes to story, Arkham Origins would be the Metal Gear Solid 3 of the Arkham Franchies. This game takes place befroe the events of Arkham Asylum, exploring the character Batman and his enemies during the earlier years of his career. A few things are explained, such as why Bane acts so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ throughout the other Arkham Games, and how the "Arkham" legacy first began. Overall, this game's story is beautifully done, and I really love the way the villains are handled. Bane is fantastic in this game, as he has yet to suffer from what would make him ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and the writers even managed to make The Joker segments entertaining, which is quite the feat given how many times we have seen the villain in the past ten years alone.
Now, let's talk about the gameplay of Arkham Origins.
Arkham Origins gameplay is nearly 100% identical to Arkham City, which is good considering this game is a sequel. Unfortunately, the small percentage that isn't included in that statement is somewhat problematic. The first thing I noticed when playing this game is that the combat seemed slightly less responsive than in previous installments, this being most noticeable when you are either trying to counter enemy attacks, or hit them before they hit you. I'm not sure whether this is because the developers slightly changed the timing of some things in combat, or the game doesn't respond to my inputs fast enough, but you will notice the difference if you have played the previous title.
Second: Predator Mode. The other Arkham games were advertised as Steatlh Action Adventure, and while this game still earns that classification, there is a MAJOR lack of Predator Mode segments in this game. Not to say they don't exist, because they do, and they are very fun, but compared to the other two titles, Predator Mode is somewhat missed in this game. It's a shame this is the case, as the few times it is featured throughout the game, there are pretty interesting situations to make the segments more challenging. Invisible mines will blow up on the perches (Gargoyles are not common in this game) and there is more interaction with the environment.
My final gripe with this game, and this is the biggest of them all, is the bugs. Unless the game has been patched since I wrote this, you are going to bump into A LOT of bugs in this game. Now, I was able to get past all of them (though a game-breaking one required me to reinstall the game) and if you are patient, they will not make the game unplayable. But they will definetly happen, and they will be annoying.
Overall, I give this game roughly a 7/10. While it didn't really introduce anything new to the Arkham series, it stands on its own pretty well, and is overall what you would expect out of a sequel. Despite its many flaws and shortcomings, it is very fun to play, and quite satisfying as a part of the Arkham Franchise. If not for the bugs, I would consider giving the game a 8/10.

I completed Max Payne a couple of days ago. It was a really fantastic experience from the beginning to the end!
Just over a decade ago a friend gave it to me as a gift on Retail CD for PC. I played it for a bit but never had a chance to complete it back then. Unfortunately the CD stopped being recognized and I gave up on it. But coincidentally 4 years ago I was gifted on Steam by another friend.
This time I decided to play it again. I never had any issues running the game on my Windows 7 system. The only issue I had was the sound being messed up. There was no sound in some parts of the game and other sounds disappeared. It is a compatibility issue with the latest operating systems. But luckily this problem was easily fixed by a Max Payne: Sound Fix! patch that is found in the Steam Community Hub Guides tab. After that the game ran flawlessly!
Anyway, the graphics aren't up to par with the latest computer technologies, but they are of a high standard and exceptional for its time. The story is compelling, if sometimes a little difficult to follow, and once you start playing it, you don't want to stop! You want to know what's around the next corner and where the story will turn next, it really does get you hooked!
Level designs are varied and the gameplay is not repetitive. There are a total of 25 chapters in the game and each and every one of them is different so it constantly keeps you engaged. You can also manually save and not rely on checkpoint savings like some of the older PC titles. This is particularly important for a game like Max Payne where you'll come across difficult enemies. Enemies range from street thugs to military commandos. The first few stages of the game will present little problems for players, as enemies will rarely engage you and create life threatening situations. The latter stages of the game present much more complex situations, bombarding you with enemies in very close quarter areas. Enemies are pretty relentless throughout the game, so it's wise to sniff out painkillers and keep plenty in stock to top up any lost health and to also make sure to manually save each time you overcome difficult enemies or scenarios!
You also have a variety of weapons to choose from. Whether a baseball bat, handguns, assault rifles, grenade launchers, snipers, etc. You have full control over the enemies. Not to mention that in every particular scenario of the game you'll find that you'll need to choose different weapons for different situations! You cannot rely solely on one weapon only, that's what I like about this game. In one situation you'll need to throw grenades and in another you'll be requiring to use the sniper to kill enemies that are shooting from far above you.
Max Payne is also the first game to introduce bullet-time effects (like those seen in the Matrix). During a gun fight Max can slow down everything around him to allow him better aim and an edge over his enemies. You could instigate the bullet-time parts of the game over and over again and they would still be as awesome to watch as the first time.
It's just great fun to let loose with any weapon and reap the benefits of destruction. Not everything is about killing, as some moments will call upon Max to solve mini puzzles, or even traverse hazardous routes in order to progress.
Overall Max Payne is a fantastic third-person shooter, full of action and energy. The story is dark and backed by immersive film noir attributes. The graphics depict New York City in a stark fashion. The gameplay is highly entertaining and a complete bullet-fest from start to finish!

Despite what people in internet are saying (ie Metacritic 6.5 score by users), this game is fantastically done game with a lot of love put into it.
The worlds are massive, don't let the "oh there's just 6 worlds" fool you. This isn't a game where you jump into a picture like in Mario and complete rather wide by really pointless map with like 3-4 objectives. Worlds are full of life and are parsed in smaller sections, often entirely flipping the whole camera angle or altering the map with environmental effect, or granting you power to climb unclimbable walls.
There's so many different powerups and moves to purchase and minigames to play and master, there's at least 2-4 weeks to play with 4-6 hours a day.
I've played it like 3 days now and I've yet to even finish 1st world completely and barely scapped the 2nd one.
YES, there are FLAWS like in any game and here is few:
1) Quiz game is not enjoyable and it should be optional, not mandatory to progress
2) Some arcade games (mini games) take a bit too long to do and start feeling repetitive. For example where you get to drive a car, just finish after 3 rounds, no need to get 2 more.
3) First boss felt like it was rushed as the last phase was quite a difficulty hike, 2nd boss took way too long to finish
4) Yes the audio while talking could have used some fine tuning
5) First transformations could have been a bit more than "go unlock this with this" and had a practical use and ability to solve any number of the puzzles and wouldn't have impaired the mobility. Not a big thing as you spend most of the game in normal form.
6) Apparently it's bad design if Game doesn't include a map to show you where to go (unless game is Dark Souls of course)
So yes some fine tuning would have made this golden gem of a game, combined with of course better intro music (because apparently Games aren't about games these days)...
The gameplay was pretty masterful and I didn't find anything wrong with controls.
I'd say the real score is between 7 - 9 depending how much emphasis you put on having those above mentioned cases impacting on your enjoyment. If you didn't mind it might be 9. If you found Quiz annoying take a point. If you found every part of these above mentioned furiating then sure call it 7.
But seriously, even Mario64 had issues with some stages.
Zelda Breath of Wild was filled with boring mountain climbing parts which were more tedious than what answering couple quiz questions and trying to finish the kart ride 2 extra times would be. Shovel Knight was and is a great game, but it's no Ninja Gaiden (NES) or DuckTales.

When I bought the game I was not sure if I was going to like it. Many reviews talked about the game having camera problems and problems in controlling the characters.
I've been playing the game for more than 7 hours, been through the 4 first worlds and collected a lot of stuff and I didn't find the problems the others were talking about.
Pros:
The controllers are responsive, I didn't die a single time because of their unresponsiveness or because of depth perception. The camera mode that tries to focus on the path can be disabled by the user, so if you don't like it, just turn it off, like I did. The "free" camera works really fine.
The graphics (textures, models, animations, particles, etc.) are beautiful, the soundtrack and sound effects are amazing.
The puns are really bad (in an extremely good way).
I really like the vast number of puzzles the game offers and how each is unique. You need to collect a lot of pagies, but I still haven't felt bored of solving their puzzles.
Also, the game offes you a lot of freedom of choice: you can choose wheter to go to the next dungeon or expand the current one, and also can solve the pagies puzzles in almost any order in all levels.
If you like challenging, beautiful and well design platformers with a lot of collectables, the game is for you.
Cons:
The game could tell you earlier about the two camera modes availabe, as many users talked badly about the game because they didn't know the mode exists.
The first world seems a lot harder to find eveything compared to the others, maybe because of its verticallity. It still is a good level, but the game can get a little boring at the start because of this, but the other worlds are amazing and really fun to play, and I did not feel bored while playing them.

I loved this game from beginning to the end. But, unfortunately I can not call this Banjo-Threeie. I have play most of Rareware's platformer games on the N64 back in the day and will say I feel it would never be as memorable as Banjo and Kazooie. Quick explaination of this: You play as a lizard and a bat who goes through a similar plight like banjo and kazooie, jumping into worlds and doing your clue finder/puzzle solving abilities. It follows pretty much hand on hand to how banjo and kazooie did.
Now what makes me say that it would never be considered as the successor is because when I played Banjo and Kazooie, we learned the game along with the bear and the bird and it took me weeks to make it to the witch because the game was hard and long. Then when we get to Banjo-Tooie they pushed the N64 to it's absolute limit they used every button you could possibly use on that alien control, all sorts of interesting concept, new ideas and showed such passion and dedication that it was probably the longest N64 game out there. And when I say it was long it still had tons of content without feeling repetitive.
Yooka-Laylee does not show the same passion as B and K did. It tries hard to be banjo and Kazooie but it only feels like a shadow of what was and not it's own game. They tried so hard to make it like Banjo and Kazooie they didn't bother to seperate them. Worse of all they lost the point of the challenge of a platformer when they give free flight in the map. It felt like it was punishing players for trying to challenge themselves to be honest. Also it was just very hollow in what it offered, the maps were short and you basically extended the maps to go back and figure out what you didn't do/what's new. They didn't have that many worlds and it only took me a few hours to beat the game with very little effort and then a few hours more to unlock everything. (Did this on the xbox with a friend.)
TL:DR
Point is this is not Banjo and Kazooie Threeie, it's just a shadow of what it wanted to be. It's actually really short and pretty easy aside from the boss fight. It punishes people that like challenges and defeats the point of a platformer. I recommend it because it's still pretty good but don't expect Rareware.

So after about 32 hours with the game and its Review build (release build) I feel confident to say that i absolutely love this game... so lets dive into why.
Video:
Text:
There is one caveat regarding Torment... If you do not enjoy reading, you will almost certainly not like this game, because there is a LOT, and i mean a LOT of reading. Dialogue, Interactions, Descriptions, Activities, inner monologue - everything primarily communicated through text, and then - maybe - through visuals.
Which means that the primary point of critique is the story... so is it any good?
yes. Yes. YES.
The combination of excellent writing, very well fleshed out characters, a unique and mind-bending universe and an endless parade of cool interactions with people and and objects make the setup for the story great... and the story, side-quests and objectives you have are all also VERY Good.
But not only due to good story: Your choices are important, your actions are critical and choices made before, affect a lot of things later in major ways. Sometimes in ways you wouldn't imagine, but even minor changes will make massive differences.
There is a just a LOT of things that you do to shape your gameplay, and that provides a lot of replay value and a lot of general gameplay value. VERY good.
Now, having set that stage: There are a few issues. The game is still not as bug-free as I would like and is missing polish in certain areas: primarily the UI. So its not a perfect game, and would benefit form a good Quality of Life pass by the developers. Just small animations issues, minor bugs and UI inconsistencies that break immersion for no particularity good reason.
The Visuals are also a bit of a mixed blessing - While the art design, direction and composition are all amazing and the sound design (including the limited Voice over work) are very good... the character customization and visuals are very restricted and not that great and the level of animation, effects and interactive elements that are more than text... are also not that great. It's not a major issue to me personally, but your mileage may vary.
Combat is the last part and here i have a few issues with the way the game does a few cool things, but ultimately - it feels very limited. The various stats, items, usables and so on are often available in combat to perform cool actions and your characters can have a wide range of abilities, but because of the massive story / dialogue focus, the game doesn't reward "working towards" combat focus - so you end up with a character that can talk down a demi-god, but still needs to use a cudgel to fight a literal sentient nightmare.  While the combat requires thinking about actions, much like the rest of the game, it doesn't have the same effect where possible consequences are exiting - merely the end result of smacking something in the head.
Thankfully - combat is infrequent unless you actively seek it out, which makes it very good indeed. Talking your way out of a sticky spot is a viable strategy and that is very much applauded.
Overall Torment is a fantastic CRPG, and i wholly recommend the title for anyone that enjoys RPGS. Unless you don't like reading, because... yeah... tons of that.

If you're going to be frustrated at this game, it'll be at how bad you are at platforming in general. Super Meat Boy may not be I wanna be the guy levels of hard but it doesn't give you any mercy. It will punish mistakes time and again. It doesn't care, Super Meat Boy will grind you into fine meat paste until you master platforming inside and out. And I couldn't take the heat. So, I got out of the kitchen. I'll admit that I don't give up on too many games. Those that I do give up on rarely receive a review but I think I got enough of an idea about SMB from what I did play of it. It's a highly polished platformer with plenty of both visible and hidden levels to test your skills. The titular character responds to the controls how you expect him to. Levels are filled with challenging obstacles such as pits of death, saw blades, crumbling walls and more. You should expect to die multiple times before you make it through a level. This is clearly the case when the game has an excellent replay system that shows each and every attempt you tried. There's a lot of content you can tackle so it's just a question of whether you can handle the difficulty.
Settings are pretty bare-boned but that's unexpected from a 2D game. V-sync has to be forced in the control panel and you will have physics problems if the framerate is above or below 60FPS. The game is well optimized though so you shouldn't run into any issues messing up your time. Resolutions, full screen on/off and volume sliders are present. Notably, you will
a controller for this game. No ifs ands or buts about it, SMB is unplayable without one. Key rebindings can only be changed in a txt file outside of the game.
I gave up at the first boss of this game. I'm not that good at platforming games of this difficulty. I'll admit that I don't usually seek the challenge in the first place either. It's still a great game from what I can see of it but the level of difficulty will probably keep most people at bay. And really, you should only pick this up if you're looking for the challenge. If not, there are other platformers out there that test you without being masochistic about it. There's not that much of a story to really talk about either. SMB gets his girlfriend kidnapped and he's trying to get her back. That's about it. It's an homage to the platformer games of old while still holding its own unique style and flair. This game is focused on one thing and one thing only: to be the best platformer-centric game it can be. And it pulls it off quite well.

The second game prove to out perform the first and is regarded as a high for the series. This makes the thrid game in the arkham series 'Origin', to be very similar to Assassins creed brotherhood. Although it couldn't be said that these are worst than thier predecessor, neither of these games really offer any ground breaking innovation to the series. let's break Arkham origins down game down into some key compenets and compare it arkham city.
Firstly the environment, The Map in Arkham origins is considerably larger than in arkham city , giving you access to what is apparently the whole of Gotham City. Despite its size however its a pretty dull map. one third of the map looks like it has been commped and pasted from Arkham city, another third consistes of a collosal bridge which you have to cross every time you want to get to the other halve of gotham, unless you use the new 'quick travel system'. This leaves only one third of the map that is new, which is fairly dissapointing. The developers have added the bat cave, however this only serves as an access point to ranked challenges and training exercises and you only interact with in a couple times in the main campaign.
Speaking of the main campaign, the story line of Arkham origins is as expected top notch. The only criticism I can think of has  to do with some of the villian. firstly some of them are rather obscure. I know some die-hard batman fans will know who some of they are, but if the majority of people have to wikipedia half of the villians in a batman game, it means your scraping the bottom of the barrel. Secondly you only fight most the villians once and then thats it. Deathstroke for instance was the first of the 8 announced assassins for the game and there was a considerably amount of hype about the fight between him and Batman. They when you get to the game you fight him in one boss fight and then he is totally defeated. These assassins are suppose to be the best in the world and are getting paid $50 MILLION to kill the batman, yet all of them seem to lack the tenacity and motivation to try more than once to kill batman. The reason behind this I believe is because the developers are trying to cram the entire storyline into the time frame of one single night, surely stretching it out to a week or at least a  couple of nights wouldn't kill the plot.
Finally there is the combat which for the most part is left untouched and retains most of its inherit awesomeness. The developers worked off the idea that 'why fix something that isn't broken' and instead opted to simply make the combat 'different'. This has ment the implementation of three new mobs to beat up: The martial artist, who is basically a regular mob that requires more countering in order to defeat; The Venom thug, essentially a mini Bane, where you have to disable his venom pack before beating him to a pulp; And finally the Enforcer thug, who act like the Abramovici brother in arkham city only sometimes the have armour which you need to remove, before you take them down. there are also some new gagdets that can be employeed in combat such as the shock gloves and the ability to do two special combo moves, however this only makes the fighting eaiser as this give the player a very easy way to beat all the mobs that are support to make the game difficult. There are also some gadgets such as the remote claw and the glue grenade which are exact ripp offs of the line launcher and freeze grenades, respectively.
Yet another similarity that Arkham origins has with Assassins creed Brotherhood is the fact that it is the first in its series to introduce multiplayer. This consists of a 3v3v2 system where two gangs (Jokers and Banes) fight over 3 control point while a third team of Batman and Robin (which is unusualy as Robin is not featured in the main game) attempt to takedown the teams siently, in order to build up an intimidation metre and scare the thugs away. Although this is a fairly unique game concept it is at the best of times glitchy. FPS aspect of the game is somewhat stale and ins't terribly exciting. The matchmaking system is fast to get you into a game, but you often have to wait for the nesicarry 8 people to join before the game starts. Despite the fact that 8 people have to be in the game in order for it to start, there always seems to be two or three people that leave the game while its loading, usually resulting in on team having an unfair advantage over the over. This is particularly noticeable when the super villians become avaliable for either villian team to grab. unless the hero team or the disadvantaged villian team is really good, the team with the most numbers will generally gain access to their teams villians, which are considerably over powered . One game it took my team 4 lives to kill an enemy Joker and I have yet to see anyone successfully kill Bane. There is also a system where you can buy, with either in game or real world money booster backs. This in itself is a sin considering I already bought the game. It is more so a sin when the game suddenly desides to wipe all your statistics including your level, unlocks and purchased goodies!
In Final Summation, Batman arkham city is indeed a good game by most standards and arguably it is as good as Arkham City , however it is certainly not any better than arkham city and leaves a lot for the next arkham title to rectify. In my opinion however Batman Arkham Origins is still a worthwhile game with pleanty of the unadulterated goodness that makes the Arkham series of of the best in its genre.          7.5/10

Now, before all of you simply glance over my words simply because I don't recommend this game to everyone, allow me to explain in detail why that is so.
Have in mind that I have not completed this game 100%, nor do I intend to; I am not a completionist, and even if I were, this game does not deserve it. I've also played both Arkham Asylum, and Arkham City, followed by Origins, all in quick succession and in proper order, over the course of about 3 weeks. I was also (un)lucky to pre-order this game with a decent discount; it cost me about 30€ or so, a good dip from the 50€ that the game retails for.
Also have in mind that I will not be talking about the online multiplayer of this game; I feel it is an unnecessary add-on to the game that does not benefit a previously exclusively single-player experience, and a great one at that.
Now, I usually don't tend to compare different games because it takes away the focus of the game at hand, but since this is a sequel (or a prequel, to be precise); a game in a series of games, I shall compare it to its predecessors simply because it makes sense. This goes more so for the quality of the previous games, and to see if this game is up to the same standard. And unfortunately, it is not.
This game, like many other in their respective franchises, such as God of War and Assassin's Creed just to name a few, suffers from a very common AAA game problem; over-iteration. Companies become greedy due to the success of previous entries, and simply start cashing in on the loyalty of players with a passion for games like this. It should also be noted that this game, unlike Arkham Asylum and City, wasn't even made by the same studio; the first two games were made by Rocksteady, whereas Origins was made by WB Studio Montreal; meaning that the entire cast was changed.
Now, before I can state why I don't recommend this game, I'll take a look at the two previous entries in the series.
Back when I started Asylum, I expected nothing of the game. It is the only game of the three that I have not done any reading on, or have not seen any video material beforehand; I explored as I went.
A week later, having finished it, and on a side note, it is the only game of the three that I have played on the Easy difficulty (and it still remains the most difficult game in the series), I came out more than pleasantly surprised. Everything, from the game's level design, to its closed, dark, gritty, and almost paranoid atmosphere, not to mention amazing characterization, was spot on. I won't even start talking about the voice acting, which was second to none. The game felt fresh. It felt new. It felt like a really high-quality piece of work.
Afterwards, I almost immediately started Arkham City. With this one, I'd done some previous reading and watched some short videos. The game received almost universal praise, and I read reviews filled with nothing but good word of it. And given the quality of Asylum, I went into the game with high expectations.
Another week later, I finished the game, but with mixed feelings. For one, the story seemed out of place, and was kind of messy all around. Other aspects of the game received no change whatsoever; it was basically Asylum with a different story. Luckily, voice acting remained on the same quality level as with Asylum; Hamill really shined with the Joker. Lastly, the game did improve in one aspect. That was the environment. It provided me with a more or less open world, shedding the closed atmosphere of Asylum, and providing me with the constant feeling of being on the move. The design of Arkham City was great, and it was a good change from the closed corridors of the Asylum, and this required a different approach from the player.
Yet, despite all this, I still prefer Asylum. It just felt better.
Lastly, I started playing Origins. I had hopes for the game. I wanted to see it correct the things City got wrong; a more coherent story, a larger world to explore, more stuff to do.
And after a while, I saw that the game failed spectacularly at all of these. Now, since I'd harbored nice feelings for the previous games, I could look over the various issues that the game has. However, by the end of the game, I realized that this game was indeed a failure. It is a failure because it takes everything enjoyable from the previous games, and then limits it.
For starters, the level design is a step back from Asylum, let alone City. The game basically tricks you into thinking you've been given this large open world, when it fact it is more limited than the closed levels of Asylum, for most of the game. There are only a handful of ways to progress, and the game is not flexible in this aspect. Adding a quick travel feature detracts from the game's supposed exploration-based nature, and you're left to realize that, despite this game having a (slightly) larger map than City, it is barren. The entire city is almost empty, and to make things worse, this is obviously artificial, and on purpose. The game feels poor in content. It even has loading times between areas if you quick travel. It is simply pathetic.
And all of this is made worse by the fact that the game doesn't try to innovate in the slightest. It sticks to the formula of 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it', and it pays for it dearly. Nothing has changed gameplay-wise, and some things are even performed worse than in previous games. The entire system, like City, is simply copy+pasted from Asylum.
Last but not least when it comes to gameplay, the game has a multitude of bugs. From what I heard and read, I actually got off easy; I only encountered two or three game-breaking bugs over the course of my playthrough. Gameplay aside, there are even more issues with the game. And that would be the story.
SPOILER warning; mild story spoilers ahead.
Now, it might be just me, but the story of Origins feels even more out of place than City. It is cluttered, and makes no time to explain itself, while at the same time letting down my expectations. For one, I expected the Joker's presence in the game to be minimal, even more so than in City. But no. They just went and had to make him the main villain. Again. For the third damn time. Now, all of this would be ok if he was up to par. But even that doesn't occur, as the change in voice actors is visible; while I have nothing against Troy Baker, by trying to be as good as Hamill just doesn't work, and makes the game feel cheap. It is something you'll notice if you played the previous games.
Second, the game disappoints in its choice of villains; because the Joker is the main man behind the scenes, this de-values all the other villains, and makes them effectively the Joker's underlings, which is terrible. None of the other villains are given proper screen time, nor are they challenging in fights. This is evident as the game has the worst boss fights in the series. It is a step down from the outright amazing boss fights with Scarecrow and Mr. Freeze, as well as the Penguin in Asylum and City respectively.
And as far as the story goes, the name of the game is misleading. This is no origins story. It is just a half-as*** attempt to cash in on the amazing work of Rocksteady. The story does not feature the true Origins of the Batman, and provides no backstory to his motivation, like Asylum does. It just takes a great character and gives him more stuff to do.
TL;DR - If you simply have to have more of Batman, play the game. However, this game works best if you haven't played any of the previous two games. If you have, and think the series was great so far, for the love of God, don't play this game. If you were a fan of Asylum, stick to it. It is by far the best game in the series, and playing this will only make you dislike the franchise.
As a side note, this review was longer, but it seems there's a character limit, so I had to shorten it. Oh well.

I have mixed opinions on this game, mainly cause I've spent 60 hours playing every single story and side mission, as well as looting every possible thing I could in the Big White.
I'll start by saying good things about the game; it is gorgeous. It has a lot of Mad Max lore easter eggs and the main story of the game is pretty good. I enjoyed the characters and the trippy Max moments he had throughout gameplay, as well as car combat and several ways of taking down enemy vehicles.
Probably my favorite side stuff was taking down convoys which are the closest thing to the Fury Road movie.
And now to the bad side; it can be VERY repetitive and frustrating to do some challenges. Doing some looting is interesting cause of the locations the devs put their effort into (like camps), but most of the looting locations are just copy/pasted and always the same: 2-3 loot crates and maybe 1 history relic. You'll rarely stumble on new car models unless you've previously maxed out the strongholds so you know where to go.
And don't even get me started on the annoying clearing minefields and challenges ("Stick It To Ya" being absolutely THE WORST challenge to accomplish).
Overall, this game reminds me of Assassin's Creed/Far Cry games. They're not bad, but they aren't anything special really. I know that once I've completed every possible thing I could and unlocked all achievements that I will never play this game again. Not because it's bad, but because it felt so good finishing it.
tl;dr - the game's like pancakes. You'll love it at first, but play it too much (like myself with 60+ hours) and you'll get sick of it.

"What does one life matter?"
Apparently, it is a question where the answer would only make sense to each individual's code of beliefs and ethics. And sometimes, for a rare few, there isn't any answer to be had at all. But much like "What can change the nature of a man?", it's not the answer where the satisfaction is derived, but the journey to that answer through self-discovery.
This game does exactly what Planescape: Torment has done way back in 1999, that is to say, it has achieved a narrative that is thick with philosophical metaphors, witty dialogue and wonderfully delightful characters. Like Planescape: Torment, it takes every known cliche, knocks it down and rebuilds it in a manner that most ordinary folks wouldn't have ever imagined, let alone foresee it.
As such, this game is really not for the faint of heart, at least when it comes to reading. The text is heavy and littered with many proses and vocabulary that are somewhat archaic in format. Throw in some in-universe colloquial slang, and many players would easily be put off by the game within the opening moments, but that is essentially the charm of the game. Soldier on and you will be rewarded with an immersive experience that probably surpasses even Pillars of Eternity.
So, what does one life matter? It doesn't, but you make it matter anyway, because it's your story to tell, and perhaps, that is actually all that really matters.
