I have mixed feelings about Yooka-Laylee. Quite a shame too, as many of the trailers leading up to its release made the game look highly appealing. Not to mention my contribution to the game when the Kickstarter was announced (I backed it day 1 for the record). Essentially, the product I and many others were greatly hoping for turned out to be mediocre at best.
As a spiritual successor to Rare's gems of the N64 era, I feel this game follows WAY too closely to what Banjo-Kazooie was like. Instead of it being a game that's authentic and feeling like an inspired game, it feels more like a copy and paste of the bear and bird with newer graphics, different characters and less fun gameplay. Not to mention all the little things about this game that just add up over time.
For instance, time after time I felt like certain challenges were strictly made to utilize the game engine's physics, especially the few challenges where you need to roll balls into goals. There were also numerous challenges that constantly reuse hoops to roll, jump or fly through. Minigames played via Rextro range from average to frustratingly stupid and the controls for said games don't help their cause much. Kartos sections take a huge learning curve to master, but often the controls were so janky to begin with and certain enemy placements are random meaning you can almost always guarantee getting hit at least once. Flying is COMPLETELY broken in this game and really makes you question why certain challenges exist if you can just fly to bypass whatever obstacles are in the way. The camera, while I think is dumb at times, even more so than the original games, is getting way more flack than it actually deserves. It's not fantastic but it's not atrocious like many people say. And the stamina bar is one of the worst ideas I've seen for a game like this. It is completely impractical with how many moves your stamina bar utilizes. Sure, butterflies can restore your stamina, but if none are nearby, you now have to play a "fun" waiting game so it'll recharge. This by far undermines much of the experience of Yooka-Laylee for me
Some of the bigger gripes I've had mostly amount to the worlds themselves. They are full of many challenges, but many areas of the game seem large just to be large. The expanding mechanic makes already big worlds into massive worlds, causing multiple instances of backtracking (which you still have to do for completion anyways with moves from later worlds) unless you opt to expand the world before entering, sans the first world. Navigating the worlds themselves is fine, but it takes a while to get from certain areas to others, especially if you're looking for collectibles or new areas you have missed. Gone are the Warp Pads and Silos from Banjo-Tooie, so it's wise to ensure you have everything before leaving. So many times the worlds have large sprawling areas for no reason other than to make the game artificially longer. This game also only has 5 worlds, plus Hivory Towers. This game would have been WAY better with smaller, more confined worlds and more of them.
There were also a few challenges when originally played before the big updates, had no prior explanation as to how you complete these types of puzzles. What comes to mind are the laser puzzles and one challenge with a sentient jacuzzi. Since the update, the laser puzzles are much clearer but the game STILL offers no explanation you can do it in the first place. This will inevitably lead most players to find the solution online, which speaks volumes on level design if most people don't what to do without getting lucky.
Several other complaints have been nullified since the big update a few months back, but for my and many others' initial experience, these small annoyances all added up into one big conglomerate of criticism that is really hard to not take note of.
Very little did I honestly have fun with this game. After the first world, I was hoping for more of the game to be like that. However, as I continued to play, moments like what I've described (and many more) have made me feel bitter and resentful at the game. It doesn't feel like a game after a while, it feels more like a glorified "chore list" disguised as a video game.
I wanted this game to be great, I really did. But copying word-for-word the formulas that worked in the past doesn't seem to be the way to go. The best comparison I can make with this game is with A Hat in Time, a game that ACTUALLY is fun to play and does everything that Yooka-Laylee did wrong, right!
Ignoring the several controversies leading up to the game, it still falls flat in terms of enjoyment. So much so I find it hard to replay the game at all, even just to goof around. I can constantly go back to games from the past with inferior graphics and whatnot and still feel like I'm having a good time. With Yooka-Laylee, I don't have that feeling in the slightest.
Despite everything, I still think Yooka-Laylee is worth a shot, even it's not up to par with its predecessors. If anything, I think Yooka-Laylee is a great step in the right direction for Playtonic. Maybe the sequel (because it's pretty clear there will be one) can learn from this game's mistakes and rectify it to be an actual good video game.
In conclusion, I would recommend ONLY for those looking for a decent collectathon and platformer. It's nothing to be amazed at, but for $40 and sometimes cheaper, why the heck not?

After watching the trailer, I wasn't going to play Spec Ops: The Line - it looked like just another war-glorifying soldier hero game, Battlefield of Duty 26. Then I read some of the reviews, many of which rave about the game's plot exploring the horrors of armed conflict, etc. On the strength of the reviews, I decided to give it a try.
Having just finished the single-player campaign, I can't bring myself to go farther than a solid
. The plot, while slightly more involved than I had feared, was still fairly shallow. Additionally, it wasn't supported by the gameplay. For a game that tries so hard to make the player consider the ethics of his actions, it gives the player remarkably few choices, and the ones it does give only highlight the lack of the others.
The gameplay is also fairly bland and repetitive. Most of the game is spent crouching behind sandbags and shooting dudes in the face. Advance to next area, find more sandbags, shoot more dudes in the face. There's very little opportunity to involve stealth, strategy, or anything but frontal assault. There are a couple of sequences where you get to do something different, like cover your squad's escape or act as a helicopter's gunner, but those are few and far between. The enemy forces are very monotone - the entirety of the game is populated with Basic Soldier™, who carries one of a handful of weapons, maybe a dozen Edged Weapon Experts, each of whom can inflict more damage with a single stab than Basic Soldier can with fifteen bullets to the face, and another dozen Heavy Troopers, who are to absorbing damage what Edged Weapon Experts are to dealing it.
I played through the game on Ubuntu 15.04 - it seems to be a solid port, although
I took about 7 hours to finish the single-player campaign.
Overall, I have to say that, unless you
love shooting dudes in the face or have always wanted to see what it's like to blow up postapocalyptic Dubai
, it's probably best to pass on Spec Ops: The Line.

If you're going to be frustrated at this game, it'll be at how bad you are at platforming in general. Super Meat Boy may not be I wanna be the guy levels of hard but it doesn't give you any mercy. It will punish mistakes time and again. It doesn't care, Super Meat Boy will grind you into fine meat paste until you master platforming inside and out. And I couldn't take the heat. So, I got out of the kitchen. I'll admit that I don't give up on too many games. Those that I do give up on rarely receive a review but I think I got enough of an idea about SMB from what I did play of it. It's a highly polished platformer with plenty of both visible and hidden levels to test your skills. The titular character responds to the controls how you expect him to. Levels are filled with challenging obstacles such as pits of death, saw blades, crumbling walls and more. You should expect to die multiple times before you make it through a level. This is clearly the case when the game has an excellent replay system that shows each and every attempt you tried. There's a lot of content you can tackle so it's just a question of whether you can handle the difficulty.
Settings are pretty bare-boned but that's unexpected from a 2D game. V-sync has to be forced in the control panel and you will have physics problems if the framerate is above or below 60FPS. The game is well optimized though so you shouldn't run into any issues messing up your time. Resolutions, full screen on/off and volume sliders are present. Notably, you will
a controller for this game. No ifs ands or buts about it, SMB is unplayable without one. Key rebindings can only be changed in a txt file outside of the game.
I gave up at the first boss of this game. I'm not that good at platforming games of this difficulty. I'll admit that I don't usually seek the challenge in the first place either. It's still a great game from what I can see of it but the level of difficulty will probably keep most people at bay. And really, you should only pick this up if you're looking for the challenge. If not, there are other platformers out there that test you without being masochistic about it. There's not that much of a story to really talk about either. SMB gets his girlfriend kidnapped and he's trying to get her back. That's about it. It's an homage to the platformer games of old while still holding its own unique style and flair. This game is focused on one thing and one thing only: to be the best platformer-centric game it can be. And it pulls it off quite well.

TL:DR - I've gotten 70+ hours of gameplay out of Hitman even before the second mission hit.
First off, there are a few issues. On release, there were a bunch of server issues, and for some reason IO has decided to kick players out of their game sessions if they disconnect, despite it being a singleplayer game. Not a decision I agree with.
I also realize that for some, the episodic release schedule will be a major turn-off as well, especially with the delays inherent in software development being shown publically for all to see.
But for those willing to look past those two issues, and who are interested in a stealth game with an emphasis on undercover tactics rather than combat ones, I honestly don't think you can go wrong with this game. At the time of writing, there are 2 small training missions and one large sandbox level, with a second out of a planned 7 similarly scalled maps total on the way within a week. Within the levels available there are numerous ways to find and kill your target. You can be quiet, you can be loud, you can kill them in a public "accident" or without anyone noticing or ever finding the body. You can bludgeon, stab, shoot, poison (three different kinds available) garrote, drop, explode, incinerate, electrocute etc etc etc your targets or anyone who gets in your way. It's possible to create all manner of diversions to remove witnesses non-lethally or simply make sure eyes are looking away from you when you go for the kill.
And of course, what makes Hitman, well, a Hitman game, is the disguise system. Each level has many disguises with different levels of access to various areas in the maps and its well worth trying each of them on and seeing what you can do with them.
For those looking for an extra challenge, the game has plenty of pre-set ones to strike your imagination - various ways to take out your target, some of which you might not have even considered without being told it was possible, as well as for discovering all opportunities or using all disguises in a level. Or, if you're really skilled, go for the Silent Assassin, Suit Only challenge, and kill only your targets, without being detected or changing outfits. Once you've exhausted all of these challenges, there are further ones in the form of escalation missions from IO and contracts from fellow players which give you new targets and restrictions.
All in all, what makes me really appreciate Hitman is the amount of different approaches you can take to get around any challenge, most of which involve more subtlety than simply running in with a rifle. (and in fact, most of the time that will get you killed quite quickly - though props to anyone able to do so and get out alive)
It is currently unfinished, so if you want to hold off for now I wouldn't blame you, especially since the current level of quality usually found in episodic and/or early access games. But hey, I managed to get 70 hours out of it without getting bored, and that was with a single map. I guarentee once it's done the game will be well worth your money.

Let's be real here, Yooka-Laylee isn't groundbreaking.
I backed this game on Kickstarter expecting the game to revive my nostalgia for the collect-a-thon genre...
It has not done that...
There's a few things fundamentally wrong with the execution and presentation of this game in my opinion.
First, the game feels clunky at times it shouldn't be. This may be an injustice to the developers, but I feel that making the game using the engine they did ultimately hurt them in the long run. Before you get all defensive, I know how long it would take to custom make a game engine, so I respect the decision to utilize Unity in order to satisfy customers in a reasonable amount of time.
Second, combining old elements with new elements. It felt like Playtonic couldn't decide between this generation's buddy duo being completely retro, or completely revolutionary. Similarly old school moves combined with big, open worlds with only an indie developer's budget made the game feel a lot slower and emptier than it should be. I hate to say it, but A Hat in Time did a lot more with 5 reasonably sized worlds than this game did with 5 BIG worlds.
Third, Flappy Flight. Without a doubt, this one move single-handedly ruined my immersion for the remainder of my unfinished playthrough. Simply put, I refuse to finish the game. Label me as ignorant, but these big, emptier-than-they-should-be worlds complete with deceptively large numbers of Pagies per world ruined my natural flow of gameplay.
Overall, since Yooka-Layle is attempting to revive the buddy duo collect-a-thon genre, I'd find it in their best interest to compare the game to Banjo-Kazooie.
The first time I played Banjo, I collected everything in Mumbo's Mountain in one sitting, and without exiting the world. With the world expansion mechanic, doing exactly that is impossible. I get it, Tribalstack Tropics is a cutesy call back to Mumbo's Mountain and Mayahem Temple, and I will admit that without expanding the world, I thouroghly enjoyed finding all the Pagies, Quills, and Ghost Writers I could.
The rest of the issues I had with the game should be managable to most people, so I'm gonna keep them to myself.
Frankly, from my perspective, a level can be as small as a couple platforms, if the developer finds a way to make it cohesive, immersive, and fun to explore, I'm all for it. There's just a certain sweet spot between size of the world, and amount of content in said world.
Unfortunately, for the $40 price tag, I cannot recommend this game. If it goes on sale for 50 or 75% off, then go ahead and pick it up. At the moment, however, if it remains $40, just pick up A Hat in Time. Or do both, especially if Yooka-Laylee goes on sale for $10.

While I have many problems with this game, I don't think it's as bad as people on the internet act like it is. First off, aside from aiming with a power, the controls in the game are actually pretty good. It’s just that about every interaction with the game feels sloppy; for example, it was common for enemies to hit you even though you’re in the middle of an attack animation at them (felt like they’d go through your attack randomly), everything you can use your tongue on feels vague and random (what I mean is, the required distance and what your tongue will actually go for is mostly beyond your control if objects are somewhat close together), it seems oddly hard to just move in a straight line and you end up commonly moving in a curvy zig-zag motion constantly correcting yourself (you eventually get used to it, but it’s very weird getting to grips with it when it isn’t a problem for me in any other game), as well as other smaller things.
The mini games are all a mixed bag ranging between horrible to okay and should have had much more time put on them (not that the mini games in Banjo-Tooie were much better).
And the level design is also very good in places, and even does a good job at leading the player on where else to go in the level; it’s just that the things ruining that are whenever you die and whenever you move to a different area. Areas are connected at several points, though this seems like a good idea, it makes getting lost very easy to do since the transition doesn’t follow the same space logic as the areas themselves and just teleport you somewhere. Now the one level where this was fixed was in the Space world level since you can get to almost all areas without teleporting and the areas you do have to teleport  to are distinct on the outside from all the others so you don’t get it mixed up with other areas (one even, straight-up, has a sign on top of it). That’s not even mentioning how very helpful the quills are for finding new areas since they pretty much say to you that you haven’t been here yet; I just wish there was something on top of the quills (or a lot more quills meant to lead you places) because once you collect a large portion of them finding the rest will have you constantly running in circles.
Of course all of that could be avoided if the levels weren’t so friggin big; which is probably what these guys like to do because I had the same problem with Banjo-Tooie back in the day (oddly enough, no one seems to point out how Tooie had this problem too but still seem to love it then complain about this game’s large levels).
Aside from all of that though, everything else is great. The music is fantastic, the character design is fantastic (Trowzer is the best♥♥♥♥♥♥♥joke ever), and the story is…well charming (but the self-awareness of the characters gets a little over played).
Fact is, I agree with most people, it’s mediocre. But I recommend Yooka-Laylee because it’s still very enjoyable in many places, just so long as you can get past its rougher points.

I love Game Grumps and absolutely ADORE this game. Even though the game is still rough on some edges (white pixels, bad recording, typos) it didn't stop me from enjoying it 100%! Like many other players, I went into the game with an idea of which dad I was going to like the most, but now I can't possibly pick up a favorite. I'm not usually big on dating sims, but this turned out much better than expected. For the positive aspects of the game: the art is crisp with vibrant colors and limited animation. Much of the background music is pleasant and akin to the music found in Animal Crossing. Lastly the bachelors truly brought forth the positive experiences that the Grumps had with their fathers.
As for the negative aspects of the game: it has quite a few typos and grammatical issues that could have been easily avoided with better editing/playtesting. The game is slightly contrived in that seven eligible (despite LGBT individuals only making up 1% of the population) bachelors all live in the same cul-de-sac (though this could be for comedic effect). There also has been talk of glitches that prevent all possible endings for the bachelors despite the game's release delay and multiple choice options to receive different endings. Also some of the mini-games could have had more polish (the radio one could have used an adjustable camera, and the gargoyle just never seemed to take unless by random chance).
Overall with both positive and negative aspects considered this game shows promise for the team's first endeavor, and hopefully it will be a sign of more innovative projects to come as the team finds its voice.

"NOTHING IS A CLICHE WHEN IT'S HAPPENING TO YOU."
Max Payne is a third person shooter set in the gritty streets of New York City. Max, an undercover cop, witnesses the murder of his wife and infant child. This urges him to go on a warpath to seek vengeance and answers. Many consider this game to be a classic, and I think it holds up to the title.
+The story is told in a graphic novel style. Artwork mostly looks like muddled photographs, but it fits the overall mood of the story. Each panel is fully voiced to great effect. Max Payne's grave tones steal the show, though the other performances are still up to par. The story itself is a classic revenge tale; it treads off the path with conspiracies and experimental drugs, but the main point of the story is Max gaining vengeance... In style.
+Action. It's spot on. I usually don't care for third person shooters. The over the shoulder cameras can be pretty janky, movement is often delayed, and overall I feel like my accuracy hits the gutter. In Max Payne, however, I never had an issue. In fact, it uses the third person camera to its advantage. With bullet time dodges, you can maneuver the character in ways that actually help you in combat. While it looks cool, it all serves a purpose. With quick wits and the right doges, you can clear rooms in a way that is immensely satisfying. Nothing is better than sweeping a group of baddies in a single slow-motion dive.
~Graphically, the game hasn't aged very well. Facial models are clearly just photgraphs and a lot of the environments don't really feature anything too impressive to look at. Animations, as well, can be a bit strange looking. Using melee weapons feels just wrong, and Max's default stance is questionable. That said, I'm sure it was good for the time.
-Environments. There aren't many. Most of the game takes place in narrow corridors, factories, and harbors. While the level design seemed to flow well enough, I wasn't too impressed with variety. Discounting the dream worlds and the satanic nightclub, Max Payne doesn't have much to offer in interesting locales.
VERDICT
Max Payne is a game everyone should try. It's fun, it's frantic, and it's worth experiencing. Fans of shooters should explore the title, as it offers much more--in terms of gameplay--than many current games. It's not a long game, clocking in at maybe seven hours, but it's worth the low price that age warrants.

Bang Bang Racing is a good overhead racing game with major issues to overlook. The first issue is every time you turn your car, the chase camera swings to adjust. Its a gentle sway, but it often goes back and forth for the most minor of adjustment. It can be stomach churning, but there is always a fixed camera angle. The second issue is that an entire event can play as if its in slow motion when others are fine. Sometimes the slow motion accelerates to the smooth speed the game usually has. Even the fireworks at the end make the game slow down. I can recommend adjusting your screen resolution, but on a computer that can play ultra max settings on grander games, its just odd.
With those out of the way, I can tell you about the game itself. The game plays great with a keyboard and mouse or just a 360 controller. It plays like a lot of overhead racers, left and right to steer with a nitro boost and you have car health. If you take enough damage your car is crippled and you'll need to crawl your way to the pit lane. You can tell a damaged car by the bellowing smoke coming out of its tailpipe. Driving through the pit near the finish line will replenish your health and nitro boost, but its out of the way and its just easier to avoid completely. Like most overhead racers you can turn on a dime and there are a number of hairpin turns on each closed circuit course. These ultra sharp turns ensure that you'll need your brake or in this game's case reverse.
You compete against seven other racers in typical races and elimination rallies that eliminate whomever is in last place when the clock runs out. There are time trials where you race against the clock. Finishing in third place or higher will unlock the next track or two. The races are brief, several laps that take half a minute each depending on the track. Coming in first unlocks a few new vehicles for the current series.
Rather than showing stats for each car, it gives you a hint and a description for each one. I assume a steering wheel means that its good at handing or steering. The roll bar icon indicates that its durable and can take a beating. The nitro means that its better at nitro and what looks like either a tire or a fan could mean its exhaust is efficient? Perhaps it accelerates faster. I assume the speedometer means that it has a better top speed. Wait I have that backward, the speedometer is the car better at acceleration and the wheel is the one with the better engine.
The meat of the game is the career that has you competing in four brief stages that I'd call a series of events rather than stages. Each one has a minimum of five events that increase by two for each stage. With the exception of the first stage, these stages are punctuated with a final championship that has you racing in several races back to back as a sort of endurance event.
The aesthetic is nice and clean and the cars are stocky little cubes that represent race cars, stock cars and muscle cars in a sort of chibi caricature form. Speaking of chibi, there are no people in the game, just bouncing heads on bleachers to cheer you on. Its a look that several other overhead racers do and Bang Bang Racing is the cleanest. Each track is beautiful and full of color. Japanese cherry blossoms on some tracks, a crystal blue watery port on another. It just looks like a game I want to play.
Each track is compact and littered with things like cones, tires and barrels that will get in your way. The barrels are either full of water or tar, they'll slow your car down depending what you hit. The real obstacle is your opposition, because they all cluster together and usually jam up early turns in each race. There's no logic here, they just cram together. You can push other cars out of the way, just as you can be pushed sideways. With the cars being so stubby, its tough to turn anyone around although I have seen a few racers get stuck driving into walls.
There's good use of stand and it will scatter onto the pavement if you drive through it. This is a nice touch of detail and it seems to affect gameplay. As you progress, you'll find tracks with shortcuts which is another nice touch. One thing that was overlooked is the game's snowy winter track without icy roads. It plays like every other track.
For anyone interested, there's four player on the same game and it could make for some fun times if you have a big screen and enough friends to play it. If you're alone, you can always play against bots and even select their difficulty. You can play through all four championship endurance races, but if you're looking for a quick fix, there's free play that lets you select the mode, track, class, laps and difficulty of your opposition.
Despite its two major flaws its still a fun game and a real toss up as to if it earns a recommendation. If the game slows down this bad for me, what will it do for you? Its only on a few early races, but those early races are your first impressions of the game.

A fun little mini racing game with cute graphics and good music!
Don't mistake me, it has some serious flaws:
* Track design is explicitly created to punish skilled and experienced racers as hazards are placed directly in the best line for many turns
* The camera swings around behind your car, and it only gets worse as you ascend in the classes, because higher speed makes it swing around more violently forcing you to rely more or less on perfect track memorization (as you can't see where you're going)
* Admittedly I did not get into the higher classes, but the AI cars more or less already became completely irrelevant in Class II and I imagine in Class III they're pointless because they seem to use the same AI and can't really handle the performance of the Class II cars
HOWEVER! It works very well, performance is great even on Intel HD Graphics, and honestly the UI and overall design are very charming. The driving mechanics are fun and well-implemented; while drifting isn't that useful in the first class, it becomes a big deal (expectedly, given what the class is) when you get to Class II. Like most racing games, the car with the bonus top speed is the best car in any given class, so once you unlock that there's not much point in using any other car in that class.
Overall I won't give it a global recommendation, but for anyone who wants to casually play a racing game that harkens back to the SNES but with the visual polish we expect in 2011 (the year the game was released) it delivers!

There is just one major bug (during the final boss fight - you will know it when you get there) with this game and the fix is rather simple. You need to go into the file called "DefaultInput.ini" and check to see that these two lines are there:
.Bindings=(Name="NumPadThree",Command="DebugCameraZoomOut | OnRelease StopDebugCameraMovement")
.Bindings=(Name="NumPadFive",Command="TriggerQuickStrike | QuickGadgetX | DebugMenuSelectX | CancelBatarangCamera | Button aQuickStrike")
For some reason the defaultinput.ini file does not have that second line which you need for the final boss.  If adding that back in does NOT solve your problem, then reduce the resolution to it's minimal settings and try that. If you have both fixes going and that does not work, good luck because that's all the help I can give.

Let the record show that I was not among the ranks of the internet controversy machine that set out to shoot this game down because of the Jontron cameo removal. I had every intention of giving this game a fair shake. Now that I have, I can say in earnest that this game did not live up to the hype.
You wouldn't think that the story, of all things, would be one of Yooka-Laylee's major downfalls, but somehow they managed to make it one. Rareware games back in the fifth generation did have a tendency to occasionally break the fourth wall, but Yooka-Laylee only has three walls as far as I'm concerned. The entire game is pervaded by self-aware apathy that is more contagious than funny. Laylee herself will constantly remind you that this is a silly video game and she can't be arsed to invest herself in it, and the same can be said about the charmless villain with no clear purpose. For what it's worth, you're trying to rescue the sentient pages of a magical book from a greedy (I think?) CEO who wants its power to rewrite reality (to what end, I couldn't tell you). I suppose Laylee just wanted to get them back so she could pawn off the book for money (again, I couldn't tell you what she's trying to accomplish, if anything), and Yooka is just an upstanding gentleman with no interesting personality quirks who's only along for the ride.
Putting aside for a second that Yooka-Laylee and its characters don't care and as a result I ended up not caring either... There is a solid foundation here. Aesthetically, this game hits all the right beats, with appealing cartoonish visuals, and music that is reminiscent of Kirkhope's older pieces (if not as memorable). The actual gameplay could have been good too. The first level seems quite promising when you've got nothing but the basics, as well as some pretty solid platforming. However, the game often introduces new abilities that trivialize its own game mechanics. It won't take long before you get an overly generous gliding ability, or a completely consequence-free ability to move underwater. I'd say the most egregious example of this though, is when you get theoretically unlimited free flight (to the game's credit, this is pretty far in), rendering any and all platforming unnecessary. Many broken abilities, such as flight, are fueled by the regenerating power bar, which refills itself within seconds if not being used. This includes a number of increasingly powerful attacks, which are to be used on utterly useless enemies that never get any more threatening or varied (the game even makes a cutesy attempt to lampshade this at some point). I know that Yooka-Laylee thinks it is parodying Banjo-Kazooie to an extent, but enemies were never this much of a non-issue in B-K, which also, might I add, restricted where you could take flight, and how long you could flap your wings.
I'd say the most noticable lack of creativity in this game, though, is the apparent dearth of ideas for levels. Instead of 8 or 9 somewhat unique worlds, you get 5, with the option to expand them later. This does add more objectives to each level, but the areas and/or people of interest are just strewn across more big empty space, full of extra collectible quills that all add up to way more than you'll ever need to purchase every ability.
I suppose my standards might have gotten a bit too high since I was a child, so, if you're feeling nostalgic for a few Nintendo 64 games, Yooka-Laylee might still tickle your fancy. The game is definitely a textbook case of style over substance though, so it might leave you feeling just a bit empty.

Okay, so i am making this as a NEGATIVE review, however let me say this is only for one big reason, wich is; CONTRACTS MODE, hear me out!
The main mission itself is really awesome and the map is huge! there is so many possibilities to take out your targets, i cannot wait for the next levels! i do agree this "episodic take" they are doin is a negative aswel for me, but i can look past it.
However a big part about these new Hitman games is CONTRACTS Mode, i loved it in Hitman: Absolution and I was glad to see it made its return here, having Contracts on these big maps would be amazing!
What i do not like about Contracts mode at this moment is the lack of features, for example i had spend hours making an awesome contract and could not wait to share it so my friends could try it out and see if they could complete it, this was a huge part of Hitman: Absolution and part of what made it so awesome for me, and i am sure many others to!
In Contracts mode in this game there is no way to share your contract with friends, or to even look for them via a simple search function, right now your contract just apears in the "Latest contracts" tab and after a while it is just gone as many new player made contracts apear, there is no way to find it back again so you might aswel have deleted it. (yes i know you can find in in the MY CONTRACTS tab, but that is only for me to see, why would i keep replaying my own contracts if there is nobody to compete with?)
Basicly what it comes down to is, Contracts mode in HITMAN 2016 is a MAJOR step back compared to Contracts mode in Hitman: Absolution.
Hitman: Absolution contracts mode had; Friends only filter contracts list & score boards, sharing contracts, easy way to look for new contracts, and an awesome rating system to see what other people think about your contract. HITMAN 2016 has none of these features sadly...
I hope Io-Interactive & Square Enix are aware of this and are working on improving the HITMAN 2016 contracts mode ASAP! but at this time i could not find any information on it that they are, all i can find is other people like me who are sad about these lacking features.
So here is my feedback for HITMAN 2016, its a real shame because the main mission is AWESOME, i cant wait for more and hopefully a much better Contracts mode! because that is what keeps me coming back to play, especialy now when you have to wait for more main missions aswel =(
Until then, my review will stay like this, but i hope i can update this soon and make it a positive!

A SURPRISINGLY good, SERIOUSLY underrated, and FANTASTIC exploration and evolution of the beloved Mad Max universe that's BURSTING with content!
The 3 elements that makes this game shine are world design, exploration, and combat. The wasteland is a vast environment alive with dangers and secrets waiting to be unlocked. The combat takes what made the Batman Arkham games work and adds a gruesome and brutal flavour to it. Top it all off with an OVERWHELMING amount of activities to do and collectables to get, and you'll be playing this for DOZENS of hours.
But the game is not without its faults:
The main story, while closely following the formula of the films that came before it, doesn't really add anything to the character of Max himself. Granted, it's always been the world that's the main focus with Max the role of the observer, but the interactions of other characters during exploration and side missions focus more on Max, especially with Griffa. However, the story really picks up in the last half of the game.
It can get pretty repetitive at times, especially with little to no variation on taking down the Top Dogs in camps. With the amount of things to do in this game, the repetitiveness can really stand out, making this game better in short sessions as opposed to long sittings.
I experienced a few crashes, but they were infrequent enough to not ruin the overall game.
One BIG gripe I have is how you can't fast travel with any other vehicle other than your Magnum Opus. If you want to drive any other car, you need to drive all the way over to your destination, especially when you need to use your dog for disarming mines. It's a baffling design choice to say the least.
All that said, I was surprised how much I enjoyed this game. I liked this game WAAAY MORE than Shadow of Mordor, which I thought was a collosal dissapointment. With the amount of things to do in this game, the recently reduced $30 price tag is an absolute steal.
If you enjoy the movies that came before this, you'd have to be absolutely mad to pass this underrated gem up.

While Max remembers what happened 3 years before we need to go back 15 years. It was in 2001 that Remedy released an action-pack video game that was the first utilising the slow-mo we got to like so much after Matrix came out. I remember it was not long after the first benchmark software, 3DMark 99 was released - one of the graphics tests included the lobby scene from the Matrix recreated spectacularly thanks to the Max Payne engine.
That's right. Max goes after the entire underworld of New York as some junkies kill his wife and baby girl. The game is pretty linear - we go from one area to the next. Everything is pretty straightforward but while making progress the action is almost constant and it is very easy to die unless we regularly turn on the slow-mo effect. Making things slower around us allows for more precision-shooting, too. I like how Max uses painkillers to make the pain go away - not health packs but regular painkillers.
The game aged a lot but still looks pretty cool. At the time Remedy's software was revolutionary in every which way. The accompanying music is a classic one - the game's theme was later on used in its sequels and became one of the signature elements of the franchise.
There are dozens of cutscenes between the various stages but these all appear in the form of comic book pages. The narrator, Max, is actually played by the guy who wrote the game's screenplay, Sam Lake. We follow Max's internal monologues - his struggle with New York's evil and at the same time with his memories; the memory of losing his loved ones, something so painful that eventually set him on this dangerous path he can never leave.
There you have it: a classic 3rd person shooter that still matters. A game that has all the ingredients to give birth to an excellent action flick: Italian-American mobsters from New York, amazing dialogues / monologues and all this touched by a little - if not too much - film noir.
I do not think there are many brands out there whose sequels became really good. If you like trying out classic games this is a must have for you especially since almost everybody who appreciates the modern technology graphics have - probably - already played the 3rd and last episode. You'll probably have a sound issue once the game starts up for the first time but thanks to the many guides available on Steam this can be solved immediately.
PS: Steer away from the film adaptation released in 2008. It is the epitome of how bad video game adaptations can turn out.

Highly recommended.

At this point, it's difficult to tell the completely-serious-ridiculousness of the 90s from actual satire. Released in 2001, Max Payne exists in a time so close to the height of 90s bravado that it hasn't quite dissipated yet, but we might finally be ready to start talking about how silly it all was. For a fifteen-year-old Playstation port, the game itself has held up surprisingly well, perhaps even gaining a bit more accessibility in the move to the PC. The interface is clean and intuitive, the transition between shooting gobs of interchangeable mooks and the fastforwardable/rewindable cutscenes is smooth, and the bullet time mechanic is game-changingly useful without entirely dominating play. Other than the platforming elements - that have no business in this game in the first place - Max Payne is still a joy to play. Even when being encouraged to abuse the quick save function to solve cheap instant-death scenarios, it doesn't stop being fun. But what makes the game memorable are the little touches: the casual nature of the conversations between enemies before you burst into a room, the sensible placement of guns and painkillers, the way Max looks towards and mentions cutscene-inducing items but lets the player activate them on his or her timescale. Where Max Payne shows its age is in the flat, pasted on faces of its character models. Everyone is made out of sharp-edged boxes and Max himself is caught in a perpetual squint that never fails to decimate his dramatic creditability. This weakness only highlights the brilliance of the graphic novel styled cutscenes though, as they can be relied upon for any moment that wants to hold on to its pathos. And that's what Max Payne is made of: a handful of brilliant choices that leave its equal amount of flaws mostly ignorable.

Bang Bang Racing doesn’t want to be just another isometric racer.
It’s design leans heavily toward that of classic arcade racing, uninterested the cartoony power ups and lightweight vehicles so pervasive in the genre, focusing its energy into crafting a very physical racing sensation even at the cost of neglecting everything else in the game.
And it definitely shows. Bang Bang Racing’s core racing experience is tight and fast, with cars that carry a deliberate weight as you spin around corners, and aggressive AI that holds tight to the line between challenging and unfair. The sense of speed feels amazing as you slam down on the boost and try not to wreck and your newfound velocity, something that’s difficult to land when you’re viewing the game from the viewpoint of a trailing helicopter. It’s some of the most engaging racing I’ve ever had in an isometric racer, but it’s also the first and last thing Bang Bang Racing ever excels at.
Though there’s a clear struggle during races as everyone fights for first, often spinning themselves out in the process, once you leave a race progression becomes hard to track. You unlock tracks and cars in a linear order, but it doesn’t feel like you’re ever advancing. Races come and go and I never got the impression I was driving better cars or racing smarter opponents from the first race to the last. The only difference between the four cups (which branch out into individual races) is the type of car you drive, but again there’s little to differentiate them by. Muscle cars felt the same as formula one cars, and as each cup uses small variations on the same courses I never had to adjust my racing style for any small subtleties the different vehicles might provide.
Track designs are universally solid, but you can only go so long on a dozen or so tracks before they start to feel tired. I appreciated the small ways Bang Bang Racing changes things up between races, be it switching race modes or opening and closing short cuts, and it was never much of an issue that I was still essentially doing the same races over and over. But I imagine that’s in large part do to the career mode lasting in the range of 2-3 hours, which works at keeping the sense of repetition at bay, but also meant I was done with the game rather quickly and found little excuse to replay races over again.
Most bothersome is a camera that can’t keep up with you. Bang Bang Racing has two options for this, one being a fixed camera typically from the side of the track, and a dynamic camera that stays at the isometric angle but turns to follow the direction of your car. Both are extremely problematic, the former because it makes it difficult to drive in a straight line or see where you’re going, and the latter for all of that and the added effect of being nauseatingly mushy. It pans slowly and clumsily, often leaving you staring in the wrong direction you need to drive and sliding around so much that I often started to feel ill and had to stop for fear of vomiting over my monitor. It tends to be more usable than the fixed camera, but at the added cost of motion sickness which may or may not affect you (for reference, I almost never experience it).
Yet for all Bang Bang Racing’s problems I kept coming back for the immensely fun and satisfying base racing experience. That I was willing to endure physical discomfort to play it should say how much I enjoyed it, and it makes it difficult to recommend for or against the game in any large capacity. I can only hope developer Digital Reality gets another crack at it and can fix the problems present here, because they’ve got a great foundation to work with packaged together in a miserable shell.

I was initially really put off by the insane hype surrounding what looked like an incredibly average game, especially when the hipster sjw crowd latched onto it. No joke, I have had people who haven’t even played the game rave on about how it’s the best thing ever. Seriously, the way some people talk about this game you'd think it solved world hunger or brought peace to the Middle East. Curiosity always gets me in the end though, and I picked it one sale, half hoping that this would be overhyped hipster trash and half hoping it was as good as the fanboy/girls said.  . and you know what?  Its a pretty good wee game.  Not great, and definitely not, in my eyes, able to justify the quasi-religious level of hype that surrounds it, but not a bad game for sure.  I actually found it to be a very enjoyable if wonky and inconsistent game.
There’s quite a bit to like about Undertale.  The music and the sound effects especially are incredible, and I appreciate that the game rewards you for being kind and doesn't force you and if anything encourages you not to hurt other characters as the best dialogue is usually what follows the non-violent option (Hear that Bethesda? You can have a nice rpg without having to murder everythng with a face).  When the humour is done well, it can be quite funny (although sometimes it is barf inducingly cringeworthy), and overall the story is enjoyable and resonates well on an emotional level.  It might be alittle to SJW in its themes of prejudice and ignorance, but the game has a nice message and I appreciate that.
However, there’s a few things that really irked me.  The graphics are downright bad.  Yeah, read it and weep fanboys and fangirls.  I understand not every indie game can be Hyper Light Drifter, but I find Undertale to be ugly – lo res can be beautiful (Sword and Sworcery? Fez?) if done with a touch of artistry, but Undertale just looks lazy and sloppy.  And this is coming from someone who remembers playing a commodore 64 on a black n white tv in the 80s.  I thought the combat system was a bit  hit and miss.  Sure, it can be  fun and rewarding figuring out how to pacify an enemy for the first time, but when you’re fighting Froggit or Aaron for the 6th time?  eesh.  Also, I found the game gets really tedious in some places, like in certain parts where you are interrupted every 2 seconds with some stupid interaction from a certain NPC.  Can’t you just let that sh*t play and the background and let me keep walking?  Really freakin tedious
So, overall, I’ll admit I went into this kinda wanting to hate it, and I came away kinda liking it, with the high points being the story and the music. Oh the musi is amazing, and can stand toe to toe with great snes scores like Secret of Mana or Chrono Trigger.  But let me reiterate that, in my opinion, while the game is good, it has more than a few flaws and some very grating and annoying parts to it. I would recommend Undertale on sale, for while it’s not quite a case of the empower's new clothes, it’s not the messiah the worshipers of the church of Undertale make it out to be.

100% completionist review
Pros:
- Classic humor/writing
- Well built platforming
- Modern geometry, making everything climable
- Excellent final boss fight
Cons:
- Camera fights you (solved by switching to manual in the camera options)
- Backtracking
- Controls could be smoother
- Not Banjo-Kazooie
This game is definitely not Banjo-Kazooie, so if that's what you want going in you'll be disappointed. But it is a modern platformer with a heavy focus on mixing classic Rare tropes and level design with new ideas. It definitely feels like something that could be slotted into the late 64 catalogue easily.
Everyone will want to immediately switch to the manual camera. Having played it through on the classic and gone back and played around with the manual camera, I can guarantee that the controls will immediately feel much tighter with this option enabled.
Playing through the game I never had trouble finding remaining quills aside from the well known Shovel Knight single quill, they were all along the path to the pagies one way or another. On the other hand, there were a few pagies that were quite hard to find, but what kind of collectathon would it be without a couple of those here and there?
While the levels look pretty and the platforming is grand for the most part, it quickly becomes obvious as you play through that very little in the levels connect to each other. Each pagie is plopped on the map somewhere and are equally fast/easy to get to, with the only barrier being the expansion. There are very few minigames besides the hoop race which has a heavy presence.
All-in-all, a lot of the elements of the game feel like they were rushed. Lack of minigames, odd characters being reused between levels, few characters in general, lack of connection between level parts, and a couple easy to reach holes in the overworld where you can go out-of-bounds. Sacrifices were apparently made during the making of this game, here's to hoping that a sequel will have enough dev time and hours to make up for it.
I give a firm recommendation to anyone wanting to have fun with a classic-style platformer without expecting it to be Banjo-Kazooie wholesale.

RELEASE THE KWAKEN! :3 I'm having so much fun with this. Went in with 0 expectations and am absolutely loving it. Controls are nice. Reminds me of the old days of PS2 a lot. Whatever problems people had were because they expected too much, at least that's my personal opinion on it. There is old school difficulty where things are not laid out for you so you have to hunt it down. However, I don't consider that a downside. It brings a level of thinking to the game and making sure that you get things as you go through if you can. 100% the game is hard but it should be hard, not a cake walk like people want it to be.
The worlds are large but managable. You can easily learn the layout of each level without difficulty. Short cuts are added in that you can unlock so you can get around each level easily. Again if you've played older games you would be used to this or at least can map it out in your head. Controls are easy to master.
The level designs are cute as are the characters. It reminds me again of a lot of older games. I think the pumpkin lanterns following you around in the swamp level was an amazing add in(Can I have them for house security?). I've been appreciating little things that they added in. Also I think I laughed for 20 minutes straight about Trowzer the Snake... They are enjoyable jokes that as long as you aren't a stick in the mud will enjoy.
Puzzles are enjoyable. They are my jam so I can easily figure them out but they have enough difficulty to them that they don't hurt your brain. If you can't do something there is a move that will help you do something, you learn this very fast.
The banter in the game is enjoyable as well.
The biggest problem I've heard about was the controls and honestly nothing is wrong with them. I don't find them too sensitive or too stiff. They are just right when using a controller.
Cons: To expand the worlds you need to go in and come out. If that isn't true then I've been having trouble with it and I apologize. You should be able to expand right after you unlock the world. It would make it easier but it really isn't that big of a deal.
The whistling tonic for rare items should probably include quills... but maybe have another tonic for locating quills and other things like that? However, it isn't that big of a problem.
Overall the game is highly enjoyable and makes me remember the old days when I was a kid. :3 Very cool.

One of the best 2D platformers ever made, revered for its incredible difficulty and absurd amount of charm. A must-buy for anyone remotely into independent games - this game and Braid are the two major titles that kickstarted the entire modern scene.

Belated recommendation. Super Meat Boy is a fantastic throwback to the earliest days of 2D platform gaming, with a few notable differences. First, the difficulty level is brutal. And I don't use that word lightly. I played a ton of sidescrollers in my day, but can't think of very many that even approach this level of difficulty. That said, SMB alleviates a lot of the frustration that usually comes with difficult games by doing away with "lives", and making respawns instantaneous. These elements, coupled with short stages, allow for levels to be retried many times (which you WILL need to do) quickly and easily. If this weren't the case, the game would almost certainly be far too frustrating for most gamers. Add in some cool music, strange cutscenes (plus lots and lots of spinning blades), and what you've got is a classic of the genre. Just be warned, unless you are some keyboard savant, you are going to need a controller to get very far, especially once you hit the later levels.

This is actually a complex game to rate, as there are a number of positives and negatives. So, without further ado, let's start by the positives:
- The setting and ruleset: This one will look like a negative, but it's actually a positive. Numenera, the tabletop RPG, sells itself as innovative both in terms of settings and rules. Sadly, it is not, in either case. That is not to say it is a bad RPG in any way. It is not. It just oversells its “science-fantasy” setting, when it is really just fantasy with an interesting makeover.
In the same sense, while it attempts to portray itself as an avant-garde, alternative game, which favors roleplaying and exploration, it is basically a simplified D20 RPG with pretentious names, not getting even close to real RP-heavy settings, such as FATE, or even WoD. Although I do realize this makes the game look very bad, it isn’t. It just isn’t what it attempts to sell itself as.
Those issues, however, doesn’t affect the PC game. The rules, which aren’t really that good for a P&P game, work really well on the PC, and the setting translated very well for the electronic media. I was actually quite impressed.
- The theme and mood: as stated above, the setting clicked very well with the engine used, and it oozes with character. In this one regard the game succeeds greatly in doing its stated purpose of being a rebirth of Planescape: Torment, with interesting scenarios and exotic NPCs.
- The plot: although only the beta has been released so far, and only for backers like me, it was easy to see that the story is well written and woven in the game itself.
And now, sadly, we move to the bad:
- Your companions: in a nutshell, many of them are bland at best, and tremendously annoying at worst. While I did like some of those, the game starts poorly, by not letting you have both the real interesting ones, which are clearly the most relevant to the story, with you at the same time. I can only hope that this changes as the story progresses, but I am not optimistic about it. The glowing Glaive (that is a warrior, for the not overly pretentious RPG players) is one of the most annoying NPCs I ever had the displeasure of having on a party, and that includes James Vega! Which brings us to two related issues…
- No romance: for some insane reasons, Numenera forbids you from having romance options. While this stance is forgivable on games such as Tyranny, where every NPC either hates you or is terrified of your very shadow, or Pillars, which basically had only the most superficial interaction with your companions – to name recent examples – Numenera, in theory at least, is a game about your interactions and relationships. And now the game intends to tell you that, in a game about interpersonal relationships, there can be no romance?
This is probably the (second) worse sin this game committed, and the one that made me want to ask for my Kickstarter money back, if that were possible. Let me be clear: I am not talking about sex scenes. I believe we all had more than enough claynimation sex scenes with Mass Effect and Dragon Age. However, the lack of romance in a game about RPing is not only prudish and a little schizophrenic, but a real offense to the sensibilities of any reasonable human being, who knows that, in a tightly knit-group of people working a living together, romance is almost certain to bloom. This was the main deal breaker for me personally, and it wasn’t even the worst problem with the game. That would be…
-Misrepresentation: one could call it more simply, lies. As I said, one of the main issues with the game are the either annoying, irrelevant or simply uninteresting companions that can join you in the game. That might have not been a problem if only there were more of them. Sadly, in a one-sided decision by inXile, they decided to cut one third of the possible companions in the game, and two of the most interesting ones at that!
Added to that, many features were cut, such as crafting. And to put the cherry on top, the company was “unable” to inform the players about said changes, only doing so a few weeks before release.
Unfortunately, despite the game’s no irrelevant qualities, I find myself unable to recommend it to other players.

I finished the first act in the current beta and I wanted to share my thoughts with the community. Now I am a long time favorite of games like Baldurs Gate and Icewind Dale + pretty much all other RPG's, but I never played Planescape Torment - unfortunately, so I was excited to try this alleged successor to what many claim to be the best RPG of all time.
First of, this game is different in the sense that it is a true rpg - meaning that you can actually avoid combat pretty much all together through diplomacy, threats and deception. Now to some, I imagine that might feel boring, but to me its really a treat to be entertained in an old-school kind of way. It feels like you are living in an excellent book, where your choices matter. Its also sci-fi fantasy, so don't expect to find much in terms of familiarity in neither the world itself or its inhabitants. Sure there are a few kinks here and there - but nothing gamebreaking, however the lack of character customization seems disappointing.
I would recommend this game to people who enjoyed a game like Pillars of Eternity for its writing - not the combat. You absolutely have to enjoy lots and lots of complex reading, so if you are a 'big words hurt my brain' kind of person, then you will probably not like this game at all. There are no fancy coup de grace killcam animations and the actual combat feels underwhelming, but I like to think of it this way; I may find the♥♥♥♥♥of a baboon ugly, but I still like to watch it sway in the brisk wind ...

I'd like to remind everybody that this game came out the same year as Knights of the Old Republic and even attempted some of the gameplay elements from the Old Republic, however it should also be known that this game fails terribly on every aspect. To iterate my point:
The level designs aren't awful, although sometimes the game doesn't exactly make clear what your objective is, so you can be stuck on the same level forever. The game wont give you any hints or anything to look back on to remind you what and where you need to go, so really you'll just have to get used to watching a lot of walkthroughs.
Combat is very important to this game, as pretty much the entire game is based around it. There really isn't a variation in gameplay design except for a few interesting levels, but those levels are too few and far in between. The combat itself is pretty awful. It's supposed to support fast paced battles, but the game processes these battles slowly, so suddenly we get a clash of contrast. Such a fast paced design doesn't support the game's engine or whatever that dictates the games pacing. It almost looks like the entirity of the game is in slow motion.
The characters are really boring and stale and just flat out unlikable. The designers really didn't know how to make these characters interact, which would be fine since the game's mostly focused on combat anyways, but there's one system that is suddenly effected by this.
It was a cool concept/design, and was really the only thing this game had going for it. I am referring to the whole jedi/sith mechanic that was implimented. This system dictated that you were to either be a jedi or a sith depending on the choices you made throughout the game. It was a cool mechanic, but there are almost no stakes whatsoever. There was never an established relationship with the characters, and they don't even mention anything about the powers you develop until a level ends, and that's it. Now I want to look at Knights of the Old Republic. They implimented the same system, but there were stakes to it. There were actual characters in the game, and they were very likable throughout the game, and they usually reacted right then and there in the game. Whenever you made a desicion that dictated you to lean more towards the sith, they would get legitimately frightened. That was cool. In this game, whenever someone mentions it, it's more like your math teacher's just telling you to "do better on your quizes". Reminder that this is a main mechanic in the game. When the player feels no remorse for the main mechanic and realizes there's no depth to said mechanic, really it kind of renders the whole mechanic useless.
This whole game is really just a waste of money. Don't buy it, you won't get anything in return except for an empty wallet.

As a seasoned player of this game, I would recommend it as a 7/10, but it is definitely not without flaws. I'll list the pros, cons and debatable features from my experience so you can decide if you think you'll enjoy it as much as I did!
Pros
- 4 Player splitscreen, a rarity on PC. I spent most of my time playing this mode.
- Simple and yet brilliantly original car damage/pit stop system
- Good variety of tracks with different routes
- Car class system lets you pick the speed you want to race at
- Plenty of unlockable car liveries
- Each racing class has a car that is strongest at something different (one for handling, one top speed etc.)
- 8 cars on track is refreshing as lots of arcade racers only have 4
Cons
- Computer controlled cars rely on "rubber banding" (If they drop too far behind they will go irrationally fast to catch you, but the same works in your favour if you fall behind)
- Compatability issues, there is no guarantee this game will work on your system, I have encountered problems with it myself
- The single player is a quite short, and once completed time trials, single races and split screen are the only other things to do
- No online multiplayer, one of the game's biggest disappointments
- No Steam workshop or modding facilities, creating your own liveries and tracks would extend the life of this game significantly
- The price is a little over the top for me, for such an inflexible game
Other features
- No Mario Kart copying pickups/powerups, one of the biggest pros of the game for me!
- Shortcuts on tracks which you'll do well to remember the positions of, but other cars will frequently utilize
- Time delayed explosive barrels, and oil barrels can be used for your benefit or doom
10/10 Would Bang Bang.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I was initially really put off by the insane hype surrounding what looked like an incredibly average game, especially when the hipster sjw crowd latched onto it. No joke, I have had people who haven’t even played the game rave on about how it’s the best thing ever. Seriously, the way some people talk about this game you'd think it solved world hunger or brought peace to the Middle East. Curiosity always gets me in the end though, and I picked it one sale, half hoping that this would be overhyped hipster trash and half hoping it was as good as the fanboy/girls said.  . and you know what?  Its a pretty good wee game.  Not great, and definitely not, in my eyes, able to justify the quasi-religious level of hype that surrounds it, but not a bad game for sure.  I actually found it to be a very enjoyable if wonky and inconsistent game.
There’s quite a bit to like about Undertale.  The music and the sound effects especially are incredible, and I appreciate that the game rewards you for being kind and doesn't force you and if anything encourages you not to hurt other characters as the best dialogue is usually what follows the non-violent option (Hear that Bethesda? You can have a nice rpg without having to murder everythng with a face).  When the humour is done well, it can be quite funny (although sometimes it is barf inducingly cringeworthy), and overall the story is enjoyable and resonates well on an emotional level.  It might be alittle to SJW in its themes of prejudice and ignorance, but the game has a nice message and I appreciate that.
However, there’s a few things that really irked me.  The graphics are downright bad.  Yeah, read it and weep fanboys and fangirls.  I understand not every indie game can be Hyper Light Drifter, but I find Undertale to be ugly – lo res can be beautiful (Sword and Sworcery? Fez?) if done with a touch of artistry, but Undertale just looks lazy and sloppy.  And this is coming from someone who remembers playing a commodore 64 on a black n white tv in the 80s.  I thought the combat system was a bit  hit and miss.  Sure, it can be  fun and rewarding figuring out how to pacify an enemy for the first time, but when you’re fighting Froggit or Aaron for the 6th time?  eesh.  Also, I found the game gets really tedious in some places, like in certain parts where you are interrupted every 2 seconds with some stupid interaction from a certain NPC.  Can’t you just let that sh*t play and the background and let me keep walking?  Really freakin tedious
So, overall, I’ll admit I went into this kinda wanting to hate it, and I came away kinda liking it, with the high points being the story and the music. Oh the musi is amazing, and can stand toe to toe with great snes scores like Secret of Mana or Chrono Trigger.  But let me reiterate that, in my opinion, while the game is good, it has more than a few flaws and some very grating and annoying parts to it. I would recommend Undertale on sale, for while it’s not quite a case of the empower's new clothes, it’s not the messiah the worshipers of the church of Undertale make it out to be.

Naysayers abound for this game and I have no idea why!  This game by far made me feel like Batman than the other two by a wide margin.  Batman in a prison and Batman in a bigger prison  is neat but actually going through Gotham City and interacting with police on the streets was a much awaited experience.  Whoever said the boss battles in Origins are dull must love generic, because in my opinion on Arkham Asylum and Arkham City boss battles was lackluster at best.  The only boss battle I enjoyed at any length was the Mr. Freeze battle where you had to use your wits to defeat him.  In Origins almost every boss battle was clearly thought out and AMAZING (Especially Deadpool).  The weather effects and the music are fantastic.  Some people have said they added snow to hide the draw distance, but I think it looks impressive regardless (Especially if you have a good PC)  Some people have also said the story was nonsensical.  I'm not sure what aspects of the story are so nonsensical but I enjoyed it greatly.  Yes, you meet Joker yet again, but the depth of the characters is really on full display here.
Now the negatives:
-The Riddler ending - DO NOT WASTE YOUR TIME!  Look it up on You tube and I promise you won't want to see the ending either.  They should have given him a lesser role if they wanted to have that ending. (Aka, not wasting a couple of hours going to every crevice of the city.)
-The bridge.  Even with the quick travel system that bridge was exhausting to go through.  And you WILL go back and forth.
-The city is alive only when you have events do to. I think this is mostly on the fact of the dev being handed this instead of having two games prior to work within their own merits (small grace, if they do another Arkham this aspect won't be so forgiving)
-Upgrades.  They are boring.  Plain and simple boring.  The fact they are connected to different systems in the game is more frustrating than anything else.  I don't know why they chose to go in this direction but it's frustrating.
-Audio tapes.  Why can't they take notes from System Shock, Deadspace, and a litany of other games where you can listen WHILE you play.  They might be great tapes but I wouldn't know, sitting on a single non-moving screen seeing the tape play is just plain boring.  No transcripts, either.
That being said, I think it's the best of the three.  I hope they fix the problems and really make the next Batman (hopefully give them a couple years to get it perfect, don't annualize it!) what it deserves to be.

Buried - This map, with the paralyzer, the ray gun mark 2, and leeroy, is too easy. Camping is the only strategy on this map. Overall it is pretty boring, and usually i dont go down, i just get bored. BTW the three maps above I do not have on PC, but on Xbox 360.
Origins - Have you ever wanted an old school zombies maps with plenty to do, enough space to do it, the original characters, and 8 wonder weapons? Then this is the map for you. With a map size rivaling that of tranzit (not really, but its big) there is plenty of room for all of the things that this map touts. 6 generators need to be powered, the first is quick revive, second is nothing (except the box and wunderfizz), third is speed cola, fourth is juggernog, fifth is staminup, and the sixth, once powered, gives you a part for... The fire staff
*Fire Staff - Easily the best non-upgraded staff, the staff of fire has a "magazine" size of 9 rounds. It shoots out a burst of 3 fireballs for each shot. Once upgraded, it has 12 shots in each clip, and can be charged to shoot 6 shots at once. The staff is now more powerful on the normal shot, and is great with the charged shot. It shoots 3 bullets in sequence. Each creates a torrent of flames on the ground that eats up any zombie that passes. All in all, it is a great staff.
*Wind Staff - The closest thing we have to another thundergun, the staff of wind shoots out a burst of air that is a 1 hit kill until round 14, i believe. When upgraded, it's power is increased, and when charged, it creates a whirlwind that sucks in all zombies near.
*Lightning Staff - The staff with the most overall ammo, the staff of lightning is the worst non-upgraded staff. I have not built this staff, so i will leave it at that.
*Ice Staff - Easily the best upgraded staff, the staff of ice reks scrubs every time you shoot it. A one hit until round 15, give or take, non upgraded, this thing packs a punch. Once upgraded, and this is the easiest to upgrade, it is the holy grail of staffs. It shoots out a blizzard of snow when half charged, and a longer one when full charged. It sucks in nearby zombies, similar to the wind staff's charge, but more powerful, and longer lasting.
*Panzer Soldat - The boss of this map, the panzer soldat is a powerhouse. Cloaked in armor that can only be penetrated at the face, it is a monstrous force to deal with. The staffs make short work of him, but it takes forever to kill him with a normal gun, like the MP40 or STG-44.

The multiplayer is a lot of fun though. It borrows a lot of the movements from the predecessor Jedi Outcast, but adds the new lightsaber customization, so that not everyone has the same lightsaber. I'm going to keep this short and simple (yeah right, who am I kidding?).
Pros
------
- The lightsaber combat is the best out of any Star Wars game I've ever played. You can use single at first, then choose between continuing with single saber or going with two sabers or a dualsaber.
- You get to choose between Human Male/Female, Twi'lek Female, Rodian Male, and the odd Kel Dor race. Presumably male. Nice variety.
- You can mod the game. Get some skins or a nice multiplayer mod (I'll get to that in a minute).
- Varied and enjoyable missions.
Cons
------
- Although the lightsaber combat is fantastic, I'm still not sure I know what I'm doing. I just sort vary up my directional attacks (move in one direction and attack a certain way, move in another and you'll attack in a different way). If all else fails, I use the dark side Rage power or Speed to get an advantage.
- Single voice actor. Per gender (at least I hope so, I haven't played females, yet). This is fine when you're human.. or maybe even Kel Dor... but it can be a little odd to hear a Rodian talk so... non-Rodian.
- Slightly confusing progression in missions. It's not too bad, but without a walkthrough, you'll get stumped a few times. Only advice I can give is to take things slowly if you get stuck. Like when you have a certain AI member with you who just so happens to be the person who opens a locked door if you wait long enough.
==========
All of my cons are relatively minor. I don't mind opening a walkthrough if I get stuck at most like... three times. It's a quick search to see where you need to go or what you need to do. It's just that the pacing gets slowed down if you haven't played the game at least once before. I really can't stress how small that complaint is for me, though. If you're easily swayed by criticism, like I tend to be (sometimes), then I can easily say that you should ignore my cons and focus entirely on the pros.
Speaking of the pros (and this is a biggie), there is an excellent mod that could really use more players. It's called "Movie Battles II" and it's a multiplayer mod that lets you play through scenario missions against another team of players. You choose your class, your skin, then set your abilities. It takes a good fifteen minutes to set your controls and get comfortable, but trust me... when you get used to it, you'll have a lot of fun.
Just don't get frustrated if you get your butt kicked. The mod is about 11 years old. Some of those players have had a lot of practice. It's that good.
Oh and just full disclosure (though it's unnecessary, I feel), I was gifted this game for free by a kindly redditor. I would have gladly paid for it, myself, if I had the cash. It's a terrific game.
Thank you, Voicy.

Don't believe the positive reviews. This game is garbage. The number one reason? The driving controls are the worst I've ever experienced. That's not input lag you're noticing, it's actually how the game was designed. If you're driving and nick even the tiniest jut from a wall, your car will spin around and come to a complete stop. Conversely, all of your enemies have perfect driving ability. Five cars will attack you at the same time, causing a stalemate where you just circle one car trying to hit it while the others take pot shots at you. If you somehow manage to bring one of them down in health, it'll inexplicably gain incredible speed when driving away, robbing you of the 6 scrap and any satisfaction that you could have gotten if it had been destroyed.
You play a whiny version of Max who reliably refuses to do anything anyone asks him to until they ask him a second time. His best friend, Chumbucket, worships Max like a god despite the fact that Max has no good ideas and treats him like a dog. Also he sounds like a muppet. You'll spend much of the game sliding around (yes, I mean sliding) on foot, accidentally overshooting things that you want to pick up. Then you'll hold down the button to pick it up, only to learn that you weren't quite in the exact position the game wanted you to be in, or you started the whole button press process too early, before the game was ready.
I think the positive reviews are from people who paid bottom dollar for this bargain bin title and were surprised to find that the graphics were good. They probably put the game down after 5 or 6 hours of play. They are the smart ones. I actually tried to play through the game and found that it's repetitive, tedious and frustrating. Don't believe the hype.
