I too was hyped for it. Waited for the release, played it on day one streaming it and all that good stuff. The game started and I was hit with that sweet sweet nostalgia from everything. The characters voices, the music, the design of the world. Everything screamed Banjo to me. Welcome back to the N64 collectathon days old friend! Entering the Hub world of Hivory Towers and getting the first pagie. Satisfying. I jumped all over and got to mess around til my hearts content. Happy as could be. I found the first world. Tribalstack Tropics and again all the love in the world. So much to collect and explore and all that good stuff. Expanding the world was a weird idea. But it worked nicely for the game and made the world not too overwhelming at first.
Sadly the game hits you with the best world first. The second level is massive. Confusing and just feels empty alot of the time and i feel like its something that just gets worse and worse as the game goes on it ends up feeling like an huge world with very little in it in areas. I think that this was something you could solve easily with some more collectables. They added the energy bar to remove the management of all the extra ideas, but think about how much more things could be spread about if they had moves require certain things. Scales or something like that to fluff up areas. If the life powerups were split into pieces in a world. They could inspire so much more exploration. I felt actually punished for exploring alot of the time. Would find hidden areas only to get in and find nothing in them. No ghost writers, quill, pagies, energy bar, nothing.
The controls are really nice for the most part besides the rolling ball. Sometimes it felt impossible to control the balls at some points which could be really annoying for percision parts. The flying was also god aweful. It amazes me that Banjo-Kazooie had better flight controls somehow when it was made so long ago. But other then those the controls are fine and feel okay.
Ability wise was good. I felt like I was getting new ones frequently and they were spaced out nicely. They all felt alot more used all over then Banjo Tooie for sure. However...every move almost draws from the energy bar which I honestly dont know why its a thing. Even the rolling which is your main source of movement around the massive worlds. You can upgrade it by collecting energy upgrades but it never feels like enough honestly.
The characters of this game are great. There are some lacking ones but the main group is amazing. Trowzer is the best idea for a game I have seen in years. Capital B is a wonderful idea for a villain and Dr.Quack was a great sidekick for him. Yooka and Laylee fit in wonderfully with the style of characters from the N64 era. All around I love the characters and how they were designed.
I do have one massive issue and its this games biggest crime for me if anything else. It lacks polish. I had enemies spawning in trees. Trapped in walls. The game does not freeze during animations meaning when your losing air under water. You cannot move. I nearly died because of a unskippable scene of a key opening something underwater. Honestly even banjo knew to do this. Also during the final boss fight I died while learning the patterns. I entered the room after to try and during the talk between Capital B and Yooka I took damage entering the room from the previous fight. Then Rextros games contain two pagies each. One for beating it and a second for beating a high score. But if you beat the high score on the first try you still need to replay the game. Some of which are stupidly long. If this was the first month of release fine, but its been 4 months already. These are obvious issues to me.
So overall i give the game a 7/10 it has alot of great ideas and potential but really just falls flat in alot of places. But when I stop thinking of it as a new Banjo kind of game I love the game itself but I have issues with it.

Max Payne is a game without a lot of the "advancements" made in the 3rd person shooter genre. The game features open yet often small levels, with very little cover or areas to hide behind. The game will often kill you suddenly and without warning, with enemies showing up out of nowhere and many blind entrances through doors walking you right into death with enemies already pointing guns at the door. And there is little to no checkpointing, with the player having to make their own with quicksaves, which they'll definitely need because as I mentioned the game will kill you suddenly and without mercy regularly.
The gameplay consists of utilizing the bullet time and dodge mechanics to outmanuver bullets, shoot more precisely and deal more damage in a short period of time to kill enemies before they kill you. The game has no cover mechanics and attempting to pick off enemies from behind cover rarely works. If you stand still in a fight, you will likely die. You must abuse horizontal movement and bullet time to your advantage to keep the enemy from getting a bead on you, because shots are often lethal.
During my first playthrough, I was frequently frustrated by the game. When I reconsidered the trial and error battles as puzzles I enjoyed myself much more. Every abrupt and sudden death which was previously unfair suddenly became elaborate puzzles I had to solve using bullet time and focus firing priority targets. By the time I reached the end of the game I realized some techniques relating to the bullet time mechanic I could use to play more efficiently and immediately played it again on the next difficulty. The second playthrough was even more fun as things were more challenging but I felt like I had only just grasped the bullet time mechanics and was making full use of it at last. When I had finished the second run I was contemplating what I could do to play better for the next difficulty. Very few games new or old compel me to do that, and it was that hard "unfairness" that made me want to come back.
The game's plot is enjoyably campy. It's the kind of sincere corniness that games had before they tried too hard at being quirky and random. It's enjoyable and skippable which makes it easier to replay the game without playing through interactive cutscenes.
Buy Max Payne if you like arcade-like 3rd person action games and trial and error difficulty.

Though it is an unneeded game in the franchise and many will be put off by its visual departure and lack of inventiveness, it is still a good game.
Pros
-Visually great! I personally like Batman's younger less blocky look. I was always a bit put off with how derpy Bruce looked in the past games. So this was a welcome change in my book.
-Atmosphere. Arkham City made me feel cold while i was playing it. It gave me the sensation that i was snug and cozy in my batsuit while all the unlucky thugs were miserabley cold. Arkham Origins makes me feel that if it wasn't for my batsuite I would be suffering from hypothermia. The added christmas vibe gives this the best apmosphere in all of the games in my opinion.
-Story. I have to confess I haven't beat the story yet but I honestly don't see it being any better or worse than the previous titles. It is a perfect excuse to suit up as Bats and beat up on a portion of the Rogue's gallery. Will update this after I have completed it.
Cons
-Multiplayer. A very creative idea and when a match gets going (after waiting anywhere from 5-20 minutes) it CAN be alot of fun. But like many mp games these days it was an after thought and this game is very evident. It's nice to see a different mp idea surface but it needed more time to stew.
-Tech. Once again we have an Arkham PC release with poorly used DX11 and Physx tech in it. I found, like Arkham City, when gliding around Gotham and DX11 is enabled the game starts spurting and stuttering so much that it pulled me out of the experience. Thankfully you can disable dx11 features to make the game a much smoother experience. Though still not 100% free of the stutter (thank you unreal engine). I disabled mine from the ini file which seemed to do a better job than simply disabling it from the in game options. And honstely, you're not missing much with these features turned off. If you are a gamer, like me, who prefers fluidity over graphical fidelity then do yourself a favor and TURN DX11 OFF.
-COD syndrome. No advancement. Nothing new to see here other than story and some new visuals. If you are expecting a change like we saw in Arkham Asylimg to Arkham City then you will be dissapointed. However don't let that stop you from enjoying a game that is still really good despite it not stepping outside of the box a bit. Here's to hoping the next game doesn't follow suit.
Despite some bumps and bruises throughout this game it is still a fantastic title. Especially to Bat fans and those who are jonesing for a bit more Arkham in their gaming library. Give it a whirl!

Thought I'd write a review for this game but, the hours I have invested in it speak for me in all honesty.  This game is the epitome of my STAR WARS wet dreams.  Custom Jedi, Lightsabers, The Force, and Stormtrooper dismemberment; what more could you ask for?  The story campaign is really good and provides a good time for everyone.  Luke Skywalker is voiced by Mark Hamill and John Williams' original STAR WARS score plays throughout the entire game.  The fanservice levels in this game are just literally off the charts!  However, where this game really shines, in my opinion, is the mods.  This game becomes ten times better once you start sinking mods into it.  The moding for this game is super easy and definitely add to the experience once you've done all you can with the vanilla game.  The mod that gave me over 400 hours by itself was the MOVIE BATTLES II multiplayer conversion mod.  I personally believe the MOVIE BATTLES II mod is the best possible mod to get for this game as it is regularly updated and transforms the battle mechanics of the game completely to make it feel like a more realistic STAR WARS experience.  And that is just one of the thousands of mods for this game floating around the internet.
So in short, game by itself is great.  The Story is ok and the STAR WARS fanservice is seemingly endless.  Game with mods is fantastic, tons of mods that add the experience in many different ways.  Highly recommend this game for any person who has ever wanted to swing a lightsaber.

This game is probably one of the sweetest I've had the pleasure of partaking in. The dialogue is as snappy as it is relatable, especially between the player character and his daughter, and it makes all the characters so incredibly natural-sounding. Another thing I enjoy about the game is that not all of the good endings are magical end-all be-all fixes for these characters. Sometimes things take time, sometimes life doesn't always let things pan out, and while potentially disappointing, it's more encouraging to see positive impacts take root in a more realistic way than the traditional "love heals all wounds" mantra dating sims tend to adhere to, especially with older characters with their own lives built up around them.
It's obviously a simple indie game worked on by a small studio, it isn't perfect, it's short, and it's got its programming quirks, but in my opinion this is far outshined by the love that was poured into the writing. So if you're here for the story, the dad jokes, and Paranormal Long Haul Ice Road Truckers, I wholeheartedly recommend picking it up.

Honestly, I'm a bit disappointed. This game doesn't really fit what I would normally see or hope to expect in dating sims, and I don't think it's because my standard is too high.
While I appreciate the game trying to be a bit more 'real', I honestly didn't expect a game called //Dream// Daddy to be so somber. Without spoiling too much, two out of the seven dads in the game you don't get a 'happy ending' with in the traditional sense. You don't get your happily ever after. While one ending can be considered 'bittersweet' and mature, I don't really need that kind of adult right-thing-to-do kind of thing in a romance game. I want them to be adorably in love and have love magically and unrealistically fixes everything in the universe dammit!
The other ending is just... weird. I think we all know who we're talking about. What is the point of a dating sim with a dude that you can't be together with? Like... he's just there to be a disappointment and a bad decision. There's no happy ending. What's the point? Why do you even play? Isn't there enough disappointment and bitterness in the real world?
After those two routes, the other storyline felt thin – like, it's cute, but the story definitely needs work. The dialogues are funny, I'll give you that, and the art is GREAT (I really like the dad builder, that was cool). The story though, I'll give it a 3/10.
The characterization is fine, I like the player character and his daughter plenty, but the daddies on the other hand somehow fell into really weird stereotypes? Some of them (cough like 3 out of 7 at least that's 40%) are downright NOT likable or unfriendly unless you're on their route, and I found myself not looking forward to doing all the routes.
Given that you can fast forward through everything, I think it would take you 24 hours tops to get all the endings and after that it's kinda boring fast :T

There's something about Garfield Kart... something one cannot ignore or forget. Indeed the community has been vocal about this particular title, putting John Lennon's immortal words of being bigger than Jesus to shame. Sorry John, Garfield Kart now ranks above the lord. But just to put it back on solid ground: it is just a game with just a little out of hand fan base. Still an unforgettable experience mind you.
I will not go into much detail about what makes Garfield Kart... Garfield Kart, but a summation would boil it down to fantastic 8bit music, quirky lovable characters and the range of emotions it is capable of invoking in you. Gameplay consists of linear exploration of a 2D top down world, interacting with characters and battling it out (or not) in short bullet hell combat sequences. Writing is comedic most of the time, drawing influence from internet culture, but can be serious or more relaxed when there is call for it. The excellent background music fits each character interaction well and tonality of the situation and the character can be sensed from the music alone. Even before a new character says anything, the music playing will tell you their intentions. Visually the game may feel a little behind at times but you will be moving through the world at a steady pace, nothing will feel repetitive. The great thing about Garfield Kart is that every interaction feels unique. You move to new locations with different climates portrayed in with different colors, meeting different characters with different traits, battling different ways and doing different things all while listening to different music. It doesn't get old. An impressive feat for an one man developer to achieve.
I'd recommend this game to anyone with just a little bit of an open mind. The music is great and you can expect internet culture referenced humor with a bit of an anime flair to it. Combat optional but bullet hell based. I did only one playthrough in six hours but apparently the more you do, the more you will love the game. I'd say ignore the fandom and judge the game for what it is. A high quality experience at an affordable price. And yes, expect the soundtrack to be making top ten lists for a while.

I'm recommending this game, but with a strong caveat: if you did play Banjo-Kazooie, or are unfamiliar with late 90s game design, this may not be the game for you.
Yooka-Laylee manages to appear as charming as Banjo-Kazooie, but unfortunately it falls short in so many areas that the two BK games shined. Perhaps most glaringly, the later levels are designed as a bunch of branching paths with one or two things to do down each, instead of having a cohesive level to roam around in. The first level pulls this feel off in spades, but every level afterwards feels less and less inspired. I've heard other people say this, but it feels like Banjo 0.5 more than anything.
Now this doesn't sound like a glowing reccomendation. BUT if you are into this genre or were an absoute fan of Banjo-Kazooie, you will enjoy this game most likely. As I said before tho, if you are unfamiliar with the era of gaming Yooka is refrencing, I'm not sure you will get a ton out of it. I'm in my mid 20's and loved both BK games to death, so I'm in the camp who got something out of this. However, I haven't even fought the final boss yet, and I haven't gone back to this game in some time, so really think about if you are the type of person who is going to enjoy this game, especially at it's current $40 price point.

I played this via Steam Family Sharing, which is great, because I'd have been pretty upset if I had spent $40 on it. I'd like to recommend it, and there will be people who would like it, but I'm afraid that in general it's not something I can recommend. Your mileage may vary.
Essentially what it comes down to is this: Yooka-Laylee has touted itself as being a spiritual successor to games like Donkey Kong 64 or Banjo-Kazooie. And it is. However, "spiritual successor" also carries certain connotations. This is not a "modern" take on the genre. It is not an "updated" game. Aside from graphically, it does not improve on the original formula in any way, which is the only thing that I would ever ask for from a sequel.
And you have to call it a sequel, because it leans just so hard on "Hey, remember Banjo-Kazooie?" There isn't enough original game here for it to stand on its own. Thats fine, I don't mind that - Banjo-Kazooie is a great game, and it's worth trying to emulate it and make a sequel for it. But the problem here is that this game isn't... fun. It's like it was made by people who have been in a bubble since the mid 90s.
20 years ago in gaming we had to accept things like twitchy controls and bad cameras. There were technological limitations and a lot of games faced those challenges. Not just Banjo-Kazooie or Donkey Kong 64, but games like Mario 64 or Spyro or the Resident Evil games. Great games, despite the limitations.
So why would you intentionally implement those same limitations now? It feels like a self-imposed handicap in the name of nostalgia - trying so hard to just make a carbon copy of a game from the late 90's. What I would have liked is something that gave me the FEELING of playing one of those games, without all the frustrations. A more pure experience. Instead, this feels like I have an emulator open and am playing a literal N64 game.
Basically, there's no reason for anyone to play this. If you want to play something that feels like the classic games, play them. Boot up your Nintendo 64 and go through Donkey Kong 64 or Banjo-Kazooie. Play something that tried to be ahead of its time, instead of something that's stuck 20 years in the past.

Huge, empty worlds that are gorgeous and exciting to explore for the first time, but are painfully tedious to scour for the last few collectables?
Only 5 worlds and a hub, but they’re all unnecessarily massive?
A bunch of annoying physics puzzles, racing challenges, and timers?
Hidden bonus challenges that make you want to tear your hair out?
Wait a minute, this isn’t Banjo-Kazooie. This is Super Mario Sunshine!
Seriously, Yooka-Laylee makes more sense when you look at it as a successor to Sunshine, a game that got just about as much hate as it got love. Like Sunshine, I feel that Yooka-Laylee simultaneously deserves all the love it gets, but also all the hate it gets. I haven’t felt so perfectly ambivalent over a game in a very long time. I had a lot of fun with this game, hence the thumbs-up, but I can perfectly understand why some people don’t like it. If you had a love/hate relationship with Sunshine, you can probably expect to feel exactly the same about Yooka-Laylee.
For starters, the game makes a good first impression. The worlds look beautiful, the controls feel solid, and the character designs are hilariously awkward, true-to-form Rareware designs. The music is fantastic,
when one of the David Wise tracks comes on. The jibberish speech and the constant barrage of fourth wall-breaking jokes and surprising double entendres often got a chuckle from me (although I have a feeling you’re going to like the jokes exactly as much as you like the game as a whole – the same way that you only really like a person’s jokes if you like that person). I felt that the best part of the game was the magical feeling of diving into a fresh new world full of details and quills and pagie challenges, and spending about an hour jumping on every rock, swimming in every puddle, getting lost and exploring every corner of the world. It was also fun to purchase all the world’s moves as soon as possible to see what they could do. While the game is far from being a Banjo-Kazooie clone, I felt it succeeded in evoking that “bring me the horizon” feel that a collect-a-thon should.
But that initial impression wears off, leaving you with quite a bit of tedium to go through. To be fair, I define a challenge as something that’s unfun to play, but fun to win, and I feel that games have every right to be frustrating, annoying, obtuse, grindy, or intentionally trolling, as long as it feels great to finally win the prize in the end. I don’t feel that games need to value your time at every second of the experience -- sometimes the initiative is supposed to come from the player to play the game, and that's fine.
With that out of the way, I’ll be blunt: there are several points where this game wants to frustrate you on purpose, and it doesn’t apologize for it. At every turn you’ve got unfairly hidden secrets, memorization-based bosses, annoying obstacle courses with tight timers, dead-ends, puzzles that don’t explain themselves, trivia quizzes, and slippery slopes that’ll send you careening into the pit. While this isn’t a Kaizo-style game by any means, it is a very trolling game that doesn’t always value your time. And that’s perfectly fine – as long as you’re in the mood for this kind of game. If you’re the kind of gamer that likes to conquer annoying challenges and laugh in their faces (and I’m not kidding,
in this game has a face), you may just love overcoming this game’s challenges. But if you feel offended that your time is being wasted, you’ll probably hate it. It’s totally subjective, and at several points during play I flip-flopped between the two mindsets repeatedly, so I understand both sides.
As far as complaints go, I suppose the biggest problem I had with the game was how hollow and samey it felt after a while. The worlds are colorful and polished, but after a while I couldn’t shake the feeling that they were just Unity sandboxes. Very detailed and pretty sandboxes, granted, but they sorely lack a dynamic feel; it doesn’t feel like your progress is doing anything besides making quills and pagies disappear from the map.
Every world checks off a few boxes: One boss, 5 ghostwriters, 200 quills, one arcade machine, one minecart ride, one pagie requiring you to find several characters who are standing around, one pagie requiring you to take a grand tour of the world through Superman 64-style rings, at least one
race through Superman 64-style rings, one or two pagies you can only get using a transformation, a few pagies requiring you to climb to the top of something, a few pagies requiring you to hit buttons, usually on a time limit, a few pagies that require you to find and use a nearby berry bush or edible object… and honestly, little else. There are only about 5 types of enemies in the game, too. This game could have done with a
dose of more variety. A
dose. But I get the feeling that a lot of planned content was cut to get the game released faster, so I guess I’ll just save my hopes for a sequel.
Subjective complaints aside, I have a few mechanical criticisms with the game:
* While I didn’t mind the difficulty of the game’s boss fights, they give almost zero tactile feedback when they take damage, so it’s hard to tell if you’re even doing damage or progressing the fight. They really need that Zelda-esque red flashing effect.
* There are some areas of the game that force a fixed camera. If you fly into these areas, steering accurately becomes almost impossible. They added a free camera option in the latest patch, but then you have to completely control every aspect of the camera at all times, and that’s a bit more trouble than it’s worth. Personally I think they should have just disabled the fixed camera if you're flying.
* In a lot of places, the clipping needs some serious work. Like in that one room in world 5 where you have to fix the pipes – they didn’t even
.
* The FOV is a bit too high. I’m guessing they did this to make the far-off distances look a bit farther away, adding to the illusion that the worlds are huge, but the ever-so-slight tunnel vision distortion makes it hard to judge distances when platforming.
* The flight power. Is it fun? Hell yes, but it also renders all the other powers obsolete, except those required by specific Metroidvania-style barriers. It also lets you cheese almost all of the platforming puzzles, which honestly felt like cheating, especially in parts like the Rampo boss or the dark cave in world 2. If you beat the challenges before getting flight, you feel like a fool, and if you beat them after getting flight, you feel like you cheated. There’s no even medium that feels satisfying.
Overall, while it’s not a good Banjo-Kazooie successor, I can’t deny that it managed to capture
of its magic (and some of Super Mario Sunshine’s magic, for that matter). I enjoyed taking in the aesthetics of the wide polished worlds, and I enjoyed the satisfaction of conquering the game’s stupid challenges, of getting trolled and trolling the game back. I personally had a 7 / 10 experience, but don’t take my word for it – this is a polarizing game, you may really like it or really hate it, but definitely try it out if you're hungering for a Nintendo-styled collect-a-thon and form your own opinion. While I’m personally not eager to play the game again anytime soon, I’m definitely looking forward to a bigger, more varied sequel if one might ever be feasible.
(Achievement hunters can expect to get 100% in as little as 15 hours, or as much as 40, depending on how much you want to use a guide. Most everything in this game is fundamentally easy, the problems are knowing where to find stuff and knowing which power to use.)

It´s not a bad game, but it is worse than Banjo Kazooie in almost every aspect besides graphics and I say this without being blinded by nostalgy.
Remember the Banjo Kazooie levels? Mumbo´s Mountain? Clanker´s Cavern? Freezeety Peak? You always had a central element (mountain, clanker, giant snowman) which eased navigation in those worlds. The levels in Banjo Tooie were bigger, but at least you had a teleport. In Yooka-Laylee you have no teleport and each world consists of clumped together areas which makes navigation very hard, since you don´t have a central point for orientation.
Gruntildas lair was such an awesome hub where every area was different. Hiwory Tower, the hub in Yooka-Laylee, feels always like the same boring factory hallway. Just like the worlds it is so unremarkable that I lost count how many times I got lost, because everything looks the same.
Quills, which are the notes in this games, are spread and hidden in the worlds rather than working as breadcumbs to lead you to interesting places. Have fun wasting your time to find the last two or three quills in every world after you got every other collectible.
Except for maybe Trowzer (Bottles replacement) most of the minor characters are pretty lame and boring.
Copying Banjos and Kazooies characters for Yooka-Laylee (Banjo/Yooka being chill and Kazooie/Laylee being cheeky) was also not the best idea since it always remind you of the original characters and those more meaningful dialogues.
Remember the awesome quiz at the end of the Banjo Games? It´s pain in this game, because
a) you have to do it 3 times before getting to the next world and
b) it´s asking you questions like "How many Quills do you have at this exact moment?" or "How many hours did you play this game yet?" which you can only answer if you looked those informations in the menu up a minute before the quiz.
I wish I could at least have the hope, that my invested money makes sure, that playtonic games can now start to pump out more rare-like games. But seeing, how devs which once upon a time developed Banjo Kazooie and now made such bad design choices like in Yooka-Laylee I don´t have much hope.
Don´t even buy it on sale, just play Banjo Kazooie one more time, unless you really really want to play another collectathon even if it´s worse than the original.

Unlike the "Force Unleashed" title recently released, Jedi Academy allows for players to customize a set of tactical and strategic force powers that define your own personal play style and greatly affect your combat experience.
Though not nearly as cinematic of an experience as modern action games (the graphics of the time were far less impressive), the combat of this game is epic in ways that modern games cannot even hope to achieve. Want to run 60 feet along a wall, swipe a stormtroopers head off as you go, backflip into the center of ten troopers, send them flying, rip their guns out of their hands, leap 20 feet in the air, bounce off of a wall, roll backwards and jam your lightsaber into a dark jedi's guts? You can do that.

Today I jumped into the Early Access build for the first time to see how it plays and get some impressions of the early parts.
First off, Torment: Tides of Numenera does not mess around with its richness in text. There's tons and tons of descriptions about the environments, dialogues offer at least 5 or 6 possible branches to go into and there are very few generic NPCs that give you a single line response. Once I'd entered the first real area (the Circus Market) I realized that I shouldn't approach and talk to everybody. It's too much! But in a good way, this led me to be more objective oriented in my play style. I finished one quest, it's about rescuing a guy who's being publicly executed. It was a very interesting premise, there were multiple ways I could've gone about it, and even in the solution I chose, I had different means of progress (do I talk a merchant into selling me an item that's not for me? Do I snatch it when they're not looking? etc).
Torment is a game that delights in the inclusion of skill checks at every opportunity which is fantastic. I do love my skill checks in my RPGs. In conclusion of the quest was satisfying and I grew to like the characters I met. They had personality and there was some notable nuance in the writing.
Overall I had a great first impression. It seems like the full game will be a real monster in terms of replayability if they keep up the standard set by this first quest anyways.

If you are a fan of Planescape: Torment, I highly suggest you pick this up. It is somewhat of a spiritual successor to that game, and it certainly feels just like it. Well worth a purchase in my book :D

Don't believe the positive reviews. This game is garbage. The number one reason? The driving controls are the worst I've ever experienced. That's not input lag you're noticing, it's actually how the game was designed. If you're driving and nick even the tiniest jut from a wall, your car will spin around and come to a complete stop. Conversely, all of your enemies have perfect driving ability. Five cars will attack you at the same time, causing a stalemate where you just circle one car trying to hit it while the others take pot shots at you. If you somehow manage to bring one of them down in health, it'll inexplicably gain incredible speed when driving away, robbing you of the 6 scrap and any satisfaction that you could have gotten if it had been destroyed.
You play a whiny version of Max who reliably refuses to do anything anyone asks him to until they ask him a second time. His best friend, Chumbucket, worships Max like a god despite the fact that Max has no good ideas and treats him like a dog. Also he sounds like a muppet. You'll spend much of the game sliding around (yes, I mean sliding) on foot, accidentally overshooting things that you want to pick up. Then you'll hold down the button to pick it up, only to learn that you weren't quite in the exact position the game wanted you to be in, or you started the whole button press process too early, before the game was ready.
I think the positive reviews are from people who paid bottom dollar for this bargain bin title and were surprised to find that the graphics were good. They probably put the game down after 5 or 6 hours of play. They are the smart ones. I actually tried to play through the game and found that it's repetitive, tedious and frustrating. Don't believe the hype.

Bang Bang Racing is pegged as a top-down “family friendly” racing game. With a similar camera angle and toy-car style as TNT Racers (released earlier this year) you’ll race with four different car classes among three gameplay modes in an attempt to earn the gold trophy in each championship circuit. Bang Bang Racing strips away things like power-ups and weapons in favor of a simple and pure racing game. Unfortunately what’s left is a rather boring racing game with little in the way of any replay value.
Aside from a boost meter that refills over time each track in Bang Bang Racing is littered with traffic cones, exploding barrels, oil slicks and other obstacles to avoid. Most of these usually cause you to slide across a turn as you helplessly watch as everyone else passes you. For the most part these obstacles aren’t difficult to avoid but in the opening moments of each race when you find yourself with very little breathing room it can be a bit too easy to get pushed into an oil slick finding yourself at the back of the pack early on. The racing itself in the game is okay at best. With the exception of the final car class there’s very little sense of speed and the handling on most cars is quite bad. This is made worse with the fact that the default camera in the game has a hard time keeping up with you. Most tracks are composed of numerous twists and turns in which the camera rotates just slow enough so that your view eventually gets blocked and you’re driving towards the screen. Switching to a fixed view camera only makes this issue even worse.
Beyond the game’s terrible rubberbanding, the AI in Bang Bang Racing is just strange. Sometimes they’d drive straight into a wall without even trying to make a turn while in other situations they’d navigate the track perfectly. In other situations I’d get passed by a car only to have it stop in front of me and slide causing my car to get stuck and watch as the rest of the cars passed in the time I fought with the controls to reverse.
Despite these things it’s not uncommon to still have fun playing racing games online with friends. I was pretty surprised when I found that, beyond leaderboards, Bang Bang Racing has no online play at all. You can still play up to four player split-screen but the lack of online is just disappointing.
The only piece of replay value in the game is the numerous skins you can unlock for each car. Unfortunately I never felt like there was much of a difference at all between cars. Despite each car having one specific special feature (better acceleration, boost etc.) I never felt like I was using a different car besides the change in appearance. This alone makes going through and unlocking extra skins seem rather pointless to me.
Bang Bang Racing isn’t a terrible game but it is boring. The handling isn’t as good as it should be and the lack of online seems bizarre. The only two positives are that it’s a nice looking game and it does sport some decent music. To be blunt I’m not sure I would recommend this to anyone at all.

It´s not a bad game, but it is worse than Banjo Kazooie in almost every aspect besides graphics and I say this without being blinded by nostalgy.
Remember the Banjo Kazooie levels? Mumbo´s Mountain? Clanker´s Cavern? Freezeety Peak? You always had a central element (mountain, clanker, giant snowman) which eased navigation in those worlds. The levels in Banjo Tooie were bigger, but at least you had a teleport. In Yooka-Laylee you have no teleport and each world consists of clumped together areas which makes navigation very hard, since you don´t have a central point for orientation.
Gruntildas lair was such an awesome hub where every area was different. Hiwory Tower, the hub in Yooka-Laylee, feels always like the same boring factory hallway. Just like the worlds it is so unremarkable that I lost count how many times I got lost, because everything looks the same.
Quills, which are the notes in this games, are spread and hidden in the worlds rather than working as breadcumbs to lead you to interesting places. Have fun wasting your time to find the last two or three quills in every world after you got every other collectible.
Except for maybe Trowzer (Bottles replacement) most of the minor characters are pretty lame and boring.
Copying Banjos and Kazooies characters for Yooka-Laylee (Banjo/Yooka being chill and Kazooie/Laylee being cheeky) was also not the best idea since it always remind you of the original characters and those more meaningful dialogues.
Remember the awesome quiz at the end of the Banjo Games? It´s pain in this game, because
a) you have to do it 3 times before getting to the next world and
b) it´s asking you questions like "How many Quills do you have at this exact moment?" or "How many hours did you play this game yet?" which you can only answer if you looked those informations in the menu up a minute before the quiz.
I wish I could at least have the hope, that my invested money makes sure, that playtonic games can now start to pump out more rare-like games. But seeing, how devs which once upon a time developed Banjo Kazooie and now made such bad design choices like in Yooka-Laylee I don´t have much hope.
Don´t even buy it on sale, just play Banjo Kazooie one more time, unless you really really want to play another collectathon even if it´s worse than the original.

“With its stellar gameplay and presentation, Euro Truck Simulator 2 set a new standard for the simulation genre.” -
Actually driving a truck with your own business in which you travel around Europe.
Driving games have never really been my thing in the past. The only reason I bought this was because one of my friends was nagging me to buy it. When I first played it, my first hour was literally crashing everywhere trying to adapt to the controls. But the more I played it, the more I loved it. You can own your own buisness and travel around a huge chunk of Europe. Definitely a must buy! Give it a chance, it's worth it.
All of my reviews are laid out in a particular format that fits the game.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is the 2nd game of the Euro Truck franchise. You drive around Europe, completing deliveries and earning money to manage your own company. You can hire drivers to work for you by also completing deliveries around Europe. You can buy your own truck and design it in anyway you choose. Make your dream come true...... but in a video game.
The gameplay is pretty simple if you've played simulation games beforehand. There are different modes for controls so for newcomers it shouldn't be too hard to adapt. Once you're used to handling your truck, it can be pretty relaxing. The game has tons of real-life radio stations for you tune in to. Your truck pretty much has things a real life truck would have, such has headlights, indicators and a horn. It even has steering wheel controller compatibility. There are 8 different camera views, so you can drive your truck at different angles. An almost basic style gameplay (Unless you go for the more advanced modes).
You don't need a super powerful PC to run the graphics at a high level. The developers have done a great job at detailing environments as best as they can. Some locations are beautiful to drive through, where as others are a bit plain and simple. The graphics aren't the best I've seen, but they're good enough to show a beauty element to it. The graphics settings are easy to navigate, should you need to change them.

When looking at some of the screenshots, I can see some people being a bit overwhelmed if they haven't played many simulation games before, but as I said before, you easily adapt. As long as you know the controls, you don't need to worry about all the things you see around your steering wheel. Managing your company can be confusing at first, but the more you play, the more you get used to it.
- Very realistic
- Huge world to explore
- Beautiful environments
- Different driving styles
- Real-life radio stations to listen and relax to. :)
- Some parts of the road make no sense. E.G. Roundabouts.
- Can be confusing for people new to simulator games.
- Some environments can be plain and/or repetitive.
As many people have said, this game is more of an experience. You don't have to like simulators to like this. You don't have to live driving games to like this. If I ever want to play a relaxing game, this would be the game I'd choose most of the time. It provides many hours of enjoyment, with plenty of things to do.
I would definitely give this game a go!
Final Verdict - 9/10.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a game that you will either love or hate. Personally, I love it. I first started playing SCS's trucking games with the 18 Wheels of Steel series. A friend gave me a copy of American Longhaul and it got tossed on the shelf as I thought I would have no interest in it. A few months later I decided to install it and after half an hour of play I was hooked. I then went on to put many hours into all the games in the series.
I received ETS 1 in a bundle one day and set it aside to play at a later date, but I never got around to it. Then one day a friend of mine told me he had bought ETS 2 after playing my copy of ETS 1 through my shared library. He was one guy that I thought would not enjoy a truck driving simulator (in fact he originally ribbed me about playing 18WOS), so I was surprised when he started raving about it. That was enough for me to buy the game and all the DLC.
Once again, I am hooked on a trucking simulator and it is great. ETS 2 is leaps and bounds above all of the previous efforts by SCS, both in terms of visuals and gameplay. There is still the problem of braindead AI drivers, but that is something you will learn to anticipate and it does not become such a problem after a while. The visuals are stunning, you just have to look at some of the screenshots to see how pretty this game is, and the truck models are fantastic. All of the trucks feel different when you drive them and you will soon find your favourites and those that you loathe to drive.
With the addition of mods, especially some of the map mods available, the replay value of the game increases. There is even a multiplayer mod that regularly sees thousands of people on some of the servers. It is quite a sight to see hundreds of people lined up trying to get into Europort.
The game is also linked to the
website which offers external contracts, events, and more. The site is only alpha at the moment, but with the imminent release of
I can see more features being revealed.
As I said this is not a game for everyone, but if you like simulators and you like trucks then you will probably like this. As for whether to purchase or hold of for ATS, I would recommend buying this and then also ATS when it is released.

The platforming itself is solid. I never came across a "that moment" where I felt like I was cheated off a ledge or clipped incorrectly. The controls are responsive and feel like they make Yooka move in exactly the way you want him too. In fact, the platforms can be too precise at times- there are a couple sections early in that let you access areas in ways you weren't intended to by "Skyrimming" up a craggy surface. Granted, this never led to any major sequence breaks, just a few extra quills and the like. Even the swimming controls feel responsive, which is rare even in stellar platformers. The one issue with the platforming is the flight power. Unlike in Banjo Kazooie, where you could only start flying on specific panels, you can engage flight literally anywhere, and keep flying until your stamina runs out. If you play the game in order, this won't really become a problem, as the final level seems designed around it more or less. However, if you rush flying, you can really break a lot of the intended platforming. Is this a flaw in the game design? Yes. But it's easily bypassed if the levels are played sequentially.
The levels themselves are competently designed. Its parent game, Banjo Kazooie, of course had superior level design. Those levels were smaller, but compat, meaning every corner of it had something going on for it. This was a huge downfall of the sequel, Banjo Tooie. Tooie had much larger levels, in fact they're similar in design to Yooka Laylee's large levels. However, where Yooka Laylee actually surpases Tooie is that it has more evens going on. Tooie had 10 jiggies per level, as did the first game, but the overall number of collectables was slashed. This made the levels feel more diluted and empty. Yooka Laylee has 25 pagies per level, and in fact more collectables than Banjo Kazooie. This prevents the levels from feeling vacant like in Banjo Tooie. It's still not perfect, however. They're too large to capture that "perfect size" feel of Banjo Kazooie, but they're still a vast improvement over Tooie's barren levels.
The writing, I will admit, is not as good as Banjo Kazooie's. Yooka Laylee uses much more fourth-wall humor than Banjo Kazooie, so take that into your own personal tastes. Thankfully, the writing never reached cringe-inducing levels. No references to outdated memes, pop-culture, or the like, it relies on puns and a heaping helping of sass from Laylee. The music is pleasant but nothing outstanding. I enjoy every track but I don't ever find myself humming along or nodding my head to the beat like I do with tracks like Click-Clock Wood or Gruntilda's Lair. The graphics are pretty. I enjoy looking at this game, it has great use of color, but of course you can see all that from the Store previews.
All in all, this is a very enjoyable game that I'm driving towards 100% in. The last games to drive me to that level of dedication were Banjo Kazooie and Ori and the Blind Forest. Is Yooka Laylee as good as those games? No. But it is still a great game. In fact, I'd say it even surpases Banjo Tooie. If you're hankering for a solid collectathon, pick it up. If you've been curious about this game, catch it on sale.

Summary: FPS kill and loot to a decent story. Fun. Violent. Harsh language. Eventually gets repetative, but that takes a while.
Lots of shooting action in this RPG/FPS hybrid. The setting has an excuse for respawns (player and enemy), recharging energy shields, weightless backpacks, and always-full magazines, which is a thoughtful touch. The story is just as rich and well constructed as the setting, with some good twists and genuinely appealing characters; that last despite the fact that everyone in the game is a terrible person.
Six categories of guns, billions of possible unique items, and a ton of customization options allow for each character to play differently from each other, even in the same class. Each level provides additional health, a point for the skill trees, and scaling damage resistance to lower level foes.
The action mixes shooting (smooth), exploration (mostly interesting), platforming (a mixed bag), and vehicle operations (opinions vary) fairly well. The environments are large and good looking, the enemies are diverse enough to force weapon swaps mid combat but few enough to master. Challenges result in Badass Ranks which can be used to improve every single character on your account.
DLCs:
Captain Scarlet and Her Pirate's Booty - Neat idea but flat. Scarlet is the only interesting character, the zones are dull, the enemies reskins of existing foes (sand worms = threshers; pirates = marauders), and the new vehicle is slow. The story is boring as well, "What?  There's treasure over there!?  I will have it!" The loot is mostly decent. Introduces the Seraph items and crystals.
Campaign of Carnage - Pretty good, though you need to be level 50 (and fully equipped) to finish all the content. The story is amusing, well paced, and flows naturally. Foes are mostly bandit reskins, but it's not a problem in this context. The supporting cast is excellent, from new faces, such as Mr. Torgue, to returning friends like Mad Moxxi and Tiny Tina. With a few unique items, and more Seraph items, the loot is pretty good.
Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt - This one starts a little slow, and the huge environments can take a while to get through (especially before you ulock the new vehicles). But the environments are gorgeous, the villain is hillarious, and Sir Hammerlock is Sir Hammerlock. The enemies are a mix of returning foes, reskins, and original challenges; the tribal shamans are both exciting and frustrating to figure out.
Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep - A must buy. Brick, Lilith, and Mordecai sit down to a fantasy table-top role playing game run by Tina, staring characters based upon the six playable classes. It is full of references to books, movies, video games, Dungeons and Dragons, television shows, and the relationships of the people at the table. (During this game, the six vault hunters of Borderlands 2 are torturing intelligence out of a captured Hyperion employee.) The foes are interesting and unique, combining elements of previous foes into new and fun variants (orcs, knights, treants, skeletons, etc.), with challenging boss battles. The in-game story is a bit simplistic, but well done; the story that unfolds from overheard table-talk is complex, heart-wrenching, and worth the price of admission. The loot ranges from okay to amazing, with some excellent new resources (I especially like the Chain Lightning grenade) and very cool 'red text' weapons. A brilliant example of DLC done correctly.
Head Hunter Packs:
All consist of two multi-part quests in a single standard-size zone.
Bloody Harvest - TK Baha refuses to stay dead, and needs you to kill a pumpkin monster. Thematic, but I was glad it ended when it did, since I was about to get bored with the zone.
Hunger - Mr. Torgue returns, with his grandma, as the host for a reality combat show. Pretty funny, and one of the most frustrating raid events of the fanchise. Lots of Hunger Games references, but almost never overtly.
Mercenary Day - They tried to pack every Christmas cliche into this one, and almost suceeded. Still, interesting new foes and some details about Marcus's and Moxxi's marriage.
Love - Moxxi wants help creating peace. Foolishly, she asks the Vault Hunters for that help. Carnage ensues. One of the tougher (non-raid) boss fights in the entire game.
Wam Bam Island - Pure reminiscence for veterans of Borderlands, as Sir Hammerlock discovers the Son of Crawmerax. The second quest has a bit of character development for each of the B2 Vault Hunters.
Borderlands 2: The quest for every piece of dlc ever.

You all know why this game is good. Many of you feel a great deal of nostalgia towards this game. So did I.
I'm writing this review to remind you that besides this game's many strong points like great story, awesome graphic novel style cutscenes, good soundtrack, spot-on voice acting, there are also flaws.
First of all, Steam version is garbage. If you run Windows 7 or newer, expect some amount of tinkering to even make it run. And it's something that developers or the store itself could have fixed very easily.
Second - this game is not really meant to run on widescreen resolutions. The hack I used caused the dot crosshair to become very small, making aiming harder, and also somewhat altered camera placement so Max's body often obstructed the line of sight.
Third - there are sound problems, which again are fixable with the external tool.
Fourth - forced vSync. You can kinda hack it off, but extremely high framerates cause some issues, which again will require you to use external tools to limit the framerate to 60 to fix them. Playing with vSync on causes aiming to feel very sloppy, almost vanilla Skyrim level bad.
Fifth - this game is brutally, ridiculously hard. There is A LOT of instances where enemies kill you LITERALLY WITHIN A SECOND. Getting past those instances is possible either through dumb luck or through quickloading 10-15 times. Enemy placement is somewhat dickish, and they also will ambush you, including from areas you just cleared. There is a special place in hell for grenade throwing enemies, as grenades explode within 1 or 1,5 seconds after landing and will kill you instantly in most cases.
Sixth - weapon spread and accuracy are pretty much constant with Max's stance and movement having no tangible effect on them. There is no recoil at all, and the fact than spread is very high with most weapons makes the combat more luck-based than skill-based.
Because of all this I can't recommend this game, at least not the Steam version. If you have not played it and still want to, get it. It deserves to be played. Perhaps its flaws only serve to thicken the noir atmosphere it's going for. It may not look like much today, but it was a breakthrough back when it was released. Just try to get it elsewhere first.

Batman: Arkham Origins should have been a standalone expansion to the Arkham series.
A quick note about glitches: from the 20 hours of gameplay, I encountered some animation bugs but sadly, one major bug that would not let me finish the game with keyboard and mouse at the climax of the game in the chapel.
While everybody is talking about the game being riddled with bugs, I cannot help but feel that Arkham Origins was made to cash in on the popularity of the Arkham series. While the story that is set on Christmas Eve is neat, the writing is sloppy, and the assassins are making a lot of dumb and contradicting decisions. Even though I played Arkham City two years ago, I can tell that some of the assets were re-used in this game. Moreover, the gameplay has not changed much, except for some additions to your equipment. So just take what made the Arkham games great, then rinse, repeat.
Fans of the Arkham games sooner or later will ask the following questions:
- Why does Batman start out with all of his equipment from Arkham City at the beginning of the game?
- Where are all the people in Arkham? I guess they are all locked inside, right...
- Why is the writing so forced in some areas, especially with the Joker?
Do not get me wrong: Arkham Origins is a very enjoyable game and there are some nice moments in it, but this whole origin story could have been dealt with much, much better.
If you played Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, you should not buy the game at full price.

If you're going to read this, then focus. Put a couple of minutes aside. Pay full attention to me, because this isn't just a review. I'm going to pour my heart into this because I feel that's what this game deserves. This isn't just something you can score.
At first, this game's story is exactly like your standard anime, but it very quickly becomes something far greater. In my 32 hour campaign, there wasn't a single second in which I wasn't enjoying the absolute hell out of everything the game had to offer me. The adorable characters, the amazing story, the graphics of all of the spells...there wasn't a single second where I wasn't entertained.
It got to the point where once I reached the end of the game, I wasn't crying just because of the way the story ended, but also because of the very fact that the game is over now. Sure I knew I could do a new game plus, but something about finishing the game was just so heart wrenching. I can't even remember the last time I shed a tear, and I am a rather stoic man, so it symbolizes a lot that this amazingly emotional game managed to make me cry in different ways at the same time.
Somehow, the repetitive combat isn't a bad thing. The spell effects of each and every spell are entertaining and beautiful enough to keep you interested in seeing them forever. Getting experience and skill points is fun no matter what, to the point where even the slightly-mandatory grinding is even fun. That's saying so much.
Perhaps the most touching, is that it's a fully realized PC port. A game built with a JRPG engine has full mouse and keyboard support. Sure it seems like it would be standard for PC ports to have such things, but seeing a lack of mouse control in recent PC ports like DMC: Special Edition, it's hard not to feel grateful that the developers worked so hard to make mouse and keyboard work everywhere in this game. The amount of love they must have for this game must rival mine. And it does not surprise me, because it's extremely easy to fall in love with this game. You will have to practice the keyboard controls a bit (it took me a little bit to find out that Page Up and Page Down helps you aim your spells in combat, and Page Up re-centers your camera when exploring dungeons) but it won't take long, and the game's turn-based nature is very conducive with this control scheme, ensuring you have as much time as you need to figure out how, and where, to aim your spells. Give it a while, and you won't notice any difference in speed from casting a spell at the right position using a keyboard or a controller.
And to top it all off; my girlfriend gifted me this game and all of its dlc's. Even if it wasn't such an amazing game, it would be worth appreciating simply because she got it for me. But it turned out to be my personal game of the year. Deandra, I love you, and I can't thank you enough for giving me this art, and I can't thank Compile Heart and Idea Factory enough for creating it.

I'm not a professional reviewer or anything but I'm 32 (golden age of gaming) years old and I've played and finished every single CRPG on the planet, some of them multiple times.  This game definitely has the potential to be among the best I've played.  The writing it fantastic but I have to say, what I like the most is how the game mechanics are setup.  Most games like this you would reload if your character fails at doing something or persuading someone, but the way Torment is set up failure can lead to something new and interesting and the best moral choice won't always lead to the best moral outcome.  I love that because it simulates real life decision making.  Nothing is black and white.
Post Release Edit:
I've just finished the game.  I definitely feel like there's a lot of room for replay because of all the branching choices. I still stand by my original words but I do feel mildly disappointed though I feel it's my fault.  Torment isn't really an CRPG in the traditional sense.  I feel it's more of a point and click adventure game with some combat elements (mind you I was a Jack so I got through many things without combat).  I was very excited to hear that the game was set 1 billion years in the future. I am a fan of all things sci-fi.  I love the bizarre and unknown and some of the concepts in the game (such as the Bloom) were genuinely cool.
However the downside is being so far out made it also somewhat unrelateable.  I had a hard time caring for any of my companions. I also believe I've been spoiled by voice acting in RPGs. I don't mind reading at all but I honestly prefer to read what an NPC said rather than a novel-like narration though the skill with which it was written has my respect.
One let down was the lack of a world map.  I though perhaps I would get to visit some of these places I heard about in the game but alas they were only lore.  I was disappointed with the overall plot though there were some twists I didn't see coming. I felt like the billion year into the future plot was really interesting but I really wish it was more organized.  I felt like there were a lot of random elements and things that didn't really fit in well together. I also wish I could delve more into the backstories of some of the more interesting elements.  For example, I wanted to know a lot more about the Bloom than what was given.
Overall, it's a good game though I believe Planescape Torment was better (though in all fairness I am a fan of that universe).  Perhaps it's just me since this is my first experience with Monte Cook, maybe if more comes out in this universe I'll grow to understand it better.

"Planescape: Torment" has been my favorite CRPG of all time since I first played it at its release in 1999.
It figuratively and literally turned the genre on its head. All the basic assumptions people take away from most CRPGs had been practically inverted wholesale.
I was a fan of the source tabletop setting released in 1994, long before the game hit the shelves, so I had looked at the video game with a very critical eye, and found every moment of its game play engaging, and its story, theme and characters utterly unique.
I was hesitant, and ultimately decided against supporting the kickstarter, mostly as I realize now due to my lack of understanding of the Numenera setting. Unlike Planescape, which had the underpinnings of D&D to start with, I was never able to wrap my head around how the Numenera setting worked. It just never clicked for me.
I knew I’d pick this up when it released, even if it was just a chance of catching some of that old Planescape:Torment nostalgia.
I also admit, I only have 3.0 hours, yes three, into this as I'm writing it. (I may update this review after I have more time with the actual release version).
However, I've played the first 10-20 minutes of the game probably 6 times, each with completely different outcomes:
From what I've seen, which I completely admit is a small sliver of the whole, this not only matches my expectations of what a spiritual successor to P:T would be, it exceeds them.
The settings are equally fantastic in the truest sense of the word. The characters I’ve seen so far, are almost as good as the initial characters you meet in P:T.
If the rest of this game matches the first 15 minutes, this will easily slide up to match Planescape:Torment as my favorite cRPG.
Where Planescape: Torment asked: “What can change the nature of a man?”
Torment: Tides of Numenera asks: “What does one life matter?”

looking forward this just
help you answer that question in the same way,through game play, story, and character development.

As a backer for this when it was announced I had decided to check in on the game to really get a feel for it and see if I was a fool for backing it or not.
Long story short, I am very happy with this game and what I have played. I have played almost 10 hours the past few days, sending in bug reports as appropriate (ran into one major one that blocked continuation/completion of a major quest and a minor issue with character creation not showing the correct Health value during creation, though it did show the correct value once you left character creation.) but overall the game is in good shape.
This game more than any other really feels like playing a tabletop RPG. There is a ton of options for making decisions (including ones that will outright kill you such as diving in the initial sequence) and ways for your character's unique traits to really shine and affect gameplay in meaningful ways.
The Tides system is also very clearly setting itself up to be the most interesting morality system ever put into game form. It really feels like I am making a unique person with unique views as I play and the system does a great job of distilling your character's motivations and thoughts into a tide.
Combat in the game is fairly basic and straight-forward. It too feels like a true representation of a Tabletop Rpg combat system. But what makes Combat great is that it is almost never the only option available to you, and indeed it is often the least interesting.
Overall, I am very excited for this game and cannot wait to play its complete form!

When I bought Voodoo Garden I didn't realize it was really a clicker game. That is OK though- I like clicker games. What I don't like, however, are bad clicker games.
Unfortunately Voodoo Garden just doesn't work for me. Some parts are ok: the art is nice and consistent, the music and sound effects are very good, and the overall vibe is nice. But the actual game is lacking in some key ways.
The game's biggest problem is just that it is very shallow. There is very little to customize and the upgrades are few and far between. The mechanics are very simplistic and also, unlike other clicker games I've played, unless the game is open it doesn't continue to collect things for you.
It also has some gameplay problems. The first is, nothing is explained. There is almost no text at all in this game and so everything is trial and error at first. Then there are some EXTREMELY annoying design flaws. One is, sometimes the you need to click a lot all over the screen to get fast moving lizards and such. But double clicks can also pick up certain objects like totems which disables your mouse until you put the object back down. This is a baffling choice in a click game. "Don't impede the clicking" is like the most basic tenet! Very frustrating. It also can be tricky to get the text under items to show up in the menu because for some reason it goes between "click to purchase" and the items name. Maybe if the  game had instructions it wouldn't need to put various things like that under EVERY object, making it hard to see the names/functions of anything easily.
Another minor issue is that picking up totems with all the sound/music muted still makes a sound, and a fairly loud one at that. It startled me the first time I did it.
My final issue is that the game just doesn't seem balanced. Each area  of the garden has different things: trees in the back, then bushes, then herbs in front, etc. But at all parts of the game it seems like my need for herbs way outweighed the space I had, even when my garden was fully expanded. Add that to a fairly slow and non-user controlled potion making system and the whole game can slow to a halt.
Because of these issues and an overall sort of laziness about it, I think Voodoo Garden is a waste of a good idea. I liked the animal sacrifice screen and thought it was clever but was disappointed when it became apparent that that was the best idea in the whole game.
Ultimately, this is just too shallow a game. I got all the achievements in less than two days. For an adult gamer, I need more to keep me engaged and since this game is both shallow and yet too mature for kids, I just wouldn't recommend it to anyone else.
Also, just a stray thought: I bet people would be really mad if someone made a Catholicism clicker game, right? Or a Judaism one?

An intense and darkly charming game, with brutal combat and some of the best vehicular combat I've seen, only to be held back by unnecessary and grind-y design choices and a plethora of bugs and glitches.
The sound design is great. Engines roar, voices fit the world and their characters, wind blows and storms bellow. You can detect threats with pinpoint accuracy if you're using surround sound, but even with just speakers you can tell where sounds are coming from. Melee combat feels savage and satisfying. It is very reminiscent of Batman's, but that's simply because it's the best way to do third person melee combat. Assassin's Creed did it before Batman, after all. Car combat takes a while to get used to and isn't nearly as fun if you're not in the Magum Opus or the Drop Kicker, but is plenty of fun when you are and feels incredibly rewarding when it works out.
But, as I said, some questionable design choices and bugs hinder the experience. Hunting down collectables is a staple of the genre, but the majority of what you'd be collecting to 100% a camp is quite literally garbage. Early game it is necessary to upgrade the magnum opus but later on whatever you'd collect is just trivial. And most locations are just these; little tents with a few enemies and a few heaps of garbage for you to stuffle over to and pick up, sometimes they'll hold a Relic or some other item that actually makes it worth visiting. But that's just action-adventure games in general. What truly holds Mad Max back, in my experience, is how buggy it is, and I've never had an issue with infamously buggy games like Skyrim or Fallout 4.
For a good 4 hours of my 38 hours, my Magnum Opus had entirely disappeared. I could not call Chum to bring it, I could not find it where I last saw it, it would not appear in any stronghold; I drove from Gastown to the bottom of the map searching every location I could think of, I restarted the game at least 4 times, and then, I pull into a stronghold and it's there and no issues followed.
That was the major issue. In addition, I've seen:
Game frozen when in the Garage section
When I would be prompted to open a bio page, it would start, then go to blank
Several items don't show the correct command prompt ("Hold E to climb ladder" when it should be "Collect Water") for instance
Recieving experience (and griffa tokens, the currency used to increase stats) for the same accomplishment over and over again (if this isn't a bug, it's a terrible design choice)
And, while not bugs, there are a number of quality of life issues with the game
Holding E to do everything
Button mashing
When using the sniper rifle (which can only be used in the car for some reason), Chum is incapable of keeping the car in place on an incline where Max can, changing your perfect vantage point into you tumbling down a cliff
Most missions are fetch quests
I would recommend Mad Max to a friend, but not without acknowledging it has many flaws

This game is getting much more flak than it deserves. Sure, the DRM isn't pleasant and the performance leaves some to be desired, but it's easily the best Hitman since Blood Money. It's a true return to roots and I for one couldn't be happier. I think the episodic release model will help keep people invested in the game longer.

Most of the reviews I see that downvote this game seem to be from fanboys whining about how awesome a game from ten years ago was (Blood Money) and nothing compares to it. After praising the game for going back to the mechanics of Blood Money, offering huge levels to explore and tons of AI to deal with, and the replay value, they all slam this game and give it a thumb down. The main complaints, and I'll address them in line:
1) Always-on DRM. Put it in offline mode. It's the same game with the same content. You can do this from the menu, you don't need to disconnect your computer or sign out of Steam. You're welcome.
2) Performance issues. I've got an old AMD Athlon processor with a single GTX 970 graphics card that has yet to see any performance issues after 13 hours in the game. As most PC gamers know, there's a lot that could cause minor issues with ANY game. Chances are, the problems these people are seeing aren't caused by the game itself but rather their particular hardware setup.
3) Episodic release. While this *may* be a legit complaint in certain ways, get over it. If you don't like it, wait until the full game is released and then purchase. Don't bash a game just because you want to play it ASAP. They aren't charging you any extra cash over what they would normally charge for the game (unless you do decide to purchase it piece-by-piece).
And seriously...go back and play Blood Money again. It was great for 2006 but it doesn't hold up. The PC version doesn't have controller support, there's little AI to have to work around minus 2 levels (Mardi Gras and the Heaven/Hell party), and the levels are tiny save the Heaven/Hell party (that level was actually kinda massive at the time).
HITMAN is a fantastic installment to the franchise offering massive levels, tons of assassination options, hundreds of AI characters throughout, and the classic "closed level"-style of gameplay that became synonymous with the franchise. If you're a HItman fan, this one is not to be missed.

First Revision: Will probably add stuff to the review later.
First off, Yooka Laylee really captured the old school nostalgic feeling for me.
The worlds were diverse and interesting for the most part, some of them had massive areas with nothing while others had plenty of things to see and do.
Controllers felt nice and snappy, camera were only annoying once or twice through the entire game and the graphics were pleasant on the eyes.
The bosses were fun and balanced just right. They required a certain amount of knowledge from the player, so you felt like the things you learned throughout the game actually matters in the end.
Last boss was very satisfying to beat since it was initially really hard going into it blind but once you learned all the patterns and what ability to use it became "easy". It felt like a good balance between the player's skill and game design challenge.
The "side quests" you do to get pagies are for the most part really fun. They range from jumping challenges, time trials, combat and straight up silly things. I won't spoil any of it though as the surprise element is required.
Enemies in the game had a good enough variety if you ignore the fact that they used the same enemy in all the levels, just with a new model attached to it. They had all the basic baddies you would expect from a game like this. Sadly, the combat isn't really that good so they are mostly used to fill out the world to make it feel alive as you can probably skip 99% of them.
Characters in the game were for the most part really funny and very typical Rare humor. Most of the minor characters was forgettable while the main characters really stuck with me.
The quiz from banjo kazooie is back, but feels very out of place. The questions are really unfair, stuff like "How many hours did you spend to get to this point?" or "How many quills have you collected?". It was okay the first time, but having it multiple times throughout the game felt really unnecessary and ruins the flow of the game.
Rextro’s mini games were a nice distraction from the main game, but nothing I would like to play hours to end. Maybe it's fun with friends, but I havn't tested this.
Transformations were fun and unique for every level and were well implemented into the levels. I didn't like the plant though.
Kartos was a fun little throwback to the 90's with minecart riding through the world. I found them fun enough, I could easily see where I was going compared to back in the 4:3 days and Donkey Kong Country where you had to have split second reactions to dodge certain obstacles. The camera in 3D do help a lot though, as it's angled in the direction you're going.
I really liked the fact that you had to search for quills, but I wish they were placed in a more logical way, as they felt very random and didn't guide the player through the level as the notes did back in Banjo Kazooie.
The crystal skulls were also stupidly well hidden in some levels and really easy to find in others (probably intended).
The co-op mode was a joke and is basically identical to the unfinished mode from banjo kazooie where the other player controls a UI element so they can interact with certain things in the game.
Yooka Laylee let's you choose which world you want to complete first, so I naturally went out to 100% World 1, and then 5 while only entering the stages in between for abilities. This means that my playthrough will be different to yours if you choose to do this in another order. This also means that you might not unlock certain abilities that I had when I did something you might find really hard but is really easy with a certain ability.
An example of this was one pagie I had to do some really hard platforming to get up to (pixel perfect jumps), but I understood why it was so hard later in the game once I unlocked the flying move.
Sound: Music was not as good as some of the older rare titles, but they still managed to have a few memorable tracks. Audio effects were generally good and I can't really remember any effects I thought "Man, this sucks!". So, as with most things, you don't notice the good things, only the bad.
Graphics: I really like this cartoony style, so I'm a bit biased. Textures were nice and "high" res so I don't see the graphics becoming outdated any time soon. Shadows were nice, animations were good, particles were satisfying, generally a very pretty game. Also works flawless in 21:9 ultrawide 100 hz.
Gameplay: Solid gameplay, really good controls and good platforming for the most parts. Really easy to pick up and play by anyone.
Replay Value: The main part of the game is the exploration and finding secrets, so the replay value is sadly a bit low as you will most likely remember most of it for a second playthrough.
Story: Nothing unique and a few forgettable characters, but the humor was on point. If you like the old Rare games humor, you will most likely have a good laugh from this as well.
I'd give it a solid 7/10.
Losing a few points to bad quills placement, not a great plot, Rextro’s arcade, enemies and the quiz being over-used.
Still relatively high as I had a really good time with it. I even finished the entire game in a weekend because I couldn't stop thinking about what to do the next day. Haven't had this feeling for years!
Overall a good game that I would recommend to anyone who wants a modern platformer.
