Tides of Numenera by nXile studios is the successor title to Torment Planescape (1999) developed by Balck Isle.
No longer based in the 2nd edition D&D universe of Planescape. We are in the 9th world of Numenera. However Torment: Tides of Numernera is wirtten by a heavy hitter in the gaming industry Chris Avellone. Chris has worked on titles such as the original Torment, Fallout 2, Baldur's Gate. This is most definitely what people are calling  "text heavy" and it's exceptional.
This is a great rendition of the pillars of eternity unity engine. Character models looks great, every district you enter has its own artistic merits and acheivment. You can't help but play to learn more about the world of Numenera.

# An updated review
Having finished the game with the Servant of the Tides DLC, I would like to update my review and say that despite my initial annoyance, the game grew on me as I've played through it. The game tells a fairly straightforward story of a man's search for immortality, but the journey to the conclusion is filled with skillful worldbuilding, interesting twists, worthwhile characters, and intriguing moral choices.
Not only are the choices you make intriguing on their own, but they also have a lasting effect on the world and the story. I have also only now discovered that your companions form an opinion of you, which further affects the story, and that I have missed several of them. This leads me to the conclusion that despite the lack of intrigue at finding yourself in an unfamiliar world, the game still offers a fair deal of replayability.
Even though I found the crises boring in the beginning, they become more interesting as you progress through the game. Not only do you gain more characters and these characters gain new skills, abilities, and cyphers, which opens up new tactical options, but I also found the later crises more inspired in their design. I particularly enjoyed one crisis, where you need to split your party into three groups. One group keeps a guard busy, while the other two groups coordinate a robbery. Sadly, most crises were just generic battles with peaceful resolution options thrown in.
Another thing that I ranted about in the original review was the lack of passage of time outside crises. Unlike the organic real-time environments of Planescape Torment, where you could be attacked at any time, TToN separated the gameplay into turn-based crises (battles) and safe exploration. This turned cities into sterile and boring environments free of danger. Sad to say that this does not change throughout the game; however, I was pleasantly surprised to find out that the game secretly measures time under the hood and that it was possible to fail timed events if you lingered for too long. This does wonders for the sense of urgency and makes the world feel more organic and alive. This also makes a particular quest lines extremely memorable as the output depends on your quick wits.
The main character has the ability to use devices called Merecasters to relive the memories (Meres) of various individuals and to alter the reality by guiding the individuals' actions. The Meres are presented via a choose-your-own-adventure gameplay that is based purely on text and on the occasional illustrations. The rest of the game is already heavy with dialogue, but the Meres go a step further and strip the remnants of gameplay, leaving only text and inviting highly creative writing.
# The original review
As a Plainscape: Torment fan and a Torment: Tides of Numenera backer, I will try to assess how Tides of Numenera measure up to their spiritual predecessor. Please note that I did not finish the game. The gameplay consists of exploration, dialogues, and battles:
- Exploration is the standard fare. I feel that the Pillars of Eternity engine was well-chosen and the game is visually appealing, propelling you to explore every nook and cranny of the bizzare game world.
- Dialogues are more engaging compared to a traditional cRPG, since having a certain skill is not enough for you to activate special dialogue options.  Instead, you and your companions will need to spend Effort. Effort is spent from a set of three pools (Might, Speed, and Intellect) that are replentished on-rest or via items. The amount of Effort you need to spend depends on your skills and on the chance of failure you are willing to accept. Overall, this mechanic makes dialogues feel fresh. Since writing was the cornerstone of Planescape: Torment, rest assured that no corners were cut here and the (numerous) writers that were involved with the game did a marvellous  job.
- Battles (called “Crises”) are turn-based and heavily scripted. You may either use items and a wide array of battle abilities, gained as a part of character progression, to attack your enemies, or you may interact with the enemies and the environment instead. Actions undertaken during crises require Effort to be spent in a fashion similar to the dialogue system.  A minor complaint is that you may not control your characters individually outside crises, only the whole party; as a result, there is no way to position your characters strategically before a crisis begins. Otherwise, the battles are engaging and will certainly bring joy to the players who prefer turn-based over real-time-with-pause combat.
As outlined above, I am fairly pleased with the individual aspects of the game.  However, a game is more than a sum of its parts and I feel that there is something essential missing here; something that made Planescape: Torment the exceptional game it is.
Planescape: Torment (PT) was built on Infinity engine – the engine that powers the cRPG classics of Baldur's Gate (BG) and Icewind Dale (ID). However, whereas BG and ID feature complex character sheets, combat logs with dice rolls, and tactical combat controls, the user interface of PT is bare and all the dice rolling is happening behind the scenes without the player's knowledge. As a matter of fact, you would not know that Planescape: Torment is an RPG unless you knew its lineage, since it plays very much like a point'n'click adventure game; this is further supported by the easy combat (compared to BG and especially ID), heavy emphasis on exploration and lengthy (visual novel tier) dialogue over combat, and by the fact that the main character cannot die. The magic of PT is that you start the game thinking that it is a point'n'click adventure game, but during the course of the game you discover that there is real-time combat, choice and consequence, faction affiliation, alignment, character abilities, and more. Combine this with the fact that both the Planescape setting and the story of PT are weird and highly unpredictable, and you end up with a game that has you questioning its every aspect including the game mechanics – a feat successfully pulled off by few other games.
Looking at Torment: Tides of Numenera (TToN), this aspect of PT is virtually lost. The complex character progression is in full sight and you are expected to spend a fair amount of time studying it. Combat is carefully separated from the exploration gameplay and turned into a heavily scripted minigame. As a result, there is no intrigue in the game mechanics, as all is laid out before you at the beginning of the game, and the exploration gameplay, which along with dialogues is where you will spend most of your playing time, is a plain point-and-click adventure game with no passage of time and with no danger to the characters.
TToN is not a bad game. It is lovingly-crafted, ticks all the boxes for a good point'n'click adventure game, and the tactical combat sets it apart from the rest of the genre. Unlike PT, however, it spends too much Effort on polishing the individual parts rather than making sure that they combine into something truly exceptional. A classic example of missing the forest for the trees in my eyes. Still a solid game, though.

TL;DR - What's available right now leaves me wanting more - I powered through it before my classes start back, and I didn't realize the beta ended when I got on the airship!! I want to play with my speedy glaive more!
Negatives :
Out of the thirteen hours I've put into the game (so far), I found one bug - Using the south eastern terminal in the Peerless quest without clearing out the southern drones will stick your party in place without the ability to move or to attack. Even if you kill off the peerless using Opportunist, you're still unable to interact with the game entirely and thus are stuck having to reload.
Along the same track, older saves from early versions will keep your game from loading, but anyone using exclusively steam won't have that issue. If it becomes a problem, go to your InXile folder inside Appdata/locallow and delete the saves folder!
Positives :
The world is phenomenal. The interaction is very Pillars of Eternity. The characters that I have met thus far have been enjoyable, though part of me wishes you could dive a little deeper into them. I'd really like to be able to gut Fulsum's hold over the Underbelly and generally just sew chaos while I pretend to be the Changing God!
The side quests are numbeous, fairly recognizable, enjoyable and more often than not completely worthwhile - I'd like to see further expansion on the invasive surgeries that you can get in Cliff's Edge, but I also run chromed out in Shadowrun so maybe that's just me.
The combat is solid. While it can be tricky to get ahold of at first, this most recent patch (Tidal Surge, Dec2016) seems to have made things a little more accessible and easier to grasp without losing *all* of the math going into combat.
Wishlist:
I'd really like to see an option to speed up combat - Specifically enemy animations and general combat speed.
I'd like to see further gear customizability - Not just for the Last Castoff, but also for their companions! I'm not saying I want to stick Rhin in a suit of full plate, but interchangability would be nice if it could be introduced somehow.
Closing thoughts:
I'm very much excited to play through this multiple times in full with different builds and party compositions. I do hope that all of our companions aren't necessarily introduced in the first city. I'm excited to see what changes happen with the Cult of the Changing God - Being a selfish and careless character for that run was really great for making them do all of my dirty work! Here's to looking forward to inXile putting out yet another phenomenal title!

- There's not much in terms of a tutorial.  While there was some tool tips every so often, it would've been nice to have been given a little more info on what to do in the beginning.
- Gold/XP can only be earned while the game is running.
- Unlike many clickers, not every process can be automated.  The player must remain active to collect many of the game's ingredients.
- Gets quite boring after awhile-- while new plants/upgrades are gradually added, none of them really add anything interesting.
Overall:
It's hard to say quite how I feel about Voodoo Garden.  While I was charmed by its aesthetics, the whole experience was ultimately lackluster.  To me, the best part of a clicker(especially a more creative clicker like this) is getting more and more efficient to the point where all processes are automatic except for overall management.  I found Voodoo Garden disappointing in the fact that the user's job never really gets much easier.  From the beginning to the end, the player is madly clicking the screen to collect ingredients that their helpers cannot collect.  It gets to be a tedious process.
Ultimately, unless you're a huge fan of mindless clickers, I'd pass this game up.

The big issues with the game is that even after the first major patch for the game it still has a number of issues that will periodically pop up and cause frustrations. In the battle against Killer Croc near the very beginning of the game, Killer Croc’s model will vanish thus leaving you unable to see him. I’ve also experienced falling into the void below the map immediately after a cut-scene finished. While the flipping-while-flying glitch isn’t that big of a deal it does scream at you that the game has problems.
The world map is physically bigger than Arkahm City’s, but City feels like it was planned much better thus City feels like a bigger game than Arkham Origins does. I enjoyed the variety of the boss battles in Origins, but on New Game Plus I frequently get hit enemies because their pre-attack movement was obscured by another enemy.
The best new component of the game is the enhanced crime scene interaction. Arkham City did a decent job with the aspect of investigating a crime scene. In Origins you do a complete crime scene recreation where you’re able to recreate what happened during the crime in 3D and then rewind or play the action to help you figure out what occurred.
If you want to continue the Arkham games then I recommend getting Origins as it’s interesting to visit some of the same interior locations from City, but I wouldn’t recommend making this your first introduction to the Arkham universe. Start with Asylum and then go to City before playing Origins.

An intense and darkly charming game, with brutal combat and some of the best vehicular combat I've seen, only to be held back by unnecessary and grind-y design choices and a plethora of bugs and glitches.
The sound design is great. Engines roar, voices fit the world and their characters, wind blows and storms bellow. You can detect threats with pinpoint accuracy if you're using surround sound, but even with just speakers you can tell where sounds are coming from. Melee combat feels savage and satisfying. It is very reminiscent of Batman's, but that's simply because it's the best way to do third person melee combat. Assassin's Creed did it before Batman, after all. Car combat takes a while to get used to and isn't nearly as fun if you're not in the Magum Opus or the Drop Kicker, but is plenty of fun when you are and feels incredibly rewarding when it works out.
But, as I said, some questionable design choices and bugs hinder the experience. Hunting down collectables is a staple of the genre, but the majority of what you'd be collecting to 100% a camp is quite literally garbage. Early game it is necessary to upgrade the magnum opus but later on whatever you'd collect is just trivial. And most locations are just these; little tents with a few enemies and a few heaps of garbage for you to stuffle over to and pick up, sometimes they'll hold a Relic or some other item that actually makes it worth visiting. But that's just action-adventure games in general. What truly holds Mad Max back, in my experience, is how buggy it is, and I've never had an issue with infamously buggy games like Skyrim or Fallout 4.
For a good 4 hours of my 38 hours, my Magnum Opus had entirely disappeared. I could not call Chum to bring it, I could not find it where I last saw it, it would not appear in any stronghold; I drove from Gastown to the bottom of the map searching every location I could think of, I restarted the game at least 4 times, and then, I pull into a stronghold and it's there and no issues followed.
That was the major issue. In addition, I've seen:
Game frozen when in the Garage section
When I would be prompted to open a bio page, it would start, then go to blank
Several items don't show the correct command prompt ("Hold E to climb ladder" when it should be "Collect Water") for instance
Recieving experience (and griffa tokens, the currency used to increase stats) for the same accomplishment over and over again (if this isn't a bug, it's a terrible design choice)
And, while not bugs, there are a number of quality of life issues with the game
Holding E to do everything
Button mashing
When using the sniper rifle (which can only be used in the car for some reason), Chum is incapable of keeping the car in place on an incline where Max can, changing your perfect vantage point into you tumbling down a cliff
Most missions are fetch quests
I would recommend Mad Max to a friend, but not without acknowledging it has many flaws

Troubles will start at the very beginning when a bunch of sith will infiltrate the Academy to provide diversion while others drain Some force residuals from the temple and steal Skywalkers log records. A new Sith cult is rising and troubles spread over the galaxy so now it's time for the new Students to go around and solve them.
With this new setting we are bound to customize our character's gender, race and appearance. Our lightsaber's hilt and color can be customized as well.
The game genere is still a third person action while wielding lightsabers, and FPS when using firearms, but this time we have Lightsaber and force powers since the very beginning,and (after an intro and a training section) we're not playing through an ordered number of levels but we're given a set of 5 levels and we can choose which mission to accept. We're not bounded to accept all of them, as 4 will be enough, but considering for each mission we can improve one light or dark force power at choice it could be wise to complete all of them. After that we will proceed with with story related cutscenes and levels and after that we will be given another set of 5 missions again, rinse and repeat.
Even though the story is nicely represented with some more coreographic cutscenes and situations it doesn't really impress and involve the way it happened with Dark Forces II or Jedi Knight 2. A good point is the choice for dark or light path, so once again we can choose which side of the force to join with one particular decision towards the end. As usual the most interesting ending is the dark side, but I'm not here to spoil anymore than this.
The engine is once again the same from Jedi Knight 2, but this time the idTech has been polished and improved further with effects, shaders, reflections and saber burn marks on enemies as well. Level design didn't give me the impression of being constant, as I've witnessed marvelous and amazing sections well designed with lot of care and attention for details and decorations, while other areas or levels are more flat or... standard.
Gameplay is the real core of this chapter as it has really been improved under many aspects. We have new set of moves such as rolling out or jump when grounded, bounce out when pushed or jumping onto walls, special attacks specific for saber combat styles and in the latest sections of the game we can wield the saber staff or two lightsabers. A particular note goes to one particular section, a mission where you must run all the way with a speeder bike. Even though it's a simplistic section I simply loved it and I'm sure EA had that secton in mind while working on Battlefront.
The soundtrack is amazing as always. As in Jedi Knight 2 it uses the Classic tunes from John Williams with dynamic tracks, so fast paced tunes will be played while you're in action, while slow movements will be played while exploring and everything wil be smoothly linked with apropriate musical passages. A bunch of new tracks have been added for specific sections.
Unfortunately the impression of this title is that of an expansion more than a new chapter. Of course there are lots of gameplay innovations, a whole new story, but still the story doesn't have the impact nor the importance of the previous chapters, the characters don't give great impressions, specially Jaden, the story is quite predictable and the level design even though it has many sections full of details and inspiration has other sections more standard making the game look... Rushed.

"Smoke rose from the sewers below like all the fires of hell were beneath us." Awesome quotes like that make Max Payne sweet as candy. The game concerns the eponymous hero and tells a peaceful story about his blissful retirement from the NYPD and how he lives happily ever after with his wife and kids. Or not. The game concerns his "Taken style" journey for vengeance after his family are brutally slain by junkies high on a new drug. Valkyrie. The game is (in my mind) split into two seperate parts, the gameplay and the story.
The gameplay concerns Max running through new york killing everyone he sees, you use different guns (a lot of them) and have the option of going into bullet time (slowing down time like a family reunion) but fundamentally the gameplay is derivative and repetitive. There's a link with the general pessimisitic film noir tone of the game and how depressed and angry Max is but that doesn't neccessarily excuse gameplay which is so lacking in variety.
The story of the game involves tracking down who was responsible for the crime and is told partly through graphic novel style scripts with gritty voiceover, partly through cutscenes using the in-game engine but probably most interestingly through the environment of the game in the form of graffiti, doodads and various TV shows which are variously sinister and funny and educational.
The main problem of the game (for me) is (as previously mentioned) the actual gameplay of the game becomes a chore one has to work through to access the storyline (which is interesting and thought provoking). I guess it's kind of like playing an RPG where all the battles seem like a means to the end of enjoying the narrative and you actually wish the game would just be super easy so you could get what you actually want out of it with the minimum of fuss.
Overall the game is very interesting and different but has that rather large flaw. Still worth a look.

Ideally, a review should be an objective evaluation of the merits and flaws of a game...but we all know that these days that's often not what happens.  Sites like Steam and Metacritic are littered with "reviews" that are expressions of agenda rather than honest appraisals.  "I'm mad that there's no crafting - 1 out of 10!"  Or "I'm counteracting the 1's with my 10!"
T:TON has attracted more than its share of such sentiments, mostly because of two reasons: angst about what some see as a betrayal of promises made during the development process, and secondly, a misunderstanding of what this game set out to do and what it is.  I'm not going to go into the former at all... I'm just going to say that if you're going to pick a cause to champion, railing against developers for normal development processes is not a very good one.  But I will talk some about the second because this game is very much worth playing for what it is, and all of the whining about what is is not, (or worse, what it "should be" in some entitled fan's imagination) is just noise.
T:TON is a heavily story/dialogue based game.  The core of its gameplay is talking to NPCs, exploring the environment, and expressing your character in the way you desire to.  This game allows you to do that to an almost unprecedented degree.  Most quests have real weight to them, with different ways to accomplish them (not all of which are immediatley obvious), real ethical decisions, and ramifications that may come much later in the game.  The NPCs are imaginative, and plentiful, and the writing is fantastic.  I would count it among the top 5 or so games I've ever played in terms of writing quality.  The environments are full of things to interact with in interesting ways.  If you are a lover of story and writing, this game is absolutely worth playing.
The systems of the game are more polarizing, though I would argue that they have considerable merit as well.  Combat IS not a focus.  It was never going to be, from the Kickstarter onwards, and it isn't.  However, those who say that you fight "once in 20 hours" or whatver are not correct.  There are many opportunities for combat if you desire it; it's just never going to be a random encounter with a trash mob.  As far as how the combat actually operates, that's a matter of taste, but the turn based system is a fit with how the game is played in general in a way that real time could never be.  In Crisis encounters (which is what the game calls combat, which should be a clue), you do not necessarily just fight, or in some cases, fight at all.  You can sometimes activate devices, or speak to your opponents.  In some cases, a Crisis is a moment of heightened drama, not a fight.  If you love constant, context-free combat, and feel that an RPG without it is boring, then you will be bored by this game.  That is not a fault of the game, or of you.  It is simply a sign that you two don't match.
I could say a lot more about this game.  The environments, especially in The Bloom, are fantastic.  I enjoy the soundtrack.  There are a wide variety of interesting items to find (loot in most games is extremely boring after you've played for a few hours and seen most of what it can be mechanically; not so here).  And again, the story, characters, writing, and breadth of choice in your interactions is non pareil.
Bottom line, if you aren't the sort to get hung up on a less than perfect running animation, or the lack of a system proposed 4 years ago that didn't end up fitting into the game, and you ARE the sort who loves to explore a unique and vibrant world, love reactivity and choice, love story and an ability to write your own unique tale, then you owe it to yourself to ignore the folks with agendas and play this game.

To be honest, the game really missed the mark. I was disappointed with it as a long time backer that it turned out such a basic game.
Cons:
-Combat is turn based and there are no random encounters, it's all combat in the exact same spots (though you don't have to fight every battle), which means you'll spend most of your time broke, undergeared,  and outclassed by enemies depending on your party config. Then in the end, the complete opposite happened, I was Oprah Rich and armed to the teeth, the game became much much easier, but the rough start made the game less enjoyable.
-Dialog is way too long. It's like reading a paragraph and a half just to greet a merchant who sells junk. I found myself skimming through a lot of it for the more trivial characters.
-It's Ugly, specificially the icons, interface, portraits, UI in general. The animation of spell effects, areas, loading screens, and 3D characters was top notch. But the 2D UI is hideous grey and came out "unfinished" looking.
-Combat difficulty fluctuates throughout the game, some areas are easy, some are cruel (endless gate comes to mind but won't spoil) and while combat can virtually be completely skipped, it woud be nice to have an actual "winnable" combat, there is no difficulty setting either.
-No auto-sort inventory button, just nitpicking but c'mon it should be standard.
Pros:
- Very well written, and author-level scripts, as a book, it was enjoyable.
- Cyphers are plentiful and can really be devastating in battle and fun to use.
- Party members are interesting and generally perform well in combat, also there is plenty of commentary from them in dialogs, banter between NPCs, and side quests for each companion.
- The Ninth World is very unique and provides an interesting setting.
- Challenges in the game can be solved in different ways depending on your style
- I felt the game had the perfect number of side quests.
- Different endings based on choices offer replay value.
In the end, even though I did enjoy my playthrough of it, and many of the side-stories or memories and how well they were written. I can't really say it's a good game worth buying. It's crap, buy it cheap because as an interactive novel it's awesome, but I wouldn't spend more than $30 on it. I have a feeling it's going to be like inXile's previous game, Wasteland 2, where it finally got to be a good game about a year and a half after release when the "director's cut" edition came out with improved graphics and fixes and such. This one is going to be no different, and that's if we're lucky enough to see a director's cut. As a backer who invested $150 I'm extremely unhappy with the final product given the amount of money raised and time allocated, it's just not a good game overall.

YOOKA-LAYLEE (PC)
PUBLISHER Team17 Digital, Inc
DEVELOPER Playtonic Games
GENRE 3-D Platformer
THE BASICS:
It's Banjo-Kazooie again – which is exactly what fans wanted – only with a lizard and a bat instead of a beat and a bird. Run around collecting cartoony things – ALL the things, for they are legion, smack cartoony bad guys, collect cartoony health/energy pickups in the form of butterflies, and explore the vast worlds on display (five worlds, each of which can be expanded). If B-K floats your boat, you're gonna love this.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
Your good-hearted character(s) find their peaceful little worldlet attacked by a bad guy who is stealing the books of the world, in hopes that he will be able to use them for world conquest. Oh, and pollution. Plenty of that. You know the drill. Find missing sentient “pagies” to put back into the magical book, collect floating feather quills to spend on new abilities, and snag the (much rarer) other collectibles in order to access temporary transformations and unlock arcade games.
CONTROLS:
Native controller support. Standard platformer controls (tho you can't move while crouched), new buttons and moves introduced gradually. Would be nice to have a handy reference on how to use unlocked powers without having to go back to the sales-snake to ask.
GRAPHICS:
It looks friendly and pretty, which is par for the course, and the modern engine does at least allow for one thing its older counterparts couldn't do – letting you actually see the bulk of the level at a glance if there are no huge obstacles in the way. Floating platforms waaaay up near the vertical limit still cast accurate shadows way down at ground level, clueing you in to the fact that “there may be something useful up there.” Little to no pop-in, and a constant 60fps or better, even on a moderate system.
SOUND:
Good music, feels cheerful and bright where needed, more somber or creepy when appropriate for the area. However, the characters all “speak” in grunts and squeaks that are immediately off-putting and grating on the ears. Would have liked an Audio option to remove or reduce voices while keeping other sound FX intact. Note that these voices extend to nearly every single menu in the game, as well, even at the title screen.
OVERALL:
Be careful what you wish for. This one goes right for the nostalgia in players and bets everything on it. Having started out as a tribute to the Banjo-Kazooie games, they held a phenomenally successful Kickstarter and gave the audience just that – a game that hearkens back to the N64 era's idea of 3-D platforming gameplay, with everything both wonderful and woeful that implies. Unfortunately, the dev team seemingly took this to mean that they should also ignore a decade and a half of improvements to how this sort of game can be done.
YL has solid gameplay, but it still feels like we've all done this before, many times. The characters are all cute critters (and yes, this includes most of the enemies and collectibles), with some closer to the creepy-cute end of the spectrum.
Side note – the “Exclusive Mode” (available when booting up the game) puts it into modal, full-screen non-windowed mode in order to allow a bit more processor time to be devoted to the game, and it helps. The downside is, in my experience, every time you Quit the game while under Exclusive mode, it crashes instead of merely doing a graceful exit (at least on Win10 64bit/Creator update). You have to access Task Manager to get rid of its crash notifier and do anything else at all. This, and other issues such as the “talking” menus, seem to indicate areas that could have been polished more in a game which is otherwise polished to a mirror sheen. For what it's worth, it's not a BAD game by any means – it's just that it could have been so much better.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Win 7+ 64bit, i5-2500 3.3GHz, 8 GB RAM, Nvidia GTS 450/Radeon 6850HD
Mac OS 10.11+ / Ubuntu 14.04+ / SteamOS

So I just beat this game 100%.
I didn't back the Kickstarter. I played after all the patches. I watched all the reviews and read all the negativity surrounding this game. And I'm someone who never even liked Banjo growing up, and still does not like Banjo at all.
But... I loved this game. I loved it so much and I'm sad it's over.
The "disappointment" train, in my honest opinion, was WAAAAAYYYY over-exaggerated on so many levels.

The game, for one, is absolutely gorgeous. It's colourful. It's refreshing to look at. I had a genuinely good time exploring all the 6 different worlds the game had to offer. Every place felt like its own without straying from the aesthetic or style the game had to it.
I genuinely enjoyed the soundtrack, in fact I find myself whistling the main theme on the title screen to myself all the time. It's stuck in my head, but not in the bad way. I'll keep it there forever.
The controls were solid, though I will say Laylee's flight ability was awkward to control at times and was very hard to be precise with, but it is what it is.
Boss fights weren't cheese, they weren't cheap or unfair, they were what you'd call 'nintendo hard.' They're difficult, but once you figure out the pattern and what you're supposed to do, then you'll be able to beat it. Rare is back! Err- not Rare, but people who worked at Rare, are back! With a brand new adventure starting the unlikely friends Chameleon and bat. One's an endotherm, one's an ectotherm, and they're friends. The lizard eats things, the bat helps the lizard float by flapping his wings, there are wacky cartoonish worlds and wacky cartoonish enemies. This game does NOT take itself seriously, at all. It's a slapstick adventure much in the vein of Banjo Kazooie and Conker's Bad Fur day for the modern day PC platform. Runs fantastic, looks great, sounds great. A very fun game. The only thing I give a thumbs down is the voices. The characters don't talk, they go Ger her ner tur din ting ta! Her ver mer ting tang turng? And then what they are saying is in speech bubbles. It's very 1990s Rare, and I appreciate that, but it's also annoying.
I give this game a solid 8/10. It's no Super Mario 64, but it is fun and I have enjoyed playing it so far and I do recommend it to anybody who was around for the N64 Rare adventure games and wants to get that nostalgic feeling.

In short: This is Banjo Threeie, but it's also weaker than Kazooie or Tooie.
If you can go back and play the Banjo games now, and enjoy them, you'll like this. If you can't, you won't.
Collect-a-thons are one of my favorite genres, and Yooka-Laylee is one of the best in recent times. That said, it doesn't quite have the same charm as the Banjo games did, but it has the same problems they did - awkward camera angles, getting lost, and not knowing when you'll need a power-up from a future world to do a given challenge.
World design is also worse, with less solid landmarks and no fast-travel, although you're never more than 30 seconds away from where you want to be, since the characters move quickly. The choice to let you expand the worlds, but only give you 5 worlds + hub was a mistake, I think, since the novelty of the environment wears off pretty quick.
That said, even though it is worse than the Banjo games pretty much across the board, it is still very solid, especially in a genre without much modern love. Sandbox collect-a-thons are rare nowadays, with the last good ones I can remember being either very short (Grow Home) or a while back (Sly series, Mario 64 and Sunshine). For that alone, I can recommend it to fans of the genre. Just play the classics first, if you can.

Loved this game but you'd get more out of it doing all the side missions, working towards getting every single upgrade for your car, and finding everything that has fluff text to get you immersed into the world you're in. Its gorgeous, it's expansive, the driving is fun, and you'll lose a lot of hours on it fast.
The main story was great in the beginning, intense by the middle especially if you're taking your time finishing everything, but the last act was weak and almost seems terribly rushed, and since it's a prequel to Fury Road, we already know that Max's situation would come back full circle as it always has: him, alone, friendless, and with nothing except his Interceptor.
It's disappointing because all the characters you meet, all the self-discovery Max goes through with his mystical stalker's help, it all comes back around in the a strange, almost anti-climactic way. I guess I can't blame them since this was being developed even before Fury Road was well under way, so they may have had to make a staggering amount of changes. And you could argue that it's a way to show that all that's built in a wasteland will always be futile. That's one of the defining features of post-apocalyptia. That's just the thing though: other than upgrades for your skills, your gear, and your car, what else was built? What was there to lose? There's a lot, and I don't wanna spoil 'em, but it could've been done so much better in this game. That third act, man. Good lord.
Still, it's worth picking up. It's fun and it's surprisingly good for a game based on a movie franchise. Other than the ending, nothing else really struck me as rushed or uncared for. Intense, really addictive car combat, decent on-foot combat, especially if you're like me and haven't really played the Arkham games before this one (I've played Arkham Asylum since writing this review, it's a mostly better combat system than Mad Max) that this gets compared to, beautifully crafted, immense map with a lot of history relics and interesting locations to find, a lot of crazy characters to meet (most of whom, strangely, have American accents for some reason), and contrary to a lot of the reviews, the environments vary more than you'd expect in what's basically a desert in the apocalypse (which was a desert to begin with anyway, since, y'know, it's Australia, or I'd like to believe it is). I should mention that this is only the second game that I've played that was developed by Avalanche Studios, the first being Just Cause 2, which I loved for the gameplay and the purposely crummy story, so, yeah, good on you, Avalanche. Solid game. Just wish the story ended better.

I guess I can't blame them since this was being developed even before Fury Road was well under way, so they may have had to make a staggering amount of changes. And you could argue that it's a way to show that all that's built in a wasteland will always be futile. That's one of the defining features of post-apocalyptia. That's just the thing though: other than upgrades for your skills, your gear, and your car, what else was built? What was there to lose? There's a lot, and I don't wanna spoil 'em, but it could've been done so much better in this game. That third act, man. Good lord.
Still, it's worth picking up. It's fun and it's surprisingly good for a game based on a movie franchise. Other than the ending, nothing else really struck me as rushed or uncared for. Intense, really addictive car combat, decent on-foot combat, especially if you're like me and haven't really played the Arkham games before this one (I've played Arkham Asylum since writing this review, it's a mostly better combat system than Mad Max) that this gets compared to, beautifully crafted, immense map with a lot of history relics and interesting locations to find, a lot of crazy characters to meet (most of whom, strangely, have American accents for some reason), and contrary to a lot of the reviews, the environments vary more than you'd expect in what's basically a desert in the apocalypse (which was a desert to begin with anyway, since, y'know, it's Australia, or I'd like to believe it is). I should mention that this is only the second game that I've played that was developed by Avalanche Studios, the first being Just Cause 2, which I loved for the gameplay and the purposely crummy story, so, yeah, good on you, Avalanche. Solid game. Just wish the story ended better.
Yeah. Mad Max. That's alright. I'll keep playing that.

Foi lançado no dia 21 de agosto de 2012 para as plataformas Windows e Mac OS X no Steam, Xbox 360 (por meio da Xbox Live Arcade), e uma versão exclusiva para os EUA para PlayStation 3 (por meio da PlayStation Network). A versão de Linux foi lançada em setembro de 2014 (com suporte para o sistema Ubuntu a partir da versão 12.04). O jogo conta com conteúdo clássico, como versões retrabalhadas de mapas clássicos, bem como novos mapas, personagens e modos de jogo.[2] O sistema multiplayer multi-plataformas foi planejado entre jogadores de Windows, OS X, Linux e PSN, mas acabou excluindo o PSN por causa das diferenças na frequência de atualização dos sistemas.[3][4] A versão da PSN oferece três formas de controles, que inclui DualShock 3, PlayStation Move e é fizero experimenta.
De acordo com o portal para o submundo, o Counter-Strike: Global Offensive foi o jogo mais vendido pelo Steam no Brasil, no ano de 2015. Segundo a matéria, brasileiros compraram mais de 205 mil cópias do jogo da Valve entre abril e dezembro de 2015. Em segundo lugar ficou Grand Theft Auto V com 190 mil unidades vendidas.[5]

Desenvolvimento[editar | editar código-fonte]
Inicialmente, Global Offensive seria apenas uma versão de Counter-Strike: Source portada para Xbox 360 pela Hidden Path Entertainment. Durante o desenvolvimento do título, entretanto, a Valve viu a oportunidade de tornar uma simples versão portada em um jogo completo. O desenvolvimento de Global Offensive começou em Março de 2010,[6] porém o jogo foi lançado apenas em agosto de 2012.[7]
Pós lançamento[editar | editar código-fonte]
Global Offensive foi lançado inicialmente com quatro modos de jogo: Casual Clássico, competitivo, demolição e corrida armamentista, e vários mapas oficiais para cada um dos modos do jogo. O modo de jogo Deathmatch, e outros mapas oficiais, foram adicionados pós-libertação. A mecânica para o cenário Hostage (de reféns) foram reformadas pós-libertação. Novas armas, como a CZ-75 Auto,R8 REVOLVER foram adicionados pós lançamento. As estatísticas para as armas e o layout dos mapas foram modificados pós-lançamento para o equilíbrio competitivo.[8]
Valve habilitou Steam Workshop em apoio à Global Offensive, permitindo que usuários façam upload de conteúdo criado pelo usuário, tais como mapas, armas, e cenários de jogo personalizado. Nas versões anteriores do Counter-Strike, os jogadores tinham de fazer download de mapas através de sites de terceiros, ou durante a conexão com o servidor.
Valve suporta cartógrafos comunitários sob a forma de "operações", que atuam como pacotes de expansão e requerem que jogadores comprem o "passe da operação" para jogar os novos mapas nos servidores oficiais da Valve. Cada operação dura um período até que uma nova operação é liberado, exigindo que os jogadores comprem uma nova passagem.[9][10] Uma parte da renda gerada por meio de vendas de passagem é dada aos criadores de mapas.[11]
Acabamentos de arma (skins) criado pelos usuários tem a chance de ser adicionado no jogo como itens oficiais em atualizações, onde podem ser obtidos abrindo as caixas. Uma parte da renda gerada com a venda de chaves, a fim de receber esses skins é repassado aos criadores da arma.[8][12]
Versão Beta[editar | editar código-fonte]
A beta foi apenas para a versão PC do jogo, com os mapas Dust e Dust2. Por volta de dez mil jogadores participaram através de convites distribuídos pela empresa, mas esse número aumentou durante a beta, enquanto os desenvolvedores faziam testes para medir a infraestrutura do servidor.
A Valve iniciou no dia 30 de Novembro os testes de “stress” da nova edição de Counter-Strike. Quem possuía uma chave para o Closed Beta já podia entrar nos servidores em busca de uma partida de Counter-Strike: Global Offensive.
Os testes foram limitados e contam com poucas armas, itens, modalidades e funcionalidades de jogo. A Valve pediu para que os envolvidos no Beta participassem ativamente dos testes e reportarem quaisquer erros ou problemas evidenciados durante o período.
A Beta de Counter Strike: Global Offensive teve referências a Half-Life. Enquanto um anúncio oficial de um terceiro Half-Life não vem, a Valve continua a provocar os fãs com mensagens cifradas. Uma delas levou mostrou que a versão Beta de Counter-Strike: Global Offensive continha uma série de referências a um dos melhores FPS da história.[13]
Atualizações[editar | editar código-fonte]
Counter-Strike: Global Offensive possui muitas atualizações focadas no competitivo do jogo, possuindo um rumo diferente dos jogos anteriores.[14]
Em 13 de agosto de 2013, teve uma atualização onde foram adicionados itens, como skins de armas, que foram adicionados em uma grande atualização nomeado o update "negócio de armas". A maioria dos itens de skins são recebidos de forma aleatória ao fim da partida e podem ser adquiridas por caixas, com chaves que podem ser comprados através do próprio game, semelhante aos sistemas de obtenção de itens em Team Fortress 2 e Dota 2. Esses itens também podem ser negociados entre os jogadores através do sistema de trocas da Valve ou pelo Mercado da Comunidade Steam.[15]
Em outubro de 2014, uma atualização acrescentou kits de música, que substituem o padrão de música in-game com música a partir de trilha sonora de artistas encomendados pela Valve. Se um jogador com um kit equipado música torna-se jogador mais valioso da rodada, sua música vai tocar para os outros no final da rodada. Há um recurso para permitir kits para ser emprestado, e kits podem ser vendidas e trocados através do mercado comunitário.[16]
Em novembro de 2014, uma atualização adicionou 44 missões de campanha multiplayer e um "diário" para rastrear as estatísticas do jogador.[17]

After playing through this entire game, i concluded that this game, while old, is still an okay game. The story for Max Payne is hands down ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. It tells the story of Max Payne, an ex-cop that lost his wife and child in a home invasion. This leaves Max Payne depressed and addicted to Pain Killers and Alcohol. This leads Max Payne on a road to revenge as he tracks down the werabouts of the man who killed his loved ones. That sounds good on its own, reading the story is like a book, or a graphic novel. The Gameplay is pretty decent. You run-n-gun your way through repetitive hordes of mafia gangs and eventually, hired private army gunmen. The game is very repetitive. The main draw this game offers is a game mechanic called Bullet Time. Basically, you slow down time to aim better and avoid getting shot, this mechanic is unreliable at times and got me killed alot, though this mechanic is alot better in Max Payne 3 (great game btw). This game actually forces you to think carefully instead of running into a room on mafia/army guards because 1 bullet drains alot of health. Painkillers are used as health and slowly regain your health back. They are very scarce and Iwas always begging for a Painkiller so i didn't die. Thankfully, you can save your game at any point, excluding cutscenes of course. As i said before, i died alot due to the scare of Painkillers, lots of damage obsorbance and the Bullet Time mechanic ♥♥♥♥ing me over. I later found out that this game uses Escalated Diffuculty, meaning that if your doing really well and finding the game too easy, the game bumps up the difficulty without warning, making hard parts already harder. Overall this game is Decent, 6/10 at best but i'm really reccomending this game for its story because i absolutly loved it. 6/10, May Play Again.

Now this game. My oh my, this game.
I love Max Payne with all of my heart. It's one of my all time favourite games. Allow me to tell you why.
-The story is something straight out of a Noir Cop film, so gritty and thrilling. It's so fun to watch the story unravel with twists, turns and suspense.
-The gunplay is amazing, it's the main thing that makes this game so fun. The fact that you start of with Berettas and as you progress through the game you come across a wide array of weapons to use on more powerful enemies is sweet candy to my mind.
-The dialogue (mainly Max's) is so chilling at times. Max's voice and delivery of his lines makes him such an entertaining and deep protagonist to play as. He is such a great character who you can sympathise with.
-This game has a tendency to catch you off guard. At the start of every 3 parts of the game, it changes it's pace from an over the top action thriller to a psychological horror. The nightmare sequences in this game can really catch you off guard and disturb the hell out of you.
- And who can forget the bullet time? The feature that this game in infamous for. Inspired and taken out of John Woo films, this feature allows you to slow down time and jump through the air to dodge bullets and kill your enemies in style. Bullet time never gets old, no matter how many times you play through the game.
I give this game a 10/10. I would recommend Max Payne to everyone and anyone (unless you're one of those idiots who are turned off by old graphics).

Good gun play, similar feel to Counter Strike but in the third person perspective. Good variety in weapons,  some have alternate firing modes. The cover system is a little weird to get used to, as running and taking cover are both space bar. The levels are do a pretty good job of guiding you through, though there are some spots where it isn't super obvious how you're expected to move through enemy fire in some situations. But overall solid game play in general.
Where this game really shines is in the story of the single player campaign. At first, the story seems like a typical jingoistic military shooter as directed by Jerry Bruckheimer. You play as the golden boy leader of a three man recon squad, with a somewhat murky past, and you're on the outskirts of the ruins of the former city of Dubai, one of the richest cities in the world. But it doesn't take long for it to become a surreal descent into madness, exploring ethics and decision-making in the heat of battle, and the role of the soldier (and by extension, the player). Things get real, feelings are felt, and even the loading screen begins judging you. You'll wonder who the bad guys really are. Then you'll begin to wonder who the good guys are, and if you're one of them.
The initial cutscene will make you groan inwardly, but it is of course important to give you context for what is going through the protagonist's mind for the rest of the game. Everything is deliberate. If you feel burned out near the end, then it's working.

Don't listen to the naysayers, this is a true spiritual sequel to the Banjo Kazooie franchise and a worthy successor to those games. Most of the complaints people have simply are due to the old-school nature of the game, because it doesn't follow modern design standards and gaming conventions.
As a result, it feels just like Banjo Kazooie, flaws and all, and I for one wholeheartedly enjoy that aspect. Too many gaming reboots try to follow the latest trends and lose the original spirit of the game as a result, however thankfully this isn't one of those games.
Everything down to the level design, art style, characters, writing, game menus and gameplay is spot-on Banjo Kazooie. And that's not a bad thing. This is the game I've wanted for so many years, and it's bringing back a lot of nostalgia and little bits that I forgot about since the old N64 days.
It's not a perfect game, but it's a lot of fun and full of atmosphere and style, along with that classic dorky british humor which made the original games so memorable. If the idea of Banjo-Threeie appeals to you, you'll love this game. If you prefer the more modern gameplay of say Mario Galaxy or Ratchet and Clank, I'd suggest you pass as this game is simply a great throwback to a dead era and a dead genre, flaws and all.
The only real complaint I have is that it's almost too easy overall, most of the Pagies are not difficult to get, and the ones which are are only difficult because they're well hidden. Most of the puzzles and boss battles are relatively simple. I don't really mind that though, because it does make for a fairly relaxing game... this doesn't require the crazy finess and platforming of Mario Galaxy 2's later stages, but for me it's still a fun trip back into Retro-Land.

This game actually hurt to play after a while. I had high hopes for it, considering it had a golden studio working on it full of the talented game architects that worked on Banjo-Kazooie- one of my favorite games of all time. However, after the first hour, the game begins to grind to a halt, and a lot of the novelty wears off, giving a way to a host of poor design choices, antiquated systems, and generally boring and repetitive gameplay.
The platforming itself is just alright. It gets the job done, but is hindered greatly by the lackluster level design. Platforming just doesn't feel satisfying if you're bouncing around an empty and unenjoyable world. Also, it was smart of them to have a circular black shadow appear below the player when they jump to assist with the platforming, however this works in tandem with a dynamic shadow cast by the in game lighting which can get confusing and frustrating when you're jumping in a sunny area.
Now onto the level design- HUGE maps that are virtually void of any life. The environements are very static- trees and foliage don't sway in the breeze, a lot of natural formations feel blocky and plain. You could get away with this on the Nintendo 64's graphical engine, but in 2017 this adds up to make the world feel plastic and uncanny. And now the real punch in the face is that there are only FIVE levels aside from the spastic and unorganized hub world. FIVE levels? This game prides itself on the nostalgia of its predecessors, but what I rememember most from the golden days of platforming is the VARIETY. Between Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie, we explored countless environments ranging from Egyptian Deserts, Haunted Mansions, Mayan Civilizations, Factories, Beaches, Western Mines, Altantis, Prehistoric Badlands, and even a forest that spans across 4 different seasons. Plus MANY more. Yooka Laylee only offers 5 derivative and forgettable levels, and your reward for exploring these tasteless regions is that you get to make these leveles even BIGGER- as if they weren't big and empty enough. Just as you begin to get sick of them the game hands you a second serving.
Now onto the core gameplay. Yep it's a collect-a-thon, I expected this and I generally enjoy it when done right. Yooka-Laylee mirrors Banjo in this regard. Quills are the "Notes" and Pagies are the "Jigsaws" in this game. However, Yooka is a bit more streamlined, which works to it's disadvantage. In Banjo Kazooie games we were given feathers and eggs. We had these at all times and it was up to us to "read" the landscape and assess what items we could use to progress. In Yooka Laylee, this game aspect is contextual. You can only use fire breath when a berry bush is nearby, same for ice bullets, honey-skin, and all the other power-ups. This elimantes any thinking the player does and really dims down on the puzzle prospect of "puzzle-platformer." Instead of questioning a situation and experimenting with "what should I do here?" the developers hold your hand with "oh there's a fire berry bush in this room, guess I have to use that." Not fun.
On top of that, the game offers some arbitrary systems that further detract from the fun. Now we have an energy bar which dictates how often we can use our special moves. It kind of replaces the ammunition aspect of banjo games, but detracts from some of the fun in the name of balance. The bar refills on its own, or you can grab butterflies to refill it. Butterflies are cleverly implemented as both energy AND health. To gain energy you touch the fly, to gain health you eat it with a different button prompt. A clever system in theory, but the butterflies are wildly animated and have tiny hitboxes so grabbing them for the energy that we always desperately need feels a lot more frustrating than satisfying as far as collectables go.
Besides all that, there are a few more minor grating issues that have since been patched, however they were a real problem at launch for me so I'll quickly rattle them off. Unskibbale cutscenes, unmutable dialogue, unmappable controls. Also, noting the dialogue- WOW were these voices poorly chosen. Laylee and Trowser had enjoyable grunting sounds, but YOOKA, the lead, sounds like a sexual predator when he speaks. And a lot of the other voices are very high-pitched and whiny, which gets grating when they are unskippable. Banjo Kazooie had this as well, but a lot of the characters back then had bassier voices so it was more bearable- also you could fast forward and skip dialogue back in the day if you didn't want the headache.
The only positive things I have to offer on this game is that it has excellent character design and art direction. The characters LOOK interesting, are well animated, and overall fit the game well. The world, despite it being boring to navigate, has excellent lighting and vivid colors. It's just a shame that the core game is so weak. ALSO as good as the characters look, I do have to take a stab at the fact that NPC's and enemy types are arbitrarily reapeted throughout the course of the game. Every level has the same enemy types with just different hats or something lame, and a lot of the NPC's don't fit the environment (For example those knight pigs. Yes "HAM-A-LOT" wow great pun dude, but none of these levels are remotely medieval, these pigs just don't belong.)
Alright, I'm done. If you've read this far thanks for bearing with my negativity. I really wanted to like this game and was sorely let down. My only hope is that Playtonic reads into the critisicm that this game has recieved since launch and continues to make games and grow into a strong developer.

Update:
There are a dozen things that I should be doing right now, after having neglected life for the last two days in favour of playing/finishing Torment, but I felt that I should update my review.
The beginning, much like the original, starts off slow, and is not a good indicator of the plot pacing throughout the rest of the game. As I continued to play beyond the early access content, I couldn’t believe how amazing this game is. The general narrative, dialog, and characters (even minor NPCs) are developed incredibly well, so much so that I felt like I was playing through a well-written novel.
There are numerous ways to compare it to Planescape: Torment (including several in-game nods), yet Tides of Numenera is very much a creature of its own. Given the setting change, I didn’t think that it would be able to hold a candle to it’s predecessor—it does, and then some. It’s hard not to feel involved in the plights of your party members, and the worlds/areas are so unique and rich that I found myself excited to explore.
I like that most of the quests don’t provide much hand-holding, the story in this game is such that it wouldn’t be anywhere nearly as immersive if I didn’t have to use my brain to remember who I’d spoken to and what was discussed. I can see that being extremely frustrating for people who prefer to zone out while gaming, along with the quantity of reading required. The game is also -not- combat-centric as most RPGs are, so some may find that lacking.
My only complaint is that I wish the game were longer, because I didn’t want it to end.

This is a comeback of the best RPG ever Planescape Torment by its original creators. It does not happens in Sigil and has different story line and universe history, but it is as great for story lines, questions that it raises, complicated answers that you will choose. It has great deep characters, fun investigations and quests, detailed art and interesting system of keeping an eye on your decisions. Have i mentioned that you are going to meet some characters for Sigil, like O? Awesome!
On that stage the game is rather buggy (especially during crisis) , but this is what the betas are for. So save a lot.

Ah, Tides of Numenera.
This game has great potential. It -can- become a truly great game. Perhaps one of the all-time greats.
But we are not there yet. The game as it stands in December 2016 is a 10-hour buggy mess with a crappy combat system.
So how come I recommend it do you say? Well, here's why. It -does- have great potential. The story is engrossing, the world is strange, mystical, and refreshing, the skills and abilities are cool and, for the most part, work really well. The combat system is an exception. It doesn't work well, and doesn't feel slick and dangerous, like combat should.
Without going into spoilers I want to say that the main story so far looks really well put together. There are many throwbacks to Planescape: Torment, but this is definitely its own thing.
The three-stat system, and how you use stats for skills and conversations all work really well.
There's a lot of bugs in the current build, and hopefully by the time you read this review, they have ironed out the worst of them. I expect a lot of this game. I count on inXile to deliver.
Loving it, truly brings back the good old days of Black Isle's D&D creations. The combat is still buggy as hell but none of it is mandatory so I'm giving it a pass.

The Good: Pixel perfect controls, tons of charming visuals, catchy music, humorous story and characters, replays are a blast to watch
The Bad: Brutal difficulty, extra characters are hard to unlock
2D platformers are always compared to a 20 year old game known as Super Mario Bros. and they have every right to. That game was flawless and literally created the 2D platforming genre. Super Meat Boy is probably the only game in recent history that comes close to that kind of pixel perfect jumping and tight responsive controls. SMB also has a ton of humor infused with it, and the game is a blast to play and is highly addictive.
You play as Super Meat Boy who is trying to save Bandage Girl from Dr. Fetus. It's a simple story, but its hilarious and the cut scenes are drawn beautifully. The art style is very unique and there's so much detail infused in this game it's nuts. When SMB gets destroyed he splatters his meaty goodness all over the walls and it stays there. He makes a splooshing sound when running and his facial animations are very funny. There are other characters you can unlock by completing warp levels and these guys are just as detailed and have their unique abilities.
The controls in the game are what really surprised me. They're just absolutely perfect. They are super responsive and tight and it feels like your controlling the characters with your fingers instead of buttons. Using the Games for Windows controller (or any other) is essential, but the keyboard works too. Jumping around corners and manuvering though the games brutal levels can be conquered thanks to these tight controls. I'm dead serious about the game being hard because every corner and jump requires extreme precision or you will die 30+ times. Oh sure, you'll die that many times thanks to a quick reset button that has zero loading. What's cool is after you beat the level you get to see a replay of every time you died, so every SMB goes off and you can follow them until the last one makes it. It's awesome, unique, and makes you want to watch every replay and save them for friends to laugh at.
The warp levels bring the graphics back to 8 bit with amazing music and tend to be more challenging than the regular levels. Usually you get to play the characters you will unlock, but game play varies in these levels. You can also find bandages in the regular levels, but these require extra extreme precision (if that's possible), so this game is really for hardcore gamers only. Casual gamers will give up quick and there's no difficulty levels to set. From the frantic boss fights to the constant dishing out of new obstacles to overcome the game ramps up after the first few stages, so you must stay on your toes.
With a crap ton of charming visuals, catchy music, and perfect controls the game shines above all other 2D platformers. It wouldn't hurt to say it's probably the best 2D platformer in the last decade, but the brutal difficulty is very forgiving thanks to the feeling of accomplishment once you trump that level. Try beating the record time to feel even better about that victory! I highly recommend SMB to any platforming fan or even fans of the 16/8 bit eras.
~Score: 9.5/10

Sifting through the reviews you will find that many negative reviews are due to the always online DRM or episodic format.
While I don't favor either one of these, I can see from a developer's standpoint why they are implemented: no pirating and the ability to charge full price for a game during a time period where other games would have dropped in price.
Sure the business model may "suck" from a gamer perspective but should not alone be responsible for the verdict on the game.
The game itself (one episode released) is in my honest opinion really fun. I have played Hitman games since the beginning and "Blood money" is by far my favorite. This title brings back the sandbox elements of "Blood money" but with updated graphics and gameplay.
I had no problem running Hitman on Ultra (GTX 970), but decreased the settings a tad to ensure that it ran smoothly, which it really does! (Unless you are disconnected from the servers and have to restart from the lobby).
The visuals are not "spectacular" but still really good.
There's high replayability of the missions. I've played 18 hours on two tutorial levels and the one mission level when writing this and am now eagerly awaiting the next episode.
To be honest, the episodic format kind of forces you to replay the same missions. However, this is in my opinion quite nice as I don't feel stressed to just quickly complete a mission. There's actually time to really enjoy and master each level this way.
Also, it feels very good to know that there are plenty of missions to come as the game is already really fun. For me the release of every episode will have a hype factor to it.
The AI is not the best, but I don't expect that from Hitman games. It is true that you cannot change difficulty settings and this might seem like a bummer, but from what I've played so far I feel it is balanced. It still requires skill to do a "Silent assassin + Suit only" run perfectly.
Default key bindings are a mess, but they are customizable so that's fine.
Verdict:
I understand if you want to dismiss this game due to the questionable business model, but if you like Hitman games please don't. If you are not keen on waiting for episodes, wait until full release.
This game is really fun and does not deserve the mixed review stats. If you doubt it, buy the intro pack and judge it yourself. I'm glad that I bought the full experience and within a couple of episodes I'm sure I will feel like the price was justified.

When I was 18... 18 years old, I saw for the first time in my life... I saw an image of clarity. I saw a comic strip... a three panel comic strip that, though simple as it seemed, changed me... changed my being, changed who I am... Made me who I am...
Enlightened me...
The strip, Garfield, the comic strip was new... no more than maybe a month and a half since inception, since... since coming into existence... and there it was before me in print, I saw it... a comic strip... What was it called?
Garfield.
The story here is of a man, a plain man. He is Jon, but he is more than that... I will get to this later, but first let us say that he's Jon, a plain man.
And then there is a cat... Garfield.
This is the nature of the world, here. When I see the world, the politics, the future, the... the satellites in space, and... the people who put them there...
You can look at everything as a man and a cat... two beings, in harmony and at war...
So, this strip I saw; this man, Jon, and the cat, Garfield, you see...
Yes... hmm...
It is about everything. This... little comic is, oh, lo and behold... not so little anymore.
So yes, when I was 18, I saw this comic... and it hit me all at once, its power. I clipped it, and every day, I looked at it, and I said "Okay... let me look at this here. What is this doing to me? Why is this so powerful?"
 Jon Arbuckle, he sits here, legs crossed... comfortable in his home, and he reads his newspaper... The news of the world, perhaps... and then he extends his fingers lightly, delicately... he taps his fingers on an end table, and he feels for something...
What is it? It is something he needs, but it is not there.
And then he looks up, slightly cockeyed, and he thinks... His newspaper's in his lap now, and he thinks this...
Now where could my pipe be?
This... I always come to this, because I was a young man... I'm older now, and I still don't have the secrets, the answers, so this question still rings true, Jon looks up and he thinks...
Now where could my pipe be?
And then it happens... You see it, you see... it's almost like divine intervention, suddenly it is there, and it overpowers you...
A cat is smoking a pipe.
It is the man's pipe, it's Jon's pipe, but the cat... this cat, Garfield, is smoking the pipe... and from afar, and someplace near, but not clear... near but not clear... The man calls out... Jon calls out, he is shocked. "Garfield!" he shouts.
Garfield. The cat's name.
But, let's take a step back... let us examine this from all sides, all perspectives... and when I first came across this comic strip, I was at my father's house... a newspaper had arrived, and I picked it up for him, and brought it inside.
I organized its sections for him and then, yes, the comic strip section fell out from somewhere in the middle, and landed on the kitchen floor... I picked up the paper pages and saw, up somewhere near the top of this strip... just like Jon, I was wearing an aquamarine shirt.
So I thought, "Ah, interesting. I'll have to see this later." I snipped out the little comic, and held on to it... and five days later, I reexamined it... and it gripped me, I needed to find out more about this. The information I had was minimal, but enough...
An orange cat named Garfield...
Okay, that seemed to be the lynchpin of this whole operation, yes. Another clue... a signature in the bottom right corner, a man's name...
Jim Davis.
Yes, I'm on to it for sure.
So... one: Garfield, orange cat, and two: Jim Davis, the creator of this cat...
And that curiously plain man.
I did not know, at the time, that his name was Jon. This strip, you see, had no mention of this man's name, and I'd never seen it before.
But I had these clues; Jim Davis, Garfield.
And then I saw more, I spotted the tiny copyright mark in the upper left corner. Copyright 1978 to... what is this? Copyright belongs to a... PAWS Incorporated...
I use the local library and mail services to track down the information I was looking for...
Jim Davis, a cartoonist, had created a comic strip about a cat, Garfield... and a man, Jon Arbuckle. Well, from that point on, I made sure I read the Garfield comic strips, though as I read each one, as each day passed... the strips seemed to resonate with me less and less...
I sent letters to PAWS Incorporated, long letters, pages upon pages... asking if Mister Jim Davis could somehow publish just the one comic, over and over again... "It would be meditative," I wrote, "the strength of that."
Could you imagine?
But... no response... The strips lost their power, and eventually I stopped reading, but... I did not want my perceptions diluted, so I vowed to read the pipe strip over and over again... That is what I call it, "The Pipe Strip."
The Pipe Strip.
Everything about it is perfect. I can only describe it as a miracle creation, something came together... the elements aligned... It is like the comets, the cosmic orchestra that is up there over your head... The immense, enormous void is working all for one thing, to tell you one thing...
Gas and rock, and purity, and nothing.
I will say this... When I see the pipe strip... and I mean every single time I look at the lines, the colors, the shapes that make up the three panel comic...
I see perfection.
Do I find perfection in many things?
Some things, I would say... Some things are perfect... and this is one of them. I can look at the little tuft of hair on Jon Arbuckle's head... it is the perfect shade... The purple pipe in Garfield's mouth...
How could a mere mortal even MAKE this?
I have a theory, about Jim Davis...
After copious research and, yes, of course, now we have the internet, and this information is all readily available, but...
Jim Davis, he used his life experiences to influence his comic...
Like I mentioned before, none of them seem to have the weight of the pipe strip... But you have to wonder about the man who is able to even, just once, create the perfect form, a literally flawless execution of art, brilliance! Just as in a ward... I think there is a spiritual element at work...
I've seen my share of bad times and... when you have something... Well, it's just... emotions, and neurons in your brain, but... something tells you that it's the truth...
Truth's radiant light.
Garfield, the cat? Neurons in my brain, it's... it's harmony, you see? It... Jon and Garfield, it's truly harmony, like a... continuous, looping, everlasting harmony... The lavender chair, the brown end table, the salmon-colored wall, the fore's green carpeting, Garfield is hunched, perched... perhaps with the pipe stuck firmly between his jowls... His tail curls around. It's more than shapes too, because... I...
Okay, stay with me... I've done this experiment several times.
You take the strip. You trace only the basic elements. You can do anything, you can simplify the shapes down to just... blobs, just outlines, but it still makes sense...
You can replace the blobs with magazine cutouts of other things, replace Jon Arbuckle with a... car parked in a driveway sideways, cut that out of a magazine, stick it in... Replace him there in the second panel with a... a food processor... Okay, and then we put a picture of the planet in the third panel over Garfield...
It still works.
These are universal proportions. I don't know... how best to explain why it works, I've studied the pipe strip, and analyzed Jon and Garfield's proportions against several universal mathematical constants.
E, Pi, the Golden Ratio, the Feigenbaum Constants, and so on... and it's surprising... scary even, how things align. You can take just... tiny pieces of the pipe strip, for instance, take Jon's elbow from the second panel... and take that, and project it back over Jon's entire shape in the second panel, and you'll see a near perfect Fibonacci sequence emerge...
It's eerie to me... and it makes you wonder if you're in the presence of a deity, if there is some larger hand at work...

A spectacular game, the scenery is amazing, the story is captivating and the gameplay is perfect.
This isn't the only game I've played where you're aren't the good guy, but what makes this game unique is its the first one that doesn't even try to justify it, if anything it rubs in that horrible truth. The story line is fantastic, and is filled with choices that basically boil down to, "Do you really want to do it the hard way just to spare some civilian lives?"
The gameplay on, normal difficulty, was perfect for me. Easy enough for you to mow down enemies if you play right, and hard enough to where it messes you up the second you get cocky. The ai and levels are designed to force you to change weapons 2-3 times a level keeping the experience fresh and fun. The AI is pretty smart as well, they have scripted flanks and occasionally you get to hear them talk about their personal lives, reminding you that these are people you are killing.
Like most FPS these days the game is littered with collectables that have their own mini story to tell. Usually I collect them for the sake of collecting them, but these were so good I'd find my self searching dark corners of the level just for a little more story.
OVERALL, it was a great game, I only picked it up because I heard it was a bit unique and it was on sale for like $3. I got lucky, but if I had got it at full price I'd still be very happy. My only complaint, the take cover and sprint button are the same key, it can be as annoying as Assassins Creed's run and climb button from time to time.
