When I first got this game I really enjoyed it. It has good music, it's cute, and I liked having my own little garden and spirits to help around. After a few hours, I felt done with the game, but I couldn't really leave it with achievements unfinished. It took me 33 hours to finally get all of them. While this game has some good points, I don't find them good enough to really recommend this game to others.
The good aspects are as I said, good music, cute game, as well as what I suppose is generally a decent concept. It's a good game for achievment hunters because if you're dedicated, you could finish them all in less time than what I took considering I wasn't paying attention 100% of the time. It helps that your spirits can help pick things like mushrooms up, so the 6666 mushrooms achievement isn't as intimidating as it seems. You can also play this game while not completely paying attention to it, allowing this game to be a good side thing if say you're doing something else or waiting for another thing to finish, you can just do some clicking around on this game in the meantime without worrying about saving progress or anything of the sort.
The not so good parts of this game include all of the clicking (one of the achievements including clicking 2000 dragonflies). A chunk of the ingredients needed to make certain recipes in order to get coins requires you to click the creatures that run/fly/etc across your screen. The coins are of importance, as they allow you to buy more plants, expand your garden, etc. which all help you level up in the long run. I also found that this game became a little tedious after a few hours and I didn't really want to continue it. I sort of reluctantly did finish it (on the side of doing other things, as I don't believe this game is one that you could just sit and completely focus your attention on without getting bored) for the part of me that needed this game to be completed before given up on. Lastly, the biggest down side to this game is that I feel like it doesn't have that much replay value. Other games you can playthrough again for different experiences or to try different styles of play, etc. With this game though, I feel like once you play through it once, if you play through again it's just the same old thing.
Honestly, I don't believe that this game is worth what it costs. I've played better games for much cheaper. I'm glad I got to experience it, but if I were given another opportunity to purchase a game like this for the price that it's at, I wouldn't do it again.

Ready to tend to your lush farmland? Welcome to the swamp your hut sits on as it is ripe to grow plants to harvest. But, you don't exactly sell what you harvest. Armed with a few recipes, the various critter parts, fruits, leaves, and so on can be combined to make various voodoo items to sell.
Armed with only a few plants, you work up your way up to getting more access to different plants and recipes with each level up. Three lanes are available to plant, the top for trees, middle for bushes, and the bottom for herbs. The beginning plants cost a decent amount but the more advanced ones will cost a lot, with the upgrades increasing the price. But these do contain ingredients for products that sell for  higher price than what you start out with. As you get more and more plants you can plant, you will eventually lose space in front of your hut so it will be time to expand. Of course the price will increase with every expansion, but more space equals more cash. I do recommend putting ghosts on the expansions, as you will need to scroll to the side at this point, but I do believe bats only bother plants on your current screen.
Various animals will walk through your garden as they can also provide some ingredients. Of course, more variety will pass through as you level up as even lizards and dragonflies will eventually visit. But be careful of the bats! They will have no mercy to steal from yur garden! I believe the bats will link up to your spirits, as they will not take the mushrooms and bogroots until the spirits can. These will most likely be the ingredients you will be short of the most, including the beehives bees will leave behind. Luckily, there are ways to get more to spawn in forms of totems. Each totem having their own design to correspond to what they will attract when lit. Sadly these come way too apart. Snakes will be one of the earliest animals you need a lot of, but the totem for them don't become available till to 20s levels.
An inventory is available, with limitations set. You have a set amount of each you can take in, with an upgrade increasing it, and once you try to harvest past it, those will be sold for one coin. Giving you a hint that you shouldn't buy anymore of those plants if you keep with having more than you can carry.
But hey, you will not be the only one that can harvest. You can buy animals, starting with a rabbit before you unlock more by leveling up, that you can fatten up by feeding them their prefered food. But if this is going to take resources away from you, why do it? Permitting that you have available spots, you will get a prompt to sacrifice the animal once it is fully fattened up to turn them into a spirit. Forever slaved to your garden as they have to pick the various plants for you. This excludes the mushrooms and bogroots until you get the upgrade. If you place them by the plants they ate, they will also get a boost in growth speed. With the upgrades going to their plucking speeds.
So later game brings you to only needing to scare off bats and picking animal parts once the spirits come in to help. What else can there be? It will occasionally rain, making spirits disappear and animals stop coming around. Even the totems will be put out due to the rain, nullifying their affects. Making you pluck everything yourself on a moment's notice to spice it up a bit. Before you know it, the rain will stop and everything will come back.
Voodoo Garden leaves you to your own devices without a tutorial or what anything does. I do wish it gave some indication of the different aspects, especially when your plants (and those who will be planted there) can diminish in production. It only took a while that bees planted a beehive there and noticed that bees are your savior, where previously I kinda freaked out thinking it would forever block the space as there were no recipes calling for beehives at that time.
Now this is not an idle game. While it does have idle aspects, Voodoo Garden is very much a clicker game and will only continue collecting and growing if it is running. With spirits helping out, you only need to click the bats and the animals walking by the plants, and even than there are recipes that do only require plant items.

ok, wow, where to begin?
well, first off, i liked the story so far as ive seen.  it's an interesting concept and keeps my attention moderately well.  The sound track is good, and i enjoy elements of the gameplay, but...
1)  the graphics are pretty awful.  I mean it, it honestly looks awful, even when comparing it to PST which this is supposed to be the successor to this game.
2)  Combat is a chore.  the few fights i actually had were pretty horrendous, the abilities were pretty pointless as you could only use it once or so and then its done for not just fights, but until you rest next.  it made combat really unsatisfying

Ive played this game no more then two hours and have already ran across over half a dozen (already documented) bugs ranging from game crashes to freezing to simple things like the portraits vibrating weirdly when the mouse scrolls over them.  I know its in early access, but im barely into the game and already finding this many issues?  seems a bit ridiculous to me.
4)  general lack of care for the characters.  When i first played PST, i instantly fell in love with one of the first characters you find.  He was unique, he was witty, and he was memorable.  The 3 companions i met so far ive played with and am trying to want to get to know, but they are just really really boring. don't get me wrong, i want to like this game.  i'm going to play it to completion (or as far along as completion goes for now), and if it changes my mind, i'll gladly rewrite this review with glowing reccomendation, but sadly, this game doesnt live up to half the example of PST. Update:  ok, as of the december 20th update, i need to revise some of my statements.  The graphics, while still lacking, are refined and look a little better. All in all, i still wouldnt reccomend the game for preorder but, maybe when its out february 28th 2017, it might be worth a try.

I'm thinking, hey, they plan for a Q1 2017 release, how unfinished can it be? Very unfinished is the answer.
No way in hell they're releasing in the first quarter of 2017.. but if they do, it's going to be quite the mess.
1. Interface is clunky, with text being cut off, even through character creation, you're picking abilites you don't know anything about because if you hover the ability the text shows up cut off! 4. While I completed their inspirational game PS:T several times and yes, it did not have a strong focus on combat, it feels like this game has contempt for combat. This would be a pretty decent game, if it didn't come from such an experienced team.
The controls are extremely loose, which makes the platforming aggravating to the point of feeling luck-based.
It lacks charm - the characters are very flat and boring, and the humor of the game is self-referential and meme-y (you get an acheivement called "SNAKE SENPAI," as an example.)
The soundtrack sounds exactly like a mish-mash of Banjo-Kazooie songs as opposed to something new and original.
One of the core gameplay mechanics is the choice of whether to expand the current world you're in or move on to the next world, but both must be done in order to fulfill all gameplay.
Meaning that there are two playstyles. Either expand the world as soon as you can and enter a huge, poorly-guided world, or have a constant back-and-forth between levels. Unfortunately, the game supports the second version, going to new worlds to unlock new abilities to use in older worlds, which makes the game feel longer than it is.
There is no real story reason for all of the collectibles. You're given a basic "If the bad guy collects all of the Pagies, they can change the world" plot, but in the game, many of the bad guy's minions themselves hold the Pagies not giving it to their boss, meaning that doesn't hold any structure, PLUS, it also means that if you collect, say, 1 Pagie, then the bad guy's plan has been foiled.
In short, the game runs on nostalgia, which wouldn't be a bad thing if it had the gameplay and story to match.

I admittedly went into this game with high expectations. Banjo-Kazooie was a formative game for me, and still stands as one of my all-time favorites. I go back to it regularly and still enjoy it every time. Yooka Laylee seemed like it could finally be the spirtual Banjo 3 I've been longing for.
But alas, Yooka Laylee does stumbles mightily. The game shows us that 3D platformers in 2017 can't just copy entire concepts from the gold standards of the genre, and become automatic hits.
The pros for Yooka-Laylee: It is an amazing looking game. From a technical perspective, the characters and environments look very well polished. The presentation, from the menu texts to the music are all charming and enjoyable callbacks to the Banjo games that give you a great first impression when you boot it up. Many of the character are fun and have cool designs, although the sound effect VO on the characters hasn't aged particularly well.
Presentation aside, the act of playing the game is where the flaws quickly become clear. The gameplay is the biggest offender that brings this game down. Controlling Yooka and Laylee just doesn't feel good. The movements don't feel quite as snappy as something like a Banjo. Certain moves have just a little bit of latency between your input and when the animation kicks in. Things like the ball roll move (the Talon Trot equivalent) up slopes or aiming for the "egg shoot" move, all feel like you're fighting the game to accomplish what you want to do. Even traversing around the worlds feels like more of a chore than you would want.
And you will be traversing a lot. The worlds in the game are large, much larger than worlds from a Banjo game. But this also ends up working against the game. The worlds are big, but large sections feel empty. Multiple times, I found myself feeling like I'd seen everything I'd like in the world, only to see I'd collected about half of the collectibles. The worlds overstay their welcome, and outside of the casino level, lack interesting set pieces to begin with. Trying to collect everything feels more like a chore than a fun activity.
There's other smaller nitpicks, like the number of collectibles in each world that require you to play the very bad minecart and arcade minigames. But overall, the tricky controls and unappealing worlds are the biggest things that strip most of the fun out of this game.
In short, I'm not mad about this game, I'm just disapointed.

Max Payne is a 3rd person shooter developed by Remedy Entertainment, and published by more companies than a candid celebrity photo. Remedy themselves proceeded to take a 7 year nap in development hell, awakening to release Alan Wake, a much worse game.
What separates Max Payne from every other 3rd person shooter ever made isn't the mechanics, although when those are good they're great, it isn't the graphics, and it isn't even the graphic-novel-style story. It's the sheer presentation, using every element, every polygon they could to bring this dripping noir to life.
Max Payne's lines and delivery of said lines, are incredible. Dialogue certainly isn't underwritten, and you'll be hearing him wax poetic more often than a Shakespeare in a themed museum.
Rest of the story? Not nearly as good. A checklist of cliches and cynicism at said cliches, with the occasional office worker posing as a big-shot mobster, obscured by listless photoshop filters. Saved by breakneck pacing, each trope being ticked off as fast as soccer fans at a losing match. The locales are all grimy, but they're not all grimy basements - from the city streets to harbors to nightclubs, to some weirder inbetweens, Max Payne keeps it fresh, and it keeps it tight.
Aforementioned mechanics to go with those locales are just as beaut - running around firing into mobsters with every weapon in New York never gets old, a far cry from the modern cover shooter. To be still is a lethal mistake.
Now, while Max Payne is worth getting and worth seeing right to the end, it's not by any means a perfect, flawless game. And I'm not talking about the concept of games "aging".
The difficulty curve gets absurdly punishing, with lategame enemies destroying you in 1-2 hits while tanking a dozen rounds to the face in return. It's there when the stylishness of mixing strafing with dives takes a massive hit - you're better off edging around corners and bottlenecking rather than taking them on, especially when it comes to rear end star constellations like grenadiers and shotgun monster-closets.
That's not what the game is about, that's not the game at its best and that's not fun.
You'll see this in action with early boss enemies making a habit of trapping you in a small room and destroying you, each one begging for a mouthful of cheese and thousand-round machinegun projectile bullet-time-vomit to the rest of the face. And despite all this F5/F9 bait, the end still manages to be anticlimactic - no details for obvious reasons, but it resorts to a glorified puzzle.
More importantly, this antique is a pain in the rear to get working. This game is old, untouched and most community patches have gone "missing". I'll just share my method for getting it working.

Deceptively simple. It was a right max pain. It shouldn't be in this state. But it works fine if you do that.
Despite everything, despite all that, this broken, old, ugly game is absolutely worth getting. Not even considered a hard-sell  - Max Payne is one of the best 3rd person, linear shooters ever made.
You'd be doing yourself a favour to give it a spin, and ride the pain train.

Sifting through the reviews you will find that many negative reviews are due to the always online DRM or episodic format.
While I don't favor either one of these, I can see from a developer's standpoint why they are implemented: no pirating and the ability to charge full price for a game during a time period where other games would have dropped in price.
Sure the business model may "suck" from a gamer perspective but should not alone be responsible for the verdict on the game.
The game itself (one episode released) is in my honest opinion really fun. I have played Hitman games since the beginning and "Blood money" is by far my favorite. This title brings back the sandbox elements of "Blood money" but with updated graphics and gameplay.
I had no problem running Hitman on Ultra (GTX 970), but decreased the settings a tad to ensure that it ran smoothly, which it really does! (Unless you are disconnected from the servers and have to restart from the lobby).
The visuals are not "spectacular" but still really good.
There's high replayability of the missions. I've played 18 hours on two tutorial levels and the one mission level when writing this and am now eagerly awaiting the next episode.
To be honest, the episodic format kind of forces you to replay the same missions. However, this is in my opinion quite nice as I don't feel stressed to just quickly complete a mission. There's actually time to really enjoy and master each level this way.
Also, it feels very good to know that there are plenty of missions to come as the game is already really fun. For me the release of every episode will have a hype factor to it.
The AI is not the best, but I don't expect that from Hitman games. It is true that you cannot change difficulty settings and this might seem like a bummer, but from what I've played so far I feel it is balanced. It still requires skill to do a "Silent assassin + Suit only" run perfectly.
Default key bindings are a mess, but they are customizable so that's fine.
Verdict:
I understand if you want to dismiss this game due to the questionable business model, but if you like Hitman games please don't. If you are not keen on waiting for episodes, wait until full release.
This game is really fun and does not deserve the mixed review stats. If you doubt it, buy the intro pack and judge it yourself. I'm glad that I bought the full experience and within a couple of episodes I'm sure I will feel like the price was justified.

There is a scene where two guys are smoking on balcony or something, talking about their lives, the sunset, their experiences, their dreams, their family, their friends. They are not very important characters, just another of the seemingly endless supply of bad guys the game throws at you. After I heard their conversation I stopped a moment before my team and I shot them. They would no longer share their stories, they probably did not expect that peaceful sunset setting over those desolate ruins of a debauched city to be the last thing they saw.
That is when I realized. I was not killing "bad guys", I was killing people. People who had as much to look towards to as I did, and has lived as fully, and I killed them. That is the feeling you should get when taking a life, not a casual dismissal as another number in the kill count, it seems game developers forget to add this most important element to shooters and action games. Shoot first ask questions later seems to be the purveying rule when addressing this genre. So far this is the only game that has made me feel the morality of such a rule. When I killed those two, I realized there was no right or wrong, just difference of opinions that could never be solved and has escalated beyond any form of civil discussion. This was meant to be a short review, with some dry humour, but this is what this game does to you. It makes you feel and regret and question until you've reached a conclusion that satisfies your morals. I still have to find it in me to find the moral compass required to pick up this game again. To steel myself against the immorality of killing and become numb to the feeling of taking a life. I have to draw the line somewhere.

Spec Ops: The Line is a well made AAA console title that unfortunately could have been absolutely friggin awesome had the developers had optimized it more for the PC.
The script was alright, but might have been better if the author had been writing an actual story for a video game than a reality play. Despite the authors pretensions, it seems to be a knock off of Francis Ford Coppola's "Apocalypse Now" with a twist ending. I don't play games like this to think, if I wanted to do so, I would play a game like "This War of Mine," which would be a much better choice.
The voice actors did a pretty good job, and I liked the soundtrack. Visually, Spec Ops: The Line looks pretty good.
The controls are kinda clunky, but I believe this may have to do with it's console roots. Also this is to be expected making the transition from d-pad to keyboard and mouse. I do wish I had more freedom though, when it came to setting up the controls.
Unfortunately one of the main things that keeps Spec Ops: The Line from being a great game is the horrible (and I do mean horrible) squad based AI. Constantly my squadies would run in front of me while I was shooting, bump me, or get in my way so I couldn't target or shoot baddies. Also they often would hide behind cover, not shoot back, and just sit there. Often they would run into hails of gun fire (even though cover was easily available), requiring me to rescue them. Even the enemy AI at times seemed to be, well, challenged. It's strange that games like Freedom Fighters (2003) and F.E.A.R. (2005), released so many years earlier, would have better squad and enemy AI.
Also the levels are very linear, so I couldn't really go off any where and explore anything. It seemed like there was only one path through, and unless was scripted, I couldn't really use tactics like flanking, rear attack, or using terrain elevation. Sometimes I would run for cover when the baddies would show up, and I would be exposed because the the thing I was trying to hide behind was off limits. A few times I had to restart from a previous checkpoint because my guy got stuck and couldn't move (glitch).
All complaints aside, I did have fun playing it. I would recommend getting the console version instead though, but if it's on sale, go ahead and buy it. 6.5 out of 10.

As someone who has more than 300 hours into Pillars, I can say that I am not too excited for Tides.
Pillars easily carries the most coheisve and dramatically presented narrative in a cRPG since Baldur's Gate 2, yet while Tides holds it's place in my library, I earnestly do not expect it to hold up as well.
inXile games tend to carry a very unfinished and unpolished feel to them, which is often overlooked due to quality writing that propells the games from start to finish. Wasteland 2 is an excellent example of this: great story ... but incomplete "product" ... and the hours I've spent with the Early Access of Tides, I get the same impression.
Recent changes have shown a clear trajectory towards simple delivery of a complex story, confirmed by developer responses on the forums to questions regarding removed features (such as a truncated introduction that has been stripped of any ingenuity and unique inspiration that it had during earlier versions). Many suspect this is due to it's concurrent console release, but I suspect there is more to it: as development has unfolded, I believe the inXile scrapped elements that weren't working, which has left visceral gaps in what remains.
Still, inXile's writers are top notch and I will play this game through to the end, but I do not expect it to have much of the replayability that PlaneScape: Torment, Baldur's Gate/2, or Pillars of Eternity possess.

Summary: FPS kill and loot to a decent story. Fun. Violent. Harsh language. Eventually gets repetative, but that takes a while.
Lots of shooting action in this RPG/FPS hybrid. The setting has an excuse for respawns (player and enemy), recharging energy shields, weightless backpacks, and always-full magazines, which is a thoughtful touch. The story is just as rich and well constructed as the setting, with some good twists and genuinely appealing characters; that last despite the fact that everyone in the game is a terrible person.
Six categories of guns, billions of possible unique items, and a ton of customization options allow for each character to play differently from each other, even in the same class. Each level provides additional health, a point for the skill trees, and scaling damage resistance to lower level foes.
The action mixes shooting (smooth), exploration (mostly interesting), platforming (a mixed bag), and vehicle operations (opinions vary) fairly well. The environments are large and good looking, the enemies are diverse enough to force weapon swaps mid combat but few enough to master. Challenges result in Badass Ranks which can be used to improve every single character on your account.
DLCs:
Captain Scarlet and Her Pirate's Booty - Neat idea but flat. Scarlet is the only interesting character, the zones are dull, the enemies reskins of existing foes (sand worms = threshers; pirates = marauders), and the new vehicle is slow. The story is boring as well, "What?  There's treasure over there!?  I will have it!" The loot is mostly decent. Introduces the Seraph items and crystals.
Campaign of Carnage - Pretty good, though you need to be level 50 (and fully equipped) to finish all the content. The story is amusing, well paced, and flows naturally. Foes are mostly bandit reskins, but it's not a problem in this context. The supporting cast is excellent, from new faces, such as Mr. Torgue, to returning friends like Mad Moxxi and Tiny Tina. With a few unique items, and more Seraph items, the loot is pretty good.
Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt - This one starts a little slow, and the huge environments can take a while to get through (especially before you ulock the new vehicles). But the environments are gorgeous, the villain is hillarious, and Sir Hammerlock is Sir Hammerlock. The enemies are a mix of returning foes, reskins, and original challenges; the tribal shamans are both exciting and frustrating to figure out.
Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep - A must buy. Brick, Lilith, and Mordecai sit down to a fantasy table-top role playing game run by Tina, staring characters based upon the six playable classes. It is full of references to books, movies, video games, Dungeons and Dragons, television shows, and the relationships of the people at the table. (During this game, the six vault hunters of Borderlands 2 are torturing intelligence out of a captured Hyperion employee.) The foes are interesting and unique, combining elements of previous foes into new and fun variants (orcs, knights, treants, skeletons, etc.), with challenging boss battles. The in-game story is a bit simplistic, but well done; the story that unfolds from overheard table-talk is complex, heart-wrenching, and worth the price of admission. The loot ranges from okay to amazing, with some excellent new resources (I especially like the Chain Lightning grenade) and very cool 'red text' weapons. A brilliant example of DLC done correctly.
Head Hunter Packs:
All consist of two multi-part quests in a single standard-size zone.
Bloody Harvest - TK Baha refuses to stay dead, and needs you to kill a pumpkin monster. Thematic, but I was glad it ended when it did, since I was about to get bored with the zone.
Hunger - Mr. Torgue returns, with his grandma, as the host for a reality combat show. Pretty funny, and one of the most frustrating raid events of the fanchise. Lots of Hunger Games references, but almost never overtly.
Mercenary Day - They tried to pack every Christmas cliche into this one, and almost suceeded. Still, interesting new foes and some details about Marcus's and Moxxi's marriage.
Love - Moxxi wants help creating peace. Foolishly, she asks the Vault Hunters for that help. Carnage ensues. One of the tougher (non-raid) boss fights in the entire game.
Wam Bam Island - Pure reminiscence for veterans of Borderlands, as Sir Hammerlock discovers the Son of Crawmerax. The second quest has a bit of character development for each of the B2 Vault Hunters.
Borderlands 2: The quest for every piece of dlc ever.

As someone who has never really liked dating sims for their lack of active and frequent direct interaction like most games, I absolutely love Dream Daddy. It is utterly charming, sexy, adorable, and thoughtful, with a surprising ratio of player interaction/decision making to passive story-telling. The dialogue and narration are so well written and evoactive that you'll have as much fun reading through the hilarious or emotionally touching text as you do stressing over which Dad Joke to make to impress your favorite father.
Anyone who says this game is too expensive in comparison to its content must not know how to play a Dating Sim. The replay value is high for a low $15; with 7 dads to romance and multiple endings for each, you'll spend hours trying to get perfect scores on your dates or perhaps self-sabotage yourself just to see what happens. It is not a perfect game by far, but it is impressive what a small "beginner" indie studio did with their very first title.

Yooka-Laylee is a 3D Platforming game that was crowd funded via Kickstarter and developed by a new team formed of ex Rare developers. This game is made as a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie. Honestly though, I had high hopes for this game. What we ended up getting is a game that has great music. and a good looking modern development on an old art style. The level design and overall gameplay itself is where I find the game to fall short. In Banjo-Kazooie the main object of collection were Jiggies, Yooka-Laylee is similar and you collect items called Pagies. A lot of the Pagies in this game are just really boring to get. The levels themselves look nice, but I never thought that any of them were all that fun to play through. I find the first Banjo-Kazooie game to be a way more fun game with a ton of awesome levels, and I felt that game also had the perfect length.
Sure there were moments of enjoyment, but by the time I got 100 pagies I just wanted to get it over with. If you love Banjo-Kazooie, you may enjoy this game. I cannot recommend it at full price however, only pick up this game on sale. It's not good enough to be $40.
(Side note: I DID back this on Kickstarter, and that is one of the factors of my high expectations, another being the developers involved)
(Side side note: I'm not giving up on Playtoic though, I think if they make a sequel they can really make something amazing with all the feedback they were given I just won't be getting it day one next time around.)

Even though published already in 2001, Max Payne still keeps on rocking. Max Payne offers an interesting and dark twisted plot which keeps you quessing until you reach the very end of the game. As a side note, the developers of Max Payne decided to create easter eggs and other interesting visual appearences, and together with an awesome storyline, these factors make you want to play the game through probably for yet another time.
Gameplaywise Max Payne is basically a run and shoot game with a very little variation between the firefights you're forced to encounter. The range of usable weapons in the game is pretty small and the amount of bullets you need to consume to be able to kill enemies is absolutely ridiculous. Also, the enemies have a bad habit to come out of the blue or suddenly throw grenades at you which are almost impossible to evade within the given time. With that being said the gameplay of Max Payne is quite fast-paced and needs to be played along with a great amount of concentration.
Despite the negative sides of Max Payne, there is also something good to say about it. The level design of the game is pretty unique, the level of voice acting is great and the facial expressions enemies as well as Max have on their faces are rather funny. Throughout the game you can find some easter eggs and references to other video game series all of which offer a nice addition to the basic run and shoot concept of the game. The dreams and hallusinations experienced by Max play a big role in creating the anxious and tense atmosphere, which is actually the basis of the whole video game series. Storyline is impressive to say the least, controllability of Max's moves is very well executed and the mods made for the game can give it some additional value.
Overall when you get used to playing Max Payne, it isn't that hard to beat on any level. I have played Max Payne through once before I owned it on Steam. After I got the Steam version, I made three more playthroughs, with every given difficulty option and had some great time with it. After the first playthrough I found myself enjoying outdated graphics, some visual appearences and precise game mechanics as well as other positive things mentioned above. Some of the downsides can be rather easily forgiven, as the game itself is quite old and with that being said, very much has happened in the video game industry since 2001. And indeed, once you find your kung fu being strong enough and you think you've got even a little bit of mercy left to be given to an oldie like this product is, you should definitely give it a good try. There's actually a chance you won't regret it.

As a 33 year old lawyer I consider myself somewhat of a "stealth gamer". It took my girlfriend 9 months to find out that I like video games... Due to a busy work schedule my Steam time is somewhat limited so I normally don't squander it writing reviews. But for this game I will make an exception.
I was not familiar with the Numenera universe before playing the early access version of this game. (I still don't feel "familiar" after completing the early access version.) I consider myself a diehard planescape fan and couldn't suppress the feeling that the developers simply couldn't afford or wouldn't dish out the necessary funds to use the the planescape universe and make a "real successor" to Plancescape Torment.
Boy, was I wrong!
After playing this for 22.5 hours it went from my "I'll look into it" pile to my "dear god, no more delays" pile.
The writing is simply stellar. The characters have incredible depth. The themes are mature and compelling. The developers have avoided the infamous genre pitfalls and clichés ("avenge loved ones, rescue princess, save the world"). Tides of Numenara is without a doubt the most original rpg I have ever played.
I hope that the decision to make the game available across many different platforms will make it more available to audiences, who have avoided the rpg genre due to the above-mentioned clichés. In my view, this title shows that great art comes in many forms - even in the form of a video game.
If you truly enjoyed Planescape Torment this is for you.

Full review here :
What has made into the final game with all the cuts and delays it’s superb, It’s detailed world full of interesting characters to meet and the side quests are very interesting. We have a robot who wants to have children, an octopus (Nychthemeron) that can only talk at night, and you can make it night just for that alone, you will meet a cult that worships the Changing God and you can tell them that you really are him to sleep for free. We meet cannibals who eat the dead to preserve their memories or people that fight in the endless battle between the Changing God's army and the opposing force.
It really is a joy to read every interesting opinion that a character has. All quests can be resolved in multiple ways.
The most interesting part of the game comes after the first major city, in the Endless Gate I had a great time listening to Inifere and trying to solve all the possible outcomes. Also, that holds one of the hardest fights that can lead to game over screen if you fail, and of course if you choose to fight. After that , aside from Miel Avast, the next major hub will be the Bloom written by George Zeits who is responsible for Mask of the Betrayer from Neverwinter Nights 2.
The Bloom area is where the game really shines, it shows it’s full potential by using the setting, writing and the great soundtrack from Mark Morgan (same composer from PS:T, Fallout, Wasteland 2)
Some examples from the Bloom : a robot who collects hosts that are only beautiful, a spaceship that has smashed into the bloom - that is huge monster like where people live, trade and so on. You can also find out what different mows want and feed them people or even your companions in order to open portals to other dimensions. It all feels very alive, and well put together.
There’s a unique crisis system here that involves using your party members to distract a tour guide while you steal an important quest item, if you resolve to violence the battle will be almost impossible. The other companions you can find throughout the game are Tybir, Rhin and Erritis. Rhin is interesting because it’s a kid that can talk to Gods and Erritis, well, he is written by Chris Avellone and you can enjoy his full potential only if you choose a certain class with a certain ability. Tybir is just the funny guy in the game, and well, that’s about it. The characters while being interesting it can't compare to PS:T.
Graphics in the game are good, especially in the bloom area, I like that we are able to zoom in very close, about the size of PS:T characters.
I have read on forums that people think T:ToN is lacking in humor but that’s not true, the game has humor but a more mature one then the first.
The whole story of the game is great written and you can have different endings based on your choices and the Tides. The Tides serve as a kind of alignment system, but a more complex one, because it can change depending on what you say to a character.
Another great addition to the game are the meres : devices that can help you get into someone's memory and change the future, there are some that you need to interact because of the story but most of them are scattered throughout the game for the player to find them.
Conclusion: I will recommend the game despite it's flaws and cut content, it’s a rough gem that can suck you into the great written story, a story that was written by 6 different actual writers and it’s complexity and narrative, detailed characters, choices that matter and reactivity all over the place will make Torment Tides of Numenera a game hard to miss for anyone that likes a real RPG and don’t bother reading. Maybe some of you will want to hold on until patches and cut content to be added, but for myself that I waited so many years to finally arrive , it’s a good experience, especially since true RPG’s with real reactivity are hard to come by today.

I really loved Planescape Torment. It had a rich, creative world with a very grown up story that was ahead of its time. The graphics really added up to the game and created a rich atmosphere.
Now to Torment: Tides of Numenera. To be honest, it is nothing like Planescape. I haven't really seen anything were I can say this is on par with its role model.
Even if you do not judge it by that high standards, it is mediocre at best.
For example the graphics. It just doesn't look good. And I am not talking from a technical standpoint, but from an artistic. In terms of colors it lacks harmonic environments, it looks dull. Compared with a newer game like Pillars of Eternity which manages to create something special with every map, it is weaker in every way. No atmospheric lightning, the maps are nowhere near that detailed.
Also through other means like sound they do not manage to create the imagination of a living, breathing city.
As for the combat, it is boring and slow. I don't know why they made the decision to go turn based. I see no reason, it isn't even very tactical.
But remember, this is still Early Access and maybe the game has greatly improved in the past month - who knows.
And that brings me to my last point:
I am really disappointed by this Early Access. There is no real involvement of the buyers. No updates, no information. If anything, this is a good example on how you should NOT do an Early Access. I am sure I am not the only buyer that is disappointed how this is going. It really looks like they just wanted to grab some early money without any real responsibility towards the buyers.
Release is out ow and its a great game. Worth the money now.

Mad Max 8/10
For what I paid ($10) this was a solid, enjoyable product. Was it perfect? No, it was not. However, it did keep me entertained for over 90 hours.
Positives:
Solid (albeit depressing) story.
A large world to explore with plenty of content.
Exceptional graphics with only a handful of minor glitches throughout my game.
Enjoyable (but repetitive) gameplay with only the occassional frustrating encounter. In other words, it's a fairly easy game on the default difficulty.
All acheivments can be completed in a single playthrough.
Negatives:
Frustrating driving mechanics and a poor handling car.
Repetiive gameplay, fetch quests and unimaginitive ground combat/enemies.
Hold the button to.....hold the button to....
One-dimensional characters abound at every location. Very cut-and-paste NPC's.
This is not art, but primarily a driving game without tremendous driving mechanics. Still, there's enough outside of the flawed driving experience to justify purchasing the product. That is, if the price and description sound enticing to you.
With better ground combat, driving mechanics and the occassional npc that didn't act exactly like every other character, it would have been a more enjoyable experience.
Beyond that, it would have been more fullfilling (for me) if there were actual roleplaying elements and I could make decisions where Max didn't come across as such a straight up S.O.B. all the time.
Basically for my rating I subtracted half a point for a handful of glitches. One point for the terrible driving mechanics and another half point for the cut-and-paste feel to the NPCS and combat. Getting swarmed by enemy vehicles around the clock got tiresome fast.
A solid, straightforward and enjoyable action/adventure game that could have been better.

is the tie-in game that was associated with and released a few months after the blockbuster movie Mad Max: Fury Road. Despite this, it shares almost nothing with the movie, the main similarities being thematic style and a main character who is modeled and voiced to resemble Tom Hardy.
The game follows Max, a lone survivor haunted by the guilt-induced specters of his deceased family, through a postapocalyptic desert wasteland on the less-than-epic mission to get his car back and hoard enough supplies to make an attempt to reach a possibly mythical land of slightly less wasted desert.
As far as overall design goes, the game very clearly shares its heritage with
. Instead of a lone, spirit-possessed ranger aiding fellow survivors, bringing down war chiefs, and murdering bands of marauding Uruks, while being guided by a seemingly subhuman creature with uncertain motivations; the player is a lone, guilt-ridden man aiding fellow survivors, bringing down war chiefs, and murdering bands of marauding ... post-apocalyptic mutant people, while being guided by a seemingly subhuman creature with uncertain motivations. There's a near-identical world map divided into regions, with fast travel between regions available once key areas of each region has been reached via slow travel. Quests, challenges, and caches of greater and lesser worth are marked on the map once discovered, once again giving achievement-oriented players plenty of grist for the grinder.
In terms of gameplay, there are three basic mechanics: driving, punching, and upgrading. The driving portion is well-done, and includes exploring the landscape, raiding enemy warbands, destroying symbols of enemy chiefs' power, hijacking enemy convoys, participating in deathraces, and even catching sick air from terrain features. The player can capture enemy vehicles and add them to her garage, giving her the ability to drive them whenever she wants, but only the main vehicle can be customized and upgraded. In addition to the basic driving combat arsenal of ramming and shooting out of the window, the player can equip a harpoon to grapple with enemy vehicles and tear down structures, pull out a rocket launcher for extra kick, or even park and practice extreme-range sniping from the back.
While driving occupies approximately 50% of gameplay time, the other 50% is spent infiltrating hostile camps, raiding groups of near-defenseless outcasts for their meager hoards of scrap, and taking down war chiefs. This is unfortunate, because the vast majority of these missions, as well as the hand-to-hand combat itself, are extremely tedious. Although there are nominally a variety of different tasks and objectives, they all boil down to: follow linear path through enemy-populated area, get rushed by a group of enemies in every open space, punch everything that bleeds, and blow up everything that doesn't.
Because the games are superficially so similar, I again can't help making the comparison here with Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor. In M-E:SoM, there was an extensive and carefully-integrated stealth mechanic, giving the player multiple options for low-conflict sneaking, quiet assassination, or chaotic bloodbath. Additionally, there were three completely separate combat trees: ranged, standard melee, and ultra-close; each one of these had a variety of special attack upgrades that could be learned in order to enhance the combat experience.
In Mad Max, you have shooting and punching. However, shooting is slow, and Max can only carry a few shells at a time. On top of that, there is no stealth option - on a good day, you can take out one or two before the group sees you, but there's no way to use cover or terrain to your advantage, let alone achieve sneak attacks or avoid combat altogether. And then there's the punching. In his arsenal, Max has Punch, Slow Punch, and Parry. All combats basically consist of parrying and counterpunching until Max is the last one standing. In boss fights, substitute dodging for parrying, since bosses tend to have unblockable attacks.
The payoff for all of this driving and punching is scrap and experience, both of which can be used to purchase upgrades in order to improve your driving and punching, as well as Max's beard, which accounts for something like 20% of his personal upgrade tree.
The environments were well-done, with lots of little details that reinforced the theme and enhanced immersion. For example, during one challenge mission,
. In another,
. The characters are varied and interesting, with the sadly notable exceptions of
and the beyond-laughably cliché damsel.
Despite its lack of meaningful connection with Fury Road and its unavoidable yet inadequate similarity to Shadow of Mordor, Mad Max is a solid game. I spent 30 hours playing it, and if they ship an expansion, I'll probably play that as well.
OK, final recommendation time: if you haven't played Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor, go play that.
If it leaves you wanting more, or if you just want to slap some armor onto the Black on Black and go wardriving, then Mad Max is for you.

In a nutshell - GTA meets Batman Arkham set in the wasteland world of Mad Max.
There is a fair amount of dispute but i feel convinced that this is a prequel and takes place just prior to Mad Max: Fury Road. More on that later.
Protip: I recommend you focus on the main storyline and secondary (blue) quests, don't get overly obsessed with doing every single sidequest else it will get too grindy and you might get bored. Just do whatever sidequests are on the way to your objectives. And don't worry about the difficulty too much and unlocking everything.
Protip2: I recommend you use a controller. Keyboard is fine (i used it) but driving can be a bit tough with it imho.
Protip3: You can continue exploring the wasteland after you finish the game. No need to rush those achievements.
+ The game is pretty damn gorgeous, with probably the best environmental effects and terrain i have possible ever seen in a game thus far. To the extent where i died several times from suddenly admiring an astounding sunset/vista...
+ They really nailed the look and feel of the movie in this game. That, and the game is very well optimized and stable.
+ Mad Max lore - ever wondered who those buzzard guys in the movie were? How about how Max got his PTSD? Or wanted to know more about Gastown? Or why the world is a desert? Or how the whole apocalypse went done. All in the game, which is a big plus.
+ Combat is smooth and similar to the Batman Arkham series. Similarly, the driving mechanics and combat are quite ok as well.
+ Some really nice easter eggs all over the place, see if you can find them all. :)
+/- Unlike the movie the focus is more on hand-to-hand rather than shooting (there is not that much). Not necessarily a bad thing imho.
- Sidequests can be too similar, and in the same vein enemies and mini-bosses tend to be just variations of each other faction-wise. As a result can be kinda grindy, but like i said its open-world so really it is up to you.
All in all i had a lot of fun with this and thoroughly enjoyed myself, highly recommended! Now its off to re-watch the awesome movie now that i have just finished this... :)

To start off I'll say that this is probably the most unexpected success of the year 2012 and probably one of the ridiculous ones'. Now to the actual game.
I'll start with
:
1.
: Now here there isn't much to explain. Astonishing views from the tall sky scrapers of Dubai and the sandy color were on the high level. It makes you believe you are in Dubai on the war zone, and not in your half broken apartment with neighbours drilling walls. Also worth noting that the demands for such beauty aren't high.
2.
: This one is very balanced. Like in some games of this types, you are playing a role of one man army, and fighting against huge huge huge amounts of enemies. Unlike in most of the games, and this is very important, you have very frequent checkpoints. So even if you die, you will not be thrown back to the beginning of      10-20 min fight as often it might happen, but rather 1-5.
3.
: During the tense fights you might not even notice it, but the music that's playing is very good, at least to my taste. Some hardcore rock really does it during the fight. Bands like Deep Purple, Alice in Chains, Bjork and others are featured in the game.
4.
: And here comes the beast - the reason this game is worth all of the fuss. Mainly, the aim of the plot was to show the tough job of the soldier, and the decision making, but also criticise the fact of the war itself, and the way we make war in general. Some touchy issues were shown like use of chemical weapons such as white phosphorus, and the unpleasant consequences that it can bring. You can accidentally vaporize a whole camp of civilians... And then you will have to deal with it.
One of the other touchy issues, although only if dug deep enough, is the USA "invasion" in the middle east countries and their interference in the local conflicts often in order to protect their own interests which brings more victims. But this discussion will not occur here.
In conclusion the plot really makes this game a big deal with very unexpected twist in the end of the game. If you play the game the second time, you will feel as if you would watch say Fight Club for the second time. You know the big twist and you can see how the game slowly leads you into it.
Regarding
, this game doesn't have too many of them. The big one is movement, and controls in general. Sometimes when you want to get behind cover the character disagrees with you, running is also a bit weird.
Another big con, and I really really really hate this one, is when one of your crew members goes down, you have to pick him up, and if not, you'll have to start over... This is the most annoying part of the game, especially on the higher difficulty levels, where you'd run towards him and die, or you just won't be quick enough. Other than that...
Enjoy the game.

I just finished the game. Spec Ops is probably the best game I have ever played. Not because it has ground-breaking gameplay (the movement is actually quite clunky) and not because of the SIK GRAFIX BRUH (I had my computer settings low so I could run the game better). But this game had the most compelling, intense, and real story. It's such a commentary on violence in our society because making those violent moves doesn't work out in the end.
SPOILER ALERT! I'm telling the full story that I experienced. I assume I only got one of the possible endings but still don't read it unless you have played the game through. Scroll down to the bottom of my review if you wanted to skip the spoilers. be warned if you read em though, it's some heavy♥♥♥♥♥♥and I'm not proud of it.
I went through the game thinking i was making the right choices, and depending on what choices you make it drastically affects the outcome. Because I chose the mindless violence side of things (as most shooters advocate) and made a lot of things more easy for me: 47 innocent civilians burned. I went into the game 2 other people in my squad (Lugo and Adams). One of them was hung by rioting civilians because of what I had done, the other threw me over a barricade and fought hundreds of soldiers until he died, and in the end it went through all the decisions I had made and their consequences. I had been hallucinating, and in the end I was face-to-face with the villain of the game, Konrad. He was dead and it turned out that I was hallucinating most things in the game. It came to a sequence where he was pointing a gun at me, saying challenging things to make me regret my decisions. He counted down from five and I let him pull the trigger. I could have shot him, but I didn't. He was a hallucination, and It ended with me dead, having commit suicide overlooking the burning city of Dubai. It hit me immediately. I did that. Because of what I did I failed my mission, and instead of saving everyone like I wanted to do, I saved no one. Never have I completed a game and felt such hardship, like it was all for nothing and that I made the wrong choices.
END OF SPOILERS
In any case, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I recommend this game to literally anyone who is even considering it. No game has been so impactful to me. One thing though: when you get it (and you should), pay attention to the story. Make the right decisions. It will be thrown back in your face if you don't.
This game does not need a score out of 10, because it's depth cannot be measured by you unless you play it.

This game is actually really good. Most people seem to want to hate the game because of having to be always online and the fact that it is being released in an episodic format. Does it suck having to be always online to be able to play a single player game? Sure. The fact of the matter is that some people, much like myself, are always online anyways so this affects me, in what I feel,  such a small way. As for the game being episodic, Square has made it abundantly clear that it was going to have this type of release, so I'm surpised (and also not surprised) that many people who write reviews use this as a negative. You purchased the game knowing what it was going to be like and if you don't enjoy, then refund it.
As for gameplay I would just like to give a few pros and cons that I have noticed in my small amount of play time.
Pros:
- Extremely open and the level provides a variety of ways to complete it.
- Actions seem to be a lot faster in this one. Dumping a body in a dumpster for instance, you don't have to watch the whole scene.
- The people who stand around a level/the scenery really makes the game atmospherically amuzing.
Cons:
- I heard that the game has slow load times, though on an SSD, this is not an issue.
- The game does not run very well. I have a 980ti/i7 4770k and I had to turn down a lot of options to get a steady 60 frames per second.
- The game crashes sometimes. I have only experienced this twice and luckily it was resolved by using DX11 instead of DX12. I can definitely see how this would turn someone off of the game.
That's about all that I can notice so far. I look forward to more levels being released because by the way it's looking, it is going to be WAY more like Blood Money than Absolution....which is like, what everyone wanted in a new Hitman game, right?

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW (after Tubular Update):
Oxygen Not Included is a colony survival simulation. You (as a commander of 3 duplicants) spawn in the middle of the asteroid with one goal - live as long as you can using the resources available all around you, slowly expanding your base getting additional crew spawning every once in a while. On the surface it looks like a nice and goofy Klei game with cute graphics and hilarious gameplay. What I didn't expect though was getting hit by the complexity of the mechanics - trying to produce oxygen taking gas densities into consideration, pressures, temperatures calculations, food management, plumbing setups, electricity, running out of fuel, avoiding polution, cleansing/refining resources, research, dealing with duplicants decor expectations and phobias (sic!), the list goes on and on! :)
The variety of setups that you can get will make your head spin. Gas/liquids pumps, food manufacturing/preparation tools, special tiles, variety of materials, automation, oxygen manufacturing tools, many different power producing machines, everything with pros and cons, forcing you to constantly shift your strategies - perfection :P Sometimes you just watch the screen, trying to wrap your head around the bubbly mess of pipes, wires, air cleansing units, research stations, cots, piles of crap (or rather 'polluted dirt' ;) used to fertilize your plants), food laying on the grond, because your dudes have ten thousand things queued up and when you finally make some crazy setup work you feel great! And then one of your duplicants urinates in your only water supply, because the outhouse was full and you didn't notice, because there was ten thousand other things to take care of and you're screwed again :P Just another day in the colony. A beautiful mess :)
All that being said, at this stage of development there's no 'end game'. I digged my way through the entire map in all 4 directions and (to put it simply) there's nothing there. No emergency teleporters, no way to some rescue ship, no distress beacons, nothing. So for now the only goal is to sustain your colony for as long as possible, which is super fun in its own right honestly :P Final game should have some sort of a goal though, just saying.
9/10

Arkham Origins is a good game especially if you are just jumping into the Batman: Arkham universe.  There are upgrades to graphics, interface and bat-gadgets from both Arkham Asylum & Arkham City.  However the game play is almost a carbon copy of the previous games (but this IS a prequel and that shouldn't be unexpected).
That said some of the side quests (notably the Enigma/Riddler quests) are nothing in comparison to Arkham Asylum's riddler quests. In Arkham Origins these are exclusively switch based puzzles without any of the Riddler-like brain teasers of the game's predecessors.  Also the game does have bugs. In my experience far less bugs than those reported on the 'net. The only actual glitches I encountered were the "Joker Beatdown glitch" and the "Infinite Fast Travel Loading Screen to Batcave" gltch.  The first is easily solved with a little googling (see below) and the second was resolved by switching from DirectX 11 to DirectX 10. Notably DirectX11 has bugged every game I've played that tried to use it so I wouldn't blame the developer for that - however the "Joker Beatdown glitch" was a let down. If you come accross this glitch this forum post on steam  should resolve it:
Many many other so-called glitches are not bugs - just markers of how difficult the game actually is. The only issues like this I faced were the game not showing that left Ctrl will cancel/retract the bat claw (and the grappeling hook), and the "grappling hook accelerator takedown" being far too difficult to do (becuase the game as too few enemies that can be taken-down this way).
All in all I really enjoyed Arkham Origins. IMHO part of the so-called problem with the game's reception is because it's hard, and because the standard for Batman: Arkham games is amazingly high. YMMV but at the harder settings Origins was more difficult that Arkham Asylum.  On the whole I'd give this 7.5 out of 10, an excellent jumping on point for the series but not up to the sky-high standards of Arkham Asylum or Arkham City.

Max Payne is an undercover detective wanting nothing else but revenge on those who ordered the hit on his wife and killed her and their newborn baby girl. Unfortunately for him, he's been burned and framed for the murder of his best friend, a DEA agent... His rage will be unleashed on New York City criminals while evading the police. What secrets will he uncover?
Don't look at the minutes passed in Max Payne here on Steam, I happen to own the retail version. And also an italian version offered by a magazine when I was on vacations back then.
So, you may bet, I loved the plot of the game. You're going from surprise to surprise and the noir ambiance is really showing Max's state of mind. Everything is done by night or underground or in dirty buildings. Even some side characters are well-written like Mona Sax, though you should play Max Payne 2 for more secrets about her. Eeer, what? Yeah, yeah, I like Mona. But I prefer the Mona of Max Payne 2 than Max Payne. Besides, you find alliances with people you would have never thought...
The gameplay is simple: you shoot, you cover yourself, you shoot, you take painkillers to ease your pain and you use your bullet time feature to slow down time to avoid bullets and to kill more enemies. Anyway, I can't say that there is really more in Max Payne apart some puzzles (well, mainly to find your way but not the puzzles like you see in casual games). You have also a lot of weapons, interesting anyway to see Max carry so much of them. From shotgun to sniper rifle with grenade launchers, don't ask how he does. But the best is perhaps the nightmare sequence, that is separating each act.
The graphics, while looking a little old today, are also very very good. The only problem I have is the fact that Max is having always the same smiling face. I mean, this is weird at the end. But really, each level is well builded and creepy in its own: from Ragnarock to the subway, passing by the Aesir Corporation so futuristic and by the docks.
The soundtrack is also quite good. The main track is quite sad.
But the best also with Max Payne, is that the story is told as a comic, with excellent voice actors. It's allowing the story to be darker and also to have subtitles.
In other words, Max Payne was an excellent title, with an excellent plot and an excellent gameplay (the bullet feature was really helpful). It's not a wonder that it got turned into a trilogy. If you like action, you have to play Max Payne. Never regretted it back then... I should replay it on Steam too....

I try only to write reviews if I've got something to add about a game that I haven't seen many other reviewers already noting. I'll make an exception with Garfield Kart. This game is just as good as every media outlet and amateur reviewer says it is. It might actually be, all things considered, the best game I've ever played. All of the hype you've heard is real. If that's all that matters to you, pick the game up right now. Read on for a bit more detail.
This game creates an experience that's far more than the sum of its parts. The excellent visuals and music, the lovely sound design, and the painstakingly well-crafted environments, NPCs, and quest and dialogue writing all combine to give this game a lived-in, realistic feel that very few games have been able to exhibit. Every corner of the world feels real. There's so much to experience across the several maps that you can simply wander from place to place for hours upon end, taking in all that there to experience. None of this is procedurally generated, either. It's all hand-crafted, and for those willing to look, there are some incredible things to find.
Early in the game, the player character Garfield meets a gungho historian off to chronicle the war. Garfield tells him not to go, that the warzone is a chaotic, anarchic wasteland and he'll be killed simply for the quality of his boots. The historian laughs it off, and offers some lasagna to Garfield. If Garfield wins, he can win a unique lasagna recipe from this NPC. Later in the game Garfield and Jon find themselves underneath a tree full of hanged civilians. Upon searching the foot of the tree, Garfield can find a half-finished history book, and the lasagna recipe the historian was carrying if it wasn't won from him earlier. The entire game is littered with moments like these; very subtle, missable details that only a minority of players will experience, yet CDPR has worked hard to place in the game anyway because they truly care about the depth of their world. I've played it through to completion several times and each time I find something new.
The quality of writing is so good that it will propel you to finish the game regardless of whether or not you like the combat. The characters are so likeable that you'll grow attached to them before too long, and the quality dialogue and voice acting makes the plot points hit that much harder. The unique thing about this game is not so much the quality of its writing, as there are quite a few games with
solid writing, but the depth to which this quality of writing goes. From the main questline to the most minor sidequest, you can always expect to be pleasantly surprised. I was hooked by the very first monster hunting sidequest in White Orchard when you discover just why this Noonwraith is roaming around the well in this small village. Each NPC seems to have a lovingly crafted backstory of their own, and even the most minor fetch quest has its own wrinkle to make it interesting. The high quality of these quests is even more impactful in a world of Mass Effect Andromeda's with their disposable, MMO inspired, procedurally generated fetch-quests. They don't make them like this anymore. This is a game in which the most minor sidequest you take on will take you nearly an hour, and it will make you stop and think about a dilemma, or a question it poses, through its quest writing. It's amazing just how much quality content the writing team put into this game. Nothing is disposable, everything in the game serves to garner an emotional reaction or ask an important question. It's packed to the brim with quality content to experience.
When it first released there was some talk of graphics downgrades, bugs, and obtuse UI. However CDPR have completely eliminated all of these issues with the most extensive round of post-release patching I've ever seen for a game. Every major bug I remember encountering has been eliminated from the game, it looks phenomenal and runs very well, and the UI flows like a dream whether you're using mouse and keyboard or a controller. In addition to this they added a ton of free DLC, so make sure you've got all that stuff set to download after you purchase the game.
To top all of this off, this game has the best DLC offerings I've ever seen in a video game, period. Better than Minerva's Den, better than Lair of the Shadow Broker. The writing in Hearts of Stone is the best I've ever seen in a DLC, and is the high point of the entire Witcher series in my opinion. And the sheer amount of content added in Blood and Wine is mind-boggling. If you buy Garfield Kart, buy the Game of the Year edition without any second thoughts.
This is a game you'll put hundreds of hours into without regret. You'll be missing the characters long after you've finished it. Any time you hear a music track from the game on YouTube you'll immediately become nostalgic for the game. Garfield Kart is truly a towering achievement in every sense of the term, it's one of the very few games in which I can't find anything to criticze. It's an absolute masterpiece, and no matter what types of games you enjoy, you should buy it and give it a shot. It might actually be better than everyone says.

Certainly not perfect, but entertaining.
Pros :
+ beautiful and coloured environments, great art direction.
+ very nice music (and nice variations when underwater/inside/...).
+ basic movement controls are very well handled (running, rolling, jumping).
+ lots of gameplay variations : transformations, tonics, arcade games, ...
+ wide levels to explore, with many hidden spots.
+ great game length, if you take the time to explore the levels and find the collectibles.
Cons :
- some controls feel wrong (mostly the flappy flight and the 'kartos' controls).
- a bit more variety for monsters would have been appreciated.
- too many bad jokes about the lack of story. Breaking the fourth wall once in a while can be fun, but not when it happens during every single dialogue.
- I have no problems with gibberish voices in games like Rayman 2 or Last Tinker. But in Yooka-Laylee, they really sound weird. Fortunately, they can be disabled in the game options.
- most of the game is well balanced, but a few challenges are way too hard (Kartos 3-4-5, Rextro's arcade 4, the 'Inept' boss, ...).
All in all, I'd recommend giving it a try if you like 3D collectathons with wide open areas (such as Spyro the Dragon, or Jak & Daxter 1, for example).

After a long break from this game I finally uninstalled it. I doubt I will get back to it anytime soon.
My main problem with this game is the level design. The concept of just five large worlds + HUB to explore is neat and all, but it doesn't work for me. The levels are empty, open and confusing. I kept wasting time in the HUB world alone because I kept getting lost! Most of the time I had no idea where to go and where I'd been. I really wish I'd had a map. In the first and second worlds a lot of the scenery is so uniform and lacking in variety that it made navigating even more difficult. The third level was thankfully slightly more sensible. I never got to the 4th world, because after 1+ hours of searching I still couldn't find it in the HUB world.
The idea of expanding the worlds was cool in theory but disappointing in practice. The additions to the first three worlds at least didn't really... Add anything new in my opinion. Just small segments of further platforming on the edges of the areas you've already explored. I must mention that I was completely infuriated by Icymetric Palace. It added nothing new to the beautiful (but confusing) snow world, just an annoying puzzle castle thing that I couldn't find my way out of. I don't understand why they felt the need to add an isometric segment to the game.
For a collectathon game Yooka-Laylee has very little to collect. Collectibles could have been made into such an useful tool to lead a player in the open worlds, too!
Overall, I also feel that the character and enemy design is quite uninspired. Two out of the three bosses I fought were underwhelming and irritating. The humor of the game is a miss for me personally. The story didn't really interest me at all.
If the playability was better I probably wouldn't mind the lacking characters and story so much... But they add to the feeling of emptiness.
But now for pros.
Like I said, the ice world is really beautiful. All the scenery in the game is quite lovely and fun. The character designs aren't to my personal taste, but they do fit the style and remind me of 90s mascot games just like they were supposed to. The music was pretty good, too.
The idea of Yooka being able to change his abilities according to what he eats was cool enough, so were the many minigames. The execution is debatable, but I did like the ideas.
I enjoyed the third level the most, since I could kind of navigate in it. It had some neat puzzles, swimming and platforming, as well as the only boss I thought had any merit to it.
Yooka-Laylee fails to live up to the hype I hear surrounded it. As just a 3D platforming fan who thought it'd be fun to play, a lot of the game mechanics and design choices left me confused and/or annoyed. Now that it's been a while since I played I still remember being frustrated more than anything else.
I got the feeling that this game tries too hard to be the same as something old. Without such a direction it could've been a lot more interesting, I think.
I wouldn't buy this game for full price. Wait for a 50% or at least 30% sale. The DLC prices, though, are on point according to my experience.
Not the collectathon revival we hoped for, but with a creative new coat of paint it's a fun platforming experience.

Ok, let me start off with saying that I have just completed the game and that I think this is a good first product for Playtonic Games as a company. However, there were far too many issues for this game to qualify as a "good" game, let alone a "spiritual successor." I love the Banjo games, but I also realized before buying Yooka-Laylee that this game wouldn't exactly be a Banjo game. I went in looking for a 3D platformer made by professionals. Unfortunately for Yooka-Laylee, I got a 3D platformer layered with inconsistencies, poor level design, and almost no unique characteristics to make it even close to being another nostalgic experience. Every NPC is pretty much as boring and forgettable as the next, besides maybe Rextro and Kartos (Kartos because he is a piece of ♥♥♥♥♥♥), which is mainly do to the fact that they are glorified talking statues with teleportation abilities.
Now there are some challenges and puzzles that left me feeling livid in Banjo because I was temporarily frusterated with them for the moment, but there are challenges and bosses in Yooka-Laylee that left me feeling very resentful, and confused as to how the level designer making the challenge didn't think there was something a little too challenging for a human being to complete it within the first 10 times they tried. Some of the challenges and bosses were pretty fun and/or seemed to be designed pretty reasonably, but most were clunky and hard to beat without being on your last butterfly of health.
The worlds could be beautiful at times, but after time you realize that there is not much to do but run around and go through mundane obstacle courses and do 15 second errands for talking light posts just to expand the level and complete more tedious courses and short errands. In the Banjo games, the characters and levels were so dynamic and interconnected. Some of the actions you would take in a world in Banjo would have an impact on other worlds and/or characters and would provide more opportunities. Banjo also had a lot of intricate ways to get to other parts of a world. In Jolly Roger's Lagoon for example, you could shoot the teeth off a big fish underwater to go inside him and rescue a character that shared a relationship with another character in the level. I didn't see that at all in Yooka-Laylee. Everything is extremely static and lacks natural emotion.
If you found that you were interested in this game because you wanted a game made by the great developers of the Banjo series (Like me) or some other game, then I would say wait until they come out with another title or two. They likely just need some warming up to create another masterpiece, as they have been out of the game for a while; pun comepletely ♥♥♥♥ing intended.
Only recommended as a time sink. Hopefully, the next one will be better.

This game definitely missed the mark in terms of capturing what was fun about their previous games. Hopefully the developers take all of the criticism, good and bad, and be able to revisit their approach to this series.
