Back from Valhalla... MAX!
This game holds so many memories for me. The endless shootouts, the screaming of Max' wife, the babyroom-spaceout-wtf-mind♥♥♥♥, Bullet Time... too much to mention. This game is one of the first really bloody games i came in contact with, and at the age of twerlve, i never had any nightmares. Luskily, because this game is also set in a pretty sinister atmosphere.
Working at the NYPD, Max is a hard working police detective. Three years ago his wife and kid got murdered by junkies, and he is remembered again when he rolls into a drug investigation. Soon he finds out that this drug and the murder of his family are connected. Desperate to cleanse the city from the drug and redeeming himself from the burden, he goes on a crusade. From an ease-in to a vertical dropdown in a rollercoaster, this game holds you by the balls from start to end.
this game is a ride, a flow. The game is divided by chapters, and obviously you start at Chapter 1. After loading screen mosly there is a quasi-funny comic, before you delve into the action. And action, well... no shortage of that. From one shootout to the next, blood everywhere, heroin syringes everywhere, painstillers everywhere... - I, for this very reason, do NOT recommend this game if you are sensitive for these things. I mean, if it's not the game, it is the amount of heroin ingame that makes you addicted to Max and his crusade. No, really...
Apart from this, but not to be taken into consideration: The fact that i had difficulties installing and running the game in Windows 7 SP1. Why i don't take this into consideration? You can't expect a game built in the early 00's to be 100% compatible with multicored PC's imho, even when it's revamped. It's engine is just not built for multicore. You want the full experience, try it on a virtual machine, find an older PC or downgrade your PC. Please do not complain about this.
If you like dense packed action this is the game for you. I think this game is worth every penny, including when it's full price.

In my opinion, the Max Payne series has the best writing of any video game series ever created.
Considering all the games I have ever played and loved, Max Payne will forever reside way, way up, in the highest reaches - in the ether - above all others, as one of my favorite experiences in gaming.
The narrative is nuanced in a way that spoils most other games. Clean story-telling with no gratuitous explanation. You won't get all of the information, but you get enough, and that's all that matters.
This was the game I cross-installed onto my cheap laptop during college in order to have it available on-the-go. I have played Max during slow days at work, I have played Max in libraries, even on a Yankee Trails bus.
While I hold Max Payne 2 and Max Payne 3 in very high regard, the first game in the series remains my favorite. It is an exeptional product with an enthralling story, entertaining gameplay, and a hero I just can't stop rooting for.

Max Payne is a little bit like buying a fifty-year-old escort: it hasn't aged well, it's not pretty, and it takes a little bit of convincing to get everything running, but it gets the job done. The performance is not stellar, but hey, maybe you got it on a discount, maybe you know a guy. This is why I don't recommend the game.
With that aside, it's pretty great. The noir is noir, the story is acceptable, the metaphors are a tired rain on a dreary autumn afternoon, never sure quite when to give up for snow. They do seem a touch forced, but there's a charm in that, along with the graphic novel-style storytelling. The gameplay is frankly, at this point, weak and stale, and enemy accuracy is wildly unpredictable, which is no fun when every bullet hurts and you're quickloading/quicksaving all the time to avoid getting scraped in a scuffle. As frustrating and tiresome as that got, I still found myself playing on to hear Max mutter exposition in his slightly congested voice. I did beat it, but I won't play the unlocked difficulty levels. Finishing was enough for me.
TL;DR: I don't recommend it, but I thoroughly enjoyed it. Prepare yourself by grabbing the sound and widescreen fixes.

Max Payne is a third person action shooter that focuses heavily on gun play and storytelling. It was probably the first game that pulled off bullet time succesfully and opened the way to other games like F.E.A.R. to improve it and modernize it. The creators of Max Payne were obviously inspired by the popular action movie of that time, The Matrix, to design the shooting mechanics and the overall action theme of Max Payne.
You play as Max Payne, an NYPD detective who sets on avenging his wife's and childs' death by the mafia that is connected with a powerful drug. As the story progresses, you unravel the darker side of the story that led to the loss of your family. The story is presented through graphic novel slides with voice over as narrative. I have to say that there are some really talented voice actors taking part in this game. The production team used many of its members to pose as the characters Max Payne and it clearly shows that they had a lot of fun doing so. The visuals are obviously dated compared to modern games and some of the basic features like mission obvectives are missing. For its time however, Max Payne was way ahead in both presentation and most importantly gameplay. It has a noire style of art design and an overall mature and dark theme which is a rare thing in our days.
The gameplay is heavily focused on gun play which at some point gets kinda repetitive and almost boring but the bullet time effect is keeping things interesting. What is really annoying though is the difficulty level. I have never played such a hard shooter like this one before. It is so unfairly hard at some points that it forces you to abuse the save load option and memorize the opponent placement. So, you will die a lot in this game. This is an unforgivingly hard game that WILL punish you!
The music isn't memorable, except for the main theme which is played through most of the game but all the songs fit with the tone and the dark theme of the game. What is memorable though is the voice of Max Payne and the whole narrative style.
All in all, Max Payne is a challenging and an original for its time shooter with a classic revenge plot and a kickass protagonist that should be played by everyone who likes to go on a rampage killing junkies ,criminals and gangsters in style.

You may need a mod or two to run this game, especially when playing in Windows 10, but when you do you'll experience an excellent game with a thrilling story with many twists and turns. The comic book style cutscenes suprisingly works well with the games noire motif. If you want a fix of Noire in gaming or want to experience an excellent retro third-person shooter that's aged quite well then you should get this game

I'm not a fan of Banjo Kazooie and Tooie, they are a product of the 90's, they were massive collectathons with stiff animation, clunky controls and poor framerates. They also featured notoriously frustrating final boss fights which beat you down hard and had you restart the entire fight all over again. Yooka Laylee is essentially Banjo Threeie, Laylee is pretty much a dead ringer for Kazooie (personality wise). The modern graphics and powers afforded by the PC ensure a smooth experience, controls feel tight and responsive, and framerate is a silky smooth 60fps, so in that regard it is a step up from its predecessors. The graphics and presentation in atleast 4 of the 5 worlds is very Rare like, with charming oogly eyes on everything and everyone.
The music is not on the same level, David Wise and Grant Kirkhope had some amazing soundtracks during the Rare SNES/N64 days, but the stuff here isnt even close to their best. Rare's classic formula is back in full swing, a couple of worlds (check), lots of jiggies (in this case, quills) and about 100 pagies needed to get to the final boss. YL features 5 worlds + 1 hub world, 4 out of the 5 worlds are actually quite good while 1 is just tedious and uninspiring (Casino world). YL follows Banjo's blue print to a T, even having the infamous death bridge quiz, where you need to get 10 answers right to advance to the next area, these are quite easy.
There were times where I lost patience, wanting to finish the game as quick as possible while other moments where I was getting bored and had to push myself to reach the finish line. Hard to believe a game in 2017 doesnt have a map or fast travel. I challenged the final boss after 103 pagies, found out his pattern after a little frustration and put him out of his misery. I'd strictly only recommend this game to fans of Rare and to people who really enjoyed the Banjo games. Here's hoping the upcoming Super Mario Odyysey impresses me and shows me that there is life yet in the open world 3D platformer cause I nearly wanted to stop playing YL a few times. Better luck next time to the ex Rare team.

I'll start this out by saying I actually quite enjoy games like this, so I'm not bothered by it being shorter or dialogue-heavy (like this review, lol). If you're not sold immediately, I recommend you watch a playthrough or wait for a sale. Dating sims are basically choose-your-own-adventure romance novellas, so if that's not your style you might never be a fan. It's a very cute game, and yes, has a lot of room for improvement, but DDADDS feels very heartfelt. I'll start with the negative, since that's probably why you're reading this review:
(Negative)
Sound design. The voices (mostly grunting noises, this game is not fully voiced as you might expect) can be too loud at times, and on the "date end" screens can be barely audible. I did not use headphones, largely because of subpar audio. Most of the characters have their lines recorded with a decent quality, but volume levels are inconsistent and Hugo sounds, frankly, like he's talking into a cup. I feel like the voiced lines are too frequent and not of the quality I anticipated from the Game Grumps. Sometimes, the character noises can be jarring, and they're often misplaced, which brings up the next negative:
Saves can, at times, not work properly. At least one of my manual saves ended up taking me back to a screen with no options, meaning I effectively had to search for another point to go back to. Those which did work often had other bugs, such as character art appearing where it shouldn't (Joseph's kids appearing during a date with Craig, for example) and the sound jumping around. Some dialogue choices you made earlier can also seem to change with saves, though it's nothing which affects date route progress. These are bugs though, but I'm optimistic that they'll be patched.
It's short and feels a bit unresolved. Granted, I haven't tried to get negative endings (are those the alternates?) with anyone but Robert, but they all seem to end themselves the same way. Many end up feeling more like friendship, and aside from some dialogue, the game ends the same way (which, if you play other games in this genre, is a big no-no)
(Positive)
This game has a lot of heart. No. Really. I expected it to be a little crass but was pleasantly surprised of how respectful it was. The dialogue is humorous, but not (usually) dirty for the sake of being dirty. I find it to be very cute and the characters are pretty multi-dimensional. If you enjoy reading and characters more than gameplay or enjoy casual gaming experiences, you'll have a good time. This ain't Dark Souls (unless your idea of that is minigolf.) I expected it to be more of a joke than it is. I'm glad it's not.
Speaking of humor, the game is chock full of it. I love the jokes. They're very modern, but not in a way that dates it. I rarely laugh out loud at things like this, but you'd never have known that if you'd watched me play.
The art is, of course, amazing. The character portraits have more attention to detail put into them than what I see from major game studios and the small animations are smooth.
Minigames help break up the dialogue, and they're pretty fun to boot. Some aren't as self-explanatory as others, but it keeps you from being buried in words, words, words. Heck, I'd like to see more of them on routes where they're not as frequent.
Negatives are usually my buy/don't buy point, so I made them more detailed. If you're new to the otome genre, there are a few free ones you can pick up to test the waters with before spending $15 here. Buying or watching or not touching at all is your choice, but I'm glad I picked it up. If this review was too long for you to read, then you probably won't find yourself happy with the game.

. MC goes on those "dates", but most of them aren't really romantic or even a way to set up romance. It's just two dudes chilling and doing their stuff and talking, and getting to know each other. I don't usually write reviews, but I feel like due to this game getting a lot of flack, I need to give my two cents to whoever's wondering if they should get this game.
I am one of the people that backed this game (the tier to just get a copy on steam). Not from nostalgia, I just enjoy 3D platformer collectathons. My childhood games are Spyro 2, 3 and the Crash trilogy, but I only played Banjo Kazooie semi recently, and felt like it was much more open for exploration, but lacked the tightness and careful design of Spyro, its Playstation counterpart. I still enjoyed the game. I'm saying this just to point out that I have a more objective view on the Banjo-Yooka comparison than people who had N64s as kids.
First thing's first, the most important thing in these types of games in my opinion, the controls. It genuinely feels good to control Yooka, much more than in banjo in my opinion. The movement is very intutive, the jumps and roll feel good, even the flying that everyone is giving crap is pretty fine (doesn't come close to Spyro though :^) ) The only real control problems I had were rotating while ducking, and how slow some of the moves come out.
Another extremely important part is the level design. This is the real crux of this game. You only get five levels (each one you can "expand", so let's say you get 10 levels, with 5 pairs of jointed levels). The greatest problem compared to Banjo is that the levels are "too open". What I mean by this is, you have vast spaces you need to cross with absolutely nothing in them way too much of the time. People in the reviews constantly say that the first two levels and the fifth is okay, while the third is bad and fourth is horrible, but I did not have that experience at all. The third is actually my favourite level, followed by the fourth, the fifth, then the first, and lastly the second. The second is by far the worst, and has the most open, useless spaces.
Another issue with the level design is the complete lack of interactivity. First of all, nothing you do in one level will affect another level (like it did in Banjo Tooie a lot, for example). Not just that, but you make almost no change in the levels themselves at all! The most drastic change would be in the very first level, where you can change a basin that runs across a level from dry, to full of water, to that water being frozen, and maybe the last level, where you kind of add a platform that doesn't even need to be there, because you get flight.
Another issue and dimension of the openness has to do with what abilities you have. Namely, the ability to fly. I really don't think this should be a mechanic that's required for the levels, and should be more of a bonus ability that you get as a reward for collecting everything. What this basically does is tell you that the levels are not contained AT ALL. Anything can be anywhere, on any pixel of the map, and the only way to be sure is to go back to every level and fly to every single cliff and crevace and check. not just that, but that means you can skip 90% of the platforming by just getting the bare minimum until you get flying.
Speaking of flying, the energy meter. It's not like in Banjo where you can use kazooie to run infinitely. Now you have an energy meter for whatever you doing, functioning similarly to the feathers in BK. While I think having an energy meter and time limited ammo is an improvement to the feather system, the roll should not cost energy. Luckily you can make it so the roll doesn't waste much. The main problem is still the flying. You're supposed to fly across the entire world, but every 20 seconds or so (that's with most of the energy upgrades), you have to stand by for the same amount to get your energy back. It's just a waste of time and does nothing to make flying easier or harder, just more tedious, and annoying, because they expect you to fly everywhere anyway.
The enemies are just a nuissance, but I feel like that's what they were intended to be. Almost no thought process involved with them, or the attack system. The main focus is the platforming and movement, so I can forgive this. The biggest annoyance of a mob would be the big fat orange corplets, that have WAY too much health, and just one boring attack, as well as the invincibility eyes of possesion.
The bosses are much more thought out, but have the same problems as in banjo. Just repeat the same thing you've been doing but slightly harder until the boss is declared defeated. If you die, you repeat the entire boss. This isn't as much of an issue for the level bosses, as they're never that long, but Jesus Christ, the final boss is HORRIBLE with this. There are like 6-7 phases, each having different things you have to guess how to deal with. It wouldn't be annoying if you had checkpoints between the phases, but if you don't guess well enough, you have to repeat the entire "fight" again. A real sour taste in my mouth. Instead of the final boss putting the focus on what the rest of the game was about, platforming, it just showcases all the problems with the "fighting system" this game has. It should've been something like the final boss of Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones, another game with a huge focus on platforming as opposed to fighting (even though the fighting was actually pretty good).
The collectables are fine. You get pagies (read: Jiggies) by doing small challenges, either platforming or minigames issued by the side characters. The ghost writers are like Jinjos, but more interestingly designed. The quills are the notes, only just put randomly about, instead of as a way to guide the player to areas. Again, the problem is less with the quills themselves, but with the open level design and ability to fly. There are no restrictions to where a collectible can be in the level.
The music is fine, I guess. Wasn't interesting enough on its own, so I'd put a podcast in the background or something. Same goes for story and characters. Just kind of ok. The characters being not that great is more tragic, because there was great potential, but again, everyone lacks interactivity. At almost no point to the characters acknowledge the existence of one another, which just seems odd, especially for the characters that are there in multiple levels.
The camera used to be much worse, but was improved somewhat. Much better than BK, at least. You also couldn't skip the god-awful and boring cutscenes, but a patch fixed that as well. And gave you the ability to skip dialogue in general faster. So kudos on that. Still don't know how they're gonna fix that level design with a patch though.
I know all you've heard is criticism, but I genuinely enjoyed the game, with all the niggles it caused me. It's satisfying to collect stuff and do the platforming challenges, It's satisfying to move around and explore in general, especially in the levels that aren't the second level. I seriously hate that level. I'd recommend it for the same price I got it for, around 15€. Any more than that, I don't think it'd be worth the money. Not enough content, and not groundbreaking enough to warrant that much. It's just a bit of mindless, collectathon fun.

The base game is great, and the reason I bought this game. I used to play this long ago and since I noticed it was on steam, I got it. The reason I stayed, however, was because of the mods, 1 particular mod in fact called Movie Battles II. Movie Battles II is a competitive multiplayer mod, with tons of new features and player models. There are plenty of people still playing this mod and it's still getting updated, which is remarkable for a game this old.
Movie Battles adds loads of maps and new gamemodes like Open (Rebels vs Empire with classes such as Wookiee, Mandalorian, Clone trooper and Storm trooper, Jedi and Sith etc.), Duel (A mode for Jedi/Sith only as it is supposed to be lightsaber duelling), Full Authentic (Like Open except that it's supposed to be an authentic battle from the movies or other media like the games, and thus it has limited slots for certain characters e.g. there can't be 2 lukes at the same time).
Overall if you buy Jedi Academy or already own it, be sure to download Movie Battles II as well, as it's a fantastic mod for an already great game.

I have so many good memories from this game. Not from the specific one, but its sequel but that's the reason i know the series anyways. I am lucky that someone gave me the fall of max payne on PS as a gift, which was a significant part of my childhood. I recently bought this one and finished it for the first time. The fact that i have finished the sequel numerous times while knowing absolutely nothing about the original felt awkward. Well, it's about time i wrote a review.
The plot follows Max Payne, a NYPD cop in the '90s, who was living the "American Dream" before his wife and child were murdered. Three years later,he is working undercover in a drug case, which is connected to the death of his family, when he is framed for his partner's death. Now he has to work alone to uncover the truth.
It takes about 8 hours to complete
To begin with, it's a classic third person action ***(-adventure)*** shooter, with a great storyline and interesting action sequences, considering the year it was made.
+ Mainstream story but with a very interesting plot, but unfortunately, it seems that it's a small part of the game
+ Great Soundtrack
+ Graphic novels replace cinematic cutscenes, but not entirely, since there are still some.
+ Bullet time
+ Shootouts are too many to handle (dayum)
- Almost the entire game consists of shooting, shooting and shooting except:
- The prologues of each part which are not only kind of pointless but can also become really frustrating.
- ***Concerning the gameplay, there was no serious effort on map creation since they usually become boring, and simple. Not to mention the fact that they sometimes cover more than a chapter. Comparing them to the sequel's, they are not good, and deprive the of its potential of being consider an adventure game. Someone can easily assume that, at some points, it is like a hack 'n slash. game***
- Also, i was disapointed by the small variety of weapons. Commiting a genocide with berettas, deagle and occasionaly an M4 can get really boring. Additionally, the ammount of bullets it takes to bring someone down (excluding headshots) is ridiculous.
- Last but not least, the ability to save the game whenever you like makes the game less challenging, since this function can be abused, but no one, since the experience is ruined.
Concluding, i recommend grabbing the game only on sale (usually ~75%) since i dont think it's worth full price.

A small scale point and click mystery game, with a unique art style, but more importantly a story that will enthrall you through in-game conversations  with good writing and good voice acting.
This is a short story, disguised as a 4 screen point and click mystery adventure, that is actually a series of conversations with characters you don't even see in-game. But let me tell you why it's so good.
As a game, the puzzles are mostly simple and make sense. You have no inventory so it's a very streamlined experience. The bulk of the game is conversations with Maggie's neighbors, which are done through the thin walls of her apartment, so you don't see most of them visually. However, the conversations are where the game shines. The neighbors, despite being a voice on the other side of a wall, all come off as fleshed out people, they feel real. The quality of the writing and voice acting was my favorite part of this game. I was honestly impressed by what I thought was a low-budget indie-game. And grew to like several of the characters, which I also think is the mark of good writing.
To speak to sound design, as someone who lives in New York City, and played this game with headphones, I had to take my headphones off a few times to check if the sounds I was hearing where in-game, or outside my own apartment building. The credits page is 2 screens long, and the second page is sound licensing, so if you want a true big-city sound experience, this game does it the best I've ever heard. The goofy sound effects are fun, but the real city noises I did have trouble distingusing from in-game, or the real city outside my own window.
You are sometimes given dialog path decisions to determine the other character's opinion of Maggie. Though I feel the scope of the game requires only one true path through the game, I still enjoyed the occasional "I agree", "No you're wrong!" option, and it makes me consider a second play-through to see what would happen if I picked other options. Again, the conversations are the strong point, so I would want to hear more of them. I also enjoyed the prerogative this game has that this binary decision isn't "good" or "bad" and more "what would advance the plot" so you are sometimes forced into picking what would normally be "bad" because you know it's the only way the story would make sense. Which is a nice diversion from the triple-A "moral" games, which get on my nerves, and I enjoyed the dedication to story in this game.
As stated before, the game is short, it took me a little over 2 hours to get from beginning to end. But it is very much a mystery story. Throughout the game they hint at what the conclusion could be, and I drew my own conclusions based on the clues, and while I was close, the ending took me by surprise. And I very much enjoyed not only the ending to the story, but the the plot wrap-up where everything was completely explained by the information already given, which I think is the mark of a good mystery story.
Watch the trailer, the last quarter is actual gameplay, it'll give you a sense of the animation and visual quality. But the bulk of the game is in story telling, and character development that is really the quality of this game. The single conversation the trailer shows with a character is so limited, and that's really the game's strength. It's a fun mystery, lead by conversations, and I think the trailer relies too much on the artistic style, which ends up being a small part of the experience.
I enjoyed my time with Maggie, and would reccomend it to others.

I'm just gonna start with some complaining to get it out of the way, but trust me, if I didn't like this game, I wouldn't bother to write this.
First, the tone is kind of all over the place. One minute I'm cackling at a cactus elaborately dissing the sun, the other it's the genuinely tragic story about lies, manipulation and attempted murder.
Didn't really get why we had to painstakingly give the police guy four bottles one by one and watch him drink each of it. I thought that maybe it was going to be a plotpoint later, like Randy gets angry that you gave away X beer bottles, but nope?
Beauty's voiceacting sounds a little too bored and emotionless. It's cute in small doses, but she has to dramatically narrate at the end a lot. I really enjoyed Shrimp and Cheesey's voices, though.
I'm also still confused whether Beauty and Dunc are the actual inhabitants of this world, or Maggie just imagined herself some friends. I mean, Randy knew about Beauty's existence, but all the other characters we see look humanoid.
Aside from that, I really like the artwork (hell, I basically bought the game because of it), and the characters are fun and likeable. The bit with the cop and the pirated music made me laugh out loud.
I love that this game has a retro feeling to it. It's like I'm playing some old point-and-click adventure from the classic era, I have a huge soft spot for that.
Also, I gotta say, it would've been really easy to ridicule a fat girl who watches TV in her undies all day and gushes about her flamboyant husbando, but the game just lovingly pokes fun at her, and I respect that.
As someone who also tried developing games in a team of two people, I kinda admire the way you managed to cut so many corners. The game takes place in one room, you never see most of the characters you talk to, the major plotpoint is described over the radio, the main character is a simplified white blob that's easy to animate, the other two major characters are just a cactus and a radish... And I don't mean it in a bad way, since a) the game is short enough so that you don't get tired of it b) the voiceacting adds more character to the people we can't see c) it's claustrophobic, but it fits Maggie, who doesn't go out much and just focuses on her boyfriend. It's so cleverly low-budget, it's impressive.
Overall, a cute little experience. Can't say I didn't have fun. Kudos to you guys.

Maggie's Apartment is one of the best written point and click adventures I have played.  Its fantastic visuals and simple yet satisfying game play make this a must have.
The artwork and animation are visually stunning.  Character movements are not programmed sprite sliding around on the screen but rather fully animated natural movements.  Maggie bounces, shakes and shimmies at every interaction.  There are few backgrounds, but this is to the effect of the creative design.  But the backgrounds that are included feel lived in and characterize Maggie and her world.
The game play mechanics are a simplified form of point and click. The entire game takes place in Maggie’s apartment. Her only interactions are to her house plants and her neighbors through the walls. You would think this would make the game feel small and restrictive, but it doesn’t, there is a lot to learn talking to the walls.  Further, Maggie cannot pick up any items. Instead you drag items as the lay in her apartment to what you want to interact with.  This works really well, since you never leave the apartment, it is very intuitive and lets Maggie assemble the mess she lives in.  The game play is simple and revolves around the concept of discovery.  It is not so much as puzzling out how to do something but discovering solutions.
Voice acting in the game was brilliant as well.  Characters were well developed and every voice personified them perfectly.  No phoned in acting here, accents (albeit cartoonish) were well done and unique to the characters. Even the sound engineering was spot on.  Voices were muffled in a way that made you feel like you were listening through walls.  Moreover, the radio in the apartment played music which doubled as the menu to control sound in the game (clever).
Maggie’s Apartment is fine example of excellent writing.  Maggie is deeply flawed and incredibly endearing.  For the entire story, Maggie is mostly naked and exposed, while in the supposed safety of her apartment. In contrast the private and intimate lives of those around her seep through the walls easily.  Even outside Maggie’s apartment the game makes a point to show that everything going on around is completely exposed. These concepts re-enforce the revelation of the truth. And, without spoiling the game to much, its conclusion is wonderful. The dialogue is engrossing and with every revelation I was eager to learn more.  Plotting and theme are creative and build an argument that has very real truth to it. Put simply, this game is written splendidly.
Maggie's Apartment scores perfect tens on all counts. Art and animation were lively, voice acting and music where brilliant, and the game play was simple yet fun. But the star of the show was the well written story. Honestly, there are so many reasons to recommend this game it is difficult to count.

As someone who has adored Howard's artwork and previous freeware game releases, I was extremely excited when the trailer for Maggie's Apartment was released, and eagerly waited for the official release of the game. Now that I've played it, would I say that my hype was deserved? Yes, absolutely.
Maggie's Apartment is a wonderful game, and it feels like a love letter to the kind of wonder and excitement that 90s point-and-click games held back in their heydey, and especially the charm of the Humongous Entertainment games. The animation style, while largely minimal, does exactly what it needs to, and combined with the offbeat character designs feels charming and friendly to look at. The warmth of the visuals also provides an interesting contrast to the sorrows of the plot, but you'll have to find out exactly how for yourself. The writing and voicework for the game is also top-notch, as every character's voice and dialogue feels completely natural to them, and the writing feels clever without being smarmy or annoying.
The game is not without its flaws, but I'd say largely they're the kind of flaws that the majority of point-and-click games suffer from. Figuring out how to progress can be baffling and require solutions that are hard to logically reach unless you remember the old point-and-click gameplay standby of "examine everything, try to combine every object with every other object, exhaust every dialogue choice". The minimalist animation style, while charming, also means that during some of the conversations (and some of them go on for QUITE a while, as some characters love to talk about nothing in order to cover up the SOMETHING that's the real issue they're having) there's not a lot to look at, and I found myself looking away from the game during these points, which felt like a crime, because it IS a very beautiful game.
If you're a point-and-click fan, or someone who loves to play games for character intriuge, or who loves the look of hand-drawn animation, I'd absolutely recommend the game. I would not recommend it for kids (unless you got some weird kids) because as charming as the style is, the game deals with some fairly dark concepts here and there, and the ending is fairly intense. Overall though, it's a game I'm still thinking about and feel strongly affectionate for, even if it took me far too long to get around to finishing it.

Every single thing about this game has so much character, ESPECIALLY little Maggie. We all know what it's like to be in a situation where you're blinded by love, and this game took it to the extreme in such a simple, almost silly way. Even the "serious" stuff about this game is funny, but the point still gets across. Maggie was, of course, the main reason this game was so dang good. She's a cute, short, chubby girl who is WAY too lost in her hopeless romantic outlook, just like me! It was honestly a bit humbling to see a character so much like myself in a story like this. I feel wonderful after playing this, because I really feel like I UNDERSTAND what Maggie goes through. It's not just a surface-level conflict, even if it is a bit SILLY of a conflict.
In short, this game was fantastic. If I was playing it with no distractions, I'm a bit convinced I would've cried at least a little near the end, especially since I know pain like what Maggie experiences. Good music, good art, good jokes, everything was wonderful! I want to be sad it was so short, but I feel like it would've overstayed it's welcome otherwise.
For anyone looking to play a short, silly, and strangely thought-provoking game, Maggie's Apartment is perfect for you.

Here comes the bad:
This game came with my R9 390, so I'm not copmpletely upset, just disappointed. At this time I can't recommend this game until something is done about the always-online stuff. I stopped pirating games once I could afford to buy them and for the convenience of being able to play games offline or online without hassle or worry since my copy was legitimate. Implementing heavily obstructive DRM and requiring online connectivity for a SINGLE-PLAYER experience is pretty much giving paying customers the middle finger. Let people who buy your game enjoy it, intagible assets like customer goodwill goes a long way guys...

"Dream Daddy" is a game with great humor and huge potential, that, despite it's charm, left me disappointed. Don't get me wrong, this is very entertaining game and it will probably make you laugh, but it isn't working out as a good dating sim or romance story.
I can't believe no one ever did something like that before. Playing as single dad, who is dating other
single dads is something unique and refreshing among bunch of angsty teenage boys you usually encounter in BL visual novels.
Dads are great. Each of them not only looks different, but has unique personality and style. I fell in love with some of those guys
and I just wish could spend more time with every one of them.
Writing is great. You will probably laugh a lot.
I love how this game shows relationship between protagonist and his daughter. Plus, Amanda is adorable.
Game description states, that it was voiced by Game Grumps. There is no "voice acting". There are few grunts that are repeated way too often, to the point, where it's actually annoying and dumb. You can't turn it off, which is another issue.
Like proper skipping (without unseen text) and text speed regulation.
Like I've mentioned above, I really enjoyed all of the pursuable characters, but in every single case, "romance" happens way to quick, with rushed ending, that also doesn't make much sense. For example since Craig
. MC goes on those "dates", but most of them aren't really romantic or even a way to set up romance. It's just two dudes chilling and doing their stuff and talking, and getting to know each other. That's nice, but when after two meetings, said dudes suddenly discover that they are really into each other, it just doesn't seem compelling. Especially, since we are talking about gay relationship. No one really discuss anything and ask if the other person like men IN THAT WAY, they just go with the flow, which is unrealistic.
It's about 8-9 hours long. That's not bad. What is bad, is the fact, that games FEELS too short and rushed. I think I would prefer if there were less, but better established routes, with more in-game time.
To sum it up: if you like LGBT themed games and enjoy solid dose of bad puns and some clever writing, you will  like this game. If you expect it to be a good dating sim though, you probably won't feel satisfied with what you'll get.

I got my Dream Daddy (Robert), but will play through the rest of the Daddy Dates to see how they pan out. The game is short if you stick with one dad, but if you go out on the dates with all the dads, the game will have replayability value to see how all the Dream Daddys stack up to the initial one you end up choosing. Before choosing Robert, I went out on one Mat date, one Joseph date, one Brian date, two Craig dates, and two Damien dates.
To sum this game up, Dream Daddy is a dating sim. That's the short of it. You move with your daughter, Amanda, to a cul-de-sac inhabited by other single dads. You go out on dates with them (2 initial dates, and then the third decides your Dream Daddy), all the while still being a dad to your daughter and sharing all the good times with her...and all the bad.
I went into this game expecting something goofy and off-the-wall. Surprisingly, I was wrong, but in a good way! The animations were charming, the characters were well-designed, the dialogue was funny, quirky, and had heart and soul put into it. I was surprised at how much I connected with Dad and Amanda, as well as with my dad of choice. The writing I have to say is this game's biggest strength.
The voice acting (funny Sim-like grunts and various short phrases) fit the tone of the game, though I did not care for the way Hugo's voice was recorded (it sounded like it was in a tin can). Also, there are some times where your character says to a dad that a certain thing happened and you didn't come across that moment in the game yet/at all, and it breaks the immersion experience a bit.
To me it was worth the money I spent on it. If you want a game with heart behind it, and a game where you can get some laughs, play Dream Daddy. It is well worth your money...and your time. :)

First off, this has been my first foray into the Ninth World of Numenera. I gotta say, I wish I had more opportunities to have experienced it sooner. It's a lovely mixture of SciFi and Fantasy that keeps me coming for more.
I'll be blunt with you, friends - The game is still in development as of this posting, but a big new patch was released today, promising many lovely updates to make an already entertaining slice of the game (It IS still being made, after all) into an overall better polished, and more tasteful slice.
If you're a fan of old school RPGs, or enjoy sci fi - Hell. Come give the game a shot when it's released. You'll get a kick out of it.

A lot of praise has been given to this title for the writing, and rightfully so. The vocabulary and structure are an elegant delight to read and makes the intimidating undertaking of reading millions of words on a monitor before completion something to actually look forward to.
But TTON's strength also lies in the quality of the encounters. They are surprisingly imaginative when taken separately. As you'll gather enough pieces to form a story, it only gets better.
All of this is spiced up by interaction with alien tools and skills that get you through strange situations, refreshingly different than typical RPG mythos.

Now I've been through the early access version meticulously (expected bugs included) and in spite of the few glitches, it's obvious what a completely awesome and amazing story this is.
I totally and gleefully look forward to the finished version.
Lifting the legacy of Planescape Torment is, in my eyes, quite an impossibility. I've kept coming back to that game like a favourite story since it was released, but I almost think they might succeed.
In creating a setting so different, and yet so similar, I feel like I'm being given all the same philosophical, ambiguous and metaphysical strangeness, but in a new world without it being just old stuff reiterated. The atmosphere is different, the characters, the tone. And yet somehow, it's recognisable as a successor.

Long story short, this is the kind of story that I will likely keep coming back to in the future too.
I can't wait to see the finished product.
10/10

Torment: Tides of Numenera is intended to be the spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment, which has been said to be one of the best RPGs created and I am inclined to agree. The settings, writing and characters were all rich in detail.
I am happy to say that, so far, TToN is shaping up to also be a masterpiece to be remembered.
At first the settings will seem alien to you and you'll feel slightly confused, but gradually everything will make sense if you open your mind to concepts that would otherwise seem impossible to comprehend under normal circumstances.
You'll end up wanting to explore every corner of every area, finding secrets, speaking to the locals or simply examining strange, otherwordly technology in the hopes to gain some sort of advantage through them.
Many of the quests will not give you a sense of what is the right and what is the wrong decision, leaving it up to you to decide what the best course of action is based entirely on your personal interpretation and opinion and even then you might be wondering "was that truly the best choice there was?"
An example containing spoilers: At some stage you will find a creature in a bar, lamenting the fact that he lost contact to the rest of his civilization, whose purpose it was to guide others. The most obvious choice would be to use your powers to rid his mind of the sadness enveloping his thoughts. After you do so his sadness turns into cold determination as he sets out, not to guide people, but to dictate over their lives with an iron fist. (Or that is how I interpreted the turn of events. Correct me if I'm wrong.)
Would I recommend the game as it is now? Yes, if you can accept the fact that it is not finished, but you want a glimpse of what is to come. Otherwise just wait until its full release.

This game has come out roughly around the same time Halo:  CE has, and this game has aged much better than its spacey FPS counterpart.  For a third person shooter, this game sets a benchmark, and its set pretty damn high.  It may be old, it may be grimy, but it still holds up well with surprisingly solid controls, and a great story showing an inside look at the criminal underworld of organized crime.
What's more amazing (as shown in many Rockstar games) is their unique ability to create their own world with its own advertisements and even TV shows.  Kong Whiskey.  Captain Baseball Bat Boy.  Lords & Ladies.  Aseir Corporation, etc.  The game provides a surprisingly immersive environment comparable to a Valve game.  You even get a part of the game where the 4th Wall is broken in a silly way.  Overall, this game is a shining gem of the turn of the century.

I bought this back in 2015 as a way to tide me over and scratch that post-apocalypse itch before Fallout 4 hit. Little did I know however was just how much this game would surprise me. Fallout 4 launched and well...I was let down by it - badly. This on the other hand kept making me return for more. It's not a long game but it is a beautifully realised one graphically and in the way its world feels. The driving feels excellent - the vehicle mods make tangible differences to your car whilst the vehicular combat is wild and bombastic. The on foot combat is similarly tight and immensely satisfying with Arkham Asylum-esque combos and counter prompts. Another positive to this game is the audio and the ambient musical score, which really set the tone for the vast swathes of wasteland you'll be traversing. In short, I would easily play this again through to completion rather than bang my head against the cack handed game that is Fallout 4.
Pros -
- Graphically gorgeous (and well optimised on lower end systems so I hear)
- Tightvehicle handling
- Satisfying vehicle and on foot combat
- Haunting soundscapes
- Appropriate bleakness and misery
- Australians
Cons -
- Slightly short
- Certain mission types can be slightly dull (I'm looking at you mine clearing)

Just for context I am one of the post kickstarter backers who pledged on the site for 75$. Do I regret buying the game? No, not really. Do I regret backing for extras? Yeah kinda. Torment is devisive game at the moment and I feel that the game is simply not worth it at this time. I may reccomend it at a price drop but there are a number of reasons I cannot reccomend it at the time. So lets break down why I feel this game just isnt what I had hoped for.
The Good:
-2D backgrounds are really well drawn
-Story is good (not great just good) and setting is very unique
-Lots of choice and consequence
The Bad:
-The writing is bloated and a slog to read (they need an editor seriously)
-If you play peacefully 99% of the game is reading and going back and forth between NPC's
-The crisis have a novel idea but feel rather dull and uninteresting.
-Lacks any meaningfull mechanical RPG mechanics outside of conversations
-Lots of cut content
-Feels like a visual choose your own adventure vs an actual isometric CRPG
-Console versions are completely pointless as no regular console player is gonna buy this
-exploration is pointless if you dont do any of the combat
If you want a proper CRPG with good writing/conversations AND fun gameplay buy Wasteland 2 and/or Pillars of Eternity. If you liked Planescape Torment and want a game with a kinda similar feel (although Planescape felt more like a game tbh) then sure buy it. But if you want a proper CRPG look elsewhere.

It doesn't look very good today, and we've seen the central mechanic copied a thousand times since, but this is a classic of action gaming that's proven very influential over the years, for better or worse. Even if it hasn't aged the best, the copious helping of noir style and dead-serious melodrama mixed with weird humour make this one still worthwhile, and I recommend running through it as part of a full trilogy run.
It comes from a simpler time where shooters could just be about shooting everyone, with no vehicle sections, no hacking minigames, no rpg elements, no sandbox elements, no moral choices, no collectibles, no quicktime events, no... well, you get the idea. It can seem like a relic today, but I appreciate the simplicity and devotion to doing one thing and doing it well. Coupled with one of my favourite video game protagonists, and this one remains a fond memory even when played today.

In these days of miserable sheisters, developer pond life and microtransactions in early access games (i'm looking at you Ylands) it is a breath of fresh air to see a developer with some moral fibre. Has Klei ever put a foot wrong? Certainly not with Oxygen Not Included. Priced according to value, a tight schedule of meaningful updates, a game that continues to grow and reach ever more subtle layers of complexity. I only wish that Klei games could be duplicated like its charming characters and there were several Klei studios making games. This is how Early Acces games should be developed and brought to market. Klei continue to offer the very best of games with integrity, decency and value. There simply is nobody better and its come to a sorry pass that common decency that ought to be a given stands out from the crowd.
If you like colony management games it doesn't get much better than this, if you're on the fence about backing an early access game, it doesn't get much better than this, if you like complexity, replayability and a challenge, it doesn't get much better than this. If you want to support one of the finest studios out there, it doesn't geet much better than this. If you want the rare privilege of buying the game and just getting the game without being nickel and dimed and generally shafted, it doesn't get much better than this.
I'm so tired of gaming industry shenanigans that has left such a sour taste in the mouth whilst gaming and I cannot tell you how pleasant it is to get what I pay for, and to hand over the cash to people who so thoroughly deserve it and ask only for a fair return on a hard days work. Thankyou Klei, and hats off to you

So, went into B:AO having finished both B:AC & B:AA, both of which I thought were pretty great. City was a masterpiece, a counterpoint of amazing design, story and combat. Origins; sadly not as much. So why am I recommending it? Well, it is really good, beautifully designed, intelligent, but you can’t help feeling that the game is pushing you down the path of one beat-em-up to the next. The scenes are amazing, but certain environments feel completely underused. The have fantastic atmosphere but the inane radio conversations with Alfred, who for some reason in the game is a master hacker, spy, and psychologist despite being 75 and a butler… none of the canon suggests otherwise.
When Arkham City came out, it was what Assassins Creed 2 did for the original AC; built on a great idea and then took it somewhere better with the sequels (mostly.) The entire Assassins Creed series has been built on the idea of pushing the environment, the story and the combat styles. Now both AC and the Batman series have a lot in common in terms of gameplay, combat options etc. So why then did WB stop inventing when there was so much opportunity? The combat is IDENTICAL to Arkham City, very few additions have been made. For the first time, you feel Batman is underpowered in combat (until you get the gloves…) but even then, you feel anaemic in hand-to-hand as you hit some street thug for the 12th time and he still gets up for more?  The combo’s are still pretty cool, and the unlocks are decent too (although no clear guideline as to HOW you should develop you character or options of gameplay (Hint: upgrade ALL your physical combat abilities as quickly as possible in your first play through, you won’t be doing much else but forced button mashing for the majority of the game, right up to the end.)
Spiderman 3 -proof you don’t need to cram in every super villain in a single story. So why do we have 15+ in this game? Is it because at the last minute, everyone agreed that there wasn’t enough story without it? And the combat with all but a few is more irritating than awesome. I REALLY didn’t enjoy most of the encounters, not because of the difficulty, but they just felt forced. Randomly, the game throws in another half-dozen “heavies” mid-boss fight who basically just get in the way. You spend a few minutes swatting them off you like flies before heading back to the main guy only to realise that 1 more well timed mini-game “press Y to counter” and he/she was toast?!?
My other pet peeve in the game was the tiny combat spaces. This game is huge, wide open spaces, but you will spend most of the game in micro-combat arenas trying to put some space between yourself and the group of 17 henchmen, all WAY to close to really open up and deliver some serious combo blows. This is with the exception of the “bird” side mission run-up where you have 20+ encounters in nice, open spaces. It feels great until the final “bird” fight which is massively disappointing.
Lastly, I have to mention the utility belt and amazing no-you-can’t-attach-there-right-now grapnel gun. Good game design dictates that you create natural feeling limitations and barriers to keep players in the sandbox environment you have created. And with good reason. It would suck to suddenly end up “IDSPSPOPD-ing” off the map. (That’s a Doom reference kids, ask you dad.) But why, when you are Batman, flying through the city and jumping from tower to tower does THAT tower suddenly not let you attach to the balcony, or that one, or that one?!?! What’s going on? Was it because the buildings are too high for the render, or is it because the developers through it would give an unfair advantage in tactical environments? NEWSFLASH – Batman punches people with sniper rifles and machine guns by the handful. The odds aren’t exactly stacked in his favour… Now I admit, in some scenarios, the limitations of the environment are necessary, but when one bridge strut allows you to power-grapple and the next one drops you on your♥♥♥♥♥ that’s poor design.
I have read a couple of other reviews of this game and agree with a lot of them. You get the feeling the studio and the game developers simply ran out of time to polish it quite right before deadline and so shipped out a slightly buggy, almost masterpiece that is aching for better treatment. A sad and experience ruining oversight. Batman: Arkham Origins is primed for some genius to mod the ever-loving sh!t out of it into something better, if WB ever lets them…

Garfield Kart. Ah, Garfield Kart. Where do I begin with my beloved Garfield Kart?
Well, Garfield Kart is probably the best game I've ever played (hence my playtime). Everything about it is truly incredible. From the beautifully rendered 3D graphics, to the immersive, fun gameplay, everything about this game adds up to an overall wonderful experience. Also of note is the beautiful music, which required an entire orchestra, which, I must say, was completely worth it. It adds so much to the great experience of Garfield Kart.

Now, on the gameplay. It is truly innovative. The game is played using the arrow keys and various other buttons to drift and use items and whatnot. I know that playing a racing game with the arrow keys may, to some, sound like playing Dark Souls with a keyboard and mouse, but rest assured, once you try it, you'll never be able to go back to the old way of playing racing games.  It really adds a lot to the experience, that you couldn't get by using a controller.
Also on the topic gameplay, the characters. Each one has their own quirks and characteristics. Some, like the big G-Man himself, are more all-rounders that can do well in any vehicle or any driving style.  Others, like John, are more specialized and require a lot of practice with their specific style to do well. Overall, there is a nice variety that allows so much replayability.
Now, onto the graphics. They're amazing. Each character is beautifully rendered in 3D. I know some people say that graphics don't really matter, but in this game, they really make a difference. I don't think the game would be quite the same if the graphics were worse. Also, oh my god. Those female characters are HOT! Check out the Rule 34 for this game immediately (though, after this review of course).
So, you may be wondering how the game runs. And, I must say, it's runs SO smoothly. Even on my rig, which is pretty cheap, I can get upwards of 200 frames. It's just optimized so incredibly well. How they did this, I have no idea, but it's truly amazing.
To wrap it all up, get this game. It has beautiful graphics, fun, innovative gameplay, great music, and it all runs super well. All of that is only five dollars. ONE OF THE BEST GAMES EVER MADE. And it's only the price of a sandwich from Subway, if you live in 2010. Just get it, dude. Now. Do it. NOW. You won't regret it.

Jedi Academy is, simply put, one of the best Star Wars games I've ever played. The story is ... okay, I guess? It's not bad but it's no BioWare KOTOR epic story. Whatever. It's got some interesting (no longer canon, thanks Disney) stuff about ancient Sith Lords that's cool if you're into (no-longer-canon) lore. The graphics are pretty good, especially for a 2003 game they've held up pretty well.
But the game is really significant for one very important reason. No Star Wars game before or since has ever captured the feeling of wielding a lightsaber as well as this one. You know, that thing all of us who have ever seen a Star Wars movie have always dreamed of? This is the game that does it best. Other Star Wars games at best make you feel like you're wielding a regular sword that's been given a Star Wars mod. In Jedi Academy, I felt like I was truly wielding a deadly beam of light. I'm a traditional one-saber kind of gal myself, but I also love how the game put real thought into developing fighting styles for wielding 2 lightsabers or a double-bladed Darth Maul style saber as well.
I also really like the ability to choose between a variety of missions instead of being forced along a totally strict linear path. It's not anywhere near total sandbox freedom, but being able to quit out of a frustrating mission and try a different one instead is nice.
tl;dr: THE BEST LIGHTSABER COMBAT IN ANY STAR WARS GAME EVER

This is a solid older title.
Unlike a lot of older titles, the difficulty in this game is actually a bit on the easy side, partly because the AI is braindead but also because your Force Powers are awesomely powerful. You will plow through most enemies once you get a handle on the mechanics, though special enemies that crop up in a couple of missions will require some finesse.
Saber combat is this game's highlight. This game came out before QTEs became a standard feature of combat games, but it still manages to feel fluid and satisfying, allowing for a few different fighting styles, from noob-friendly flurries to rapid-swapping between saber stances to catch an opponent off-guard. The saber also reflects blaster shots and is throwable, so it's a very versatile weapon - so versatile that you'll only rarely need to use the other weapons at all.
The story is nothing special - it's the typical "stop those dastardly Sith/Imperials from galactic domination" story. There is some character customization but it is primitive by modern standards. The game is structured around five-mission sets of varying style and difficulty (of which you have to do at least four in any order) punctuated by longer, mandatory ones that advance the story. The main plot is a bit hamstrung by this since that means there are only about four plot-advancing missions, but this structure does successfully convey the feeling of the everyday life of a Jedi, taking errands all over the galaxy.
Along the way you unlock Force Powers. Not all the Force Powers are equally useful, but there are a few powerful and very fun ones. Fully upgraded Mind Trick allows you to turn an enemy for 30 seconds, Grip allows you to fling enemies into walls or off ledges, Lightning allows you to devastate an entire roomful of baddies at once. Do note that the default key-bindings kind of suck, and I recommend re-binding them to your preference in the control options.
The graphics, as expected of an old game, are servicable but unremarkable. The sound design though, is excellent. From the music to the way every weapon and enemy sounds, this SOUNDS like a Star Wars game. And the voice acting is superb all round, including Jennifer Hale for the female Jaden.
At only a few dollars on sale, and with a fairly short SP campaign (~12-15 hours) I would say it's at least worth a try!

Just played a bit of it, but I can already enumerate some points. First, I died before I could even start the game. How? In an awesome way, but I won't give you spoilers. Since the first lines of the narration, you`re already choosing your destiny and changing whatever you don't know you're going to change, and that's simply terrifying and gratifying at the same time. About the "Planescape: Torment premise", well, I might say the whole package is all in it, even if many thing are not implemented and "well developed" yet, you can "feel" it`s all there.  I can give a couple of examples from what I`ve already experienced: alien-ish and complete freakish ambientation, great character development, "things" so bizarre simply apread all over places for you to interact and figure (what the hell) is it about, dense and metaphysical dialogues that give you the creeps and "haunt" your decision-making. Aside of that, you're simply thrown into the world without knowledge or making sense of anything. It's strange. The most common word not for the begining of the game but for the whole of it.
I'm sincerely SUPER excited for what's coming next (patches and updates) and still exploring and understanding everything we already have. It's not something simple to make a game whose main premise is to continue the legacy of one of the greatest RPG's ever made. It's really a BOLD proposition, but I have to say, the guys in InXile are treading the right path towards this goal.

I have played the first bits of the game and so far, I am very much impressed. The writing is top-notch, and it really brought back those times when an RPG game really puts you in the shoes of your character. The amount of lore, the presence of literary power, and philosophical queries places this game in my list of video games as gesamntkunstwerk (total art), as an experience. Truly, the developers are one of those legendary people who are sent to this world to create these type of games.
The game has its performance issues, of course, since it is still on Early Access. A load of bugs, optimization issues, and in my case, I experience tons of lag especially in the beginning of the game. Hopefully, the developers will do work on these issues and I wish them luck on that.
To sum up, this is the type of game you should buy and play because it immerses you into a world that is merely a reflection of our own. The decisions of the Last Castoff are refractions of your decisions in your own life. I think video games (open-ended/open-world RPG's in particular [tho T:ToN is more open-ended]) are an existential commodity that serves as a prism to our own experiences in life. And with the emergence of games like Torment: Tides of Numenera, I think its players will get to answer questions about individuality, the weight of their choices in this tapestry of life, and most importantly, they will get a glimpse of the essence of their existence.

Unapologetically Queer: This is Dream Daddy.
Yes, a queer game made it to the #1 top seller on Steam despite how toxic the internet can be towards queer topics and especially in games.  In DDaDDS (Dream Daddy: A Dad Dating Simulator) you take on the role of a widowed father of one, Amanda.  In this story-driven, choose-your-path simulator you end up moving into a Cul de Sac (Up until this point, I always thought it was Cul ve Sac!  I learned something from a video game!).  Your daughter Amanda is going off to college soon, and it seems like your only source of interaction are going to be all these hawt dads that coincidentally, live on the same Cul de Sac as you (Super convinced it’s the Matrix for daddies)
A Happy Ending?
Dating is hard, and in a videogame, it’s a lot harder.  DDaDDS presents you with opportunities to make your own choice in decisions that will affect the outcome of the storylines you partake in.  The stories I experienced were with my daughter Amanda, and Craig.  Picking the “right” choices are very important if you’re looking to romance your daddy, or have a good relationship with your daughter.  At first, it felt like the game was giving me many choices, allowing me to continue with my “own story”  However, when I got to the end of the third date with Craig, he ended up rejecting me.  I had realized that on the 2nd date, I had to “do better” (Daddies will indicate with different “glows”, like Hearts, Dark Clouds, and of course, EGGPLANTS).  It’s a reminder that every decision you make in real life can affect outcomes.  Luckily, in DDaDDs, you can easily rewind time by loading an auto-save from before the time you screwed up.  In a weird way, this game has caused me to be more wary of my actions in any future friendships I’ll have.
If you’re like me, you’ll get swept away in the writing of this game.  From the dad-jokes (Obama Jokes) that give you an honest chuckle, to the hypothetical scenarios where I’d catch myself thinking “How would I handle this with my child?” (Oh honey, I’ll never have one, I’m too selfish and fabulous).  The writing is so convincing, you may even fall for your digital daddy but then realize, oh he’s just a hologram.
The great things about this game, could go on and on.  To sum it all up in a sentence: Streamer Mode to remove any non-royality free music, great customizable options for your Dadsona (though more outfits would be greatly appreciated!), and dare I say it: The Dad Tips during loading screens BEAT any Sims loading screen tips and will provide wise wisdom to last a lifetime.
So, now that you’ve read my recommendation, get your Dadsona on and date some dads!

There's something refreshing about Maggie's Apartment that I can't quite put my finger on.
Something that's important to know going in is that it's a very small, self-contained story. It feels like you're learning just as much about Maggie and her relationships as you are about the mystery. I'm not going to spoil what happens, but the game definitely has some interesting commentary on celebrity culture and idolization.
I really like the art style in this. It has kind of an 80's quality to it, for lack of a better description. Lots of highly-saturated colors and dramatic, rubbery character designs reminiscent of the work of Craig McCracken or David Feiss (the person who animated this is a Calarts student if you couldn't already tell). I dig the designs of Rascal and Randy in particular- they're both very funny and memorable. I know it's not a huge deal for point n' click games to be hand-animated, but I think it's honorable here nonetheless, especially given how much care is given when it comes to basic movements, like climbing onto a couch.
As with many point n' click adventure games, Maggie's Apartment can be a little cryptic sometimes- there are points where you have to exhaust every single character's dialogue options (sometimes multiple times) to advance the plot. Keep that in mind particularly when talking to Rascal. The game also doesn't explain this right away, but instead of having an inventory, you just click and drag objects in the room to other objects. Sometimes both objects are move-able, and sometimes only one, like when objects need to interact with the window or the Randy poster.
I was kind of hoping the game would have some branching paths, but it appears to be a series of puzzles based around a linear, predetermined path. This is honestly fine by me- it's a game made by a couple of art students, not programmers. Play this game for the art, the story, and the comedy, but it's probably not what you want if you're looking for a challenge.

This game is really interesting to me. Usually people like games similar to GTA or Need For Speed, which I do like as well, but I also like simulators, like this one. They can really teach you how a lot of the things work, and how to properly drive, check your mirrors, etc.. The tasks are pretty simple. Choose a quick job, drive from point A to B. Along the way you may run crash, run out of fuel, or you may just end up with a traffic ticket. You are able to create your own company, but you don't really have the necessary funds from the beginning of the game in order to buy a truck, a garage, or hire workers. I'd also like to add that the creators of ETS2 are going to release American Truck Simulator next month (at the time this is being written) so that is also something else to keep an eye out for.

+ Tight platforming

: Controls work well.  I played 100% with the controller so I can't speak to how well the keyboard and mouse work.
: This game very much hearkens back to Banjo-Kazooie.  You start a level and have to find and collect all of the coins (feathers) and get your trophies (pages).  However, each level is essentially just a collection of set pieces with open space between them.  Nearly none of the areas has any sense of cohesion and you could just about see the boundary line for each section.
Each level has two forms: beginner, then expanded.  I'd recommend doing beginner first to get a general layout down before the level gets too wide to really grasp.  As there's almost nothing tying the levels together they can be VERY wide making it hard to orient yourself.
: Beautifully up-resed N64 goodness.  Every character is well crafted, however there are only a handful of enemies in the whole game.
: Story is laughably simplistic, however, this is par for the course for games like this.  The story works just fine: Bad guy collects things that you have to get back so he can't use things to take over the world.
: You'll get several hours of collectathon goodness, however you'll miss the elements that really tied the told games together into a whole.  I found myself really enjoying exploring each time I got a new power, however by the end I was really just wanting it to be over

You're sitting in a room, alone.  Before you hover images, passing in rapid sequence, but conveying a comforting sense of the entirety of a whole.  You sift through their details - an odd protuberance in an unexpected place, a comforting voice passing through the air behind you - and ponder.  While you draw no closer to these images physically, your mind and will are progressively and inexorably more deeply involved in the events you observe, these same events you even direct, to some extent.  You notice that, in reflections of reflections, you weigh heavy questions.  They pass through lesser used corridors in your mind, and prompt at once both introspection and alarm.  You realize then that you just spent the greater part of an afternoon, and the equivalent of the price of a quality meal for two, on a simulacrum, still in its fledgling state, of worlds only known to a glimmering few, and you yearn to know - to feel - more.
If you've read this far, congratulations.  You'll see more like this, lots more, as you wade, wander, and weigh your options through this newest world of Torment.
After starting over twice, and a good, what, 30 hours at this point?  I finally found an in-canon expositor who at least helped me, the human playing this game, understand that numenera is a plural noun indicating objects, not a singular proper noun indicating a place.  I know what two of the five tides regard, and my latest protagonist is happily balanced among all of them.
[Edit] So, I am apparently a ponderously slow exploratory player, and I'm okay with that.  I do believe the reason the series is named Torment is because it's (almost) impossible to die.  That seems fitting, for someone who took almost 50 hours to get through the beta.  Pro tip: don't leave town.
Having resolved 16-odd quests, and with 2 remaining, now I'm seriously jonesing to get on with the rest of this.  I can only guess that, as a secret-finder and prose-reader (I really LIKE the Meres!), I'll probably lose ~200 hours of my life in this game.  I can't wait for the hideous stench of the Bloom to fill my nostrils... ugh, wait, maybe I can? [/edit]
Highly recommended for your Bartle's exploratory types!  Feel free to look elsewhere for bullet-time, spraying gibs, skimpy outfits, collisions, porridge, wanton violence or wontons.  You're on earth, a billion years in the future, and you've got all the time in the world to read through tomes of narrative, linking slender chains in your mind, piecing together yourself, and all the whys of all the voids, within and without.
Grand. Fictional. Terrifying. Alluring. Fun. Interesting. Human.
Can't wait for the final release...  It's already an impressive work of art!

UPDATE: I've been playing the final game now, but not on PC.
FIRST OFF: My gaming PC broke like a week before the game published. I had no ready cash to sink in to a PC, so I bought it (again) on PS4. So I cannot comment on the technical side of the game on this review. On PS4, it works better than expected (I didn't expect much, to be honest). It's a bit sluggish and not super amazing looking. But honestly, it's not like anyone played Planescape for graphics, either.
IN SHORT: Very text heavy RPG, basically a novel of ginormous size that you can wander through and read all the accompanying lore. There is very little combat, and all of it can be avoided. There is a number of systems at play in game that are not very well explained and take a long time (in some cases) to figure out. Despite some items having a lot of lore attached to them, they are often just random throwaway stuff that you're just meant to sell away.
SLIGHTLY MORE NUANCE: Torment Tides of Numenera, I am glad to say works as intended. It has a story that is mostly about thematic depth, interesting conversations, very interesting lore, and more text than you can possibly imagine. This is probably a guinness world record, isn't it?
It also, at least on first glance, seems to have quite a lot of options that make difference. It's hard to say if this is actually true unless you play the game several times over. But at first playthrough it seems to be hinting at quite the number of decisions.
I am not saying the crisis system is the best system ever, but it does bring an interesting de-emphasis to combat. You don't need to fight a damn thing in this game, and often you should be thinking: should I even fight?
In conclusion; if you liked Torment: Planescape, you will like this game. Unless like so many, you are blinded by nostalgia. The fact is that most gamers are nostalgic to a fatal degree and can't grasp that some things will never have the same impact once you've experienced them once (like playing a truly story driven RPG first time, like Planescape). It doesn't mean Numenera is worse than Planescape, it means you are different. I think Numenera is better than Planescape, but mostly because of presentation and technical things. Planescape was horrible game when it came to combat, and the whole DnD aspect dragged it down badly. The strange world of Numenera lifts this game up, and the systems don't in general get too much in the way of the game. However, I haven't finished this game yet so I can't say for sure that the story is as good.
I might update this review once I finish the game, or I might not. Who cares? This is just my opinion anyway.
Like I said, I recommend this game for those who want a story driven, text infused, very slow paced game with mostly optional combat in a very surreal world.
