I had very high expectations for this game. Was upset when the release date had to be pushed back, but I completely understood and was 100% fine with that.
Still, this game did not nearly rise to my expectations.
Let me get some pros out of the way:
-Art. Loved the characters and their differences.
-Very diverse personalities are represented.
-Colorful, fun, good looking aesthetic-wise.
There may be just a few more, none that come to mind straight away.
Now, the cons:
-The idea that the game is "voiced" gives the idea that there are more than just grunts and hums.
-While the art was great, it would have been nice to seen more than 3 facial expressions per character. Especially Ernest. The poor kid was just trying to watch a movie that he was supposedly interested in and looked like he'd just drank too much dish detergent two minutes before.
-Grammar. The grammatical errors were abundant and prominent (to myself, that is). I couldn't go a minute without cringing due to a missed comma. It was very poor. While others may not have noticed it as much, I couldn't go very far without noticing frequent mistakes.
-There is not much detail that goes behind the dates. The player is virtually unable to form any "connection" with any of the dads, as the dates only scratch the surface behind furthering the relationships.
-While I know the player's dad is supposed to act as awkward comic relief, it goes overboard. We get it, Stephen, you don't like to run and would rather be eating a burger alone in a corner. Sure, he's thinking about how to deal with Amanda's departure to college, but should it really come up in almost every conversation in the game?
-Not all dads have "happy" endings. Some have both "good" and "bad", depending on how the dates went, but it seems as though some only have "bad" or "neutral" endings. If this is a fun, LGBT+ positive game, shouldn't it portray happy, healthy relationships?
-Relating to my previous comment: the "cult" ending. While I, myself, have not reached this ending, I have heard about its possibility through some deep code-digging. This is horrifying, to say the least. As I said, should a fun, LGBT-based game have something as horrific as that? Portraying gay relationships as unattainable, or unrealistic? Nah, I didn't think so, either.
-The ending seems to be the exact same, no matter the dad you pick. While your relationship with one dad will be changed quite a bit in the end, all paths lead to Amanda's graduation party. The same graduation party. Every time. Just seems to me like the writing ending-wise seems a bit lax.
-Not too many options for the player's dadsona. Although, of course, I may be a little biased, as I am the type of person that enjoys creating their Sim more than actually playing the game.
And, again, there may be some more, but nothing comes to mind.
TL;DR: Don't bother with the game, especially with the $15 price tag. The cons outweigh the pros; I'm disappointed and wish I could go back.
I was so hyped, too. I'm guessing that could be a big part of the disappointment: too much hype for what hadn't even been released yet.

I'm not too familiar with the artist so I'm a bit of an outsider here, although I believe the lead artists are students so I assume this is a student project; but this game popped up on my feed and on occasion I like to take a chance with off-beat, unusual point and clicks. It's a genre with a lot of very interesting experiments.
This is a quirky, charming, extremely experimental little game that revolves around a neat twist. The artstyle is simplistic but has a kind of old style caricature comic strip charm to it. There's a few inconsistencies with the animation, but It's pretty obvious this was done on a student's budget so it's perfectly excusable and the personality of the protagonist in all of her little actions makes up for it. The game also has a kind of dark sense of humor, but it's subdued and doesn't overdo it.
As it is a priced release, I do have to point a few things out though. Even by point and click standards, some clues and overall the progression of events the player must trigger to move things forward can be especially vague. The ability to actually drag items isn't really even hinted and I only discovered it after fanatical clicks on the screen by accident. There's a minor glitch involving the mini fridge becoming unclickable (that has an easy fix as stated on the hub. Nonetheless though, I gotta note it.). The game crashed a few times when accessing the menu for me as well.
Finally, in the "not bad not good" notes territory...the game is quite short. Not necessarily a negative, as the game is obviously a bit of an experiment and short and to the point can be a big plus. However aspects of the story, keeping things as vague as possible in order to avoid spoilers, go unresolved by the end. The game concludes its main plot well enough, but there's a certain something big that isn't really explained. I can only assume it's meant to be interpretive, but it might leave some confused as there isn't really even much in way of hint as to what to make of said detail.
All and all though, it's an interesting little experimental scene of a game. A part of me does wish it were a bit longer perhaps, but that's kind of a good thing to. Just know that it is just that, an experiment. I might say as well that  for the type of game it is and the short length...it might be a bit overpriced, however it's certainly not a purchase I regret. If you like quirky little experiments once in a while and have your expectations in perspective, I'd give it a go.

Hitman may have been a great game, yet poor design choices and always-online drm garrotes Agent 47 and leaves this game gurgling in the toilet.
What's Good:
Our first map offering, Paris, is quite detailed and a large playground of murder. I have no issue with the new design being centered around repeating this large map with varying objectives. It's fun trying to complete escalations as the mission difficulty slowly increases. I used to play Blood Money in the same way, completing a mission and then trying a new angle. So it's cool that they've built this in with their unlock and challenge system.
Kills are satisfying in that there appear to be multiple options. There are some of the bigger more staged options and I would recommend turning off the Opportunities hints as they basically hold your hand. Beyond that though it's fun turning people chaotic so you can sneak up behind someone and stab them with a lethal injection. The core of the game (map design, ai, sound, visuals) is great.
What's not good:
I'm always amazed how developers can create something good and then shoot themselves in their own foot. I don't play Hitman for multiplayer. Leaderboards are why the game has always-on drm. And it's felt. On my final part of an escalation mission, I was disconnected randomly and bounced back to the main menu. This negated all the work I had just done. To have my play interrupted by a feature that I care nothing about in a game that isnt about other people is beyond infuriating. I appreaciate them trying to tap into community content with the contracts feature. But we don't need always on drm for that.
Also the episodic release schedule is confusing for a hitman game. The story isn't compelling enough for me to WANT to see what happens next. Which has to be the case for Episodic release to work. Instead you walk away feeling like you have a very small repetitive game.
BOTTOMLINE:
Core mechanics are great but the game is hampered by always on drm and episodic release schedule. Not enough content to keep you motivated to continue playing.

Not really a review, just a response to many of the negative comments that have recently appeared.
This game is good. It smashes Absolution to pieces and has redeemed the devs from what was effectively franchise death. So far all the complaints I have seen regarding this game have nothing to do with gameplay. People are whining about loading times, and small graphical glitches, and the menu layout. Come on!!! If that's all you have to complain about then surely that tells you more about the types of people reviewing, not the developers.
Episodic releases. Firstly, I never expected a new mission on April 1st as that would have been less than a month since release. Secondly, it's worth the extra wait! I spent a very long time playing Blood Money. I completed it on 360, PS2 and PC. It was great. So this new game still doesn't match Blood Money, but again, look at Absolution. I've spent more time on The Showstopper alone than the entire Absolution game. Heck, I spent just as much time on the beta release than the Absolution game. I much prefer this episodic release with all these extra mission types than waiting until they complete package in the summer or later. Thanks to the episodic release I've been able to play Hitman now.
If you are considering buying this game weigh up the pro's and con's. It's got good gameplay, plenty to do, it won't waste your time, there's new content to look forward to and keep you excited and interesting. The bad? Out of game issues such as loading times, poor menu layouts, longer wait than expected for new content. In game it has occasional glitches (like all games) and sometimes has some graphical issues (nothing I've personally experienced).

What can I say? Meh. It's ok but I'm not excited to continue playing it mainly because of the lack of a storyline. It's a collection of set piece contracts all happening in the same place. Paris is just a series on unconnected contracts set in a palace during a fashion show. Memorize the layout of the palace and go through the motions soley for the purpose of collecting a number of achiievements. For me there is not a lot of excitement in redoing what amounts to a level over and over again.

I've played every Hitman game to date and this feels like a step in the right direction. Performance is good, audio is good, I haven't had a single crash or any issues. Most importantly this feels like a proper Hitman game, unlike Absolution. The need to be always online is a slight annoyance but it's not going to stop me playing.
All in all a good game taking the series back to its open world roots.
Edit: Now that all the levels are out for the game I still recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the previous hitman titles.

I've been following the development of Prison Architect since Alpha 15. When it was officially launched today, I gave the new features a try, and have to admit I have very mixed feelings.
First, the base sandbox game is TONS of fun! It's a prison management system, where you are free to treat prisoners with downright cruelty or as if they are on holiday. You can focus on strict profit, or on reformation. The basics are fairly simple, yet there is plenty to learn.The sandbox alone I'd recommend to anyone.
With the new release, there were two main additions: The campaign and the Escape mode. T
The campaign I DO NOT recommend. For me, it completely threw off the pixelated, cartoony vibe of the early access. It was dark, crude, and downright vulgar. Maybe that's reminescent of the darker side of certain prisons, but it completely threw off the overall feeling of the Prison Architect I knew and loved! It took the game from what I'd consider the upper end of "E: Everyone" to the upper end of "M: Mature". It is not for children. It's probably not for adults. It's definitely not for me.
(Side note: I created a Mod called "Family Friendly Mod", which tuned down the adult content of the campaign. It's now at about a "T:Teen" level, or about what you find on "Prison Break".)
However, the Escape Mode is AWESOME!!! You can play it on any saved prison, which allows you to customize your difficulty. It needs a little rebalancing, but playing an an OP legendary prisoner, racking up your murder trials, setting fire to a prison... It's like a whole new game within the game. A++

Oxygen Not Included is a management game from Klei, the people who made Don’t Starve and Invisible Inc, which is my personal favorite. ONI is best thought of as a cartoony galactic disaster waiting to happen. Much is done in the style of Rimworld but viewed from a side-on angle. Everything happens below the surface of a distant planet, or possibly an asteroid (at least, I didn’t reach any surface during my upward digging).
Colonize and survive. Once you have the required research, you can build gas and liquid pumps, temperature management devices, medical bays, and much more. Many of these machines require power, too. As with everything else, research is a task you set out for your colonists, who will run around and do the jobs you’ve created for them. You’re always looking ahead to the next piece of tech you can implement in your base.
Besides precious oxygen, players will have to manage their heat, water and energy levels as they continue expanding their rocky home. Everything can be recycled in Oxygen Not Included, including toxic air and even the waste of domesticated animals and or your colonist if you really wanted to survive using completely green energy.
All in all, how you advance your colony is up to you. Since there is so much complexity bubbling underneath a layer of simplicity, there is a multitude of strategies that the player can take to achieve your end goals. Are you going to be trapped in an endless feedback loop of the struggle to survive, or are you going to thrive under the pressures of this atmosphere? Will you become the space oil baron that you didn’t think you could be? Or will you find your stride in the utilization of thermal energy? These are questions that you have to ask yourself, as just as far are you willing to push your colonists?

Although I have very little play time as of writing this review, I can confirm that Garfield Kart is one of the most revolutary steps in gaming history. Atrefacts Studies really out done themselves in this racing game starring the Garfield and his friends in hopes of winning the 1st place gold cup.
1. Graphics - the graphics for Garfield Kart are absolutly breath-taking. This puts The Witcher 3 and other greak looking games to shame. I have a pretty powerful computer but not even my PC can handle all the power that is needed to run this game. I was constanly getting 10 to 20 FPS, so you're gonna need a beefy PC to run this game.
2. Story - throughout all my playtime I can assure you that I felt the characters' feeling, emotions, and everything that was thrown at me. The lore and story in Garfield Kart is massive. There is so much to learn and read about in the lore of Garfield and his friends.
3. Controls - if you've played franchises like Mario Kart, you'll feel right at home with this game. I'm happy to say that the controls for Garfield Kart are on point. It took me a little of getting used to the drifting (or what this game calls it: skidding) but after about 5 minutes I was fine. Not only does it support keyboard controls but it supports a controller!
4. Multiplayer - as of right now, any form of multiplayer is not present in Garfield Kart, but I'm fine with that. The devs worked hard enough on the campaign and graphics so it's expected for the MP not to be present just yet. I'm sure this will be added some time in the future.
5. Soundtrack/Music - Sonic Mania? Put that game's soundtrack to the side, THIS is your new OST to jam to! The soundtrack for Garfield Kart is so catchy and great. I feel so relaxed, yet happy and sort of energetic hearing the songs in Garfield Kart. If you don't get a chance to get the game (although it's only 5 bucks), make sure to search the music on YouTube. It's definetly a good listen as you'll start jamming to the amazing tracks found in this game.
6. Final Verdict - Garfield Kart is definetly a contender for GOTY for me. From the music to the graphics, Garfield Kart is a joy to play. Please pick this game up if you haven't already.

I'm writing this review after having completed the game twice, once without the significant patch and once with it.
Both of my playthroughs have been very positive experiences, although the patch makes the overall experience feel much more inviting.
The collectathon genre as a whole isn't for everyone, but it's a genre I love for the satisfaction of finishing loads of fun little tasks, getting caught off guard by some hefty challenges, and exploring fanciful worlds at a leisurely pace, always finding new stuff to do.  For me personally, Yooka-Laylee is easily one of the most enjoyable games in the genre.  What weaknesses it has (like having to beat Rextro's arcade games twice to earn the Pagie for beating the high score) barely detract from the experience for me.
I'll also state for the record that the Capital Cashino is my favorite world, and I have no issues with the Icymetric Palace.
Legitimately don't understand the complaints with those areas.
I grew up with the Banjo games and honestly consider Yooka-Laylee more enjoyable than either of them.  This is among my all-time favorite games now, and I'm eager to see what Playtonic has in store next.

Coming into this game, I didn't have many expectations. I just wanted a game that felt similar to the first Banjo-Kazooie game, and that's exactly what I got, but it isn't exactly what I hoped it'd be.
Firstly, let's go through the positives; The new duo is good. I like Laylee's sarcastic approach to the situation, and Yooka's politeness, yet I do think this is too reminiscant of Banjo & Kazooie. Capital. B is a wonderful villian, the dialouge he gives Yooka & Laylee is really funny, and fits his character well. Trowzer is amazing. My main nitpick with Bottles is because he didn't have much personality. He was there as a tutorial, and didn't differentiate himself from other NPCs in the game. Rextro was also a favorite of mine, I enjoyed having a polygonal character in the game, to differentiate it from modern game, and really stand out. As for other characters like Dr. Quacka and Dr. Puzz, they're OK. They really can't fill the gap Grunt's Pot and Mumbo had. However, I must say each world is aesthetically pleasing, as each world has a wonderful piece of music to go with it. Pagies & Quills fit this game so much. It's wonderful to see the character the Pagies had, such as the one that couldn't slip out the bars of a cage on one of the worlds. Quills play a key aspect in the game, and work well with the book theme in the game. The bosses in each level is a wonderful addition to the game. The closest you'd get to a Boss in BK, would be someone who'd take a few hits to defeat, but end up giving you a Jiggy. Another really cool addition is the Tonics you get from Vendi. They really do benefit you quite a lot, and I like the limitation of only having 1 being equipt at a time was nice, and it allowed you to change your gameplay.
However, no game is perfect. Yooka-Laylee has it flaws.
I did not like the expansion feature. For the first 3 Worlds, it felt nice, having new areas to explore. But by the 4th & 5th levels, you couldn't do much without having to expand the world I honestly would've taken 5 more worlds over the expnsion feature. Once a world is expanded, it's harder to find collectables (which is annoying if you're like me, and want to 100% the game.). Kartos Minecart Mini-Games weren't as good as I hoped they'd be. It felt klunky to control, and having a boss being centered around fighting someone on a track, WITH Kartos didn't do well. I hate the new ways the duo gets moves. I love Trowzer to pieces, but I hate having to then purchace moves with my Quills. It really caught me off gaurd, when I had to constantly check my totals to see how many Quills I needed to find. The energy bar is a terrible feature. The greatness of the BK came from it's collectathon idea. Whether you had to hunt Notes, or Red Feathers, it felt great finding them, because you knew you could then progress through Grunty's Lair, or finally get that Jiggy you were looking for. Yet, in Yooka-Laylee, they throw that out the window. Only giving you an energy bar for all your moves. Whilst on the topic of moves, I did NOT enjoy being able to cast anything at any time. The joy of flying in BK was because you first had to hunt down the Flying Pad. With Yooka-Laylee it takes the rarity you would have on finding it, and gives you the ability to fly at will, but in it's defense, is good due to how vertical the levels are. Transformations are also a letdown. I only saw me using transformations for 1 Pagie. Maybe, at max, 3. And the transformations barely fitted the levels, half the time you would transform and wonder what you can use it for. Like, how does a Pirate Ship go in a space themed level? The glory of the Transformations in BK came from the fact you didn't find them often. You could go to Mumbo's Mountain, and not see Mumbo's Skull until Bubblegloop Swamp. In Yooka-Laylee, it's gaurenteed you'll find one, at a cost of 1 Mollycool. Unlike in BK, where you'd have to find a certain amount of Mumbo Tokens.
Apart from that, I have minor nitpicks. Such as, a few HUD issues that nag me, aside from that it's a wonderful game. It really did feel like a Banjo game, and it really made the players smile. I recommend you snag this game, I promise you won't regret it.

My first idle / clicker game was Adventure Capitalist; I loved the art style, the simple idea and the multiplication of numbers. I wanted to achieve 100 %, almost did, but then developers decided to implement more and more different maps, new achievements, etc. So I kind of stopped playing Adventure Capitalist, just randomly take a look once in a while. Other clickers followed, very addictive in the beginning, but mostly I stopped them before I got 100 % of the achievements.
What does this all have to do with VOODOO GARDEN? Actually directly nothing, except the fact that VOODOO GARDEN gets the clicker genre right. You actually have to click in the game; you cannot just use some clicker fake programme and rely on the automatic idle mode. You need to be in the game to proceed further, that means you can't just start the game once in a while, like most idle games that count time offline. But of course you can easily play it in the background without losing anything (not like Fallout Shelter with its monster attacks).
You are the owner of a swamp land. You plant bushes and trees in order to collect (click) fruits and vegetables, mushrooms and many more. With those ingredients the game automatically produces different forms of products (from poisonous potions to the Voodoo puppet). Production finished, you receive money you can spend on better and more vegetation. In the beginning you have to click on the vegetation yourself to collect the ingredients, then later you can buy animals (chicken to goats), which you feed until they are fat enough to be harvested. The spirits of the dead animals help you to collect the ingredients automatically, that means you don't have to click on them yourself (idle aspect of the game).
The game is based on an experience points and level up system which allows you to unlock different vegetation or stronger animals on higher levels.
Most potions or products require pieces of wild animals / insects in order to be created. Those automatically run into your garden. The spirits do not collect them automatically, which means you have to click on them yourself (real clicker).
You cannot collect indefinite numbers of ingredients, at a certain point the counter stops and gives you a coin instead.
The production line can be prioritized, which leads to a certain amount of tactical planning. Especially when it comes to the achievements which for example are “collect 2000 dragon flies”. The collection of the dragon is not counted if your stock is full, so you need to first produce something with dragon flies in order to empty your stock and before you click on the dragon fly.
Besides of this simple but tactical mechanic you can build totems to attract a specific kind of animal / insect. You can level up every form of bushes, trees you plant or other products.
Following what I liked and what I did not like, knowing that I highly recommend the game, even to people that have never played an idle or clicker game before.

Finished game. Took my time. Did side quests. Pleasurable. But also, some negatives.
Game feels short. A few acts short. Sagus, intermission, Bloom, and final act. Feels like there should be 2-3 more steps on the way there somewhere. Game is nowhere near as long as old torment, or icewind dale, or baldurgs gate. Storyline is fairly predictable, once you hit mid-game you can see where its going. A few twists but nothing mind-blowing.
Another gripe, is bland companions. None of them were honestly interesting. Just...people, with their own problems and a short quest to solve it. Few paragraphs of text allocated to their background and quest. Meh. Now old torment, THAT had memorable companions. Floating skull, fallen angel, suit of armor, that githyanki or whatever... Those were interesting. Numenera companions, by comparison....bland. less then bland even. I finished game with half companion slots empty, because I could not care less - and because i did not need their abilities truth be told.
Gameplay - you can talk your way past every single fight - this is not always interesting, like cheating. Also, once you get a full level and some mid-level gear, you can steamroll the NPCs - combat is unbalanced a bit, either its too hard, or becomes too easy. By end game you can become literally unkillable - you regenerate HP faster then you take damage, with certain gear and skills. Oh and you get a nice sword that bypasses all armor and resistances. Unbalanced.
But main gripe is that skill checks are incredibly easy. You literally CANT fail past a certain point, and that point is a third of the game in. Game gives you all these various proficiencies, like lore-mechanical, or weapons, but, honestly, you dont need most of them, skill checks are that easy.
overall, its a nice game. Worth a playthough. But nothing spectacular.

*Updated After Full Release* - As, I'd hoped, the complaints below have been addressed. This game is a worthy purchase if you're a fan of Planescape Torment or Numenera
________________________________________________________________________
Let me start by saying that I hope I'm able to change this review someday. I love Numenera,  I loved the original Torment, and the small parts of this game that work show a lot of promise.
That said, the "game" is far too incomplete to get a recommendation at this time. It's at a very early alpha level of bugginess, such that all but the most patient of gamers will not be able to tolerate it. If you don't imagine yourself happily persevering after the fourth time you've crashed during character creation, you should probably wait a while before checking this game out.
Even if you are prepared to save after every action and reload a lot, brace yourself for a shocking lack of content. You'll get a quest, head out for the dungeon, and then get a dialog telling you to imagine you just completed the quest. At the current state of development, the game is very thin.
These two complaints should be addressed as development progresses. One thing that won't change is that this game looks and plays like a game from 1999. Thats not a bad thing, it's just what a gamer like me wants, but it's not for everyone.
Those complaints aside, I haven't returned it and continue to slog through it. Why? Because it's a great portrayal of the Numenera setting and system. Because the writing is top quality and the dialog trees are extensive. Because I suspect that I will love this game when it's done and don't want to wait for them to finish it.
So, if you're the kind of person who loves Planescape and plays in a weekly tabletop Numenera game, this title is worth a look. Otherwise, I'd keep my eye on the forums and pick it up when it's got a little more meat on it's bones.

I'm not a native speaker, but I like reading English novels. I loved every piece of the stories in the game, and actually, quality of the stories was the only thing that made me keep playing this game. However, if I had wanted just good readings, I would have bought a book.
Every feature in this game is not that desirable except stories, and if I have to point out things, I think I should talk about  2.animation  3.combat  4.voice acting. I saw some people saying that this is a story-driven game and the other things are not needed, but this is not 'Planescape: Torment' in 1999. If an essential feature of the game can be developed as a firm structure, and it can enrich the whole game without hurting or shortening stories, I don't see any reason to prevent it.
If you like reading books, you'll be satisfied just for good stories. I like novels, movies, and TV shows which focuses on sophisticated stories, and I haven't seen any stories like T:TON. Describing the stories of this game with my sloppy words will only debase the true value of it because there are not many writers who can describe 'a world unlike any other' better than this team. So here's an example of the stories in the game, some words from a person whom you get to meet in the game.
However, I think not everyone will like this game because it contains too many reading materials. It was hard to read all these vast amounts of texts, and it was much harder than 'Pillars of Eternity'. Actually, You'll have to spend 85% of your time for reading, and 95% if you choose to avoid or resolve the crisis(combat). In my case, I liked it cause I liked those stories, but I think it could be a huge threshold for those who don't like or are not familiar with reading.
When I was choosing each action, I expected they would show me some animations, or at least some glow on each mirror. However, all I could see during the whole sequence was the exact same static picture without any changes or movements. It's basically a picture book which I have to read multiple pages of scripts separately. It doesn't feel like a real world. I'm not saying they have to make some fabulous fantastic actions. Is it really that hard to make one bit of red or blue shining line, or at least some glow? I can't imagine that devs are somehow apathetic or lazy. This scene really made me think if there had been anything wrong with development progress.
This is just one example of many things. I couldn't see any animations when 'the clock mission' started, and 'master foreman'(enormous robot) didn't even blink even when I was talking to him(But he was still talking and shouting). If it is a really hard part and can't be changed technically, I can accept that. But small effects in the important scene can't be hard and can't hurt stories. I can't understand why they didn't do anything about them.
I don't think these issues are just some minor bugs or mistakes. If devs don't change their whole perspective, we'll have to read scripts on the lifeless and static picture book for most of the time.
As you all know, 'Wasteland 2' and 'Divinity: Original Sin' had similar combat system. For instance, if you have 12 action points in 1 turn, you get to move(2pt), heal/buff/debuff(3pt), attack(5pt) and spare 2 points. In T:TON, simply put, you can use only 1 action(use item/skill/attack) and 1 move in 1 turn. Combats actually work like this.
[Initiative]
Enemy1 > Enemy2 > Team1 > Team2 > Enemy3 > Team3
The reason I didn't include moving is because it doesn't actually matter in combat. First, cost and benefit(distance) of the moving is fixed. Second, moving rarely affects to the attacks because it has fixed cost. Third, moving is not about strategic decision making in the field, rather about choosing whom I will attack on this turn, like a card game. If you want to hit enemyX, you can just go to X and hit X, and there're no limits or disengagements or anything. Forth, I've tried many combats by using several saving files, so I can assure you that the enemies are not that smart. There's nothing special you can strategically gain from moving. In conclusion, It's basically not different from typical card games.
At first, I thought 'sacrificing stats to increase hit chance and damage' was a brilliant idea. However, since maintaining stats are not that hard, it doesn't actually matter that much, at least for now. There are some alternative options like intimidation, persuasion, or using numenera, but they're nothing but another type of attacks. Some could say it's inevitable cause it's based on the board game Numenera, but they were monotonous and tedious combats for me anyway.
I simplified many things for the explanation, but it's not that different from the big picture. I don't think little tweaks could fix this matter.
I think voice acting is important in animation movies and games. Think about any animation movie and imagine that you have to watch it without any voices. I always couldn't understand why they don't put voices in RPG. Funny thing is, they always show us an advertisement with voice actors performing their breathtaking lines, but in actual games, we can't hear anything on 80~90% of the scripts. I don't know much about voice actors, but even Youtubers make videos of full voice version. When I heard they raised over 5,000k, first thing got in my mind was a little hope that devs could show us full voice version of Torment. But I couldn't hear any signs or promises yet.
1. Vast amounts of good stories, if you like reading novels. (10/10)
1. Vast amounts of good stories, if you don't like or are not familiar with reading. (5/10)
2. Lack of animations on the important scenes. (6/10)
3. Combats are too simple. fundamentally similar to a card game. (7/10)
4. Lack of voice actors, at least for now. and couldn't see any promises. (?/10)

It's been said before, many, many times, but this is easily the most underrated semi-major title of 2015. If you're a fan of the movies, especially Fury Road, it does some fan service to those willing to pay attention, and an ending that could just as well lead up to the beginning of Fury Road. Maneuvering and hand to hand combat weren't the best you could get, but Max is also partially disabled right from the start. Car combat is incredibly fun, and building yours up and collecting others don't get boring (it did not for me, anyway). The map is massive, the car physics are easy to work with, and the game isn't always easy. It's also gorgeous.
I don't doubt many people playing this found boring points, as I did occasionally just driving in the great beyond. There's plenty to do if you want a game that has a lot of busywork, like finding photos and messages scattered across the land. There's always somebody to battle and blow up. I played a lot of games in 2015, but as far as ones that came out that year, I did manage to edge out more gameplay out of Mad Max (which I bought just to kill the time before Fallout 4) than I ever anticipated. Highly recommend you buy the game, especially since it is regular dropping under $15. The game got no paid DLC, it basically came and went, but it left a lasting impression!

Just buy it when you feel the price is right. As for me... I had some suspension of disbelief, but it quickly spiraled away with events that made little to no sense. I figure I wasn't this game's target audience, and I base that on how the game goes from being silly to serious as a heart attack... and I sort of only value serious material I can connect with. If you're asking me to value characters, I need empathy. Without that, it's easier just to go to reddit and look at pet gifs... just as much clicking, just as random, and no real struggle with random calls back to adult life and its misery.
I think you can give this game a fair shake for the art, which is great. But I had hoped for more than just the visuals. I kind of wanted to feel connected. I respect a lot of the other folks that liked this story, so feel free to disagree. I've just played a lot of different point-and-click games, and could very well be the snob here. If it wasn't for the art, I'd be asking for my money back.
I ended up not finishing the story (I am pretty sure I was two clicks away, but it was just too frustrating)... and while I can't describe where I stopped, I'm sure you'll know it when you hit it and think "So, this is supposed to be tragic? If I do go back to the game, it'll be to pull the graphics out...

Maggie's Apartment is Anatola Howard's (a.k.a. Maroon Racoon's) first commercial game project. When examined alongside her previous free games, Pen Palz and 4 Lung Boy, Maggie's Apartment is both similar in nature and noticably more developed than either of them.
This is a game that wants you to have a certain experience inside the safety of a video game; an experience that, if you've ever had it in real life, you will know might well be one of the hardest things to go through/make someone else go through there is. And every single element of this game's narrative and plot is drenched in metaphor and foreshadowing towards its ultimate goals: Empathy, and understanding.
Not only charming and, at points, hilariously written and voice-acted, Maggie's Apartment is an incredibly smart and thought-provoking game. The art is extremely detailed and the designs are wonderfully imaginative. Every character has a unique voice (both in writing and acting) and many will stick with you for a long time.
Despite only being about 3 and a half hours in length, Maggie's Apartment is adventure gaming bliss. You owe it to yourself to check it out.

at the end

After discovering the Vampire Magician disguise whilst roaming the attic, I wondered if I could combine my new favorite disguise with my favorite method of getting close to the second target (Mrs. Margolis) which involves obtaining a V.I.P Pass and either climbing to the roof unseen, or walking through the guards, flashing your pass and allowing yourself to be searched.
Some information in case you haven’t played the game. If you obtain the previously mentioned V.I.P Pass you can enter the auction run by your target. Upon sitting down in a chair like everyone else in the auction, Mrs. Margolis will walk over to 47 to introduce herself. After giving the very convincing fake name of Tobias Reaper, 47 will now have access to the entirety of the auction as if he was supposed to be there. My goal was to do this not in 47’s signature suit, but in the Vampire Magician disguise which looks like something out of a steampunk convention.
It started out well enough. Having put on the Vampire Magician disguise I was seized by the excitement brought about by dressing like a middle schooler who snuck into the theater classes prop room and hastily ran out the door into a guard. Having convinced him that I indeed was supposed to be here by pummeling him unconscious violently, I tried in vain to hide him in a nearby box. Unfortunately he was caught against a crate and his whole body horrifically disappeared inside sans his arm which stuck out like a sore….arm (as the thumb as glitched into the ground). Having recovered from the shock I snuck my way out and back towards the ground floor to obtain my V.I.P Pass from a bathroom. So far, nothing had gone irreparably wrong. I walked towards the guards to hand them my pass and to my surprise they refused to speak with me. They even made fun of my outfit and would not allow me to hand them my pass. “No matter!” I thought out loud. There is more than one way to skin a cat (specifically 4,553. And I wouldn’t know that if my neighbors would stop letting them roam free so they crap in my garden). I snuck quietly over to a conveniently placed drainage pipe that led to the roof near the auction I was trying to infiltrate. After the guards were no longer facing me, I climb up onto the balcony and walked dramatically into the chair filled room where the auction took place, my detection meter rapidly filling as I rushed towards the chair were 47 must sit in order to trigger the meeting with the target. However I could not sit down in the chair. Just like the guards outside, my disguise prevented me from becoming Tobias Reaper and gaining convenient access to my target. Before I could voice my disappointment every guard in a five mile radius drew their pistols and turned me from a Vampire Magician, to a Human Collender.
To summarize, Vampire Magicians cannot be V.I.Ps to an auction where shady and eccentric powerplayers go to buy information.

Batman Arkham Origins in my opinion is the best Batman game of all time. It has revamped the Detective mode which makes you feel like that you are the Dark Knight. The plot for Arkham Origins is the main antagonist, Black Mask, has offered up a £50m contract for anyone who brings him Batman's head. This has attracted a group of lethal, costumed bounty hunters and assassins to Gotham in search of the caped crusader. At the same time, every criminal in the city has decided to ignore the citywide curfew in place due to a recent snowstorm and use the fact that Batman is otherwise engaged to launch a bit of a crime spree. Batman has to find Black Mask and get him to cancel the bounty, stay out of the crosshairs of the assassin and put an end to the citywide crime wave.
Overall I think that this game is Excellent and should be a Game of the Year for me.

The game initially comes off like a lot of effort has been put into it (which I don't totally doubt). There are sweet mini-games, the dad is pretty customizable, there is an option for binder-dads (for dads who bind), you get to meet the dads in a manner that makes sense, and you get to make a choice in the game where it's basically one dad or the other. However, after that point, there's no juggling of schedules or dads which could, for one, make a specific playthrough more interesting (though the writing is more complicated, I'm sure more people would be tempted to buy the game just for their own exploration purposes if the game was more convoluted) and the writing more complicated and interesting since the story would be forced to develop in many interesting and specific ways. I find the depth of the game really lacks partially as a result of that. Amanda is really the only other aspect you need to juggle, but the game never gets to a point where you need to choose between Amanda's well-being and a love interest or....yourself. So, in reality, Amanda is a piece of cake to handle (she really is a great kid though) and you're not ever really juggling anything. There's not much challenge to the game besides the mini-games and being careful in your responses. Each dad route feels like it could take that next step and that the point you reach at the end of each one feels like it's the beginning of the relationship....maybe even barely? There are both good endings and bad endings in this game, but the game ultimately really only has one ending that changes slightly depending on your relationship with the dads and I guess also depending on your relationship with Amanda. It's a little disappointing in its end game and I really thought this game was going to expand out into having a part 2 after the 3 dates (as in the story really only progresses so far until you do the 3 dates). Another thing that this game lacked was, imo, significant milestones. Don't get me wrong, there's really memorable parts that are really well written and super funny (significant pro of this game: the dialogue), but I feel like there are parts that could be even more special if we had milestone art or something thrown in there. I appreciate the dad relationships and the platonic love that progresses pretty well into romantic love, but I would have loved more romance, more intimate interaction, etc. Compared to other dating games, this did better in some ways like with the mini-games. I would say the writing was better and I really want to, but I feel like I was held out on. I definitely feel like there should have been more and I am a little disappointed because I wanted to love the game so much, but having been familiar with other dating sims and even just games that weave a romantic aspect into them, my expectations were higher.

Batman: Arkham Origins is a prequel to the Arkham Asylum/Arkham City games.  Only 2 years into being Batman and helping out in Gotham, Batman has his toughest night yet since this Christmas Eve the villian Black Mask has put a bounty of 50 million dollars on his head and 8 deadly assassins are in Gotham looking to score.
The game looks really great and runs well even on my older laptop with an Nvidia GeForce 310 512MB card.  Occasionally has some small bugs like batman gliding through the air and flopping up and down constantly, or even more infamous, quick time events where the buttons don't register (If you can, use a controller).  Combat is the same as the other Batman games.  Very quick and fluid combos against large groups of enemies, or Predator set pieces where you pick off enemies one by one in sneaky fashion.
The story is much more fleshed out than the previous games as well. Without giving too many spoilers, It shows how Batman's relationship evolved with the police and Liutenant Gordon, why so many villains want him dead and how he earned his reputation in Gotham as a hero.
If you liked the previous Batman games and want more, you will definitely like this game.

I won't lie, differently from all the other reviews, I have decided to rate the game itself, and my god is it amazing. It is the first Hitman game I've played (got it bundled with my GFX card) and I've had tons of fun with it already, playing through each mission (3 so far tho) until I've done all there is to be done, and then do a bit more while waiting for further patches. The mechanics can be quirky at times, but bugs are very rare after the latest patches. Short Pros/Cons:
Pros:
- Really freaking fun, you have so much freedom, and it's realistic enough to force you to make up strategies instead of mindless mayhem
- Promising story and great atmosphere where you still decide how it plays out
- Any actions you do are well incorporated into the current mission
- No pesky limits to items (Skyrim hoarding bloodline)
- Stealth is rewarded and preferred
- Replay value is insane even for just having one mission
- All rules are well set, for example if you kill all the guards they are dead and you can escape instead of them respawning or sending in reinforcements. Very unlikely to happen though
Cons:
- Always-online requirement (way better than at release, but still annoying)
- If you want to be up-to-date with the releases, you'll have to pay continually. Game was 60 initially and 20 for GOTY edition, now you can get them both for 30 and maybe even less in the future.
Summary: (SO IS IT WORTH?)
I got this game for free, so it's hard to tell. +50% sale would be a good investment. If you buy it, make sure you meet (or don't mind) these criterias:
- Decent graphics card to make it run smoothly
- You don't mind waiting for updates for months (rather you enjoy it)
- You love stealth games with sort of "sandbox killing" and freedom

The worst part about Yooka-Laylee is that so many things are so very right with this game. I want to love it more than I do, I wanted to enjoy it more than I did, but unfortunately there are some critical mistakes that hold this game back from being the classic it should be.
There are only five worlds, and although you get to expand them and add more stuff to them, it just feels a bit lackluster. All five worlds are huge, to their credit, but their size is just a novelty. There isn’t much to do in these huge worlds other than travel from one place to another. There are some great platforming moments sprinkled throughout, but walking through empty fields of scenery to get from one moment to the next gets tiring quickly.
The controls are tight, and platforming feels good. In a strange decision, midway through the game you will gain a move that lets you fly with very little limit, and you can just use this to skip most of the platforming the game has to offer.
There are very few enemy types, and they are duplicated throughout each world. None of the enemy types really offer engaging combat, and while 3D platforming games aren’t known for their combat, it feels like a total afterthought here.
I don’t understand some of the decisions this game makes. It feels glued together in some places, but in others things are very polished.

Yooka Laylee is impressive knowing that Playtonic had only a handful of developers and $4 million budget to play with on a 3 year development cycle. A lot of my complaints in this review is likely rooted to the fact that they had relatively low resources for an ambitious game large in scope and size.
* Performance - My rig is a considered budget for 2014, but I was able to handle this game on ultra at 60 fps 1080p with very rare frame rate drops. You'll likely not see any issues in most DX11 cards, The quality of visuals to performance ratio is among the highest I have seen in any game.
* Visuals - In my opinion, this is the best part of the game. In mountains and mountains of greyscaled, gritty, and brown games, Yooka Laylee vibrant color pallette is a breath of fresh air. The textures are detailed and is consistent with style and tone of the enviornment. BK and BT players will feel at home.
* Worlds- There are five huge worlds. Unfortunately, a few maps are trope maps. Two of the maps are eerily similar to the ones you'll find in BK and BT. There are some level design snippets that felt copied and paste from one world to the next. Exploring is still a blast. There are so much to take in and enjoy. Being able to climb the tallest structure and take in the vastness of the area is an enjoyable experience. I wasn't too impressed with hub world. It felt like long corridore with too few shortcuts.
* Minigames - The minigames in YL took a deep nose dive after BT. The controls are very floaty. The mini-games felt like something you would find on a "101 Games" CD in 1999 and aren't cleverly embedded in the world like in BT. That being said, the minigames have an usual addictive quality to it.
* Pagies - The main object of the game is to progress from one world to the next by collecting pagies. What I like about YL is that you actually have to work to get the pagies. There are 145 total pagies total. I can count on one hand the number of lazily placed pagies where you just waltz up a platform to grab. There are some backtracking, but it's nothing like BT. In BT, you know by your surroundings that you'll need to backtrack later to get a collectable. In YL, this isn't really the case. You'll spend a good chunk of your time trying to figure out everything eventually giving up and returning after you learned an ability. Fortunately, this scenario is rare.
* Combat - YL is more like BK than BT. In BT you have a variety of moves in your arsenal to deal use during combat. Like BK, in YL, you really only have two or three abilities tied to getting rid of enemeis. Combat takes a backseat, which is fine since the game doesn't over fill the world with enemies. The focus on YL is platformming. If you're looking for a beat em up, then YL is not that game.
* Bosses - Bosses are a mixed bag in YL. Each boss with exception of two bosses, have at least one major flaw: hard coded camera angles designed to make you fail, lackluster personality, lazy predictable design, and fustrating mechanics. This is a huge drop from the BT series where bosses actually had personalities with much more focused and tighter designs.
* Abilities - The abilities are great YL. The problem with abilities in YL is that they are far too easy and cheap to obtain. If you grab a particular abilitiy early on, a good chunk of pagies are easy to cheese. BT handles thiat problem well by designing the world to prevent you from cheesing your way through the game. There is a tonic system where if you complete achievements you'll be granted bonuses. This is a cool system and works great. Most of the tonics are completely useless.
Despite its many minor flaws, I did enjoy this game. For $30 on sale, I felt like I got my moneys worth. I recommend this game to anyone who likes 3D platformmers. For those new to the genre, I recommend grabbing Banjo Tooie somehow and giving it a shot.

This game seemed to be
there. The graphics are vibrant and colorful and the lighting well done. The characters are great and have a lot of charm. The sense of humor is there, often poking fun at itself and the game industry in general. The gameplay feels natural as well. Jumping, spinning, pouncing. It has a lot going for it but there were a few things I discovered in my 95 minutes of playing that caused me to pull the trigger on the refund button.
First, the camera. I'm old and when I was in 9th grade the N64 came out and Mario 64 was released. This is easily the greatest 3D platformer of all-time and, in my top ten, the greatest game of all-time. Yooka Laylee has enough going for it that it starts to draw comparisons from the greats. And the fact that I do not have control of the camera and constantly have to press RB to readjust the camera behind me was a severe annoyance. They just released an update for manual camera control. I tried it. No difference from the classic control. Maybe it is bugged for me.
Second, the worlds. While there are interesting things to see and do in the first world. It felt like a bunch of ideas dumped onto an island with no cohesive structure. There is no map and so I just roam around, tracking over the same areas over and over again hoping to find something new or discover one of the collectibles, of which there are many but again, they are all thrown at you and scattered about. Not sure if I need to find them here or on another island. Do I need to pay some paiges to make this island bigger to find more stuff to collect or do I need to move on? These questions ended up frustrating me more than filling me with a sense of wonder and exploration.
Lastly, some of the game design choices. The fact that the obnoxious dialogue voices and lack of skip button made it all the way through to the final cut and only removed when players complained non-stop, and rightfully so, has me question who is giving thumbs up and thumbs down to game design decisions here. How in the world does that not get fixed before release? The devs tested that and were like.. Awesome! We've made the most annoying voices in the world unskippable! Once I tried to go to the second island and was hit with a ten question pop quiz, that was the straw that broke Yooka's back. I got the refund before it was too late. The game is expensive. I got it on sale for $30. If I'm paying $30 or more for a game it needs to be something I enjoy thoroughly and not cringe through.
That's my 2 cents. Now I take my $28.98 elsewhere. Maybe A Hat In Time will scratch that old school 3D platformer itch.

I'm not sure why this was nominated as a game with one of the best stories. Its definitely a long stretch from that with its over the top corny pictures and cheap budget voice acting, however the game is definitely fun as a fps which harbors a unique cinematic matrix trick at your characters disposal.
Made back in 2001 the graphics are somewhat dated, but the game is still entertaining and will give you a similar adventure feeling comparable to that of Half Life. It's the clever level designs and the many secret places and passages that they hide that make it a delight to explore. Personally I recommend the youtube walkthrough by countduncan if you want to find many of the secrets.
The game has 4 modes, easy, medium, hard and a time mode. Even easy is really difficult in comparison to some of the games of today and thanks to the F5 quick save at your disposal you will be practically using it after every gun shot. The time mode is just a get out of my way, mow everything down while you sprint, brandishing two uzi's or an automatic shotty. However even this is really, really, really tricky also.
So what is the story? The story involves Max Payne who 3 years ago arrived home to find his wife and child murdered by 3 addicts hyped up on a new drug called 'V'. After the funeral he takes up the offer of an old friend Alex Balder and leaves NYPD to work with the DEA and try and get this new drug off the streets. Working covertly undercover, Max Payne is set up as an operative inside the Punchinello crime family after they get a serious lead pointing their attention to an underboss known as Jack Lupino transporting the drug. This operation is so tight lipped that only Max's true identity is only known by 2 people, that is Alex Balder and B.B who is also an administrative DEA.
B.B eventually gets a tip that something BIG is going down at Roscoe Street Subway station and informs both Max and Alex to get down there and investigate. Little do they know it's a trap which exposes Max Paynes true identity to the Punchinello family. Max knowing there is no where to hide and that a hit has now been placed on his head, decides to go all Humphrey Bogart and hunt down the Don of this family himself. On his journey he will meet a variety of colorful under-bosses and assassins which he will need to take out of the equation and cater for first.
Eventually he learns more about this V drug how it was originally designed and tested by the government to try and enhance the performance and morale of soldiers during the gulf war. However the project was quickly halted in 1995 when the test results showed damning mental side effects. Problem was certain high ranking officials saw potential in this drug and decided to keep testing and manufacturing it in secret. Not long after that Max learns what connection the 3 addicts had to do with his wife and why she needed to die. Armed with the new revelation of what really happened and slightly influenced with the invigorating power of V on himself he tracks down all those responsible and kills them.
I guess in a nutshell because the story has some aspects similar to the well known and publicized MKUltra experiments the CIA performed unknowingly on many of the public, it often gets nominated as a 'great story', but seriously nothing still quite beats the original...

Beta review 26.1.2016
In short Torment is isometric cRPG. The game aims more for reactivity, choices, replayability and story telling than other RPGs. This game is successor to Planescape Torment which was released 1999. According to wikipedia, PST has been pretty frequently rewarded after year 2000. For example, 2008 IGN listed this as n. 8/10 franchises that should be resurrected, praising game for having "best writing and characterization seen in gaming". Planescape has also been frequently listed top xx all games ever done and to play, last of them being PC Gamer stating 2011 Planescape Torment being 19th greatest PC game ever done. Clearly, there's a huge demand for this successor.
Team behind the game is more or less "all star" group, having been part of creating following titles: The Bard's Tale series, Wasteland 1 & 2, Fallout 1 & 2, Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, IWD 1&2 and NWN2 expansions. (Well, Avellone left before change of year 2016 ) Also, creator of Numenera setting is involved with project as well. Mark Morgan (Fallout 1,2,NV, Planescape etc.) is composing music for Torment. The game raised 4 million USD in Kickstarter, later increrasing the amount to 5 million and it's still growing. As far as I know, this is currently a world record for a Kickstarter project related to games. The game has already delayed like one year and will be released this year, propably after summer? If I remember correct, Kickstarter was was chosen as a method to fund the game to get rid of some problems gaming industry does for developing of games.
So, a lot of promises, expections, hopes and doubts.
-
, just like developers have said. There's a lot of text to read and it is written really well and the use of words is colourful, really making your imagination running. The languange however is not anything simple, which might become problem for people who dont speak English as first languange or have fluent English otherwise. (For this, before buying, I would recommend to check Let's Play videos or something where you can see a bit of it). Dev has mentioned that this game will have about equal amount of words than Planescape had or possibly even more. (Devs have however stated that the game will be translated into: French, German, Italian, Polish, Russian and Spanish during early access.)
-
seems to play big part of the quests and world in the game. Quests seem to have multiple solutions, starting from not even taking the quest, ignoring after taking it and other solutions where you do something. Naturally, you can't solve quests in all different ways in one playthrough. 5 dimensional tide system also seems to provide replayability as they do different things for the world. You even have different prologue parts before waking up in the world of Torment. Choices in game also shifts these tides as well and might cause NPC's in world to react in different ways etc. I havent investigated this  tide thing yet.
-
Developers ask for feedback in the forum or via the feedback system provided in the game. It's nice to see that developers are actually reading the forum and recommendations, suggestions and other ideas of people in the forum, also commenting them occasionally. (To make it clear they dont do what people tell them to do, they just take the best parts or ideas that suit for their vision of the game). Also, they havent developed f.e. stores, proper UI or many items for it. I'm sure that the combat system will get some tweaks as well.
-
Numenera is odd world for a person who is not familiar with the setting before playing this. That's why the lore might feel a bit crushing at the start, but if you look around and do things, you get more familiar with it in short time. In short it's scifi world but has a touch of more usual cRPG aspects, which makes you feel more like in home if you are familiar with genre. There's a lot of advanced technology, but knowledge and how odd devices and such are used is limited. I'm not explaining theme more here, but there's a lot to wonder and be curious about (like a fountain of purple fishes flowing instead of water?)
I think the game seems really promising so far. I'm curious about what I will learn about Numenera, the story, characters etc and what kind of choices can I make. I hope the full game will show more strong philosophical aspects as well (like PST did), which, at least the question "What does one life matter?" seems to be hinting about. I also got now and then Point And Click feeling :D Also, I havent had problems with performance of the game (other than first area). If you would like to see all different outcomes of quests etc. I would say playing this beta could be like 40 hour thing to play. Otherwise it's about +10 hours.
People who want to read (a lot) and think, diving into atmosphere and environment of Numenera with their imagination. People who enjoy cRPG titles, especially Planescape: Torment. People who don't mind that you can't archive everything in one playthrough. People who enjoy traditional, narrative roleplaying things, pnp and such. (However, dont expect and hope that this game is Planescape Torment 2 - Successor means that the heart of PST is there in terms of writing, reactivity etc. but the game's setting, rules etc have nothing to do with PST..)
People who dont speak fluent English. People who expect more fast paced gaming and action. Also, people who find idea of reading a book horrible. People who think that fighting in RPG is mandatory rather than one possibility among others.
Good thing is that this game will also be released DRM free.

So. Should you buy this game?

Wow, what a fantastic, wild ride. I genuinely loved the story, characters and artwork, and the puzzles were fun too (although there were a few places I got stuck, or spots I didn't realize I could click on.)
All in all, Maggie's Apartment left a real impact on me, and I'm very curious about what happened to the characters after the events of the game. I really can't recommend this game enough if you're a fan of point n' click adventures and have a taste for mystery.

Maggie's Apartment is a point & click adventure game that roughly took me about 3 hours to finish from start to finish. Throughout the story, you meet a variety of colorful characters, most of them non-human. The dialogue itself if wonderful, and the jokes throughout the game are clever, silly, and downright smart. I am a sucker for good dialogue, so this game was an honest treat.
The story itself is very cute, and at the same time, kind of heart-wrenching towards the end. The game, however, relies on point-and-click and some puzzle solving to progress the story. I am not fond of point & click games, but I love a good puzzle. This game had a nice blend of the two, and I was invested enough in the story to get past the point-and-click aspect of the game. The difficulty is also not too hard. There are some spots that had me stumped for a little while, but I was able to progress through trial and error. Some parts were a little confusing, and the first real obstacle was finding out you can drag items to make them interact with other objects and such.
The art style is interesting but unique. I loved Maggie's design and the general art direction of the game. The sound effects and movement of the characters were perfect, and it didn't take away from the story or immersion at all. The animation is a bit choppy, but once you get used to it after a few minutes of playing, you really start to appreciate the style. There were a few instances, however, where the sound felt out of place or too low. This is not a serious problem and is easily overlooked.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of adventure, point & click, or just a good story in general.

Voodoo Garden has a fun art style and most of the mechanics found in other idle clickers. You'll plant and harvest ingredients, expand your garden, prioritize what you produce, level up to unlock more plants, and eventually have a screen full of helpers.
Sadly I didn't find Voodoo Garden as good as some of the other idle clickers out there. Also, unlike other idle clickers, there is no progression while the game is closed.
I don't currently recommend Voodoo Garden. It feels like a cookie cutter clicker game with no innovation or challenge.
The game also feels poorly optimized, my Geforce GTX 970 was constantly at 50-70% usage, seems high for a game this simple that needs to be left open constantly to progress. The game framerate gets choppy after several hours running. Since there are no configurable graphics options I used the NVIDIA Control Panel to force VSync on, this lowered GPU usage below 40%.
If the game was better optimized I would recommend it only if you are addicted to playing any idle-clicker game you can get your hands on.

At first glance, Voodoo Garden is a re-skin of Plantera, an idle game where you grow a garden indefinitely (or until you get all the achievements).
However, in its curent state,
. It is certainly a clicker, but since the game does not progress at all when it is shut down, I think it does not fit the definition of idle games. Indeed, all other idle games I know, except for some weird browser experiments, will welcome you back with a message saying how much you earned while you were away and this does not (and does not award you anything).
Like Plantera, you own a garden with a variety of plant types and animals. The garden grows slowly before your eyes and you can either let your minions harvest slowly or speed them up by clicking.
Unlike Plantera, you start with no minion (
), there is no way to automatically defend your crops (at least at lower levels) and you will earn money not by selling your harvest directly but by using them in voodoo recipes.
All in all, the one difference that will probably matter the most when comparing this game to Plantera is that prices never go down... In Plantera, whenever you buy something, its price rises, but when you sell it back, the price goes back down. This encourages experimentation: you can upgrade your plants and animals, knowing that you will be able to re-buy the lower level things later on. Here, the prices only go up, which makes the idea of selling anything kind of insane (except for getting the achievement). It seems the creator is considering removing this "feature" (imo, a bug) in a future update, but as it stands right now, Voodoo Garden will punish rather than reward experimentation. Which seems silly in a game where everything (recipes and spirit effects, not just the plants and animals) is revealed progressively, so you simply cannot plan in advance and MUST experiment, even though it is actively discouraged by the game design.
Voodoo Garden has awesome graphics and a good concept but it is riddled with baffling game design issues... Those could be fixed rather easily.
IMO, for this game to be worth anyone's time, the dev needs to do 7 things:
Until all 7 things are done, I cannot recommend this game, no matter how pretty it is (and it really is).

I always get a very nostalgic feeling when playing an old Star Wars Game. It could be becuase the graphics and style remind me of a simpler time. Either way, this game is a real gem that should be bought by any true Star Wars fan. The story takes place after episode 6 with Luke training the new set of Jedi to help the galaxy by going on various missions. There are a good amount of missions available to do that come in sets of 5 with a total of three sets of missions or 15 missions. This does not include the opening and ending levels. The graphics are not the best but it is understandable due to the date this game was released. The thing that really shines through this game is the gameplay, it is mainly done through a first person shooter perspective when using blasters, and a third person perspective when using a lightsaber. The blasters have a wide variety that you unlock as you progress giving different types to use for better results. The lightsaber however is the crowning acheivement of this game. In the beginning you can customize the hilt and color of your lightsaber with more customization unlocked down the road. The combat with the lightsabers in this game is incredible, different combinations of mouse clicks and movements yield incredible attacks that look like they were taken out of the movies. You can deflect blaster bolts, block, parry, de-limb enemies, and throw your lightsaber. The combat is so well done it really makes it fun to fight tons of sith warriors while also being functional. Pair the lightsaber fights with slomo on kill and you get for a dramatic and fun experience. This game is something to behold as its combat was ahead of its time, contained a good story and is just all around a good Star Wars game, if you are looking for a fun game to play this is it.

I am a big fan of hitman video game series and have always loved the game and appreciated any kind of changes introduced in the game. Even with Hitman Absolution, I was pretty happy with it. But this prequel to hitman video game series seriously disappoints me. Why? Well here's the list.
1. First of all, the thing that bothers me the most, "you have to be online all the time to actually play the game". Even slightest disconnection from your side or the server side (which happens more often than you think)would throw you back to the main screen. And boy, its so frustrating. To add to the problem, the servers are almost always offline.
2. You can't unlock any achievement when playing offline.
3. The game's episodic release is a turnoff. It forces you to play the same map hundreds of time under different name. Call it contracts or escalations. I for one don't mind playing a map over and over but only the one that I like. Not every one of them. It takes away that freedom from you.
4. 6 Levels over 6 months is a long time.
5. Escalations are just like any other contract but with cameras and lasers, which is easy to destroy.
6. The game is buggy. NPC's see through walls. Didn't expect that from a game which is already on episodic release. It just points that the game is released prematurely.
note: the play time on my profile is actully the time I wasted trying to connect it to the server.
I would recommend to buy it only once all the episodes are out. The game might be less buggy by that time.
[Edit : Its been more than a week since the patch v1.03 was made available and since then, not even once was I able to connect online. The online mode sucks to such a bad degree, I can't help but give it a 0/10. Definitely not recommended at all. Waste of money.]

The long awaited Banjo-Threeie has finally been released!
Well, okay, not really, but I still find myself saying "notes" instead of "quills" and "Jiggies" instead of "Pagies."
I've heard this game called a love letter to 90s collectathon platformers, but it really isn't.  It -is- a 90s collectathon platformer! Sure it was released in almost 20 years after the 90s ended, and it's a whole lot prettier, but everything's there! Platforming through impossible technicolour 3D worlds, weird NPCs, enormous amounts of innuendo in dialogue, and of course collectables, collectables, collectables!
This game even brought back that feeling of rage and frustration as you try for the 14th time to get a thing, and then wish you'd never even heard of the game much less bought it.  The "I'm going to stop playing after I get this one more thing...no...this one more thing....no...crap it's midnight!" factor is real in this game, as is the triumph of making it through a difficult part.
The game pulls no punches, and shows no mercy.  The overworld is confusing and finding the game worlds takes a whole lot more effort than it probably should.  The game worlds themselves are enormous, much larger than any of its predecessors.  This is both a good and a bad thing, as the amount of content available is huge, but finding it can be difficult.  Learning the lay of the land takes a lot of getting lost first.
I've been looking forward to this game for a long time, and it's everything I expected.  It could use polishing to improve the flow of the gameplay, but as-is, the package is excellent.
Playtonic, I'm looking forward to the sequel!

Let's start with my background: I never played any of the Banjo Kazooie games, I didn't back the game on Kickstarter, I got it during Summer Sale, and I played most of it after the polishing update came. Got it? Good. On with the review.
I went in expecting a fair quality collectathon platformer with decent controls and nice levels, and that's exactly what I got. It gets all the basics solidly done, but doesn't avoid some of the most common issues that have plauged 3D platformers since their dawn, namely slightly wonky swimming controls and the camera occasionally getting stuck on level geometry.
The standard controls and moves feel nice and responsive with an Xbox controller, the exception being the steering of the flying controls, which feels a bit too imprecise for some of the challenges. Ever so slight imprecision is a running theme with most of the vehicle transformations, and it might get somewhat frustrating in a few sections that require fast evading or platforming. Luckily, it's not too terrible.
The arcade minigames are inconsistent in quality, ranging from tolerable to teeth-grindinly frustrating. They are optional for anyone who isn't trying to 100% the game, but then again, it's a colletathon, and the entire point is to 100% it...
The levels are overall nice, with the very first one being the standout of the bunch with its sheer verticality in the expanded version. However, five levels just feels way too little, even with this much care put into them. I was left wanting more locations to explore.
Speaking of wanting more, there are only around six enemy types (as far as I remember), not counting level-specific reskins of the standard mook. Maybe two or three types more would bring nice variety to combat. The standard mook type is not very engaging to fight, so you just walk by them most of the time.
The writing is classic Rareware, but tonally it's somewhere between Banjo and Conker. The entire thing is a thinly veiled middle finger to Microsoft, which I personally find hilarious, knowing the background of the developers. There are even enemies and a boss designed after a Kinect! Plenty of references to the team's history are scattered through the game, even the unused ice key from Banjo makes an appearance.
The biggest issue I have with the game's writing, is Laylee. They tried to make her snarky and sassy, but went too far, and now she just comes off as an insufferable guanohole who insults and belittles everyone for no reason. That's not very endearing.
As for the graphics, it is a very, VERY pretty game, striking a good balance between cartoony and detailed. Sound design is solid as well, especially Yooka's footsteps on different surfaces and power-up states. Grant Kirkhope is back in the composing team, and it really shows in the style and instruments. While not his best work, it gets the job done. The melodies aren't really that memorable, but I can't really blame the man. He used up all the best melodies almost 20 years ago. Where do you even go from that?
Overall, Yooka-Laylee is decent 3D collectathon platformer with a rock-solid foundation, but it needs more of everything. Still, I would recommend it for any platformer fan whenever it's on sale. It is nice, but not full price nice. I will eagerly be waiting for a sequel to improve upon it.
If you loved Banjo-Kazooie and other games by Rare, you will Love Yooka-Laylee!

Like many other reviewers I played through Banjo-Kazooie/Tooie and like many others I loved them. Yooka-Laylee is in many ways a worthy successor, but there is room for improvement. Don't be fooled by older reviews; the latest patch really changed the game for the better. A lot of the main issues got taken care of, primarily the camera. It's still not the best out there, but it manages well enough not to hinder the experience.
The characters in this game are great. There's a lot of humor in the game and it doesn't take itself too serious. They all fit right where they're suppose to be. I could knitpick here and there (too many ''talking shopping carts'' in the third level or the same puns in the fourth), but overall this is a positive. Same goes for the music. It's well composed and though repetitive it never gets old. If you have played games like Banjo-Kazooie on the N64 you'll love the nostalgiatrip. If you haven't, this game might feel dated though.
When it comes to the downside, it's certainly the difficulty. I finished the first playthrough at 100% at around 23 hours. Which isn't too bad all things considdering, but I rarely felt really challenged. What didn't help was the fact that pretty much every level has the same types of enemies; there are 6 in total (if you don't count bosses). At some point, how many of the same creatures can you kill before it gets dull? All things considdering the game is pretty expensive for what you get. 5 levels, 1 overworld and about 25 hours of playtime. I purchased the game during the Summer Sale and that was just-about worth it for me.
All in all this game does deserve a second part, but Playtonics need to step it up a notch.
