Lengthy review ahead.
TL;DR: Not a perfect game, but extremely close to it. Absolutely recommended for anyone who's interested or enjoys dating sims. Not recommended for those uncomfortable with gay relationships, for what I hope are obvious reasons.
Pros:
+Incredibly appealing art style, creative design, and music. The game is very, very pretty, the characters are all expressive and unique, and the colors are vibrant without being gaudy.
+The writing is quirky and fun while, for the most part, knowing where to draw the line without bleeding jokes dry. I've come to enjoy the dry humor sprinkled in throughout serious subject matter, and most of the jokes are clever. There are also a few pop-culture references and fourth-wall breaking, but it is thankfully minimal enough that the few times it does happen are genuinely enjoyable.
+Surprisingly deep and mature story. For a game that markets itself the way it does, DDADDS has some wonderful serious moments in it as well. The Dads all have some depth, the story of Maple Bay is deeper than it appears, and some of the routes get downright heavy and emotional. It genuinely shocked me to see them so openly have, for instance, a chance for your character to decide whether he wanted to have a drunken one-night stand with another character or not, and have neither decision painted as wrong. There's even a hard-won, time-consuming true ending to be had for one of the characters!
+Casual LGBT+ representation and general acceptance. You're a father dating other fathers. Some fathers have male exes. You can choose the gender of your ex. You can choose whether you're implied to be a cisgender or transgender father (no impact on dialogue), and whether or not Amanda is your biological or adoptive child regardless of which choice you made at character creation and what the gender of your ex was. None of this is pointed out, questioned, made strange or shunned, at any point in the story. It's unavoidably and seriously gay, but does so in such a casual and subtle way that it's able to leave an impact on those of us who appreciate and be generally ignored by those who don't.
+Minigames! They helped break up the monotony of reading very well, and are for the most part solid and simple, but fun.
+Plethora of content. I'm 12 hours in and only through about half of the routes, and with multiple endings per-Dad, I can tell that I'll have plenty of time to sink into the game to get everything. Despite this, individual routes are relatively short, meaning you'll never feel like the game is moving at a sluggish pace.
+Easy save-scumming. You can save at every decision and you don't have to overwrite an old save to do so. You can get exactly the outcome you want most of the time just by smart saving and reloading. As a dating sim regular and a completionist, this is an extremely handy thing for getting every ending for every dad without relying on guides.
Cons:
-Minigames. They're fun when they work well, but some of them are needlessly clunky or overly simplistic, or don't have enough instruction to actually succeed at without trying a few times. The penguin game and the mini-golf game are the worst culprits. Still very bearable, just annoying to get through if you aren't lucky or good at them.
-Characters aren't always what they seem, some in a very pleasant and delightful way, and others in a way that just makes their route seem bizarrely out of left field. Some obvious plot twists are treated as a huge revelation much later, which can make the player feel a little babied. Nothing too severe, but again, mildly annoying.
-In the current version, there are some visual bugs if you reload older saves, which result mostly in characters briefly losing their glasses, but sometimes leads to a pair of creepy twins invading your romantic bro date. Please patch this, they terrify me.
-----
Overall, a 9.5/10 from me. Very fantastic game. Could use some small tweaks and have some routes or minigames that are weaker than others, but overall a high-quality, smooth, genuinely funny and endearing game that I've done nothing but love to play since buying it.

1) Best Writing Ever! Amazing story, characters and settings with personalities of their own.
2) Uniquely awe-inspiring environments with unforgettable experiences around every corner.
3) A massive project filled with love, both from the Devs and the Fans!
4) The Spiritual Successor to Planescape: Torment, and I could not be any prouder!
5) Just to clarify: This is not D&D, nor is it technically part of the D&D universe... but it's also technically could be, in a way. Afterall, Planescape: Torment took place in Sigil, and that city could take you anywhere in the universe... I wish not to debate meta/universe lines or copyrights, so I will just leave it as that. No it doesn't explicitly have any connection to the previous game, but the feel, wonderful bizarrities and incredible writing feel right at home.

Thus far, the game has been amazing. It has the updated graphics and sounds (plus voice acting!) that were needed to drive the series forward. Planescape: Torment is held dear to the hearts of many, and this game shall not disappoint! 12/10 Can't wait for the full release!
If only it weren't so late... I want to play FOREVER!

It's the closest thing we've gotten to a game like Planescape: Torment since 1999.  That's high enough praise to sell any game.

PROS:
- The Story... While I didn't get that wave of "le feels" the simplistic reviews professed, this game was definitely heavy and deep. The story is brilliantly crafted and the characters are well voice-acted, ultimately resulting in a plot that does not make you question so much "morality" as some players have said, but breaking the fourth wall and questioning the validity of "choice", particularly in games.
- Excellent shooting, guns feel weighty and effective. Ammo reserves are small forcing you to be tactically prudent and careful.
- Graphics are artistically beautiful. On the technical side, they are aging a bit, but I got my 60 FPS.
- Levels, albeit very linear, are designed very well. Absolutely beautiful with some destructable objects, some of which can be used to harm foes.
CONS:
- Arrays of unfriendly and abysmal checkpoints. This game was made in 2012 and there are still checkpoints before cutscenes and scripted events, making you sit through them until the "skip" option pops up about ten seconds later.
- Multiplayer is a throwaway. This didn't bother me, but it might some. The devs did not intend on implementing multiplayer until the publisher forced them to, so don't let it rub off on your overall opinion.
- Don't like turret sections? Too bad! About a dozen of these son'-guns in this game.
- Some story elements seem shoe-horned, such as the unavoidable war crimes you commit perhaps intended to make the player feel remorseful.
- Squad commanding is a rather two-dimensional feature. You didn't miss out on a lot, but it would have been nice to see something with a little more Republic Commando/Rainbow Six-esque depth.
- Probably the biggest complaint of all is that this was obviously a console port. The mouse smoothing and acceleration can only be disabled by decrypting the .ini. Some buttons are annoyingly bound to a myriad of actions. Sprinting, taking cover, and reviving your buddies is all bound to the same button and you can't change that, trying to perform one action and performing another has gotten me killed dozens of times.

OVERALL:
Had it not been for the story, it's just another modern military FPS with all the guns you recognize in a pretty environment. With the story, it's fairly impactful, sort of a reflection on games in general. The six hours it took me to complete justifies the $6 it was purchased at, but definitely not the normal $30.

Garfield is a fat and free-spirited orange cat who lives with his owner, Jon Arbuckle. Garfield passes his time by antagonizing Jon and teasing an aggressive neighbor Doberman Pinscher, Luca. Aside from Jon, Garfield maintains an unlikely friendship with a helpful mouse, Louis. He also socializes with his fellow neighborhood cats, including Garfield's stooge Nermal and Arlene.
Meanwhile, a local television host, Happy Chapman, known for his cat "Persnikitty" is introduced as supposedly a happy man. In reality he is allergic to cats, jealous of his brother Walter J. Chapman, a news reporter, and destined to be more successful by performing on TV show Good Day New York. Jon has made a habit of bringing Garfield to the veterinarian, in order to see vet Dr. Liz Wilson (whom he is in love with). Jon tries to ask her out, but due to a misunderstanding, he is given custody of a stray dog, Odie. Regardless, Jon and Liz begin dating. Garfield is jealous of Odie and tries to get rid of him. Odie is brought to a canine talent show, where Liz is a judge. Garfield gets involved in an altercation there with other animals, which moves Odie to the center of the ring, where he begins dancing to "Hey Mama" by the Black Eyed Peas.
His improvised performance is a hit. Happy Chapman, who also is a judge of the dog show is impressed with Odie, and offers Jon a television deal for Odie, but Jon declines. After Garfield accidentally make a mess inside Jon's house, Jon punishes Garfield by forcing him to sleep outside for one night. Odie comes out to comfort Garfield but Garfield locks Odie out. Nermal and Arlene witness this as Odie runs away; he is then picked up by an elderly woman named Mrs. Baker. Jon searches with Liz for Odie while the neighborhood animals treat Garfield as an outcast. Meanwhile, Chapman and his assistant Wendell find a notice Mrs. Baker created of Odie and, recognizing the lucrative possibilities, claim Odie as Happy's own.
When Garfield sees Odie on television and hears Chapman announce he and Odie are going to New York City, Garfield sets out to rescue Odie. Jon discovers Garfield missing so Jon and Liz start searching. Garfield gets into the broadcast tower via the air vents but he is blown around violently. Garfield finds Odie locked in a room; Chapman enters and secures a shock collar to Odie, which, when activated, releases an electric discharge that forces him to perform tricks.
Chapman heads for the train station with Garfield in close pursuit. However, an animal control officer catches Garfield mistaking him as a runaway. Mrs. Baker tells Jon that Chapman took Odie, but Jon believes Garfield was taken too and he and Liz race to Telegraph Tower and then to the train station, after learning Chapman has left. Garfield is released from the pound by Chapman's abandoned feline star, Persnikitty, who is really named Sir Roland. Chapman boards a Texas-bound train, with Odie in the luggage car. Garfield arrives only to see the train depart. Garfield sneaks into the train system control room and frantically switches the tracks, leading to an impending train wreck. Garfield hits an emergency control and causes Chapman/Odie's train to return to the station. Garfield frees Odie and they exit the train. However, Chapman chases them. Chapman threatens Odie with the shock collar, but is stopped by Garfield's friends and animals from the pound, led by Sir Roland. They swarm and attack Chapman, allowing Odie and Garfield to escape.
The shock collar is now on Chapman who gets shocked. Jon and Liz arrive to reclaim the animals and find Chapman disoriented. Jon punches Chapman in the face for stealing his pets, and leaves with Liz and the two animals. Chapman is arrested for his supposed involvement with the trains, as well as for abducting Odie. Garfield regains the respect of his animal friends as a hero. Back at home, Liz and Jon form a relationship, while Garfield learns a lesson about friendship.

This is one of those special-place-in-my-heart games that elicits some kind of catharsis every time it's played.  The setting, gameplay, soundtrack, dialogue, artwork - it all comes together in this strange culmination of dark justice.   Max Payne loses in the end, whether he wins or not.  He's doomed from the start, and a lot of games don't torture their heroes this much.  So from the beginning you're in this nothing-to-lose mentality alongside our protagonist.  The mechanics even support this idea, as you can restart from the last point of death if you mash the quicksave button like an underlying arc from a Lost episode.  Events replay like you went back in time a few seconds prior to your blundered encounter and decided to duck left instead of right.  The gaming community criticized this feature when it released all those years ago, and people are still kind of iffy on it because of its linear drive.  This game really is a comic come to life.  The setting is as much a character as Max is, rife with loneliness and torment - slowly picked apart by what can only be described as a 100-year winter.  New York City is the target of the Norse Gods' "♥♥♥♥-this-place-in-particular" ice beam of misery, effectively isolating Max and a thousand goons to do glorious battle in Thunderdome 2.0.  The reason this game is and will always be timeless is because you don't need to inject yourself into 2001 to appreciate this title for all that it is.  It's a story that can be told over and over.

A solid arcadey pool game with a variety of modes. Despite the small playerbase and no previously promised snooker mode, I recommend it to any
pool fan, especially on sale.
+ User-friendly mechanics

+ Witty descriptions
+ Fitting soundtrack

Pool Nation is an arcadey pool simulation game. This one takes the player to the world of fancy lounges, chillout music, and jump shots.
The game is very accessible: tutorials are short but cover important basics to get one started. One can also adjust the aiming aid level (novice -> veteran -> pro -> champion -> off) which is a huge plus. Players can test their skills against the AI opponents in VS and Career modes, as well as against other people, and solo in the Endurance mode. The last mode is a time trial and requires quick thinking and precise shots, as the balls spawn faster as the time goes by and when the ball count on the table reaches 24, the game is over.
The career mode is divided into two tournaments (9-ball and 8-ball), each with four cups. There are 12 matches in each cup plus a couple of bonus matches in lesser known modes, such as killer, 3-ball, speed pool, and the like. Each of the matches has two optional challenges to complete, for instance finishing a match with a skill shot, a ball streak, etc. Completing certain matches unlocks cosmetics. There are loads of decals, cues, and ball sets to be earned and the only problem is that they seem to reset to default ones every time the game is started. It is a minor issue but worth mentioning nonetheless.
This game looks and sounds great. The sounds of cue action combined with jazzy muzaks in the background create a laid-back atmosphere. Sit back, take the weight off your shoulders, and pot the balls like a boss – this game lets one do just that. Furthermore, the AI is fair for the most part and the difficulty curve is not very steep, making the experience very pleasant and virtually rage-free.
Overall, I recommend getting this game on sale to any fan of billiards games. While it may not be a realistic simulation and its playerbase may be really small, this game can provide hours of entertainment and satisfy the itch for some pool action. It indeed is a shame that the snooker mode was not delivered, given how much fun this game is.

Batman Arkham Origins puts you in the shoes of a "rookie" batman,which seems to rely in brute force over outsmarting his opponents like in the other installments of the series.
This is not a bad thing, as you play the game, you can see the evolution of batman from just a "myth" to the feared legend he has always been.
Gameplay wise, the mechanics of the game have been polished completely, and are now better than ever, however, some of the boss fights, while amazing. tend to become repetitive and lack luster once you are halfway done the bosse's health bar.
The series has also recieved a graphic overhaul and looks way better than its brothers do, however, the Physx implementation  is terribly done and leaves a lot of desire, as the papers and strings that use this seem to run at a whole different frame rate and look out of place. Another inclusion of physx is the "dynamic" snow in which Batman and his enemies leave footprints/trail in the snow.
However,in some part of the game the use of Physx means you are going to take a HUGE impact in perfromance,even if you have a really beefy computer; and I don't mean just a 10-15 fps drop, no, I mean going from smooth as butter, to as jittery as Jell-O;when I reached that point of the game, I had to turn of Physx to continue playing,because leaving it on would have meant playing at around 15 fps.
Story wise, the game is marvelous, as it expands the background of the Dark Knight in almost a comic/graphic novel like fashion. There are many references/homages that comic fans will love to see being put in the game.
As an Arkham series game, I see why it might not be as well received as the other games,as it bring almost nothing new to the table.
But if you take it as a standalone Batman game, it might be the best one yet, if it makes any sense.
9/10

Campaign - I haven't played the campaign yet but I am planning to so I am not going to talk about it much however from what I have heard it is a great campaign like most CoDs are and worth playing if you have the game.

Awesome Zombies - The Zombie map you get with the base game is called 'Green Run' it is split up to 4 separate maps (Tranzit, Town, Farm and Bus Depot). Tranzit contains Town, Farm and Bus Depot all in one huge map with a buildable wonder weapon and a bus. Traniz was a flop in my opinion. The map was terribly executed with the way that you can't choose when the bus goes (freeze it somewhere), the wonder weapon overheats and blows up in seconds and the fog is annoying as hell. Town is a great survival map - Some people hate the Lava I personally like it because if you are new to zombies it teaches you about being aware. Bus Depot has no perks or pack-a-punch which is a challenege and really fun solo or co-op. Farm has perks but no pack-a-punch and is a great map. All the DLCs are worth it if you are going to play Zombies a decent amount of time however don't expect to play with people - each DLC map has about 30-70 people playing whereas Tranzit, Town, Bus Depot and Farm have 300 all together playing.
Overall I give the game a 9.5/10. If you are an avid Call of Duty player you cannot miss out on this game and is a must have for anyone looking for a fun, supported and well optimised FPS game.

So, I got this game for the campaign, and not for the multiplayer. I'll review it based on that.
So, the first modern warfare game had a pretty good and more realistic campaign. Since then, the Call of Duty series has just gone crazier and crazier, trying to be more intense than the last game. Probably because they have not really innovated anything at all and the games feel plain boring. With some pollish perhaps we will all still be "blown" away a little. Apprantely, people still buy this games like crazy.
Still, this game has one of the better campaigns though because the settings, weapons and tech are interesting and creates some variety. The whole future thing plays well, making the game a little different and more fresh than other campaigns.
What is good?
It runs well on most machines, and it still looks pretty well. The productions values are top notch with nice cutscenes. Perhaps not my style, or not very interesting, but nevertheless very well done. It is nonstop action. If you take this as an "action movie ride", you can have a good time. Varied game play and sections. Not too difficult if you are looking for an game easy to get into.
What is not so good?
It is SHORT. You probably knew that, but for the asking price, this is still absolutely ridicolous. The game takes itself too seriously, and this just makes it silly. It is quite difficult to understand what is going on, or even care for any character. The game is truly set up to impress you ONCE. I mean many action sequences, that suddenly happens (often in slow motion), where you are supposed to something cool, totally lose their charm when you fail a couple of times and have to redo that sequence. It just turns frustrating. The magic is gone instantly.
There is no freedom whatsoever - If you do something that the game (devs) did not have in mind, it is pretty much insta-death. It does not feel like you made something stupid, but that you just died for no reason taking a step in the "wrong" direction. It can become very frustrating because you might not always understand what is going on. You cannot really take your time either, or you usually explode in some way or another.
Game is often confusing because it really tries too hard to make it intense and busy. In most cases it actually feels like you did not do that much in the end, but that the game sort of led you through.
I still rate this reckommended if you can find a cheap deal, because it is rather entertaining if you know what you are going in for, and you might get a lot out of the multiplayer as well if you are into that. Personally, I find multiplayer way too frustrating though.
I still say Bad Company 2 is the best military shooter out there still. Campaign and online.
Cheers!

This game is a fun building game with procedurally generated random worlds and enough variables and enough possible build orders and game strategies that you can start over many times to try new ideas.  One example is how you deal with stress and illness.
Too much stress makes people susceptible to illness from germs.  You could try to deal with this by focusing on building aesthetically pleasing living/working areas and high quality food which will keep them from getting stressed.  If that's not to your liking then you could choose to let them be a bit stressed but build artificial means of stress relief such as massage tables to keep their stress low enough that they mostly don't get ill.  Or maybe you don't worry too much about their stress and instead you focus on high quality medical care so that when they do get ill they recover quickly.  Perhaps you'd rather solve this problem by focusing on building a very clean and sterile environment so that even if they are stressed they won't be around any germs so they won't become ill  You might even take pleasure in abusing your duplicants, providing them no toilets and only the minimum care needed to keep them from dying, making them stressed and sick on purpose so that they will cry , vomit, and pee all over the place creating resources to power your twisted experiments.  Depending on which option you choose you will want to research different technologies first and choose different people with strengths and vulnerabilities that work best with the path you have chosen.  Depending on how you play it your facility's operation might more resemble a prison, a research center, a farming commune, an art museum,  a hospital, or a waste reclamation plant.
I enjoy experimenting and trying to build my base it in different ways.  If you like that sort of experimental building gameplay then I highly recommend this title.  It has much the same charm as Prison Architect.  If you like that game then I thinkk you would probably like this too.
To get the most enjoyment out of this game, don't go looking for Lets Play videos or guides.  The fun is in figuring out how to succeed, trying and failing in different ways and refining your gameplay then trying again.  You'll lose that if you start out by having someone else that has already done it 50 times tell you exactly what to do.

As someone who didn’t get into collect-o-thons until Rare Replay, I find myself in an interesting position to judge Yooka Laylee; I did not grow up with these games but I am familiar with the classics. The small refinements to the Banjo Kazooie formula help make YL one of my favorite collect-o-thongs to complete while the nostalgia diminishes its execution. Unlike other games that rely on nostalgia, the developers relied too much on the past without understanding how to make them enjoyable to both old fans and new.
What puzzles me the most about YL is why it is being heralded as the reason this genre is outdated in today’s market by people who never liked these games as well as dismissed by hardcore gamers  who let the small flaws tarnish everything. These people aren’t wrong for having a different opinion; its the hardline attitudes that stand in the way of improving upon all YL's many great moments and numerous faults.
As someone who likes Mighty No. 9, Shovel Knight and Yooka Laylee, it may appear a mess of contradictions to someone who doesn’t know why I enjoy each game. There’s a management of expectations behind the nostalgia, hype/funding, and gameplay that are reasons why only one has succeeded while the others are lambasted by fans and critics alike.
MN9 is a victim of high expectations by both critics and fans that was overblown by its faults due to set-backs for release, its launch debacle and its devleopment. At its core, MN9 was a classic MegaMan game for both good and bad that used a the X series’ emphasis on skill and speed as adding versality and practicality to the boss upgrades to entice diehards. As a backer of MN9, I loved it because it took all the things I liked about MM and added something to the classic formula, while fans of X and more casual players did not enjoy it.
SK was a game adored by critics and fans who wanted a game that relied on nostalgia but instead of giving them what they wanted it was made to be based on what people think they remember about NES games. The modern additions as well as accessible options for changing the difficulty let most fans enjoy the game, and cheat codes allowed players to amp it up for hardcore audiences to get more out of it. As someone who knew nothing about SK, it was a fun experience if too reliant on the accessible options to make a challenging experience while the DLC deviated from SK’s strengths.
YL is different from both cases because like MN9 it relies on its nostalgic appeal and core gameplay from Rare’s platformer days while also innovating with tonics and abilities to be more accessible to newer audiences like SK. Its hype was strong but I don’t believe it was guilty of overblowing expectations to everyone, nor do I think the game compromised its overall challenge for newcomers. What YL did do wrong was to give a false sense of reward for secrets to backers, not including me, from the Toy Box demo and fail to understand the limitations of its nostalgia design as well as iron-out its overall lack of polish in its gameplay.
Of all the criticisms levied at YL, this is the most toxic to state because it seeks to dismiss an entire genre due to one game rather than the purpose of the genre not of interest to the critic. Collect-o-thons by their very nature are platforming adventures into playgrounds of a variety of challenges, puzzles and gimmicks to make the act of exploration entertaining. When people complain about barren areas, needless backtracking to expand worlds, the limited number of worlds, and the variety of platforming challenges, I cannot but help to think these people miss the point of these games.
As someone who is not a fan of traditional JRPGs that rely on boring turn-based combat, it would be equally dismissive of me to say that turn-based combat or JRPGs are outdated. Games like XCOM, Valkyria Chronicles and Darkest Dungeon can make turn-based combat rewarding or the Earthbounders (LISA, Citizens of the Earth, Undertale and the Earthbound series) can make JRPGs engaging for people like me. All these games have their niche audiences and deserve to have a place in today’s markets for people who do enjoy them, so the argument that “X” is outdated should never be used.
What should be talked about are what are some commonly accepted tropes about collect-o-thons that could be changed for the better or offer something different. People who complain about the lack of navigation failed to utilize the world-expanding capabilities to help them learn the layouts in two-steps, and I would encourage people not to expand worlds until they have opened all five. Environments vary in their size and the thematic challenges to keep variety without using the same puzzle twice, especially the Casino level. Platforming challenges can be made easier or more difficult with tonics, and the worst dilemma of these games of finding all the Notes/Coins/Feathers can be solved with a tonic just to help you find what you’re missing. (I don’t believe this last trope is required for these games when finding the main collectables is the real reward, but I understand the idea of signposts.) This last change is something I have always hated about collect-o-thons and why I love YL so much because it addresses the problem without ruining the exploration.

None of this is to say that YL is perfect, and I doubt anyone would disagree with the statement.
The most obvious fault is the camera being stuck on the terrain is something you can mitigate, but it’s the overall lack of polish on the controls that bothers me. Gimmicks like Kratos’ Minecart or Rex-Tro’s Arcades are well-meant attempts for variety but the simplicity and clunky controls ruin their enjoyment. Character noises, while not as much of an issue to me with the update, are still a relic of the past that could have been tweaked to be less frequent in conversations. Abilities that are meant to make the game more accessible like the flight ability can sometimes ruin the challenge itself if you rely on it. It’s these nuisances and many little things that constantly remind you that the overall experience is not without its apparent flaws.
However, a reoccurring issue that leaves this game with a sour taste compared to other nostalgic games is an overall desire to get back at modern gaming with its type of humor and jabs at certain practices within the industry. This idea didn’t occur to me until the Casino Boss Fight where you are fighting I.N.E.P.T., a motion-sensor security device that invades your personal space to damage you as well as suffering from near-sightedness. The fact that a boss could ridicule Microsoft’s KINECT so blatantly while being on Xbox One shows how much vengeance is behind YL, and it doesn’t work in the game’s favor. Many jokes come off as cynical jabs at modern gaming that may annoy some and feel out of place toward others, but the overall tone of these jokes that gaming back then was so archaic it was bad and now also full of rubbish is something I did not expect to feel from a game. The point is it’s easier to root for the underdog when it finally gets its chance to shine, but it’s hard to feel sorry for the underdog when it uses that moment to bite the next person’s ankle.
While I wouldn’t ever put Yooka Laylee into one of my favorite platformers for many reasons listed as well as shoe-horned nostalgia moments that don’t understand why they worked (ex. Quizzes), I would welcome a sequel.
All Yooka Laylee would have to do is learn to improve on its errors and learn to adapt with modern times rather act the nihilist in burning the past, forgoing the present and not considering its future potential that it could easily achieve with enough understanding of its place in gaming.

At the time of writing this review I've done two playthroughs of the game and I've loved every minute of them.
Setting aside that this game was published by Game Grumps, for a group of people who were working on their first game this is amazing. There's always going to be a few nitpicks, a couple of typos here and there and my friend experienced a small continuity error in her playthrough, but overall for what you're paying you're getting a lot of game. There's some nods to Game Grumps within the game (such as outfits and quotes), however I feel like it should be pointed out that this game can 100% be played as a standalone game without any prior knowledge of the publishers.
People are complaining about the price, but this game is around 1/4 of what big new release games go for currently and yes, the routes individually aren't the longest, but as with all dating sims the intention is that you'll complete several, if not all of the routes. There's different endings for each dad and selecting different options throughout the game can get you different reactions, routes and endings. If you complete the game fully and do all of these routes as intended, this game will take you a while to get through.
Overall, this game does what it intends to do well, it's a dating sim and it follows the dating sim formula perfectly. I can't help but feel like those complaining were going into the game expecting more than a dating sim, because as someone who's played several dating sims in the past I can safely say that this is my favourite I've played to date.

, I think it's safe to say, I know what I'm talking about.

, by far, it one of the most stellar games I've ever played in my life. It's historical accuracy is astonishing, a true piece of art. Let's get started by the games perfect representation of Russia in World War 2. This game legit shows so many details, minor and major about the Eastern Front. It's like every detail makes you feel like you're actually experiencing it. The trenches, the cold atmosphere, not to mention the outstanding sounds, they are the most top tier quality I've heard in a game for a long time, it's just.. so immersive. The story of Efreitor Garfield of the 10th Lasagna Division NKVD and his comrades is just so beautiful. The Russian soldier's goal is to keep eachother alive, developing relationships with one another, save many, and kill the Nazi scum. Efreitor Garfield, Private Odie, and Private Nermal must rescue their recently captured commander, Lieutenant Arbuckle (Jon) from the Nazi Werchmant, and SS. They succeed, but a price (I'll let you figure it out.)
Another piece I'd like to talk about is the graphics. One word. Astonishing. The best game I've ever layed my eyes on. Everything looks.. real. They even made the lasagna textures full. Now what generous developers do that! Ok, I'm getting carried away, but for real, best graphics. You need a real beefy PC for this masterpiece, with it's stunning textures, models, bumpmaps, effects, post processing, and extreme polish.
To conclude, this is honestly the hands down best World War 2/Cold War game I've ever played, please, if you want a life-changing experience, purchase
for a whopping $5 in USD, today!

I can easily spend a few meditative hours hauling cargo across Europe, it's addictive. When you've just completed a run, it's like "well, one more won't hurt", and so on :)
I do recommend a set of steering wheels for controls though. That makes the experience much better compared to keyboard controls (or game pad).

The beta is a bit rough, but it's the first beta build so that's just going to happen.  That said, it was still very playable and enjoyable.  What really struck me about the game was the sense of otherness that the main city oozed out of each and every one of its pores.  Even after investigation I don't know what half of the ancient machines that scatter the city do, but they're all beautiful and intriguing.
Remember those question based character creation segments in a lot of older RPGs?  Well this game found a way to take that concept and make it not suck.  Basically how you solve the games initial set of problems determines your class and early stats in a way that feels organic.  You're literally discovering yourelf.  Don't worry, though, if you don't like the results, you get a chance to change them to what you want to play before jumping into the game world proper.
I don't have a solid review of the game's combat, because I didn't really fight anyone per se.  I wanted to see if you could solve everything without dealing a single HP of damage, and for everything I stumbled upon that was an option!
The strongest point of the beta is probably the writing.  It was a delight!

I've put in a decent chunk of time in to the Torment beta over the weekend and while its obviously clunky and unfinished I had a great deal of fun with it.
There are so many people you can talk to in Sagus, the first city, that you can easily spend over 5 hours just going around and annoying people with endless questions. Best thing about it is that pretty much every single bit of dialogue is well written and all of the characters have some sort of compelling story to tell, if you can get them to share it.
For example there's a cannibalistic cult that lives in the depths of the city and rather than the usual RPG business of having you kill them Torment actually managed to convince me to not just leave them alone but concede that they might have a good point...
However, while the story really is amazing, possibly just as good or even better than Planescape: Torment's the combat, graphics and performance still need a lot of work done to them.
The combat right now is best described as generic low-level DND combat with the one big difference being the various items and background objects you can use (the titular Numenera) if you have either the necessary skill or knowledge to activate them without blowing yourself up in the process. I'm guessing things will become a whole lot more interesting once you get a few more abilities under your belt but since you're mostly stuck as a low level character during the beta it was fairly meek.
The performance is also a bit of a sore spot. Its not uncommon to have your game freeze for a couple of seconds mid combat or while interacting with particularly complex background objects or even when simply accessing your inventory or any menu besides the dialogue one.
In other words, while Torment has an amazing story that's well worth exploring, it is still very much so a beta and as such I'd recommend you buy it either because you want to support the developers or because you want to soak in the story. Just don't buy it expecting a finished game because it most certainly isn't one just yet.
I've also done a video where I go far more in-depth about Torment so if you're looking for more info I welcome you to take a look:

Torment is a worthy successor to Planescape.
A new universe to play around with keeps things fresh while some familiar RPG mechanics stay similar to other games, and the lore is expansive to say the least. With the option to complete pretty much any crisis (the battle scenes) peacefully given the right skills and lucky rolls, pacifist runs are possible. Using the environment to your benefit in these crises is very satisfying when it works, too.
Be aware that as an early access game there are quite a few bugs, some that can break things to the extent that a reload is required, so save frequently!
I can't wait to play the full game!

As of right now, I cannot recommend this game for mainly because of bad gas/liquid mechanics.
Oxygen Not Included has a lot of focus on water and gas distribution systems. However, the current implementation makes designing said systems for your colony an experience of frustration. Every time you try to make a system that has more than one producer and/or consumer for water/gas, you run a risk of messing it up so badly that you'll have to redo the whole thing. For instance, it is very easy to completely stop the water from moving in the tubes accidentially, making half your tube tiles bursting with water, while the second half is completely dry for no obvious reason (I've found WHY this happens by searching the forums, but haven't seen any workaround other than "don't do complex systems" essentially).
Until the liquid/gas mechanics get a rework, I really cannot recommend this game unless you're willing to fight with very counterintuitive quirks with their distribution.

This could be called a "good first try" from Playtonic Games, a fledgling company that includes many of the original Rareware developers who worked on such classics as Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo-Kazooie.  If not obvious from the name of the game alone, Yooka-Laylee wants very hard to invoke memories of Banjo-Kazooie, and in fact was Kickstarted under the promise of being a spiritual successor to the franchise.  Because of this the game will inevitably be compared to the original, and in doing so it cannot hope to live up to the classic's nostalgia, pedigree, or its own crowdfunded hype.  But taken independent of anything else (as this review will attempt to do), the game is a fun and solid 3D platformer-adventure experience, marred by occasional design flaws and shortcuts (probably the result of a new company working with a small budget).
The premise of the game is enjoyably absurd: an over-the-top evil businessman is stealing all the world's books so his publishing company will have a monopoly on the market.  In the process he steals a magic tome of great power from the protagonists, who must infiltrate his corporate headquarters to get it back.  The formula is tried and true:  a hub world that splits off into individual main worlds, wherein are hidden a variety of collectables, and the player must collect a certain number of them to progress further in the game.  Collectables are protected by platforming segments, puzzles, and minigames, some of which require backtracking after the player has obtained more special abilities in later areas.  The difficulty level of these challenges is all over the place, and puzzles in the first world might be just as easy or hard as ones in the last world.  Each world is colorful, thematic, and full of wacky characters.  Of note is that Yooka-Laylee only has five worlds (a small amount for this genre), but compensates by having twice as many collectables per level.  The worlds sadly aren’t QUITE twice as large as the average 3D platformer, so a lot of challenges are out in the open and fairly short.
While Yooka-Laylee is more or less linear with a clear level hierarchy, the design allows for an unexpected amount of explorative freedom.  Levels are actually two-tiered: they begin small with only certain areas unlocked, and can be expanded by spending collectibles.  Since these collectibles must ALSO be spent on unlocking new worlds, the player is allowed to choose for themselves whether to delve further into an area that piques their interest, or move on to something new.  Many of the special moves are technically optional and can be obtained in any order; the game accommodates by cutting down on a lot of arbitrary halts to exploration, particularly the dreaded invisible walls.  Instead, nearly every ledge, crevice, and object is fully-modeled and solid enough to jump on: with a clever application of jumps and air techniques, what seems like an impassable barrier without the right move can be bypassed, and exploration can continue without the game breaking as a result, since it’s already been designed with freedom in mind.
The dialog and humor of the game is pun-laden and very hit-or-miss, which can be tiring considering the game is chock full of it.  Many jokes are good for a smirk and a chuckle, but just as many are sarcastic and shallow, without much bite; something a grade-schooler might say to look cool.  The game also relies HEAVILY on fourth-wall humor to poke fun at bad video game tropes, often at its own expense, perhaps to distract from the fact that the developers did not have the time, money, or foresight to properly avoid said tropes themselves.
Enemies and combat are more of an afterthought in Yooka-Laylee.  There is a very small pool of generic baddies that gets reused from world to world, and they are both easily avoided and easily dispatched to regain health when needed.  There is one boss per world, but "boss" is hardly a fitting term for them: with one exception they are all located in random side rooms, guard nothing, are irrelevant to the world they are in, and are just another minigame to learn and complete.  It's almost shocking when the final boss rolls around, and the player is suddenly subjected to an action-packed beatdown present nowhere else in the game.
The game design overall feels cobbled together, and rather than any glaring problem, it's the little things which bring it down.  Both the hub and the worlds feel more like a bunch of incongruous parts glued together, rather than a cohesive whole.  NPCs are placed seemingly at random in the world, and while enjoyably goofy in design they have minimal thematic polish or personality to make them stand out.  Even the reoccurring NPCs that show up in every world to offer unique minigames feel no more special than any other minigame.  And while the motifs of books and shady business practices add charm throughout the world, the story ultimately does nothing to capitalize on it, and every character's actions and motivations end up ringing hollow.
A lot of hate and disappointment has been piled upon Yooka-Laylee for not living up to the adventure game watermark set by Banjo-Kazooie.  While many pieces of criticism are quite valid, this should not and does not invalidate its existence as a game.  No new game should have to be compared to the bundle of emotions and memories invoked by an old cherished classic, as such a comparison cannot hope to be considered unbiased (though to be fair, Yooka-Laylee INVITES such a comparison by its very existence, so perhaps it deserves what’s coming to it).  It should also be acknowledged that Playtonic Games is not Rareware:  they did not have nearly the budget, manpower, time, or experience that Rareware had when developing Banjo-Kazooie.  If anything, it should be considered impressive that Playtonic created what they did, given what they had to work with.  This, plus the simple fact that Yooka-Laylee is a right fun and solid game by itself, makes it worthy of recognition, and future work by Playtonic should be looked forward to hopefully.

Beta review - 26.01.16
You can't help comparing Tides of Numenera with its spiritual predecessor Planescape: Torment. For good or ill, this is not PS:T 2. Without Avellone, there is a noticeable shift in writing and the setting itself greatly differs from Planescape. I had worried that it would be a pale imitation, a weak creation that mimics but does not understand what made Planescape: Torment so great.
I was wrong. I am not very far in the game, but after having talked to many NPCs and finished several quests, I feel like I have a good gauge of Tides of Numenera.
1. The writing is superb. I still miss Avellone, but the new writers raise many interesting questions about legacy, always finding a new unusual facet to explore and introduce you to. It's not a shallow game, which comes as a great relief to me.
2. The choices are introspective. The game not only asks what you would do, but why and how? It is very refreshing to be asked to ponder on my motives, especially compared to Pillars of Eternity, whose choices took a more results and action oriented view.
3. The gameplay and combat looks promising. I can't say more, as the game is yet unbalanced and I only experienced 2 crisises yet.
4. Bugs and lack of optimization. Currently, the game lags pretty hard 3-year old gaming laptop. The loading times are exruciating. Smaller levels need 3-5 minutes, the big marketplace requires whole 10-15 minutes.
Overall, I recommend the game, but only buy it right now if you have either an extremely powerful PC or a lot of patience for the loading times. I had the patience, but doubt that many other people will.
If you think this is a proper successor to Planescape Torment then it's not.

Being a regular player and GM in the world of Numenera, this game could only please me. It really feels like it's coming from where it claims it's coming (or something like that). Moreover, this fantastic universe of weird stuff and strange people is taken over by cool devs from a nice studio with the goal of reproducing the experience Planescape : Torment was while not forgetting to enhance it. So it's like a dinosaur of the oldschool rpg world but with a facelift, featuring a marvelous -but super weird- universe, dialogues where you can actually go pretty deep (not in all cases, but i don't care if i can't discuss the meaning of life with the guard patrolling the area), sceneries where you can actually feel the work which is provided by the devs, and a crisis system which is refreshing the good ol' pen'n'paper turn based system without disorienting the nostalgic ones, giving a sense of returning to the roots of the style which made some of us lovers of all this game can represent : a good videogame, a good adaptation of the pen and paper rpg Numenera, but also a great storytelling in which your choices feel decisive.
Prepare yourself for tons and tons of dialogue though, so if it's not something you're searching for or if you simply think you'll not be able to stand it after a while, i would suggest you to go your own way on another wonderful steam page !

This is easily one of the most complex survival sims I have ever had the privillege to play. It is absolutely brutal and unforgiving. For that reason it makes your eventual triumph even better. So sit back my friends and let me tell you a tale of an asteroid.
The three of my duplicants spawn into the asteroid and procede to clear out the area. As more dupes spawn we begin research into a tech which would allow us to create oxygen and hydrogen from water. At this point the oxylite ore (or compressed oxygen) has become almost depleted as a result of my rapid expansion. To buy time the dupes begin escavating oxygen pockets nearby. When we get the tech required to produce oxygen the way I want to I sigh (this is going to be a long game).
Using a few of the mealwood seeds (are we really that desperate to eat lice...) we place a farm under the spawn and the carbon dioxide begins to flood it. We place a food supply in the carbon dioxide (cool food won't rot now). Gradually we get more dupes and water begins to become a luxery; just out of my luck I find a gyser and jury-rig a pump from the gyser to the base's water supply. As an interesting note the water is so hot it is killing the germs (nice...I like this realistic touch).
Fast forward and we're pumping oceans of hydrogen to power generators while we tuck the chlorine away (hoping it doesn't kill anyone this time). Eventually power shortages and a surplus of coal mean coal power is on the menu. Next thing I know the entire bottom level is flooding with carbon dioxide and about to reach the cots.
Mysteriously woodmeal farm starts to fail due to overheating (ooh so boiling hot water is heating up the crops...awesome). I build a cooling system to allow part of the farm to continue to function. Eventually we begin frying mush bars to make up for the food shortages. I build a new farm away from the heat and slightly elevated (maybe that was a bad idea).
Fast forward we are a colony of 25 dupes and roughly 25% are dedicated to tasks I do at will. Eventually however I notice a serious problem...we're almost out of water...we were using it faster than it could be produced. The hydrogen generators laugh at me. Fortunately I am getting close to oil and the waste water should be enough to fuel the colony to 50 dupes. As a quick solution I drain a pocket of water into my base and continue construction, I can see the oil and all problems will be solved soon...
...yet I was wrong the temperature difference of the new pool of water dropped the temperature low enough that my cleaned water was not having the germs removed after being dropped back into the main pool. Immune systems start to fail (I'm getting concerned). Then my medical bay fills as people are diagnosed with food posioning. One or two doesn't worry me...when I get the fifth guy I see the problem, but at that point it was too late. The heater installed in the water supply for just this fails (there's not enough water to heat). Illness swept through the base and my workforce was down. In the middle of this we run out of coal and the power production drops...we can't run the gas pumps to remove the hydrogen. The hydrogen leaks from the ceiling and into the lower floors...the plants can't grow in hydrogen and the dupes can only spend a few minutes in it. Health plumets further as polluted water covers every surface. Then the food shortages come through and with a dwindling workforce of 10 I order plans for a recovery knowing they won't be alive long enough for the new farm to produce the crop. Dupes begin to attack the machinary or just cry as they count their days. One by one they starve to death until the last one who I didn't think would make it manages to grab a little bit of food.
In the end there were 2 dupes (one was ready to spawn during this collapse) and 24 bodies along with parts of the base that had basically flooded with fluid and hydrogen gas. I let them harvest food and get the power back online so they don't suffocate. One by one new dupes spawn and the base is gradually repaired. The machines are repaired, the dead are buried, and the hydrogen clears back into the ceilings. At a population of 10 I figured it was a good time to finally get the oil.
The extra oxygen pumped from the hydrogen ceilings is directed to exosuits. Now we can walk though the coldest biomes or the crude oil at the bottom. When we finally break through to the crude oil I smile...the coal around the base is almost cleared out and I need a new power source (or I could just make a few dupes run in a hamster ball all day). The crude oil bursts through the gap we cut and starts melting the ice biome we were in previously.
10/10 Would kill my base again to see it rise from the ashes.
Cons: We need more content and more diverse map generators, but this is early access and we will likely be getting those shortly. Tech tree doesn't make much sense in places (for example trapping animals is at the end while automation requires refined metal which is a mid-tier tech, but can be researched in the early game. Tutorial is kinda lacking and the game maybe too complex for some, but to me that complexity is what makes it fun.

First off, I'm going to add a positive review for this game to balance out all the unfair negative reviews. I want to being by saying that the actual game itself is an incredible experience.
If you enjoyed Blood Money's massive sandbox expanse, with numerous methods of assassination, then this is definitely going to be enjoyable for you. It is a substantial departure from the linearity of Hitman: Absolution.
However, it is far from the perfect game. I will agree with a lot of the points raised by those who have posted a negative review, which are:
-Always-Online DRM (which intereferes with the loading times and stability when playing with an unstable internet connection)
-Poor PC performance & optimisation (*EDIT: Now much more optimised and runs smoothly)
-Inconsistent AI behaviour and reaction to distractions.
Just keep in mind, that the game itself is not the problem. The game itself is actually incredibly enjoyable, and that is how we will feel about it in a year's time, when the game is complete. (*EDIT: I still 100% agree with this, now all the episodes are out) The issues all arise from temporary issues. (poor optimisation , always-online DRM [which unfortunately will not likely be changed] and the lacklustre business model.) (*EDIT: Which have now been mostly addressed)
TL,DR Summary: While the game isn't perfect, it is still very entertaining and a must-buy for fans of the original Hitman franchise, who enjoyed open levels with interesting NPCs and a backstory of intrigue.

6.5/10 - The artwork and most of the writing is great, but that can't mask the obvious problems. The game costs twice as much as other dating sims and is maybe half as polished. Not all of the problems are graphics or something that can simply be patched away, either. REALLY wanted to like this game, and still do, but genuinely disappointed. Would recommend if it goes down in price, goes through bug patches, but I don't think the issues with the writing will ever get resolved.
PROS:
- clean, fun User Interface with beautiful colours
- really cool character designs
- retains good sense of humour while also being heartfelt and engaging
- great soundtrack
- intersperses mini-games and such throughout the otherwise classic visual novel/choose your own adventure dating sim style
- decently robust character creation options
- flexibility in dating options, characters breaking out of cliche tropes
- enough realism with what characters are struggling with to get emotionally attached
CONS:
- visual glitches (character sprites jumping in and out of frame with bad timing)
- HUGE audio balancing issues (some character voices are incredibly loud, especially Goth Dad, while others are too quiet)
- virtually non-existent options menu (can't change audio balance, can't resize window after starting up program) that can't be accessed unless to save and quit to main menu
- can't easily have 2 characters going at the same time, save file system sucks compared to the majority of other dating sims
- minor text/dialogue discrepancies (game not remembering choices you made/saying the exact opposite of choices you made, improperly describing sprites or objects displayed on screen, like when a character is holding a wine glass when they're supposed to be drinking whiskey)
- very little choice in MC's personality (just get used to being awkward, sarcastic, and mildly trendy), which especially comes through when non-dateable characters (particularly women) are being portrayed as horny, aggressive harpies that the main (gay) characters have to fend off (awkwardly hostile to bisexuality, which doubled down when the game forgot that I had chosen to have a dead wife rather than a dead husband...) Honestly, not as friendly or inclusive as people are going to brag about.
- character sprites never change outfit, and you can't/don't change your own outfit, which starts to feel weird if you or NPCs are e.g. wearing a graphic tshirt to a formal affair
- really no way to tell if you're choosing the "right" answer in some cases. too many multiple-choice paths rely on inside jokes and niche humour that don't come across as strong as they should be. Written in a way where you can tell all writers involved genuinely felt they were in-tune with pop culture and modern slang and whatnot, even though that's not the case. Expected of a game about dorky out of touch dads, but still frustrating.
- Kind of ridiculous when characters who look under 30 & like they popped out of a fashion catalogue complain about being old and out of touch with their kids, but also talk to each other over social media using millennial-speak.
- my dadsona's forehead is heckin' huge, and you're either a twink, bear, or jacked to all hell (and choosing "jacked to all hell" makes it contradictory since your character eats sweets and junk food 24/7 and complains to his college buddy about how out of shape he is)

Pool Nation resides in a niche genre that anyone interested knows generally what to expect. Like most people, I'm mainly concerned with a pool game feeling right. That means there must be a finely tuned physics engine in place to mimic physical actions and reactions, whether it be a simple or advanced system. Pool Nation absolutely meets this requirement and then some. It provide the player with a very nicely crafted physics system to experience billiards virtually. Of course, the actual game trumps experiencing it virtually, but the imitation is overall convincing and worthwhile. Not only is the core game well constructed, but the development team made sure to provide the extras that keeps players interested. It's definitely worth the buy if you're looking for a solid pool game, especially considering its fair sale price.

Micro-management hell. I get it is in development, great, this is a review of the early access. Nothing is well explained. Really this game should have a step by step guide/tutorial, like a 'demo' scenario from the main game where it starts with a fresh base and guides you through every single function & feature of the game. It's simply too much to take in, it reminds me a tad of Kerbal Space Program. I see how it appeals to people, but the general populace of players who enjoy survival games like Don't Starve, this is NOT for you. It's insane how complex it is, the entire game is built around "Logic Gates" for multiple things. Electricians should have a blast with this (I'm serious) as it is essentially you creating multiple pathways for multiple currents that can't cross or interchange. I can see why a lot of people disliked the Germs update, you're already battling hunger, oxygen and a need for expansion, all the sudden you're suffering from germ infested oxygen, your people are going to the bathroom on themselves for no reason instead of using the bathroom which just floods everywhere for ever and ever... it's a nightmare. This is not a game you 'recover' from mistakes either, the game IS a learning curve. So everytime I start a new game, I'll get a little further, realize a design flaw I had and that's that, time to start a new game, there is no going back and changing it, resources are very very limited and any major investment that doesn't pan out basically means you're done. I wish I had more positive notes here, but really it's not easy. The art style is fun, just like don't starve. The UI is mostly intuitive but different types of gas and germs should be more visually represented, you have to constantly switch through visual filters to really see whats going on. You spend as much time trying to figure out what you need to do as you do actually doing it. This is a game for 'planners', people who enjoy spending as much time if not more planning on how they're going to do a thing as they are going to spend actually doing it. Honestly, I'm really disappointed. I was hoping for more of a Don't Starve in space game, if I could I would return this but I'm out of the return policy period on Steam. Even on discount, this wasn't worth. I'll probably dump a few more hours into it just to not feel like buying it was a total waste but after that, it'll get uninstalled and forgotten about forever more. It has no enjoyable hook for me and certainly no long term fun factor. It is novel at best and tedium personified at worst. Where as Don't Starve made the complex/tedious aspects of out door survival simplified so you could focus on the exploration and basic aspects of survival, ONI does the exact opposite and force feeds you every single annoying aspects and nuanced hardship. Everything needs to be designed (Air flow network, liquid management networks, etc), nothing is plug and play in that you can't just drop some venting or such, you have to lay ductwork, build in fan systems and put vents on them, blah blah blah and everything you build has to be maintained and reloaded with dwindling resources, it's a zero sum game. Overall, ONI wants to be good, but the developers are WAY too focused on making this a hardcore in depth full space colony building sim as opposed to something... well, fun. The game wants to be Sim City but tries to make it 3 times harder and more complex, fun for some, but I can't imagine this will experience anywhere near the success as Don't Starve, it's more work than play.
The art, the Sounds, There's nothing not to like, if you enjoy creating/designing/solving problems, this game is for you !

As a veteran Hitman fan, I would like to share my experience with you about the pro's and con's of this game.
Pro's:
Visually striking, looks very nice environmentally.
High replayability value, considering the episodic format of this game, includes many challenges, assassinations etc.
Character models and motion capture seem much better than in previous games.
Plays and feels much like Hitman Bloodmoney, more open non linear level design with the ability to stage accidents.
Con's:
Always online DRM for a single player game like Hitman is just nonsense.
Frequent disconnections from Square Enix poorly optimized servers, made the game unplayable for the first few weeks of release, however I have seen improvement, as not experienced any disconnections within the last few days.
If connection to the server fails and you are playing, you are forced back to the title menu, where you will lose all progress within that session, unless you manually save.
I have experienced random crashing of the game while playing, just randomly crashes to desktop displaying Hitman has stopped working. Using latest Nvidia game ready drivers, MSI GTX 970 4G, Windows 10 Pro X64, 16gb DDR3 Ram, 250GB SSD for System, 1TB Western Digital 7200RPM for steam games, 2TB Western Digital Green for Storage.
Feel melee combat is not upto standard, as other enemies can hear you and you are quickly compromised, unable to have a choice of silently dispatching an enemy who enters into melee combat with you or instantly killing them as an option would be nice.
The way it works at the moment is you just enter into a melee animation, similar to Hitman Absolution, however you perform an awesome melee takedown animation, yet still have to press a button to knock them out? Which kind of makes the melee takedown animation pretty pointless in my opinion.
Dissapointed with lack of other animations and features not included in this game, which were fundamental aspects of previous Hitman games, such as; ability to take human shields, customization of all weaponary with the ability to add scopes and upgrade ammunition types.
No safehouse / Hideout with shooting range to show off your aquired weaponary from previous levels.
No Professional difficulty or other difficulty levels for that matter, which were present in Hitman Bloodmoney and what hardcore fans of this franshise truly miss.
Still awaiting the elusive contracts, which has been delayed.
Episodic formula does not bother me, however the time between releases of these episodes does. Almost 2 months wait for Episode 2: Sapienza?
The game feels like I am testing a BETA, Episode 1 has been buggy, such as; random crashes, frame rate drops, very poor servers which constantly go down and force me to restart a session over and over. I feel the episodic format was introduced due to the possibility of the game been largely unfinished before release?
Always online DRM is really killing this franshise, as Hitman has always been a singleplayer game, the only need for online connectivity, should be for contracts mode and to receive updates and new challenges IMO.
The way this works at the moment is that you are getting locked out of been able to complete challenges offline, and also the ability to use unlocked weaponary offline. The game feels very limited in offline mode and is hugely crippled by this always online DRM.
I just hope IOI are listening to these reviews and to the surveys they handed out recently to help fix these problems and turn this into a game of the year contender.
My suggestion is wait until episode 2 releases and also wait for IOI to patch the game, essentially wait and see if they have listened to their customers and fans who purchased this game via the recent surveys.
I would be happy if they released a patch to disable always online DRM and enable challenges and unlocked weaponary, elusive contracts and escalations in offline mode. I do not care for competitive leaderboards for a singleplayer game.

It's a good game if you're looking for a hitman experience.  However, it's super short, I mean 2 hours and you pretty much used up your $15's worth.
The AI - I wish there was a neutral rating because the AI is definitely buggy and a step back from the previous installments.  People who notice you will lock on to you no matter what (through walls and stuff) but the easiest way to avoid that is to just run which in previous games would have raised even more suspicion if you ran the moment they looked at you.
Controls - it sucks so much for pc because it obviously was designed as a console first and pc second.  I quickly got used to them after a few changes but it just shows how much quality they sacrificed just to get us to shell out some money for an incomplete game.
Missions - it's really just 1 mission for 15 bucks, the 2 tutorial missions isn't that fun since they're both super easy with disguises/methods literally just laid out for you.  The mission provided has a ton of people around, so it's fun for the silent killers with so many eyes and it's fun when you just want to go psycho.
The good - there are a ton of new ways to kill someone and they definitely spent a lot of time to come up with all these various methods of kills.  They also removed all those scripted events from Absolution and it's more sandbox now.  I have no idea why game developers back then all thought we liked super linear games like Max Payne 3 (which kind of killed that franchise for me).  I'm glad they went back to the original sandbox gameplay, it was like when JC Penny decided to never have "sales" anymore and the company declared bankrupcy shortly afterwards since the CEO obviously didn't know crap about the business.
Performance - really poorly optimized, I have SLI gtx 980's and it runs noticibly like crap with everything turned up.  I know that the game is designed for ATI graphic cards but 2 top of the line NVIDIA's should handle this game with everything on max.  I ran the game on a 4k monitor and had to use medium settings to play properly.
Overall - this game is definitely rushed.  I wasn't so anxious for a hitman game that I couldn't wait for a full release vs. a 1 level beta.  Bad AI, people/things falling through floors, obviously the business execs were desperate for some cash and didn't care about quality of the game at all.  I mean, I probably would still buy the next episode since being a hitman is fun but it's getting real close for me to just give up on this franchise completely.
TLDR - Unfortunately, great games like Dragon Age, Hitman, Mass Effect are all falling into the hands of executives looking to get rich quick and they don't care how badly they kill the Franchise.  At least they didn't just copy and paste levels like Dragon Age 2.  I hope that nobody is going to mess up Dishonored 2, hitman 6 is probably going to be fun next year when it's out of beta but I probably would have moved on by then.

The Cold War was a state of geopolitical tension after World War II between powers in the Eastern Bloc (the Soviet Union and its satellite states) and powers in the Western Bloc (the United States, its NATO allies and others). Historians do not fully agree on the dates, but a common timeframe is the period between 1947, the year the Truman Doctrine (a U.S. foreign policy pledging to aid nations threatened by Soviet expansionism) was announced, and 1991, the year the Soviet Union collapsed.
The term "cold" is used because there was no large-scale fighting directly between the two sides involved in the conflict, although there were major regional wars, known as proxy wars, supported by the two sides. The Cold War split the temporary wartime alliance against Nazi Germany, leaving the Soviet Union and the United States as two superpowers with profound economic and political differences. The USSR was a Marxist–Leninist state led by its Communist Party of the Soviet Union, who in turn were led by a leader, with different titles over time, and a small committee called the Politburo. The Party controlled the press, the military, the economy and many organizations. It also controlled the other states in the Eastern Bloc, and funded Communist parties around the world, sometimes in competition with Communist China, particularly following the Sino-Soviet split of the 1960s. In opposition stood the West, staunchly democratic and capitalist with a free press and independent organizations. A small neutral bloc arose with the Non-Aligned Movement; it sought good relations with both sides. The two superpowers never engaged directly in full-scale armed combat, but they were heavily armed in preparation for a possible all-out nuclear world war. Each side had a nuclear strategy that discouraged an attack by the other side, on the basis that such an attack would lead to the total destruction of the attacker: the doctrine of mutually assured destruction (MAD). Aside from the development of the two sides' nuclear arsenals, and their deployment of conventional military forces, the struggle for dominance was expressed via proxy wars around the globe, psychological warfare, massive propaganda campaigns and espionage, rivalry at sports events, and technological competitions such as the Space Race.
The first phase of the Cold War began in the first two years after the end of the Second World War in 1945. The USSR consolidated its control over the states of the Eastern Bloc, while the United States began a strategy of global containment to challenge Soviet power, extending military and financial aid to the countries of Western Europe (for example, supporting the anti-communist side in the Greek Civil War) and creating the NATO alliance. The Berlin Blockade (1948–49) was the first major crisis of the Cold War. With the victory of the communist side in the Chinese Civil War and the outbreak of the Korean War (1950–53), the conflict expanded. The USSR and USA competed for influence in Latin America, and the decolonizing states of Africa and Asia. Meanwhile, the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was stopped by the Soviets. The expansion and escalation sparked more crises, such as the Suez Crisis (1956), the Berlin Crisis of 1961, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. Following the Cuban Missile Crisis, a new phase began that saw the Sino-Soviet split complicate relations within the communist sphere, while US allies, particularly France, demonstrated greater independence of action. The USSR crushed the 1968 Prague Spring liberalization program in Czechoslovakia, and the Vietnam War (1955–75) ended with the defeat of the US-backed Republic of Vietnam, prompting further adjustments
