I’m not a “VIDEO games” person but a “video GAMES” one. You won’t see me praising a game like Heavy Rain because of its dull gameplay mechanics, neither over-crediting it for its TV movie-quality plot, what you would read from me about Telltale’s The Walking Dead series is that they are good interactive movies, perhaps calling them good “games” would be hard for me. But this one, this one it’s a bold act of rebellion, even when the game itself is nothing impressive, it is one of those few cases where I'm inclined to recommend a game I didn't enjoyed a lot playing to.
Spec Ops: The Line should be played, it deserves to be played, at least to experience what it does well and how it was a failed but respectable attempt to make a AAA game with an actually adult narrative and distancing itself from the cheap “play this to feel more mature” trend on gaming narrative that started more or less a couple of years after the 7th generation of consoles.
The GAME
In Spec Ops: The Line you won’t find a hidden gem with terrific mechanics, in fact, the game feels like a tasteless Gears of War clone, it feels like the genre of the game was chosen just to appeal to a bigger audience, if they had developed a top-down shooter or a strategy game a la “XCOM: Enemy Unknown” they would had saved a considerable amount of money, and even been able to invest more on its gameplay and get more or less the same sales they got (roughly 1.13M according to VGChartz).
This doesn’t mean the game is horrible, in fact, It’s decent, and even good at times, it isn’t boring and it’s A.I. isn’t bad, for example, in the hardest difficulty (which is the only one I played), it also has a fresh level design which helps to bring variety to the experience, using verticality pretty more often than third and first person shooters regularly do.
So, in short, the game is not painful to play, but it isn’t also memorable gameplay-wise and you will feel no need to replay it.
The Portrait
One of the three things this game does right, and the first of them you will notice, is its environment, the ashes of Dubai are real, and not because the game is ridiculously photorealistic (which is not), but because it’s meant to communicate something, not a feeling, not a direct message, but a story, you know something more than a sandstorm happened there. The devastation and helplessness, the man-made disaster over the implacable overtaking of nature against a metropolis turning it into a no man’s land are tangible.
The designers did a good job (most of the time) trying to immerse the player by mixing the “COVER HERE PLOX” structures among the rest of the environment and they try to constantly draw the players towards what is left of the civilization to give us a break from the sand. The people designing its environment probable spent most of the time guessing: What would people do if “this” happened? The environment results believable and satisfying to watch too.
The Chant
The sound effects are decent and the voice acting accomplishes what it’s meant for. What the game does well is the music, instead of using an over the top generic film soundtrack, the game uses a soundtrack of rock music and its specter of derived genres, constantly portraying what is happening in front of you, sometimes even with some bit of irony, most of it has heavy feelings and a couple of tracks which could be considered as portraying an "angry" or "desperate" feeling, it counts with names as Nine Inch Nails, Deep Purple and Jimmy Hendrix.
The music also lets the sound effects of the sandstorms, broken glasses and guns take the main role when it’s needed. The radio signals also play an important role in the immersion and are a nice way of telling us what’s happening instead of leaving such task in its entirety to the cut-scenes.
Another interesting part related to the story is what I would consider as a "cliche" being used many, many times in games to tell us the "background" of the story, is the way of letting us get into the story by finding some intel recordings through the map, which may I say there is nothing bad with it, mostly because it's related to an already interesting story, but it's just another "checklist" type of feature, similar to its completely unnecessary multiplayer.
The Book
The story of Spec Ops: The Line is based in a classic war novel called “Hearth of Darkness” written by the Polish Author Joseph Conrad (something the writers of this game don't try to hide) and they let you know that in the first moments of the game (I highly recommend the book, ONCE you have played the game).
The story revolves around the 33rd Battalion, a combat unit sent to help Dubai’s citizens to evacuate after a series of sandstorms downplayed or ignored  by the high class and politicians of the city turned it into remnants of what it was. The 33rd was thought lost, but suddenly the US Government gets a looped message from the Colonel John Konrad about the situation of the city and the failure of its mission.
The game starts with the three-man operative from the Special Forces Delta conformed Martin Walker, John Lugo and Alphanso Adams entering to Dubai and trying to find what happened to the 33rd. The game has some twists, moral decisions, and many hard moments, it portrays war as what it is: murder, and a side trying to conquer the other, while its portrayal of the “occupation” is way lighter than how the book is based on portrays colonization, it’s very admirable to have people getting out of the safe-zone of bro-patriotic-BS found in most AAA war games, with silly “good vs. bad” plots. While it doesn’t goes deep about the political causes of a conflict, it’s a reminder of how distorted a leader’s mind can be and/or how harmful can people be by justifying their narcissistic needs by making up “the enemy” as “the evil” as an excuse for the urge to fight that “evil” which isn’t more than a result of our a need to rationalize the actions we commit or condone, probably our only scapegoat as simple mortals in one of the sides; a way of finding inner peace, perhaps full of emptiness, but enough to let us believe our own lie. First let’s take action; justification can come later as corpses can’t reply anyway. We are all heroes.
Score: 60/100.

If you've been around the internet, most likely you've already heard of this game. It's commonly praised for it's good plot, good characters, and unconventional way it looks at an RPG. Instead of telling what's already been said by others, I'll just talk about how killing is viewed here.
One of the morals in this game is that killing is wrong. Normaly this bugs the hell out of me. Telling people that they shouldn't go around murdering each other is good and all, but most things never really tell you why and just expect you to know that its bad thing to do so. This game is one of the few things that gives you a reason, and does so organicaly by how the story unfolds, but first, I'd like to talk about how this moral is treated in most things.
In most other works, you are told that murder is wrong, but then are shown the most unredeemable jerkface in existence.
They have commited countless crimes and will continue to do so if allowed to live, yet the best you should do is imprison them even though there's no real reason to keep them alive. Some of these works make things worse by having a hero that has already killed countless minions from fighting, but are then disalowed to execute the main villain because of some lame reason such as being out of revenge, hatred, or somehow "not worth it". None of these works give a compeling reason that killing is bad, and things usualy get worse because sparing the villain allows them to escape and do a bit of murdering themselves.
That is what I usualy see about this moral, and why I absolutley hate it. And then came Undertale. To explain why this moral is presented so well, I'll give a bit of my experience playing.
First off, it's plain advertised as a game where "no one has to die". It says this, but does not exactly stop you from killing things, or even murdering everything if you so please.
In most RPGs where your allowed to pick a fight with just about any NPC you can, I usualy start by going axe crazy beating up everyone. It's something you usualy can't do in games, and it's often hilarious when all the guards come and start pummeling you. I often murder everything I can just because I can in these games, and this was almost true with Undertale. It's not exactly and open world game where you can pick fights with NPCs, but killing everything you run into is still something you can do.
I had first jumped into the game thinking I'd do just that, beating up every monster that crosses my path like in every other RPG. once I met Toriel however, that quickly changed.
Toriel, as her name subtley suggest, is the tutorial character. She shows you a practice dummy to learn the basics of combat in this game. Instead of telling you to fight however, she tells you to talk to it instead. Since it was a different thing to do from other games, I chose to see what the non-violent method does.
Already this game encraged me to take the peaceful route, and let me just emphasize that it ENCOURAGED, it didn't force me, I was still able to hit the dummy if I wanted to, but I chose the other option.
Since the non-violent option is actualy the non-standard thing to do in most turn based RPGs, I found myself using it instead of fighting. When I bumped into actual monsters to fight, one of them was presented as being really weak and is "too sensitive to fight". I continued using the non-violent method.
Toriel eventualy become my first boss fight because to continue the game, I had to prove I was strong enough. This was when I first used the fight command, and I instantly regreted it when I accidentaly killed her. At first I continued and thought I'd find out how to not kill her on my next playthrough, but I felt so bad that I restarted. This game had encouraged me not to kill, and now I felt so bad that I had a reason to figure out how not to kill someone. This was enforced by the fact that in my 2nd attempt, I noticed that Toriel dosen't even have any intent on killing you, if her last hit can kill you, she stops attacking and I noticed her next attack would avoid hitting me even if I tried to run into it.
After figuring out how to spare her, Toriel's job was done, she really was the tutorial of the game, and had taught me how to play non-violently.
I went through the rest of the game with the full intent on sparing everyone I encountered instead of my initial plan of going axe crazy. And that's just the thing, I already had the INTENT to not kill. I didn't spare everyone because it's what I was supposed to do or because it's what I decided to do for the playthrough, I spared everyone because I WANTED to, and why woulden't I.
Throughout the game, the rest of the monsters were actualy pretty friendly. There was no reason to kill anyone and most bosses actualy seemed like Toriel, as in, they never really wanted to harm me. Sometimes I thought that there should of been a somewhat evil boss to make me decide if I should kill or not, but it wasen't the point of the game, or atleast not yet. By the end, it turns out there really is one of those unredeemably evil bosses. I had fully decided that it'd be the only person I'd kill, but by the time I had the choice, I ended up choosing to spare them. That boss actualy threatend to do horrible things If I let them live, but I still chose to spare them. Eventualy, they sort of made good on those threats, but at the absolute end of the game, I had learned the truth and never regreted my choice to spare that boss earlier.
By the end of the game, I was given a new view on the moral of killing.
In other works, you are told murder is bad. You are then presented a villain who you should spare, and then makes you regret having to let them live while still telling you that murder is wrong.
Here in Undertale however, you are encouraged to take a more peaceful route. You are presented with characters you wouldn't want to hurt, and are given a villain that you will be glad to have saved. Instead of telling you why killing is wrong, Undertale gives you a reason not to kill, and that alone is a reason why this game is truley great, and worth getting.

PROS:
- clean, fun User Interface with beautiful colours
- really cool character designs
- retains good sense of humour while also being heartfelt and engaging
- great soundtrack
- intersperses mini-games and such throughout the otherwise classic visual novel/choose your own adventure dating sim style
- decently robust character creation options
- flexibility in dating options, characters breaking out of cliche tropes
- enough realism with what characters are struggling with to get emotionally attached
CONS:
- visual glitches (character sprites jumping in and out of frame with bad timing)
- HUGE audio balancing issues (some character voices are incredibly loud, especially Goth Dad, while others are too quiet)
- virtually non-existent options menu (can't change audio balance, can't resize window after starting up program) that can't be accessed unless to save and quit to main menu
- can't easily have 2 characters going at the same time, save file system sucks compared to the majority of other dating sims
- minor text/dialogue discrepancies (game not remembering choices you made/saying the exact opposite of choices you made, improperly describing sprites or objects displayed on screen, like when a character is holding a wine glass when they're supposed to be drinking whiskey)
- very little choice in MC's personality (just get used to being awkward, sarcastic, and mildly trendy), which especially comes through when non-dateable characters (particularly women) are being portrayed as horny, aggressive harpies that the main (gay) characters have to fend off (awkwardly hostile to bisexuality, which doubled down when the game forgot that I had chosen to have a dead wife rather than a dead husband...) Honestly, not as friendly or inclusive as people are going to brag about.
- character sprites never change outfit, and you can't/don't change your own outfit, which starts to feel weird if you or NPCs are e.g. wearing a graphic tshirt to a formal affair
- really no way to tell if you're choosing the "right" answer in some cases. too many multiple-choice paths rely on inside jokes and niche humour that don't come across as strong as they should be. Written in a way where you can tell all writers involved genuinely felt they were in-tune with pop culture and modern slang and whatnot, even though that's not the case. Expected of a game about dorky out of touch dads, but still frustrating.
- Kind of ridiculous when characters who look under 30 & like they popped out of a fashion catalogue complain about being old and out of touch with their kids, but also talk to each other over social media using millennial-speak.
- my dadsona's forehead is heckin' huge, and you're either a twink, bear, or jacked to all hell (and choosing "jacked to all hell" makes it contradictory since your character eats sweets and junk food 24/7 and complains to his college buddy about how out of shape he is)

UPDATE: In light of comments made by the developers, I'm updating this review. My personal feelings are unchanged but the thing that ruined the game for me is something that has been fixed, as much as it can be.
I can't personally speak for the overall plot or all the dates, having only played for a short amount of time, but the bits I did see were wholesome and cute. All the dads have distinct and fun personalities, and the writing is just bursting with dad puns and jokes. It's also refreshingly diverse, allowing you to choose between having had a husband or wife, and with canonically trans and gay characters. The art style is cute, the dad customisation is fun and diverse, and the music is good.
. Each date is broken up with a minigame, which range from fun (if a little nonsensical) to frustrating (I'm looking at you, mini golf). Another complaints I've heard is that, while the ending is slightly different depending on which dad you romanced, the actual plot doesn't change beyond a few details, and it's possible when fastforwarding to skip through new lines of dialogue. The player dad is a fun and well-written character, but I feel pushes you slightly towards some dads rather than others. There's also the question of the voice acting -- 'fully voiced' here means 'various repetitive 'oh's and 'ahs'', unfortunately not always matched up well to the dialogue ('Dad!' Amanda yelled, while talking to a completely different character). The sound quality for Hugo and Damien is also pretty poor, and the voice acting in general leaves a lot to be desired. The female characters are also unfortunately written, and considering there are only two or three of them that's not a good look. If there were lots of ladies, having one be an alcoholic and neglectful mother would be fine and good and interesting! But if she makes up 50% of the female characters in the game? Less great.
This game sells itself as a cutesy gay dating sim, and in 90% of the game it delivers. But it seems to be going the way of a lot of games, adding in grimdark elements despite its genre. In four of the seven romances (and maybe more), it is possible for the player dad to die. There's one character with whom it's impossible to get a happy ending (especially upsetting, as his story could have been a really positive one rarely seen in media). And then there's the secret ending.
And this is where the update comes into play. The secret ending has been confirmed by word of god to be an unfinished Halloween DLC ending. It's not part of the game proper, and it's impossible to actually get it; the only way we even know it exists is through datamining. Hopefully this means that for new players coming to the game it won't even be an issue, so if you're wanting to play the game and unlikely to go looking for the secrets, the rest of this review hopefully won't apply. All you might want to read on for is content warnings in case you do come across things relating to the secret ending in fandom.
Of course this will be different for everyone, and that's totally valid, but for me I don't think I can go back to Dream Daddy. It's a relief to know the secret ending isn't really part of the game, and I don't want to hold LGBTQ+ games and creators to higher standards than cishet ones, but the shock of finding out about this secret ending, and the way that is tie togethers and explain a lot of the elements in the actual game, means that it's overshadowed and coloured the whole of the rest of the game for me. From my original review: It's an ending that is, frankly, unnecessarily dark and horror-orientated, and turns the rest of the game from a goofy dad dating game to something far more sinister and uncomfortable.
For anyone looking for content warnings, they're here:
.
And for anyone who, like me, got curious enough they just wanted to know what's going on:
.
Some people really like the ARG/secret-finding element, or just aren't bothered. And it's confirmed not to be part of the game, for most people won't be part of your experience. Personally, I find that for a game that marketed itself towards an LGBTQ+ and specifically gay male audience to turn around and have this kind of a grimdark twist, for nothing more than shock value, is pretty skeevy honestly. In any other dating sim I'd be all too happy to start theorising with the best of them, but this one was meant to be light and cute and gay, and instead we get this. Comparing a grimdark twist in an LGBTQ+ game to those in games targeted towards cishet audiences is to completely miss the point. And sure, if there were hundreds gay dating simulators I'd have no problem with some of them following the dark twist convention. But there aren't.
It's fine if this doesn't bother you, in fact I'm really pleased if it doesn't. I'd love to be among those people who can still enjoy the game. Just please understand that there are people for whom this has really coloured their experience, and our not being comfortable playing the game is just as valid as others' enjoyment of it.
Anyway, I'm leaving this review just so hopefully people don't get caught out if this is the kind of thing that will bother them. I am, however, updating it to be a recommendation of the game, because I hope that anyone not bothered by the whole secret ending debacle will still get and enjoy the game. It has a few flaws, sure, but overall it's exactly the cute and fun dating sim it marketed itself to be. And it's an all-too-rare LGBTQ+ game marketed towards non-cishet people, which is why I'm really glad to be able to recommend it.

It was a fun game initially (although work management/priority system was a mess, and still is), but new mechanics proved to be a burden, so it's even less fun, and still bugged & messy with its algorithms. You start building a colony and it's fun and cute for a couple hours, but then the messiness starts to pile up and nothing gets done without your constant micromanagement, which leads to frustration, and you think, why did I even buy this. So if you don't want that, then don't buy.
Guess I'll list some points.
+ visual style, everything's cute and steampunk-y.
+ fun to toy with your growing colony for some (rather short) amount of time.
- priorities don't mean anything, it's either at 9 aka "do it right now" or anything <9 "never gets done". At first, when you don't have a lot of stuff going on, normal priorities do work, but after a while you just have to control everything yourself, and eventually you can't, and everything starts to break down.
- the more the devs add, the more complicated and frustrating it gets, similar to Rimworld which was a very fun and simple game at first but then grew into too convoluted, with miserable non-healthy addicts everywhere.
- a lot of stuff is still just broken and weird. Such as liquids mechanics, gas/pressure mechanics, or duplicant behaviour.
Overall... some stuff will get fixed (let's hope so), but I'm convinced that it'll also just become too complicated and un-simple to be fun.

Death is a great teacher. Failure in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is, as it always has been for this series, the greatest way to learn where you should have gone, what you shouldn't have done, and how you could have done better. Counter-Strike players spend a lot of time learning -- consequently, they are always getting better.
Growth is an important factor in Global Offensive, especially if you're coming into Counter-Strike fresh or after a sabbatical. This is an extremely hardcore, skill-based first-person shooter, and it forces you to think differently than other modern shooters. If you’re a Call of Duty player, you’re going to need to change your play style to succeed here. Counter-Strike also tries developing into something new here as well, despite doing little to push itself beyond what it’s always done best. Global Offensive modifies old maps to keep veterans on their toes, and introduces official new modes that encourage different play styles for the first time in almost 15 years.
Video Review

4:36
For the uninitiated, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a small-scale, team-based first-person shooter with permanent death. When a counter-terrorist kills a terrorist planting explosives in a classic Defusal match, or a CT escort swallows a sniper round in Hostage Rescue, the victim is dead for good and doesn't respawn until the next round. As such, players on both sides must exercise skill and care. The bomb objective, meanwhile, gives everyone a purpose. Of course matches end when everyone on a team is dead, but a clever and coordinated terrorist team will give the CTs the slip, plant their bomb, and protect the bomb site. Between rounds, everyone spends earned cash on better gear and guns, and the cycle continues.
Pieces of the Counter-Strike formula are dated at this point, but the superb heart and soul of Global Offensive is timeless. Teams are small, guns are lethal, and rounds are short. There's an addictive just-one-more-round quality to it, because there's a constant desire to do better than last time, to earn a satisfying kill, or to win in a new way. Call of Duty and Battlefield vets will wonder why they can't sprint to escape enemy fire or look down the iron sights to improve aim; Counter-Strike players will feel like they walked into their redecorated home. Certain map redesigns will catch hardcore fans off guard, but the changes are for the best -- the underpass choke point in de_dust, for instance, has a new escape route.
Even in the face of genre evolution, Global Offensive doesn’t care to adapt. CSGO is so dedicated to Counter-Strike's aging ideals despite market and trend changes that it brute-forces its way to success. Part of what makes it such an engaging competitive game is that killing in Global Offensive requires a wholly different skill set than other shooters. Everyone is limited to what they have and can see, with little room for character modification or on-the-fly advantages. Running and gunning is a useless play style, even if you've bought a helmet and kevlar that round, to the point that someone standing still is more likely to score the kill. Walking, crouching, or standing are your best bets to reduce the inaccurate spray of machine-gun fire.

Consequently, killing in Global Offensive feels good. There's a sickening sensation to dropping someone dead because you know they're not coming back. It's also satisfying knowing you used limited resources to play smarter than your victim. If players aren't watching corners, providing covering fire, or using smoke grenades and flashbangs, they're more likely to take a headshot from a more delicate and patient triggerman. The desire to experience that distinct feeling is a strong motivator to keep playing, even when you're getting steamrolled by an obviously better team.
If you've played Counter-Strike before, Global Offensive probably sounds a whole lot like Counter-Strike. Like Counter-Strike: Source before it, Global Offensive exists simply to modernize the look of the classic competitive shooter, while doing little to disrupt the core form and function. At the same time, it does enough to color outside the lines of tradition to justify your time and effort.Fire is one of the most interesting new combat variables. Molotov cocktails and incendiary grenades either roast groups of guys or force them in another direction. Flames are a useful distraction or scare tactic, too. They're particularly useful during Demolition matches, which focus the fight at a single bomb site rather than giving terrorists two to pick between. The new and modified maps in this mode aren't as big as classic Counter-Strike arenas – entire sections have been cut off to direct teams toward a central location – but their thoughtful design is as intricate as ever. The Lake map is a standout -- there's a wide open yet densely populated yard around the bomb site, which is inside a sizable lakeside home with plenty of vantage points and hiding spots. To separate Demolition from Defusal, players can't buy between rounds. Instead, it takes a cue from the other new mode, Arms Race, in which each kill unlocks another weapon instantly. The better you do, the more you have to switch up the way you play, and because Demolition is so fast you'll need to be quick on your feet.Unlike other game types, Arms Race allows for respawns. It's the most chaotic and care-free mode in Global Offensive, with players throwing caution to the wind for the sake of climbing the kill ladder as quickly as possible. It's a shame there are only two maps in Arms Race -- a problem that will more likely persist on consoles than PC.
If you have the option, playing the PC version is unquestionably the best way to experience Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. Mods, mouse and keyboard, and the usual PC-only options are better than the ports. Plus, Valve is much better about long-term PC support -- it abandoned Team Fortress 2 on consoles, and Portal 2's level editor was PC exclusive. If you prefer to play on consoles, Global Offensive is the same great game, with the following special bits:
PlayStation 3
For those who want to play on PlayStation 3 but don’t want to deal with the imprecision of analog sticks, Counter-Strike: GO supports mouse and keyboard, giving it a pretty noticeable edge over the Xbox 360 version. If you’re feeling saucy, Move is another option, although nuance dies with the motion controller. Move is accurate, and your quick reflexes will score kills, but the unavoidable instability of holding a remote will give your cursor some seriously unpleasant wobble. Worse, moving the wand quickly can confuse the controller, which often and irritatingly misinterprets basic left/right looks as a want to turn around 180 degrees.
Xbox 360
Aside from the lack of keyboard/mouse input, the Xbox 360 version of Global Offensive is functionally identical to that on PS3 -- the new radial user-interface on both platforms is as elegant as it is on PC. Because it’s a hardcore competitive game, Counter-Strike blocks party chat in an effort to combat cheating, forcing players with headsets to play with friends or brave the Wild West of obscenity that is Xbox Live.
The Verdict
Global Offensive is definitely a Counter-Strike sequel -- it looks and feels familiar, with minor tweaks here and there to help balance old issues and surprise longtime players. This is a demanding, skill-based multiplayer game that's as satisfying now as it ever was, but it's for a specific kind of player. If you're not willing to learn to play different than you're used to, look elsewhere. Otherwise, this is a top-tier tactics game that will probably share the long-tailed legacy of its predecessors.

As a veteran Hitman fan, I would like to share my experience with you about the pro's and con's of this game.
Pro's:
Visually striking, looks very nice environmentally.
High replayability value, considering the episodic format of this game, includes many challenges, assassinations etc.
Character models and motion capture seem much better than in previous games.
Plays and feels much like Hitman Bloodmoney, more open non linear level design with the ability to stage accidents.
Con's:
Always online DRM for a single player game like Hitman is just nonsense.
Frequent disconnections from Square Enix poorly optimized servers, made the game unplayable for the first few weeks of release, however I have seen improvement, as not experienced any disconnections within the last few days.
If connection to the server fails and you are playing, you are forced back to the title menu, where you will lose all progress within that session, unless you manually save.
I have experienced random crashing of the game while playing, just randomly crashes to desktop displaying Hitman has stopped working. Using latest Nvidia game ready drivers, MSI GTX 970 4G, Windows 10 Pro X64, 16gb DDR3 Ram, 250GB SSD for System, 1TB Western Digital 7200RPM for steam games, 2TB Western Digital Green for Storage.
Feel melee combat is not upto standard, as other enemies can hear you and you are quickly compromised, unable to have a choice of silently dispatching an enemy who enters into melee combat with you or instantly killing them as an option would be nice.
The way it works at the moment is you just enter into a melee animation, similar to Hitman Absolution, however you perform an awesome melee takedown animation, yet still have to press a button to knock them out? Which kind of makes the melee takedown animation pretty pointless in my opinion.
Dissapointed with lack of other animations and features not included in this game, which were fundamental aspects of previous Hitman games, such as; ability to take human shields, customization of all weaponary with the ability to add scopes and upgrade ammunition types.
No safehouse / Hideout with shooting range to show off your aquired weaponary from previous levels.
No Professional difficulty or other difficulty levels for that matter, which were present in Hitman Bloodmoney and what hardcore fans of this franshise truly miss.
Still awaiting the elusive contracts, which has been delayed.
Episodic formula does not bother me, however the time between releases of these episodes does. Almost 2 months wait for Episode 2: Sapienza?
The game feels like I am testing a BETA, Episode 1 has been buggy, such as; random crashes, frame rate drops, very poor servers which constantly go down and force me to restart a session over and over. I feel the episodic format was introduced due to the possibility of the game been largely unfinished before release?
Always online DRM is really killing this franshise, as Hitman has always been a singleplayer game, the only need for online connectivity, should be for contracts mode and to receive updates and new challenges IMO.
The way this works at the moment is that you are getting locked out of been able to complete challenges offline, and also the ability to use unlocked weaponary offline. The game feels very limited in offline mode and is hugely crippled by this always online DRM.

It's a good game if you're looking for a hitman experience.  However, it's super short, I mean 2 hours and you pretty much used up your $15's worth.
The AI - I wish there was a neutral rating because the AI is definitely buggy and a step back from the previous installments.  People who notice you will lock on to you no matter what (through walls and stuff) but the easiest way to avoid that is to just run which in previous games would have raised even more suspicion if you ran the moment they looked at you.
Controls - it sucks so much for pc because it obviously was designed as a console first and pc second.  I quickly got used to them after a few changes but it just shows how much quality they sacrificed just to get us to shell out some money for an incomplete game.
Missions - it's really just 1 mission for 15 bucks, the 2 tutorial missions isn't that fun since they're both super easy with disguises/methods literally just laid out for you.  The mission provided has a ton of people around, so it's fun for the silent killers with so many eyes and it's fun when you just want to go psycho.
The good - there are a ton of new ways to kill someone and they definitely spent a lot of time to come up with all these various methods of kills.  They also removed all those scripted events from Absolution and it's more sandbox now.  I have no idea why game developers back then all thought we liked super linear games like Max Payne 3 (which kind of killed that franchise for me).  I'm glad they went back to the original sandbox gameplay, it was like when JC Penny decided to never have "sales" anymore and the company declared bankrupcy shortly afterwards since the CEO obviously didn't know crap about the business.
Performance - really poorly optimized, I have SLI gtx 980's and it runs noticibly like crap with everything turned up.  I know that the game is designed for ATI graphic cards but 2 top of the line NVIDIA's should handle this game with everything on max.  I ran the game on a 4k monitor and had to use medium settings to play properly.
Overall - this game is definitely rushed.  I wasn't so anxious for a hitman game that I couldn't wait for a full release vs. a 1 level beta.  Bad AI, people/things falling through floors, obviously the business execs were desperate for some cash and didn't care about quality of the game at all.  I mean, I probably would still buy the next episode since being a hitman is fun but it's getting real close for me to just give up on this franchise completely.
TLDR - Unfortunately, great games like Dragon Age, Hitman, Mass Effect are all falling into the hands of executives looking to get rich quick and they don't care how badly they kill the Franchise.  At least they didn't just copy and paste levels like Dragon Age 2.  I hope that nobody is going to mess up Dishonored 2, hitman 6 is probably going to be fun next year when it's out of beta but I probably would have moved on by then.

This game is really interesting to me. Usually people like games similar to GTA or Need For Speed, which I do like as well, but I also like simulators, like this one. They can really teach you how a lot of the things work, and how to properly drive, check your mirrors, etc.. The tasks are pretty simple. Choose a quick job, drive from point A to B. Along the way you may run crash, run out of fuel, or you may just end up with a traffic ticket. You are able to create your own company, but you don't really have the necessary funds from the beginning of the game in order to buy a truck, a garage, or hire workers. So in all reality, you have to grind out all of the quick jobs in order to even get to that point. Time consuming, sure, but along the way it becomes a second nature to you.
Customization for trucks is great. I believe there are paint job DLCs, which I find to be really nice! Makes your truck stand out from the others and be something unique. You can change basically anything on your truck, from the engine to the transmission, and even the cosmetic stuff, like mirrors, wheels, and much more. Lots of reputable truck manufactuers are present in the game, such as Scania, Volvo, Mercedes-Benz, and many others. The choices are great. Trailers have a good amount of variety as well, and there are a lot of weight differences in them as well.. which is very important.
I would honestly give this game a 8/10. Since it's a huge open world game, a lot of the cities look very similar. I'm sure it's necessary to due that to make it run smoothly and to keep everything working properly. I'm really excited and interested to see what else will be added to this game.. I'd also like to add that the creators of ETS2 are going to release American Truck Simulator next month (at the time this is being written) so that is also something else to keep an eye out for.

Disclaimer: I am a mild Batman geek, so my knowledge on the subject isn't wonderful. I do, however, own and have beaten Arkham Asylum and Arkham City multiple times. As well, spoilers from the entire Arkham franchise may be included, beware.
First off, I do not meet the minimum system requirements for this game, nor for any of its predecessors. They ran well, and as this game shares the same engine as Arkham City, I thought that it would work. I assure that it does, and I'm very satisfied with my experience thus far. The story is very well done, besting Arkham Asylum's, but not Arkham City's. There are numerous twists and turns that I didn't expect, and I was constantly excited to press on through the game. The boss fights as a whole are refreshing, although some of them, like the Firefly boss fight, are somewhat rehashes of fights from the other two games, in this case the Arkham City Clayface boss fight. One of the highest points of the game for me, though, is the open-environment of a complete Gotham City. The game keeps you travelling from one end of the city to the next, and although you can "fast-travel" with the Batwing, I prefer to commute manually. I really don't have any thoughts on the multiplayer, as I do not plan on trying it out because I have no interest in it.
My biggest problem with the game (albeit a minute one) is that I can, in some cases, blatantly tell that the series changed developers. The music, while fantastic, has a different style to it, for one thing. Further, there are numerous aesthetic changes, such as making Gordon look more like Gary Oldman, and less like a younger version of him compared to Arkham Asylum. I could go on, but this really does not hinder the game all that much.
In some ways, in which I will not elaborate on due to extreme spoilers, this could be a standalone game outside of the franchise altogether, due to unparalleled events between the three games. However, this game is without a doubt on par with the outstanding quality of the last two games.
I was fortunate enough to have bought this game for only $24.99 due to the 2013 Holiday Sale Daily Deal, but with the experience that I have had thus far, I would've gladly payed full price. I plan on purchasing the season pass.  Absolutely recommended,

Apocalypse Now:  Dubai
The combat is solid enough, controls are slightly strange but entirely passable.   I'm not personally a fan of games on rails but this one is a decent roller coaster ride that makes the rails a bit more acceptable for me.
Enemies react to being shot in limbs appropriately and shotguns feel great, which is honestly a rarity in games.
The game gives a lot of forced prompts for commands and actions you have to or are only capable of doing at those moments which is strange and irritating.  The giant flashing prompts on the screen forcing your hand really take you out of the immersion of the story, which could be pretty good if the prompts didn't reinforce an arcade shooter feel.  The cover system is done fairly well, although i found myself fighting with the controls in many instances because it's just a few slight changes from what standard shooters bring you to expect.
I have run into some instances where invisible barriers would block my shots and they threw in the generic heavily armored (Commonly known as bulldozer) type unit who can be frustrating to an extreme when most enemies react appropriately, a sticky grenade or an RPG on his facemask will do little more than break the mask off and stun him.  The bare face of his still requires significant amounts of shots to kill him with any weapon despite being unarmored which means damage is based on body parts and not types of armored cover.  In a shooter, this can be pretty irritating but expected from the lazier ones, so it might not bother other people as much.
Ammo can be quite scarce for you and you alone as your team mates have unlimited ammo, dreadful aim, and unlimited grenades but can only be used in designated situations or of their own personal choosing.  They also pick their own cover in your general area which can occasionally put them on the wrong side of it, forcing your hand to go save them in the open during a bad enough situation to get them downed.
I haven't tried the Multiplayer or Co-Op yet so I can't comment on those.
Combat  7/10
Story      7/10
Controls 6/10
Visuals   7/10
Docking score for the excessive HUD prompts and the heavily armored Bulldozer unit because those are just lazy, especially considering the environment.
I'd have to give the game a 6/10 overall
The game is good for a few bucks, I would recommend it if you can catch it on a decent sale.

Hoping for a sweet, fun dating simulator where you can date hot single dads? You might get that! Or you might get a psychological horror game that promotes domestic abuse and cheating!
Dream Daddy: A Dad Dating simulator is, at first glance, a funny and sweet game. But be careful, you might accidentally die by falling off a waterfall or backflipping into a table or a number of other things! Thats right, there's at least ONE death per route! So long as you stick to the good options for the good daddies the game wants you to date, you'll find an enjoyable experience that's pretty short lived.
But where does the psychological horror and domestic abuse and cheating come into play, you might ask. Look no further than one of the poster boys, Joseph!
Joseph is kind and fun youth pastor with four children and a wife named Mary. Mary is an alcoholic who neglets her children and cheats on her husband. If you play through Joseph's route, you get one of three endings. Two of which he stays in an abusive relationship with Mary. The third one is a hidden ending where this ravishing young pastor who loves children, Jesus, wicked dance moves, sailing and margaritaville is actually a cult leader/demonic entity! Yep, you read that right! And apparently he feasts off the other dads energy and miiiiiight have also killed their wives or forced a divorce!
In all seriousness, the game was pretty good up until I played through Joseph's route. I got the 'good' ending where he stays with his wife, but continues to have an affair with the Main Character. This game really screwed over his character and gives a message saying "hey, if you're in an abusive relationship with someone you should stay with them" or, if on the very so rare chance you get the secret ending "never trust anyone because if you do they'll betray you! See this guy you thought was a nice religious figure coming to terms with his sexuality? PSYCH! He's a demon feeding off your and your friends souls :D"
ASIDE from Joseph, the other characters routes were funny and endearing. The art was so so lovely and the moments with them were sweet as well as the main storyline with your daughter. I teared up a bit, for sure. However, it's a pretty short game. If you were to straight up do one character's route, not dating any of the others, it's about an hour or more. And if you skip past the main story points where who you date doesnt matter, it's maybe 30 minutes. Overall the game is about 7 hours total if you don't reread all the main story parts (like helping Amanda with her friend-crisis).
TL;DR
ART STYLE- 5/5
Beautiful and diverse characters with simple, but nice backgrounds.
MUSIC- 4/5
A little too loud but otherwise amazing original music that really fit the tone.
CHARACTERS- 3/5
All of the characters were extremely well written, though some of them were either not so great or straight up terrible towards the end (mostly Joseph in his own route and other dads in routes that weren't their own)
STORY- 2/5
There are really only 4 scenes with each dad after their introduction. 3 dates that get progressively more romantic, and then an end scene. Most characters have 2 ends, a good one and a bad one, with a few exceptions. The first 3 scenes are incredibly sweet and really show off the characters. The endings are usually getting dumped or being asked to wait until things get better, which is ok but there wasn't really a super happy ending- at least not as far as I got. The main story which is mostly helping your daughter is pretty sweet and realistic, but very short. Overall, there's not much of a story so much as 4 scenes pasted on top of a thinly written semi-story.
I wish there was another option other than Yes, i recommend this game and No, i do not recommend this game. Some parts of it were really great! But Joseph's character and route really got to me and disturbed me. I believe the game would have been much better if his happy ending was "Hey, i'm going to get a divorce with Mary. Can you wait for me and be there for me while this goes through?" because you should never stay in an unhealthy relationship.
So no, I wouldn't recommend this game unless you don't care about ever doing Joseph's routes. And, if that is the case, I wouldn't recommend buying it for $15. On sale, maybe.
(My reasoning for that, even if you dont wanna play joseph's route, is that it's pretty short, even more so without completing all the routes)

Just to mention since a lot of the negative reviews seem to be based in expectations not met for this game I feel I should mention:
-This is a dating sim. If you don't like dating sims, you won't like this game.
-This game is PRODUCED by Game Grumps. This means they funded and helped out with it as you can see in the credits. Don't expect its humor or writing to be exactly like Game Grumps when it's not a game based in their writing.
-This game is a visual novel. If you don't like reading, you won't like this game.
-This game features "partial voice acting". This means it has flavor voice clips and is not fully narrated or acted. I agree that just calling it voice acted is misleading.
On to the actual review.
I've played a lot of dating sim and visual novel games and I'm very pleased with this one! Your decisions matter in reasonable but not blatantly obvious ways and the characters are very charmingly written. I'd say the only routes I didn't care much for were Craig and Joseph's. Craig's felt plain and Joseph's... Well, it was realistic but it still spoiled the fun. As for the rest, many of them have very heartfelt moments in them, a fun sense of humor, and some very human flaws and quirks for the characters. Even Damien, who starts off looking like a joke character, ends up showing a very relatable side of himself in his storyline. And like most of the positive reviews mention, your relationship with your daughter is well fleshed out and very sweet. You end up caring about her, which is pretty much vital if you're going to make being a parent the theme of your game. The art was gorgeous and there were nice little touches to each environment to make them feel lively, especially the characters' homes. It's hard to talk about the story writing without spoiling anything so I'll just mention all of the characters have more to them than what you assume when you first meet them and it's fun to get to know more about them.
For negatives, there are a few. The game has a couple of audio problems. One voice actor's microphone was clearly not as good as the others and it shows, especially since for some reason his character speaks much louder than any other character. It would be nice to see Hugo's volume adjusted in a future update. There are a couple of moments where it feels a little cheap that they reused a background without editting it even while stating something completely contrary to the art (such as pointing out the night sky in a clearly daytime backdrop, or mentioning it's almost sundown in a background that shows it's already night time). And my last criticism has to do with the medium itself. Dating Sims often feature a CG (in this game, they've decided to call them pin-ups) for each important event in the story. So I was very disappointed that they only made one for each Dad and they only show after the credits. Some of them are much higher quality than a CG usually would be, so I would find this forgiveable if they were all that way. But two of them aren't even shaded, as they are done by a variety of different artists. It's very inconsistent and disappointing, especially since I got what I consider the highest quality ones (Brian's and Robert's) first only to later end up with what felt like pictures that weren't even complete. I hope if this team does future projects, they'll include more CGs in their games.
TLDR: I like dating games. This dating game had A+ to B+ writing and A+ sprites and A+ to C art. If they make another dating game (or any visual novel) I'll probably buy it.

Early Access Review - Written during the Automation update
==========================================
As an early access game Oxygen Not Included is an excellent example of how many developers should treat open Beta.  The game has a solid core concept and runs well on it's own, with a clear area to report bugs when encountered.  The splash screen even has a countdown to the next developer update, keeping an air of transparency about how often they expect to speak about the build process and what they learn from players.
So, how is gameplay?
The level of complexity and depth in the game's core concepts is cleverly softened/made palatable by the amusing and well executed cartoon artstyle of game sprites.  The game also does not work to hasten your colony's demise in sudden and unexpected events... rather, as a player, you see doom creeping closer and closer as you piece together what you did wrong long term and then seek new ways to correct your mistakes.  The game lets you make mistakes and gives you a satisfying feeling of bounce back that I sincerely hope will be preserved as more features are added.
Resource management is a huge aspect of things, but do not expect to be carefully counting what you have just to push a bit forward.  Most objects are built using resources that begin quite abundant, with the option to build those same items with new materials later on for bonuses that may or may not turn the tide.
The sidescroller view does create some artificial roadblocks on how you build, but the ability to watch things unfold as if you are watching a digital artfarm makes it all worth the limitation.
Who would like this game?  Fans of SimCity that want to avoid the inescapable downward spiral so many games can get stuck in.  Anyone that likes the growing genre of "engineering puzzle" games such as Mini Metro and PolyBridge.
Who may want to avoid?  Anyone that needs a structured "level" mechanic (there is no master plotline, at least not yet.  Just implied lore.), anyone that dislikes learning by trial and error, if you disliked Minecraft because it's "just building with blocks".
Personally I love what I am playing and look forward to watching this game develop and change.

I'm only 20 hours in, but I can tell already that I'll be playing many, many more.  I enjoy complexity in a game, especially with plenty of opportunity to tweak and optimize my creations/world.
If you've "one more block"ed in Minecraft or "one more tweak"ed in Factorio and you like complexity, buy this game.

Ancient Space is a something, that could be called "2.5D close quarters space strategy".  Maps are split into sectors linked by warp gates and sectors are again split into multiple, well, for a lack of a better word, areas. It is possible to build structures only in those areas and only at limited locations (typically 2-3 per area, less or more possible). You tend to adopt a "attack and build strategy", attacking the next area, building up its defences (structures also help to extend your population cap). This gives the game a relatively leasurely pace, where you usually have time to plan on you next move. Add active pause and you get the deal. This is general flow broken up by some timed missions, where rushing past an area is important. In general, building is only ever to support your fleet. Your carrier(s) are the actual center of the game.
If you are into such games, you will like Ancient Space.
Your ships have special abilities with a cooldown and using them at the right point (note again: active pause) against the right parts of the enemy armada is quite important.
Pro:
- closed quarter strategy
- takes a more slow approach (minus those missions when it doesn't), but there are still pitched battles.
- graphics are decent, the space backdrops and missions are nice.
Cons:
- The multi-sector approach takes getting used to, especially on those missions where your fleet needs to be split between sectors.
- The micromanagement is limited to use of abilties. The rest is more or less melee-range fleet battle, i.e. a mess.
- Would you be able to zoom in, you would miss details on the ships. But you cannot zoom in that far.
- Fleet customization is limited. The fleet upgrades DO have an effect, but they don't necessarily feel immediately effective.
-  The space battles feel a little lackluster.
Still, I'd like to see more from this universe, possibly with more customization options, a more extensive campaign with more backstore and exploration.

Max Payne. Maximum pain. His name hides his destiny, never to find peace, to lose everyone he cares about, constantly to be in pain and always be on the edge of life and death. This is the tragic story of the title character of the revolutionary Max Payne.
In one faithful night, everything he loves is gone in a blink of an eye and the world around him crumble. Arriving home he find his baby daughter and wife killed by junkies, under the influence of a new found drug on the streets of NY, called Valkyre or just V. After the funeral Max transfer to DEA and goes undercover, determine to find where the drug comes from. Only two agents, Alex and B.B. knows who he is. Three years later, Max finally have break on the Valkyre case. He recieve a messege from B.B. to meet Alex. Max have a bad feeling about this and he wasn't wrong. Alex get killed and he takes the blame for the murder. With nothing left to lose, Max takes the path of vengeance. He is been chased by everyone – police, mobsters, freaks and so on. This wild chase is happening in the middle of huge winter storm, as if it comes end of the world. From here follows twist and turns, betrayls, meeting with insane villians, bad guys helping you with information, corruptions, blackmail and so on. The story is one of the best things here. It's written by Sam Lake, who is the face of Max. The script is full of metaphors and references to scandinavian mythology. It's brilliantly written.
Cutscene are great and original. They are looking like graphic novel with neo-noir vibe and the voice of James McCaffrey make them even more memorable. Because of the moderate budget, Sam Lake is the face of the main characters and friends and colleagues are other people in the game. The cutscenes are filled with the inner monologs of Max, from which we find out the story and his mental state.
Even so many years later all this is still kind of impressive. But what is most memorable and revolutionary is in the gameplay section. The thing i'm talking about is bullet-time. It gives you more time to react and make more accurate shots. You can see to the silhouette of Max an hourglass. There is shown how much bullet-time you have. With a press of a button everything slows down and you can even see where the bullets fly. If you dive in it takes little part of it, so you have to decide how to use it. The hourglass drains quickly and the only way to fiil it is to kill enemies without using bullet-time. You have to use it wisely, because slowing down time is essential for reaching the end. The game is highly inspired by Hong Kong action movie, especially those of John Woo.
The game is old school and doesn't have regenerating health. You restore it by the most logical thing for the game – painkillers. You find them in spread around the levels. Sometimes they are not in obvious places.
The feeling of using bullet-time and blast through small group of bad guys is awesome.You are almost invulnerable. But you are not. Max life is fragile and even on the lowest difficulty, you can die in a blink of an eye. The game is hard, but fair. She will  kick your♥♥♥♥♥right from the start and ask do you want more. Most of the times when you die, it's player fault. Some enemies are cheaply placed and you don't have enough time to react. So quick save is alway an option. I don't want to know how is in the higher difficulties.
Max have substantial, but fairly standard arsenal of weapons – pistols, shotgun, double barrel shotgun, assault rifle, uzi, granade launcher, granades, sniper, Molotov and my favorite – Jackhammer. In close range is irreplaceable. The only weapon i don't like is the shotgun. The reloading speed is slow and i often die, when i use it. Here you can find one interesting and innovative thing. When you shoot with the sniper, the camera follows the bullet. Sound familiar? Few years later this will be the main feature in Sniper Elite.
The level design is awesome. They fairly diverse – abandone buildings, harbor, mansion and so on. Some places are even turn in to a brothel. There you can see, especially in the abandon buildings, the darkside of NY. The atmosphere is dark, grimm and depressing, particularly when you see the consequences on people using Valkyre. Death is above them and waiting to collect their souls. There are other more bright places like mansion, skyscraper and so on. But there heavily armed men are waiting for you. There are two different level. Little anoying to navigate, but they are not long. They are dreams, representing the mental state of Max, his fears, desires and the guilt he feels all the time. Dark and confused like himself.
The graphics are bad, but it's 14 year old game. This is the biggest problem here. Human models are not pretty to look at and not different enough. When you take in account release date, modest budget of 3 milion dollars for four years and the small Remedy team, it's not suprising. But in the end the game sold 7,5 million copies.
14 years later the sound design is still impressive. Guns doesn't sound bombastic, they are not too loud. When using pistol, you hear pistol.
The voice acting is fantastic. Even people with small roles are doing great job, but most memorable is of James McCafferey. There is an actior voicing one of the bosses, lunatic using V, can make you shiver, when you hear him talking.
You will remmember the music in Max Payne, especially the singnature music theme. Deep beat, followed by piano and little bit later guitar and drums can be heard. All this sets the mood for the sad and dark story of Max. The others are also good. Energetic tracks with pinch of tension in the style of 80's action movies. Some places don't have music playing and this just adds to the atmosphere. Phenomenal soundtrack. When you consider the budget of Remedy, all of this is incredible. Modern games should take a notes.
This game is classic and everyone have to play. It even run great on Windows 7. You have the feeling you are in John Woo movie, where hero pour a rain of bullets and skillfully avoid them. Despite that the graphics didn't age  well, every person have to see the roots of this series and the beginning of bullet-time. It doesn't matter how other games call it. The foundation is laid here. The story and gameplay are still great. Fantastic soundtrack, great and inovative gameplay, original and interesting cutscene, superb action. Here is also laid the foundation of one of the most beloved games from me – Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne. I highly recommend it.

Pro:
1.	Relatively good graphic.
2.	Some of the soundtrack are pretty good.
3.	You get free Origin DLC which contains the remake of the first game.
4.	Quite a few different looking ships.
5.	The energy grid is really creative.
Con:
1.	The campaign is really bugged. I have to re-load and redo several missions quite a few times so continue the story.
Example #1, one mission required me to leave one area for another area, I used T-Jump device to teleport to the destination and apparently it doesn’t count, took me 30 mins to figure why the story is not continuing.
Example #2, at the end of the story, very last submission, you will need to destroy Brotherhood’s mothership. However, if you spent too much time on the previous submission and NPC have already reduce the mothership’s HP to 0 and you will stuck here forever with an invincible mothership that’s just won’t go booom. This took me at least three re-loads and a 5-mins google search to figure out. I had scream out loud at the time I passed, ‘are you me? Coding program without doing any test?’ And guess what, there is another bug just following that, I have no idea what’s working behind the scene but apparently there was a lot of I/O on my disk and lagged final CG to the level of unwatchable. BTW, I reload twice to get passed this one
Example #3, there are some bugs related to the whole HP system, sometime my ship would explode during the battle with tons of HP in hull system 1 sec ago and sometime my ship simply became invincible (remember that mothership…) with a negative HP (integer overflow?)
2.	The battle is really boring and can get repetitive real quick. This is the biggest con of this game which eventually led me to remove it from my library after finishing the campaign. Normally I would spend a magnitude of more time on similar space adventure sand box.
Yes, there are a long list of available ships and a big combination of pilot ability + ship ability. Still I can’t find much difference operating a gunship or a Titan class monolith.
The absence of weapon groups made this even worse. Now you only have two weapon classes, light and heavy (shockwave, missile, and torpedo). It’s hard to create a fighting strategic which starting by disabling enemy’s shield first under this situation. Also, the difference between missile and torpedo is really small. In other games torpedo normally deliver more damage at the cost of homing ability and flying speed. It’s not the case here, otherwise it would be pretty interesting to modify a small stealth-enabled gunship to a deadly killing machine.
Carrier is a little overpowered while being underpowered. Its fighter teams can be a big threat to regular enemy but somehow setting target on several stationary entities won’t work. Besides, I totally understand fighters or bombers can be damaged but I can’t find a clue on it happens. Maybe they were hit by shockwave or mines but I have never seem any partial damaged fighter group. It’s either intact or just gone in the empty space after a big boom.
Weapons have very limited working angles, which is reasonable for light weapon but I have no idea why developers would make it the same on the missiles. You would have to completely show your side to your enemy to fire a missile installed on your ship sides. Seriously? You can teleport troops to the enemy ship yet you can’t transmit locking data from your main sensor to the side weaponry?
Enemy AI is either non-existing in this game or this is just one extremely aggressive world. A most basic gunship would open fire to my ship, the biggest and most powerful vessel in the game, and will fight to its death without a second thought.
Well, I can keep going on this list but I guess you should have some ideas by now.

Ok, its no homeworld. Still...
Ever try to fight multiple battles at the same time using the same, limited pool of units? In addition, you can't just spam a single unit as the battle plays out like a massive game of rock-paper-scisors. Some units are strong against fighters but do little damage to big targets, another is good at taking down hard targets but will lose to fighters. Space here is also 3D, alveit limited 3D as the individual maps are fairly small.
Thing is, do you think you can handle defending a target on one map, attacking a base on a second, protecting your flagship on a third map while being actively attacked on a fourth? Your basically playing multiple levels of an RTS at the same time, and units can move between levels. You can only control one group at a time, so generally need to leave at least some of the decision to the basic AI. All of this happens in realtime.
This game gets hard, even more so if you play on hardcore, which disables tactical pause. It is rare your completely safe even if all enemy units are destroyed. However, the game is also fairly flexible as you get to choose your tactics and ships each level. You can play aggressive, defensive, stealthy. Use big units or small units of your choice. There are a limited number of points where you can put down support buildings, which can repair, protect, attack fighers, attack capitals, and so on. The enemy doesn't play fair, often having multiple points where enemy ships can spawn, though you can destroy these like any other building. Expect to be outnumbered often and just deal with it.
So this is a mix between Homeworld, Warcraft,  and Command and Conquer. If you don't mind a difficult RTS which requires tactics and dividing your attention, give this a spin.

It took me a couple of tries before I could give this game a fair shake. Even after the hype had waned for this game, the mechanics of this game were difficult to look past initially. As mentioned, I played this game largely ignorant of the hype and community surrounding it, and it took me a few tries before I could invest myself properly in the game, but once I invested myself in the game, I did not regret doing so.
Undertale is a curious game in many regards. Though it is not the first to do so, most other games before it would be hard pressed to incorporate pacifism as a main gameplay feature and execute it so well.  As an addendum to that, the game hardly shys away from berating the player for choosing to kill. There is a boldness to the game, that it takes the player actions seriously that is investing and immersive. The game manages to react accordingly to the choices made by the player and in doing so it strengthens the player's bond with the game. The weight the player's actions have on the world is empowering but not without consequence, a hallmark of good rpgs.
Mechanically speaking, Undertale is rather basic, the core of Undertale's gameplay revolves around bullet hell mechanics, maneuvering a heart (representative of your soul) away from a variation of projectiles and obstacles. The game thankfully attempts to add some variation, to this, by adding blue attacks, which are thwarted by not moving, and orange attacks which are bypassed by moving through them. There are also moments where the game will add the ability to fire projectiles, or turn the bullet hell formula more towards platforming. The variations are certainly appreciated, though the base mechanics alone, are serviceable at best. What's there is decently polished, but I've often got the feeling what I was experiencing was just a simplified version of something I played before. It's a game that offers me a simplified version of Battle Garegga and calls it a day, seeks to placate me with a watered down Galaga and then tells me to reserve my gripes about gameplay or the bare bones platforming segments.
However, the mechanics differ based on how you react. If you're going the pacifism route, you'll be faced with something of a little puzzle on how to spare your opponent. Usually that devolves into making the right menu choice in act, or if it's a boss, choosing the right act and then outlasting their attacks against you usually. That's the gist of it anyway, with some mild variation here and there. The puzzles presented usually are pretty straightforward and hardly difficult to figure out, which doesn't lend itself well to replayability. The other option, is to fight, and that really just devolves into a timing mini game with very little actual variation on that mechanic. The game can occasionally be difficult, but it's hardly a consistent difficulty, the game is quite forgiving and unfortunately, some of the final bosses are laughably easy.
Turn based RPGS have historically had issue making gameplay that could stand well on it's own, and I don't think Undertale is an exception. It tries harder than most RPGS before it, but unfortunately, the gameplay still leaves me wanting more, I can't find myself confidently saying the gameplay can stand on it's own.
Fortunately, Undertale takes precedent from Turn Based RPGS in all the right ways too. The game tells an investing story, full of charming characters and interesting personalities. The game is full of creative designs and interesting encounters and tops itself off with an endearing, quirky, self referential humor about itself. It does tend to wear it's Earthbound influences on it's sleeve at times, which can cheapen the experience, but otherwise, I'd be among the many to laud this game as having an excellent and heartfelt story with lovable characters, oh and the music is quite catchy. [Minor spoilers ahead] I can in fact admit that I, being an ugly bag of mostly water with pathetic human feelings, could not bring myself to do a Genocide run. The thought of having to kill Papyrus (a video game character) offended my primitive illogical human brain. Of course, that means that, I as a reviewer, have failed at my job of giving a complete review, and thus any criticism forwarded towards me for that is completely warranted, perhaps such offense is on the grounds for completey invalidating my review, and that would be understandable.
However, I think that very fact serves as a testament to the charm and personality of Undertale's characters.
Although, Undertale's universe does have a few aspects that hurt the experience. Particularly, certain characters will break the 4th wall a few times and reference the Save and Load feature, as well as talk to the player directly. A certain boss fight runs with the idea in fact, and this embracing of totally shattering the 4th wall hurts the experience somewhat and manages to rip the player away from any immersion that was there. Tonally the game is fairly consistent save for a single level near the end of the True Pacifist run, which jumps form cheery and jubilant to snapping into dark and disturbing territory without any sort of appreciable foreshadowing to this tonal shift. It cause this segment to stand out quite obviously, while the level itself and the mood given isn't bad, it's jarring.
The Genocide run as I mentioned is not something I could do, but judging from what I watched and the feedback many have given off, I'd be inclined to agree that it seems significantly less enjoyable than a standard run, especially since player control is often taken away at many key moments. (Ironically my watching of the run is referenced by one of the game's character's verbatim as being even worse than players actually doing it!) The Genocide run is also notable for cutting a fair bit of the standard game content and perhaps the most interesting of all, completing a genocide run permanently alters future endings, the pacifist run notably becomes tinged with a creepypasta twist. On some levels, it feels a bit cringey and juvenile in execution, perhaps because of the striking similarity it has with some creepastas, but I still found the concept overall interesting and furthermore, it heavily reinforces the theme of consequence, which I find quite laudable.
There is some replayabiltiy to be had, particularly if you want the True Pacifist ending, you'll have to play through twice. Though, aside from the possibility of a Genocide Run, any further replayability loses it's value rapidly. The aspects that make Undertale stand out are it's universe and characters. Most people will come to Undertale for the story, and remarkably few will claim they came for the mechanics or gameplay. Undertale is not a bad game for having it's mechanics supported by it's story rather than the other way around, and as such it's a game you'll fondly remember, rather than a game you'll still be playing by the end of the year for it's gameplay.
Undertale is a good game, but in this reviewer's opinion, great might be an exaggeration. I'd opt instead, to describe it as a memorable experience.

When I put this into my cart, I expected a simple Mario Kart knockoff with everyone's favorite lasagna-eating monday-hating overweight feline instead of a plump plumber.. I was horribly mistaken, however, as Garfield Kart not only blew my expectations out of the water, but solidifies itself as the best game I've ever played. It starts with a simple tutorial with Garfield walking through each era of history, showing that everything important that has ever happened can be linked back to Jim Davis, the best person on the entire planet.
Soon after, the game begins to delve into the socioeconomic issues of America, especially during the Bush administration. This leads as a segway into the life of a young african teen in northwest Detroit and the struggles he experienced on a daily basis. It truly opened my eyes to the racial devide of the country I've lived in for most of my life. It's as if this game hit on a topic that the corrupt media had hidden away from our eyes.
Garfield and his owner, Jon, then began a socialist uprising in the heart of America, quickly gaining support of most of the country. As their power grew, the corrupt establishment grew worried that their power was soon to be stolen. So the US government began to rapidly produce Right-Wing Death Squads to eradicate the utopia Garfield had created. After a civil war between the Commie Cats Club and the Right-Wing Death Squads that raged for well over 16 years, the CCC finally took Washington D.C., effectively taking America. The Democatic Republic of Lasagnaland was finally established.
Now that Garfield had no resistance, he could finally enact his master plan: go-kart racing. He converted the entire state of Kansas into a big race track where he could challenge Jon, Odie, and some big rat thing to endless races through the once-proud wheat field. The rest of the story rests with the player to decide. I won't spoil the endings, but they will have your jaw on the floor.

I'm just not a fan of this game. I want to get into it. I like complex games and designing a working colony with various struggles thrown at me along the way. I like gathering and managing resources.
I cannot stand the way this game is designed, though. I much prefer Rimworld and I realize why now-depth. What I mean by that is: this is a 2D side scrolling game. There is no depth to the rooms you can build. It's like you're endlessly building hallways and sticking stuff in the hallways. Everything's lined up side by side and nothing can be placed behind anything-this makes everything needlessly tedious and complex in my opinion.
Try adding this restriction to Rimworld or another colony building game you enjoy: you can only build rooms one block deep and only stick items side by side in that room. How much fun is that? That is this game. It could be SO much greater and more fun to play, but it's held back by the fact that it literally has no depth and it forces you to build a weird sprawling 2D colony.
Again, for how complex these game wants to be, it needs to give players the ability to build real rooms and stick items and decorations in those rooms in a logical way. Having everything take up 1 or 2 blocks and have to be stuck side by side creates easily avoided design limitations.
If that was the intention behind designing the game this way: to make it so difficult and tedious to try and circumvent the design limitations to build a functioning colony anyway, that's cool-it's just not for me. Sadly, that also means I can't recommend it. To me this game is a good example of how not to design a complex and difficult base building game. I think there's a reason all the others go for a top down view. The base building is far less restrictive that way.
