After having played and mostly enjoyed every addition to the Arkham franchise, it's with some level of internal debate that I say Arkham Origins is probably my favorite of the lot thanks in no small part to the sum of it's factors. This game has it's ups and downs, to be sure; but we'll get to those in a moment. From a technical standpoint it's beautiful, the combat and mechanics are more or less what you'd expect from previous Arkham titles but with more polish and care. Sound and graphical designs were both on point, the DLC (Cold Cold Heart, not the other challenge maps fluff) was a fun time, overall packaged as a solid game with few real flaws in ways of anything but minor bugs.
Also a friendly warning, this review does contain some spoilers for the main story.
Singleplayer's story works as an origin to Arkham Asylum and not Batman himself, though the maturing of the Bat is very evident over the course of the game. I feel somewhat disappointed to see the game pulled a villian swap, ultimately making me feel as though the emphasis on Black Mask during promotion was ultimately a waste as he barely appears at all. No prizes if you guess who he gets replaced by.
Though where that falls short, other bits manage to shine. The boss fights are a -HUGE- improvement over past Arkham games, and character developement is rich and plentiful. Gotham is fairly attractive and fun to explore, even if half of it was copy-pasted from Arkham City, it still has a flavor of freshness. The topping on the cake is, as unexpected as it was, actually Bane. He's portrayed faithfully to the comics, his fights feel imposing and his general portrayel is fantastically improved upon from previous forays. One complaint on Gotham itself was the whole "Oh, yeah. The civillians are all not around because curfew or something."
I mean c'mon, it's Gotham for Christ's sake. Have some people walking the streets, everything feels so dull and lifeless when there's nobody around aside from the random thugs strutting about the rooftops. In the cases of Arkham City and hell even Arkham Knight there's some level of excuse as to why everyone's just sort of gone.
I'd like to preface the review with the now-defunct multiplayer. Competitive multiplayer was an odd yet welcome addition that expanded upon the vanilla game's longevity alongside the thrill of putting your Dark Knight prowess up against other players. It was fairly exciting at the right times, but it had many bugs and issues such as a lack of drop-in feature for ongoing games and the possibility of incredibly unbalanced teams if too many players dropped out on one side, making the match more of a one-sided steamroll than any actual sort of competition. There were three teams in this mode, two using conventional firearms and one being none other than the Dark Knight himself accompanied by his stalwart sidekick Robin. The two competing teams were to fight it out in a series of maps spanning Gotham City with control-point based objectives that each team would need to capture, these points would rapidly exhaust the enemy team's "ticket" count until it reached zero, where upon the enemy team would need to murder the remaining players to fully win the round.
Then of course there was Batman himself. Your goal as the bat was to use stealth, ambushes and clever traps to take down the roaming thugs to raise "fear", a system that once filled would result in an absolute victory for the caped crusaders.
Not that any of that matters now, seeing how the multiplayer servers were shut down. I genuinely wish a lot of you guys were able to play it when it was still at it's height, it was honestly a blast.
Overall, the game is worth a shot if you're a Batman fan or are new to the Arkham series. I reccomend it, as even where it fell short, it was still a good game if.

The game we asked for but not the game we wanted.
I write this review as a fan of the Arkham series with a huge preference towards Arkham City.  If you believe that makes me biassed I suppose I would be a fool to disagree.
However, on with my thoughts on this game.  I was one of the people who experienced delays with getting their game and the issues I experienced with installing it have been well documented on the forum.  So after finally getting it installed I started playing with the mindset "I really want to like this but I am already hating it", so I was extremely biassed from the outset.  Then the game started and the intro was not really on par with the previous titles.
With Arkham City, the story was broken relatively slowly.  Origins certainly upped the ante and decided upon a bit of a more "up tempo" beginning.  A bit of a video, a quick change, into the action and off to Black Gate Prison we go for the obligatory "prologue"/"training" level.  This is something very common in games now.  The prologue not only trains you (if you're not already familiar with the Arkham controls) but gives you a quick intro to the story.  After that you're in the city of Gotham, going about doing the ususal goon punching.
The story develops at a pace that is a bit start/stop.  After you face the first boss (who I was surprised to face so early) you then hit the city (both figuratively and literally) fullfilling quests that at times feel a little hollow.  There has been many comments about the larger city scape being not much more than a cut and paste affair.  Which is true, there are often quite literally parts which show that WB Montreal had access to the assets from the previous games and were explicitly told to use them.  (I even noticed in the end credits that part of the Rocksteady team that worked on the previous titles were drafted in to help with the game build.)  But then, reusing assets is nothing new and has been happening in the animation world for years.
When the developers announced this and did the usual publicity, the adage that was reinforced was "if it ain't broke don't fix it" and it's fair to say that's almost true.  However I think they also forgot the "if it's fixed, then don't break it" which is how I feel the combat is sometimes - that is broken.  There are times that I find myself swearing at the game because I have felt the combat is not as good as it perhaps should have been.  Teleporting enemies, bats that are a foot longer than they're shown in the modelling, counters not working correctly.  It's tough to get the timing of the combat in this game at times with the game breaking the rhythm that you've learned to play to (and that's after adapting my combat technique from the City one to the Origins one).  Yes, I kind of excused that at first, after all we're playing a less refined Batman earlier in his career but when a game breaks the rhythm and timing that it has established, that's a bit off.
Yes, there's reused world space assets, yes there's reused goons, (both of these things are how games in a series are made) and no this game did not innovate as much as the others.  The one area they did innovate gets overlooked and that's the crime scene analysis and detective vision.  There's more reason to use detective vision in this game with all the hidden pieces to find but the new Crime Scene Investigation (or CSI:Gotham) part are marred by the fact that they're not used all that often and they are nothing more than interactive cut-scenes with a large portion of hand-holding.  It's not a case of finding the evidence but looking where you're told to look.  Anyone who's been gaming for a reasonable amount of time is quite adept at finding those elements in games on there own - either by deductive reasoning or by understanding video game mechanics.  The whole hand-holding you through those parts just ruined any innovation they had brought in.
Ok, so that's the "packaging" of the game - what about the story?
Well, ladies and gents, if you're looking for a really meaty story about the origins of Batman then watch those films with Christian Bale.  This game is about the Origins of the Arkham trilogy (which is only a trilogy due to the fact they bought this a third title out).  While it tries very hard to make it's mark on the series, it just come across to me as a "tribute" to the Arkam series rather than a title that deserves to be in the trilogy on it's own merits.  Reused assets aside, there are story elements that are all too annoying to forgive.  (no spoilers but there was one part when I shouted at my computer and turned the game off for all of ten minutes questioning the whole "did you really pull that?")
There are contrivances to every story in the world, but the contrivances of this game are, not to be melodramatic (unlike this point in the game), plain unforgivable.  This game tries really hard not to be but just ends up being contrived.  Shoe-horning elements in to fit the canon and making a foul up of it along the way.  The plot twists never shocked me and the contrivances annoyed me.  Which is a shame because, by and large, the performaces of the voice actors wasn't wholly terrible.
You could easily forgive and forget that Troy Baker wasn't Mark Hammill.  While trying to put his own "mark" on his performance of his part (see what I did there?) he did well in aping Mark Hammill's performance.  The performance of Roger Craig Smith was passable when he could remember that he was playing the Arkham Batman and not the Christian Bale Batman.  (It was funny if I noticed this change mid sentence and even funnier when he did a full Bale/Arkham/Bale conversion in one conversation).
The criticisms of others saying "oh, but it's nothing new" either missed the point of buying another game in the same series (which is to get more of what we already knew, so where's the fail?) or completly overlooked what was new and innovative (which didn't always work).  At least this could run in DX11 straight out of the box which left use with a very pretty game.
If you're a fan of the series, you probably already bought it and have made up your mind about it.  If you're not a fan of the series, then consider this Arkham Batman light (all the taste but only half the calories), not a bad contribution if it's the first ever Batman game you played.  Which I suppose is not a bad thing.
If anything could be considered a fail in regards to this game, that is the setting.  Setting a Batman game (or any game for that matter) to a Christmas backdrop and releasing it in October produces two problems.  One, when the game is beaten before christmas and you've played quite a few hours of it, you're sick of Christmas before Advent begins.  Two - it's Batman.  If you're going to send out a lot of people to hunt down a double-hard vigilante who wears a costume resembling a bat then Christmas is not the best time (especially when you release a game in October). The best time (as voiced by my partner) is surely Halloween?  Setting a game at Christmas makes replayability a bit weird.  Afterall who wants to be thinking of Christmas in May?  And replayability of a game is a major selling point to me, personally.  Horror can be done all year round but Christmas Eve defines a very short period of replayability to me.
We Batman fans however wanted another Batman game and that's what we got.  Unfortunately, we didn't get the game we expected but it seems foolhardy to be compaining about getting what you asked for.  Rocksteady set the bar so high that it was always going to be tough for this game to be an "instant classic" and while it doesn't quite live up to it's predessors it's definitely a good introduction to the series for newcommers.  I have my own theories about this but it's beyond the scope of this review.

Batman: Arkham Origins is seen as the third child that the gaming community never wanted, but it astounds both negatively and positively with its release. With its flaws publicly displayed, the story still manages to begin the legacy of Batman with a jolt of darkness not seen previously in the series. As Batman avoids the his fifty million dollar bounty, his rogue gallery is as interesting as it could be without pulling the staples from previous titles. Though Batman: Arkham Origins reverts back to the combat-driven narrative, the title overall branches out with new elements that push through some of the repetitions the Arkham games are known for.

Max Payne was released in 2001. Even after so many years it still remain one of my favorite games ever. It's just perfect. So why did I fall in love with Max Payne?
- Shooting.
Those weapons are really made well. If you are using shotgun it feels like shotgun, it can send bad guys flying for few meters, but you also can fly pretty high too. Throught whole game you use all of the weapons in game. Shooting in Max Payne is pure fun.
- Slow motion.
Probably the best slowmo in history of gaming. I mean it. Even Matrix games never had slowmo this amazing. Jumping from the corner to surprise your enemies, jumping throught the doors to surprise your enemies, and slowly falling on the ground, but faster their dead bodies.
- Story and characters.
There are great and memorable characters in this game. The story in form of comic is interesting as the story itself.
"Clear as vodka."
"No Payne, No Gain."
And of course full of specific humour. Narration is perfect too.
- Music.
Just at the very beggining you have hard time starting game. Why? Max Payne have this amazing theme music. It makes you wait for the whole thing, it's playing, and playing, and you can't stop listening to it. When I heard it first time I had chills. It's perfect, it describes perfect, without use of any words, what kind of game Max Payne is. You will want to hear more of it as you progress with the story.
- Difficult level.
Max Payne isn't a easy game. Even while playing on lowest difficult level the bad guys can pack whole shotgun shell in your head, or something on your back, and kill you without any problem. Same with them throwing grenades or molotov cocktails. Once they will get better stuff than pistols you will need something more than just slowmo to get rid of them. It's easy to get hurt and there aren't enough painkillers to get rid of all this Payne...
To be honest, I could praise this game all the time. Don't mind that it's an old game. It aged very well, graphics still looks great (at least for me) and it's full of things that you won't find in gaming nowadays. Even people playing Max Payne for the first time, so many years after release, are surprised how they could miss something like that. If you haven't played it, you must do it. You won't regret it.

This game is excellent.
It is a comic-like 2D version of running a prison. The game has a lot of depth, and at the same time is fairly easy and straight forward.
I would reccomend watching "Let's play" videos before starting into the game-- or actually playing the campaign. The campaign acts as a story tutorial for the open-ended concept.
The basics, you build a little prison. You hire some gaurds, cooks, and janitors. You build some cells, a mess hall, a shower, and a yard. And a big fence.
Then the game gets hard, the cons start rolling in. They start crying "Oh I have an addiction" "Oh, I'm bleeding because I tried to fight a guard and they beat me up" "Oh I'm angry I don't have a window" "Oh, I'm angry I can't see my family"-- ect.
The cons start fights, cost you money and man power. You make them happy. You think, this game is easy, I can take on max cons. They come in and wreck you. You learn. You adapt.
The game is great. It is hard, but not too hard. The game is rewarding. The game is fantastic.
Get out your wallet and buy it. You will not regret.

Undertale. I am sure most gamers have heard this title's name and if you haven't played it, you may wonder what all of the fuss is about. I was one of these people until I finally decided to give the game a go a few months ago. Upon first look, Undertale doesn't look like much. What is true when the gaming industry started is still true today....how a game looks doesn't mean it is not a great game. You cannot judge a book by its cover and in today's age when we have 100 GB games with ultra realistic graphics it still remains true. Undertale may not be the most visually appealing game out there but if you judge it by that alone, you are missing out on one of gaming's most memorable rides. I will keep this as short and sweet as possible. After 47 hours in Undertale, I still feel it has more to offer. The story is simply captivating, it will test your every emotion based on the choices you make. This is one of the most immersive games I have played in quite some time. The writing is SO good, especially for the main characters of this game, you FEEL what they feel. You feel like you are in the game, in their world. The battle system is like nothing I have ever seen before. A totally unique take on turn-based RPG gameplay that will test your emotions, morals, reflexes, and memorization every battle. Add to this one of the best and addictive sound tracks I have heard in a game in a long time makes for a truly and wholey, unique experience. I listen to the OST of this game even when not playing it, that is how good it is. I highly recommend everyone giving Undertale a try but especially RPG fans!

Disappointing... Yooka-Laylee gets so much right, but the core of the game just doesn't work. I had high hopes for the game, but vast, empty levels and a lack of direction make the exploration and collecting boring.
The first level was fun, if at times frustrating, but the level design just gets worse from there. The game gives barely any feedback as to what areas of a level are completeable with the abilities you have unlocked. Most areas in a level look almost exactly the same, there is practically no way to tell whether you have already been in an area or not. It feels like the levels were just designed to be huge, regardless of whether they are fun to play, or even actually contain anything at all. Add to that a bunch of invisible walls, a camera that has a tendency to get stuck behind obstacles, broken and repetitive boss fights, and contrived yet stupidly easy puzzles, and the result just isn't very compelling.

What makes the game good:
- Pretty colors
- Unlocking new skills is a blast
- Some bosses and puzzles are actually challenging
- It is fun to explore

I saw the reviews and thought "It couldn't really be that bad could it? It's a genre that is more designed and catered for children, and grown-ups are reviewing it - of course it's not going to feel like the magic of your own childhood"
First off, I backed this game on kickstarter and I must admit, the soundtrack and artbook are pretty lack-lustre so not even that was worth it. All the same, as a backer, and being a little late to actually playing the game because of life-things happening, I saw the reviews and tried to disregard them, but I've tried playing the game twice now, and while at first, yes the game does have an element of charm with it's nice pastel colours, bright environments and quirky characters; this is soon lost amongst bland, scattered, empty, lifeless worlds wherein enemies as so few and far between that you'll think you're playing some Bethesda RPG.
I didn't get past the first world because of the frustration this game implanted in me. The camera is aweful where you'll have that classic jerky zoom problem where it can't figure out how to deal with little ledges. It also has issues of fixed camera angles at the dumbest of places e.g. jumping on a platform will automatically rotate the camera to be side on because it assumes you want to do the challenge associated with it, equally, there was another challenge that involved climbing a slide but at the bottom, you have to be close enough for the camera to face the slide, move one pixel away and it will then snap 180 degrees so the direction you were previously running in is now trying to take you in the opposite direction to where you intended... Dumb stuff like that.
As I've said, enemies are generic, simple spin attack to win and there you go. Often they will just sit and stare at you waiting to be attacked... considering there are so few of them... maybe make them a challenge?
The 'challenges' that I encountered in order to get my collectables to progress were also dull and unimaginative - race a cloud, turn into a flower and bob around super slowly to turn buds into plants, body slam some blocks, complete a time trial kart race-course with the worst controls that feel as though you have no grip at all, find ghosts that require 'catching' and other dumb things that aren't explained and are just left there for you to either perservere with or come back to later. Let me tell you this;
The essence of the game is a collectathon so you'll be trying to get these 'pagies' and 'feathers' to progress both your worlds and your abilities. The latter is easy enough, the former are your main collectables. After you get a few, you can expand a world you have visited already. So, where previously I climbed and explored within levels only to find a random, inexplicable dead end where a path just stops, I now have a HUGE number of additional platforms and areas to explore, each at different corners of the world meaning I have more walking/rolling time through the level just to explore each of these new additions. Except these too aren't any extra fun and just add to the arbitrary nature of tasks the game has to offer with things like new bosses with silly slide climbing, indoor areas with more 'Come back when you have the power' locked doors and side-scrolling platforms. But get this - in a side-scrolling platform section, you still have 3d movement but a fixed camera so you can't see just a little gap at the deep end of a platform so you can slip down and have to start over... This is exactly what I mean when I say this game is just infuriating and poorly designed.
Did I mention you have different abilities - I didn't play enough to really be able to experiment with them, but what I can say is built into the abilities is another fatal design decision -
. You'd have thought that, with the size and scattered nature of the world design, that they'd at least let you move quickly right? Nope - rolling takes stamina from your incredibly small stamina bar meaning you'll need to recharge often. That is unless you roll through a butterfly which will refill your bar... except the butterflies are so hard to judge in terms of depth that colliding with them is a further frustration. Why did they add a stamina bar you may ask - so that they can have an arbitrary challenge of roll-racing a cloud around a track where you have to beat it on a single lap where you have to get these butterflies in order to prevent your stamina bar from depleting meaning you have to recharge, meaning you lose the race. It's that simple. It's just arbitrary, pointless and most importantly;
In conclusion - I tried so hard to like this game, to give it a chance that I thought critics were not giving it. I kickstarted this game thinking "I haven't really played a classic 3D platformer like this before, let's see what I missed in my childhood". I come away disappointed in the soundtrack, the artbook, and most importantly; in the game, it has even put me off 3D platformers. I must admit defeat - while critics were able to sit through 'mine-kart' challenges and multiple worlds within this game, I gave in after only just expanding my first world; I haven't even come across these notorious mine-kart sections, and goodness knows I don't want to.
I even heard there is a patch coming to sort out the voices etc, but trust me, that will be the least of your concerns.
TL:DR - It's a half baked mess, a similar cooking-related, developer referencing pun would refer to this game as under-cooked
meat. I can't see how the nostalgia factor is ostensibly a saving grace for this game among fans of Banjo-Kazooie etc... It's just bland.
Oh, and if you're thinking of buying this for your kids - don't. I can see many controllers, keyboards, mice and screens being broken in frustration.

Story Time
I was a junior at high school, lowpoint of my life, I was super depressed, and everyday all I wanted was death. I cried myself to sleep every night, and whenever I tried to talk to someone about it, they would just insult me and call me a ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Even my own parents didn't love me, as whenever I tried to tell them how I feel, they shut me off and told me to be normal. I overhear them talk, wishing that I had been put up for adoption. I was bullied at school and had no friends. I was a pathetic husk of a man, drifting to class to class, at this point completely numb all other emotion other than unrelenting sadness and anger at myself. "Why can't I express myself, why must I live like this?" I often pondered.
But one day, one life changing day, I was looking threw the steam store. It was the summer sale, and I had some money for helping my uncle at his farm. I often do it for free out of respect for him, and because he is a nice guy, and it lets me spend time with him, but he said I did a really good job, and gave me some money. I've never really had much money growing up but when ever I did, I Usually bought games. I've always enjoyed them more than other media. They let me be someone who I'm not. Someone who People like. Anyway, I saw this game, Garfield kart. My god this game. Little did I know then, that it would change my life. Anyway, I thought it looked like a horrid game, just to make a quick buck off of a brand. I purchased it, mainly because I wanted to see how bad it was. When I launched I was opened with an angelic piece of music, blowing my expectations out of the water, which wasn't hard to do though. It was at that moment, when I heard that music, I felt something, something I haven't felt in a long time. Something good. I started to play the game, and around the 2nd lap, I realized something, I was in a custom game, and had it set to unlimited laps. I went to exit the game, but as I was about to do it, just seconds away from hitting the leave game option, I realized something. The whole idea of repeating a cycle forever with nothing changing reminded me of my life, going from class to class, day to day, feeling the exact same sadness. I broke down in tears, and left, wishing that leaving that game, would have some effect of my life, and leave my "cycle". I continued crying for hours, and when I calmed down, I noticed something. A track builder. This made me realize that I am in complete control over my life. I am free to forge my own path, and if I had to repeat a cycle, I was going to make sure that it was a damn good one.
When the next school year started, It was my senior year. I had decided after playing garfield kart and my whole cycle revelation, that I can make my own path, and was going to make some friends. There was this guy, Ben was his name, who had similar intrest as me and I wanted to become his friend as he seemed like a nice guy. It was with him that I learned to communicate, express emotions and feelings, and most of all, be happy.
After high school ended, I got something I never thought I would get. A scholarship, a full ride. I was on my school's fishing team, and I was pretty good at it, as I went with my uncle and he taught me how to be a really good fisherman. I never thought I was that good at it though. I went to college to be a game developer. I wanted to give people similar experiences as garfield kart gave me. In class I met this one guy, and he invited me over to come over to his apartment with some of his friends to play some Mario Kart. I said sure and went over. going over there was the best decision of my life. I met 5 people, 4 boys and one girl. This girl was the most amazing women I've ever seen. Everything was perfect about her, her hair, her eyes, and her personality. It was love at first sight. We hit it off really well together at that party, and she was my first real friend since ben. During that party my roommate texted me that his girlfriend was staying the night, and asked me to not come back to our dorm for privacy. I asked the people there and the girl said that I could spend the night with her. I took her up on that offer and went home with her. later that night, we talked. Talked about our past. When I was telling her about my highschool years, and the sadness that came with them, I burst into tears. I couldn't help it. But she didn't make fun of me, like other people would. She heard me out, she talked with me about it, and thus, 18 years of bottled up sadness came out.
It's been 3 years since that night. Me and her are now married, and have a child on the way and if there's one thing I have to say, it's this,
Thank you Garfield Kart.

Would I recommend this game? To an extent, yes.
>Positives- The game is, at it's core, very fun. Your basic goal is to drive around, crash into people, beat people up and loot for scrap. It is repetitive, dull, but satisfying as all hell, and if you are looking for a simple game that features such things, then this is the game for you. On top of that, the game runs VERY well, perfectly optimised with a nice selection of graphical settings for varying types of pc horse power, with controls that are decent on mouse/keyboard and excellent controller support. At Maxed out settings (sorry for the pun) the game looks amazing, which works amazingly with the high-quality animations, giving you something beutiful to look at as you drive into and punch people to death with a cheeky recreation of the Batman Arkham combat system (whether it is a rip off is entirely for you to judge) and vehicle combat that could only be described as Wacky Racers on steroids.
>Negatives- As much as it pains me to say this, Mad Max has a decent amount of shortcomings, which are depressing to say the least. The story is so dull it might as well not exist, with no meaningful goal or aim to work towards story-wise you are left pretty isolated in that regard. Characters, with the exeption of Chum Bucket and that Wanderer turtle-looking guy, are hollow, unimaginative and so basic that you may even mistake then as unimportant npc's, with poorly written dialogue and stock motives that leave you with nothing to care about. The gameplay can, and for most people will, get repetitive, where even something like taking on twenty enemies at once could make you fall asle....zzzzzzzz. And finally, the price. The game is currently sold for fourty euro/dollars/pounds, which is too much of an asking price in my opinion. Thirty would be perfect given what you get, and getting the game on sale is a necessity.
>conclusion- If you can pick up Mad Max on sale, do it, that is if you feel that you are interested in what I consider as positive and are okay with dealing with and/or are okay with what I consider as negative. All in all, I feel very sorry for this game. It could have been so much more, and I believe that a sequel, if done right, could be masterful. Avalanche Studios, just like how the original Mad Max movie had issues and the sequel improved on the formulae drastically, I believe that a sequel to this game could be your Magnum Opus, in which you take what good you have done here and iron out the missteps, improving the negatives and perfecting something decent to make it wonderful, just like the trasition from the first movie to the second.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 has that sneaky perception of actually becoming one of your greatest casual games of all time.  Regardless if you're a driver enthusiast or not (and I'm not,) this title does so much to keep your interest that it's difficult to put down.
As probably unsurprising for a simulator, the gameplay is pretty solid - as well as it being visually appealing game that a mid-level computer could easily handle.
The simple A-to-B structure of accepting jobs in this game and having a start and end point are somewhat obvious and straight forward.  Completing jobs come with rewards such as money and level experiences.  When you have enough dough, ETS2 gives you the opportunity to start your own garage, where you can invest and gain more employees to help your venture.  You can then purchase more garages in every city you explore as you become a transit superpower, obtaining some high-power and ultimately big-money jobs.
The money you earn also goes to the trucks you purhcase as the game gives you the option of fixing and modding your fleet.  You'll be finding yourself visiting these garages more than frequently to keep your truck in tip-top spec and upgrading certain aspects, such as tires, lights, gearboxes, mirrors and paint jobs.
You only ever get to see your own personal truck at one time in your fleet as the game simulates how your other employees do in-game, so don't expect to see your fellow inmates on the road, but it doesn't detract anything from the experience.  The simulation calcuates (somewhat randomly) each employee based on their current experience, whether if their aspects are based on long-distance, fuel consumption, high-value cargo and so on.  The employees receive their big checks and you get a small portion of it.  The more employees and garages you obtain, the better the intake.
Graphically it's actually gorgeous.  The roads are perfectly structured, alongside the buildings, greenery and sky.  The night/day cycle is always a delight, particularly when you are driving through a long 28hour job.  The AI is somewhat smart (and it continues to get smarter as the patches for the game persist) although at times you'll find it frustrating and it can lead to instances of AI cars crashing into you - and you have to pay for it.  The roads are structured really well, but you'll find some roads just a tad too narrow.  They're not impossible, obviously, but you may be finding that you've come to a dead halt just to try turn a very awkward lane.
ETS2 has longevity written all over it.  With its constant job vacancies, truck modding, not to mention the Steam achievements that are available, there are plenty of things to keep your interest in this game.  The community is strong, and the fact the latest client has the ability to connect to SCS Software's 'World of Trucks' entity, it goes from strength-to-strength.
A game I can totally recommend to anyone who cannot drive.  At all.  And be good at it and feel pretty damn good about it too.

I like what this game is trying to do. Single-player story-driven RTS? Hell yes. Beautiful space environments? More please. Three dimensional space combat? I want it! Sadly, as much as it pains me to say this, there are just too many flaws in the execution for the game to be as enjoyable as it should be.
Let's start with the worst - there are some serious technical issues going on here. I've had the game hang permanently once, and I've had a save file corrupted, which I'm honestly not used to seeing in games these days. I also had a gamebreaking bug in the mission Psychonauts (I think that's Mission 7?) where the object tied to a mission objective simply never appeared, forcing me to enable cheats through a config file and auto-win the mission. This kind of stuff is a real shame, doubly so because the game seems to have been abandoned fairly quickly after launch, with no hope of patches.
Less utterly broken, but still really bad, is unit pathfinding. It can be incredibly difficult to get your units to do what you want, especially if you're trying to make use of 3D movement. I've repeatedly tried to navigate my fleet above or below objects in 3D only to have them move back down to the basic plane of movement, putting them in the way of enemy fire or getting stuck behind obstacles. Units also seem to sometimes just forget their move orders, and some abilities seem to break sometimes. The Dreadnought, for example, has a triple-blast cannon ability that obliterates buildings and does heavy damage to units, but sometimes it just doesn't seem to fire all or any of its shots despite triggering the cooldown. All of this means that half the time unit command is smooth, and the other half of the time it's infuriating.
Even when it works, the gameplay design isn't flawless. Issuing targeted commands on units that are closed together is tricky, requiring you to pause and angle the camera to select what you actually want rather than all the icons beside it. A lot of combat must be either really difficult or finnicky, because I spent a lot of time waiting around to build up my forces before tackling tougher points of resistence, as going in full-force is often your only hope.
The game does indeed look great, but unfortunately it's best to play at a distance a lot of the time, so you see the unit icons much more than you see the detailed units. The sound design and music are well-done, the cutscenes look cool, and the story overall is fairly interesting, though there are a few predictable beats (sudden but inevitable betrayal!), and a few threads left hanging that, I fear, will never get resolved in a sequel.
Ultimately, it boils down to that - Ancient Space has some good ideas that are marred by poor execution in a few key areas, and it's really begging for a sequel, or a massive patch, that fixes these things. Sadly I doubt it will get either, and as such I can't really recommend this unless you're willing to deal with a fair amount of technical frustrations while playing.

if your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I consider DDADDS, for what it is, a really wonderful game. It's not perfect, but it's definitely a great shot for the team's first game and it's easy to see a lot of love has clearly gone into it. You might feel it's not worth the $15, especially if you don't play this genre, but I think it's an acceptable price and was willing to pay that solely to support the efforts of a small team that worked hard to provide a game that is funny, charming, and sweet. It does take a certain sense of humor to enjoy the game, which relies a lot on puns and jokes based around anxiety, internet culture, and day-time tv, but if that sounds like something you'd enjoy, it's worth it. The characters are fun and varied and, as a queer NB player, the trans and bi/pan inclusivity is much appreciated. If you regularly enjoy dating sims, I don't think you'll regret adding this one to your list. If you're not into this genre, your mileage may vary and it might be worth it to wait on a sale if you really want to try it out.
(Very long and thorough review below - includes some major and some minor spoilers)
Story wise, DDADDS is par for the course. You meet your options, you go on your dates, you get your cg. But each dad offers an arc that primarily deals with their own emotional insecurities that you can help them overcome. Mat and
, Craig and
, Damien and
, etc. As a person that has their own emotional issues and has dealt with anxiety and depression, it was nice to see these types of issues addressed and supported. Each character has a problem and takes steps to address said problem rather than solely having the love of the player-character solve it for them. You don't kiss Robert's bad decisions away, you confront him with the hard truth that he can't change unless he puts in the effort to make that change in himself. The relationship between Amanda and her dad is also great to watch play out.
When looking at the game as a whole, I consider the $15 price just fine. It came out to around 11 hours of content for me playing through each route once and, with my experience, that's pretty standard for a dating sim like this. If you go in with the plans to only play one route and ignore others, then yes, it'll be a pretty short game. But you're not paying the price of one route, you're paying the price of all the routes. I can agree with the slight disappointment of feeling like you don't actually Date your Dream Daddy in this Daddy Dating Simulator (since the third date focuses on the climax of your relationship and the resolution of their emotional issue), but I think it's a good end from a writing standpoint.
I found the art in this game to be really well done. There's a lot of criticism about the backgrounds and character sprites clashing, but I'm in disagreement with that being an issue at all. It's a visual novel and your attention is supposed to be on the characters - they are more detailed because they are the focus. The background serves its purpose of being a background and doesn't really need to be more than that.
There are some minor criticisms to be made about the dadsona art of the game. The dadsona creator really does clash with the style of the other characters. I can understand and assume it's because they wanted a somewhat simpler style to provide more character creation options, but it's still just a tad distracting. There's also at least one hair  and a few accessories (that I've seen) that don't seem to be colored in properly, but it's just a minor visual bug and you can choose pieces that don't look like that (though some, like the big grin lips, you may not see unless you chose a certain color and have started into the game). It is unfortunate it went missed while they were polishing the game, but I don't consider it a deal breaker.
I would have liked there to be more CGS (the "special" pictures you get through playing a vn and going down someone's route - in DDADDS's case, they are the pinups you receive at each good end), even some with Amanda. CGs are one reason you get a lot of replayability value in visual novels - you want to fill up your gallery. I don't think not having them really takes away from the game's worth, but it would have added a lot to see an illustration of Mat's expression as he
or to see Hugo beaming as
. I did enjoy the unique art styles for each of the pinups we received, though I got a bit confused when Mat's (whose route I completed first) matched the character art of the game and the others didn't. It may have been more consistent visually to either make them all match or have someone else draw Mat's too.
There's very little of it, and that's kind of the point of a visual
. For everyone who thought it was boring to have to go through large chunks of text, that's just what visual novels are. It's like complaining about too much shooting in a First Person Shooter. If you dislike having to go through a lot of text, even with the fast forward option, you will not enjoy this game.
were a definite surprise. They're interesting enough to break up the potential monotony of the text, but simple enough that they don't take a lot to get through. That being said, they can be frustrating with a lack of clear instructions. Mat's minigame had controls that didn't seem to respond correctly all of the time, it wasn't clear you could turn the pieces of Damien's gargoyle upside down, and Hugo's game is odd in that you really don't know if you're winning or losing while you're playing.
is about what I expected. Again, most VNs don't have voice acting at all, and when they do, this is what you're more likely to get. I can understand feeling a bit misled when the store page simply says "voiced" and not something like "partially voiced." But it's faster for me to just read the lines than wait for the character to get finished speaking them, so I actually prefer this for visual novel games.
is another staple of dating sims. While it can be a pain to realize that making one wrong decision all the way at the beginning of the game affected the ending (//coughs
), it's par for the course. You're supposed to go through and make the "right" decisions to get the most appropriate ending. That's your gameplay. But this is the saving grace of a single route being relatively short, you can go back to correct anything you missed and get your good ending within about 45 minutes if you're fastfowarding through. This is also a game where it doesn't hurt you to explore other routes within a playthrough and I appreciate that. I kept getting worried I'd trigger some sort of argument between Damien and another Dad because I did his two dates first before exploring the others and the game would accuse me of cheating on him when I was just trying to explore as much of the game as possible. Thankfully, it didn't, and that made reloading back to the pre-date 3 saves for everybody's final scenes very easy. That being said...
as a whole is one I don't particularly like. I'm used to the ren.py format, where you manage a good number of saves yourself. The consistent auto saving was very nice, but I really disliked how it would occasionally delete your saves to keep things less cluttered. It likely won't be an issue for you if you're vigilant about your saves, but it's slightly annoying to have to keep checking to make sure your pre-date 3 dadbook save hasn't been pushed into the bin.

I really wanted to give this game a recommendation. If, after reading this, you're still interested: by all means, get it! Just wait for it to go on sale, though.
Anyway, I'm seriously considering requesting a refund for a few reasons I'll outline below, but first, the things I liked about the game:
-The writing was mostly good. I felt like the characters were genuinely relatable and even funny at times (Robert's Dadbook was hilarious, for instance, as was the first "date" I had with him which consisted of him not showing up at all and then, at the end of a day spent at home, the day getting ranked. I laughed out loud).
-The art for the NPCs and backgrounds was gorgeous! The characters all had a smooth, polished look and the scenery was vivid. The music was also excellent and wasn't distracting, which are the two things I really want from games like this music-wise. (And I loved the cameo by PUP!)
-The autosave feature was a blessing, and I like that there were multiple autosave files. At one point, my computer froze and the only reason I was able to continue without losing more than a few lines of dialogue was because of its diligence.
-The ability to create dadsonas is a neat feature. I haven't seen it done much at all in otome games.
-The minigames were charming and enjoyable, and I liked the ranking feature at the end of the date with the neat little bars for different traits that were relevant to the dad in question. There was obviously a lot of care put into the dates themselves and I felt like the game really shined in that respect.
-Dadbook was both a clever and fun way to keep track of dates and communicate with the NPCs. I've seen it done in similar ways, but this felt like a more realistic and intuitive twist on it.
-The approval/disapproval indicator based on your conversational choices was cute and absolutely an excellent way to convey that a character liked or disliked something; both good and bad were instantly recognizable as such.
And, sadly, for the bad:
-The game is very, very short for $15. Three dates per dad? Ouch. I understand that with seven dads, that equals 21 dates total, but I'd honestly prefer fewer dads and more dates with each of them if it's a matter of choosing between the two.
-Were there cutscenes? I didn't see any thus far, but I only got one date in with a couple of the dads, so I guess it's understandable that there weren't any yet. Cutscenes are always nice, though, even if they aren't specifically romantic. Ones of Amanda would've been sweet early on.
-The inability to change the volume for different parts of the game's audio meant that I had to listen to the assorted grunts and other human mouth noises. I personally don't like voicing in otome games. I'd have liked the ability to decrease the volume on those while still being able to hear the music.
-The inability to change the text speed. I read faster than the text appeared and don't like the gradually-appearing text, as I find it distracting. I'd have loved to be able to make the text instantly appear every time without clicking. There were even a few times that I accidentally clicked more than once and ended up skipping past a line of dialogue, which was frustrating.
-While I appreciated the dadsona creator, based on the fact that it was there and that a default name wasn't suggested, I expected the main character to be a total tabula rasa. I was surprised to find that he wasn't and would've loved to have played the character with an intended name and/or appearance, possibly with variations on the latter (Hustle Cat is an example of this). The main character was fun and interesting in his own right, and I would've enjoyed seeing him as a fully-fleshed out individual instead of a surprise personality hiding beneath the appearance of total customizability. It made trying to play as my own dad OC rather difficult, honestly.
-Another note on the dadsona maker: while I appreciate, again, that it exists, the options were limited and some were odd-looking. The eyes were difficult to pick between because a full half of them seemed jokey, there were no beards without mustaches, roughly half of the eyebrows looked angry, and compared to the other characters, the dad looked...flat. Thinner lines and a touch more shading might've helped on that front.
-Yet more on the dadsona front: I wish there was an option to disable the portrait from being seen entirely, as the lack of emoting by said portrait meant that the facial expression didn't match the tone of the text half the time. It was a bit jarring. (My dad OC was smiling at one point while admonishing Amanda for being out past the time she'd said she'd be home and for not texting him that she was safe.)
-About the editing/grammar of the game: while I may randomly capitalize words for emphasis in casual conversations with friends, seeing it done in a video game is awkward and jarring. The game, beer, whiskey, etc.: they don't need to be capitalized. It's weird.
-And finally, the reason I ultimately ended up considering getting a refund on the game: I really, honestly expected better treatment of women from a game marketed towards queer people. I expect the Evil Jealous/Cheating Romantic Villainess in yaoibait, which is why I avoid it and a fair number of straight otome games, but I absolutely do not want to see
adult female NPC as a mean, conniving obstacle in the way of you, the player's, romance. If it was just Mary, the literal only adult female NPC with her own art that I'd seen so far, and there were other supportive or friendly women or exes who also had art, it wouldn't have been a statement.
It was, however, during the first date with Craig that I realized that this was going to be the norm. Amanda pointed out that men and women can be friends, and it felt hypocritical that, as far as the adults went, that simply...wasn't true. At all. I'm hoping that if I'd stuck it out, I'd have seen that Mary and Joseph were equally unhappy with each other in their marriage, but he seemed devoted from the outset and saddled with, again, the only female adult NPC with art who was a less than ideal spouse. If another adult female character revealed herself to be...something other than an enemy? An obstacle? A misogynistic narrative tool to create conflict? Man, I'd have loved to see that sooner.
It may have been unintentional, but making three out of three adult female NPCs (Mary, with art, and Janet and Martha, without it) be barriers to romance is a statement, and one that should've been taken into consideration. Let men and women be friends and please, absolutely do
make female NPCs all romantic rivals or beloved daughters with no variation on those two distinct themes. Friendly exes, queer women, etc.? They all exist and a game marketed towards queer people deserves better than the echoes of misogynisitic yaoibait games.

I'm going to be completely honest. Maybe I expected too much out of someone's first game, but I ended up pretty disappointed. The art for characters (NPCs, at least) is AMAZING, the dialogue made me chuckle a couple times, and I loved the inclusiveness. But there wasn't much else to enjoy.
First off, the background art. It doesn't fit in with how the characters look, and it really doesn't feel like much effort was put into it. One that really bothered me was an aquarium one, where the fish looked like something a 10-year old would draw (it was literally shaky lines for the body, and misshapen circles for eyes. No exaggeration.)
The character creator's art style also stuck out like a sore thumb. Compared to the art for the Daddies, your dadsona was cartoony, and minimally shaded.  Some hairstyles also weren't coloured in properly, with white pixels near the outlines. You didn't have different personality options for your Dad, either. You could pick a muscled body type in the character creator but your Dad would still say multiple times throughout the game that he doesn't like exercising, isn't in shape, etc. He's also incredibly awkward, no matter what. Fortunately, I like that kind of character, but it sucks that it can't be tweaked even a little bit.
The voice acting was comprised mainly of grunting. The volume of some lines were incredibly loud, whereas others were so quiet I couldn't even figure out what they were saying. Also LOTS of text, but that's pretty typical of a dating simulator.
This is more of a personal issue, but with the one bad ending I got I was given a VERY bad first impression of that character, and it really ruined him for me. I'm sure there was a way to go about making bad endings without making the characters feel like complete jerks (this is specifically about Robert though, I couldn't tell you about the other bad endings.) At least one of the "good" endings doesn't feel at all like a good one, either. (I kept replaying it trying to get the "good" ending, only to find out that I actually did.)
It's also very short. You get 3 dates with a character, a few scenes with your daughter, then an epilogue that is nearly the same every time. I put a bunch of hours into reloading save files (which tend to delete on their own, too?) thinking that I was missing something and that there was more to the game. There wasn't. $15 USD is a lot to pay for 3 dates.
I was expecting a lot out of this game, but it's just your generic dating simulator. I tried really hard to enjoy it, because I had been so excited for it, but it just wasn't worth the money. I'd recommend waiting for a sale if you're thinking about buying it.

Only issue I had with the powers was that I didn't find myself needing any of them apart from heal and lightning.  Once you max out lightning you can clear out an entire room of non force users in a second.  It may be over powered, but that doesn't mean it's not fun.  My biggest issue with the game is that the story isn't that good.  It's more just an excuse to give your character a reason to get into all these fights.  On top of that there's a tacked on morality choice at the last part of the game that seems to just exist to give you a reason to replay the game.  Ignoring  the story this is a great game with the best Jedi combat I've ever played.  If EA's smart they'll bring this series back... but then again if they did they'd have microtransactions to unlock stuff they gave you in the old ones for free.

There are a few things to keep in mind: there are tons of bugs. I had to restart from checkpoint a few times (on an elevator below the GDCP most frequently, and once during the Bird quest so I could interrogate someone.) However, I managed to complete the game.
The third bossfight (Deathstroke) is the hardest. I suggest, before you get to The Final Offer (as that's where he'll show up) to get all the combat upgrades you can, including bullet armor as he also has a gun. And master quick fire batclaw, as it's one of the best ways to stop him in his tracks so you can beat on him.
Don't bother fast-traveling, and if you have to (to the batcave and back) bring a book to read or something. The fast-travel sequences are boringly long, to the point where I only did it if I needed to go to the bathroom or something, and didn't want to pause the game.
One other big complaint: a lot of the dialogue is demeaning, and gets repetitive fast. Batman will very frequently interrupt the game to remind you to get on task, even if you are working on the task he wants you to, and during a hostage sequence, the people will say over and over again: "you have to let us out! There's a bomb in there!" I started to ignore the crimes in progress at the end, as it got fairly repetitive, with the dialogue repeating over and over again. (guys robbing ATM, beating on other criminal, turf wars between gangs, turf wars between police, a group beating on an officer for having a brother who works at blackgate, ect.)
I wish subtitles were included for non-plot-related mook chatter, as they were often funny and interesting, but I had trouble hearing all of it sometimes--this is just me, not really the game's fault. It just feels like someone who is deaf who plays this game would be missing a lot of it simply due to not getting subtitles for mook-chatter.
I'm also glad I didn't need to log into windows live to play the game, as it always makes playing the game at college (in-between classes of course) difficult, since they block the gaming port.
Zero Punctuation claims the map is smaller than City. It looks bigger, but it's true--it is smaller. It also claims there's no reason for why there are only mooks around, like that's all Gotham is. Repeatedly, however, we hear the town is under lockdown due to 'increased criminal activity' though it is very noticable that still, there are no female mooks except ninjas.
Now, for a game full of bossfights, I have to give it applause for keeping things interesting.
It got a bit boring/frustrating to beat Bane up THREE times (seriously, we've fought him in every game now) though the third Bane fight did have something interesting (you'll have to use stealth.) Deadshot's was fun, especially when he would point his sniper at enemies and tell them to stop slacking off. The Joker's was a bit jarring due to being intercut with brief images of them fighting together, breaking up the action a bit. Firefly's whole sequence was pretty good, and I enjoyed his "is this bat spit!?" exclamation when he gets hit by a glue grenade. Shiva's battle was nothing new, but nothing frustrating either. Electrocutioner's battle was hilarious. Killer Croc was also nothing new, though he's easier to fight this time around. Anarkay is fairly easy to beat, but not as easy as Black Mask. Mad Hatter's sequence once again paled in comparison to the Scarecrow sequence in the first game, but that is to be expected, but Copperhead helping with that wasn't.
Origins ponders two questions: "should Batman work alone?" and "is Batman's no-kill rule harmful, or helpful?" making the plot just as good as the other games.

Story Time
I was a junior at high school, lowpoint of my life, I was super depressed, and everyday all I wanted was death. I cried myself to sleep every night, and whenever I tried to talk to someone about it, they would just insult me and call me a ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Even my own parents didn't love me, as whenever I tried to tell them how I feel, they shut me off and told me to be normal. I overhear them talk, wishing that I had been put up for adoption. I was bullied at school and had no friends. I was a pathetic husk of a man, drifting to class to class, at this point completely numb all other emotion other than unrelenting sadness and anger at myself. "Why can't I express myself, why must I live like this?" I often pondered.
But one day, one life changing day, I was looking threw the steam store. It was the summer sale, and I had some money for helping my uncle at his farm. I often do it for free out of respect for him, and because he is a nice guy, and it lets me spend time with him, but he said I did a really good job, and gave me some money. I've never really had much money growing up but when ever I did, I Usually bought games. I've always enjoyed them more than other media. They let me be someone who I'm not. Someone who People like. Anyway, I saw this game, Garfield kart. My god this game. Little did I know then, that it would change my life. Anyway, I thought it looked like a horrid game, just to make a quick buck off of a brand. I purchased it, mainly because I wanted to see how bad it was. When I launched I was opened with an angelic piece of music, blowing my expectations out of the water, which wasn't hard to do though. It was at that moment, when I heard that music, I felt something, something I haven't felt in a long time. Something good. I started to play the game, and around the 2nd lap, I realized something, I was in a custom game, and had it set to unlimited laps. I went to exit the game, but as I was about to do it, just seconds away from hitting the leave game option, I realized something. The whole idea of repeating a cycle forever with nothing changing reminded me of my life, going from class to class, day to day, feeling the exact same sadness. I broke down in tears, and left, wishing that leaving that game, would have some effect of my life, and leave my "cycle". I continued crying for hours, and when I calmed down, I noticed something. A track builder. This made me realize that I am in complete control over my life. I am free to forge my own path, and if I had to repeat a cycle, I was going to make sure that it was a damn good one.
When the next school year started, It was my senior year. I had decided after playing garfield kart and my whole cycle revelation, that I can make my own path, and was going to make some friends. There was this guy, Ben was his name, who had similar intrest as me and I wanted to become his friend as he seemed like a nice guy. It was with him that I learned to communicate, express emotions and feelings, and most of all, be happy.
After high school ended, I got something I never thought I would get. A scholarship, a full ride. I was on my school's fishing team, and I was pretty good at it, as I went with my uncle and he taught me how to be a really good fisherman. I never thought I was that good at it though. I went to college to be a game developer. I wanted to give people similar experiences as garfield kart gave me. In class I met this one guy, and he invited me over to come over to his apartment with some of his friends to play some Mario Kart. I said sure and went over. going over there was the best decision of my life. I met 5 people, 4 boys and one girl. This girl was the most amazing women I've ever seen. Everything was perfect about her, her hair, her eyes, and her personality. It was love at first sight. We hit it off really well together at that party, and she was my first real friend since ben. During that party my roommate texted me that his girlfriend was staying the night, and asked me to not come back to our dorm for privacy. I asked the people there and the girl said that I could spend the night with her. I took her up on that offer and went home with her. later that night, we talked. Talked about our past. When I was telling her about my highschool years, and the sadness that came with them, I burst into tears. I couldn't help it. But she didn't make fun of me, like other people would. She heard me out, she talked with me about it, and thus, 18 years of bottled up sadness came out.
It's been 3 years since that night. Me and her are now married, and have a child on the way and if there's one thing I have to say, it's this,
Thank you Garfield Kart.

I'd like to harken back to the words of Jay Wilson, original lead developer of Blizzard's Diablo 3: "No one will remember if the game is late, only if it's great."
I highlight this because I think Yooka Laylee would have been amazing if it had another year of work.
I did like the game for what it was supposed to be, which is a nostalgia-driven remaster for 90s kids; however, I think it requires a bit of eye-squinting and teeth-grinding through the game's obvious flaws that stand well in the way of its pros.
If I were to describe Yooka-Laylee in one word, it would be "deflating". In a nutshell, the game feels unfinished from a lack of playtesting. I'm sure most people know the background of the game by now regarding how it arose, what it aimed to be, and how it met or failed to meet those expectations. I played through BK, BT, and DK64 a bit before playing this game to make sure that I wasn't comparing through rose-tinted glasses. Also, I have heard the argument that this game should be judged for what it is, instead of judging it against BK/BT/DK64. That'd be great if the game didn't make its sales marketing itself as a successor to those games...
I highly recommend watching the following videos that articulate my sentiments with a corresponding example of what they mean.

that addresses the patchable issues. Patchable issues include things like lack of rebinding Keyboard/Mouse controls, adding pause music, better camera control, consistent dialogue skip options, volume control on voices, a "restart" button for the minigames (which was in DK64 18 years ago), and more. Yes, all of those previous issues were included in the final game that was supposedly "finished"!
However, the following issues are not really "patchable" without a different game; they are design flaws. I feel terrible for what I'm about to say. I know that no one sets out to intentionally make a bad game, and I wanted nothing more for this game to be great. I did play it and beat the final boss, but have you ever been playing a game and found yourself just wanting to "get it done"? Because Yooka-Laylee reeks of that down the stretch. Also, the game is too expensive for what it is!

After beating the game and after all the commotion surronding this game died down I feel I can give an honest review/opinion on this game. To begin this is not what it was cracked up to be. When I think of a spiritual successor the precedent set is not just being similar to the game your succeeding, but to modernize and refining the formula, in this case the rare style 3D platformer. When I picked up this game that was I was expecting the obvious flaws with the rare style 3D platformer to be addressed and solved. After playing I look back and feel nothing but dissapointment because of how this game is almost a complete carbon copy of the formula just with a fresh coat of paint on it. I'd like to address one argument though alot of people argue they "delivered exactly what they promised" to support the game. I consider this a bad excuse and argument to defend this game as as I said the rare style 3D platformer has aged horribly and furhter does not excuse not addressing the problems with the formula. Spiritual succesors are suppost to stand on their own two feet and be superior to what they are succeding not be a clone. Now to address specifically what is wrong here.
1. There is alot of tedious and repetitive busywork here. Most of the challenges are bad timed loop sections of varying difficulty, Poorly designed boss battles that flat out aren't fun because of the desin, and especially the transformations which serves no prupose other then to get 1 or 2 pagies, and the cart sections feel kinda unfair and annoying to control. The arcade games to me serve no purpose at all and being way to easy and tedious like most of the busywork I just mentioned. Th
2. The worlds while mostly look great, feel empty with nothing to do even though the collectiable list would say otherwise. The visual communication is bad and even before you expand the world can easily get lost with no sense of direction. World one and maybe World two are arguably the most fun the rest look almost thrown together with bad art design in my opinion. The casino level don't get me started worst world in the game. This makes going through the levels and finding out what to do extremly tedious combined with the actual tasks mostly busywork really bring down the fun.
3. The control's are also sub par. This problem was evident in the banjo games and have transfered into yooka laylee and to me this is inexusable. Flight for example is horrible as the camera along with the controlls make it impossible to fly straight and it may just be me the camera follows you way to closely while flying further hindering control. The transformations also control bad with percise movements all but impossible meaning you accidently say drive off a cliff in the snow stage when you didn't mean to. Alot has to do with the camera which tends to move way to easily without user input which contributes to the control problem mostly.
Now there is fun to be had if your a hard core fan of this but these issues with the game really hinder the experience which is a major flaw with how much of a carbon copy the mechanics of yooka laylee of the banjo games. The bad level design, bad controls, and more make it again only dedicated fans can put up with but even then to me these problems are inexcusable given how much time playtonic had to reflect on the banjo style planformer formula. I do hope there is a sequel with the problmes addressed as I do see promise here but honestly this game does not bring back the 3D platformer or mascot platforming not by a longshot, it only serves those extremly had core fans who can look past the flaws.

I can't say I've mastered this game, and knowing my own attention span vs. the learning curve for Klei games (at least based on Don't Starve) I probably never will.
There are a few bits of weirdness I'm willing to chalk up to the beta (sound effects looping after whatever should be causing them has stopped, strange pathing - like a character making a trip to the top of the ladder, not for supplies, before running back down to start on the next rung of the ladder that he's building), so it doesn't exactly seem fair to count those little quirks as a real 'negative' at this point.
It actually has no real negatives considering what it is.  It's not a simulator, it's not something where you build a stable equilibrium that you can then relax and start exploring in a position of relative safety and comfort.  There's no logical reason to assume that this is a game like that - complaining about it is like buying a copy of Space Invaders and then complaining about the lack of characterization as compared to Final Fantasy VII.  Unless you happen to have the kind of thought process that lets you plan out how you should progress from the beginning, you will NEVER be safe or comfortable.  That is the point of the game, so there's no sense getting upset about it.  I paid for it, after all.  (If that last sentence gives the impression that *I* was hoping to make a stable system and eventually tried to eat my own computer out of frustration, then . . . accurate.)
The characters are cute, the sound effects are each distinct enough that you can get a sense of what's happening just from the audio, the music is whimsical and fits the art style pretty much perfectly.  The research trees mostly make sense, and while it's not too hard to research everything early (if you really focus on it) I'm sure as development progresses, that'll be less and less true.
I guess if I think about it, I can come up with a few little gripes, things that maybe make it more challenging than it needs to be at this point.  Some sort of lateral air movement would be a big help - for god's sake, the icon on "Utilities" is a fan, but I CAN'T BUILD A FAN.  The ability to handle appliances that need water by adding water manually rather than a pipe would be good, too (obviously that wouldn't work for all, but it should be an option for at least some that don't use water so quickly that plumbing is a logical necessity).
All in all, though, those are minor quibbles with what's in essence already a very functional and engaging game.  I'll likely never finish it, but that doesn't mean that I won't at least have some fun failing.

I ended up streaming this monster 3 days in a row for 10 hours each. This game ruined my sleeping schedule I played 48 hours in about 4 days 10/10
.....But seriously, this game is already a huge amount of fun despite being in EA. Premise is: You select three duplicants (your lemmings or so) with the stats you want them to have. The three first duplicants are very important since you can choose them as you see fit, debuffs and all. Then you're inexplicably transported into a chasm and need to survive by building a colony. The game has a fantastic balance between all the necessary ressources, and overdoing it can be costly! (For example, one of the oxygen producers also produces hydrogen, not accounting for this factor costed me my first game.)
You cannot control your duplicants directly, instead you give them orders, but so far it doesn't feel like they're complete idiots. Being able to set chores and tasks on a 1 to 9 priority scale is fantastic as well. For instance, tasks like watering plants, or sweeping debris, or charging batteries, and refueling generators are done automatically. If you want your crops to be the top priority, you can set it to 6 instead of the basic 5. This ensures that they will work on crops before anything else, even if your generators are right beside your bed. If you need a ladder ASAP, set it's construction to 9, and they will literally jump through flames to get it done as fast as possible.
Everything you'd thing be a factor is a factor. Germs. Oxygen. Food. Stress. Decor and quality of life is super important. Even heat. It's the first time I see these elements all being present in such a glorious harmony. Since you're in a closed space, heat has nowhere to go. And it's not like some other game where heat radiators are a yes/no factor, instead, heat is a cumulative and dangerous type of energy. You need to vent it out or plan for it ahead of time. If you put too many batteries in the heart of your base, temperatures will rise and keep rising up to the point where crops will die, and you with them. Machines also have a thermal breaking point. Same with electricity: If you put too many things on one circuit, it will break. and that's bad. That's how I lost my second game.
Even gasses are more realistic than it's counterparts. The gasses and liquids are counted as grams. You can actually overpressure rooms, which can have nasty effects on your duplicants. They have weight too. It's not perfect (CO2 tents to go down-right instead of just down) but it gives you a nice idea of how to do. That's how I lost my third game, there were so many gases overflowing in my base, oxygen couldn't replace it. In the case of carbon dioxide and Chlorine, the best thing to do is either to trap it somewhere via filters, or dig a huge pit for it to accumulate there on it's own. Both CO2 and Chlorine are ressources per say and they have their uses. In fact...
recycling your ressources is super important. Doing a base that is functional, pretty to the eye and which can recycle most of the things is a real challenge to accomplish. You will fail a few times. It is however, hyper satisfying once you set up a network of functioning power lines, and your gasses are going where you want them to go, and your farms are up and hey you finally have a functional bathroom with showers and everything. Rare are the games which gives you all of these in such a great balance.
It's totally worth it's price. I've been the lucky one and bought it 40% off, but trust me when I say that some full-price games of the same genre sometimes give you less. And knowing Klei, they'll just keep injecting content till you're tired of it. Oh and there's a mod workshop. Not garanteeing quality mods yet (it's pretty much language mods right now), but hell it's a nice bonus. Go enjoy yourself!
