This review is essentially a reminder....to myself.
Most of the time when I write a review, it's not just preserving a memory, it's putting a time-stamp on it.
Eventually I'll play through Max Payne again, or maybe I'll play through its sequels. When that time comes around, I want to have something to compare and contrast with. This is also so that I don't fall into making the same discussions, or focus on material that I've already covered in a previous review.
It's my personal Hell.
Speaking of Hell, Max Payne sure went through some♥♥♥♥♥♥didn't he? He was practically touching the American Dream, but then it all fell apart in a New York Minute. His blood-soaked tale of revenge is about as good as 3rd-person shooter storylines need to be. The plot is great, the characters are memorable, and the writing is artsy...well the good kinda artsy. It's enough to make you care, enough to make you imagine, but not so into itself that it comes off as pretentious trash. Max Payne is a bit more cultured than you'd expect from a homage to John Woo films and Noir comics.
But let's focus on the game itself. Max Payne 1 is a classic. Despite being released nearly 14 years ago, it still holds up and is great fun today (grab the widescreen fix). These days we tend to demand more from our videogames. When we pay however much it is that we're willing to, we expect our videogame to do a lot. The third-person shooter is no longer allowed to just be about shooting people, aliens, robots, mutants, or all of the above. There has to be stealth-elements, a vehicle, some turrets, and a segment where you walk slowly and wait for the exposition to finish.
Max Payne 1 is almost quaint by comparison. There's some platforming, a moment where you don't have a single gun, and stupid pet tricks (shooting switches & trip-wires). Otherwise all you're going to do be doing is shooting people. Walk into a room, bad guys appear, and you shoot them. All of the encounters are scripted, and if your eye is quick enough you can sometimes see thugs appear out of thin air. Shockingly, this standardized approach manages to maintain its high level of quality entertainment, for the 7+ hours a first-playthrough is likely to take.
Where similar games fall to the depths of mediocrity and banality, Max Payne rises above. This is precisely because it gets the primary form of interaction (shooting people) absolutely perfect. Let's start with the bullet. Your mission is to put bullets into enemies while trying to keep them out of Max Payne. There's none of that hit-scan nonsense in this game. While you can't always see the bullets as they travel, you know where they're coming from, and where they're going. These bullets travel at the same speed, cut through friend and foe alike(always a plus when bad guys accidentally shoot each other), always leave an impact. This isn't something you're liable to notice when you start the game, but over time you will acquire a new-found appreciation for bullets and the mechanics that revolve around them.
The most important strategy is to keep moving. Enemies tend to aim for your head/chest, so you're most vulnerable when standing still or getting up from a dodge. Gun-battles are short and to the point; either you die in a couple seconds, or the bad guys die in 10-15 seconds. Making shots count is important, especially if you're using the slow-motion dodge. Bullet-time can also be very effective when used properly. It's not free, and you'll get yourself killed trying to play Neo, but it's good for those times where you need a moment or two to figure things out, even during a gun-fight. Otherwise, your best strategy is liable to be F5/F9ing your way to success (though it's not so effective on the hardest difficulty).
The most interesting aspect of Max Payne is that once you think you've finally grasped how the game works, it's about to end. This is where you move onto the next difficulty, and see if you've really learned anything. When a game focuses almost entirely on one element, you will find yourself focusing on that same element as well. With every firefight you learn something new, you calculate how many shots you can make with each gun while dodging, you mull over every situation and what you could do to not only survive it, but to own it. The controls, mechanics, and everything else that makes the genre work is done in spectacular fashion.
I'd write more, but I think you should play this game and see for yourself. Although I would be shocked if you haven't played it already.

(Spoilers)  I would think with my history of video games that I would have played this classic sooner but lastly I haven't.  I recently beat the game and am generally pleased with it.  For the time it was released (2001) It was impressive.  Playing it now some of the graphics seem dated, especially the character models, however that doesn’t mean it’s a bad game.  The story is excellent and is what kept me playing through wanting to know how it all ended.  The “cut scenes” were a nice change from typical video games, being done in a graphic novel type of way.  The cinematics we’re innovative at the time and to this day still hold up for some pretty cool moments (that final helicopter crash).  Game play was pretty fun, the main thing being the slow motion bullet time.  It had a very Matrix feel and made the game play that much more fun.  That being said the big problem I had with the game was the difficulty.  I don’t mind a games difficulty if it’s the players skill and not the games fault.  This was not the case, I found it extremely frustrating the amount of health lost when hit with enemy fire yet the amount of shots it took to take down that enemy.  It only added to the frustration when I would die having to start back at the beginning, even more annoying was the un-skipable cut scenes that I saw countless times.  I found myself hitting escape and saving my game after every group of enemies I killed.  This for me really ruined the immersion of the game which, for a game like this I felt was important.  Maybe not everyone had this problem and it could just be me.  That being said after thinking about replay value, sound, story, gameplay, graphics, everything I could think of I would give this game a 7.5/10

I love this game for 2 player local co-op.  We use 2 Steam Controllers and play via my Steam Link.
This is a fun little pool game that is great for players of all skill levels.  The controls are very intuitive and have been easily picked up by my 75 year old father and others.   We all like the music and find it contributes nicely to the overall relaxing nature of 2 player pool.
One of the great features is the versatile aiming aid which shows players the exact path of the cue ball and object ball as they aim and adjust spin and power.  As players get better they can shorten the length of the aid to increase the player skill required to make the shots.  In 2 player local co-op each player may choose the length of the aiming aid independent of the other player.  This means experts can have a very short aiming aid while less-experienced players may have a longer one.  This is a nifty way to handicap games that doesn't make new players feel pandered-to in my experience.
A couple of negatives are that the physics are a bit questionable at times, and the aiming aid can permit some absolutely ludicrous shots that would be impossible outside of a physics simulation.  The single player career seems to be nothing more than a way to purposefully gate content... even though you bought the game if you want all the locations and wingdings unlocked you have to buy the "unlock" DLC or slog through the laborious and completely unfun "career".
All in all, I recommend this game for local co-op play and pretty much no other reason.  Several times I've checked out the online lobbies and couldn't find anybody to ever play with though YMMV.

"REMEMBER, ABILITIES AREN'T INHERENTLY GOOD OR EVIL... IT'S HOW YOU USE THEM
-Jedi Academy is the follow up to Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast. It uses the same assets and--with the exception of two new lightsaber styles--has mostly the same gameplay. The graphics haven't aged well and weren't that great to begin with. The script is poorly written and the acting is terrible. Level design is hit or miss, with many platforming sections that just don't work and one vehicular segment that is god-awful. There's a lot wrong with this game.
-But stay with me here.
-Jedi Academy, despite it's numerous flaws, is one of the most entertaining Star Wars games in existence. It, along with Jedi Outcast, nail lightsaber combat with a very responsive system where every directional movement cooresponds with a unique saber slash. The force abilities aren't balanced that well, but they work well in the flow of combat.
-You will enjoy destroying many stormtroopers, as they are the general cannon fodder of the game. After that, you will enjoy fighting dark jedi who become increasingly more frequent as the game goes on. Play your cards right in the end and you will be fighting four or five at a time in frantic combat.
-Along with the saber you can use a variety of weapons, but really they're only useful for certain segments. 99% of the game will be spent chopping people up, and that's okay.
-The story isn't all that compelling, though it has a few parts with great ideas. Kyle Katarn is at your side for a large portion of the game, though often you'll feel annoyed that you aren't playing as him. While you get to create your character's appearance and saber style, you have no control over who they are. Jaden, the main character, is essentially a blank slate who has been victim of incredibly lazy writing. It's hard to tell who to blame for the shoddy voice acting, but it seems like the direction of the script really didn't give anyone room to work with. All the story cutscenes use in-game engine graphics and animations, so it leads to very wooden conversations and some hilariously bad acrobatics.
-If you can get over the half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥story you'll get to experience some great combat and a unique handful of levels that go across several different planets. Even if you don't like Star Wars, this is something you could probably get into. Anyone with an appreciation for melee combat done right will find something to like here. Even if you don't care for the story, there's always online multiplayer (which I hear is still active) to participate in.
FINAL VERDICT
-Lots of flaws with this one, but it's a rough gem. Not many Star Wars game are this enjoyable. If you're looking for a good fix for Jedi action, skip buying the new Battlefront and give this one a try. It's a better game--cheaper too. While I'd ultimately say Jedi Outcast is the better one, Jedi Academy undisputably is more accessible and consistently entertaining. Give it a shot.

It took me a couple of tries before I could give this game a fair shake. Even after the hype had waned for this game, the mechanics of this game were difficult to look past initially. As mentioned, I played this game largely ignorant of the hype and community surrounding it, and it took me a few tries before I could invest myself properly in the game, but once I invested myself in the game, I did not regret doing so.
Undertale is a curious game in many regards. Though it is not the first to do so, most other games before it would be hard pressed to incorporate pacifism as a main gameplay feature and execute it so well.  As an addendum to that, the game hardly shys away from berating the player for choosing to kill. There is a boldness to the game, that it takes the player actions seriously that is investing and immersive. The game manages to react accordingly to the choices made by the player and in doing so it strengthens the player's bond with the game. The weight the player's actions have on the world is empowering but not without consequence, a hallmark of good rpgs.
Mechanically speaking, Undertale is rather basic, the core of Undertale's gameplay revolves around bullet hell mechanics, maneuvering a heart (representative of your soul) away from a variation of projectiles and obstacles. The game thankfully attempts to add some variation, to this, by adding blue attacks, which are thwarted by not moving, and orange attacks which are bypassed by moving through them. There are also moments where the game will add the ability to fire projectiles, or turn the bullet hell formula more towards platforming. The variations are certainly appreciated, though the base mechanics alone, are serviceable at best. What's there is decently polished, but I've often got the feeling what I was experiencing was just a simplified version of something I played before. It's a game that offers me a simplified version of Battle Garegga and calls it a day, seeks to placate me with a watered down Galaga and then tells me to reserve my gripes about gameplay or the bare bones platforming segments.
However, the mechanics differ based on how you react. If you're going the pacifism route, you'll be faced with something of a little puzzle on how to spare your opponent. Usually that devolves into making the right menu choice in act, or if it's a boss, choosing the right act and then outlasting their attacks against you usually. That's the gist of it anyway, with some mild variation here and there. The puzzles presented usually are pretty straightforward and hardly difficult to figure out, which doesn't lend itself well to replayability. The other option, is to fight, and that really just devolves into a timing mini game with very little actual variation on that mechanic. The game can occasionally be difficult, but it's hardly a consistent difficulty, the game is quite forgiving and unfortunately, some of the final bosses are laughably easy.
Turn based RPGS have historically had issue making gameplay that could stand well on it's own, and I don't think Undertale is an exception. It tries harder than most RPGS before it, but unfortunately, the gameplay still leaves me wanting more, I can't find myself confidently saying the gameplay can stand on it's own.
Fortunately, Undertale takes precedent from Turn Based RPGS in all the right ways too. The game tells an investing story, full of charming characters and interesting personalities. The game is full of creative designs and interesting encounters and tops itself off with an endearing, quirky, self referential humor about itself. It does tend to wear it's Earthbound influences on it's sleeve at times, which can cheapen the experience, but otherwise, I'd be among the many to laud this game as having an excellent and heartfelt story with lovable characters, oh and the music is quite catchy. [Minor spoilers ahead] I can in fact admit that I, being an ugly bag of mostly water with pathetic human feelings, could not bring myself to do a Genocide run. The thought of having to kill Papyrus (a video game character) offended my primitive illogical human brain. Of course, that means that, I as a reviewer, have failed at my job of giving a complete review, and thus any criticism forwarded towards me for that is completely warranted, perhaps such offense is on the grounds for completey invalidating my review, and that would be understandable.
However, I think that very fact serves as a testament to the charm and personality of Undertale's characters.
Although, Undertale's universe does have a few aspects that hurt the experience. Particularly, certain characters will break the 4th wall a few times and reference the Save and Load feature, as well as talk to the player directly. A certain boss fight runs with the idea in fact, and this embracing of totally shattering the 4th wall hurts the experience somewhat and manages to rip the player away from any immersion that was there. Tonally the game is fairly consistent save for a single level near the end of the True Pacifist run, which jumps form cheery and jubilant to snapping into dark and disturbing territory without any sort of appreciable foreshadowing to this tonal shift. It cause this segment to stand out quite obviously, while the level itself and the mood given isn't bad, it's jarring.
The Genocide run as I mentioned is not something I could do, but judging from what I watched and the feedback many have given off, I'd be inclined to agree that it seems significantly less enjoyable than a standard run, especially since player control is often taken away at many key moments. (Ironically my watching of the run is referenced by one of the game's character's verbatim as being even worse than players actually doing it!) The Genocide run is also notable for cutting a fair bit of the standard game content and perhaps the most interesting of all, completing a genocide run permanently alters future endings, the pacifist run notably becomes tinged with a creepypasta twist. On some levels, it feels a bit cringey and juvenile in execution, perhaps because of the striking similarity it has with some creepastas, but I still found the concept overall interesting and furthermore, it heavily reinforces the theme of consequence, which I find quite laudable.
There is some replayabiltiy to be had, particularly if you want the True Pacifist ending, you'll have to play through twice. Though, aside from the possibility of a Genocide Run, any further replayability loses it's value rapidly. The aspects that make Undertale stand out are it's universe and characters. Most people will come to Undertale for the story, and remarkably few will claim they came for the mechanics or gameplay. Undertale is not a bad game for having it's mechanics supported by it's story rather than the other way around, and as such it's a game you'll fondly remember, rather than a game you'll still be playing by the end of the year for it's gameplay.
Undertale is a good game, but in this reviewer's opinion, great might be an exaggeration. I'd opt instead, to describe it as a memorable experience.

I don't often go out of my way to review games. But this game? As a a gamer in the first person shooter era - and especially being an American - I feel this piece of art should be experienced unspoilt by everyone. No other game will make you feel so strongly connected to a storyline as this one will.
Spec Ops the line has fairly average third person shooter mechanics. This sounds like a negative: it isn't. Why? Because Spec Ops: The Line is a commentary as much as it is a game. Since the story is what makes this game gold, I'll avoid saying too much, but the game does a good job of making the player aware of the struggles on all sides of war. On top of this, it continually references the destructive military culture of America, and questions the player whether they are truly okay with the way media treats war in general.
It's all done in a way that simply poses a question : Do you feel like a hero yet?
Really great game, worth the buy

An RTS set in the future and in space. Large fleets of warships exchanging fire. Everything from small frigates to extremely large super carriers and battle cruisers. Sounds good? I thought it did. Watched a few videos, read the reviews, and thought I would give it a go anyway. The entire premise sounds fantastic, but the game has one really fatal flaw that makes it almost unplayable. I will explain further on.
+ Diverse amount of ships, creating strategy and counter strategy
+ The environment looks really nice
+ Particle effects look not too bad, explosions and lasers look pretty awesome in huge fleet battles
+ Upgrading system for the fleet and your carrier allow for different playstyles
+ Limited amount of ships that you can build, forcing you to choose the best ship for the job
+ Music is pretty good, though the effects sound a little washed out
+ Replayability is pretty good via skirmishing, even without multiplayer
+/- Graphics could look slightly better, what I mean is if you zoom all the way in on a ship, it looks really pixelated. Not a huge deal, but the textures could have been better.
+/- No grinding, and only a limited amount of scrap collected per mission make it hard to have a good fleet all the time. Upgrades can be resold for full value, but the upgrade phase is before the next mission, and without any kind of brief it is hard to anticipate what you would be facing.
While there is only one negative point I can think of so far, it is the biggest and most glaring issue with this game. It take the playability of this game down to almost zero. All of the positives and neutrals do absolutely nothing to allieviate this one, and only one, negative point. Here it is,
- Ship pathfinding and obstacle negotiation is
Seems like that would not be a huge deal? Well, this is a strategy game, in space, with spaceships. And the pathfinding is terrible, and they can't fly their way out of a wet paper bag. I got this in a bundle package, and it seemed to be a pretty decent real-time strategy game. Unfortunately, the game doesn't translate the strategy aspect too well into a game. Why? Because it has a fatal flaw: THE CONTROLS ARE TERRIBLE. This is a game-breaker folks.
Yes, it's a 3D environment, yes, you need 3-axis controls to work with it properly, but that's not what this game provides. Instead, it provides linear movement keys in the different directions with a counter-intuitive mouse "rotate" that is a camera-rotate instead of a field rotate, making the player end up having to do a lot of unnecessary motions to really get a 3D control.
And... at the same time, as I found out the hard way, your playing field is still... badadum-tish... painfully 2D. So, you end up with all the pains of a clumsy 3D camera to have a single-plane game.
That's not even talking about losing centering and focus all the time on the units you're supposed to control...
It doesn't matter that the environments look nice or that the tutorials are good or that the missions available are varied and interesting if the game fails miserably at what it should be focusing on: providing an efficient interface for the user to make tactical decisions, preferably in real-time.
The game tries to remedy this by having a tactical pause, so you can pause the action at any time to redirect ships and fleets to the desired points but... that kind of defeats the real-time part of RTS. And in the end, you end up doing this a lot: Pause the game -- fight with controls, selections and clumsy orders to send the desired ships in the correct formations to do the right thing -- unpause, watch the scene unfold a little -- pause again, rinse and repeat.
That's just not fun to play.
Perhaps, if the game developers get smart and adjust this setup, they can make it work -- potentially the only real way I see this game setup work is if it would be rewritten for multi-touch screen, or completely re-do the way the game is controlled and presented. The terrible mouse+keyboard interaction at least doesn't work.

On the surface, Cory In The House looks like your average licensed TV Show handheld shovelware. But underneath that, is one of the biggest revolutions the medium has ever seen. Funny, smart, deep, timeless. Read on to find out why this stands as one of the finest licensed video games of all time, or indeed, one of the finest video games of all time. You play as Cory, the kid from the TV show who finds himself living in the White House. The gameplay is simple; you need to sneak around the various rooms and do various tasks, which often involve talking to someone or getting to a certain room. It sounds simple, but between the deep stat management systems, varied character patrol routes, and the amazing dialogue options, the gameplay is top-notch, making the likes of Metal Gear Solid pale in comparison (including on storytelling prowess, more on that later). The mini-games like the lock-picking are so deep, they could be sold as full games themselves. The graphics are life-like, the character portraits are so realistic you will think you are watching the show! I haven't seen such good graphics on a handheld game, ever. The audio is as good as a DS game can sound, it's all in there, from the sound effects to the catchy theme from the TV show.As an audio-visual experience, Cory in the House delivers the best on the DS. What truly shines however, is the dialogue and the smart humor in the game. The dialogue here is comical to kids, but truly hilarious to adults, which are more likely to get the more subtle jokes. And yet, it's full of life lessons and themes that resonates to all of us, children and adults alike. It's like watching the best Pixar film of your life. The writing here may live on as a timeless example of comedy. What they have pulled off here may be one day looked back as "the Shakespeare of comedy". Overall, this game is a hidden masterpiece, one that will change the way video games are made. Just give it time. For now, you can be privileged enough to play this masterpiece while the rest of the world is still unaware of its implications and future impact on the medium. They will catch up, eventually.

When I was 18... 18 years old, I saw for the first time in my life... I saw an image of clarity. I saw a comic strip... a three panel comic strip that, though simple as it seemed, changed me... changed my being, changed who I am... Made me who I am...
Enlightened me...
The strip, Garfield, the comic strip was new... no more than maybe a month and a half since inception, since... since coming into existence... and there it was before me in print, I saw it... a comic strip... What was it called?
Garfield.
The story here is of a man, a plain man. He is Jon, but he is more than that... I will get to this later, but first let us say that he's Jon, a plain man.
And then there is a cat... Garfield.
This is the nature of the world, here. When I see the world, the politics, the future, the... the satellites in space, and... the people who put them there...
You can look at everything as a man and a cat... two beings, in harmony and at war...
So, this strip I saw; this man, Jon, and the cat, Garfield, you see...
Yes... hmm...
It is about everything. This... little comic is, oh, lo and behold... not so little anymore.
So yes, when I was 18, I saw this comic... and it hit me all at once, its power. I clipped it, and every day, I looked at it, and I said "Okay... let me look at this here. What is this doing to me? Why is this so powerful?"
Jon Arbuckle, he sits here, legs crossed... comfortable in his home, and he reads his newspaper... The news of the world, perhaps... and then he extends his fingers lightly, delicately... he taps his fingers on an end table, and he feels for something...
What is it? It is something he needs, but it is not there.
And then he looks up, slightly cockeyed, and he thinks... His newspaper's in his lap now, and he thinks this...
Now where could my pipe be?
This... I always come to this, because I was a young man... I'm older now, and I still don't have the secrets, the answers, so this question still rings true, Jon looks up and he thinks...
Now where could my pipe be?
And then it happens... You see it, you see... it's almost like divine intervention, suddenly it is there, and it overpowers you...
A cat is smoking a pipe.
It is the man's pipe, it's Jon's pipe, but the cat... this cat, Garfield, is smoking the pipe... and from afar, and someplace near, but not clear... near but not clear... The man calls out... Jon calls out, he is shocked. "Garfield!" he shouts.
Garfield. The cat's name.
But, let's take a step back... let us examine this from all sides, all perspectives... and when I first came across this comic strip, I was at my father's house... a newspaper had arrived, and I picked it up for him, and brought it inside.
I organized its sections for him and then, yes, the comic strip section fell out from somewhere in the middle, and landed on the kitchen floor... I picked up the paper pages and saw, up somewhere near the top of this strip... just like Jon, I was wearing an aquamarine shirt.
So I thought, "Ah, interesting. I'll have to see this later." I snipped out the little comic, and held on to it... and five days later, I reexamined it... and it gripped me, I needed to find out more about this. The information I had was minimal, but enough...
An orange cat named Garfield...
Okay, that seemed to be the lynchpin of this whole operation, yes. Another clue... a signature in the bottom right corner, a man's name...
Jim Davis.
Yes, I'm on to it for sure.
So... one: Garfield, orange cat, and two: Jim Davis, the creator of this cat...
And that curiously plain man.
I did not know, at the time, that his name was Jon. This strip, you see, had no mention of this man's name, and I'd never seen it before.
But I had these clues; Jim Davis, Garfield.
And then I saw more, I spotted the tiny copyright mark in the upper left corner. Copyright 1978 to... what is this? Copyright belongs to a... PAWS Incorporated...
I use the local library and mail services to track down the information I was looking for...
Jim Davis, a cartoonist, had created a comic strip about a cat, Garfield... and a man, Jon Arbuckle. Well, from that point on, I made sure I read the Garfield comic strips, though as I read each one, as each day passed... the strips seemed to resonate with me less and less...
I sent letters to PAWS Incorporated, long letters, pages upon pages... asking if Mister Jim Davis could somehow publish just the one comic, over and over again... "It would be meditative," I wrote, "the strength of that."
Could you imagine?
But... no response... The strips lost their power, and eventually I stopped reading, but... I did not want my perceptions diluted, so I vowed to read the pipe strip over and over again... That is what I call it, "The Pipe Strip."
The Pipe Strip.
Everything about it is perfect. I can only describe it as a miracle creation, something came together... the elements aligned... It is like the comets, the cosmic orchestra that is up there over your head... The immense, enormous void is working all for one thing, to tell you one thing...
Gas and rock, and purity, and nothing.
I will say this... When I see the pipe strip... and I mean every single time I look at the lines, the colors, the shapes that make up the three panel comic...
I see perfection.
Do I find perfection in many things?
Some things, I would say... Some things are perfect... and this is one of them. I can look at the little tuft of hair on Jon Arbuckle's head... it is the perfect shade... The purple pipe in Garfield's mouth...
How could a mere mortal even MAKE this?
I have a theory, about Jim Davis...
After copious research and, yes, of course, now we have the internet, and this information is all readily available, but...
Jim Davis, he used his life experiences to influence his comic...
Like I mentioned before, none of them seem to have the weight of the pipe strip... But you have to wonder about the man who is able to even, just once, create the perfect form, a literally flawless execution of art, brilliance! Just as in a ward... I think there is a spiritual element at work...
I've seen my share of bad times and... when you have something... Well, it's just... emotions, and neurons in your brain, but... something tells you that it's the truth...
Truth's radiant light.
Garfield, the cat? Neurons in my brain, it's... it's harmony, you see? It... Jon and Garfield, it's truly harmony, like a... continuous, looping, everlasting harmony... The lavender chair, the brown end table, the salmon-colored wall, the fore's green carpeting, Garfield is hunched, perched... perhaps with the pipe stuck firmly between his jowls... His tail curls around. It's more than shapes too, because... I...
Okay, stay with me... I've done this experiment several times.
You take the strip. You trace only the basic elements. You can do anything, you can simplify the shapes down to just... blobs, just outlines, but it still makes sense...
You can replace the blobs with magazine cutouts of other things, replace Jon Arbuckle with a... car parked in a driveway sideways, cut that out of a magazine, stick it in... Replace him there in the second panel with a... a food processor... Okay, and then we put a picture of the planet in the third panel over Garfield...
It still works.
These are universal proportions. I don't know... how best to explain why it works, I've studied the pipe strip, and analyzed Jon and Garfield's proportions against several universal mathematical constants.
E, Pi, the Golden Ratio, the Feigenbaum Constants, and so on... and it's surprising... scary even, how things align. You can take just... tiny pieces of the pipe strip, for instance, take Jon's elbow from the second panel... and take that, and project it back over Jon's entire shape in the second panel, and you'll see a near perfect Fibonacci sequence emerge...
It's eerie to me... and it makes you wonder if you're in the presence of a deity, if there is some larger hand at work...

As far as the "first game" this company has made this is a good start I'd say, but the fact that senior Rare developers made this sets the bar a LOT higher than usual. For what it is (that being a platformer in 2017) it's good, controls extremely well, environments look beatiful (although the design isn't all too good), and the initial Rare charm is still there in some of the writing and characters.
That being said it's worth mentioning the faults, of such there are a few that could be a deciding factor in wether or not you would want to buy this game.
The first thing you'll notice upon playing this game that could be aggrivating is the camera. Now it goes without saying that there are a lot of games with high praise that have a less than pleasant camera experience (examples being Super Mario 64 and LOZ OOT), so this doesn't RUIN the game just sours the experience.
Second thing that you may or may not notice after running around for a bit is that the environments, even though they're very nice looking, are confusing as hell to navigate efficiently. The amount of just running around from world to world trying to figure out what to do or where to go chewed up close to 1/3rd of my playtime. This annoyence isn't lost within the actual worlds either it still persists. You'll find yourself wondering if you've been to certain places already and being intimidated by the size of the levels in general. Only to find out that half of it is inaccessable until you collect enough pageies. Not a lot the devs can do to remedy this problem, which is a shame because this was the games biggest downfall in my opinion.
The third thing I found to be a fault is more of a personal thing so take it as you will. The delvelopers of this game clearly know their fanbase, a lot of them were huge fans of Rare themselves and such games as Banjo Kazooie, Conker, JFG, etc. So they sort of use this knowledge to their advantage in ways that might highten the experience for some familiar with the heiritage of the company but closes out others who are new to these devs and/or these types of games in general. Plainly speaking there is a lot of nostalgia factor to this game and its incredibly clear. You may not mind this but for me (even being a huge fan of the developers since childhood) it sorta of came off as "hey look remember when we made those games?"
In conclusion I'd say that this game has a lot of initial charm to it, as well as great controls and an okay cast of characters. It can be fun to play and shows the real skill the developers at Playtonic have in terms of making a game look and feel good.....buuuut if you're looking for that game that rekindles your passion for platformers just wait until this company (or others) can get a better idea of what the consumers want and/or it gets a little cheaper.

Back when I learned that a 3D platformer was coming out for the PC, I was suprised. Then they said it was a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie, a game I've never played but recieves high praise from everybody. It was time to give Yooka-Laylee a shot.
This game is so happy! Which is a good thing. So many games nowadays have a dark atmosphere, this game takes a fresh break from that. Bright colors, great music, interesting worlds, it makes something special. The main characters, Yooka and Laylee, are very well animated making them feel alive. They have a can-do buddy dynamic that's very satisfying.
When interacting with the world's characters, Yooka and Laylee have something to say, with many funny and punny lines, and jokes too. Yooka is always polite, and Laylee has witty remarks that made me laugh.
There are interesting worlds to explore, entertaining music, and various challenges in each. I don't agree with the major criticisms out there. My only criticism would be that some of the challenges and minigames are very difficult, which requires playing them many times. It's the most enjoyable simulator for pool that I've played on steam. My favorite pool game, so far, has been Virtual Pool 4. This game is a bit more arcadey and social driven than that game, but it is still really enjoyable for someone that is into playing pool.
In short:
+ Good graphics compared to other pool games
+ Entertaining game modes
+ Multiplayer
+ Unlockables
+ Trick shots
+ Social content
+ Creatable content
+ Pretty much endless replayability since it is pool
+ Easy for a beginner trying to get into a pool sim
- Sometimes a bit buggy when trying to move or shoot with the mouse
- A little bit arcadey for pool especially when comparing physics to real life or even VP4, but forgiveable since it isn't trying to actually be a hardcore sim
- Sometimes a bit more focused on everything else except for the actual game of pool itself
Overall, it's a great game for the price. I'd definitely would recommend this to a friend interested in pool sims.

Pros:

I tried so hard to like this game, i really did. But instead of a fun and engaging story i ended up going through one route without a satisfying payoff.
There's BARELY any romantic moments in this game (and for a dating simulator that's very dissapointing). Kissing and other stuff is set to the most minimal setting possible. I picked one route but later left it on in the background cause i lost interest and did something else. It feels like such a let down cause i thought this would be a great game to represent the LGBT community but it felt more or less of a let down. I wouldn't call this a Dating Simulator but more of less "hanging out with Dads": On the route that i choose it consisted of hanging out with Brian (The only character i actually liked compared to everyone else so i had my hopes up) whom you do some fishing and some friendly competition. In the end route --SPOILERS-- you set your differences and just kiss...yep...that's it, there's nothing else. Of course later on after the route is completed and you get to the epilogue it just has you and Brian just talk for a bit, hug, and that's it. There's no emotional moments, nothing that really makes you feel connected to a character. There was just no actual pay off that makes you say "That was a good story". It felt more rushed liked i was in a Disney Princess film: no time for development and no time to actually relate to them. Take for example Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 5 (or 4, 3, etc.). While a strange example to compare to this game they're both at least similar in terms of a "Dating Sim" aspect. In both games there's options to be friends with anyone but you also get to choose who you want to have a romantic route with. However, in Persona 5 you get to learn about the character's history, problems, and experience in the world that help you develop a more long lasting relationship with the character (until you beat the game of course) but even then they give you a good send off. In Dream Daddy, you get to talk to Brian for a bit and do some nice mini games but i wanted to know more about him, his backstory and why he was so competitive, but instead the game does a time skip and sends you to a few months later for the epilogue where the level of the relationship just feels the same. I would even bare to say that Morenatsu has better character development than this game. Other examples would be Niles from Fire Emblem Fates and the romantic options in Fallout 4 (even when these routes didn't matter on the gender of the protagonist you at least had a connection to the characters whether it be relating to their backstories or something deeper).
I'm not homophobic as I am gay myself but this game just feels mediocre and doesn't live up to the title. I expected romantic moments and lots of emotional scenes but ended up just talking to a random NPC without having a connection to them. You expected something at least longer of a romantic route but each character route gets 3 scenes (each of which only last for 30-45 mins) until they ship you off Disney-Princess style and say "YOU'RE TOGETHER CONGRATS!" without a satisfying pay off.
I wouldn't mind waiting a lot longer if it meant diving a lot more into each person's backstory and personality. I'm not hating on the developers, you guys did a fantastic job on the artwork, music, and many other aspects of the game (customization, choices, etc.) but i would've loved to have more development in the characters i chose. Also, where's the Voice Acting? If i recall most of the voice acting consisted of random grunts or noises from the character that complimented the next line said.
It might be a fun game to others but i just felt so uninterested in the characters and expected something better. Is it dumb of me to expect something out of a dating sim called "Dream Daddy"? Pretty much, but i just wanted to throw my two cents in if anything. I know Game Grumps isn't known to take things seriously (I've been a big fan of them ever since they started back when they played their first game "Goof Troop") but i guess it's just me expecting too much from a game. I guess it's just not my cup of tea, sorry.

Hitman 2016 is a distillilation of the entirety of its legacy into a very fine and tasty blend, that makes it the best in the Hitman franchise.
For those living under a rock, Hitman is basically an "Assassin" simulator - you're dropped into an area with one objective: Assassinate your Target(s). The game then lets you go about finding, planning and killing your prey. You primarily infiltrate areas by donning disguises and trying to blend in with the NPCs
The star of the game are the levels - they are absolutely huge AND dense. Exploration is a critical part of your experience as you discover new routes into the target's mansion or a hidden Safe House which also doubles as the Surveillance room.
Each level is a giant sandbox and that sandbox has hundreds of NPCs going about their routines - these routines can be messed with and exploited. Set off a fire alarm...and the fashion show attendees walk out to the nearest gathering point.
The Disguise system has been refined and is perhaps the best version in the franchise yet. You can disguise yourself as almost anyone - Security, Wait staff etc. - and each disguise has its perks - Dress up as Security and you can carry a weapon in plain sight, dress up as a Waiter and you can poison drinks without alarming anyone.
If you're a Gardener and you're roaming around the Kitchen...you WILL be told to leave. Its very logical and the system doesn't break easily.
Furthermore, there is the 'Enforcer' NPC type - these are NPCs who belong to your disguise group and WILL get suspicious (and finally alarmed) if you linger around them too much. It adds a surprising amount of depth to the infiltration gameplay.
I'll end with an Anecdote:
Paris
I pull the fire alarm. The guests attending the show walk out in an orderly fashion and the security staff start sweeping the area for disturbances
My target and his personal bodyguard, however, make a run for it. Excellent.
I know exactly where they are headed, I know exactly what I have to do. Disguised as a Bodyguard, I patiently wait at the basement Security Room. My prey arrives - the Bodyguard is an old hand and knows all security staff by name...he starts to get suspicious.
I start walking out, remoted detonator in hand - I push the button as I walk out. The plastic duck filled with C4 takes care of my target. Contract completed.
As I'm heading out to the exit on the first floor, I alarm a Bodyguard - another old hand - he calls after me: "Stop! right there!"...I keep walking...I lure him into a maintanence closet I know to be empty and put up my arms in surrender - the moment he is in range, I have him disarmed and KO'd.
The nosy BG taken care of, I casually walk out the main door.

If my display picture is still displayed as "3d Realms", and my username is still the same, then some people may think my review is biased, so I'll give it to you straight.
I'm guilty of not being able to play Max Payne until 2013. I also only became part of 3d Realms in 2015.
That being said, I experienced the series firsthand early in the year, and it blew me away. I also have no "nostalgic" value for it, so my review is based on how I played it and experienced it as a gamer in modern times.
This game is amazing, but takes some getting used to. Old-school health system, and extremely fast paced action make this an interesting title, where even low difficulty may take some modern gamers by surprise. The game is set in an awesome dark 1990s Noir setting with lots of interesting story to hear, and the awesome writing of the legendary Sam Lake (writer for Alan Wake by Remedy), coupled with the occasional bits of humour and witty one-liners.
Lots of fast-paced gun action with bullet time makes for a gritty New York cop story, and definitely something worth experiencing. The story extends over the next two games (Max Payne 2 and Max Payne 3).
If you want some oldschool (read: CHALLENGING) action for a change, this game is the one for you. Don't expect regenerating health and the ability to take 10000 bullets without dying whilst jelly jam runs down the screen. You will get shot, and you will probably die quite a few times on your first playthrough, but the experience is made fun by the awesome setting, bullettime action and the witty (and occasionally humourous) dialogue.
I wouldn't recommend this if you want a more modern cover-based shooter with good graphics.

Undertale. I am sure most gamers have heard this title's name and if you haven't played it, you may wonder what all of the fuss is about. I was one of these people until I finally decided to give the game a go a few months ago. Upon first look, Undertale doesn't look like much. What is true when the gaming industry started is still true today....how a game looks doesn't mean it is not a great game. You cannot judge a book by its cover and in today's age when we have 100 GB games with ultra realistic graphics it still remains true. Undertale may not be the most visually appealing game out there but if you judge it by that alone, you are missing out on one of gaming's most memorable rides. I will keep this as short and sweet as possible. After 47 hours in Undertale, I still feel it has more to offer. The story is simply captivating, it will test your every emotion based on the choices you make. This is one of the most immersive games I have played in quite some time. The writing is SO good, especially for the main characters of this game, you FEEL what they feel. You feel like you are in the game, in their world. The battle system is like nothing I have ever seen before. A totally unique take on turn-based RPG gameplay that will test your emotions, morals, reflexes, and memorization every battle. Add to this one of the best and addictive sound tracks I have heard in a game in a long time makes for a truly and wholey, unique experience. I listen to the OST of this game even when not playing it, that is how good it is. I highly recommend everyone giving Undertale a try but especially RPG fans!

Spec Ops: The Line is a very unique game, it has cliche cover based gameplay and the standard Middle Eastern terrorist thing going on, but it slowly gets very, very, very good. The gameplay is boring and people will insist that's intentional to catch you off guard with the plot, but I don't buy it. Still, this unique experience makes up for it; if you like Gears of War style gameplay, you'll like this. Sand can occasionally be shot at through glass to kill your enemies and all the setpieces feel nice. Sound is good, realistic gunshots and explosions and voice acting are all good. The main protagonist is voiced by Nathan Drake, which is good because Nolan North is a skilled voice actor. The plot, which I heavily advise you to go into the game knowing nothing about, is heavily inspired by Heart of Darkness and, without giving away anything, is a mind♥♥♥♥ of impressive proportions. You play Martin Walker, a Delta Force or so soldier who's on a recon mission in disaster affected Dubai, when your mission turns to finding survivors of military and civilian nature. Your teammates who, while written well and excellently voice acted, are simple shoot-enemies-respond-to-simple-order AI cyborgs. That said, they are a very welcome addition to the plot and I suppose the gameplay since they don't hinder you. Radioman, a secondary antagonist of sorts, is written and voice acted to perfection as well, he's the kind of enemy that you love to see, yet want desperately to kill. The game is normally priced at 30 dollars at the time of this writing, which I can understand you not wanting to shell out for B gameplay, but you should put it on your wishlist for the future.

I was excited for Yooka-Laylee and immediately preordered it when I was able to. I even bought the digital deluxe version with the soundtrack. I was
excited. However, it pains me to say that I cannot recommend Yooka-Laylee. While the initial couple of hours show great promise, the rest of the time as you finish off the other 4 worlds is horribly unpolished.
I wish I could sum it up in a couple sentences, but I really can't. There are just so many little problems that show that the development team haven't learned anything from the past 20 years nor do they play their own game.
One of the biggest problems for me is the quizzes. I know this has been beaten to death before, but they really are awful. There's no indicator that you're about to be hit with one, many of them are incredibly pedantic like naming a specific character when the characters rarely say anything interesting, so I found myself skipping the dialog all the time.
Is that my fault? Well, that's up to you to decide. However when you beat the final quiz Laylee makes a "witty" comment about how you won't need to pay attention anymore for the awful quizzes. It's a desperate attempt at tongue-in-cheek humor but when the quizzes themselves aren't enjoyable the joke comes off as insulting rather than amusing.
Ok the quizzes are bad, but is that it? Well, no. The game is also plagued with a variety of minigames in each world. There's one that's supposed to a retro arcade game and another which is the cart one. All of the arcade ones vastly outstay their welcome, especially if you're trying to beat the high score. Prepare to play something you don't want to. The cart one is also unfun. It's novel the first time, but they appear in every game world which means you will be repeating it at least 5 times, perhaps more depending on your skill level.
If they were just unfun that would be one thing, but the game is so poorly designed that it turns what could just be a speedbump into something that will likely frustrate you. You cannot restart these unless you die. That means that if you make a small mistake, you cannot just press start. What happens when you die? You get a loading screen and then annoying dialog asking you why you're awful. Well isn't that just pleasant. Then you click yes and have another loading screen. Thankfully on PC the loading screns are really short, however it's hard not to look at this as just annoying. Both the arcade and the cart ones do NOT let you see what your target goal is on the HUD. You only see your current score. Additionally for the cart one, there are brakes and a boost you can perform. They have a short cooldown timer however there is NO HUD indicator for them. WHY????? bad. Expect to have a bad time.

A surprising stand-out part of the game is all the interactions with your daughter Amanda - she's such an endearing character and you just want to be the best dad you can be for her.
In terms of negatives, at this time it's really unclear how to get a good ending with some of the dads (Joseph, for example), but I think that's just part of the difficulty of the game and completely normal for a dating simulator. I also agree with a lot of people that more options in the character creation would be great. In some places like the mouth and eyes there seems to be more joke options than serious ones.
All in all, I highly recommend this game if you like great art, hilarious dialogue, and corgis in scarves. Just be prepared to feel some things.

Despite the game running late on release, I wasn't even upset. The game devs were on top of it and very apologetic. They promised a game without major hiccups and bugs. Of my seven playthroughs, I saw none. There were a handful of typos, but honestly, who cares. I'm crediting the game for its theme, writing, interaction, and intrigue. Not their spelling errors which are easy to glaze over when putting it into the game.
Each dad had a very unique story. One I totally bombed, and plan on going back through to figure out where I went wrong. The rest of the dads had very well rounded characters. Each dad also had unique children to play by their side. Your interactions with dads and children led to different pros and cons in each storyline. It was really fun, and quite the challenge to chose the right answers.
One of the very unique things about this game took me by surprise. The visibility of transgendered people. There was an option in the very beginning for you to be a female to male dad. Never before have I encountered such an option in games I've played. So thank you, game designers. You guys took a big leap, and I feel it's going to pay off.
The minigames. Talk about panic inducing. I was taken off guard each time because they were not what I was expecting. Was I mad that they were super hard? No. I was laughing every time because if their suddeness and their difficulty. They were cheesy and fun.
The voice acting? I was expecting more. But, just because my expectations were high, doesn't mean it had to be delivered. There was enough to add simple elements to the game. The end of date quotes also made me chuckle.
Will I play this again? Heck yeah. I'm not even done playing it yet. I want to unlock all the secrets and dad endings. Overall, this cute, short visual novel brought me much joy. It gave me what I expected from a dad on dad dating game. Humor, excitement, mystery, grunting, and realllly bad dad jokes.
I look forward to these guys making another game. As a gay dude, I really thank you guys for showing we're just like everyone else.

Dream Daddy was a highly anticipated title this summer. You, a widowed father, and your daughter Amanda move to a new house and are neighbors to a bunch of hot eligible dads. Coming from an array of personalities and backgrounds  one of these studs will become your dream daddy. It's up to the player to jump into the shoes of your dadsona to both help your daughter in her senior year of highschool before she heads off to college and revamp your lovelife.
The game is fairly progressive in repesentation. It's nice the fact that characters and their sexual orientation or identities were not a heavy focus. In fact the first interaction with one of the dads has him asking if the missus is around, if you had picked that you were widowed to another man you correct him and it's pretty much the end of that. There's no real big shocked reaction which is what I truly like about it. Being widowed to another man percieved to be normal.
There are many other pros to this game as well. The artwork and soundtrack is very pleasing. Your daughter Amanda is very loveable you two have a very good father/daughter relationship. The story is fairly charming. A number of the numerous dad jokes are timed and implemented well. The personality of the other dads and their kids are unique and varied.
While yes I do in fact recommend this game, I feel as if it was still lacking in one major area.
The relationship between dads feels rushed on some routes. While there are super charming and feel good moments I feel myself wanting more. One thing I have really enjoyed from some previous sims I've played in the past, was that there was a story after the game. You find out what happens to the couple after they get together. It would be nice to learn about your dadsona, the dad of your dreams, and their kids after you get together and Amanda is in college. Even if it were a little tidbit. I feel like that would've made the relationships you earn in DDADDS much more rewarding.
On another note there was a glitch you encounter that is funny and terrifying. The delightful twins from down the cul-de-sac can get stuck on your screen while loading a save. While at first it's funny, it quickly becomes very unnerving. It took a while to figure out how to fix it. (To fix this reload to previous saves before the glitch. Might take a few tries)
TL;DR:
Pros:
-Progressive
-Artwork is lovely
-Music is great
-Character personalities are unique
-A good number of the countless dad puns are timed and implimented well
-Amanda is a great daughter
Cons:
-Ending of your relationship with other dads is lacking. I want to know more about after getting together. What happens in the near future, how the relationship is working out, etc.
-The twins glitch is terrifying

Ever wanted to know what it feels like to be in a Jedi duel ... Then play this game Multi-player. Its a very old game now, but is still mechanically the best feeling online melee fighting system i have ever encountered (and i have encountered many)
There is however an issue, if you are new to this game the learning curve is rather large.  Many have tried to play and very few acctually bother sticking around.  Main reason is its not satisfying playing 1000 fights and losing every one hands down without feeling you even understand why.
Most skill based games follow similar formats these days, FPS for example has not really changed format ever .. you just point a cursor at something and click .. pretty simple really.
This game is unique in that you have to genuinly learn attack, defense, timing and movement to stand a chance of winning a fight.  Its same principals as learning a martial art, and there are some real masters in this game.
If you can't see past your ego whining because your getting your butt whooped all the time and get annoyed at the games obvious desire to undermine your belief that you would instantly make an awesome Jedi, then you will simply get frustrated by JA.
However if you decide to stick with it and learn the ways of the lightsaber, have the patience to train real skills over time,
The satisfaction is like no other game i have ever come across.
The fights are amazing if you know what you are doing, with so many ways to mix in combat styles, each person plays slightly differently and if you keep an open mind you will learn from every fight. They just look and feel awesome.
If you are thinking about this game there is only one question you need ask yourself ....
"Do I have what it takes to be Jedi?"

if your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Before I get into the review, a little history:
Garflied Kart was originally announced in 1997, around the same time as its now conisdered "sister game" Duke Nukem Forever. The game immediatley recieved immense attention, the trailer nearly broke the then barely funtioning internet. People were excited to finally be able to play the first fully licensed Triple A Garflied game.
But then, tragedy struck. In April of 1998, the development team [REDACTED] suddenly dissapeared. No trace was left of them, and after a thorough year long investigation by the government, it the team was determeined to have died. All hope was lost for Garfield Kart, and as Duke Nukem Forever development staggared, doubts started to set into people's minds.
Th epublic tried to keep hope, but when 2012 hit, and Duke Nukem Forever was realesed, people lost all hope for Garflied Kart. They believed that if it ever even did come out, it would just be like Duke Nukem Forever, an overhyped pile of trash.
But they were wrong.
Little did the public know, [REDACTED] was apparently cyber attacked by what some people have speculated to be crazed Mario Kart fans, who didn't want any true competition to flood the market. It is rumored that these activists were hired by Jim Davis himself, though no news of whether this is somfiemed yet, or why he would want that. But after the cyber attack, [REDACTED] went into hiding for ever a year, until they were found by Humongus entertainment, who was willing to fund them, as long as they went into hiding an dnever revealed their original name. They developed the game in secret, and after nearly two decades, it was finally released, to the joy of the community, and the wrath of it's enemies.
Now as for the review,
Pros:
+game is beautiful, art style isn't realistec, but looks more amazing than anything I've ever seen before
+Charcters are vivid, I have some sort of connection with each charcter, I even feel for the villans of this game as well as the heroes
+Gameplay is fast paste and demanding, looking away for merely a second will result in your character's death, may be too intense for some
+Amazing story, I haven't felt this emotional about a plot since watching The Godfather, I refuse to spoil any of it here
+Replay value is off the charts, You could play over the campaign twenty times and find something new each time!
+The amaount of hidden content and secrets in this game is amazing. The puzzle pieces in the game lead to amazing hidden maps and secrets about Garfield, Jim Davs, the developers, and the history of the world itself! There's far too many to list here, but the most recent one I found is that if you take the shout Jon makes when using a lasagna, and slow it down 800%, you'll find that it's actually a secret recording of JFK planning his fake death witrh the government and his killer!
+Multiplayer is very solid
Cons (yes there actually are some):
-The 3DS port is far superior than the PC port. Mianly because there were actual ways to hack into the 3DS system to find hidden files within the hardware to find more hidden levels and evil world secrets. Many of these had to eb either changed to just puzzle pieces or scrapped entirely because of the limiting nature of the PC.

Initial Impressions: The best of Absolution, combined with the freedom offered in Blood Money. If you tend to go for the core missions in a game you'd better steer clear of this one, as it only has two tutorials and one level. Paris is huge though, with plenty of replay value just to finish off the challenges and the side contracts, but don't just take my word for it: Buy the Intro Pack and decide for yourself. Hey if you don't like it, you've saved plenty of your time and money by foregoing the whole bundle.
I wrote a review before this one but a slip of the fingers removed all of the text before I could copy anything, bummer. So short version it is...
Gameplay is quite like Absolution, with the NPC/guard suspicion-o-meter wheezing wind every time you get closer to trouble but what's odd here is that 47's disguise can trick some of his similarly-uniformed peers: If 47 takes up a Palace Staff disguise, only some of the other Palace staff will be able to see through it, and these guys are known to 47(how? superior intuition?) marked with a dot above their head. Instinct is now unlimited, but it doesn't allow you to trick guards at close range, like Absolution. However you do have enough time to make a fast walking pass about three meters away from a same-dress person before you start raising eyebrows. Not sure if this system ultimately betters gameplay, and I'm still undecided at ten hours.
Since Paris Mansion is so big and rich it can be a little off-putting at first to explore all the little nooks, but once you've got your key points memorized(service corridors, scaffoldings, locations of vital tools and guards that are easily pacified out of sight) the other contracts/challenges just build on your base knowledge, and the confusion slowly vanishes. Compared to Absolution the gameplay feels toned down in terms of skill requirement, to compensate for the open-world experience. The puzzle element however is present at its par best with other Hitman games.
Two of the new gameplay elements are worth explaining here, the first of which is Opportunities. This is basically the game holding your hand and guiding you through one of the many murder methods available in the level. Some of the plans are complex so it's worth having this feature around, with Diana's commentary supplementing the opportunity-revealing conversations you overheard. It's not full-on nanny mode though, as you have to use your head to convert the Opportunity into a kill yourself. I predict it'll be a mainstay for the series, especially as the plot gets lengthier maybe you get more choices, more Opportunities to execute from one base Opportunity. Just airing it out in case Square hears me..
Next is Escalation which is a short mini-mission, repeated five times with increasing difficulty. So far I haven't felt as though I could do with just jumping ahead to the most difficult part, and five times is relatively easy  compared to the >1200 retries I've gone through in total for Absolution. Certainly getting the first try down perfect will make subsequent escalations just entertainingly more difficult. If you're sloppy though you will be punished further down the difficulty scale. I can't attest to the staying power of this one, but it seems promising so far. Perhaps a variable escalation with some levels having less and more retries is the way to go. Again, if Square is somehow tuning in.
Overall, if you're a fan of the Hitman series, I definitely recommend this. I hate the new pricing and pre-booking stuff as much as the next guy, always-online DRM even more but if you're willing to overlook these setbacks you'll find a gem of a game.

By no means just as good as said films, but for a computer game (which often focuses on things like controls ahead of storytelling) it is a well-written story. It puts your character in the centre of something he did not anticipate, and you along for the ride.
After you've finished the game, if you also go back and review the events that lead up to the end, you will notice little details here and there that hint at the hows and whys of the story.

My only complaint about this game is that it is at times challenging to the point of frustration even on the lowest difficulty setting. For this reason, I would not recommend it to those who are not already familiar with the RTS genre.
That issue aside, this is a very good game that I would strongly recommend to RTS fans. It's a fairly old school experience that reminded me of the original StarCraft and the old Dune games, but while it's not especially innovative, it's not blindly clinging to the past, either, and it has enough modern ideas and mission diversity to not feel like retread of old games. It's an homage to the RTS greats of the past, but not an attempt to ape them.
The story is pretty strong -- though suffering slightly due to technical limitations -- and the soundtrack is one of the best I've heard. Ambience is something RTS games tend to struggle with, but Ancient Space does a wonderful job of making you feel isolated and alone in a vast and often hostile universe.
Plus it has Phlox in it.
All in all, a game more than worth its minimal price tag.

If you're looking for a solid, classic-style 3D platformer, Yooka-Laylee delivers exactly that experience. It's a care-free adventure through colourful and vibrant worlds, with many quirky characters to interact with along the way.
Yooka-Laylee is ALMOST BUT NOT QUITE as good as the games it takes inspiration from (Banjo-Kazooie, Banjo-Tooie) and I say that with the smallest amount of regret. As fun as the game is, there are a few things that it just doesn't quite do as well as its predecessors:
--Level Design: The worlds don't feel quite as cohesive, with layouts that feel a bit haphazard and NPCs that don't always feel like they belong, leaving the worlds to feel a bit messy, and not as believable as as they could be.
--Characters: The NPCs and even some of the main characters feel slightly less interesting and compelling than their Banjo-Kazooie counterparts.
--Overall Polish: Just minor details, but I think the game could have benefitted from another few months of development, to smooth some rough edges here and there. Having said that, there is an upcoming polish update from Playtonic (at the time of writing this) that will seek to address some of these issues.
I think it's only fair to compare this game to the ones it's meant to recapture, and I think it does a pretty good job. Despite a few shortcomings compared to the original Banjo games, Yooka-Laylee is still a GREAT GAME, and I expect that it will only improve with time and patches.

I grew up with Spyro on the PS1, and never had an N64, so when I heard of this game, I was excited not only for a new collectathon, but also to experience the work of the devs behind the other half of the platformers I never got to experience, without sacrificing controls or graphics.  In all I was very pleasantly surprised with the result, and enjoyed my time through 90% of the game, with the few hiccups just being for a couple pagies near the end.  In short, I give the game an 8-9/10 and give varience because your enjoyment can be somewhat linked to puzzle solving.
First the controls.  I played on a gamepad, so if you plan to play this on keyboard disregard this and form your own opinion.  I enjoyed them, they were smooth and the rolling was like if spyro's charge had a tighter turn radius.  That said, the depth of field caused me a little trouble in races when jumping for butterflies, which can of course just be chalked up to me having bad sense of depth.  Other than that, the aiming in first person is nice, the reticle doesn't snap back after tilting upward like some other platformers, most of the transformations handle alright, jumping feels generous enough to keep things moving rather than testing, and swimming nowhere near other games in terms of bad handling.
Secondly the graphics.  This was a big point for me because the world is stylized, meaning it can hold on its own for much longer than just trying to make things realistic and become dated later on.  Along with that point, you get a good sense of what you can and can't interact with in the envrionment, barring a couple puzzles, as well as terrain you can stand or roll on, or just need to avoid.  This translates well with you being able to climb on a great many things a creative person might see as an alternate path or shortcut to the same destination, or just exploring your limits in these often expansive worlds.
Third the progression. The power progression in the game is the nicest I've ever had the pleasure of playing with by far, with constantly getting new powers, often several at once, and they only keep building up your ability to make the terrain your ♥♥♥♥♥ as you learn to use them in new way to get extra distance or height, until the last power which straight up gives you full control over navigating the map, more than any platformer I've ever played can attest to, and that level of freedom should be commended. On top of that, the level progression is also refreshing, as you can either opt to continue playing in a level you're enjoying, or just try to blaze through the game to get all the powers you need to 100% each level before testing the limits of them.
The only places where my enjoyment was brought down a bit were the Kartos minigames and Rextro minigames essentially, and the last slide puzzle in the over world. ♥♥♥♥ that slide.  Anyway the only reason I didn't like these as much is because I'm not a big arcade player, I don't generally like score attacks and doing the same thing over and over in order to better myself through sheer repitition doesn't appeal at all.  By all means, both start off innocently enough, with both in the first world doing a good job of easing you in, but that difficulty curves upward faster than an exponential equation, and require near-perfect playing of the minigames by the last world.  That said, it only diminished my enjoyment of the game slightly because 1; I opted to do a 100% run, and 2; I'm not into arcade style games, everything else passes with flying colors in my book.
