I have to say, while I have quite a few criticisms of the game, the one really, really good thing about it is that it feels, looks and sounds like a Banjo-Kazooie Game.
At times it almost feels like Kirkhope is almost plagiarizing himself, to the point where the first world music kind of sounds like the first world from Banjo Tooie. It's very bright and colorful and every major character fits perfectly into the game and their respective worlds. In terms of control I probably haven't played a platformer like this since Banjo Tooie. It's just so close in terms of control feel. The only complaint in that regard is really in terms of camera control, because it really is absolutely dreadful at times. It's really weird how many of the same people, that were able to create a better camera in the N64 era, now suddenly seem to struggley with it.
Another criticism I have is that the team had some great ideas that they didn't really execute that well. I really liked the idea to expand the worlds, but they shouldn't allow me to expand worlds by simply collecting a few pagies. Or at least make them more. I only saw the first world unexpanded, as I could expand the other 4 immediately when I reached them.
The other problem that comes with this is the backtracking. If you are smart you simply do everything you can each world and then revisit each once you have all the moves. But some people who may not be too familiar with games like that may find it very tedious.
You could easily have solved both issues by only unlocking the expanded worlds after reaching some kinds of switches after the 5th world and incorporating the backtracking more into the general flow of the game. Of course the unexpanded worlds should be solvable completely with all the moves you can have at that point (which they may already be, again I never played another unexp. one after the first).
I also think there were too many different NPCs.  Some of them also lacked in character. I really liked Trowzer and Rextro, but I still can't remember that squid doctor who transforms you, mostly because she has unmemorable lines and is just not that interesting design wise. Those three were all recurring and as I said especially Rextro and Trowzer generally worked for me in that context. But Kartos was also in every stage. And that weird sheld too. and you usually have three or four local characters, some being just local clones like snowmen or shopping carts, but some others like that alien invader who seem like they could play a major role in a multi pagie quest have a couple of lines and give you maybe two pagies. It seems to me like they went the Tooie route instead of the BK route in that regard. Banjo and Kazooie didn't have nearly as many characters as it's sequel and that alone helped making them memorable.
But let's also have a critical look at the main cast, starting with Yooka and Laylee obviously. They are clearly intended to be Banjo and Kazooie, but also not really. Banjo was kind naive and nice, where as Kazooie was sarcastic and mean at times, but both Yooka and Laylee are pretty similar. Laylee isn't really the problem here, but Yooka seems to be closer to a Kazooie at times than a Banjo. I also think both of them have too many lines, some being pretty unnecessary. Overall they are fine, and I honestly expected to dislike them.
Now to the other side, Capital B and Dr. Qwhack (probably spelled him wrong). I really don't like Capital B, he seems really forced as a villain. He has some good lines, but overall he appears kind of bland. The fight at the end doesn't help him either, being more of a game of patience than anything else. Qwhack on the other hand seems like he could have been a great villain, and I really liked his quizzes. I really hope he gets promoted in the next game, you can do so much with him in terms of machines.
Now finally I want to talk about the worlds a little bit. The first world is still my favourite, especially once it's expanded. On the other hand I found the Ice world pretty boring. The idea with the Isometric palace is pretty nice, but the fadeouts make traversing it kind of tedious. Now that I mention it, the fadeouts are very stiff in contrast to BK and BT, where you felt like you appeared and you could almost immediately move. Here you appear, wait for the camera to adjust and then you can move. After readjusting the camera manually, because instead of appearing close behind you it always shows you walking out of the loading zone from the front.
But let's get on with the worlds. World 3 is also not that special, but world 4, the Capital Cashino, was really fun. Same goes for the Galleon Gallaxy. Just really good ideas done pretty well. The one issue in all worlds though is finding all of the collectibles. For one it feels almost like 200 quills isn't actually enough to fill these worlds. That's probably what made the cashino so great, because adding the coins kind of filled the world with more stuff. Still, it's amazing how this game feels more like BT in regards of Note collecting despite Tooie reducing the notes from 100 single notes to 20 5-notes and one twenty. Here every single quill is an individual, and while I like that it lacks the feel of Kazooie where you could just rack them up quickly after another due to the sheer world size spreading them apart.
I really liked the ghostwriters, even though I'm not sure anyone ever tells you how to catch them. Once you know it's fine, but it can be really frustrating to wonder why you suddenly catched one.
I think at this point I've written more than enough, but I could probably even add more.
In general I would say this game is well worth it's money, it's incredebly fun when everything comes together and only mildly annoying when it doesn't (that reminds me, I said I liked Rextro, but not all of his games are exactly good). If you liked 3D platformers from the early 3D era this is a game for you. If you never played one I feel like this is a fair introduction. It's not the best one, but it reflects the strength and weaknesses of the genre pretty well.

A good attempt by the folks at Playtonic. Yooka-Laylee is made in the vein of Rare's classic, Banjo-Kazooie. There are many similarities, but also some distinct differences.
Instead of collecting honeycombs, you now collect "Pagies," golden pages from a pirate treasure book. The main villain, Capital B, is a large bumble bee who has stolen the pirate treasure book to make his superiors wealthier. The protagonists, Yooka (the green chameleon-looking lizard) and Laylee (the purple bat), have similar traits to Banjo and Kazooie. Yooka/Banjo are relatively clueless and neutral, while Laylee/Kazooie often insult NPCs with their more direct way of communication. Golden feathers are present, instead of music notes and the characters work in tandem, similar to Banjo and Kazooie. Jinjos are now colorful ghost-looking things that require you to capture them in certain ways.
The main difference between the two franchises is that with modern technology, the levels can be larger. Once you collect enough Pagies, you can expand worlds to unlock new areas (and thus, more Pagies to capture). While this seems like a good thing in theory, it actually makes the levels larger than they need to be. Some levels certainly pull this off better than others, but Worlds 1 and 5 get really convoluted once expanded. It's not like Banjo-Kazooie, where you can theoretically be dropped anywhere in a level and know exactly where you are (provided you've played the game before).
Additonally, you see a lot of the same NPCs in each World. While some don't seem too far out of place (Trowzer, the move vendor and Kartos, God of Ore), it's a bit jarring seeing Dr. Puzz (transformation NPC) and Vendi (tonic vendor) ripped from one world and stuck into another. Most world-specific NPCs (snowmen, shopping carts) lack personality. I really wish Playtonic spent more time creating a wider cast of world-specific NPCs, instead of cramming all the main NPCs into each world.
Exploration in this game is fun. You'll enjoy running through new areas and seeing what's around each corner. However, it can get to be a bit much after a specific time period. After 3-4 hours, I'd need to stop and play a different game. I didn't experience this while playing Banjo-Kazooie. Overall, exploration is fun, but not perfect since navigation can be difficult in places.
Also, Kartos sections are a drag. They're 2D side-scrolling minecart levels (like Donkey Kong Country had), except you can accelerate/decelerate and shoot a cannon (3-second cooldown). However, instead of only needing to finish the level and collect a few KONG letters for an extra reward, Kartos has you collect a certain number of jewels in order to receive his Pagie. World 1 and 2's Kartos sections aren't so bad, but because the required number of jewels increases with each world, these sections get longer and longer. World 3's Kartos section is about 2 minutes long. The issue is that there is little room for error on these sections, meaning you can be 90 seconds into a run, make a small mistake, and not get the Pagie. You have to slowly learn these sections in order to collect enough jewels, while not falling off the map (not super common, but possible). Also, the cannon sucks. More often than not, it fires straight into the ground for me and I hit an enemy, losing precious jewels.
The other part of this game I really don't like are the Duck Quizzes. Capital B's main minion, a duck, has at least two sections (haven't quite finished the game yet - I've just expanded World 5) where you're asked 10 questions to advance to another part of Hivory Towers (the hub world). Get 3 wrong and you have to start all over. These quizzes aren't difficult, but I missed numerous questions rapidly tapping A to advance duck boy's dialogue. I just don't really like the quizzes, since it takes you away from exploration and platforming to scroll through lines of text and select the correct answer.
Finally, I'm not a huge fan of the hub world, Hivory Towers. There are Pagies to collect here, which is nice, but similar to the expanded versions of Worlds, Hivory Towers can be difficult to navigate. Especially after you take a week off from the game.
I know it seems like I'm complaining a lot about Yooka-Laylee, but it's really a solid 3D platformer. However, since it comes from the old team at Rare, this game is gonna get compared to the masterpiece that is Banjo-Kazooie. I feel like the smaller, more numerous and varied worlds in Banjo-Kazooie are better than the 5 expanded worlds of Yooka-Laylee. At the end of the day, this game is a hub world, a green island world, ice world, poison swamp world, casino world, and space world with a whole lotta stuff jammed into the map once it gets expanded. The Pagies are numerous and varied, but I'd rather the worlds be more condensed.
If you like Banjo-Kazooie, this game is worth a shot. Just don't expect it to be quite as good.
TL;DR: Yooka-Laylee is like Banjo-Kazooie, but with 5 really large (and slightly congested) Worlds and a few annoying concepts thrown in here and there. Still a fun game. If you're skeptical, wait until it's $20.

The folks from Rare have made a worthy successor to Banjo-Kazooie with this one. It's the classic 3D platforming and collecting you would expect, with modern polish on the controls and graphics.
Opinion on cost: Wait for it to sell for ~$20 before you decide to buy it, unless you know for sure that this is the kind of game you'll enjoy. $40 is a bit steep for this kind of game, given that the graphics aren't anything mind-blowing and a typical playthrough is probably ~15-20 hours.
Pros:
-Top-notch performance; 144Hz of higher with an outdated GPU (GTX 780Ti) and an old i5-4670k (though it's overclocked)
-Tight controls, as you would expect in a platformer, but they feel even better here than they did in Rare's old 3D games on the N64. A huge imporvement.
-Great music!
-Flawless controller integration makes this a perfect game for Big Picture mode (console config) and a big TV.
A few cons:
-Playing with mouse and keyboard is a miserable experience because you can't remap the controls. The controls on keyboard are also not as fluid because keyboards have no analog joystick...kinda mandatory.
-No manual saving (you need to do something to trigger autosave in order to be sure the game is saving your progress)
-No advanced PC settings... you can only set resolution and overall graphics quality. No individual settings or target monitor settings to be found.

millions: Banjo-Kazooie Nuts & Bolts.

Max Payne was the originator of the film noir PC game. It combined elements of mystery intruige and shock very well. The opening scene in which Payne's wife and baby daughter are killed is more than enough to draw sympathy from gamers for him. It also acts as a fine incentive to blow the bad guys away.  The quest for justice and revenge is well told and the gameplay is well defined. The slow motion system allows players to create excellent moments of killing gangsters. The death poses are well choreographed and the set pieces are excellently designed. The music is a mixture of dynamic and classical. Max can't do any of the more innovative attack moves that Max Payne 3 introduced, but leaping forwards, to the side, backwards, rolling, are still available actions to perform.
Before Max Payne, there were no games that were such effective pieces of transmedia. After, came all of them. They would not have been without Max Payne. Any action and Film Noir film fan will like this game. It is both fun to play and has a story that is very suspenseful, inventive and startling throughout.

Pros:
-Massive nonlinear level
-Wide range of tools/disguises
-Can turn off/on features like instinct/map/objectives
-Art style that stays true to the series
Cons:
-Offline/online save games are seperate
-PS4 exclusive contracts
-Disconencting from the internet takes you to the main menu
-Need to wait for a prompt(button press to pop up) to do almost any action, which can be buggy.
-Extremely small difference between graphic settings
Bugs/glitches:
-The remote explosive falls through the world 50% of the time
-Guards sometimes see through the floor/walls
-NPCs sometimes fall partially through the floor not allowing you to drag their body
-The button to push people standing close to a ledge doesn't always show up.
-Both DX11 & 12 have lighting, crashing, and freezing problems on certain PCs.
-Kills that would otherwise deduct points for bodies found, witnesses, etc do not if you leave the mission(escape) simultaneously.
Personal Dislikes:
-Killing someone who witnessed a crime doesn't erase their observation from the final score.
-Accidents can trigger both bodies found and non-targets killed.
-Garrote and lethal injection do the exact same thing. (Can't use lethal injection to poison drinks)
-No blood outside of a couple select (bladed) weapons
-Can't push people at will or down stairs
Personal Likes:
-Feels like a true successor to Blood Money
-Original voice actor (David Bateson)
-More opportunities for accidents than previous games
Verdict:
I recommend this game because despite the cons, bugs, and dislikes the game is still very fun. Potential to be the best game in the series is there if the bugs & cons are fixed, and a few tweaks are made to the scoring system.

Dream Daddy is a fun dating simulator that focuses on Dad on Dad romances.
Pluses:
+Player character has a personality. All to often, dating sims create a rather bland or simple player character. This one has a lot of personality - though it may not be your own.
+ The daughter character is not annoying.
+Fun dialogue. While the game isn't fully voice acted (there's a lot of humming and grunting, when you fast forward through dialogue, it sometimes sounds like an orgy) the dialogue with characters feels unique. The dads aren't just carbon copies of each other.
+ The potential dating partners are actually varied. There are some I really liked, and some I just plain had no interest in. Just like real life.
+ Intriguing plots for characters. While the endings for some of the dads come out of left field, their plots and character arcs are, for the most part, interesting.
+ Fair amount of locations. Some dating sims only offer a few locations or background. This game offers more than I am used to seeing.
+ The game focuses on Male/Male relationships, which is exceedingly rare in the gaming world. It also allows for the possibility of bisexuality in both the player character and some of the datable dads.  This can be appealing in and of itself given the lack of general options out there in the dating sim world.
Negatives:
- Low Replay value. You run into a lot of repetition in the game itself.  In fact, the developers knew this because there's literally a fast forward button you can use to skip scenes until you need to make a decision. If you're a casual player instead of a trophy hunter, just save the game after you've met each dad for the first time. That way, you can date away without worries and without taking the time to redo the intro sequences.
- Overly simplistic or overly difficult mini games. There isn't much variety in the mini games, and they're unevenly spread out amongst the dads. Most mini games just allow you to spam a button and win, while there are incredibly difficult ones that give you a lot of trouble. This isn't HuniePop where the mini games actually offer increasing challenges and are fun in their own accord. They seem made for memes and not much else.

- Dad endings. Not all of the dads have logical or good endings. Well, they all have a 'good' ending, technically speaking. But that 'good' ending might not be actually "good" catch my drift? If you really like one of the dads, their 'good' ending might leave you feeling terrible. What is worse is that sometimes these endings feel like they came out of nowhere and have no relation to the dad you've been courting. This can be frustrating to the player if they really felt invested in the person they'd actually been getting to know. The "twist" endings are more The Happening than The Sixth Sense.
Neutrals:
= There are still some bugs in the game. Sometimes when you reload a save, characters that have left will hang out next to the dad you are trying to romance. (This is creepy when it is your kid watching you make a move on another guy.) Sometimes mini games won't work properly when you reload the scene that they were in, causing frustration. Sometimes your character will refer to your daughter's other dad even if you indicated that your former spouse was her mother. These, of course, may be fixed by the time you read this review as I am doing this the day after the game was released.
= Actions that don't line up. Sometimes, characters do or say things that don't like up with previous actions. Some of this is just general dating sim stuff. This isn't the Witcher III where there ar 12 different endings for every quest you go on. But sometimes this causes dialogues to seemingly come out of the blue. If you're done being with friends with somebody because they really messed you over, why are you going out for ice cream with them the next day?
= Lack of a neutral paths. Sometimes, you just really want an option between being a jerk or being somebody's one true love. In this game, you get "scores" on your dates. Which help lead to the ending you can get with each dad. But if you want to, say encourage the ambitions of one dad without becoming his lover, you can't do that.
Overall, I recommend this game. You'll get $14.99 worth of gameplay out of it. It isn't the best dating sim ever. But it isn't tragically bad either. And it's one of the few dating sims that focuses on Male/Male dating.

Right off the bat, I want to say that this game gets better the longer you play it. I know that's weird to say out the gate, but as a backer who's first impressions upon completion were not great, I figured it was important.
Yooka-Laylee is a 3D platformer collectathon in the vein of Banjo-Kazooie made by the same people only in an indie setting. You start off with basic moveset, go to different worlds through a hub-world, learn new moves, do random tasks to get collectables, and eventually get enough stuff (in this case "Pagies") to fight the final boss. There's also some humor in there, though most of it's pretty dry.
This game has pretty tight controls. Everything is responsive for the most part, with the only real exceptions being the tounge move and turning. The tounge move sometimes doesn't go to what you want, eating things offscreen that are technically closer than what you're looking at. Turning is a rounded turn; that is to say, you cannot turn around in place. Beyond those two things, controls feel good and movement is fun.
Gameplay as a whole is also pretty good. Objectives in levels are interesting enough and varied throughout. Some objectives are way easier than they need to be, and some can be almost completely irrelevant with movesets gotten later in the game. This challenge diconomy unfortunately makes some parts feel like no challenge has been presented and some parts unfair. The worst part of the gameplay is early on when the game feels the need to explain every single thing to the player. However, I found that partway through the first world (and taking a few days off from the game), I was able to get past the direct dialouge and enjoy the gameplay.
Speaking of dialouge, the story is really simple. Villain is evil and wants your magical item which you are trying to get back. Story and dialouge are a wash, though there are some great lines by random characters throughout. That being said, the character designs are pretty good and varied. There are plenty of characters to keep interest to the end.
And the game looks great. Lots of small details. Lots of bright colors. Lots of interesting settings. A+ in that department.
But a very big problem that they made was the "expand world" mechanic. Basically, every world has 25 pagies, with only 10 of them being available at first. This basic world is much smaller than the expanded one or is missing many key features. Because of this, after world two I didn't enter a world unless I could expand it at the same time, which was fairly easy at that point considering there are 25 pagies in every expanded world and the first world only takes 3 to expand. Basically a bad mechanic that I imediately found a work around for.
So, let's look at the possitive/negative bullet list:
+Gameplay is fun and varied
+Controls are tight most of the time
+Level design is big yet intricate
+Bosses are unique. One even surprised me when it popped up
+Character design is on point
+Looks great
~Story is ok, but basic
~Dialouge can be a slog to get through
~Some dialouge is not skippable (learning new moves dialouge for instance)
~Some challenges early on can become irrelevant with later movesets
-Basic enemies are the same throughout. After world two, only one basic enemy is introduced.
-Challenge is all over the place with some challenges feeling too easy and some feeling unfair
-There is no reason for the "expand world" mechanic, as worlds feel small otherwise
-The beginning is tutorial hell up through part of world 1 (this doesn't seem bad, but with unskippable dialouge and slow cutscenes, it drags on)
-The camera doesn't play nice
-Game feels like knockoff Banjo-Kazooie which it kinda technically is (actually not a bad point if you don't mind)
tl;dr: Game gets good once you get past the tutorial bits. Always expand the world before entering or you'll feel the budget constraints. A good buy on sale.

Just beat the game with 101 Pagies. An overall fun 22hr experience (if you're just going for story completion). It played perfectly on Linux. I only had one issue with Rampo not rendering correctly during a boss fight, but it wasn't game-breaking at all, strictly cosmetic.
The game worked PERFECTLY on LINUX (Xubuntu and Ubuntu Mate 16.04.x)! I have to give it to the devs for making such a nostalgic experience. The controls on my Dualshock 4 controller worked fine although the button prompts were for Xbox 360.
Story is the basic good vs evil in a platformer game. Nothing special here. Characters are generic, but comical and entertaining. Writing was funny at some parts, but mostly because of the high level of cheesiness. It often felt like forced humor, but I got a small amount of chuckles out of the experience.
Audio is OK. The voice sounds are ear-grating and annoying as crap during "cutscenes" where dialogue skipping is disabled. Not a big deal though. I like David Wise's music for Diddy Kong Racing, but the songs in this game weren't very memorable for me. They "feel good" if that makes sense... nostalgic? Childlike? Reminiscent of simpler times? something along those lines, but outside of that, they got boring quickly. I ended up listening to my own tunes while playing.
Gameplay is what you should expect from a platformer inspired by the classics of the N64. The camera was annoying at some parts, but nowhere near as frustrating as so many people made it out to seem. Not perfect, not horrible, just slightly flawed. Again, not game-breaking at all.
Performance: PERFECT on LINUX! THANK YOU DEVS! Smooth framerate (nVidia GTX 970, i5, etc.) Only lagged in the toxic areas when the graphics were set to MAX.
Fun? For the most part, yeah. Strangely, I felt more interested in the other 3D platformer available for Linux called "Poi," but that doesn't mean that I didn't have fun with Yooka-Laylee. This game isn't one that I can play straight through. I'd play in short bursts, put it down for a few days, then come back. Your mileage may vary.
I think the game is worth $40 as far as content is concerned, but if I were to do it all over again, I would've waited for a sale. I know that sounds contradictory, but I'm not sure how else to express it. The amount of content available is worth the current price of $40, but because the game felt rendundant after a while, it feels like it'd be better on a sale. This is entirely subjective though. It is definitely due to my own experiences with games in this genre.
Check it out if you like 3D Platformers reminiscent of the mid-late 90's and early 2000's. Skip it if you can't see yourself getting back into that genre. If you want a $15 version of this game with maybe half to three-quarters the amount of hours of playtime, check out "Poi" instead (it's similar to Super Mario 64).
...and remember, no matter what distro you use, out of many: one Linux. Peace!

Very promising so far, after six hours. I paid full price as a paid-up (and ageing) member of the Banjo fanclub, principally because I would like to support the developer and ensure that this franchise flourishes in future. Whether it justifies GBP35 currently is a matter for lengthy debate.
Various people have commented on the camera - it is hard for me to be critical, having grown up with some truly dreadful camera work - I think most of the problems seem to have arisen with keyboard and mouse, which certainly does NOT lend itself to this scenario! It is difficult for me to see this game through the eyes of somebody who did not grow up with NES, Master System etc., so I stop short of making subjective criticisms of the game. If we see a sequel, then I think based on this effort, it should be a spectacular. It is very interesting to witness the gradual porting of titles previously confined to the console world such as wrestling, and indeed 3D platformers, to the PC. It will be fascinating to see how this convergence unfolds in the years to come.
There are certainly much bigger and more complex games available for similar money, but I think this has a charm that enables it to punch well above its weight. Depending on how eager you are to wade through it, I would estimate this game will give you between 12-20 hours of gameplay. The side-games are exactly that, and are pleasant enough but do not enhance the game in any meaningful way.
I'm afraid I must agree with people who criticise the voices, I find myself hammering the A button to proceed as fast as possible (you can skip through MOST) - I gather this is something that is being rectified. It absolutely WAS endearing in the original N64 titles, but you were mindful whilst you were playing it that it was only by virtue of having proceeded with cartridges that Nintendo were less able to do what Sony and others were doing at the time with CD audio.
Technical info
---------------
They very definitely err on the side of caution with CPU spec, which is no bad thing. Ran fine on max settings around 50fps on my previous set-up (FX4300 / GTX950 2gb / Win7 / 360 controller / 8gb 1600) and it is running even more splendidly on the new spec (FX6300 / GTX 1050ti / Win10 / 360 controller / 8gb 1866). I would think on lowest settings you would be able to get this working on a very modest rig, and the graphical quality is actually surprisingly good at that level.
If you are having trouble with drivers for 360 controller, just ignore them completely and try just plug and play - my version of Win10 seemed perfectly happy with that, in fact I am rather surprised how well it is coping with backwards compatibility issues, decades of experience led me to expect a bloodbath. For low and mid-range machines, the in-game V-sync setting seems unusually resource intensive, and mine ran better without. I imagine if you are running a high end card on a 60hz monitor you will want to enable V-Sync or equivalent in the card's control panel settings for better results - NVid card settings seem often to out-perform the developers' own settings. I cannot comment on AMD cards.
Verdict
-------
Great fun. If you love(d) Banjo, get it at any price. If you do not feel any nostalgic attachment and prefer to spend your money more rationally (!!!), then I think it would be perfectly reasonable to wait for the price to fall a little.

As one of many Kickstarter Backers who donated because of how much they loved Banjo-Kazooie, I can definitively say that this game probably isn't worth your time, as much as I don't want to say so.
Music is great, and the overall graphic style is delightful and pleasant to look at, and some characters are designed really well, but then there's others that stick out like a sore thumb and look like they've just been stapled to the ground whereever they're standing, with a remarkably lower design quality.
The controls are a weird mix of really responsive and janky as all hell. Jumping, gliding, and rolling are all done pretty well, and they're more than good enough for accurate platforming most of the time, but you jank around from a complete standstill to a full sprint with the touch of a stick. And flying is so abysmally difficult and awkward to control that it feels like trying to guide a blind paraplegic penguin through a tornado with nothing but sign language.
It's impossible to do efficiently, is what I'm saying.
There's a lot of 90s platforming design practices that carry over back into Yooka-Laylee, like little gated areas that allow for teleportation across the map, or making the inside of buildings bigger than the outside, and those are all fine and dandy. But it also carries over a camera that's less competent than a toddler in an accounting firm and less effective than a hand-held cactus in a firefight.
I'm not even going to go into detail on the game's terrible boss fights (final boss especially, it's quite long and has SO much flying), crashes, glitches, and pure lack of support for anyone using a keyboard and mouse. I had a gamepad to play, and it's a 3D platformer, so using a gamepad makes way more sense, but still, not having a corresponding key on the keyboard for the 'B' Button is just ridiculous.
If you're the type of person that's not really into collecting things, don't get this game. You won't like it.
If you're the type of person who LOVES platforming, don't get this game. There's no platforming of substance here, it's just not what the game was designed for.
If you're the type of person that loved Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie, and you want to experience a game like it again, don't get this game. It's not very much like Banjo-Kazooie, despite all the googly eyes on everything and weird voices. It was designed differently than Banjo-Kazooie, and it's not worse for trying to not be Banjo-Kazooie, but for many other reasons, it's not a great game. Just dust off your old N64 cart and play Banjo again. You'll save $40 and the experience will be better.
If you're the type of person that kinda liked Banjo-Kazooie, and wants a game where you can explore things and not have any sort of major stress while playing a game, you could probably pick this up. Kinda either or, a game like Grow Home or Stardew Valley do the same sort of thing.
All in all, Yooka-Laylee isn't a terrible game. But it's certainly not all that good either.
Also those recurring quiz sections where the questions are ridiculously arbitrary and it takes 9 and a half centuries for the stupid duck to ask his damn question every single time? Those quiz sections have a special place in he seventh circle of hell, a type of damnation reserved exclusively for the excrements of Lucifer's excretory system itself.

Read a lot of the negative reviews before I decided to add my thumbs up. They seem to fall into a few categories, optimization, gameplay, and multiplayer/co-op complaints. So I'll address all three.
1. Multiplayer - Was forced on the dev, is horrible. Don't buy this for multiplayer, and don't bother trying it if you haven't.
2. Optimization - this is a thorny one. I have never had a problem with frame rate on either of my two rigs, but I have a pretty nice setup, and I have no idea how common the problems are. Do some research on the requirements before you spend any money on the game.
3. Gameplay. Yes the game is repetitive, yes it uses many extremely common tropes of cover-based shooters.
However in the context of the meta-narrative I consider that working as intended. I have done several playthroughs (despite my recorded hours) and taken copious notes of how responsive the mechanics are. They degrade as the game goes on. Meaning - I never had trouble sticking to cover, controlling sprint, or reloading in the first part of the game on any playthrough. I had trouble with all of them in the final act on every playthrough. This indicates intent to me. It fits with the scaling difficulty and brutality of the final act of the game. Walker/You break down as you go, and it is reflected in every single aspect of the experience.
The game is aware of the artifice. If that sounds like something that would♥♥♥♥♥♥you off rather than pique your interest, I recommend grabbing the game. I would also check out "Killing is Harmless" which is a critical analysis of the game. It covers a lot of stuff I don't have time to write about here.
I consider this game to be one of the greatest games ever made, but a recommendation comes with some caveats other than those mentioned above. Some experience with shooters will be necessary to fully appreciate the deconstruction taking place here. Without that, it may simply appear to be an example of, rather than a response to the genre. In my opinion, it also requires a straight playthrough. Meaning - set aside a full day or so, and just play the whole game. Don't break it into chunks, take time off between sessions, or fracture the experience.
Outside of that narrow band of specifications I wouldn't recommend this game to be honest, even as one of my favorites.

From start to finish, this was a really fun game. All of its various elements worked well together, and the game is as stable and bug-free as you'd hope it to be. The setting is intriguing and fun, even though it's handled as a bit of flavor rather than the focus of the game. The focus is simple: you're killing bad guys with your fists and your car. Along the way there are goals to accomplish. Most of those goals are optional, and you aren't penalized if you only focus on the main storyline while avoiding the somewhat repetative sidetracks. I loved the sidetracks, except for the races, which were just hard enough for me to only bother finishing a couple (I'd rather bash heads).
I would criticize the repetative aspect of the game, but it works to train you in getting better, and the most repetative part is also the most enjoyable: driving a nigh-indestructable scrap hot rod! Where I really wanted more from the game is in the survival aspect. There is so much water that it's hard to want for it. Fuel is simple never, ever an issue at all. Maybe since the game revolves around Gastown that makes sense, but I would have had to blow up or ignore 5 gas cans in a row to ever risk running on fumes. You do not get the sense that surviving the ravages of Nature is an issue for Max, even though it is hammered over and over that survival is an issue for everyone else. That keeps the focus more on the combat, but I would have liked to have a "survival is hard" option.
The plot is extremely simple and offers few twists and turns, but the dialogue throughout is immersive, engaging, and bordering on exceptional. Where the story part of the game really shines is in the ending: maybe the best end for a video game I've ever experienced. Play the game and experience it for yourself; it is not an ending you can appreciate without having played through the whole thing.

This is a review I’ve been planning for months. Why? Simply because the Starpoint Gemini 2 key that came into my possession was part of a clever and generous marketing campaign which promoted Starpoint Gemini Warlords. In other words, developer Little Green Men Games offered their second Steam project, free of charge to anyone who wanted to added it to their collection, during a certain time frame. Thousands of Steam users linked the game and obviously, half of my own list of Steam friends. I appreciated the gesture and delayed or not, my review for Starpoint Gemini 2 is finally here. I will compare it to Warlords, on some occasions but I fully intend to highlight the series’ strengths even before the 3rd and so far, latest iteration was released. One thing became clear from the start: LGM is a developer that takes user feedback and transforms it into gameplay features, fixes and additions.
As a direct sequel to Starpoint Gemini, veteran players may already be familiar with Gabriel Faulkner. A former space station commander and agent of the Gemini League, Gabriel is briefly introduced in Starpoint Gemini 2, before his untimely death that would prove to be a catalyst to a mystery of epic proportions and deadly consequences across the Gemini star system. Players shall assume control of Adrian Faulkner, Gabriel’s son and heir to a modest trade fleet from which only a gunship survived the aforementioned assassintation near Planet Trinity. Adrian begins his journey in the Trinity Free States, but he’ll soon be given a choice: either follow in his late father’s footsteps and also find his killers in the process during the Campaign Mode or abandon his past contacts and allegiances while attempting to make a name for himself in the Freeroam Mode.
I may even compare Starpoint Gemini 2 with Freelancer (space simulation masterpiece from 2003), since they prove similar from a gameplay perspective at least. But I really appreciate that players can access Freeroam within 15 minutes of starting the game, as opposed to Freelancer’s case where you had to see the entire storyline through before being offered a “clean slate” in regards to all in-game factions and sheer freedom of opportunities and choices. So you could essentially go straight for the space pirate/smuggler career and join the factions that are normally hostile during the Campaign missions. I’d still recommend you play through the story first, since it proves to be a comprehensive introduction onto a title that is very thorough. The map is huge so you’ll probably spend a dozen hours just exploring it while the multitude of side missions and freelancing (even smaller odd jobs) ensure that not a single dull moment shall be in sight.
Starpoint Gemini 2 uses Whale Engine 2.0 which is proprietary to LGM. A developer who crafted and upgraded their own graphics engine over time, I’m certain that I don’t have to explain the kind of dedication that this tasks requires. Since it shares its “DNA” so close to Warlords, I guess that I shouldn’t have been surprised that 4K@60fps was not a feasible option. I didn’t wish to run the game close to 30 frames per second so I decided to accept playing in 2K resolution and thus I was spared of any further frame rate issues. The graphics themselves are gorgeous and the loading times (both textures and in general) were fast by SSD standards. It’s a 2014 release, not very old even by IT&C notions and the game can be also enjoyed on less powerful systems since it has a long list of graphical options which can be tweaked to accommodate anything from budget laptops to “beastly specced” workstations.
I would have liked to say that I never ran across a crash to desktop, but sadly one of these gaming banes occurred right during the process of saving the game. A nasty affair, but I was fortunate that the autosaves didn’t force me to backtrack too much. Save your game progress frequently and especially before starting either a main mission or secondary one. The freelancing errands seem to spawn randomly based on your in-game level and reputation. They disappear just as inexplicably as they pop on the map and vanish if you load a previous save file. Early game, they are your main source of income since even trading will require that you buy an initially expensive freighter. The ability to hide the entire HUD (which is feature and detail rich by the way) for screenshots, really pleased me. If only more games would integrate this option…
The soundtrack and the voice acting never gave me any issues. They aren’t repetitive or lacking in quality. Not all dialogue scenes feature recorded lines over the displayed subtitles but when they do, the actors sound convincing enough even if there are some funny situations, such a bald Caucasian man which speaks in a Jamaican accent of English. Rastafari or not, he offered me a good laugh. As for the OST, I was more busy running errands and earning credits than to sit back and listen closely.
As in the case of most space sims, the gameplay is the true highlight and not the narrative. When you're given the option to ignore the story altogether and carve your own name however you see fit, you know that you’ll have a lot to see and do, even outside some scripted missions. If you played any similar games from this genre, you know that shooting down other ships is only a small part of the overall experience. Exploration and trading are also genre staples but the Starpoint Gemini series raised the stakes by throwing business and fleet management into the equation. You won’t become a manager of a space station or command several ships as soon as you could in Starpoint Gemini Warlords, but by taking things more slowly, Gemini 2 is more in tune to Freelancer. Is it a good thing though? I can't say for certain, but I know that I'm not a big fan of grinding.
Earning credits in the first few hours of the Campaign, won’t be hard but rather dreary. If you think that you can save up just enough for a decent freighter and that you’ll soon be swimming in credits from trading, you’re wrong. Short routes don’t net much of a profit, not to mention that the commodity prices seem to both fluctuate and are not very intuitively displayed. You have to navigate through several menus most of the time, from price checking to setting up an itinerary which won’t end in your ship being blown up by pirates. As I mentioned already, you seem to have quite a large number of sworn enemies and factions, before you’ll even leave the tutorial phase. Fast travelling across the map, is costly since the series' titular T-Gates place a hefty fee which would only strain your dwindling budget past an acceptable threshold.
On the upside, once you’re a highroller, the Gemini star system is your oyster. You’ll be able to choose between 70 ships of various design, shape or power and then proceed to customize them further by renanaming  and adding a personalized symbol that might also double as your company logo. Can’t fully repaint the ships though, but perhaps it’s for the best. Pink dreadnoughts are the last thing you’d want to see in a serious simulation. It will take a lot until credits are no longer an issue. In the same amount of time I already managed my faction’s war efforts (fleets AND space station plus auxiliary platforms) in Gemini Warlords, I was barely able to afford my second ship in Starpoint Gemini 2. In Warlords I had already bought and switched five ships, each bigger than the previous one.

A Freelancer substitute with less overall character. Get on significant sale.

but what I disliked the most is how sensitive or downright quick-time-event like some of the minigames are, and how some mini games have a huge flaw.
Like with the penguin minigame. I knocked the penguins out of my view, thinking they'd not be able to get out from above, turns out they don't even need to get out through the door, but they can go through the ♥♥♥♥ing wall that's out of your view/reach.
and with the mini golf game you dont even get to control anything, all you have to do is wait for that .001 second golden moment that gives a hole-in one. With me it went so fast that before I could consider what angle was the best (after spending a long time trying to figure out where the angle would take the ball) I had apperiantly ran out of time and the ball was hit without me promting it.
It's already hard enough to consider a good angle without not being able to control anything and the angle on which you look out on the minigolf course, but add an invisible timer to the mix and you're just making it downright unplayable.

despite all this I still think it's a nice and quirky game, but seriously tho, reconsider some of the controls in those minigames, please.

"Ancient Space" is a really decent entry into the space RTS genre, which (very refreshingly) gets away from the ironically boring routine of just having to be fast, fast, FAST!
Indeed, the game pretty much goes in the opposite direction. Many missions are downright...contemplative in pacing. However, this isn't to say that there aren't some pulse-pounding moments where you have to think quickly. Indeed, if you forget that you can "get on the gas," you probably won't complete all the missions.
Going along with the previous paragraph, I'm very pleased to say that this title emphasizes giving things thought, especially in terms of figuring out what fleet configuration works for you. Frantic micromanagement really isn't the order of the day, although some micromanagement helps you get the most out of your units. The friendly ship AI isn't brilliant, but it's good enough that you can often let them make a number of decisions themselves. This emphasis on strategy (as opposed to hotkey mashing) even applies to those moments where you can't dawdle: You have to recognize what's going on and react swiftly but deliberately, whether it's proceeding with a certain kind of build or just running away.
No, the game doesn't reach "Homeworld-franchise" territory. The scale of the game is too limited for that, both in the story and the way the game plays. "Ancient Space" is really a number of interconnected, constrained arenas that do become relatively easy to predict. (At the same time, I have to give a nod to the developers choosing a workable and recognizable mechanic, and then sticking with it consistently.) Also, this isn't a game about battles with tens upon tens of ships. Resources tend to be pretty thin, though steady, and your unit cap never goes much beyond 20. Unlike in other offerings, you're simply prevented from being able to "overwhelm" the enemy - and a person might argue that this helps to keep things interesting.
On the story side, the scope of the narrative is surprisingly human-scale. This does allow for some interesting intrigue and a pretty decent plot-twist, but it doesn't quite fire the imagination like a "Homeworld" game might. "Sprawling" and "epic" just don't describe the way "Ancient Space" feels, and sprawling epicness is what's required for a "Homeworld" experience. There has to be a confluence of visual style, musical depth, and narrative context that conveys an almost mystical sense of size. This game doesn't get to that point, and it may be that it just wasn't meant to. That is to say that "Ancient Space" isn't a bad setpiece at all. It's just that the metaphorical walls aren't very far apart.
There are some "mechanical" errors to be found. I had some moments where ships would infuriatingly fail to pathfind, and perhaps connected with that, I had a couple of occasions where ships would just halt for no apparent reason.
But those are only little dings. "Ancient Space" is a good game, and definitely worth a playthrough. It seems to have been crafted well, and it scratches the RTS itch in a slightly different way than other contenders in the genre. I say, "Good On Ya" to CreativeForge for putting this thing together. I enjoyed it.

I just finished this game.
-You will remember all the characters in this game.  It's the first game in a long time that made me remember or want to remember the characters inside of it.
-The combat system is not only ingrossing, but can be down right difficult and is perfectly balanced.
-There are many ways to go into this game.  Kill everyone, Don't kill anyone, or be a nuetral ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  lol. -Very few video games have brought tears to my eyes.  Hell I rarely have cried in my life period.  This game had me on the verge of tears pretty hard that i had to hold them back.
-Pay attention to items in the game.  They have different stats and such.
-If you think you are stuck you are wrong.  Just go back and try a different route.  Trust me i got stuck on a part and realized i was just a idiot for not tracing back and seeing a different route i could have taken.
-The games story is actually really good and you really need to play multiple playthroughs to understand what really is going on.  Or just watch other peoples videos like i did after i beat the game.  Up to you.  Still good plot twists and turns there.

Oh my god- where should I start; It usually is not my way to uninstall a game after having played less than five to ten hours- I try to give every game a fair chance to accommodate steap learning curves and quirky game mechanics. It really is rare that I drop a game after a couple of hours.
Starpoint Gemini 2 disappoints across the board from the start. Controlling your vessel is so finnicky and nervous and switching between the control modes is disorienting and confusing, especially considering the fact that the third control option "turret control" is only available during mouse control but then switches the control mode to keyboard control.
The turret control mode is so disorienting and with no aiming help correcting for enemy speed and direction becomes impossible. Also, while fruitlessy attempting to keep track of enemy ships that swirl around you like angry hornets, you have to steer your ship using your keyboard. Now I know some of you will say "well you need more time getting used to it". Well, that may be true if it wasn't so damn frustrating and unrewarding that you don't even want to spend more time.
Another highly frustrating factor is grinding for loot. There is no easy way to separate valuables from trash and the general value of looted/mined items is so low that the whole endeavor doesn't make sense anyway.
Next, autopilot will happily crash into anything in your way. Not a desireable feature when travel times can range in minutes (get up to get a drink? Better not risk leaving that gameboy brained autopilot unattended for a second). Travel times are too long in gerneral anyways.
I feel like I had another couple of things on my mind that I hated but oh well, that seems enough I guess...
Why can't make anyone a "Sid Meyer's Pirates" conversion into space? That would be the best space exploration/survival ever! (I'm looking forward to Sunless Skies, but atm the price tag is too steep).

While I love the concept of the game, and the art styles, honestly I'm pretty disappointed. There are some fundamental flaws that really should have been ironed out beforehand for a £10.99 game.
-The story is cute but not very deep and there's not much content.
-The make a dad character creator has tons of silly options (heart eyes etc) and very few normal looking options. There was ~3 happy mouths and all of them were weird? Also the style of your character is different to the other sprites, which really clashes as it's on screen most of the time.
-The voice lines are jarring and repetitive- every line starts with a 'HUH' or similar, which often doesn't make any sense with what's being said.
-Some of the mini games are boring as hell e.g. the concert one where you have to get through a crowd to find your date just involves walking forward for 1+ mins. They just feel really shoe-horned in
-There's continuity errors- I said my last partner was a woman in a conversation with Amanda, then later on my character got sad over the loss of Amanda's dad? This should have been picked up before the game was released.
-It's a little boring... there's not many options to choose from, you just scroll through a lot of text. I'm a fast reader that enjoys visual novel style games but I'd like a bit more influence over the story.
I'm not saying this game isn't worth playing- it's still fun, especially if you play with friends! It's also super inclusive and I really appreciate that. But it's not worth the price tag, maybe wait for a sale.

An old review of mine, written in 2001. Unedited:
I don’t know how to start. Really, I don’t. Maybe I should remind you about the movie known as Matrix, a movie that set a new standard in film industry, a movie that used breathtaking special effects never seen before. Slow motion, rotating camera, bullets ripping the air and the main character avoiding them… Fantastic, wasn’t it? There are some that didn’t like the movie, but I’ve never heard of a person who said that those effects weren’t amazing. This game is very similar to the Matrix, not only because of great effects but by its charm as well.
I am pretty much sure that many, many gamers have at least heard of the Remedy’s game years ago. It’s been in the making for more than 4 years now and mutated from the first person shooter into the third person view action game. Yes, it was intended to be in first person view, but the game physics and the type of action didn’t allow such thing. Even the publisher has changed. It was supposed to be 3D Realms, but they “only” produced the game, which at the end was published by GOD Games, the company that’s actually younger than this product! That tells you a lot about the time needed to complete Max Payne, doesn’t it?
Okay, lets get to the story. Actually, you can see the background story by playing through the introduction at the start of the game. Max is, or better to say was, an ordinary police officer, a New York PD detective working on the “usual” cases, solving the “usual” murders in the Big Apple. He was pretty good at what he did and was offered an “inside job” in the local mafia family. But Max had other plans in his life - a beautiful wife and a baby daughter. All he ever wanted was to be with them, but all that changed after they were brutally murdered by a group of junkies. Three years later, Max is on the inside job, in the Puncinello family. Only two people know his true identity, but after one of them gets killed while the other ones whereabouts become unknown. Max’ life is in real danger, especially after the mafia discovered him and launched a major offensive to capture and kill him. What a mess! Now both the police and the mafia are after our main character. It is your job to help poor Max’ survive in the unfriendly world as he learns a lot about the conspiracy, the drug lords, the people behind the murder of his family and military involvement in secret projects.
As I said, the game is played from the third person view. You can see the complete Max in the middle of the lower part of the screen. The controls are pretty easy. You use arrow keys to move back and forth, or to strafe left and right. Mouse is used for turning left and right and firing the weapons. Other than that you only need to know the keys for weapon selection, slow motion (more about that later), use, jump and crouch. That’s all! There are no items to be carried around and used when needed. Actually, you can collect painkillers and get back some of lost health and that’s the only non-firing item that can be collected. Back to the main screen. Except for the Max, the bottom screen features the health bar presented as little, empty Max who fills with red color as he gets shot. Next to it is a small sand clock, which shows how much slow motion you have left (as I said, more about it later) and a number of painkillers left. Other than that there are weapon stats that show up in the top part of the screen, but only during the weapon selection.
The graphics are simply gorgeous! A lot of attention is given to small details, which can be best seen during the shooting scenes between Max and multiple enemies. The play areas are always large, with a lot of rooms, furniture, buildings and other objects (unlike Oni, another fast paced action game with great gameplay but incredibly empty play areas!). Everything you see can be shot at. Not everything will be destroyed though, but holes from bullets or shotgun shrapnel will be there. Same goes with the sound. You will hear thugs talking between themselves about their wives, mother-in-law, guns, movies… That is of course until they see or hear you. I was amazed at duration of a show on the turned-on TV somewhere in one of the hotels in which game takes place. I just stood there, listened to the conversation in some soap opera, and they kept talking and talking and talking… so I turned off the darn TV! The speech was incredibly long!
Now to the best part of the game – slow motion action or so-called bullet mode. Once you turn it on, the time slows down so both you and your opponents move slower, the bullets fired from the weapons move slowly so you can dodge them (Neo, Matrix was an expert in this). This slow-mo mode enables you to aim faster at your enemies as well, giving you an incredible advantage over the others. You know, it is pretty hard to explain how great this feature is, you simply have to see it to get the idea. Even the screenshots can’t show all the action. Heck, the screenshots can’t show anything at all! Another great feature is automatic zoom-in to the great kills. If you shoot a thug in an interesting way (a neck shot, multiple head shots and such), the game will zoom the enemy that was just shot, move the camera around him and show his death in a slow motion. Another thing that can not be fully described by words or screenshots!
As Max advances further into the game, you will notice other great features. What I really like are the cut-scenes. Unlike most of the latest games, the cut-scenes in Max Payne are not movies or still pictures. They’re made as a comic strip, with hand-drawn Max, conversation bubbles and such. I like Max’ speeches and philosophy shown here!
The downfalls of this game are a rarity. Aside from very linear story and lack of everything except shooting, the biggest disadvantage of Max Payne is – its shortness. It is possible to complete the whole game in just one day (if you do not explore a bit and actually play the game for straight 10 hours or so). Remedy tried to make it more fun by making several modes of playing through the game. Once you complete it in the normal mode (the only one available once you install the game), you will unlock the hard level and eventually the hardest (once you complete hard) and a time limited mode. But neither is really interesting to play since there are no big changes to the original story.
Max Payne is a revolutionary product, no doubt about that. Bullet mode is simply fantastic and alone worth buying this game. The action is great, slow motion and zooming set new standards in action games, the story is brilliant… But it still seems to me like this title was an experiment, a prequel to the real thing. Only that can explain the shortness of such a great game. Should you buy it? Decide that yourself. If you’re looking for a game that’ll keep you busy for a long time then don’t, but if you’re eager to see something new and great then get it right away. You will not be disappointed!

Story pros and cons:
+Deep story filled with some of the best narration I've heard- props to Remedy
+Comic style cutscenes are unique and help give an artistic vision to the story
+ Chilling concept revolving around the murder of his wife and child due to madmen on a drug called Valkyr
+ Character cracks some light-hearted jokes even in his time of desperation making the situation for the player more comfortable and helps with character development
-The jokes that Max Payne gives sometimes makes it hard to take him seriously
-Disturbing drug induced sequences
-Plot ending was somewhat anti-climatic and the last part was compared to the rest of the game too easy (not even considered a boss fight)
-Some character voices are annoying to say the least
Gamplay pros and cons:
+Bullet time is a an interesting and well designed mechanic
+Large selection of weaponry
+State of the art (for its time) particle system when bullets impact objects
+Interaction with objects provides immersion
+Weapons are sorted nicely in the upper part of the screen and fits with the rest of the UI.
+Enemies have conversations and sometimes interact with Payne's actions
-Some weapons are underpowered such as the shotguns (excluding the jackhammer), especially the dual barrel shotgun
-Sniper rifles are almost useless because enemies even on the easiest difficulty are extremly accurate with weapons like shotguns and uzi's and most of the areas in this game aren't large enough to make use of it
- Grenades have a deadly area of effect, even standing a few metres away from the blast you're lucky not to have a large chunk of your health taken away.
- Enemies are insanly accurate with the weapons, sometimes they'll use shotguns and manage to hit you from several metres away continously and destroy you with them. The player however somehow can't manage to kill enemies with a dual barrel shotgun at close range. Go figure!
-Uzi's do more damage close range than shotguns!? *scratches head* they can also take multiple enemies out so once you get the Uzi the shotguns become almost instantly unreliable
-Bosses are just buffed up in terms of health, they don't provide any interesting mechanics or tactic behind them. Some of the bosses are so ridicolous that even with multiple headshots, blasts from grenades etc still won't kill them on the easiest difficulty.
-Easiest difficulty is for some reason stupidly hard. I can't tell you how many times I've died and had my trigger finger on the quick saves.
-No auto saves.
Sound pro's and cons:
+Great gun sound effects
+Narration is crisp and clear considering its age
+Somewhat humerous death sounds
+Memmorable Soundtrack
-Lack of sound options means that you can't adjust the volume of the voice, sound effects and music seperatly
-Voice during comic style cutscenes are louder than in game
-No voice/music sound problems on Windows 7 and 8 requires you to go through the trouble of patching it.
Overall this game offers what looks like a simple plot which is executed rather well and complex and the narration is on par with Alan Wake which is also made by Remedy, I wholeheartedly recommend you go play that game over this one if you're looking for a very strong voice narration driven game because while this one provides that, it does so at the cost of mediocre gameplay, fustrating difficulty, absurd bosses and unbalanced weaponry. I haven't played Max Payne 2 yet so I can't recommend that game over this one.
With all that being said, I give the game a fair score of 6.5/10. There's fun to be had here, just remember that this game has aged and not necessarily in a good way.

The game does many things well. Once you try and play as intended, the UI becomes more intuitive and the gameplay fluid. Ignore the plot if you are easily frustrated by weak stories, it does help you visit the map though.
- Use mouse and keyboard to play, they work perfectly. This is a casual game, not a flying simulation, you don't need a joystick.
- You need to master mouse3. Mouse1 to fly, mouse2 to fire and the ever so important mouse3 for the context menu.
- Equipment is vital and plentiful, use and abuse it. You may take on bigger enemies than you if you understand how equipement works.
- Improve your systems as soon as you can, it is worth the expense.
-
You have equipped the best weapons you can, let them do their job. Turrets certainly do not concentrate their fire on one target, but they will do short work on weak enemies and leave the strongest for the end.
- Use "v" while flying to inspect enemy ships, and see if they are worth attacking or it is better to run away.
- Use "k" to see your ship and your target at the same time. This is meant to help you capping (but I prefer a different method).
- Verifiy enemy difficulty before attacking. Simple as that.
- Trade is viable as soon as you can afford a freighter, but you'll earn experience a little bit too fast in my opinion. Some short circuits (buy at station A sell some at station B while buying more, then sell what is left at station C) have been implemented in the game, you don't need to run through half the map to make a living (not like in other games which are developed to complicate your life).
- Capping enemies is the best way of making money. Read a guide if you find it difficult.
- Capping is limited only by the number of marines sold in stations, when they run out of marines, you have to change station.
- Regions have a level of difficulty, if too many enemies attack you, go to a quieter place. On the other hand, friendly regions bordering with enemy regions are perfect hunting grounds.
- If you feel overpowered fly towards neutral, or even better, allied space, where other ships will help you.
- Combat, once I understood how to cap and the importance of "Fire at Will".
- The easy way of trade.
- T-portal system.
- Ship improvements and enhancements.
- Ship models.
- Game progression.
- Side missions scaling.
- No bugs.
- The plot.
- Station models.
- A little bit too easy after the initial (relative) difficulty spike.
- Voice acting. They are not necessarily bad, on the contrary, they tried to give some depth to their parts, but they are not native English speakers, which sometimes is even a postive point.
- You know what you are targeting only if you are looking directly at it, no information on your target if it is out of your field of view, aside from its direction.
- Once you become allied with half the factions the game becomes too easy.
- Capping ships is overpowered, it becomes less and less hazardous the more you invest in improvements on your ship.
tl;dr;
I was quite pleased beating six ships, of which two were dubbed "impossible".

In short - heavy Homeworld-inspired space RTS, with few interesting ideas and worth playing, despite lacking the final polish.
In each of 15 missions (plus few skirmish scenarios, without typical "random" skirmish and no multiplayer) you are tasked with various main and optional objectives from the range of typical RTS tasks - convoy escorts, strategic points capturing and holding, scanning/picking up objects and such. Most of them have to be taken on simultaneously, which, along with rather fast combat, makes active pause really important, not to mention fleet composition (since your "replicants" aka squad cap is usually smaller than needed and enemy nearly always have advantage in numbers). Ships are generally divided into 4 categories (small, medium, large and "extra large" + buildings) and while you unlock new models automatically with progress, it is possible to capture enemy ships as well, which increase options. Upgrading ships with parts found along the missions in preparation screen between them, as well as selecting officers for battle (providing various active buffs or abilities during the mission) and researching new modules for your main ship is also possible.
Story, however, suffer from rather poor presentation - most background information, treated often by characters as oblivious, is skipped or hidden in ships/discoveries descriptions. Voices are poorly done. Abilities to hold fire against selected targets or adjusting units speed to slowest ones are missing and would be really needed in many situations. Missions are heavy scripted and thus some have to be repeated few times, always with same or similar results. Camera controls are problematic sometimes (many users instinctively use zoom along with WSAD keys to operate camera in third dimension, only to find that said zooming is heavy restricted. Devs replied that they never intended zoom to be used as camera controls, as keys Q and E covers moving in up and down - explanation can can be understood, but is still less intuitive than it could be).
Overall 7/10 or even 8/10 game. Maybe not the best space RTS out there - but we had almost nothing new lately and game is still fun. Ending suggest sequel, so maybe next time it will go better?
By the way - if you experience heavy fps drops during the game and graphical options dont do anything - try to manually add the game to your GPU control panel list.

Its a Banjo game, but...
Banjo is my earliest gaming memory, and I did not kickstart this game, I paid the $39.99 release price.  With that in mind, Yooka-Laylee is one of the most disappointing games I have played.  My primary problem is that Yooka is advertised as a "spiritual successor;" however, this game does not actually succeed on any of the promises of the original games.  They put a new skin on an old game, added way too many collectibles solely for the sake of collecting, and didn't seem to try with any of the writing. I wanted to love this game! However, there is no challenge, no heart, and no reason for me to keep playing.  Its colorful, but dull.  Its controls work, but the camera is awful. The music is good, but not very catchy. It has the spirit of a Banjo game, but none of the actual love.  It feels like all of the old banjo mechanics were thrown into a 2017 game, and so it starts to drag with the feeling that you've done this all before.  This game is a blast for maybe 2 hours of nostalgia, but then the frustration sets in because it feel like banjo, but it is not banjo.  If it was $19.99, maybe buy it for the nostalgia, but at $39.99 it is an overpriced, functional, but not very good game. In the end, it feels like a banjo game, but there are just too many "buts" for me to recommend this game to anyone lacking some kind of banjo nostalgia.  If you have the nostalgia it is worth a look, but not for the price, if you want to start getting into this genre then there are better games out there than Yooka-Laylee.

been a diehard Banjo fan since the halcyon days of the N64, so of course i was massively hyped for Yooka-Laylee when the kickstarter pitch hit the net. and of course, i ended up preordering this when i got my gaming computer set up months back. is it the Banjo renaissance we've been hoping for? not really. does it have problems? hoo yes. is it a bad game? absolutely not.
a handful of reviewers/commenters i've seen have said "it's literally banjo-kazooie with a different coat of paint", and honestly i both disagree and agree with this. it's definitely distinct from BK in a number of ways, but at the same time it borrows elements from Banjo-Kazooie, Banjo-Tooie, and even Nuts'N'Bolts (though i only bring this up since both N&B and YL have massive worlds).
oddly enough, a good chunk of the problems YL has seem to be specific to YL and not the Banjo games they're a successor to.
one of these is the aforementioned massive worlds. i'm a fan of exploration, but while i did have a blast exploring around, the levels don't seem to be designed all too well; there's quite a deal of empty space that isn't utilized well, and it can be easy to get lost in a level you're not familiar with. this is most prominently a problem in World 3, where the main areas look same-y in design and there doesn't seem to be a lot of landmarks to guide you around like in BK or BT. while on this note, the large scale of the worlds means it can be really annoying when you're trying to hunt for all 200 quills on each level.
the core gameplay is good and classic, but the extra minigames tend to suffer. reused assets aside, Rextro's minigames in particular tend to control really clunkily (namely in Kartos Karting and Hurdle Hijinx; good luck getting the high scores on those). as far the minecart challenges, they seem to be sorta 2.5d perspective (think a roller coaster ride) rather than straight up 2D-esque sidescrolling; the 2.5 perspective would be okay if it didn't seriously mess with shooting or judging when to jump.
most of the other problems i've noticed seem to be minor. the camera can be quite finicky, a lot of the minor character designs aren't that memorable, and a good half of the boss fights aren't too memorable either despite some good ideas. some puzzles could have been explained better too, though honestly i mostly have this complaint with anything involving lasers. might be because of my bad memory, but nowhere in the game does it say anything like "by the way you can use your invisibility move to redirect lasers".
also the meta humor can get pretty grating for the most part but that's probably because i'm not all a fan of that kind of humor.
however, YL does have a lot of strengths to it. main controls are fluid, the world setpeices are gorgeous, there's a lot of freedom in letting you choose how to progress through the game, the collectathon stuff has been streamlined to a degree (almost all collectibles are focused on progression; resource-based abilities a la BK's flying and eggs are now reliant on a power bar or timed powerups), collecting pagies and expanding worlds is satisfying as heck, and of course you have Grant Kirkhope and David Wise's excellent music work.
Yooka-Laylee isn't a perfect game, and definitely inferior to its Banjo ancestors, but it's a solid platformer in its own right. i hope Playtonic takes any criticism as drive to improve should they end up making a Tooka-Laylee. despite the flaws, i definitely had a blast with the game. c:
i wouldn't recommend getting it at full price unless you're an absolute diehard Banjo fan, but it's worth a pickup if it goes on sale. just don't go in expecting it'll be anything like Banjo.

Early-access game. Despite this, Rust can be pretty fun if you manage to learn how to play the game properly. Greed and lack of a user-friendly system make this an easy target for bad reviews. But bear with me for a second here...
I spent the first 100 hours of my game-time on  pure PvE servers, learning the basics. This also gave me an opportunity to meet some like-minded individuals who were also trying to learn the game without the constant fear of being no-scoped from across the map with a bolt-action rifle. Instead, we spent our time hunting the various animals in the game to get a grasp on how the firing mechanics worked, improving our aim at certain distances. With the addition of the three-day cycle helicopter, we also learned (the hard way) how to hide from it, and when the time came, how to fight it.
Venturing onto a PvP server without a group (unless you're really skilled at shooting people and you're mlg or something edgy like that) is probably a really dumb mistake. You're going to die unless you have some numbers, and even then it's a roll of the dice whether you live or die. But I feel like that's part of what makes this game about survival. The person who shoots you and takes your stuff was probably shot not moments later. It's not a perfect embodiment, but it comes pretty close to the adage "a dog-eat-dog world".
I would recommend Rust to anyone who is willing to shrug off the imperfection that comes with a game in development and can look past what is there now to what could eventually become an amazing thing. This game has the potential to be a lot of fun. You just have to be willing to give it a chance.

Best lightsaber combat of all time.
Story:
This game follows your own custom created character on his journey as a jedi. You embark on missions for the academy and unravel a mystery all while learning new force powers and fighting hundreds of enemies across dozens of Star Wars locales. Whether you stay on the path of the jedi, or stray to the dark side is completely up to you.
Gameplay:
Truly the best lightsaber combat of any Star Wars video game. Simple, yet if you put the time in you can learn all sorts of tricks to fully master it. There are 3 different styles of lightsaber to learn. A single lightsaber with 3 different fighting styles (Light, Medium and Heavy) Two lightsabers (but you can turn one of them off and fight in the single saber light stance) and finally a saber staff, which is a double bladed saber that you can turn one side off and fight in the single saber medium stance.
In addition there are also about a dozen other weapons that range from basic blasters to snipers, rocket launchers, and even electric charge guns.
And of course it wouldn't be a StarWars game without force powers. Dark Side powers like Choke, Lightning and Drain. Lightside powers like Heal, Mind Trick and Absorb, and neutral powers like push, pull and jump. And so much more.
Multiplayer:
This game still has a rather large community, and the modding community has already made some fantastic content for this game.
Overall:
This game is one of my favorite games ever made...I feel like even all these years later it still really holds up. If you like Star Wars, you will really enjoy this game if you haven't played it already.
----> 10/10 <----
