Arkham Origins is the third instalment of the Arkham universe for Batman and set as a prequel. Although it bears many similarities to the other games developped by Rocksteady, this particular title was done by splash damage, and bears some of the mannerisms of that studio.
Although Origins is not by any means a bad game, many of the mechanics that are traditional to the arkham universe seem clumsily implemented; the freeflow combat system sees an enormous difficulty spike midway through the game and quickly devolves into repeated countering and gadget-spamming.
The game punishes you for being agressive, and does not reward you for taking risks in any circumstance. Furthermore, the predator sequences poorly implement stealth, with enemies seeing through walls and grates. The greatest challenge in these moments though, is the terrain, as it always seems to work against you in some form.
Although these flaws may seem harsh, they don't destroy the experience completely; Origins remains a solid addition to the Arkham universe and isn't unfun in any respect, but for a fully priced title the results feel slightly unpolished and a little underwhelming in general. For sale price though, you'll be spending a good 10-20 hours on the campaign, if you don't muck too long on the collectibles, which is something fairly surprising for a high fidelity AAA release.

Single player gameplay is riddled with bugs, no where near as polished as the first 2. Bugs like getting stuck in an area or resulting in your death were the most annoying. On the plus side, the story is brilliant IMHO and some of the new gadgets were fun to play with.
I liked the riddles in the first 2 because it gave you clues as to where you're meant to scan at each location. In this game, you're  suppose to scan anarky tags and cyrus pinkney journals but you're given no clues to as where they are other than the fact they're somewhere on prominent buildings around the city. Am I meant to seriously walk around the entire city with detective vision on and look around every corner and under every ceiling and archway to find these? No thank you.
Multiplayer concept is good - if you actually manage to get a game. You can spend half an hour of your time having your connection dropped consistently and never get a game. If you're an achievement ♥♥♥♥♥, you can spend a lot of time trying to get a game for those multiplayer achievements.
Overall, such a disappointment for a AAA game and definitely not worth the full price if you're looking to get the most of what this game has to offer. It's like the initial release was a beta version, no idea how it got past QA. If you're just looking for a good single player action game with a good story, go for it.

Would I recommend paying full price for this when a newer game that seems to address this one's shortcomings and adds more or missing features (Starpoint Gemini: Warlords) is out? No, not ever. But it's probably worth picking up during a hefty sale.
The story mode is ... iffy. It's poorly written, both in terms of how the story goes and how the characters behave and in terms of the written English employed by the developers. The voice acting... I had to turn voices off completely. Playing this game as a less directed experience (which is entirely possible) might be more your style. I am a pirate and only the jerk factions like me.
This game is pretty nice when you want to fly around in space and tweak things a bit but you just don't have the energy for micromanaging every aspect of a full 3x/4x experience. There's some nice "dogfighting" to be had in small space boats, and strategic fighting (resource management and positioning) in big ones. The variation between and within classes of boat matters, and most boats remain viable throughout the game (especially if you don't play the story mode). There's a good amount of customisation you can do to your boat, more in terms of performance than appearance.
But there's not
much of any given element. Just enough that it matters plenty.
Just be aware that there are no player industry mechanics and there is no empire-building. Also be aware there are some technical issues with the game (such as the performance-tanking nebula visuals).
In general, it's pleasant enough to pick up on sale.

This is exactly the sequel of the franchise I was hopîng for!
The new Hitman goes back to the roots of Blood Money and provides a huge sandbox level with endless possibilities. No more nonsense 'hide from the police' levels like in Absolution but true Hitman levels with clear targets.
The 'Mastery' mode allows you to replay a level again and again, each time unlocking new items or locations to take on your targets. I've now spent over 30 hrs on the Paris level and I still feel there are different ways how to approach it.
The escalations spice it up even more, providing challenges which make you rethink the whole level ("where the hell did they find a sabre??"). This is truly the Hitman game I was hoping for, I'm loving every minute of it.
The only negative point for this game is the online requirement. I don't mind being online since my connection is always on, but in nearly every escalation mission I get disconnected ...
Since it's impossible to save during an escalation mission it means I have to start all over again which is really a nuissance. Each time I get a 'server error' and when reconnecting I'm instantly reconnected, but my progress is lost.
I wonder how this will work out with the elusive targets since those contracts can apparently be taken only once, so when the connection drops ...
In addition to the connection issues the game has some minor flaws: clipping issues, incorrect voiceover or NPC reactions etc but nothing game-breaking.
Initially I was sceptic about the episodic releases, but now I have to admit this is excellent: in case the game was released as a single game I would probably play each level just once and move on to the next. Now however I play the same level over and over to complete all challenges and find all secrets which is great. I'm each time finding new ways to approach the level.
Overal I give this version an 8/10 due to the connection issues. When they fix this it will definitely become 10/10!

First of all, game strikes out on the whole "space fleet battle" concept, that's cherished by many homeworld fans. It's more like Starcraft with ships instead of marines. Maps are full-3D and filled with gigantic space objects you have to fly around but despite stunning looks that doesn't affect battles since ships don't have weak zones or blind spots to exploit with different attack angles.
So we've got a very basic space-themed story-oriented RTS with nice visuals, fleet upgrading between missions, battles on multiple maps at the same time (when "sectors" aren't used as simple map-extender) and very interesting voice acting, where characters keep themselves forcibly calm and professional that transfers their stress and despair surprisingly good.
Biggest issue I got so far is poor performance on my gtx670. I noticed drops to 20fps in some large battles and it made me consider giving it a negative review. Overall it keeps framerate on the reasonable level and judging by the forum that's my personal issues that won't necessarily happen to others.
The game also lacks basic skirmish mode and any form of multiplayer hence replayability is a bit shallow, that may be a dealbreaker for many people.
However, if you are fan of space-themed games, this one could satisfy you. It's got solid story, nice fleet-customization and overall good gameplay.

Summary: Just buy Homeworld 2 for less.
After 2 hours of download, got through the tutorial thinking "OK, this is simplistic but reasonably straight forward, and the graphics are decent."  Started the first mission, realized I wasn't having fun and didn't want to play.  Thinking about it a day later, I realize the following:
1) The AI is "Dumb": enemy ships run straight from a spawning "wormhole" to destroy a freighter.  No clumping up to make it harder, no shooting at my ships which are defending the freighter, they just spawn one at a time and make a bee line to the freighter and start shooting at it.  Why?
2) Because they are pirates and they want to capture...  ...um, yes, they did say the pirates would want to capture (something) on the freighters, but they are doing this by destroying the freighters?
3) And they're succeeding.  Not because my ships can't kill them fast enough, (my ships are kicking the crap out of them) but because I can't tell my ships to kill them fast enough.  There's no quick key grouping of ships so I can highlight a bunch of them, assign them to group 1, and then select them later by pressing "1" and tell them to do something.  Noooo, I must go up to the upper left hand corner of the screen and double click on one to get all of that type, then assign them, then double click on the other type, and assign them separately.  Then when that enemy is dead, I get to do it again.  I do not like clicky games.  If I wanted to play a clicky game, I'd play a clicky game, not an RTS game.
4) But if I set my ships to aggressive tactics, they should just look for the next/closest set of enemies and go after them next.  Right?  This misunderstanding led me to fail the first mission at least 3 times, because no, they don't go after the next nearest enemy, or anything else.  They just sit there, and if something comes along, they shoot at it, but they don't even follow it once it flys right past and goes out of range.
5) Resource collecting is... what?  There are fixed locations in space with a little gas cloud around one and some lightning around the other that you can 'build' collectors at, which are about 1/10th the size of the associated cloud but which accumulate resources forever?
Nothing makes sense!!!
6) Soooo.... I've finally worked out how to get my ships to kill the pirates fast enough to keep one of the freighters alive on the 5th or 6th try at the first objective, first mission, and this has been going on for ~10 minutes, and the freighter is sooooo sloooooow that it's taking this long for it to travel less thatn 1/3rd the way across the map which my fighters can travel across in less than 15 seco... wait!
7) OMG the maps are tiny!  And the ships are tiny too, so they need an icon for you to click on to select them as they fly across the screen which completely obscures the actual ships.  But your ships can fly from one side to the other in about 15 seconds, maybe 20, so you never actually see any of the 3D graphics for your ships because you're zoomed out as far as you can so that they and the enemy don't go racing off where you can't see.  So all you really see is some georgeous background (which you promptly ignore), some large floaty things that are in the way of what you want to look at (which you promptly ignore), and the 2D icons for your ships and your enemy's ships, which all look the same except one set is blue and the other set is orange.
8) But that zoom and speed thing brings us to more things that don't make sense.  Each 'map' has one or more wormhole entrances which take you to another map.  But there are still resouces within 15 seconds flight time of these wormhole entrances.  Like no one is going to have flown by, said "Hey, that'll make me some money." and set up shop and scooped everything up?  Or how about a toll collector: "Nope, can't go through this here wormhole unless you pay me a gazillion resource.  What, can't pay?  Have fun with that whole 'light speed' thing."
But lets get back to
6) I'm moving right along, suffering through the first objective of the first mission, playing it for the 5th or 6th time because I set the game to stupid hard, but actually 'making progress' in that the freighter is oh so slowly making its way along (insert more stuff that doesn't make sense)... and the game crashes.
I took it as a sign and uninstalled the game.
Yeah, I really can't comment on the story line, or the voice acting, or ship upgrades, or anything after the first objective of the first mission.  Never got that far, and don't expect to, unless I run into a play through on youtube.  At 100x speed.  Seriously, buy the old Homeworld 2, add in patch 1.1, and have a ball for <$10.00.  Add in the free Complex 9.1 mod and you've got so much PvC and PvP potential... Ancient can't hold a candle to it.

The Story, Voice, Music and overall ambiency is in my opinion, very well done. I like the way they used "ingamestoryreasons" to justify enclosed places and the use of buildings, which can be customized to heal, or shoot a specific damage type, or support, or whatever, like tower defense.
With respect to the main gameplay mechanic - ship combat - I think it resembles much Nexus, but it is done in a more micro-intense matter, because you have to SPACEBAR-pause every few seconds to allocate a power, swap repairs, spawn a replacement unit, or issue new orders. This game is thus not really real time strategy but more real time tactics, like ground control, with some Z-axis movement to call it 3D.
Personally, the gameplay is fun and challenging even on the easier settings, and must be downright nightmare ragemode on the hardest settings.
With respect to the RPG elements... Depending on objectives you accomplish (if you even can), you receive some rewards like additional superpower (from officers), or additional secret officers. Also by collecting the yellow anomalies (which is IMHO mandatory) you gain powerups like extra resources, or materials for upgrading the fleet/carrier at the start of each mission.
My only wish was that customization had been given more freedom because now you can only customize a hull by selecing between 3 or 4 narrow options like +1 armor, or +1 XL damage or +20 speed.
Customization wrt to the mothership (carrier) is much more free, and you can choose between an offensive or defensive version that have advantages and disavantages. I have run with the Defensive one because it gives more resources per second, and you can build on its advantages by selecting from like 40 different upgrades, or round it out to your desire.
Now my main issue with this game is not even the common (like once every 6 hours) crashes, which is understandable for a very small company product, but on the choice of the engine and the way the map layouts railroad and constrict you. I know you made the game good and adapted it to work in these constraints but I'd like to think the game would have come out better if made to work in a more open envronment, specially since in some of the missiong that are really tight, camera positioning is a pain in the butt and very frustrating not being able to see clearly whats on the area and being unable to zoom out, or worse, having to look from the bottom up (this is a problem because there is a definite up/down layout and you sort of need to be able to look from the top down).
TL;DR: This game is definetly worth $20, and if you liked ground control, homeworld 1 or nexus jupiter incident, go for it. But please watch a gameplay video before buying so you can understand how different the game actually is and plays than those aforementioned titles.

Early-access game. Despite this, Rust can be pretty fun if you manage to learn how to play the game properly. Greed and lack of a user-friendly system make this an easy target for bad reviews. But bear with me for a second here...
I spent the first 100 hours of my game-time on  pure PvE servers, learning the basics. This also gave me an opportunity to meet some like-minded individuals who were also trying to learn the game without the constant fear of being no-scoped from across the map with a bolt-action rifle. Instead, we spent our time hunting the various animals in the game to get a grasp on how the firing mechanics worked, improving our aim at certain distances. With the addition of the three-day cycle helicopter, we also learned (the hard way) how to hide from it, and when the time came, how to fight it.
Venturing onto a PvP server without a group (unless you're really skilled at shooting people and you're mlg or something edgy like that) is probably a really dumb mistake. You're going to die unless you have some numbers, and even then it's a roll of the dice whether you live or die. But I feel like that's part of what makes this game about survival. The person who shoots you and takes your stuff was probably shot not moments later. It's not a perfect embodiment, but it comes pretty close to the adage "a dog-eat-dog world".
I would recommend Rust to anyone who is willing to shrug off the imperfection that comes with a game in development and can look past what is there now to what could eventually become an amazing thing. This game has the potential to be a lot of fun. You just have to be willing to give it a chance.

A truly fun game. SPG2 takes a lot of the best aspects of space simulators and combines that with high-paced, massive-ship combat, as well as a handful of RPG elements. There are skills and perks (that you gain by leveling primarily) that make you a better killing machine, and ships to compliment every style of play. You can be a trader just trying to make an honest buck, or you can take to piracy and capture and sell (or pilot) victim ships. There's also a reputation system among the factions, and there's a faction to support every style of play as well.
The game certainly has its downsides. Loading in new areas is a little clunky, with the game occasionally stuttering, and the backdrop very suddenly changing, but these can be easily overlooked and foreshadowed by the great gameplay. Other than that, there are few downsides I can actually spot. Like some RPGs, enemies do scale with the area they're in. While their level will match yours (plus or minus a few levels), the NPCs in tougher areas will fly tougher ships, and this can sometimes hinder progress in the main storyline.
Much like games of the same type, there is a good deal of down time where you're not really doing a whole lot, or you're just travelling. However, the game manages to strike a nice balance in that you'll often spend as much, or even more, time actually taking on missions or chasing bounties.
Overally, while I certainly have my gripes about the game, that isn't a long enough list for me to not love this game, and the pros heavily outweigh the cons in every department. And, for those of you who may see this as a pro, you don't need to have played the first game to understand the story of this one. However, they did port the first game into this one as a free DLC.

This is exactly the sequel of the franchise I was hopîng for!
The new Hitman goes back to the roots of Blood Money and provides a huge sandbox level with endless possibilities. No more nonsense 'hide from the police' levels like in Absolution but true Hitman levels with clear targets.
The 'Mastery' mode allows you to replay a level again and again, each time unlocking new items or locations to take on your targets. I've now spent over 30 hrs on the Paris level and I still feel there are different ways how to approach it.
The escalations spice it up even more, providing challenges which make you rethink the whole level ("where the hell did they find a sabre??"). This is truly the Hitman game I was hoping for, I'm loving every minute of it.
The only negative point for this game is the online requirement. I don't mind being online since my connection is always on, but in nearly every escalation mission I get disconnected ...
Since it's impossible to save during an escalation mission it means I have to start all over again which is really a nuissance. Each time I get a 'server error' and when reconnecting I'm instantly reconnected, but my progress is lost.
I wonder how this will work out with the elusive targets since those contracts can apparently be taken only once, so when the connection drops ...
In addition to the connection issues the game has some minor flaws: clipping issues, incorrect voiceover or NPC reactions etc but nothing game-breaking.
Initially I was sceptic about the episodic releases, but now I have to admit this is excellent: in case the game was released as a single game I would probably play each level just once and move on to the next. Now however I play the same level over and over to complete all challenges and find all secrets which is great. I'm each time finding new ways to approach the level.
Overal I give this version an 8/10 due to the connection issues. When they fix this it will definitely become 10/10!

30 minute of gameplay. That's all it took to get fed up with the exceedingly poor PC version that - despite being originally designed for PC - feels like a rushed port that the devs cobbled together the day before launch.
The lack of graphics settings makes for a choppy framerate on lower-end computers that also makes any and all inputs a good 1/2 second delayed. This makes even the simplest of fine-tuned platforming a chore, constantly having to fight the battle between overshooting, undershooting, and a camera that makes missing platforms altogether a regular occurrence.
This game is also quite literally unplayable on keyboard and mouse. As I don't have a controller to hook up to my pc, this is my only option. If you're wondering if I simply mean that it's a chore to play on KBM instead of actually "unplayable" no, I literally mean unplayable, as there is NO B BUTTON MAPPED. Are you serious, Playtonic? I want to love this game. It looks beautiful, it has amazing music that even just off the get-go seems like it would do Banjo proud, and the mechanics I've seen so far seem like they would be fun to play.
As someone who backed this for WiiU, only to be forced to settle for the PC release and have that be unplayable, I'm crushed that Playtonic has screwed me over so much with their lack of simple foresight. If we get a patch that allows graphics settings (which will HOPEFULLY get rid of the ridiculously large input delay) and custom key bindings (or hell, even just a freaking B button mapped to the keyboard) I'm sure this review will change. Until then, however, this game is a chore that overcomes any fun I've tried to have with it.

Let me start by saying that I love 3D Platformers; from Banjo-Kazooie and Super Mario to Ratchet & Clank and Jak & Daxter, even the more obscure ones like Rocket: Robot on Wheels and Space Station Silicon Valley. Because of this I backed this game on kickstarter and I will say that I was not disappointed.
Yooka-Laylee is a good game. I enjoyed the characters and story and I loved exploring a new world, then expanding it and seeing what new areas opened up. The worlds are beautiful and huge and can definitely be overwhelming when you first get into one, but after exploring a bit you can generally find your way around. The music sounds like it could have come directly from Banjo-Kazooie and was perfect for the game. I loved the varied moves and gameplay mechanics as well.
I have seen several reviews that complained about the camera. I will admit the camera is not the best, but it is by no means the worst. I never found myself missing a jump or dying because of a camera issue. Anyone who has played a 3D Platformer should be fine with the camera controls.
Another complain I see a lot is about Dr. Quack's quizzes. I always enjoyed the quiz sections from Banjo-Kazooie and was happy to see that return. Dr. Quack's quizzes are short and simple. He will ask you 10 questions each time, but if you answer the questions quickly he'll actually only ask you 5 each time. The questions are not difficult; I only got one wrong throughout the whole game, and every other time I was able to answer the questions quickly enough.
Overall, I enjoyed every minute of Yooka-Laylee and I am happy to possibly see gaming return to the 3D Platformer genre. I do recommend this game to anyone who likes 3D Platformers or anyone who just wants a lighthearted and friendly adventure.

I bought this game when it was in Alpha 1.  It has come a long way since then, but even back then you could tell this was something special.  It's not just a good game, it's an incredible game.  The graphical style is quirky and it's cartoony nature belies the brutality of it all.  You will mess up initially, your prisons will not go according to plan.  I still find it challenging after more than 170 hours over the last several years.
But this is a game I've time and again revisted and played for hours on end.  It rewards you for experimentation and for trying new things.  There is no one correct path.  But most importantly this game while fun also makes you think.  You find yourself committing the worst of the worst to permanent solitary confinement because it's an effective way to deal with them but that's a horrendous thing to do to another human being, locking them in a small cell with no toilet or bed, fed only enough to stave off death.  But it works.
This game with story mode, Escape mode, and the Sandbox will provide you with hundreds of hours of entertainment for years and years to come, I know because I've already experienced that.  It feels polished, it runs great, and it is made by a company with integrity and common sense.  More than that, in my opinion it's one of the greatest games ever made.  If I could only own five games, it'd be this, XCOM:EU, Civ 5, CKII, and Cities Skylines.  It deserves your money, and you deserve to experience it.

Now that I've had the chance to play this game for a few hours, I can tell you that this 20 dollar purchase was very reasonable. A lot of people are comparing this game to HomeWorld, but that is an unfair comparison as you are dealing with apples and oranges.
Homeworld was great for what it offered. Massive fleet battles, graphics that were amazing for their time. A compelling story.
Ancient Space didn't try to copy Homeworld.
PROS :
The voice acting as has been stated by other reviewers are great. The story is plausible and pallatable in the same way Nexus: The Juptier Incident had a fresh spin on the old space genre.
The level of detail on the ships is great. Perhaps, because I do have a good video card, I can play it on max settings and the detail really shines.
The way you control your ships is intuitive and I felt the learning curve was negligible.
The "hero commanders" that are activated via the interface that can cast spells or debuffs(shields, more armor, more attack, enemy is more vulnerable, and so on) is a nice addition.
Having stationary platforms that help you crawl is a creative and fun idea. Has a small Command & Conquer feel to it.
CONS :
As some have mentioned, the graphical requirements are pretty high. People are having performance issues. I am not one of them.
The AI. It seems like waves of enemies continue to come your way. That's not so bad, but the game doesnt teach you that you basically just set up your units in specific areas of interest, following the rock paper scissor approach depending on what the enemy is throwing at you. You dont tell your ships what to attack as much as tell them where to be, ready for an attack. And when you get swarmed, you can issue orders to target fire on a specific ship. Point is, its more like moving chess pieces into position, and then using it, than just go and attack this target the way Homeworld did it.
I think this is a great game, relatively speaking. I hope that future projects come to fruition as a result of Ancient Space.

Let's talk about what this isn't : Homeworld 3.
This is a story driven RTS game set in space, without the strategic complexity or depth of the homeworld series.
Why do I say this? First off, for a game set in 3 dimensional space there is no Z axis!  Battles predominantly revolve around rock/paper/scissors style ship weapons and resource generation is per tick, based on owning fixed points on the map.
I enjoyed it but I was disappointed there wasn't more complexity ala homeworld.

If you love RTS, then you need to give this game a shot!
I have played many RTS games and love ones that are space themed and this is the BEST one thus far.  I have played Sins of a Solar Empire, Galaxy Civ. and many others... Thank you for creating this!  Keep in mind that this is currently meant to be a single player game strategy only.  You have 4 unit classifications in this game, and each classification has its own selection of units.  Small, which would obviously be small fighter craft and bombers and others.  Medium, which consists of corvette or Frigate like space craft.  Large, which has cruiser size space craft.  And finally EXTRA LARGE, my favorite, which consists of dreadnaughts, and some other giants of space....  Also base building and capture points,  dont forget that.

I'm currently 5-6 missions in the game.
I always wanted a space RTS where you could fly and ficht into megastructures.  Now I can finally enjoy it.
The game is good, and the scenario is simple but fun.  Sure, it's not on the level of Homeworld, or Nexus-TJI, but up to now I enjoy the game.
There are a few cons, though, but nothing that a few patches can't solve.  Here are some of main issues I have:
-The main one would be the camera being unable to zoom-out enough to have a full view of the battle.  Seriously, they (the creators) should work on that, as it makes seriously hinder the gameplay.
-Ship movement sometimes seems erratic:  ships get caught into the megastructures (or into each others), and it can be quite tedious to direct them waypoint by waypoint. (then again, it might be better if the camera could zoom out far enough)
-3D movement is not explained in the tutorial or in the control menu. (Either that or I was really distracted when playing the tutorial).  It took me quite a while to figure it out. ("g" to summon movement disk, then "left ctrl" to ajust altitude, btw)  It is also somewhat buggy, and I often have to give the order twice.
Outside of those few points, which are quite easy to deal with once you get used to the game, I have no complains at all about the game.

Let me start by saying that I love 3D Platformers; from Banjo-Kazooie and Super Mario to Ratchet & Clank and Jak & Daxter, even the more obscure ones like Rocket: Robot on Wheels and Space Station Silicon Valley. Because of this I backed this game on kickstarter and I will say that I was not disappointed.
Yooka-Laylee is a good game. I enjoyed the characters and story and I loved exploring a new world, then expanding it and seeing what new areas opened up. The worlds are beautiful and huge and can definitely be overwhelming when you first get into one, but after exploring a bit you can generally find your way around. The music sounds like it could have come directly from Banjo-Kazooie and was perfect for the game. I loved the varied moves and gameplay mechanics as well.
I have seen several reviews that complained about the camera. I will admit the camera is not the best, but it is by no means the worst. I never found myself missing a jump or dying because of a camera issue. Anyone who has played a 3D Platformer should be fine with the camera controls.
Another complain I see a lot is about Dr. Quack's quizzes. I always enjoyed the quiz sections from Banjo-Kazooie and was happy to see that return. Dr. Quack's quizzes are short and simple. He will ask you 10 questions each time, but if you answer the questions quickly he'll actually only ask you 5 each time. The questions are not difficult; I only got one wrong throughout the whole game, and every other time I was able to answer the questions quickly enough.
Overall, I enjoyed every minute of Yooka-Laylee and I am happy to possibly see gaming return to the 3D Platformer genre. I do recommend this game to anyone who likes 3D Platformers or anyone who just wants a lighthearted and friendly adventure.

Pros:
- Basic platforming is decent
- Good variety of moves
- Lack of bugs
- Some nice music and art design
Cons:
- Worlds are far too large. Collectibles are very spread out so there's not as much to do as it first seems.
- Forced backtracking, as some collectibles are blocked off until you get the right move or expand the world
- Too few worlds and enemy types
- The flight move trivializes a lot of the platforming
- Challenges are either ridiculously simple, or frustrating due to poor controls
- Poor controls in minigames, minecart sections and in certain transformations
- Some poor enemy/boss/environment design which will make you take unfair damage
- Game rules aren't consistent. Even if it seems like there should be multiple solutions to an obstacle, only the intended one ever works. e.g. there are two special moves which are both used to break glass, but any actual piece of glass will only respond to one of them.
- Slippery surfaces take away nearly all control from you which can make you fall directly into a damage/death pit. But it's not intuitive or obvious which surfaces are slippery and which aren't.
- Game lacks polish. Things like no victory dance/jingle for picking up a pagie make on overall big impact on the feel of the game. There's no real rewards for collecting more than what's absolutely necessary to progress.
- Lots of minor QoL issues such as unskippable dialogue/cutscenes, the game not telling you about useful controls/features of moves, or needing to complete every arcade game twice even if you got the high score the first time. Overall many features feel tacked-on and barebones.
- Very meager story and characterization, even compared to classic Rare comes. Unsatisfactory ending that teases a sequel instead of concluding the story.
My advice: Give this a miss and hope that the sequel is better, if they ever make one.

A fun blast to the past and it pulls on your nostalgia strings and gets you hooked if you loved Banjo Kazooie. Unfortunately the game does suffer from some flaws and bad designs in some areas. Gloomy Gem Grotto for example is one of the most annoying challenges you'll have to complete for a Pagie. The Kartos minigames are challenging but annoying and repetitive. Did he really have to pop in all 5 worlds? Luckily it doesn't take long to get the hang of it and pass the challenge. Now the Rextro games are a different story. The first 3 are fine. a little bit challenging but doable. But the last two? Absolutely horrible. It's not fun, it's not a way to spend your time but if you want to 100% this game you will have to endure. The thing that makes these two games unbearable is because of the LACK OF RECOVERY for this game. This is apparent when you fall into the swamp of the 3rd world. If you can't make it to ground within a few jumps, you'll probably die because unlike Banjo-Kazooie you have a VERY small recovery window (seconds of invincibilty) so in those arcade games, if you land in the wrong spot you'll just die again and again. It's soooo aggravating. The worlds also become less interesting as you progress through the game. The 2nd world is great on the outside but the inside castle parts are not fun. The 3rd world is pretty good but hard to navigate, although you do get to turn into a pirahna swarm which was awesome. The casino world is fun but collecting 100 tokens can turn the experience sour and the last world is just kind of meh. You spend a majority of it sailing as a pirate ship which sounds a lot cooler than it actually is. It sails slower than the 1st Wind Waker boat even at full speed and it looks unimpressive. The world is designed beautifully but the contents of it are just lackluster. The boss fights aren't great with the exception of the 3rd and 4th ones. Finally there's an excrutiating slide challenge for a Pagie in Hivory Towers because you have to learn how to control how you slide. Still not as bad as Hurdle Challenge and Up N'Ova.
TL;DR? There are challenges that are incredibly unfun, recovery problems, sloppy controls when rolling and flying and camera problems add to why the challenges are so frustrating.

DDADDS is both a loving parody of dating sims and a dating sim itself. If you're familiar with the genre you'll know what to expect- most of the interaction is through dialogue choices. There's a few mini-games, but if you're expecting more, you'll be disappointed.
DDADDS is- in a word- cute. It's very sweet for the most part- there's a few implications of NSFW content, but the most that actually is shown is shirtlessness. The romancable characters are charming, and while a few character arcs are pretty predictable (there's a lot of 'find hidden depths/secret interests and help the dad come to terms with/accept it' style plot), that's sort of what I was expecting from this game. Not too deep, but sweet and enjoyable. Like if a sherbet dib dab was turned into a game.
I do feel like the wider plot, which focuses on more your relationship with your daughter than any of the love interests, does limit the romance plot. However you play, the ending is sort of the same. The different romance arcs are enjoyable, but they're constricted by the overarching 'Amanda goes to college' plot. I don't know how or if this could be fixed, so I'm willing to let it slide, but it does mean that the game is repetitive on replay. There are also still some bugs, and there is some inconsistency- Hugo's VA's audio quality is lower than the other dads, and it's noticeable.
The only other thing I really have to say about the game is that I think the different dads are well designed- they all have very distinct visual styles and personalities. The personalities can be a little archetypical at times ('here is hipster dad' 'here is fitness dad') but I think that's a feature of the dating sim genre in general. It is worth noting that one of the romances is a trans man, and IMO he has the best and most respectful writing I've ever seen for a trans character not written by a trans writer.
Overall, I really enjoyed playing DDADDS. It's fluffy, silly, not serious fun, and if that's what you're looking for, I'd recommend it!

I was worried about this game being developed by WB Montreal instead of Rocksteady. Overall I think it hurt the game, but it's not as bad as I thought it'd be. Let me start by saying - it's a great game. If you loved previous two games, you're going to love this one as well... since it's basically the same thing. The story is great, as in all Arkham games, but for me it's nowhere near Arkham City level sadly. Gotham is much bigger this time, just as dev said it would be, but half of that is copy & pasted from AC. Sure, there's some fun in it when you see how that part of Gotham looked before Arkham City, but it gets boring really soon, and with half of the missions and riddler collectibles placed there it really starded to feel like I'm playing a DLC for Arkham City after 2-3 hours.
Combat remained mostly unchanged, thankfully, with some new gadgets thrown in by developers, like electric gloves for example, in an effort to make it more interesting, but they failed completely and it feels like AC combat system really. I have to say that gadgets are the thing that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off the most, as almost all of them are reused. One of them (Ice Grenede, which is given to you by Mr Freeze in AC) was replaced by Glue Granade... which is exactly the same thing. They also doesn't make sense since you had to obtain almost all of them (except for Batarang and Batclaw) in AA or AC and Origins is supposed to take place before them!
Graphics are similarly unimpressive. They look identical to AC graphics, but AC came out in 2011! I did like, however, new menus, new HUD elements and that they took the effort to optimize their game which means it runs much, much better than Arkham City.
So in conclusion it's Arkham City with new storyline and new villains in an effort to tell the origins story. On one hand it's good they didn't messed with it so the combat system, collectibles and visual style remained the same. On the other it's about enough of vent crawling, jumping between gargoyles, detective mode and same, lame♥♥♥♥♥ repetitive, extremely boring missions. I really hope Rocksteady is busy making proper sequel to Arkham City using Unreal 4 and that they can innovate. I really enjoyed this game, but I don't think I'm going to buy what is essentially the same game 4th time next year. 8.5 / 10

Ok. Batman AO is the newest in the Batman video game franchise.I understand that i'm a few months late(As usual), but I just picked it up during the Steam winter sale. Now to summarize my thoughts of the previous two games: Asylum was meh. Average graphics, typical Batman story, and pretty good gameplay. City was a better meh. Meh graphics, Great gameplay and and a Batman story. AO, on the other wing is, well, Batman approved.
AOs story is a bit better than typical Bats fair. Black Mask breaks out of prison, then hires 7 of the worlds best killers to do their job. Now without venturing into spoiler water, things are not always as they seem. Now the reason that I said that this was better than the typical Bats story is that, this being an origins story, most of the major villains of Arkham don't really know about Batman yet. Outside of Penguin and Joker, the rest of the villains are part of the lesser characters list on WB games site.
Now I need another paragraph. Now as you may have guessed, most of the game is based around killing these villains. The major ones that I remember are Deadshot, Copperhead, Bane, Firefly, Anarchy, Slade Wilson, and the Electrocutioner. As you may have guessed, these serve as the games boss battles. And those being boss battles, they are the games low point. They all attack as their respective weight classes normal foes would. Bane charges and has to be killed with beatdowns, Wilson must be killed using a lot of counters, and copperhead using blocks. No variety here...
Ok, so you may have noticed that I am yet to mention graphics. Well, there pretty good. Snow looks nice, the Bat-suit is detailed down to the depth of which the bat on his chest can be measured, and night never looked so good. The facial animations are solid, and the regular animations look, well, smooth. The game could have used a tad bit of polish, but, this being the 7th or 8th year of the consoles, I can forgive them.
About the combat...it is Batalitious. It is largely unchanged from the previous games. It may not have innovated much, but neither bid Borderlands and it worked. It seems a lot less gadget based than City, but yet again, who said that was a bad thing. It is based around a series of counters, blocks, and special takedowns, that, when stringed together, work perfectly. It is a system that few games have been able to master, and, thankfully, Batman AO has.
Then again, theres the mulitplayer. For the most part, it revolves around crappy third-person shooting, with occasional games playing as the Bat. There isn't really a lot to be said here. In MP, there are 3 teams: Banes thugs, Jokers lunatics, and Batman/Robin. Joker and Bane fight it out with the standard fair of shottys, snipers, and HMGS. Its for the most part sub-par shooting that is extremely dated. And well they're off killing eachother, Bats and Robin(Who never shows up in SP) are able to sneak around on lions and pick of gunmen. Its similar to Spies vs. Mercs in Splinter Cell, and is well...meh
Last, I just wanted to spend a few words talking about the sound. The games base sound is solid, the guns are, well, guns, and the outside winds are good. The music is sub-meh, and for the most part forgettable. The voice actors, on the other wing, are pretty solid, and at least worthy of a sentence.
Well, the verdict. Good graphics, great story, decent sound and amazing gameplay. Maybe its been too long since i last played a good game, but in my book, this counts as one

When I first heard about the game, I was a little concerned that it would be crass and ironic. Given that the Game Grumps' typical repitoire of comedy consists of♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes and giggling about sex, I wasn't sure if a "daddy dating simulator" from the Grumps team would be right for me.
As it turns out, the game is surprisingly wholesome. The highlight of the experience is the relationship between your dad character and his daughter, which is a heartwarming coming of age story. It almost feels as if the "dad dating" aspect of the game was tacked on and pales in comparison to the father/daughter story I found particularly charming. That alone is well worth the $15 price of admission.
As far as the "dating" part goes, I only completed one path so far, with the big guy Brian. I found it sweet and wholesome, and I was very pleased with the story. So far I haven't seen anything overtly sexual or uncomfortable. I was glad that the endgame seemed to be simply love and not sex. I haven't played any other dates so far, but I am hoping it will be that way for the others too. My only complaint is echoed by other reviewers: it is very short. It takes 3 dates to find the dad of your dreams, and thus if you have your heart set on dating just one dad, you'll find there isn't a lot of content for you. However, for 15 bucks, there are plenty of dads to choose from and a lot of writing that went into developing each one, so I do think they delivered just enough content to satisfy.
Additionally, there are a few graphical and programming errors that I think could be polished out with an upcoming patch. The hairstyle I picked for my dad, for example, had transparent pixels between the lineart and flat colors, allowing the background to show through in a glaringly obvious way. And there was an instance in which the game forgot the gender of the player character's deceased spouse. Given what I've read in other reviews, this seems to be a recurring trend. Also, as far as visual novels go, the choices you can make are rather limited and linear. It would be nice to have more choices more often, even if it's just for roleplaying flavor. A lot of the personality traits of the player character are pretty set in stone.
For 15$ though, the game is fine. It could use a polish patch, but I believe the amount of content it delivers is satisfying enough for the price tag. More content definitely wouldn't hurt, but the game accomplishes what it sets out to do. If you're on the fence about buying it, definitely pick it up if you're interested in a heartwarming coming of age story.

Sauce:
Olive oil
1 pound lean ground beef (chuck)
1/2 onion, diced, about 3/4 cup
1/2 large bell pepper (green, red, or yellow), stem and core removed, diced, about 3/4 cup
2 cloves garlic, minced
1 28-ounce can good quality tomato sauce
3 ounces (half a 6-oz can) tomato paste
1 14-ounce can crushed tomatoes
2 Tbsp chopped fresh oregano or 2 teaspoons dried oregano
1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley (preferably flat leaf), packed
1 Tbsp Italian Seasoning
Pinch of garlic powder and/or garlic salt
1 Tbsp red or white wine vinegar
1 Tbsp to 1/4 cup sugar (to taste, optional)
Salt
Lasagna:
1/2 lb dry lasagna noodles (requires 9 lasagna noodles - unbroken)
15 ounces Ricotta cheese
1 1/2 lb (24 ounces) Mozzarella cheese, grated or sliced
1/4 lb (4 ounces) freshly grated Parmesan cheese
Cooking Utensils You'll Need:
A large skillet to brown the beef, bell pepper, and onion
A large pot (8 to 12-quarts) for cooking the pasta
A medium sized pot (3 to 4 quarts) to simmer the sauce
13" x 9" x 2" lasagna pan, preferably pyrex or stainless steel (avoid aluminum pans if you can, they can react with the acidity of the sauce)
A large colander to drain the noodles
A couple large sheet pans to cool the noodles
A large slotted cooking spoon
A large wooden cooking spoon
A chef's knife or large paring knife to cut the vegetables
MethodHide Photos
1 Put pasta water on to boil: Put a large pot of salted water (1 Tbsp salt for every 2 quarts of water) on the stovetop on high heat. It can take a while for a large pot of water to come to a boil (this will be your pasta water), so prepare the sauce in the next steps while the water is heating.
2 Brown the ground beef: In a large skillet heat 2 teaspoons of olive oil on medium high heat. Add the ground beef and cook it until it is lightly browned on all sides.

Remove the beef with a slotted spoon to a bowl. If there is more than a tablespoon of fat left in the pan (there shouldn't be if you are using lean ground beef) remove it from the pan.
3 Cook the bell pepper, onions, garlic, add back the beef: Add the diced bell pepper and onions to skillet (in the photo we are using yellow bell pepper and red onions).
Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until the onions are translucent and the peppers softened. Add the minced garlic and cook half a minute more.
Return the browned ground beef to the pan. Stir to combine, reduce the heat to low and cook for another 5 minutes.

4 Transfer to medium sized pot, add tomatoes and remaining sauce ingredients to build the sauce: Transfer the beef pepper onion mixture to a medium sized (3 to 4 quart) pot. Add the crushed tomatoes, tomato sauce, and tomato paste to the pot.
Add the parsley, oregano, and Italian seasonings, adjusting the amounts to taste. Sprinkle with garlic powder and/or garlic salt, to taste.
Sprinkle with red or white wine vinegar. Stir in sugar, a tablespoon at a time, tasting after each addition, to taste. (The amount of sugar needed will vary, depending on how acidic the tomatoes are that you are using.)
Add salt to taste, and note that you will later be adding Parmesan, which is salty.

Bring the sauce to a simmer and lower the heat to low to maintain a low simmer.  Cook for 15-45 minutes, stirring often. Scrape the bottom of the pot every so often so nothing sticks to the bottom and scorches.
Remove from heat.
5 Boil and drain the lasagna noodles: By now the salted water you started heating in step one should be boiling. Add the dry lasagna noodles and cook then per package directions (al dente). (Note noodles may be cooked in advance.)
Stir often to prevent from sticking. Make sure that water remains at a full rolling boil during the entire cooking to prevent noodles from sticking.
When ready, drain in a colander and rinse with cool water, gently separating any noodles that may be sticking together.

Spread a little olive oil on a large rimmed baking sheet, and lay out the cooked noodles on this sheet, turning them over so that they get coated with a little of the olive oil. This will prevent them from sticking together.
6 Assemble the lasagna: In a 13x9x2-inch casserole or lasagna dish, ladle a cup of sauce and spread it over the bottom of the dish. Arrange one layer of lasagna noodles lengthwise (about 3 long noodles, edge may overlap, depending on your pan) over the sauce. Ladle a third of the remaining sauce over the noodles.

Sprinkle a layer of a third of the grated mozzarella on top of lasagna sauce. Add half of the ricotta cheese, by placing cheese dollops every couple inches. Sprinkle the grated parmesan cheese evenly over the top of ricotta cheese.

Apply second layer of noodles, top it with half of the remaining sauce. Add half of the remaining Mozzarella, the remaining ricotta cheese, and another thin sprinkling of Parmesan.
Finish with another layer of noodles. Spread the remaining sauce over the top layer of noodles and sprinkle with the remaining Mozzarella cheese.

7 Bake: Tent the lasagna pan with aluminum foil (not touching noodles or sauce). Bake at 375°F for 45 minutes. Allow to cool before serving.
May be reheated in conventional oven or microwave. Leave aluminum tent on for storage. (Try to keep the aluminum foil from touching the sauce.)

It's Hitman again, and better than ever.
All my support to this game, both as a gamer and as a developer. They knew perfectly well what made hitman tick and they went back to the roots and improved its strong points instead of trying weird formulas or investing time on unneded features. I felt like replaying and replaying and replaying a mission like I used to in the old days, and it's not like I can do this very often lately.
The mastery incentive is a very good idea to add motivation to try the different assassination styles. It makes you feel encouraged to play in a messier, but sometimes funnier way from time to time without feeling that the game is scowling at you for not making the perfect run. I'm all for silent assassin ranks, I'm sure we all cleared blood money, contracts and the original games with perfect records, but sometimes assassinating the victim in plain sight and making a huge mess or actually using remote explosives without feeling that you're playing the game wrong is fun as well. Here you can actually gain something from it and unlock new things.
If the episodic system allows the developers to create missions as good as the paris one, it will be more than worth the wait.
And if you don't like the episodic system... just wait a few months and buy the whole thing instead of giving the game abyssal scores for a characteristic that was well known long before release. Production time and budget are two of the worst challenges in game developement, and responsible for a lot of dramatic amputations that kill the game quality. If they needed to resort to this formula to avoid having to compromise the final game quality, let them try. If they keep the quality this first mission has, it will be more than worth it. And considering there is the possibility of only buying the starter pack, which is very reasonably priced, it's not like they are robbing anyone.
We'll see how this one turns out. I'm confident that the other missions will meet my expectations. I could be wrong, who knows, but I'm gonna bet on them!

Enter the next era of HITMAN
At first glance, the game feels like you are back in absolution. Flawless graphics,great lighting effects and all the glamour that absolution boasted and offered. But there the similarities ends. What we have here is a game that combines the very best of Blood money's sandbox killing with absolutions fluid controls. Also, gone is the ultra stupid Tag and Execute system introduced in absolution. It doesnt make sense for 47 to have it and they have righted it by removing it. Instinct does not feel intrusive in comparison to absolution and gives you great wealth of information. In fact too much information at times which may or may not break individual game experience. Game level design is beautiful and huge and at times confuses me. I must admit that this is not a design flaw but rather my inexperience in detailing the floorplans but it just goes to show that to execute a perfect crime, planning and intel must be sought after in advance. There are of course some gripe with the game. The Shortness of the first level left me wanting more but yet unsatisfied at the same time. Perhaps the abrupt ending of the first episode felt like a kick in the stomach giving me a bitter taste of having to wait a month for the next part of the game. It is a month too long in reality and hopefully, the developers will push out the nex epi in due time. The next gripe in mind is the amount of buttons for each actions. In blood money, my fingers never have to move across the keyboard to access my inventory. Everything was reachable within my left hand but in this game, everything was jumbled. Inventory had to be accessed with "I" button and some buttons on the left that are keybound arent even used during the first epi. Design flaw perhaps? It is stupid and inconvenient. Developers should look to follow blood money or absolution's key mapping instead to provide better controls. The third gripe i have is the buggy AI. At times, certain actions performed by 47 will cause the AI to actually stop doing what they were intended to do...forever. And by certain actions, i did not mean killing. A good example is one of the target did not go to the affected laptop as intended no matter how long i waited there. The target was just standing in the patio doing nothing surrounded by all the guest and not moving! How am i suppose to kill anything if the target is bugged and not programmed properly?! Fix it squeenix/IO! The last gripe i have though is the opportunities. It is absolutely intrusive and should not be too obvious for players. With it, i feel like im being coddled and it felt way much more intrusive copared to instinct in absolution. The good thing however is that you can customise the UI to display lesser of these opportunities to down right zero help. Outside of these gripes, im relatively pleased with the game and how it turned out. Keep it up IO and hope to see the next release soon!
P.S For those who preordered the full priced game and are griping about the price, Deal with it. You were given the information and choice to purchase episode by episode before hand. So do not go saying how it is not worth whatever amount you paid in advance because of the episodic release.

This game is very nice to look at and the controls are intuitive for a 3D space game. The issue I have at this point is that it is a very linear game. Instead of an open world where you can take over bases, collect resources, and build a fleet you are led down a path of doing each of these things only to the extent that you need to in order to complete the current mission. The ability for your ships to navigate to a chosen location without getting caught on rocks/portals/etc is also an issue in some missions.
As it is now, I rarely need to setup a base of operations once I remove the previous owners from a zone. Instead I just setup a base on the one or two tiles that will give me resources over time and then max out my fleet according to replicant count and move to the next location down the designated path. I assume this gripe is not as big of an issue when playing on hard difficulty, but it would be nice for the game to require you to make use of bases regardless of difficulty.
I'm having fun with the game in it's current state, but I am at the point where I want more, and I'm not sure that I'll get it out of the available campaign. I hope this game is expanded upon in some way in the future to allow for different types of gameplay similar to my description above.

Not bad, but severely underwhelming.  It's the sort of thing you would find in the $5 bin at WalMart and be pleasantly surprised by. Worth purchasing on sale, maybe, but at full price there's far better games out there.
The big upside is that it's extremely challenging. Not because of the enemy AI or anything, no it's hard due to the sheer ridiculous swarms of enemy ships you will face - missions are generally pretty short and brutal slugfests hopelessly outnumbered which you can win by being equal parts clever and lucky.
The story is alright but extremely generic. It's somewhat nonsensical to me to send in your precious, irreplaceable carrier for every mission and to abandon your fleet whenever you leave the sector, but then I'm not some masterful tactician so who am I to say.
The maps are not open, as was implied - they are typically divided into 3 small sectors connected by warp gates. The only place you can build is fixed positions and the only thing you can build is turrets.
Ship pathfinding is hilariously bad. You can somewhat overcome this by manually instructing your ships around every small obstacle but this obviously presents an absolute nightmare situation doing a lot of things, like trying to send ships reinforce other ships in a major fleet fight, or trying to not smash your keyboard and froth at the mouth in your chair.
I could go on but I think you get the point. It has potential, yes. It's not a bad game. But it's far outclassed, even by games decades older than it (yes I mean Homeworld 2). And I wouldn't reccommend anyone buy it at full price.

tldr; set compatibility mode for maxpayne.exe in the max payne directory to Windows 98/Windows ME + run as administrator.

Quick-save happy action game squarely of the old school variety. At the time of release there was just nothing else like Max Payne. The Matrix was fresh in the minds of the masses. System Shock 2, Half-Life, Deus Ex, had all been released. PC gaming couldn't get any better. Or so we thought.
Controls may seem wonky to youngins raised on the buttery smooth engines of late. Mechanics may seem unpolished if you're used to a skill ceiling in reach of "everyone". Max Payne can both challenge and frustrate you. Gameplay-as-story was new and had only been woven succesfully into a handful of titles. It stands as a great example of a "pure" game, hitting all the highs the medium has to offer. It hasn't aged quite as gracefully as other classics, but strap into a comfy chair with at least a few hours to spare, turn the lights down and your sound up and prepare to enjoy an excellent affair of cinematic gaming in the dark underworld of a frozen New York City.

Ok, this has been driving me crazy for seven movies now, and I know you're going to roll your eyes, but hear me out: Harry Potter should have carried a 1911.
Here's why:
Think about how quickly the entire WWWIII (Wizarding-World War III) would have ended if all of the good guys had simply armed up with good ol' American hot lead.
Basilisk? Let's see how tough it is when you shoot it with a .470 Nitro Express. Worried about its Medusa-gaze? Wear night vision goggles. The image is light-amplified and re-transmitted to your eyes. You aren't looking at it--you're looking at a picture of it.
Imagine how epic the first movie would be if Harry had put a breeching charge on the bathroom wall, flash-banged the hole, and then went in wearing NVGs and a Kevlar-weave stab-vest, carrying a SPAS-12.
And have you noticed that only Europe seems to a problem with Deatheaters? Maybe it's because Americans have spent the last 200 years shooting deer, playing GTA: Vice City, and keeping an eye out for black helicopters over their compounds. Meanwhile, Brits have been cutting their steaks with spoons. Remember: gun-control means that Voldemort wins. God made wizards and God made muggles, but Samuel Colt made them equal.
Now I know what you're going to say: "But a wizard could just disarm someone with a gun!" Yeah, well they can also disarm someone with a wand (as they do many times throughout the books/movies). But which is faster: saying a spell or pulling a trigger?
Avada Kedavra, meet Avtomat Kalashnikova.
Imagine Harry out in the woods, wearing his invisibility cloak, carrying a .50bmg Barrett, turning Deatheaters into pink mist, scratching a lightning bolt into his rifle stock for each kill. I don't think Madam Pomfrey has any spells that can scrape your brains off of the trees and put you back together after something like that. Voldemort's wand may be 13.5 inches with a Phoenix-feather core, but Harry's would be 0.50 inches with a tungsten core. Let's see Voldy wave his at 3,000 feet per second. Better hope you have some Essence of Dittany for that sucking chest wound.
I can see it now...Voldemort roaring with evil laughter and boasting to Harry that he can't be killed, since he is protected by seven Horcruxes, only to have Harry give a crooked grin, flick his cigarette butt away, and deliver what would easily be the best one-liner in the entire series:
"Well then I guess it's a good thing my 1911 holds 7+1."
And that is why Harry Potter should have carried a 1911.

Yooka-Laylee is a perfect example of a Kickstarter that delivered exactly what it said it would.  For better or for worse.
If you're familiar with the Kickstarter, then you know exactly what you're getting into: An old-school collectathon-style game from some of the devs who refined the genre in the 90s.  If what you wanted was more sprawling worlds in which you can lose yourself, tons silly tasks to carry out for rewards, NPCs who are somehow both charming and utterly annoying at the same time, plenty of backtracking to open new areas with new abilities, and all of it rendered with much better textures, more detailed models, and other technological advancements the 90s could only dream of, then you've found your game.
On the other hand, if you never liked the collectathon genre in the first place, this will definitely not change your mind.  No matter what it was that may have turned you off the genre before, it's probably on display here, including goals that may not be well-indicated in worlds whose sheer sizes make them difficult to keep in your head (with no on-screen maps, either), the same sort of gibberish-voices that some people just can't stand, slightly clunky 90s-era level design, a camera that seems dedicated to fighting your every move (admittedly, a patch is in the works for this), and tediously combing every single inch of every world just to find that one stupid minor collectable in each that's stopping you from 100% completion.  This game was made for people who didn't mind all that and are maybe even nostalgic for it, and the makers are not ashamed of it in the least.
My personal opinion?  I like it.  I knew what I was getting into when I backed it, and they delivered.  It's another set of worlds to explore, another set of things to collect, and another strange assortment of characters to get to know.  What can I say?  It hit my nostalgia center in the right way, warts and all.  I just can't really blame anyone who doesn't like it.

As someone who use to play Banjo-Tooie and Kazooie religiously throughout life, poured countless, hundreds of hours into them, Banjo-Tooie is easily my alltime favourite game, I can safely say Yooka-Laylee is just a Spiritual Sucessor to the games, it takes heavy inspiration from those games and it's quite fun, but it is not the Banjo-Threeie I was expecting, There are many, many elements that Banjo-Tooie and Kazooie have that make those games legendary, sadly Yooka-Laylee lacks these elements, let me go into some of the cons;
The Hubs are often confusing to navigate and you can get lost easily.
The levels I've played so far 1 - 3 are sometimes confusing to navigate and figure out what you need to do, especially when you play a non-expanded level, there's dead ends and missing parts that make everything very confusing and forces you to get enough pagies to expand it to figure it out easily.
The character designs don't quite fit the levels sometimes, alot of the enemies just feel like they've been copied and pasted and given a different art style and model to fit the level, where's Banjo-Tooie and Kazooie had very, very unique creatures per level.
The Boss FIghts I've currently had have been pretty annoying and boring, and not voerly creative like the ones in Banjo-Tooie and Kazooie, and speaking of bosses
*SPOILER WARNING*
And lastly, Rextro's arcade games are often a ♥♥♥♥♥ to play and you have to play them twice for two pagies, Kartos Racing is the worst thing I've ever played, it controls like♥♥♥♥♥♥
The game however does feel quite nice to play, the camera and controls are pretty solid for a platformer like Banjo, the music is great and it's a blast to play, the sounds are quite fun to listen to and some of the puzzles are quite fun.. sometimes, and the only technical issues I've had so far are just the odd occaisional frame drop, Originally I was praising this game as a great Banjo-Threeie but taking a step back and looking at it, it's not a Banjo game at all, just a platformer with heavy inspiration from Banjo, and yes I played Banjo-Tooie shorty after binge-playing this game for 7 hours.
All n All, If you aren't expecting a Banjo-Kazooie/Tooie clone and want a good platformer, then get this game, otherwise, get it on sale, it's deffinately worth a play, and alot of fun, I rate it 7/10.

I did 100% in Yooka-Laylee and it was overall a very enjoyable experience! Not as good as Banjo-Kazooie, but not far behind for sure. Only complaints, like many others, is that the levels are too big for nothing in general (the amount of stuff to do and pick up doesn't justify the size. The second level, the ice one, being the greatest offender imo) and the camera is really bad (probably the one retro aspect they could've skipped on without anyone complaining haha). Other than that it's exactly what we asked for, a spiritual successor to Banjo with a completely 90s 3D platformer feel. Which is exactly what they marketed.
I don't understand the other complaints, it seems people expected something else and/or were misinformed. It's a game made by the veterans of Rare and it's the Banjo-Threeie they always wanted to do but couldn't because of copyrights. So they did exactly that but with another skin on it and a very smaller budget they would've had and QoA support from a publisher. And considering all of that, we got something very good out of these conditions.

Max Payne is the first title to the highly acclaimed Max Payne franchise. Originally developed by Remedy Games back in 2001, it has then received multiple awards for its story telling, gameplay and graphics from critics and gamers alike.
Max Payne is a third-person action game where the player takes the role of a hard-boiled, no non-sense New York City cop named, you guessed it, Max Payne, who is on a mission to avenge the death of his wife and infant daughter in the hands of vagrants who were high on a street drug named Valkyr. He sets of to find the people responsible for the production and distribution of Valkyr who he holds responsible for his family's death.
+ Story: - At first glance the story seems to be a cliché cop drama, and, yes I would agree, HOWEVER, it's the presentation, execution and overall delivery of the story that makes the original Max Payne a gem on action drama story telling.
+ Gameplay: - This was the fist game to incorporate the now popular 'Bullet Time' effect where time basically slows down allowing the player more accuracy for combat while at the same time adding theatrical spice to the gunplay. This might not be relevant to the current generation of gamers but back in 2001, it was one of the game's highest selling points.
+ Voice Acting: - Fantastic voice acting from the cast specially on the character of Max Payne with his dark humour and gritty personality.
+ Atmospheric: - The graphics for its time is top notch and delivers a very dark and depressing world that reflects the slowly changing personality of Max. From the dank and cold city streets to the surreal nightmarish realm of Max's dreams, the game stands tall on atmosphere and immersion.
- Bugged Sound for Windows Vista/7/possibly 8: - Being 13 years old, the game does suffer from compatibility issues. Gameplay wise, it functions well enough but users will encounter a bug that renders no audio in the game. (Note: LINK TO THE FIX IS AT THE BOTTOM OF THIS REVIEW)
- Replayability: - Linear story is FINE, its a good way to tell a narrative story in a directed pace but Linearity does sacrifice replayability at degree because after finishing the story there is little reason to play it through a second time around. Like a good action movie, it's best to be played again after some time has passed.
- Facial Animation: - Max has a permanent facial expression where the devs tried to give him a gritty look but they just ended up making him look smug and/or constipated expression through out the game. Good thing the Comic Book cut sences are there to save the day.
Max Payne is a GREAT GAME that started a great franchise. It brought us the mainstream Bullet Time effect that most action shooter gamers has come to incorporate and embrace as a core game mechanic. It showed us a perfect blend of action and storytelling in one single game without sacrificing gameplay and mechanics.
It is a fast paced brutal 3rd person shooter that fans of the genre should not miss out on. Sale or full price, this game is worth the money and worth the time.

I've been playing RTS games since C&C. The Homeworld series has, since I first played it, been one of my all time favourite RTS series. The gameplay was simple, intuitive and elegant. The ships had interesting designs and looked, for the time and even now, beautiful. The Avatar looked like a brawler. It oozed a kind of raw power. It was a moving chunk of armour that was armed to the teeth. The Qwar'Jet, it's Taiidani counter part was equally as daunting. The units were varied, several different kinds of fighters (of which the Taiidani were the more visually interesting in my opinion). The fighter furballs raging around formations of assault frigates and walls of Ion Cannon Frigates to the destroyers and cruisers duking it out in battles of attrition were spectacular. Following trails of your fighters as they jinked, dodged and spun through enemy formations, firing pot shots at what they could or covering each other. It was and still is visually stunning.
Even though there were only two or three characters, Homeworld had ambience to spare. Certainly the gameplay of the second trumped the first at the cost of the ambience and much of the heart and soul. It's gameplay was superior, even if the number of usable fighters and ship classes were halved, the changing of individual fighters to squads cleaned up a lot of the flotsam of maintaining your fighter's numbers. It was, in my opinion of gameplay, superior. I was seriously disappointed that there was no Homeworld 3 and I'm hoping against hope that Gearbox don't ♥♥♥♥ each and everything up with the remake and possible sequel.
Why these two paragraphs about Homeworld in a review for a completely different game? I just want people to understand where I'm coming from when I say that Ancient Space is a mess.
