To paraphrase a certain quirky games reviewer - "Ancient Space is Like Homeworld but..."
(Also... ancient space? isn't most space ancient?)
Imagine for a minute you're playing Homeworld with persistent ramifications level to level (the more you suck early on, the tougher later levels will be - so don't suck)... well Ancient Space has none of that. Careful resource management? Nope. A large variet of units? Nah. Major differences between your ships and the baddies? Nu-uh. Massive truely 3D space environments where you have to think tactically in three dimensions? Sorry - but it does pretend fairly well.
No. Ancient Space (which in TeamSpeak is pronounced "AAAAAAAncient Spaaaaaaaaaaaaaaace") instead goes down the Dawn of War route to being a game.
There are persistent resource points - which given the infinite nature of space, are of course severly limited in number and fixed. You can only place "buildings" on the fixed resource points (really they're turrets. Either good vs Cap ships OR small and medium ships, radar, repair, or slow the enemy) which is lucky as the AI is too stupid to try going around them.
The resources are infinite - being one of those X resource/time types, which is mostly fine, but it robs you of the risk vs reward of trying to go further and further out from your base to mine/dig/harvest stuff that was present in RTS games since Dune 2
Ship numbers are insanely low. Don't expect to re-enact cool space battles from films or previous games... the most I've seen so far was 21 slots (some ships take more than one slot). I say ship numbers are low - they're low for you. The enemy have no such troubles, and their production times are much shorter (so the poxy ships that disable your pop up so often that they get very annoying very quickly).
Ships are ... boring really. 2 or 3 of each size of ship (eventually 4 different fight sized ships! woo). The limitations on numbers and the small variety mean that Corsairs are the best thing since sliced-starships. They can imobilise an enemy and then capture it 6 of them takes on every resource area/enemy building facility I've come across) and you could build more.
Space is apparently not 3D... it pretends to be... but it's really just a blanket over some bumpy things (like it was in the original Doom). Why do I say this? because you can't direct your ships up or down... there are some floaty circles in space which are higher or lower than each other and if you click on them then your ships will dutifully move there - but you can't positions ships half-way without fist commanding them to move somewhere then stopping them midway. Homeworld might have been more years ago than I'd like to admit, but they worked out how to go up and down back then. Then there's the fact that the circles of space being transparent which occasionally causes ships to go somewhere you didn't think you were clicking because the context sensitive movement system though you wanted to go somewhere closer to the camera than you knew about. Seriously the movement in this game is almost poor enough to be a bug - not quite, but really... meh!
Between missions do your actions carry any weight? No. You can upgrade some ships a bit (and one ship a lot) by spending points which are arbitarily doled out at the end of each mission. Ships you build vanish mysteriously to be replaced by an entirely different fleet of ships the mission designers thought would see you through.
In Homeworld you had your entire race with you on one ship - because your previous home had been bombed into a radioactive hellish nightmare type affair... so it made sense that you lose your mothership, you lose. In this game despite travelling everywhere by fixed, reliable and free warp gates, you send your utterly irreplaceable carrier on every mission... not just outside the last gate so you can send reinforcements through as and when they're needed... because, reasons.
But the graphics are awesome right? Well, they're ok I guess - we are unfortunately in a time where graphics are pretty good even in low budget titles. Sure things are pretty, but no prettier than X3 for instance and that's several years old. Textures are alright, models are ok... nothing says "OMG! THIS IS AWESOME I WILL NOW DRY HUMP MY MONITOR" though.
Also, the levels are small - it's space! Why must things be so small... Warp-gates are the only way to get from one sector to another so there's no inbetween space, and the sectors themselves are tiny (compared to Homeworld).
I know by now people will be wondering why compare it to Homeworld so much? Well to those people - go play Homeworld then play this... you'll see that at no time has there been an original idea design wise. This game is trying to be Homeworld and a bit more.
People really seemed fixated on Skirmish mode in forum posts running up to release - there are three skirmish missions. No free form - decide things yourself missions... nope, 3 specific missions. The first is a Horde type game "survive as long as possible"...
There's no multiplayer. No Co-op, no Versus mode. I've heard people counter with "well, that means they can focus on the single player story" ... Well, Aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaancient Spaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaace is clearly aping both Homeworld and Dawn of War - both games had rich developed single player experiences AND multiplayer.
I can't recommend this game - not because it's terrible, not because it's below average, but simply because it's trying to be two games which were both better examples of being them. Had Homeworld and Dawn of War not existed then this would be good. But they do exist, and having played them, this feels more like a poor copy that it would otherwise.
Allow me to move ships UP and DOWN in space
Allow me to play the game with friends (co-op campaign or competitive)
Allow me to build a fleet of ships (not a couple of ships)
Allow me to take ships from one mission to another
Allow me to choose a strategy from a variety of ships and play styles (rather than severly limiting my choices by having so few unit types - best ships in the game are the Corsair and Cutlass and you have to capture those)
Increase the number of skirmish options
Fix those and you'll have a game that's almost as good as Homeworld (which if Gearbox are reading - a release date for the remaster would be nice). Till then you have an average game which doesn't stand out enough to recommend - even at £14.99

Ancient Space is a 3D, space based, story heavy, single player, real time strategy game (RTS).
The Great:
- Gorgeous 3D space environments that should be the standard for space RTS games going forward
- RPG mechanics such as gear and specializations customization added to ships and capital ships that make you wonder why no one else has done it this well in an RTS game before
- Detailed and intricate RTS with RPG aspects gameplay works very well - a solid foundation to build upon
- Voice-acting and story are well above average for the genre
The Good:
- Intuitive control scheme
- Varying difficulty
- Nice pacing such that it is almost always interesting but not exhausting or stressful
The Bad:
- Some technical glitches present
- Graphics options are nearly non-existent
- Missions can run long at times and sometimes contain tedious overlong sections
- Occasional excessive difficulty
- This game would do very well to include Steam Workshop support for easy modding support
Overall:
This looks to be a very worthy addition to the RTS genre.  While a slightly tighter and more forgiving campaign might have proved better,  at $20, and given how much the game innovates in some ways (e.g. adding "gear" to your fleet of ships and the overall art direction) it is hard to find much to complain about.  If you like strategy games or RTS games in particular, you should definitely pick this game up.

Though the arsenal isn't perfect, most weapons are still usable in many situations, unlike in successive iterations (who uses LMGs in Ghosts or Advanced Warfare?), and though gadgets are too damn many as always, they're not excessively spammable and do not replace the standard weaponry. C4 and Gaymore are still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ unfortunately. It's not perfect, but it's fun, the game speed hits the sweet spot between rushing and tactical gameplay and generally it's fun to play a multiplayer match.
-Pick 10 class creator is well-thought and allows for creative equipment settings, without being as perk-filled as Ghosts' Pick 13 or whatever it was.
-The maps have some flaws pointed out in the cons, but are rich of cover and alternative routes and are generally enjoyable. Their design is far from splendid, but it's functional and nice. The setting is extremely generic, though.
-The graphics are below standard as always for this genre of games, but are a nice step forward compared to Modern Warfare 3, and the PC conversion is rather good for COD standards, running smoothly and even offering some sort of FOV slider (though very limited in range).
-The campaign is probably the last attempt so far in a COD game to make a decent single player experience. The plot is interesting enough, there are many different situations, voiceover is decent (the italian one, my language, in particular) and there are even multiple endings and variations caused by the player's actions. Nice one.
-The game modes are mostly fun and functional in multiplayer, with some exeptions, and are varied enough to offer the average player various choices when it comes down to choose what to play. As long as there are players.
CONS
-This problem isn't related to the game, but to the fact that it's on PC: COD community on this platform is a little more mature than the console one (don't let me think about them...), but it's small. There are few thousands of players playing this game as of now for the most part of the day, and it can be hard or impossible to find a match in certain game modes. And, with such a small choice of hosts, the chance of finding a laggy game is rather high.
-No dedicated server, by the way. It was 2012, already late enough to miss this very important part of a serious online game, and now it's 2015 and Advanced Warfare still hasn't any. Are we gonna have this amazing "privilege" eventually?
-The arsenal has been rebalanced wildly and has no clearly OP weapons anymore (not that much OP, at least), but it's tiny. Excessive amounts of assault rifles and submachine guns and barely any shotgun, sniper rifle or pistol.
-The maps are too damn circular, allowing for an excessive chance of being spawnkilled by a flanking enemy. Also, spawn is badly calculated as always, either throwing you way too far from the action or in front of an enemy player, sentencing you to instantaneous death.
-The DLC amount and price in this series has been an insanity since Black Ops, and hasn't improved. At least 50 euros (season pass) to obtain a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of new maps that maybe weren't really needed and inevitably split the community and one new overcomplicated zombie map. Oh, and one new weapon. This is crazy.
-Zombie has become so super convoluted it's sickening me. Once a grizzly survival in condensed map facing endless hoardes of zombie, it's now become an easter egg hunting with the annoyance of endless hoardes of zombies. ♥♥♥♥ me, this sucks.
-Some equipment in multiplayer is OP as hell. Stun grenades have an excessive range, an excessive duration and an excessive effect, turning the victim into a helpless statue every time they hit. Obviously, they're used continously. C4 and Claymore, apart from being flat out annoying, are the camper's easy button and have an excessive power.
-This is just my personal opinion, but i think splitting Domination in two rounds is just stupid. It breaks the rhythm of the gameplay and it's just pointless. If a team suck, there are already extremely favorable all-over-the-map spawns that allow for unfair counterattack and backstab. There was no need for this annoying feature. Unfortunately, it didn't change in the successive installments.
Thus, Black Ops II isn't flawless. And yet, it's the least unbalanced and funniest of the recent COD experiences. Though it isn't a new game anymore, it's still enjoyable without having to face the terrifying optimization and balance that Ghosts has and the atrocious Advanced Warfare jump-spam gameplay, not to mention their awful map designs. So if you want a decent COD game that isn't dated 2009, this might just be your choice

Starpoint Gemini 2 is a space game like Elite and Frontier of old. You can have different ships, and rig them with different sets of weapons of different types, and then fly around to your hearts content fighting random enemies, hauling cargo, and so on.
The nags
- The campaign seems wooden in its story and voice acting

All in all, if you happen to get the game with a nice price and like to pimp your spaceship, Starpoint Gemini 2 can be worth a try!

(TL;DR version of this review available at the bottom.)
Picked this up during the brief period it was free on Steam. It's a space trading and combat game obviously heavily influenced by Freelancer. The most significant departures from Freelancer, apart from the obvious graphical advances a decade brings, are the combat mechanics, which are still decently action- and maneuver-oriented (but easy to cheese), and an overall lack of polish. The game is still being worked on, though, so that might change months or years from now.
At lowest settings the game runs decently well on my 2011-era midrange laptop, a "potato" by today's standards, and I expect that any decent modern machine will be able to run this game in a much prettier configuration. It already looks good enough even on the low end.
The biggest problem the game has at the moment is it doesn't do nearly enough to get a new player up to speed. The campaign itself offers no help whatsoever to teach players the game. The only tutorials you get are small-font text help screens which appear whenever the player happens to blunder into a new element of the gameplay. There's a lot of stuff to learn, and most of your education will come from trial and error or from just poking around the UI. It will take time, but it's less tedious than it sounds. Still, IMO it's a process that ought instead to have been interweaved into the early stages of the game's campaign, or at least mostly taken care of in a separate tutorial section, as any game of this level of complexity ought to.
The combat is quite fun, once you figure out what you're doing. It's clear this component of the game has had the greatest share of thought and effort put into it, and once you explore the mechanics past its surface presentation you discover effective fighting techniques that make you a very dangerous scrapper in just about any ship.
One piece of advice: ditch the default camera and gunnery mode for something better. Use turret view for camera control, WASD+QE to maneuver, and fire-at-will mode together, and you'll enjoy combat. If you use the standard setup meant to imitate Freelancer, you're going to be constantly frustrated and far easier to kill. Freelancer's tail-chasing dogfight combat style doesn't make sense in a game where virtually every ship can fire in any direction.
The trading and progression systems work quite similarly to Freelancer: sell off what you pick up from combat or mining, save up for bigger and better ships. The larger classes of ship are gated behind a level requirement, and you gain levels by accumulating XP from combat and completing missions. Your reputation value determines which factions are hostile or friendly, a value which is also adjusted through combat and missions. The cash value of goods vary between locales, making trade routes possible (but honestly not worth it, considering how much more you stand to make through combat).
Immersion factor is mediocre; the general activity level of ships coming and going through Gemini are about the same as Freelancer, but the fact that ships and stations in Freelancer audibly talked to each other, and to the player, helped to sell the illusion of a bustling interstellar civilization. There is no comm traffic between NPCs here, and that makes the game world feel more sparse. NPCs wander around until they get into trouble, at which point they either die, or they win and wander around some more until the process repeats itself. No NPCs are seen mining asteroid fields, running trade routes, or in any other way pretending to be scratching out a living in Gemini.
If you decide to try the campaign, be prepared for disappointment. It is easily the weakest aspect of this game as of this writing, and feels tacked on to a game that wasn't originally designed to feature one. The dialogue is HORRENDOUS. Badly written, badly acted. I ended up taking my headphones off during cutscenes because I couldn't stand to listen to any more of them. The only positive thing the campaign contributes is a big chunk of money and XP for completing their missions, accelerating your progression some. It's barely worth it, though, because the campaign is NOT enjoyable or well-made.
Despite my criticisms, though, I still think this game is worth playing. A lot more work needs to be put in to rework some dead-end features and polish the experience, but it's already a plenty decent game that won't be a waste of your time. As far as the price goes, though, the current price ($34.99) is much too high. I'd consider this game barely worth the money at $20, a decent value at $15. Basically, wait for a sale before picking this up.
TL;DR version: If you enjoyed Freelancer's gameplay, you'll like this. Worth buying at $20 or less. Avoid the campaign. You'll need to put in your own legwork to learn the game's mechanics because it's bad at teaching them to you. Combat is fun once you break away from the default setup. Let this game grow on you.

It's like Arkham City but worse. Still alright. It's obviously a quick cash-in, It's nowhere near as polished as AC, and the amount of copy/paste is staggering. But it's not bad.
I like games about punching people, and they more or less improved the punching people mechanics from Arkham City. The counter window is smaller, and the people punch you more aggressively. Origins has to be played more defensively, with less button mashing and more gadget use. At least on hard, normal is still easy. They tacked on some new enemy types in Origins too, which kind of work.
So punching people is the most functional part of the game. There's a lot of dumb bs in the rest of it though.
The story of the game makes no sense for the first half but it picks up once the Joker shows up, because the Joker is easy to write. The hyped up assassin plot is barely even relevant to the story: at no point does it feel like there's assassins trying to hunt you down. 4 out of 8 assassins are reused from they previous games because finding new villains is hard and takes work. Half of the assassins get reduced to sidequests, too, so it's actually Batman who's going after the assassins. The sidequests are kind of nonsensical. Deadshot tries to fight you in a tiny confined space in a sneak mission, even though he has a sniper rifle and could just set up camp somewhere and drop you when you glide by. I mean come on.
I liked the Bane fight. The developers probably liked it too because they make you repeat it.
The new crime-scene reconstruction thing is brainless and tedious. You don't even have to look for clues anymore, they give you a trail of red triangles to follow. Wow!
All the AC sidequests have been copy/pasted here. Origins packs watered-down Riddler trophies (now enigma trophies), Bane Canisters (now black mask canisters) and the Zasz mission where you rush after phones (they're bombs this time). The added sidequests are mostly about punching people on the streets, which is something you'll do anyway, so that too is lazy.
Many parts of the game feel like pointless filler, as if it was compulsory to pad out the game with reused assets. For some reason you go after the Penguin again and his boat hideout is laid out suspiciously like his museum from AC. You also♥♥♥♥♥♥around in the Steel Mill for a bit, go figure. Batman also gets poisoned again, presumably because they wanted to reuse his "poisoned" walk cycle. Then Batman goes on to have a bunch of lame hallucinations because that is part of the formula.
Origins has a neat, dark winter wonderland setting, and gliding around the moody art deco town is all kinds of atmospheric. They did managed to ♥♥♥♥ up the grapnel gun a bit (it doesn't latch on to some buildings for some reason) and the map design is not nearly as tightly structured around gameplay as in AC. There's also no civilians in Gotham apparently, because of excuses. They should have at least put SOME civilians standing around here and there, but no, that's extraneous and all the corners had to be cut.

Max Payne is a 3rd person shooter with a unique mechanic known as Bullet Time. While in this mode, Max leaps in a direction and slows down time allowing the player to take down multiple foes with ease. Damn, it is such an awesome feature. Great for stylish kills/takedowns.
Story is absolutely amazing. You play as a New York cop who seeks revenge after such drug-fuelled thugs cross paths with you. As you go through the campaign, the tale gets darker and more intense though never losing it's humour. Ending was also great.
Gameplay wise, it is one of the most fun action games I've played alongside Mafia - Lost City of Heaven (which is an incredible game). There is a lot of satisfaction in slowing down time and killing a whole bunch of dudes heavily armed with SMGs, shotguns and Berettas.
Graphics are dated though that's to be expected as Max Payne came out in 2001, though is still serviceable.
All in all, I'd recommend this game for all fans of action games with great stories.

After playing the training scenarios and the first campaign mission (about half an hour) I have to say I am underwhelmed.  Some might say that's too short to draw a conclusion but I have already run into enough disappointment with this game that I've lost interest in it.  I'll break it down into pros and cons:
Pros:  The graphics are good and the backdrops look great.  The voice acting is pretty decent as well.  I also thought the soundtrack was strong.  The ship models look good and the moving hardpoints are a nice touch.
Cons:  The "movement" of the ships, for some reason I cannot quite put my finger on, just does not seem right.  It definitely feels more Sins of a Solar Empire than Homeworld to me.  As a absolutely HUGE Homeworld fan (one of my favorite game series of all time) I was not impressed with this game.  Another big disappointment is the explosions.  In a game like this they should really make the explosions feel powerful and awesome and this game fails tremendously in that reguard.  Large captial ships explode extremely quickly and with a visual and auditory fidelity not up to par with Homeworld 2, a game 11 years its senior.  In Homeworld 2 when a captial ship was destroyed it was EPIC.  In this game it's forgettable.  Weapon effects are largely in the same boat... just underwhelming and almost immediately boring.  Another complaint was that I felt largely underprepared for the first mission following the training scenarios.  The first mission throws several objectives at you and immediately drops you in combat.
Overall I'd say that while I respect the intentions of the developer and almost always welcome a sci-fi/space oriented game I just cannot give this game my recommendation.  A few strong aspects are completely overwhelmed by multiple negative ones.

I've done a video with my playing through some first impressions. In general, I enjoyed the game. HOWEVER - if you were hoping for a homeworld replacement (as I was), don't expect to find it here. This is more a basic RTS with a few other elements. It's fun, I enjoyed playing, but didn't give me the pure joy of Homeworld.
If you approach it with more generic expectations, I believe you can find a decent amount enjoyable about this game, making it worth the price.
EDIT: Took out a comment regarding 3D movement based on Developer note. Will further explore, although I don't believe it'll change my review too much. Still an enjoyable game, still a bit less than I was hoping for, but fun.

The polish is merely polygon-deep.
I've seen quite a few small bugs (and they are small - save for one crash).  Several parts of this game are best described as 'annoying'.  The near silent ships (much moreso than homeworld), the level design (endless reinforcements for the enemy thus far, plus a buggy skirmish level), the incredible slowness of every ship, including fighters, the weapon discharges that appear out of nowhere, with no effects or moving turret (only applies to some of the ships), the halfhearted RTS control/command based on +1 defense rather than something real (homeworld 1 geometric formations that affected position->results, not +1 attributes).
The story might be good - can't say yet.
Don't buy - yet, at least.  See if the basics are fixed up first.

I will flesh out this review more when I finish the Campaign and try Skirmishes.  My tenative review of the game is that it is quite good, especially considering the price.
Story/Campaign:
The tone of the story is short, but effective.  The form of delivery for the story is modeled after general RTS Campaigns such as Company of Heroes or the Homewrold franchise.  Campaign missions tend to allow the player to move at their own pace.  In one mission (I believe mission 3 or 4), I sincerely messed up an assault on an enemy position, and paid the price in time and resources, but was able to recover and press on to completion.  The difficulty can be quite hard, but once you know the high-value targets (Warpgates/Repair Stations), things seem to resolve themselves quickly.
Units:
Unit design is distinct both in art and play.  Ancient Space uses the tried and true RPS style of unit countering, in the case of this game different weapon systems are more or less effective based on the hull size of the opponent.  Once you begin customizing your units with upgrades (between missions), you can truly give your own fleet a wide range of effectiveness.  It is unfortunate how limited some of the upgrade option can be though.
Art:
This is a catagory where the game tends to knock it out of the park.  Each sector looks distinct and interesting, and the background space is at times awe-inspiring.  All told, the artists for Ancient Space have created a vibrant and interesting space environment that I could likely look at for hours, assuming of course that I have eliminated the enemy Warpgates.

Thus far I've only played the first few missions so this is just an initial impression.
I see a few people comparing this to Homeworld but truth be told, though it shares certain elements like the space theme and the 3D movement, the game doesn't share much more with Homeworld.
It's more accurately described as an area control type game and much more comparable to the likes of Ground Control/World in Conflict mixed with elements of Conquest Frontier Wars (the warp routes and different sectors). Each unit has a specific role and powers to which you have to micromanage each of their ability(ies). Resources are acquired by capturing specific areas and building stations on them to which resources will then trickle in over time. Each station in turn can have a certain add-on (only 1 add-on per station) build on it that adds certain actions and powers. Like turrets as an example. Between missions you can upgrade your unit's stats or abilities and you can choose which Officers to take with on your next mission, who each will have different effects during the next mission.
The game is quite difficult, not because of particularly difficult AI but rather because it feels like each mission was designed to be played in a certain way but sometimes there is no clear indication of what the devs intended you to do. So a lot of trial and error. This could also only be due to my inexperience with the game.
There is obviously more to the game but I’ll write a proper review once I’ve spend more time in the game. And thus far I’m more on the optimistic side. Just don’t get this with the impression that it plays like Homeworld but rather that it has a rich atmosphere and strong character like Homeworld. The thematic Battlestar Galactica-ish music also helps with this regard.

I've played with numerous space RTS games in the past and I have to say I like Ancient Space. I'm at Mission 4 and until this point it has a very good atmosphere, something what only older games, Homeworld or Conquest: Frontier Wars were able to give. And maybe I've played space RTS, such as Homeworld a long time ago, and I played that one on hard, but this is the first time I've lost on normal (I've lost a few times already, first during Mission 1 and then right at the beginning of Mission 3 and a few times after that. It's not an easy game.).
As a storywriter, as that's my job IRL, what I like the most that here the characters sounds life like. They don't explain evident elements, but tell it well, like if they would part of their life. This is something what I miss from others games and what I really like here, as this gave the first good impression during the first cutscene, namely that we have a character who doesn't feel the necessity to explain the whys or whens in the log, but tells everything natural.
The only thing what I've found strange that the were no VO during the tutorial and I miss the unit feedbacks (However they're synthetics, so I can live with it.). And the narrators are also doing their job well. What I also liked is that during the tutorial, the music was also able to give a great atmosphere, something what many games are unable to. And if I already speak about the music, as it's one of the necessary element, I have to say it is also great and very atmospheric.
I still have to get used to the controls and such, but I already see that the upgrades and scannable elements also make sense, and they don't feel as just filler elements, but they're really give something for your units, so as the officers and their skills. Overall, after the first few hours, I'm pretty impressed with the game as it's giving back something what only older games, such as Homeworld or Conquest: Frontier Wars were able to give. I believe Ancient Space worth the investment and your time.

Essentially this game is Army Of Two: Desert Reskin Edition ft. meatheads and a good twist ending.
The only reason this game has good reviews is because the Spec Ops community suppresses negative ratings by downvoting them into oblivion. If you actually want to see unbiased reviews, look at the "funny" section where a few have surfaced through. I know people will gripe about me only having 50 minutes played. I had to use a custom launcher because it kept crashing on startup. This review will cover the mechanics first, then the plot.
This game is so linear its basically a 5 hour movie that pauses itself every minute or so for you to unpause it with a quicktime event or pressing a button to climb over something. The guns feel awful, never run out of ammo, and you'll never use anything the enemy isn't carrying at the time. Everything consists of setpieces with less thought put into them than MoH Warfighter. You will shoot enemies in a linear environment from cover for about 3 rooms, have yet another encounter with a turret that lasts all of about 5 seconds, then predict perfectly that you will be ambushed by infinite waves of enemies. In these ambushes you have to simply rely on trial and error and waiting. In every ambush there is a special spot you're supposed to be or you will be killed. For example, in the first ambush you have to run across an open field of sand to a broken building and get behind one of two pieces of cover. Lets say you picked the left, you'll be blown up with a rocket launcher setpiece and killed instantly. You restart, try to fight back and get killed within seconds because you want to have a good time, I guess. Eventually, after a few retrys, you'll find the magic position that won't get you killed, sit there for about 3 minutes until another setpiece is activated and you somehow all get away unscathed. You will look around and suddenly realize that you are now conveniently at the exact location you were heading to in the first place.
This game introduces nothing innovative whatsoever other than the option of shooting a window about every 30 minutes to drop sand on enemies. It seems like more of a gimmick to me than anything else. The movement couldn't even be spared, either. Imagine if Gears of War and Army of Two had a crippled child that was put on the indie games section of XBOX 360. Spec Ops just a step above that. It also doesn't help that the friendly AI is constantly in your way and consistently fails to understand orders outside the context of linear setpieces, which is always a "press M3 to continue this game" resulting in your teammates actually doing their jobs.
Since everyone regards this game so highly due to its story and 99% of the plot is driven by cutscenes, I'm going to look at as a movie. If this was submitted for a film class, I'd give it an A-. I enjoyed the dramatic shift in tone and the twist endings, but that's all that really stuck out. It feels a bit shoehorned at times but I pushed through the generic cliches of modern shooters that is spec ops to reach the ending and the finale was great. However, it didn't make up for the lack of intuitive gameplay. My only qualm for the plot is the poor character development for everyone other than the main character and his squad. There weren't any memorable enemies and the leaders of the various factions you fight are basically just "guys." They don't have anything special to them and I'm bound to forget them within a week or two from now.

Free at the moment and not a bad game for that price at all. In fact it is probably worth buying anyway. But it has some bugs and gotchyas that are hard to get over. The gotchyas come in the form of how the game is designed: With a main quest that leads you by the nose but then does not give you good controls to follow the instructions given. And that quite literally. There is no "follow" command despite being in the "context menu" as a greyed out option.
In the main quest this means when it comes time for you to follow the lead ship you must speed along using PTE (power to engines) mode until you overtake that ship then slow down and let them disappear again, and so on until the eventual cutscene/dramatic moment. Not particularly game breaking UNLESS you happen to fail to understand how to keep up with the ship you must follow, in which case you get a warning that you will have to reload and then you will be given no alternative but to do just that. Ah...but you can't save unless you are in a starbase (the menu gives you options there). But you can't save during missions. (Meaning the main mission!)
Otherwise the game has a pretty cool non-linear quest system that lets you build up cash, reputation and experience levels (which do little but give you small advantages here and there.) The faction system seems kind of black n white/bland but I like the ideas anyway and the way your reputation goes up and down (according to your actions) makes sense to me.
There are some things that don't make a lot of sense but mostly they are nitpicks. And the VO acting is atrocious. Don't sit through the main quest too many times in a row. You might go insane with the badly read dialogue and the fact that all the voices are provided by two VO actors. But this is window dressing on a game that has a lot of potential.

It's Hitman again, and better than ever.
All my support to this game, both as a gamer and as a developer. They knew perfectly well what made hitman tick and they went back to the roots and improved its strong points instead of trying weird formulas or investing time on unneded features. I felt like replaying and replaying and replaying a mission like I used to in the old days, and it's not like I can do this very often lately.
The mastery incentive is a very good idea to add motivation to try the different assassination styles. It makes you feel encouraged to play in a messier, but sometimes funnier way from time to time without feeling that the game is scowling at you for not making the perfect run. I'm all for silent assassin ranks, I'm sure we all cleared blood money, contracts and the original games with perfect records, but sometimes assassinating the victim in plain sight and making a huge mess or actually using remote explosives without feeling that you're playing the game wrong is fun as well. Here you can actually gain something from it and unlock new things.
If the episodic system allows the developers to create missions as good as the paris one, it will be more than worth the wait.
And if you don't like the episodic system... just wait a few months and buy the whole thing instead of giving the game abyssal scores for a characteristic that was well known long before release. Production time and budget are two of the worst challenges in game developement, and responsible for a lot of dramatic amputations that kill the game quality. If they needed to resort to this formula to avoid having to compromise the final game quality, let them try. If they keep the quality this first mission has, it will be more than worth it. And considering there is the possibility of only buying the starter pack, which is very reasonably priced, it's not like they are robbing anyone.
We'll see how this one turns out. I'm confident that the other missions will meet my expectations. I could be wrong, who knows, but I'm gonna bet on them!

Enter the next era of HITMAN
At first glance, the game feels like you are back in absolution. Flawless graphics,great lighting effects and all the glamour that absolution boasted and offered. But there the similarities ends. What we have here is a game that combines the very best of Blood money's sandbox killing with absolutions fluid controls. Also, gone is the ultra stupid Tag and Execute system introduced in absolution. It doesnt make sense for 47 to have it and they have righted it by removing it. Instinct does not feel intrusive in comparison to absolution and gives you great wealth of information. In fact too much information at times which may or may not break individual game experience. Game level design is beautiful and huge and at times confuses me. I must admit that this is not a design flaw but rather my inexperience in detailing the floorplans but it just goes to show that to execute a perfect crime, planning and intel must be sought after in advance. There are of course some gripe with the game. The Shortness of the first level left me wanting more but yet unsatisfied at the same time. Perhaps the abrupt ending of the first episode felt like a kick in the stomach giving me a bitter taste of having to wait a month for the next part of the game. It is a month too long in reality and hopefully, the developers will push out the nex epi in due time. The next gripe in mind is the amount of buttons for each actions. In blood money, my fingers never have to move across the keyboard to access my inventory. Everything was reachable within my left hand but in this game, everything was jumbled. Inventory had to be accessed with "I" button and some buttons on the left that are keybound arent even used during the first epi. Design flaw perhaps? It is stupid and inconvenient. Developers should look to follow blood money or absolution's key mapping instead to provide better controls. The third gripe i have is the buggy AI. At times, certain actions performed by 47 will cause the AI to actually stop doing what they were intended to do...forever. And by certain actions, i did not mean killing. A good example is one of the target did not go to the affected laptop as intended no matter how long i waited there. The target was just standing in the patio doing nothing surrounded by all the guest and not moving! How am i suppose to kill anything if the target is bugged and not programmed properly?! Fix it squeenix/IO! The last gripe i have though is the opportunities. It is absolutely intrusive and should not be too obvious for players. With it, i feel like im being coddled and it felt way much more intrusive copared to instinct in absolution. The good thing however is that you can customise the UI to display lesser of these opportunities to down right zero help. Outside of these gripes, im relatively pleased with the game and how it turned out. Keep it up IO and hope to see the next release soon!
P.S For those who preordered the full priced game and are griping about the price, Deal with it. You were given the information and choice to purchase episode by episode before hand. So do not go saying how it is not worth whatever amount you paid in advance because of the episodic release.

Yooka & Laylee is a truly well functioning time machine.
Devoloped by former people from Rare, they set out to re-create what they had done with the Banjo series on the N64. When being so close in formula, there is bound to be some problems. Camera being the most notable one, but if you are like me and many others from that era of gaming, this won't be much of a hassle for you, as it's kinda part of the charm by now, and easy to avoid unless you trully feel the need to hump those walls in thight spaces.
Running around in a sandbox platformer with fetch quests would be best way to describe what you will be spending your time with in this game. The duo is just as dynamic as Banjo & Kazooie, if not more. Much like B&K, Yooka being the more sensible one, while Laylee usualy mocks other characters you stumble upon, like Retro Rex, 'an old dinosour that still lives in the 90's.
You can progress in any order you like, you can actually take on the very last boss without confronting any of the other bosses. Unlocking the five world does not require much effort, but you will be needing to revisit all the worlds at some point if you want to collect everything, as each world gives you new moves to conquer challanges you could not complete earlier.
If you have played 3D platformers from the 90's, you know what you can expect, more of the same platforming from its golden age. If not. This is a good opportunity to try it out with all its ups and downs in a more accessible state and better graphics. (Because all games are judged on their graphics, right?)
Anyway... Y&L is truly worth your attention, not because it's a really good recreations of what once was, it's also one of the few alternatives to 3D platforming in recent years where genre and budgets are based on sales charts.

The whole reason that Yooka-Laylee exists is because of those nostalgic feelings we get when we think of some of the best 3D platformers in the N64 era: games like Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo-Kazooie. But that connection that Yooka-Laylee establishes early on with nostalgia is both a gift and a curse: as its attempts to recreate the magic of those past games force it into decisions that harm every element of the overall game's structure. In short, it tries so hard to be the new prince of Rareware, that it forgets why those Rareware games did so well in the first place. It has the individual elements, the pieces of that original series: but it falls apart when attempting to combine them together to make one flowing overall product.
Which is sad, because the base engine and performance here is pretty great for a 3D platformer in 2017.
There are flashes of brilliance here when the game decides to be a little creative: when forcing the player to use their skills in unconventional ways to solve puzzles. Some of the early level design is really well done, as the world's structure in the first 2 worlds really work from a gameplay and a presentation perspective, making you want to explore like Indiana Jones.
But that quickly falls apart, as the game starts to get into a rhythm: which is REALLY BAD for a 3D platformer. You start to see challenges that aren't different enough from each other to stand apart, and the ability to fly completely wrecks the difficulty curve for the game due to the lack of limitations on it. Then you starts to see the cracks all over the place: as elements from the original game start to show up: but they don't make sense for the world or the story that was built for Yooka and Laylee. It becomes less about wanting to explore at this point: and more you racing to the end just because you want the game to be over.
The last several levels have major gameplay design problems, and it's very easy to forget what challenges you've done, and where the next set of challenges is. The upgrade to 25 pagies in an area is too much to handle without some maps/information to help offset it, and it becomes a grind in the wrong way. This,  on top of the fact that you keep on waiting for those sparks from the early level, but they never come.
Yooka-Laylee is a sale title for me, but given Steam's review system, I have to not recommend it to the overall public. It does have a place in the collection of Exploring fans and is great for kids: but those looking for a comparable experience to Banjo-Kazooie are going to be let down.

Small guide to play properly:
Download Gameranger in order to find servers.
Once you start playing you'll notice the graphics are quite bad.
You can fix that by getting the console up using SHIFT + ~.
Then type the following commands:
r_customwidth 1920
r_customheight 1080
r_mode -1
vid_restart
Now you have alot better graphics.
Hosting  a server through Gameranger might be a little tricky.
It might happen that whenever you want to host on high graphics, your game crashes whenever you change maps or modes.
The only way for me to fix that is, by manually changing the graphics to 800x600, then change whatever you want to change and use the commands again to tune up the graphics.

Undertale. How do I describe this game with spoiling? The game is brilliant and you should go in as blind as you possibly can. After beating all the main endings of the game I feel confident that I can tell all the great things about Undertale.
Pros
Taking from the classic RPG and JRPG tropes, Undertale twists the system in hilarious, over the top, and sometimes sadening ways. From the beginning you are treated to it's intelligent story and its satirical comedy that makes it unique. The world of Undertale is very fleshed out and has lots of very interesting plot points that one can speculate about. Essentially this game is Army Of Two: Desert Reskin Edition ft. meatheads and a good twist ending.
The only reason this game has good reviews is because the Spec Ops community suppresses negative ratings by downvoting them into oblivion. If you actually want to see unbiased reviews, look at the "funny" section where a few have surfaced through. I know people will gripe about me only having 50 minutes played. I had to use a custom launcher because it kept crashing on startup. This review will cover the mechanics first, then the plot.
This game is so linear its basically a 5 hour movie that pauses itself every minute or so for you to unpause it with a quicktime event or pressing a button to climb over something. The guns feel awful, never run out of ammo, and you'll never use anything the enemy isn't carrying at the time. Everything consists of setpieces with less thought put into them than MoH Warfighter. You will shoot enemies in a linear environment from cover for about 3 rooms, have yet another encounter with a turret that lasts all of about 5 seconds, then predict perfectly that you will be ambushed by infinite waves of enemies. In these ambushes you have to simply rely on trial and error and waiting. In every ambush there is a special spot you're supposed to be or you will be killed. For example, in the first ambush you have to run across an open field of sand to a broken building and get behind one of two pieces of cover. Lets say you picked the left, you'll be blown up with a rocket launcher setpiece and killed instantly. You restart, try to fight back and get killed within seconds because you want to have a good time, I guess. Eventually, after a few retrys, you'll find the magic position that won't get you killed, sit there for about 3 minutes until another setpiece is activated and you somehow all get away unscathed. You will look around and suddenly realize that you are now conveniently at the exact location you were heading to in the first place.
This game introduces nothing innovative whatsoever other than the option of shooting a window about every 30 minutes to drop sand on enemies. It seems like more of a gimmick to me than anything else. The movement couldn't even be spared, either. Imagine if Gears of War and Army of Two had a crippled child that was put on the indie games section of XBOX 360. Spec Ops just a step above that. It also doesn't help that the friendly AI is constantly in your way and consistently fails to understand orders outside the context of linear setpieces, which is always a "press M3 to continue this game" resulting in your teammates actually doing their jobs.
Since everyone regards this game so highly due to its story and 99% of the plot is driven by cutscenes, I'm going to look at as a movie. If this was submitted for a film class, I'd give it an A-. I enjoyed the dramatic shift in tone and the twist endings, but that's all that really stuck out. It feels a bit shoehorned at times but I pushed through the generic cliches of modern shooters that is spec ops to reach the ending and the finale was great. However, it didn't make up for the lack of intuitive gameplay. My only qualm for the plot is the poor character development for everyone other than the main character and his squad. There weren't any memorable enemies and the leaders of the various factions you fight are basically just "guys." They don't have anything special to them and I'm bound to forget them within a week or two from now.
Scores with 5/10 being average
Gameplay: 2/10
Story: 8/10
Overall for the game itself: 3/10
If you really want to enjoy this game, please do yourself a favor and just watch the cutscenes online and save $30 and 4 hours of your time. The plot is really the only thing Spec Ops: The Line has going for it.

- the reputation system is a bit simplistic, basically lawful-vs-evil, but it works. You can play as a ruthless pirate too :) Some factions will be hostile to you, regardless of your actions (because of story constrains).
- heavier ships are almost always better, there is no point in flying smaller craft later on
- the story is nothing to write home about, the voice acting is pretty amateur, sometimes nonexistent
- the graphics is dated, but it is to be expected, the game is 3 years old
But don't let these things discourage you, there is plenty of good here:
+ space is pretty and has a good variety with dust clouds, asteroid belts, space stations, anomalies and so on
+ there is a large variety of ships and ship classes
+ there are many weapons, modules, mods, so you can customize and tweak your ship to your play-style or the current mission
+ you can hire NPC mercenaries to help you out in tougher situations
+ you can capture enemy ships and sell them for lots of money or keep them for your personal use, or just collect them in the hangar, like I did :)  Also because off this, pretty much every ship you see out there can be yours for the gold or the iron price :)
+ you can only save at stations, so you take a risk every time you venture out into space
+ beside the main mission line there are secondary missions for the big factions and random mercenary work
+ the DLC missions add a couple extra hours of gameplay and new ships (especially the Titan, which is a beast as the name suggests)
In conclusion: It's not perfect, but if it is on sale, and you like Freelancer-type games, go for it.

Undertale. How do I describe this game with spoiling? The game is brilliant and you should go in as blind as you possibly can. After beating all the main endings of the game I feel confident that I can tell all the great things about Undertale.
Pros
Taking from the classic RPG and JRPG tropes, Undertale twists the system in hilarious, over the top, and sometimes sadening ways. From the beginning you are treated to it's intelligent story and its satirical comedy that makes it unique. The world of Undertale is very fleshed out and has lots of very interesting plot points that one can speculate about. Good luck trying to find all the secrets and endings, the amount of work Toby Fox put into this game is crazy. You will never be able to find all the dialouge he created. You will also be pleased to note that Toby Fox tried to make the backtracking and grinding in this game very optional. Thank you so much.
Cons
The first section of the game is quite bland texture wise, don't let that turn you off though. Once you get further the textures become stunning. Sometimes new gameplay elements aren't introduced very well. The puzzles are meh, but that's kind of the joke. Sometimes the protagonists movements may get a little funky, but it is just visual.
The game is brilliant. Every single thing about this game from the secrets to the dialouge is well crafted. Totally worth the ten dollars you spend to buy the game.

Initially, my expectations for Jedi Academy were lower than how the game turned out to be because of how much of the series was changed from the Dark Forces titles to Jedi Outcast. However, the changes made in Jedi Outcast as well as Jedi Academy from the originals are easier to accept when Jedi Academy intentional disassociates itself from its predecessors by not focusing on Kyle Katarn, and more so continuing with the fan-service attitude of Outcast into a more fleshed out experience.
This expectation is important to illustrate as while I do not find Outcast or Academy to be great games when it’s labeled under the greatness of Dark Forces this does not mean they are bad games. People who find entertainment from the simplified combat of shallow lightsaber controls in an RPG-lite experience for replayability as well as the multiplayer and modding community will find something to enjoy if you always wanted to live the fantasy of being the Jedi you always dreamed of with friends.
This statement is said with all good intentions; in an ironic change of perspectives from Outcast, Jedi Academy’s overreliance on the lore established from the film is what make the game so entertaining throughout the whole experience.
From the moment the game starts, you are allowed to create a preselection of Jedi characters as you develop your own lightsaber playstyle and revisit the famous locales of the films and fight alongside heroes like Chewbacca, Katarn and Skywalker as well as fighting against famous antagonists like the Yetis from Hoth, Boba Fett and the Sith Apprentice from Jedi Outcast. These are established with a variety of missions that give more creative structure to the gameplay as some are simple reconnaissance missions whereas others are scavenging pieces of tech while playing floor-lava with a sandworm on Tatooine. Some of these missions are more aggravating than fun such as the racer-bike mission or the stealth mission with a Rancor. Thankfully, not all missions are required to progress the game, so the ones that are not tied to the main plotline can be ignored. In spite of the varying quality of its content, the context for its fanservice as well as changes the core gameplay goes a long way from tiring out the depreciative gains of being a Jedi from the start that ruined Outcast.
While I will lament the decision for the series to rely more on fanservice than on original stories and characters, the enjoyment from fighting alongside your favorite Star Wars heroes in the series to defeat the Sith along with its most infamous villains of the films or the previous game is something with innate satisfaction whether you enjoy the change or not. The same cannot be same for the combat.
One comment that allured me initially to the Dark Forces series was the emphasis on Jedi Academy on having the best lightsaber duel gameplay in any Star Wars game to date, and I fail to understand this claim after playing the game for myself.
Throughout the Dark Forces games, the controls for Lightsaber combat has boiled down to holding the left-mouse button to attack and the right-mouse button to do a special maneuver or throwing the lightsaber. The notable addition to the same framework is the combo-based fighting system that relies more on rhythmic combinations of the same one-button for various attacks that utilize jumping, crouching and weapon styles to make up for the lack of complexity. On the surface, all these options should make the combat feel great to experience.
The drawback to the combat system is the memorization of the animations and move-sets to pull them off, which when limited to a single button is too unclear for the player to get a feel of the controls. Another major issue is the inability to read the enemy Jedi attacks as well as knowing when a hit is registered in the turmoil of the constant clashing of lightsabers. The result of these two problems makes the combat feel more based around luck rather than skill, and perhaps that is because the controls are balanced for multiplayer rather than singleplayer AI where cleaving through hordes of Stormtroopers, Droids or Smugglers is the main source of satisfaction from the gameplay.
As for the rest of the gameplay for singleplayer, it improves upon the limitations of Outcast by expanding the player’s arsenal with time with various lightsaber styles and progression systems along with Force abilities from the start. Unfortunately, this system makes replaying the campaign lacking as there is no NG+ mode or a way to unlock all available options from the start to encourage more variation in playstyles or builds unless you use cheat codes.
What saddens me the most about this series is that despite the many shortcomings I have with both Jedi Outcast and Jedi Academy, the series’ deviation for more Jedi-styled gameplay deserves more modern adaptions with modern ideas to expand upon its limited combat skills. Something that incorporates the weapon style arts of The Witcher or the deliberate combat systems of Dark Souls and/or For Honor could be the foundation for a greater game to be create. This idea wouldn’t be without a fanbase to support it as the player base surrounding this game and the modding scene still thriving after so long shows that there is a foundation worth redeeming in the future of Star Wars.

Despite what Oxygen Not Included may initially appear to be, it's anything but a simple game. It's simple on the surface, and easy to get into: Here's your little dudes, don't kill them. But as your base expands and resources become scarcer, you'll encounter new, and often subtle, challenges. I'm about 8 hours into this game and I realized I had grossly underestimated Oxygen Not Included. Beneath the cutesy colony builder surface, this game is a hardcore system designer rivaling Factorio in complexity. The challenges are subtle, and often times you won't realized you've encountered them at first, but they are definitely there.
If you're a fan of the Rimworld or Dwarf Fortress style of "starts off simple and soon becomes a monster of machines simultaneously killing you and keeping you alive", you'll love Oxygen Not Included.

I'll expand upon this review later as I play through more of the game. The time that I've spent on it so far is merely a review of my first impression of the first 5 missions.
Compared to other RTS games, this game doesn't really do anything that better games, such as Homeworld, haven't already brought to the table. The difficulty is pretty damn hard due to the way the AI are unfairly given so many units that are all thrown upon you. The game is not difficult because of an intelligent AI, but more because you have to face overwhelming numbers most of the time which sometimes leaves you feeling cheated when you're beaten.
Example:
In mission 2, you have to face roughly 50 units with your 12. The enemy are given battleships and frigates and many fighter squadrons. You only have a carrier, a battleship and 9 squadrons of fighters/bombers. You cannot build frigates yet, and frigates are good against fighters, so your fighters get mowed down while they try to hit the enemy fighter squadrons which counter your bombers. Even then, frigates are fairly decent against bombers, which doesn't make much sense. To win, you have to have your fleet at the center of the map where your turret's angle of fire (if you haven't built many turrets, you are screwed and have to restart; the trigger which spawns all of these units is unexpected and you won't have enough time to build the turrets to counter the threat) can deal the most damage on the incoming enemy units and allow you pick off the early incoming units one by one until the battleships arrive, rather than having a massive wall of enemy units focusing on your mission critical capital ships (if you lose either the carrier or battleship, you fail).
To each mission, there is a specific formula to how you should beat each mission (e.g. you have to build/upgrade these units, attack these units at this time, use this special ability etc all in this order to win the mission, you will find it extremely hard to do it any other way). This then becomes a gruelling trial and error affair where you have to figure out the formula and win, which sometimes frustrates you to no end and limits your tactical options to win the mission. Some tactical choices you make earlier in the mission render the later part of the mission next to impossible to win, resulting in you having to go back and restart.
This game looks pretty much your typical RTS game, but not what you'd entirely expect. It may not introduce many new things to the genre, but it does keep you on your toes and is unforgiving. This can be interesting, especially for people who want a challenge.
I do not wish to give this a negative recommendation, I'd rather give it a neutral rating (some will hate it, some will love it, some will think it's just okay). But, since there is no such option, and I'd rather lean a little to the negative side, I have given it a negative recommendation. I'd suggest you wait for the eventual sale to come around if you wish to get this game, just incase you get disappointed with it.

Before going forward with this reveiw I will mark it as a game I wouldn't reccommend, however, my feelings are pretty neutral on the game over all.
When I first heard about the game I was very excited, a vn with lovely art and a light hearted plot sounded like just the thing I needed. However, I do have some complaints along with some praise for the game, as someone who is very familiar with VNs from large studios like PArade and Nitro+Chiral and also ones from independednt makers.
Pros:
-the art is lovely and has a nice feel to it over all, I'm pretty picky on style and art in general when it comes to VNs
-the story is nince and light hearted, for what i've played.
-characters are distinct and don't blend into eachother , design or personality wise
-the music is fine, nothing to write home about, but it fits the game. I only wish they had an ending song rather than recycling the theme, but whatever
Cons:
-routes are super short, especially for this being a $15 game, I expected a good few hours of play time with each persuable character rather than 3 short dates. Thhis game had the quality of something I'd expect to find for free on newgrounds rather than for sale.
-from what I've played, two completed routes, the characters don't really have a significant character arc and the character building fell flat for me and they ended up feeling very 2 dimentional and not fleshed out.
-the scenes with your daoughter's problems and such feel forced into the story, like they didn't finish writing everything and just decided to jam her arc into the story rather poorly.
-while I love the art, the backgrounds and character sprites clash bady from a stylistic point of view. Especially since some backgorunds seem more solidly lined and others looks rough and sketchy. It doesn't blend well.
-the main character's customized sprite also has the same problem with style clashing, which could have easily been fixed by doing the same kind of shading and line density as the npc sprites.
-the game has little to no replay value. It's a one and done nothing game that didn't even have CGs to collect other than a pinup for completeing a route.
-mini games felt b a d to play and more of a time waster than anything. They were tedious and not very fun, thanks for trying though
Overall I did have some fun with the game, but I'd recommend saving your money for something with higher quality, better character building and an overall more compelling story. I'd recommend the game No, Thank You!!! which has been officially licenced in the US and can be bought right here:
But if you decide to buy the game that's on you and this is just my opinion, take it with a grain of salt.

Leonardo da Vinci's "Horse and Rider" statue was never going to be what people remembered him for in the many thousands of years that followed. Why? Because it was never made. The mold itself was created by Da Vinci but work was halted for unknown reasons and the mold itself vanished into obscurity until it was recently on tour in 2012. Could the mold be considered a masterpeice? No, it is a curiousity and nothing more and it wouldn't really be a 'must see' item when placed in a museum or gallery if other works of art such as his Vitruvian Man or the Mona Lisa. And that is also the reasoning why I cannot recommend SPG2 - it's a mold of a good game and not a good game in itself.
I say this for a number of reasons but let me first address some points raised in other reviews.
It was said by some that much of the game is spent struggling with the controls and the clunky GUI. That SPG2 has you spending most of your time traveling between points on the map in uneventful tedium and that the game is horribly repetative.  All of that is true but only because people aren't playing the game properly and this in part of the fault of the developers who did an absolutely terrible job of introducing the game via a meaningful tutorial or easing players into the game through quests. It's like complaining that Fallout 4 is tedious because you never realized there was a fast-travel systrem or that your character had the ability to run - so you walked everywhere. To be fair here, SPG2 ships handle like the mechs from Mechwarrior or tanks. Or they handle like a 6DOF shooter. But due to the developers permitting players to change between control schemes as they play by just touching a key you can understand how some people would get confused. Personally I found setting the  control to the 3rd person view and just using the spacebar to switch between turrets and ship steering was the best way to go. In reality though the developers needlessly overcomplicated things. But the unexplained complications didn't end there as you also need to get to grasp with an unexplained radial menu and power management systems. Plus the ship customisation makes it hard to tell if turrets which says "Av Damage: 50, Rate of Fire: 0.5" means that the DPS is 100 or that the DPS is 25 which is why the average is 50. Space travel is actually very fast but again it isn't very well explained. Through playing the game I discovered that Power To Engines, plus setting power management to Engines AND using an inexpensive speed boost consumable allows you to travel 10'000 units in around 60 seconds which is more than enough to get you from starport to another or to hop between freelance quests. But unless you happen to sit down and read through the manual you'd never understand even half of that.
But enough of the bad, what does SPG2 which is good? Well, it does a fair bit. There is a wide variety of quests available and things to do for money and XP. My run through took over 40 hours and that is with a bit of sidequesting and taking time to get the best ship possible in Gemini fitted with the top tier enhancements and hardware. In terms of value for money, at the full price you'd get a fair bit of entertainment for your cash. For me however, this was on my wishlist for months and then I picked it up for free during the give-away they did when SPG:Warlords was released. The combat itself is more tactical than it may seem at first. Ship positioning is key since you're piloting frigages, carriers and dreadnoughts and can't really dodge incoming fire unless you're very far away from the source. Rotating the ship when shields are taking too much damage while managing power systems, targetting vessels, using abilities and keeping an eye on your fighter squadrons (if you have a hanger onboard) all gives you the kind of micromanagement you normally only get in an RTS and that keeps things interesting. For a time....
The trouble is that SPG2 is not finished. Not that parts of the game are missing, but that you can tell there hasn't been much effort put into balance and polishing. The GUI is clunky and parts of it seem redundant. Cash becomes trivial when you learn to capture ships and either sell them or keep them for yourself. Your level/rank limits what types of ship you are cerified for but you can pick up courier missions within dangerous space intended for players more than 20 levels higher than you are and get some very easy progression. However this means combat becomes a risky and less rewarding way of leveling as a result. A captured ship is worth hundreds of thousands if not millions of credits but a cargohold full of valuable goods would only get you a 10th of that amount at best. Worse still is that pirates may spawn right next to a station or planet so capturing them and towing them to a starport is done very quickly. So all of this means you progress so fast that you quickly end up with nothing more to strive for. With a Helios Dreadnought at your command, tens of millions of credits in the bank gathering dust and 2 level 60 mercenaries backing you up you can steamroll through the storyline missions very quickly and it all ends with a final quest that is buggy and may force you to reload a save and even after completion the marker and the ships involved remain at that point in space for some odd reason.
It would be fair to compare SPG2 to games like Fallout or Eldarscrolls where you explore a world, have random encounters with dangerous hostiles, make friends or enemies with various factions, have an opitional main storyline and spend your time collecting gear or questing to progress. And SPG2 would be in the same league for quality had they not caused the game to be so shallow with its progression and RPG elements or taken the time to polish what they already had for content. I know that SPG:Warlords introduces a X4 aspect and frankly that seems to me like exactly what this game would have needed to be worth recommending. If it has been done properly.
As it stands though I would never recommend SPG2 to anyone even on discount as it is a very disapointing and shallow experience. The mold of what could have been a damn good game had more effort been made.

If you are like me, it is difficult choosing between two similar titles. Although they appear similar on the surface, you will be playing them entirely differently.

ONI- puzzle-like problem solving. Play around with chemistry. Less complex in overall scope, but more complex when dealing with individual problems. Choose this if you love fixing problems with creative solutions.

My first thoughts on the game was
"Another one of thos Modern Warfare or Battlefield games eh? We good guys, we kill bad guys, yipee!"
(Long review ahead...)
No, it seems that this game doesn't play it that way. This game really focus a lot on storyline. It isn't too much story based too. The action is as good as it's story and as I followed the story, I realized I actually was forced to make choices and that kind of make me feel bad for certain decisions...
Honestly, the story was so dark, in the end, all I felt was "Did I even choose the right options... This is all my fault...?"
I would replay it again and choose different options. I want to see if I could change some things. I want to see if I could save more people than kill more like what I did on my first blind play through. It was so intense too in combat. It's no run and gun here. Do that and prepare to die. You have to take your time, analyze the field and react quickly. The game forces you to be stressed and it's a good thing because it forces me to think during every battle.
My expectations had been exceeded greatly and I am actually pleased that this game was worth my time. I wish more war games were like this. Not many games execute a good storyline in a war but this one nails it down to the ground. Graphics are bautiful, voice acting is pretty close to perfect and they act in a very rational way as if it wasn't scripted. It felt like a real war instead of a game. It seriously felt like watching a real quarrel against the men.
10/10, I will replay it again with different options and hopefully I made the right choices, either way I don't think the ending will change, right...? Unless I decide to bang all the soldiers at the end...

Rating: 9/10
Budget: Worth it
Lenght: It takes a skilled player at least two days to beat the single player campaign. It features a great multiplayer mode, and even still (2016) has an online multiplayer community, but good luck beating the average Wizard who still plays this!
Replayability: I tend to replay it once every two-three years, but it has good replayability mainly because the game features and advancement system, a some incredibly memorable and fun missions and two endings.
Imagine if Jedi Outcast didn't have a 100% linear story, came with character creation and even the option to pick what fighting style you wanted to use, choose your lightsaber color and hilt and had a non-linear character advancement system.
In Academy, you advance your character by getting 1 new force power per level you beat. There are 5 levels per segment of the game - Each segment is separated by a number of story missions that you have to beat.
You can actually beat only 4 missions per segment if you want, and advance without beating the final mission - This is a good way to avoid that one mission you hate, but unfortunately, the game doesn't let you know how this actually works!
My friend did this, thinking he could just do the mission he skipped later, but that wasn't the case - and he missed out on a fun mission and a force power.
Unlike in Jedi Outcast, in this game you start as a Jedi with a lightsaber. In the very first mission, your only force power is lightsaber throw Rank 1 (not sure why they even gave you this one!), but you do start with a lightsaber, but from mission two and onwards, you have access to force powers at level 1, and after the second game segment you get to pick if you wanna upgrade to dual lightsaber, a saber staff or master the one saber.
After the first segment, you get to pick if you want the strong style or the fast style.
You can advance your powers in the game how ever you want, but it's recommended to take the first rank of healing. I actually personally recommend not taking further ranks, because I feel it makes the game too easy. Enemies do not use healing, except through force drain (taking YOUR health), a very ineffective method of healing to be frank, so I feel it makes the game too easy to have the ability to heal while fighting also.
Without healing though, the game is next to impossible to beat, because unlike in Outcast, you can't pick up bacta tanks and use them when you're hurt, and there are fewer medkits around.
The game has a bit of a learning curve, and is outdated in the graphics department, but there are mods that help with that.
Over all, a great game.

Splash Damage Got a bit of a heckling when they announced they were going to be taking over the beloved arkham series of games, which had become outrageously popular, even with those not familiar with the batman lore.
Origins waas set before aslyum and city, with some familiar faces and some not so familiar.. all with a general hostality to the bat.  With a train load of assassins out to kill Batman before christmas and return Gotham to the corrupt cops and devious villains from the mind of Bob Kane.  It almost seems fitting that I am writing this just before christmas.
So should you buy this game? Despite not knowing much about the Batman Franchise and having played the other two I was initially questioning my reasoning behind purchasing this game. Now I'm a single player kind of player so this wont cover the multiplayer ( which is unique and worth checking out, if a little buggy ).
Environment wise the open world city does seem slightly overwhelming at first. With challenges, unlockables and side quests practically throwing themselves at you its very easy to get sidetracked and explore somewhere new.  Goons challenge you without fear, seeing as the bat isnt suppossed to be real.
The familar fighting mechanics is back, this seems that Splash Damage have put there own twist on the core mechanics that were in the previous two but somehow feels less solid. It is by no means a bad mechanic and is comfortable and satisfying to play as the caped crusader, knocking a few heads together. I do not believe there are any new animations and the familar gadgets are back, with some being unlocked through story progression. This aides to the open world, making you want to go back with your new gadget to collect that elusive trophy ( or if your like me... keep progressing I have other games to play )
Now this game was buggy at release, this has seemingly been fixed through various patches ( mind you this is about 4gb in total ) I did not personally find glitches or problems further than the camera getting stuck in the wall when fighting large numbers of goons in enclosed spaces.
You may also feel slightly cheated if you were a big fan of arkham city and put many hours into that as about 50% of the city layout is " copy and pasted " from that game. So if you havent played the first two games... this is not the wrong place to start, just expect a fair amount of deja vu when you playe Arkham City.
The story of the game is actually quite good. The game focused a lot more on improving the "Worlds Greatest Detective" in Batman with a whole new crime scene mechanic, which has been implemented into the story and side missions. The Villans are easy to hate and the boss battles ( of which there are 8 individual encounters, with a certain popular muscular varient reoccuring ) are challenging and genuinly fun to play through. The voice acting is top notch. Without having been told prior I would not have noticed this game had new actors on lead roles, they made a cracking first impression which held throughout.
So if you are after a 3rd person action game with an open world setting that doesnt involve shooting everything this is well worth a shot
