Hitman is a very enjoyable murder sandbox. It's highly responsive to your actions, allowing you to manipulate the environment in complicated ways. At first, when you step into the Paris level, it can seem overwhelming. After 15 hours, my understanding of the level is considerable, enough to have completed every challenge in the primary level, and yet I keep learning new things about the environment, new ways to cause accidents, glasses to poison, so on. I have barely touched other contracts, except for one of the escalations, which are true tests of skill as an assassin. Such contracts, and later the elusive ones, also continue to be added. For the $15 I paid for the intro pack, what I've received so far has been worth it. And if the later released levels are on par with Paris, this is going to be well worth the ultimate purchase price.
On the downside, there are still a fair number of technical issues, and being online is almost essential. Loading times are around 20 sec off SSD with 16GB ram, fps hovers around 45 at 1440p with a GTX 980ti on medium settings. While I am looking forward to these issues being fixed, the slow, methodical nature of hitman means that 45fps doesn't hinder my ability to play too much, though I am looking forward to these issues being fixed.
7/10 A return to the glory of Blood Money brought down somewhat by the technical issues. I only plan to buy the episodes one at a time, and suggest the same unless you are supremely confident.

Don't buy this game right now if you can help it.
Optimization is REALLY bad, I'm running at 1080p on an overclocked  i7 4770k backed by a single GTX 980 and 16GB of RAM and it dips below 30fps frequently. It's very possible that Square Enix knows this, and makes the game "episodic" to buy the devs more time to fix it...at least I hope they plan to fix it. How they messed up this badly I don't know - Absolution ran smoothly all the time on my old, slightly weaker machine.
Gameplay itself is actually very good. If you run around, you will find "Challenges" in which the game essentially holds your hand to fulfill an objective. Overall it's a much easier game to get into than any Hitman before it (remember the last mission of Silent Assassin when you fought alone against 30 guys with sniper rifles all camping in a church?). One drawback is that you die pretty easily (2-3 gunshots) so mass shooting your way through is probably not going to work most of the time unlike Absolution.
Graphics look okay even on medium, but not spectacular on ultra either. For the hardware requirement I expected more. But this game honestly has never been about awesome graphics. It looks as good as or better than Absolution if memory serves me correctly, and I'm fine with it. At least 47's head actually looks round now instead of jagged thanks to the power of 1080p and AA/AF.
I admit, I am a Hitman fanatic like most of you. If you are like me and have a decent PC, I think you will love the experience more than hate. If you're not, don't bother right now - at least wait until it is 3-4 episodes in and see if the situation gets better. I'm sure this review section will constantly get updated as episodes come out.

Having played through the game, and 100%-ing it I can safely say it's good, but isn't without its flaws. Overall the game is a competent enough collect-a-thon, but banking off of nostalgia alone won’t save a game every time it releases. I don’t have too many gripes with this game, but there are some key points that stand out to where I could never give this game a perfect score. Fixing them however could easily make the game better.
- While it’s no Banjo-Kazooie/Donkey Kong Country it is a breath of fresh air to hear Kirkhope and Wise again. Although the soundtrack may be new there have been some parts in the game I felt myself humming along the music no matter the instrument. It’s also great to finally have that dynamic music feel back where it changes in the area/being underwater.
- There are some flaws in the world design here and there in the form of leaks (holes in the map), but the worlds each have a wonderful skybox as well as a nice running theme in each. Although the maps are rather large (forgiven by the fact there’s 25 pagies and 200 quills in each level) it does feel nice to be able to explore them, and familiarize one’s self with the layout much like I did in Kazooie/Tooie.
- The main focus of the game, and generally the reason some bought it (if even for the nostalgic factor) I like that Notes and Jiggies have been exchanged for Pagies and Quills. There’s even the Ghost Writers which in their own way are just Jinjos with a special touch. I also enjoy the Energy/Health pickups as they add to the progression of the skills.
- Although some people may complain about it I found the humor that the Pagies, NPCs, and even Laylee brought the table refreshing as it reminded me of Kazooie, and how snarky she was to most of the oblivious NPCs. I especially enjoyed the Pagie in World 5’s Cosmic Cavern.
- As far as the pairing goes I enjoy both Yooka and Laylee as characters, and it’s nice to a see a duo again in a collect-a-thon game. Although they may be simple design-wise they still fit in the world, and have a nice flow together with their attitudes.
- I enjoy most of the NPCs in the game, and feel as though they’re a nice addition in some way or another due to either their personality, or just overall appearance. However I feel that Vendi (Tonic Machine) Feels VERY out of place, and looks as though she’s in the wrong game (It’s definitely the lighting on her).
- The bosses in this game feel incredibly tacked on, and have little to no substance to them. I feel that if the bosses for World(s) 1 and 2 (Especially 2) were changed or heavily reworked they could be better, but both just being wall-type bosses really ruins things. Also having a health bar may help, or better choreographing their health (if bars weren’t an option).
- The main grunt-like enemies are all just the same monster with the same noises, animations, and mechanics, but only have a different skin. Banjo-Kazooie may not have been amazing in the enemy department, but each monster in the differing worlds at least felt like they belonged there instead of feeling like some clone made in a factory wearing a costume.
- Pickup range for the butterflies was somewhat of a problem at times, and caused a few fails here and there on some of the challenges. The tongue-grab mechanic is fine, but the range for picking up butterflies in Reptile Roll is rather short to the point where missing a butterfly could very well mean the loss of a challenge. Expanding it slightly would help immensely.
They feel very unnecessary at times, and or some of them just go for much longer than needed (doesn’t help you play them twice for another Pagie). Many people have voiced their concerns on this matter in the forums as well as easy fixes/changes to them. For the most part the arcade games just feel lazy, and the repeat version of them feels lazier as they’re just like “filler content” for the Pagies.
- The ability itself is great, but makes the game near the end a whole lot easier (although some of the challenges near the end are unbearable). Having the ability cost energy in conjunction with the capabilities it has fixes running into the issue of low feathers in Kazooie as well as the lack of flight pads, but at the cost of difficulty It makes most if not all exploration outside of the challenges later on a breeze.
- In most if not all games this should not be an issue. Just allow either the dialogue to be skipped, or add a skip button to those that don’t care for the minimal story to continue on with the game faster. It would add more replay-value, and allow speed-runners a better place in the community.
I grew up with Banjo Kazooie/Tooie, and DK64. I may be biased in some regards due to nostalgia, but I can safely say this game is at least good for what it is. I would recommend getting it, but if you really wish to wait just get it on sale.
Overall 6/10 | Good, but isn’t perfect. It should be treated as just a walk down memory lane as to why some enjoyed games like it in the past, and should be a constant reminder of those games.

Update TLDR: Newest patch has greatly improved some of the technical aspects I had problems with, but the game still feels a bit empty.  I'd recommend getting the game on a sale.
This game is okay.  That's my overal perspective I have on the game. I know there's a lot of people expecting this to be the next great platformer revival, but this isn't the game you are looking for.  This game feels like the developers were on pace to make a great game, but had to rush it out the door 6 months early because they were running out of Kickstarter cash.
There's a lot of polish that wasn't really applied to this game that was desparately needed and the result is these big worlds that are pretty, but are also pretty empty. The worlds feel way to big to be interesting.  They have these gigantic worlds and almost nothing to fill them with except for quills.  The non-completionist collectibles are a little strange too, some of them have dual purposes that take a little bit of trial and error to understand how it works. The butterflies give health, but only if you use your tongue to eat them, but if you run into them, they give you energy? Would it have killed you to have two different powerups instead?  It certainly would have added more stuff to the game, even if it's not much.
Another problem with the game is the powerup system. Granted, most sections of any game that is patterned after Banjo Kazooie has the problem that once you have collected all the special moves, earlier sections are much easier, but the difficulty curve drops off completely once you have the ability to fly, removing any difficulty in the game whatsoever.  At least in Banjo Kazooie you couldn't just fly wherever you want, there were some limitations, and that's how the game stayed difficult.  There's this part of the last level where there's these teleporters that have been made completely useless because you can fly.  You can't even access the level without getting this fly ability first.
Controls in the game can get a little weird when you are trying to swim or fly as well.  They chose this strange control system where pressing one button makes you swim upward, pressing another makes you swim downward and not pressing buttons keeps you at the same level and you just simply steer with the control stick. Contrast that with previous 3D platformers and it takes a bit of getting used to.  Strange control choices in my opinion and they weren't good choices, but after the initial shock, the controls started to make a little bit of sense once you switched from the default camera to one that isn't jerking your field of view around.
The story is incredibly boring too. Here you are minding your own business when some guy steals all the books in the world. You got to go get your book back...for some reason and that's all they give you to work with. Shoot, even going with the cliched "they took your sister" plotline was more interesting than this.
(I think hitboxes have been improved in the recent patch though.) That, or the enemy will have way too many invincibility frames and not enough time to be open to attack, especially if you got hit during that aforementioned time they were invincible.
The puzzles in this game fall into two catagories: Too simple or too unintuitive.  There's nothing in this game that is all that difficult, but there are a couple of puzzles that are so vague that I had to look online to figure out how they worked.
I felt the inclusion of minigames was a waste of time personally.  They improved the controls in the newest patch, but the games are still pretty plain and uninteresting. I think the game would have done better if they had scrapped them instead.
I think another problem I saw with the game was that the I had no compelling reason to be interested in any of the characters.  The main characters are fine to a point, and a couple of the side characters are interesting enough, but all the minor characters just get reused on the five different worlds.  There's almost no unique or interesting themed characters from world to world, just ones copied and pasted from previous worlds. They don't even look like they belong.  The pig knights get reused in 3 of the five worlds.
You know that snarky funny dialogue you enjoyed in past Rare games? This doesn't have it.  They substitute fun dialogue with a bunch of 4th wall jokes, which at this point is becoming the puns of the comedy world.  We get it, you know you are in a game, that bit is tired and you need to write better jokes.
If there's some good that came out of this game, I would say the character designs are pretty good, the worlds do have a lot of charm to them in spite of the lack of interesting stuff to do. The music is pretty spot on, but that's about the limit of the good stuff that I can credit the game.
Overall, I can't recommend purchasing this at full price. $40 is way to steep for this.  I got this game as a Kickstarter for $15, and that's probably a fair price for it in my opinion.  Even still, I feel there are a lot of better options out there that have done the 3D platformer better.  I was really hoping the developers were "returning to their roots" for this game and were going to be making this a great experience, but I get the feeling the developers got uninspired and lost interest partway through and were just trying to get it out the door because they weren't really interested in the game anymore.

I think I've got enough time and playthrough to give this game a, in my opinion, fair review, unlike most ive read where they played like 4 hours and groaned.   Right off, yeah its a spritual successor of Banjo-Kazooie.  It looks like it, feels like it, sounds like it, its kind of one of those "Yeah it sure is" things.  Is it better than B-K or B-K Tooie?   Well better than Tooie is easy but i wouldnt say it's better than B-K just because it's NEWER, i'd honestly put them on the same level, if not B-K a bit higher.  But i'll just dig right in.
Visually, it's a colorful and vibrant game, with beautiful hand painted back grounds and skyboxes.  Some of the characters are a bit...off, I mean Yooka's (The chameleon) eyes are a just a bit too big but hey, its's a cartoony style, I get it.  Really, visuals is where it pulls off the most credit, this thing just looks very very nice where it counts.  Polished details on anything you spend a lot of time looking at, and small things for you to watch for once you get used to playing it and have time to look around.  The lighting can be a little too dark or not correct in some areas.  Just kind of leaving you to take an extra second to be aware of whats actually going on there.  But it's a minor gripe really.  Otherwise, the amount of time they must've spent on Yooka and Laylees animations for everything is stunning due to even simple abilites having high details from Yooka ducking and covering his ears while shutting his eyes after waiting for Laylee to do her thing (yeah the bat is female, who knew right?)
Ill make the audio a quick one.  If you know who Grant Kirkhope is, you understand.  If not Google his name for fun and check out how cool this guy is.  One of the best in the business when it comes to orchestrating together a videogame sound track.  Even within the same map in different areas of it, the music SEAMLESSLY transitions to a different variation of the theme track of the map.  Maybe its darker or spookier, or lighter and more cheerful.  But each is a stylized variation of the base theme.   Which I enjoyed quite a bit with each area just because it kept things lively and kept your attention for a good part of the game just listening to the music.  The voice acting, for what VAing in a B-K game is worth, is pretty spot on.  Without them actually saying any real words just making different sounds and you read the text.  A few of the voices really made me laugh pretty hard so job well done on the auido fellas.
Controls will be quick too.  Most of the general controls are fair.  Swimming is probably the worst.  That can disorient you really fast and youre stuck going in a circle while you drown, fun.  But for the most part, Yooka controls pretty fair.  When you learn to fly with Laylee then you have a whole cluster♥♥♥♥ of♥♥♥♥♥♥you need to learn, and im still not good at it, just due to the erratic flying controls they gave to make it a challenge, thanks guys :V.  But you tend to land where your shadow is, theres not too many limits to movement, as Yooka can go from his trot to a baby step in a matter of a second.  So controls, you're ok, but okay is where I leave you.
Ok so now we come to the heart of it: the game itself.  Theres 5 worlds, each can be "expanded" meaning what it means, they just get more things to do added to them once you get enough of the main collectable, quills.  (I dont really wanna get into the story and spoil it all so try and play along like you understand if you dont sorry <3) Now these maps have SO MUCH to do in them that it doesnt make the game short at all.  Theres plenty to do in each, and MOST of it is entertaining, sadly otherwise if its not entertaining, it's really ♥♥♥♥ing dull or annoying.  There's easy things to do, but then it jumps to, youre stuck staring and thinking about it, or cheat and look up a video explaining it.  So the gap really isnt fun to deal with either.  Rather it has the very hard stuff sure, but how about a test of inbetween next time fellas?  that being said, you unlock new abilites by purchasing them with quills from a snake character named Trowzer (that name is so entertaining with the character). So that means, yes, you have to go back and play levels once you have new abilites so you can complete certain parts of it.  So if you're a fan of returning to play levels, then you got it.  In addition to the abilites Yooka can eat certain berries or objects to gain their power, shooting fire or snowballs, turning into a heavy iron weight, glowing to light areas, becoming electrified etc.  That was one thing I really loved was the different power ups, it made you had to do what was most of the time, simple problem solving, instead of just bashing through it.
Now about those fun little worlds, they sure can be a big beautiful mess.  Sure they all look nice and have lots going on, problem is, thats just it.  Theres SO MUCH crammed into these worlds, without many landmarks to remember where youre at sometimes, that you get lost and disoriented, or in my case trying to 100% it, you can remember easily where youve been or not because nothing really dynamically changes when you progress, and if anything changes its very minor.  So trying to keep track of what you've done or where you are at is a major problem that im not sure how it got that bad honestly.  Thats probably the worst part about it is that, the first 2 worlds are fairly simple to keep track of, but by world 3 onward, its a struggle, the 4th is a literal maze type map, which really, seems redundant because in some ways each map feels like one anyways, so good effort fellas.  All-in-all, the worlds are ok-ish kinda, just do whatever you can to try and remember what you've done or where you've been because they will not help you at all.
The bosses and minions.  The little minions you run across are a simple button press everytime to wipe out of the way, no big deal, usually give you a butterfly for health meter to regain a spot.  Not much to say besides, meh about them really. Nothing special, dont really add anything to the game, but they also dont ruin it I guess.  Now the bosses, are interesting, each one themed for each world as you could imagine, and from W1-W5 are each challenging in their own way, none are excessively hard, but require more brain than braun once you get into the final stages of trying to beat them.  Whereas at first you could spam everything to get damage on them, when towards the end, you need to pay close attention and beat a pattern, or time something right on.  Also all but one of the bosses were comical in the usual B-K/Y-L manner.  Good writing, great choice for the VA cant talk it down much.
To wrap it up though without spelling out the whole game, it's what i'd call, mostly good, with an unhealthy amount of bad in it.  Is it an original idea and concept based off of B-K? No not really, its pretty much a newer mock up.  Its not like they went out and made it a successor that is it's own thing, they basically reskinned it in a sense while moving somethings around to sell it as is.  But does that make it a bad game necessarily? No not at all.  I had quite a bit of fun most of the time doing all the challenges and puzzles.  got stuck on a few, and honestly frustrated a few times because the timing and controls on some are quite...."interesting".  It's charming, fairly harmless in existing as a game to a big name like B-K, and honestly, it's a fun 3D platformer to pick up if you haven't played one in a while, just wait until its on sale, should honestly be $20 to be fair.

The game certainly has its flaws and flubs, but none of these were interfering in my gameplay experience so much that I'd consider it a dealbreaker. I can get behind most of the negative reviews for the game, but I cannot understand how most people suggest the game is not worth it based on these mistakes.
Its a solid 3D platformer and when you loved Banjo-Kazooie, you will love this.

Yooka-Laylee's a lazy game. Two million dollars via kickstarter was probably just pocketed, or else wasted on god knows what. Poor game design litters the entire game. Certain abilities you learn don't compliment some of the level design. There's only 5 worlds. The bossfights range from nice to horrible. Half the characters you meet are recycled into all the other worlds. Visual fidelity is inconsistent.
One of my biggest issues is that you can unlock a flight move in the game that totally breaks the level design of most of the game. The developers tried to make it so you only unlock this flight ability before the last world, but the awful world hub's design resulted in the player being able to easily just open each world without playing in them for very long, unlock a bunch of moves awarded to you for progression and then return to start actually playing the worlds with a full moveset. This results in a lot of jumping and gliding and obstacle puzzles that can be totally bypassed by your flight ability. I do like the freedom of movement and exploration you get in Yooka-Laylee, but this issue goes beyond that and ends up being counter productive to the game design.
It's a disappointing game, but in the end it still scratches a certain "colorful collectathon" itch.

Now don't get me wrong, the game can be enjoyable, but it has problems.
I can't really recommend it for the full price tag. If the price drops significantly maybe, I took it when it was free.
What are the problems?
Well the controls are a bit clunky. Sometimes the goto option is bugging out and trying to get past the object you are going to, so you collide into it. For example once I had a goto on a planet to leave a VIP there, instead we crashed in the planet… I doubt he liked his travel. Or if you start form some station and the goto destination is on the opposite direction, the ship start to bump into the station and trying to get through it.
The voice acting is horrific, the tutorial is terrible. The interface is a bit strange at times, like there is tab for loadout which shows you your weapons and you can buy new ones, then there is systems which shows you almost the same thing, and then there are enhancements where you can upgrade your systems…
But as I said the game is still enjoyable, if you can get past those things. The ship design is great. Almost all ships look good. The space is nice as well, it’s colorful and empty at the same time. It’s not hyper realistic so you see only black empty space and little dots for stars, you see nebulas and other great looking skyboxes, but they are not too much. (for example Rebel Galaxy, although really pretty, it’s a bit too much, I feel like swimming in a jar of jam with different flavors). There are a lot of different things you can do and different ways to approach the game. You can mine, you can trade, you can fight pirates, you can fight the bad guys or the good guys. You can send troopers to board their ship and overtake it, and then you can either sell it, or use it for yourself. You can hire mercs, so you can form a small fleet, I think 3 is the limit. Basically it still have that feeling of a space sandbox.
But in the end it feels like unfinished product for me. Like it is released with the early mechanics in place. You know how devs just make some things at start of development so they can control the game, but later they overhaul them and make them a lot more fluid and intuitive. Well here that part was skipped.
Also note that there is no dogfighting. If you think you can play the game like Freelancer – chase the enemy and attack them, you are wrong. This is more of a sea-ship-fighting. And actually the manual targeting is not so good as well. So, in a way, it’s more of a “command and manage” game.

As for the Undertale community; give it a wide berth since the most vocal fans seem to be adolescents going through puberty.

Nearly ten year ago the snowy rain fell on Hull like all the angels in heaven had decided to colloquially urinate at the same time. And so opened this innovative action adventure for me: I had a weekend to kill, it was snowing outside, and I had no heating. I didn't want the intellectually intensity of a strategy game, nor did I want to frenetic multitasking of a RTS. With a blanket on my legs, I sat down and completed this game in 10 hours without even a toilet break. And the first thing I did? Began again. After a toilet break.
Max Payne pitches perfect progressive difficulty. Action games shouldn't - in my busy world - kill you more than three times at the same point more than three times. You shouldn't be slugging through a game with a face as pained as Payne's permanently constipated expression. Instead you should be smiling appreciatively at just how awesome it feels to burst horizontally through a door (in slow motion) and expertly twisting through your hips as you innerringly shoot three baddies with your John Woo pistols before time jolts back into the present and all three baddies fall down at the same time. Whump.
This is not a serious game, but it is seriously evocative. The weapons, even now, feel powerful. I can remember a scene where a baddie hideing behind an apartment door unfortunately proclaims that he intends to shoot you as you come in. He doesn't, but you should, expect to leap towards him while simultaneously opening said door while unleashing a full shotgun blast to his chest that lifts him several feet in the air. You can almost hear Chuck, I mean Max, saying, "not today bozo."
These scenes occur tirelessly throughout the game. Face an impossible situation. Engage bullet time (copied from the Matrix). Shoot all enemies. Read film noir comics.
While the game itself is not so serious, what should be a series consideration is the known (and ongoing) compatibility issues with steam. Unfortunately the download can open fail to name the weapons file correctly which can result in the game simply not starting. While I managed to get it work (on occasion) you cannot expect Steam to help you out on this one. Much better to buy on amazon.
Fortunately the game gleefully leads you on a deeply humorous (if a little silly) adventure once you have got the thing working. The dialogue between the baddies is priceless. Not to mention the subplot of the Lords and Ladies TV series - "My Lord! My Lady! My Lord!" - which goes on for about twenty minutes if you halt your carnage to watch the many analogue TV sets scattered throughout the game. Take this game for what it is - a romping film-noir - and you'll find an outstandingly crafted adventure that is also a piece of gaming history.

Just finished off 100%-ing Yooka Laylee, and I have to say, I really enjoyed this game. It is absolutely a worthy followup to the Banjo Kazooie games. Yooka and Laylee make a great pair, with Yooka's smooth charm offsetting Laylee's downright diabolical wit quite nicely. The cast of characters in the game is diverse, ranging from a rain cloud with some...shall we say, cloud-stipation, to space alien frog people, and the banter between them and the buddy duo is always fun. I really enjoyed this game's sense of humor (something that I think has been lost in most of the other reviews I've read), and I loved the game's mix of challenge and exploration. Worlds are themed quite nicely and are diverse, ranging from Central American-themed ruins to a literal cosmic ocean. There are more collectibles than you can shake a curly green tail at, and exploration is almost always rewarded with something useful.
To address some of the common complaints I've seen in other reviews:
1) In order to reach the final boss, you need to grab about 70% of the game's main collectibles, called Pagies. That's 100 out of 145. This is easily done, as each of the game's five worlds has 25 pagies, and the main hub has 20. Without really trying I had collected 100 Pagies within the first few minutes of entering the 5th world, Galleon Galaxy.
2) The hub world is circuitous, but there are shortcuts out the wazoo, so navigation is never an issue. You can get where you're going in no time flat, and backtracking is painless as a result.
3) The controls are sensitive and responsive, but not touchy. Getting Yooka to do what you want, when you want, is never an issue.
4) It is pretty obvious when you do not yet have the tools to get a Pagie. Encounter a big block of ice that you can't figure out what to do with? That's because you don't have the move yet. Can't figure out how to redirect that laser beam? That's because you don't have the invisibility cloak yet. That gorge looks like you have to fly over it, but you can't? That's because you don't have the ability yet. If you're a semi-conscious human being, it's easy to figure out what you need to revisit later.
5) Challenges are fun, and while you may not succeed at some of them on the first try, it is almost never due to poor game design. I say "almost" because there were a few instances where the game got in the way -- for instance, on the final phase of the final boss, the camera is atrocious. For most all challenges, you should be able to one-shot it with any modicum of skill, or worst case, the game makes it easy to retry challenges quickly, so you can easily learn from mistakes and get in as many attempts as you want.
6) The camera: It's not great. It's not terrible either. It's semi-active, in that it repositions itself occasionally as you move through the world, so if you're looking for a more passive system where you have complete freedom to manipulate the camera, you're going to find that you're fighting the camera quite often.
7) The music is hummable, as you would expect from the duo of Kirkhope and Wise. I found it to be mostly unremarkable though, which was somewhat disappointing. There is no Click Clock Wood or Freezeezy Peak or Gruntilda's Lair in this game, and that's unfortunate, because I know these guys are capable of some real gems.
TL;DR - It took me about 30 hours to 100% the game, and I enjoyed it quite a bit. It's by no means perfect, but it is what Playtonic promised in their Kickstarter, it is polished, it is fun, and it is well worth the full price of the game. Here's hoping for Yooka Laylee 2 some time soon!

As for the Undertale community; give it a wide berth since the most vocal fans seem to be adolescents going through puberty.

There are no easy to access and easy to leave hyperlanes (I think that's what they were called) like in Freelancer, where you could zip around the galaxy, jump out of the lane to do a mission and fly back to a nearby gate to keep flying. The quick travel that's in the game is expensive to use early on. While it seems to be pretty cheap for players in the later portions of the game, it looks like it will take FOREVER to discover the relevant areas of the map. The campaign missions are generally a minute of content separated by 10-15 minutes of flying to the next destionation.
Even with all that, I'd still recommend the game. The thing that really annoyed me is the main story mission, recommended for level 10 (I'm 17 atm), where you have to follow some peoople on a raid. It involves destroying a station with a near inifinte supploy of hitpoints. I might watch a movie and let it finish, just to see how long it's going to take.

This game has the potential to be a hit or miss. There is no tutorial what so ever, though I'm writing this having started only one playthrough I don't remember what happened at the start. I have played several different space-sims and this one has to be one of the most unique.
Ship types vary (that means how you fight with them too)- Most games put you into the cockpit of a starfighter, bomber or gunship at the largest. This game lets you pilot for fighter all the way up to dreadnaught class ships. This means there are different ways to fight based on the ship you are in. Most spacesims will have the point and fire style and this game does have that. A you move to larger class ships that style of flying doesn't work. You have to change to a "turrent view" control style. Here you take a view from out side the ship using the ASDW as well as Q and E to change the direction of flight while you aim with your turrets with the mouse. I found this to be very annoying at the start but after a few hours I got the hang of it and have no problem taking on multi larger ships at once now.
Income source - The ships in this game are rediculously expensive some of them ranging in the millions just from the start. You can kill ships for income which is nice plus sell the cargo they drop once destroyed. There is the option to mine gas clouds and asterout fields. You can also buy resources and trade from station to station. The main was to earn coin however is by a mechanism I have never seen before.
Ship capturing - This is the best part of this game and a very import aspect to it. It is hard to collect money by any of the methods described above to buy a ship. This gem of a mechanic also does not get a tutorial so its hard to learn about it, had to google how to capture ships. Once you get the hang of this the game becomes very easy. You basically send troops to the enemy ship and once they capture it, kill all hostile troops and destroy their internal systems, you can tow it to a nearby planet or station. There you can either sell it for cash, sometimes millions per ship, or you can place it in your hanger where you can use it whenever you want.
Questing - There is a main story that I havent really worked on as I do enjoy capturing ships trying to find the most powerful out there. There are side quest as well. There are also missions which are basically go scan this thing cature that guy or kill this group of bandits. The main story line that I have done I have found to be very annoying. It sends you to one side of the map to do a mission then sends you right back to the other side, I hate this kind of story telling and the main reason why I haven't really competed the main story after so many hours.
Things I dont like - sometimes you will enter empty space trying to find a specific class of ship and once it finally appears alone and have it half way to being captured 20 ships will just jump in out of nowhere and start shooting. You die in seconds. You can't skill dialogue or cut seens. If you get killed during a mission you have to wait through all the talking again.
Overall -  I do enjoy the game but not for long periods of time. I think the game could have been better. It is different, don't expect it to be like just any other spacesim. Go into the game prepared to learn, without a tutorial, a new playing style. Not worth the $35 price tag but if you see it on sale for twenty-ish dollars I would say definately get the game.

My expierence with Max Payne before playing this game was a short stint on Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne when I was younger. Although I liked it alot, I never thought to revisit it or explore the series. With the games now being so cheap here on Steam I decided to give them a full playthrough each.
To sum up how I feel about this game, I'd find it hard to not recommend it. Yes the visuals have dated, but not to the extent that it looks ugly. The game offers all modern resolutions and run (at least for me) as smooth as butter.
Infact the only real issue I had with the game in terms of running it was a sound bug with was easily fixed with a small player created patch, it's likely you'll have to do the same.
Gameplay wise, it's a run of the mill third person shooter. The real sell point of this game aside from it's story is the bullet time ability. One click of a button and you'll enter bullet time, being able to perform rolls, jumps and dodges. It's not just a gimmick either, the game's high difficulty means you'll have to make use of it, but that's okay because it feels so smooth and natural to pull off bullet time kills.
The story and character of Max Payne is the other real catch here. Max is troubled, his deep poetic self expression through the game is well placed and well wrote. You'll find him describing just about everything you come across of note with a clever, noir style of depressive reckoning. The story is one of vengence, it's not out of place and keeps the action following nicely.
I would highly recommend giving this game ago. It's dated sure, but not to the point where you can't enjoy it.

The game has a combination of features from Starbound, Rimworld, and Sheltered. Unfortunately, while it does take many of the good elements from these games, it introduces a whole new set of problems.
For example in Starbound you have base building but you are given the freedom to explore. In this game there is plenty to explore but most of your time will be taken up by exhaustingly menial tasks. If you send a character out to do a task that is too far away you are likely to see them urinate themselves or run back to the comfort of oxygen. It makes exploration a very slow crawl where you have to provide bathroom breaks nearly every ten tiles or they will urinate all over the map...and when they urinate or vomit it literally goes everywhere.
Unlike Rimworld where you can queue multiple food types and give priority to certain ones, the queue system for food in this game is linear. For example if you want to make higher quality food you can either add it to the queue with everything else or create an entirely new object to process food and give it a higher priority. Many things in this game operate in a linear fashion which reduces creativity and complexity.  This game has a very similar character creation system where there are positive and negative traits along with a smattering of skills. It's hard to really enjoy the personalities of the characters in this game though because they don't interact with each other unless it is task-related. The most character development you get from them is when one of their negative traits trigger.
The game borrows a lot of elements from Sheltered as well, but it doesn't give you the satisfaction of working towards anything but your own survival. Once you build up a safe habitat for your people all you really can do is build it up more or start a new base. You can fight creatures but it's mostly pointless to kill them and there aren't any aliens or huminoids that will come knocking on your door. All of the abandoned buildings I've found have been just that...abandoned buildings. In all three of the games previously mentioned you can go out and explore or engage in combat once you've built up a base, and I think ultimately that is really where this game is lacking.
The game is obviously Early Access so it's not finished. My recommendation is that if you can play a game like Starbound, Rimworld, or Sheltered then there isn't much added benefit to getting this game.

In a world where everyone's a hero when they launch a shooter, Spec Ops: The Line crushed that stereotype. Never had a game make me question my morality as much as Spec Ops: The line. This game surpassed the level of a game, bringing to me what I can only described as "a very real experience".
The strong emotions of the graphics and voice acting emersed me into a setting where I ponder over every decision I made while playing as the protagonist. I can still vividly remember the very first time I was shown the repercussions after I made a "mistake". Without revealing spoilers, I can only say I regretted so hard I did not make a save before making that decision and it "haunted" me for the rest of the game, quite literally.
Together with This War of Mine, I'm pretty sure Spec Ops: The Line can be arguably the next most realistic war game ever scripted. It introduces as a shooter, but jolts you back up and shake you vigorously, reminding you that every single round that connects with an "enemy", someone out there lost their loved one.
I have been late in picking up Spec Ops: The Line, and I regret letting it grow dust in my collection and not playing it sooner. The experience of this game is as good as reading a great novel. Kudos to the screenwriters for writing such an outstanding story.

You don't just play Hitman. You prepare, you plan, you think - and then you act, react, and adapt.
The episodic release is great for me because it gives me time to explore each map without feeling pressured to move on. The overall narrative flow will inevitably suffer from this jagged monthly instalment plan, but I’m not playing for the plot: I’m playing to carry out assassinations.
I’ve had no performance issues on my PC (2.67 GHz i7, 11 GB RAM, Asus GeForce GTX 960, Creative X-Fi). I’ve lost connection twice, but that’s at my end not IO’s.  On a big screen with surround sound this game plays very well.
The music is appropriately unobtrusive, the sound design is well-executed (I like the squeaky shoe when you change direction quickly). The incidental dialogue between characters is engaging and revealing of either their personality or a situation you can take advantage of. I love this kind of emergent game design, where the level itself provides opportunities for trying out different schemes.
The Escalations provide alternative targets but the player-made targets are lacking. I’d like to see more detail on player-made missions to decide if it’s worth my time trying out. I’m really looking forward to the Elusive Targets as one-shot (ha) opportunities to play.
Hitman assesses player progression through an XP meter, with each ‘level’ of experience unlocking new starting locations, disguises, and equipment.  This puts a really neat slant on missions, encouraging creativity in a Blood Money way.
I think IO has really hit the nail on the head here. This is what it’s like to be Léon, the professional assassin. Moving silently and unnoticed through your potential victims you’re constantly reminded of your difference as a character every time a ‘Subdue’ marker pops up as you approach someone from behind.
Hitman is focused and on point. Level design is challenging, engaging, and stimulating both aesthetically and mechanically. This is a game of opportunity and choice – go play! :D

Some may ask, how do you take such a deep and philosophical character such as Jim Davis' Garfield and turn it into a racing game? Surely such a pitch is destined for disaster but I must beg to differ. Now, I am a man who is passionate about his gaming terminal, having sunk thousands into creating the perfect gaming machine, as finely tuned as a Formula 1 car or a grand piano. So, naturally, I set the graphics setting to "Very High" Yeah, my PC can take it, it has taken on Tripple A releases of the highest graphical settings at 60fps so a little Garfield game won't be any challenge right? Heh, you know little about Garfield if you think your £10,000 computer is gonna get you anywhere out of Loser town. The mere philosophical questions the game asks your computer to ponder makes this game unfit for anything but Space-grade, NASA produced machines to handle. Just a single race in and my computer looked like it was playing a powerpoint presentation given by a five-year-old with autism who didn't know what a right arrow key was. I was crawling, and you can't win these extreme races by crawling.
I accepted my fate, I turned the graphics down to very low and closed down every other app running on my terminal at that time, except for my media player that was playing Scott Joplin's 'The Entertainer' at x2 speed on repeat. I began the game and I felt like I was playing a 2005 game that had been poorly ported to the PSP, but I was fast, and that's all that counts.
I began the tutorial race. "Heh, this is easy, kid's stuff," I said to myself. I completed all the tasks as asked without breaking a sweat and managing to keep one hand on my stiffy at the exact same time. Then they introduced my NPC competitors and Jon Arbuckle flew past me like an Eagle high on crack. Everything I knew about my very existence was brought into question when I went sprawling to last place. I always thought myself as a master of racing games? I had spent hours as a child in the local arcade ramming all my spare change into large racing cabinets while I set the highest high scores ever set in human history. I would sit in those big cushioned seats with Bruce Springsteen blasting from my Sony Walkman. I was a speed demon with the precise control as a neurosurgeon or a man who is shaving his pubes with a cut-throat razor. Each turn and gearshift were acted out with pure sophistication conjured only by a man with experience and a national talent for the road. And that man is me.
Yet, here I was, getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me like a wounded soldier caught in a bomb blast. I wasn't getting it just handed to me, Odie was serving it up on a red cushion and a royal platter. I was humiliated. But I was also determined. I withdrew every penny from my savings account and hopped onto a flight to Brazil.
I arrived at night. At the airport, I hopped into a taxi and lit a cigarette. The driver asked me my business in Brazil. I told him I had come to get fast, he then said something in his strange dark skin language I didn't understand, but I got the gist, he told me I would never get first place in Garfield Kart. So ♥♥♥♥ing killed him and stole his wallet.
Later that very same night I found myself deep within the Amazon rainforest, completely naked, I clothes would only slow me down and I needed to be fast. As my eyes adjusted to the darkness it grew sensitive to even the dimmest of light. Reflections of the moon from the moisture on the leaves shone like tiny pin♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in my vision. That's when I saw it, two shining globes of yellow and red, lying in patient waiting behind a wall of leaves, each the size of the body pillows I cuddle at night to take the pain of loneliness away.  Our glances met and it's soft breath's deformed into a piercing roar. Not the mighty roar of a lion, but instead the knife-like hiss-howl hybrids of a Jaguar.
In that moment of sheer, overwhelming terror, everything around me ground to a halt, the Jaguar froze in mid-air, the blood hungry look of pure anger that scarred along its face levitated just a foot away from mine. It was in that moment I began to learn what it was like to be fast. Kronos hit play once more and I could hear the streams flow once more. I brought my right arm thundering around to meet the attacker, in the damn FACE. My incredible speed took the beast off-guard and it went spiralling to the side, flailing in mid air before all 140kg of its monstrous mass smacked into the moss covered stone. I was fast, but it was faster. Within moments it regained all of its power and came shooting towards me like a bullet, I leapt over it and onto it's back as it shot under me.
It was then, as I wrapped my arms around its throat did I realise the creature had cut me with its initial attack. A large incision, about seven inches in length was cut like a deep trench in my forearm, blood seeping steadily. Now it was my turn. I tightened my grip like a hungry anaconda around the Jaguar's neck, it hissed and howled at me in rage and spun violently, trying to throw me off like a bull you see in those crappy Western style restaurants that they sometimes do competitions for. Only this wasn't a hunk of poorly made plastic with a motor and soft padding underneath to catch your fall. This was an organic being with no other primary desires than to destroy me. How pathetic. Just as I could feel it's breath shortening he leapt up onto it's back and slammed down onto me, nearly cracking every bone in my body. Recovery time was minimal, I had to be fast. Already I could see it's unsheathed claws come racing towards me like Jon Arbuckle once had. Garfield Kart felt like a lifetime away from me now. That's when I saw it. The Jaguar represented Garfield, and I was Jon, I was faster, I was the superior being, I WAS THE OWNER. I'M WHO FEEDS YOU, I'M WHO KEEPS YOU ALIVE AND KEEPS YOU WARM. AAAAAAGGHGHHH.
I rolled over, all pain left my mind along with any human sanity. I resorted to the same primaeval functions the Jaguar was running on. Both of us halted, eying each other with caution and respect. We were Gladiators, but we had not been thrust into a Colosseum by a tyrannical Roman emperor, we were simply encapsulated in nature, put there by whatever mad God rules over this cosmos. Then I felt it, beneath my left heel was nothing, I dared a glance around. We were on the edge of a cliff, a seemingly endless drop hung bellow us, any bottom was hidden by a canopy of trees and a thick mist. When I had brought my head around again the Jaguar was in mid air once more, this time with no anger, but a villainous grin that said "I win"
Slow down there, Garfield. Not quite.
As it shot towards me I slid to the side like a bolt of lightning. I was at one spot one instant, another the next. I was too fast for Garfield. I spun and slammed the palm of my hand - with my fingers bent and flattened so that they were all flush - into the Jaguar's side, I felt a crack and could see the aftermath of my attack of stunning speed ripple through the beast's skin. A howl of pain and realisation when it saw the drop beneath that greeted and threatened to eat it whole. It spiralled around like a terrified fidget spinner and caught its claws in my calf, I screamed in agony as I was pulled down into the abyss along with Garfield. I was fast; but, alas, not fast enough.
There was this part here that I had written where I was found by tribesmen, made king and re-created Garfield comic strips in stone tablets until I found a man faster than me but then review would be too long.
Once back home in England, I sat down at my terminal, now drenched in a thick layer of dust. I turned it on and went to play Garfield Kart. I had defeated the fastest animal alive and ran at record breaking speeds nearly every day of the past five years. I was fast, but was I fast enough? I booted it up, hit "Single Race" and began. By the end, I had come 3rd Place. That was fast enough for me.
10/10, very fun game, would recommend.

Firstly, I was not a gamer back when platformers were popular, I missed out on that era of gaming thanks to a lack of consol. I kickstarted this game because it was a game type that I always felt I'd enjoy but never got to experience. I'm glad to have joined in! Many say that the nostalgia is almost too overbearing, I disagree. The game offers much in the line of unique experience. One of my absolute favorite aspects this game offers is the total freedom of exploration it offers, both in traversing the different zones (no invisible walls!) and in its puzzle solving. If you can find a way to circumvent an obstacle that generally has a planned solution, the game does not stop you from using it. I was also impressed that the game managed to make certain abilities powerful and rewarding without making them the go-to for every situation.
One thing this game doesn't do is hand-holding. Due to the nature of allowing free exploration, you'll often find obstacles that you simply can't bypass until you unlock a certain ability. I've found some backlash from that aspect, but I actually think it plays as a strength. It encourages progression and backtracking simultaneously, without telling me to do either. The puzzles themselves vary from challenging or intuitive to simple and quick, and are all generally satisfying.
Control wise, I was extremely satisfied with how well the characters handled. As a platformer, knowing where you are and having control of your character is essential, and I never felt a lack of confidence when jumping from one platform to another.
I adore the protagonists Yooka and Laylee, both for character design and personality. While they don't get a ton of developement, they get plenty of dialogue that really makes them enjoyable to play with. I admit the voices can be grating from time to time, particularly with Dr. Quack and Capital B, but you grow used to it. text:
Yooka-Laylee was marketed as a throwback to classic Rareware 3-D, platforming collectothons, and as a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie. Question is... does it hold up? In my honest opinion... ABSOLUTELY!!! I grew up playing all of Rareware's titles. My three most played games of my childhood are Super Mario 64, DK 64, and Banjo-Kazooie. It has a certain charm that can only be described as magical. The aesthetic immediatley pulls you in. Everything pops out in a vibrant manner. The game just oozes polish. The developers took this project very seriously and it shows.
There are, however, some draw-backs. The game feels almost too much like Banjo-Kazooie, but there is enough variety in the levels to differentiate itself from its spiritual predecessor.
The two key elements at the core of this game are "exploration and expansion." Your basic move set allows for some really intense exploration, and every map is large enough for you to learn in properly the first time you visit it. The second part is the expansion. After you collect enough of the primary collectable, you have the option to open up a new world or expand the current one. This choice allows for some gameplay elements, and alows for deeper level exploration. This mechanic really shows off the creativity of the developers. Each expansion for each level feels like a breath of fresh air as new paths are revealed to you.
The controls are extremely fluid. The weight and feel of Yooka and Laylee are perfect... when they're on the ground. When you transition into the roll mode, your control of the characters become almost non exsistent, and can become very frustrating when trying to scale some areas that require pinpoint platforming. Also, some of the character transformations control schemes can feel very wonky. I slight movement of the joystick (I did my playthrough on a Xbox One controller) could spell disaster when on a small moving platform. Other than that, the jumping is spot on. I appreciate the detail of a dark circle that appears under Yooka when he jumps so that way you can see where you are going to land.
Honestly, the worst thing about this game is the camera. You have no control over it. It suffers from Super Mario 64-idis where it seems to either get caught on ever wall when you're in an enclosed area, or it zooms up right behnd blocking your vision for virtually no reason. However, this is a minor complaint. The poor camera doesn't deter from my overall enjoyment of the game whatsoever. These occurance only happened on rare occassions. For the most part, it follows Yooka and Laylee pretty consistantly.
In summary, Yooka-Laylee is an extremely enjoyable experienced. As soon as I started playing, I thought to myself, "This is what Banjo-Threeie could've been." That is honestly the best way to describe this game. It is the true sequel to Banjo-Tooie. There are countless hours of fun to be had with this game. Don't listen to other reviewers who give this a bad score. If you love classic gaming with a modern touch, this is the game for you. Yooka-Laylee has officially revived a dying genre of games I thought had been long dead. Hopefully Playtonic will continue to make future installments to this instant classic. I already cannot wait for Yooka-Toolie!

For those who want a short version :
- Have you played Banjo-Kazooie ? Then you will like this game
- Have you NOT played Banjo-Kazooie ? What are you doing with your life ?!
- Are you one of those mutants who actually disliked Banjo-Kazooie ? Why are you even reading this ?
Now for the long version :
This game is a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie and its sequel, Banjo-Tooie. Now add all the usual stuff and you pretty much know what this game is, except that JonTron isn't the one having trouble in the toilets anymore. I suppose that if you're reading this far, you're pretty familiar with this kind of game, and if you're not, i suggest you look for another review among the thousands available. In terms of map size, this game is slightly larger/longer than Banjo-Kazooie but slightly smaller/shorter than Tooie, except that instead of having the usual 9 or so worlds, it only has 5 gigantic ones. Music notes are still there (except that they're now called quills), and you'll find 200 of them in each world (instead of the usual 100). As for the jigsaw pieces (now pagies), there's 25 in each world (instead of the old 10).
The level design is pretty much what you'd expect from a Banjo styled game (collect-a-thon), nothing to criticize on that point. However, i often found myself wondering where to go to find the next pagie, a problem i don't recall having when i played the original two games as a child. Another thing is that with only 5 worlds, the game lacks a bit of diversity in its environments, and you may find yourself bored of a world if you're going to try and find everything in it at once (which isn't really possible except for the last world, since you're going to have to come back to old worlds once you've learned new moves)
I would have prefered the game to be slightly longer, perhaps with an additional world or two, even if that meant having "only" 20 pagies per world instead of 25. Moreover, i found a few of them to be quite lazily placed, and definitely lacking in "value" (having only 10 of them per world meant that it actually mattered when you got one, whereas here it just feels as if you're collecting some kind of currency, which becomes even more obvious when you realize that everything is so cheap and you don't actually need to spend a good 40% of the game's total items (contrarily to BK where having all collectibles helped you a lot in the final battle against Rhyming Greenwitch)).
As for the gameplay itself, it's really interesting and dynamic : all the transformations have a cool gimmick, just like in the previous games, and the special moves are creative and really distinctive from the ones used by the BK duo. That is, until approximatively 2/3 into the game, where you learn the flappy flight move, which allows you to fly, the difference with BK and BT however being that you can use it whenever and wherever you want, which creates some huge problems in the first few worlds, completely removing any challenge from all platforming sections, since you can now just skip them by flying. I honestly don't understand why they didn't use the flight platforms the same way they did in BK and BT, since that allowed flight to be used restrictively, and only in areas where it was needed, which made it into a cool move, and not some way to go and cheat the early puzzles.
Those problems put aside, i still had a blast with the game, and would definitely recommend it to any fan of the Banjo series out there. It's also a good game to get introduced to the series, since the moveset is quite easy to understand and the difficulty is well balanced (not excruciably hard nor laughably easy, you'll find yourself dying on some bosses quite a few times, at least it was the case for me, but maybe i just suck ?).
My final verdict for Yooka Laylee is an 8/10 :
- minus 1 point for being slightly too short
- minus 1 point for the flight move not being handled as well as it could have

I rarely review games and only do so when I really REALLY enjoy the title.
I've known about Max Payne for years, I've watched my brother play it over 8 years ago and actually picked it up before. I didn't play much of it because I remember having some difficulties.
Fast forward to 2 days ago- See Max Payne on sale for like 3 bucks. That's a deal for any game, I'll give it a shot.
I got news for you, this game is incredible. It's one long action movie that is intricate and leaves you like a junkie looking for more Valkyr. Have you seen Max Payne the movie?? Yes? No? Either way, forget that movie- Play the game and you will NOT regret it.
As Max Payne, you get put into a tragic situation that only your guns can solve. You work your way up, and just when you think you've reached the top- You realize you've only scratched the surface.
Like I said before, there's the incredible story followed by great controls that make sense. Slow-Mo feature that works like bread and butter. The game IS challenging, if you're thinking slow mo makes stuff easy- you're wrong. Great length- Not long enough where you just want to get it done, not short enough where you feel like you've been gypped out of your cash.
The graphics are dated- The game was released almost 14 years ago on the MAX-FX engine. It's what you would expect from a game released in 2001. The faces on these characters are also priceless- taking and giving damage yields grimacing results that has it's own charm.
To sum up- The game's great- About 75% of the way through the game, I turned it off- Went to the steam store and bought Max Payne 2 and 3. I couldn't get enough. If you're a fan of the noir genre, this is for you. If you're a fan of action, this is for you, if you play fps and think that third person shooters wouldnt suit you, you're wrong- this game is for you. If you want to feel nostalgic and get a warm christmassy NYC vibe- THIS GAME IS FOR YOU.
9.5/10 Loses half a point for the lack of diverse weaponry- I feel like I only got stuff that got the job done, but on the other hand- I am just a NYC copper. You get pretty much whatever a cop would get. (With the exception of an M79)
Max Payne 2 is done downloading- I wont waste any more time writing this up!

Space, the final frontier. These are the voyages of a game that has been a lot of fun.
There are similar games out there to this, no doubt. In fact, it seems to be one of the great truths in life that, no matter where in time you are so long as it's after the release of Elite, very little will change besides the graphics. What does matter are the controls, exploration, the story, and (let's face it) combat.
The controls are, simply put, very basic. This is good for cruising in your Space Ferrari through the galaxy. There are no headaches to be found here.
Exploration? Save for a few interesting space anomalies you have to learn to navigate and finding new stations to trade with... Well... You won't find much here to work with. The galaxy itself is very 2D, which is helpful for navigation, but you rarely decide to veer wildly off the beaten path unless those pirates REALLY♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
Story and plot in this game are, while interesting, fairly light. You can play with or without it. Having done both, I'm actually a fan of sticking to the plot. There's still a lot to do and see in the galaxy, but you'd likely never think of going to these places without a little hand holding.
Last, and by no means least, is combat. I'll say it plain. This was a lot of fun for me. The smaller ships force you to line up your shots and take the time to learn more about the combat system. Larger ships get, my favorite, turrets. You can either fly about, positioning yourself to take less damage and letting your turrets automatically target enemies or take control yourself to aim at that dreadnought that just decided to pop in for a fight.
My one sole complaint concerning combat are the missiles. I hate them. Powerful, yes, but fickle.
Each ship, of which there are many, can be customized very nicely. What made things even more fun were the mods. I had a great deal of fun flying around in the Galaxy-class starship from Star Trek.
I will note that this game does not have the intricate controls and fleet building that the X series has. It doesn't have the exploration that Elite: Dangerous or NMS have either. What it does is find a happy place in the middle and let you kick some space butt.

The difficulties I have with Pool Nation start in the fact that I already know ho to play pool. I will explain: The english in Pool Nation does not accurately represent the way in which a ball would travel with said spin. Top and bottom english when making a cut shot can cause the cue ball to travel more left or right on the deflection, and this is not represented at all.
Left/right english isn't actually as useful on a pool table as an amateur might think. I rarely use left/right english in real pool, as top/bottom english can account for most necessary ball control.
As I can best explain it: Top and bottom english account most for how the cue ball deflects off the object ball, and left/right english effects the way the cue ball deflects off rails. There is a small amount of effect with left/right on ball deflection, and top/bottom on rail deflection, but it is very slight.
This has to do with the fact that the rail is a solid unmovable force, and ball deflection is sympathetic to mass/friction.
My previous pool experience makes this game very unintuitive!

TL;DR; Do not buy the game or following episodes before ALWAYS ONLINE DRM is removed !!!
Review(25.03.16):
This game is good, has a strong concept and can be great with updates. However it saddens me to speak about not game play but always online DRM in this review because in its current state I can not recommend due to it. Even if they say it has offline play, it does not include major features that you PAYED for.
You can not earn challenges, you can not play escalations missions and other stuff while offline. What is worse not one of these features requires always online. Game could have easily download required mission data and let you play offline, then upload your score online. As of right now you can spend long time in an escalation mission, disconnected, and lose all of your progress and therefore your precious time. I also could not unlock various challenges in the main mission including Silent Assassin even if I got them several times. This is again (and I guess) due to synchronization failure between server and local data. In the end I got tired doing the same things over and over again.
I do not have any sympathy for a game that does not respect your time. We see other online games keep track saves, your progress for ages and for a pseudo-online game to not have these features or implement this online DRM in the first place is not acceptable.
Developer Io-Interactive said that they want this game to be living experience. They said that they would improvise the game with constant feedback coming from players. I too think this kind of iteration and episodic format is really suitable for game like HITMAN that has a complex social simulation. If they are to keep their words this is where they start, with removing or compensating ALWAYS ONLINE DRM.
While I am writing this review, the average user score is at 53%. If they insist with their policies, I do not think people will buy further episodes. I also will be devastated to see such potential goes to waste in the hands of incapable developers and publishers.
I will change the review accordingly if these issues are resolved. Please DO NOT BUY THIS GAME OR THE UPCOMING EPISODES before this nonsense ALWAYS ONLINE DRM issue is addressed.

A long time ago, I read Joseph Conrad's The Heart of Darkness. That book featured Marlow's journey down the Congo river in search of a man named Kurtz. As Marlow and his crew descended down this river on their boat, they discended into darkness and saw unfathomable savagery. They witnessed the true brutality of man and discovered horrors that can drive a man insane. I was pleasantly surprised to discover that Specs Ops was based off of Heart of Darkness.
Like the film adaption of Heart of Darkness, Apocalypse Now, Specs Ops attempts to modernize the story of Heart of Darkness and add a military element. However, instead of the setting being in Vietnam like Apocalpyse Now, Specs Ops takes place in the Middle East. I enjoyed seeing all the little parallels to Apocalpyse Now and Heart of Darkness. A big theme in The Heart of Darkness was one man not being worth all the danger and inevitable carnage, but the main character dragging the crew along anyway because of obsession and mental instablity. Specs Ops offers parallels to Heart of Darkness and offers its own little unique spin to this internal conflict.
The game is also very fun to play. However, I did have a few problems. There are a few instances where the game is frustrating. Sometimes I'll be taking cover from fire, my health will be low, and an enemy will throw a grenade. This leads to either two choices: die from the grenade or die sprinting into gunfire. These levels are very small, many of them have limited places to take cover from gunfire. It's a tedious experience to die over and over because the cramped level design leaves you nowhere to take cover when a grenade happens to fly in your direction. It doesn't leave players feeling like they died because of an honest mistake. I also encountered glitches where the sniper rifles wouldn't register a lot of headshots. Incidentally, the stealth mechanics and tactical commands feel bare bones and leave much to be desired.
Despite all my problems, I would recommend this game. There are a few problems, but it doesn't ruin the experience entirely. The game is a little short (under seven hours), but the story and atmosphere are absolutely chilling. It's a well directed game. If you ever see this game on sale, be sure to buy it!

Spec Ops: The Line, was a breath of fresh air in the FPS genre for me. The interactive terrain was enjoyable and the use of it could have a dramatic impact on how many of the firefights turned out. The Suicide Mode was suitably hard and challenging - and the game play mechancs were smooth and made the game fluid and fun to play.
The biggest pro of the game is the story. It is an enjoyable story with elements that many FPS  games don't touch on and this was the best part about the game in my opinion. When you hit the end of the game, those final moments, it really makes you reflect on what you did earlier in the game and wonder - did I make that choice? I also enjoyed the fact that there was no best weapon that could be picked up and used the rest of the game. Yooka-Laylee is the spiritual successor to Banjo Kazooie as Mighty No. 9 was suppose to be for Megaman. So lets see if Yooka-Laylee fall short or is a true successor to its predecessor.
Story/World/Characters:
Yooka-Laylee is about a chameleon, Yooka, and his female batty counterpart, Laylee. They are enjoying their new home at Shipwreck Creek, when Capital Bee steal Laylee book. Scattering its pages, or Pagies, in the process. Yooka and Laylee set out on their adventure to reclaim their pagies and stop Capital Bee. That the story in a nutshell. Its pretty straight forward. No real twists or turns. Which in honesty is what Banjo Kazooie did. Its kinda like a Saturday morning cartoon. You know what going to but you have fun watching it. You meet all types of items with googly eyes on them (a typical Rare staple). Heck even their characters I can pair up perfectly with their respective Banjo counterpart, it terms of what they bring to the game. You got your heroes (Yooka & Laylee = Banjo & Kazooie), your move tutors (Trowzer = Bottles), the person who transform you (Mumbo = Dr. Puzz), etc. It even got a snarky humor to it. For example Trowzer is a snake in pants (trouser snake) and Yooka & Laylee ship/home is called the "Bat-Ship Crazy." You got all type of humor like this in the game.
Gameplay:
This is your basic collecthon. You got Pagies which you use to progress through the game and unlock new levels. There only 5 levels but each level can be made larger. The levels are nice enough to look at and when you expand them they get large enough to buy you more time in that world. But I would have liked 2 or more worlds or at the very least had the expansion in the worlds add move variety to that world.
With the Pagies, you got Quills to collect. These will allow you to purchase more moves from Trowzer which will allow you ease at navigating the worlds or grant you the ability to earn more pagies. I would have liked more moves or if the moves were more expensive. It felt like toward world 4 & 5 I had more than enough Quills to buy all the moves in the games and lost some of my enthusiasm for hunting for addition quills in World 5.
You also got ghosts to collect. These are like Jinjos from Banjo Kazooie. Collect all five in a world and you get a pagies. I did like how they add new method to getting them. In Banjo Kazooie you only had to walk up and grab them but in Yooka Laylee you have do small like things to capture each one (I don't want to spoil it).
Yooka and Laylee come with you basic move sets: They got attacks, jumps, double jumps, spring jumps, etc. And as you progress in the games you get more moves. You also can gain MollyCools to give to Dr Puzz so she can transform you into a world themed creature or vehicle to navigate the level. I would have liked in the transformation could have been more animal themed than item/vehicle themed (but then again this is a personal thing; I would have preferred if many of the NPCs was more animals than items). There also Retro the pixel T-rex who offer you an arcade minigame to get a pagie. Not to mention Kartos the minecart who take you into some old school Donkey Kong kart racing minigames to get a pagie. Now all these mini games are optional and I found that none them was hard enough or obnoxious enough to overstay their welcome.
The platforming in Yooka Laylee feel decent enough and the combat is well... basic (kinda like Banjo Kazooie). The camera is like that of any old school N64 camera. By that I mean, you'll find yourself having to constantly adjust it. I've never got really annoyed with the camera except when I was flying. Felt like the camera would cause me to miss things when in flight. That being said, the game is easy, real easy (like Banjo Kazooie). If you're just trying to blaze through the game then you could be done in like a couple of hours. The only real part that slow player down is the 100 Pagies door that prevent you from fighting the final boss. I found myself unlock new worlds before I've fully explored the previous level. The only hard part to the game is trying to collect everything in the game. While the majority of pagies are easy to collect, some are just a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to obtain (there one pagie toward the end in Hivory Tower that involves a slide, that is particularly frustrating to get). Each level got their own boss which are easy enough. Also the quizzes make a return like from Banjo Kazooie, but this time they are LESS annoying. In Banjo Kazooie these quizzes felt like they just drag on and on, but now they are limited to 10 questions which you could reduce this number to 5 if you answer question quick enough.
Other complaint is I felt the collectible easter eggs really didn't do anything. Felt kinda lack luster.
Music/Visual:
Music composed by the same people who did Banjo Kazooie so the music fit the level nicely enough and the game is pleasant enough to look at. The game look colorful and music match the color visual of each level. Never once did I run into a part of the game where I said "this song is getting annoying" or "this level look like crap"
Final Comments:
This is a Banjo Kazooie clone... which isn't a bad thing. Banjo Kazooie was a good game, with it share of flaws and Yooka Laylee share these flaws but also share it's good qualities. As a backer, I felt I got exactly what I was promised at the beginning of the kickstarter. I asked for a modern day Banjo Kazooie clone and I got exactly that. No more, no less. So as a backer I'm satisfied, but as a gamer... I wished that had tried to add a little more content. But than again I must also remember that when I played Banjo Kazooie as a kid, it seem longer only because I was younger and inexperienced with games. Back then player guides and word of mouth was the only way to get help, but now the internet we can get any answer for any part of a game we want. Making any Pagie that seem out of reach, easier to obtain. Going back and playing Banjo I found that many of these complaint with Yooka was also in its predecessor.
So to make it short, if you looking for a nostalgic throwback to classic Rare collecthon games like Donkey Kong 64, Banjo Kazooie, and Banjo-Tooie then this game is worth it. But if you new to collecthon like these, then wait for the price to go down to  about half. At $39.99 its a little too high for those who don't have a huge nostalgic boner, but at $15~$25 range you're getting a good game.
