It's a decent game worth the buy if you think you'd like it but I'd recommend waiting for a sale, since it does have several frustrating, missing, or unpolished parts throughout. If you haven't played Banjo-Kazooie and are not put-off by N64 graphics, i'd play that instead on the platform of your choice.
Yooka-Laylee looks great and controls well for most parts, with a few notable exceptions. Your basic running, jumping, attacking and flutter jumps are responsive and easy to master. Rolling is fun and easy in mostly straight directions, but can get frustrating on tight turns where jumping is needed as well in which case things get slippery and there are strange sudden velocity changes when jumping from almost stationary. Flying is very freeing and fine for long distances but similar to rolling, it is difficult to control at low velocties and more precise landings.
There are five large worlds - very large - but after playing them I prefer the nine varied smaller worlds in Banjo-Kazooie. There's a comparable number of collectibles total through Yooka's five and Banjo's nine but with Yooka-Laylee there are few really defining landmarks in the levels and it is very easy to get lost, wandering about aimlessly. Perhaps as an unintended  result of modern consoles and capabilities, lots of detailed plants cliffs and other decorative objects look great in screenshots but add to the confusion, lack of direction, and difficulty in mentally mapping-out levels.
If you're familiar with Banjo-Kazooie, it's interesting to think about those smaller worlds. Most are a mainly a large central area with a defining landmark. The island in treasure trove cove. Clanker in clanker's cavern. The pyramid in Gobi's, snowman in freezeezy, mansion in mad monster, the ship in rusty bucket, and the tree in click clock. It was simple but worked wonders at helping you keep your bearings and never getting lost. Banjo-Tooie strayed from this a bit with larger more levels and rightfully received some negativity over it. Yooka in it's endeavor to deliever large expansive worlds unfortunately also lost this very positive feature of smaller worlds. Given that Yooka-Laylee happened with a kickstarter and many eyes on a deadline, the cynic in me thinks the large world approach was chosen partly for the ease of development, since it is easier to expand a world with more of the same assets than to imagine and create entirely new environments and characters.
Ideally I like to play a great game and complete it 100%, but only if it is enjoyable. Yooka is enjoyable enough for me to complete the game but I don't plan to do any more considering the frustration some challenges with awkward controls, some very horribly designed and dull minigames (which you have to beat each twice to get two separate pagies - the laziest way for devs to increase the number of collectibles in a game), and the boring and tedious task of collecting every quill. Even here I find note-collecting in Banjo better, where they are usually together in larger groups with larger hitboxes instead of picking up individual quills here and there, with the added work of hunting them down through the unnecessarily large levels.
In other aspects, there are a few fun characters in Yooka-Laylee with great designs and witty banter but Yooka and Laylee themselves seem a bit lacking in personality. Even a small thing like adding some articles of clothing to their designs would bring out some much-needed personality.
The music is for the most part great with a few catchy tunes but perhaps not as memorable and varied as those of Banjo. It's admittedly hard for me to objectively judge the audio without letting nostalgia cloud my judgement though.
Lastly Yooka-Laylee just feels generally unpolished in various areas. The camera shows a goal in a challenge but doesn't smoothly transition back to where you are standing, instead snapping back to your latst camera rotation which can be jarring. The minecart games don't list the gem goal anywhere beyond the opening dialogue and doesn't display your end result at the end. Enemies hit you after completing challeges during the screen transitions. The stamina bar feels unecessary and just annoying most of the time. Butterflies can be difficult to find to restore health but it doesn't matter anyway because nothing is lost when you die - you just respawn at the entrance of the last door you went through. There are some slippery slopes you're supposed to roll up but some you cannot and no easy way to tell the difference. Sliding on your butt controls terribly too and if you missed a quill on the slop on the way down, tough luck - you gotta climb back up and through whatever you just did again if you want them all.
Grab the game when it's on sale enough for you and enjoy a play-through, but I recommend skipping any frustrating parts and not going for 100% completion.

While I've always been in love with Jedi Knight; Jedi Outcast 2, I have my issues with it's sequel, Jedi Academy. Do I think the game is good, however? Well, it does say "Recommended", right? However, as I usually do, I will keep the bad stuff of the game ahead.
First and foremost, while the game doesn't have as many as the previous game, it still has a few graphical errors with modern games. Mainly resolutions being 4:3, but those are fixed quite easily.
What is probably the biggest problem, however, ain't the graphics but the direction the game takes. Remember the enthralling storyline the previous game had? Not here. In here instead, Kyle becomes a secondary character, and instead you create your own character, which sounds great on paper... But falls flat, as you're only given the choice of your combat style, being male or female, your outfit and race, and later on the game, what ending you want. You can also choose what missions to do, but that's kinda pointless as you have to clear at least 4 of the 5 given missions to advance the game.
And that's another thing, the missions themselves are... Well, dissapointing compared to the previous game. Jedi Academy goes more for an "arcade" style, with items arround it and quantity of enemies over quality. Not until later in the game you're given a proper challenge, and even then half the enemies will be easy to kill by pushing them down a cliff and similar stuff. It also doesn't help at all that the game is WAY more short than the previous.
It's third problem, is a character itself. Rosh. At the first minute of your playthrough you meet this guy, and even since then you will most likely hate him already. He's a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ a worthless meatbag, and a bad character overall. And the hilarious part is that the writers of the game probably knew it, and
.
The last issue this game has, is that weapons are irrelevant. From the start of the game you'll have your light-saber, and you'll BARELY use anything else, which is a shame, as the game still has it's great FPS action there from the previous game. It does force you to use them in one of the missions, and there is a new cool weapon, but that's it.
All that aside, however, what do we have left? An enjoyable game were you get to feel like a motherf#cking Badass Jedi. Likely because of the incompetent enemies, but a Badass never the less.
Light-saber combat is not only great, but it beats the previous game. Not only there are a few new moves, but there are also 2 new styles of combat: using two light-sabers at the same time, or using a dual-blade saber. There are also some sort of special attacks that can be used when hitting Mouse 1 and Mouse 2 at the same time, which consumes half your Force bar, but deal insane damage.
About force powers, they're still there. Some have changed whoever, some have been erased, and some others have been added. The game does f#ck it when it gives you the choice of getting them at the order you desire, as they can make the game EXTREMELY EASY early on (such as the Lightning force power at LVL3, which nearly instantly kills most enemies of the early game, and deals high damage to enemy jedis, even pushing them back). Later in the game you'll have to get used to them to advance, and they can also be used to find cool secret areas, although there are not nearly as many as in the previous game.
The multiplayer is also back in action, having more content and active players than the previous game, mainly because it has nearly all the crap it had before, but with some new aditions. Tons of models to choose for yourself (also having the option of making a custom one for yourself, like in the singleplayer game), and tons of maps and gamemodes as well.
The game is also easily modabble, for the people out there who want to add crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥to the game, but that's up to you. It does help, however, to add better animations, textures and such.
Is the game good? Yes. You'll have fun. However, if you're looking for a singleplayer experience, go play Jedi Knight; Jedi Outcast 2, as it delivers WAAAAAAAAAAY better than Jedi Academy. If you're looking for multiplayer action or mods, then this one's for you, and it's a solid purchase on a sale.

It's the classic Rare collect-a-thon platformer formula same as it was circa November 20, 2000.
The camera snags rarely but otherwise is fine, the levels are huge once expanded so you have to explore and cover ground to find stuff, the controls are tight for the stuff you'll be doing all the time but wonky for the stuff you'll rarely do, there's an even break between the challenges that are a hit and the ones that are a miss and once you get certain moves, the actual platforming becomes trivial.
The game isn't bad, it's just not great.
The biggest issue is that the devolopers haven't pulled from the vast font of trial and error in design in the intervening 17 years between their prime and now. They have not included any of the quality of life improvments most games feature now such as a map or compass, a quick way to get to unlocked levels or even a way to warp between levels when you're in them and none of the minigames have a way to quickly restart them if you fail. The game will tell you the total number of collectables you have for a given level but gives you no indications of where the ones you missed are even after beating the final boss.
There is also a lack of creativity in the tasks you need to do when collecting things. The quiz segemnts between the different zones of the hub promise a fun spin on things and a mounting challenge but the board never gets more complex than a straight line and the questions never become more complicated than the first quiz, this is a great metaphor for the rest of the game.
If you've recently replayed the banjo games and you really want more, by all means dive right in, just don't expect things to get as crazy as 'Kazooie or 'Tooie.
If you want to play a servicable collect-a-thon, this would not be my first reccomendation but it would be on the list.
If you want a challenging platformer there are better offerings in the genre.

A game very reminiscent of good old platforming games (Banjo-Tooie in this case). I personally love 3D-platforming, it is one of my favourite genres, so I've been looking forward to Yooka Laylee since I first heard of it. When I finally got it and started playing it I had mixed emotions. It feels a bit overly complicated, with few worlds, many collectibles and quite a bit of backtracking. Not unlike the 90's platforming games Yooka Laylee can be pretty frustrating at times, some times due to your own fault, and sometimes the game likes giving you the middle finger. I did complete the game however, 100% collectibles and all achievements complete.
I really wanted to love this game, but sadly I can't just ignore all the problems it has. It is an okay game. I enjoyed a good deal of it but so many things were frustrating and / or poorly designed that I can not recommend this game in good conscience. I really hope the game designers learn from this game and make a better sequel, or new game.
Pros:
+ The game design is amazing. The characters are all really well-made, the levels in particular looks great, every character is distinctly different from every other character, in a good way.
+ Sound design. Whenever you pick up a collectible or complete a puzzle you get a satisfying little jingle. It motivates you to get more of them. Very cool sound design in this game.
+ Music. While sometimes a "little too much like Banjo-Kazooie/Tooie" most of the music is great and memorable.
+ Collectibles. Many are in plain sight, many are well-hidden, just like its supposed to be.
+ Chameleon swim animation. It looks great. Chameleons look so silly when they swim.
+ Animations in general. Most of them work really well. Sometimes some things clip through something else, but expecting everything to be flawless isn't realistic.
+ Abilities. There are a good number of abilities in the game, most are fitting and useful.
Cons:
- Enemy variaty is basically zero. You have your ground-slogging enemies, your swimming enemies and your flying, shooting enemies, and a few re-skins of the same kinds. That's about it.
- Controls and camera. The camera works fine about 85% of the time, but I've been close to falling to my death several times because the camera decided to change around, and suddenly I was walking toward the edge instead of away from it. As in many platforming games of the 90's your characters "slide" a bit after moving in any direction, something that I think is fine as long as you keep it very subtle. They had all the chances to make it subtle. They didn't.
- HUD. For some reason the game developers decided that you don't need to see how much HP you have left, so a few seconds after taking damage, your health bar disappears. To find out how damaged you are in a boss fight (where your attention is elsewhere) you'll have to pause the game. Not optimal.
- Music length feels too short on some levels, making it feel repetetive.
- Story. This is a personal preference, but I wasn't invested in the story at all.
- Inconsistence. Some puzzles and actions works wonderfully and are fairly straight-forward. Others require you to use your abilities in ways you didn't think they were supposed (or able) to be used in. This is both good and frustrating. Mostly frustrating.
-  Frustrating mini-games. To advance (or at least to beat one boss/ aim for 100% completion) you'll need to complete an annoying mini-game with horrible unresponsive controls and THEN fight the boss, using the same horrible unresponsive controls. Or being "forced" to play arcade games (like flappy bird for instance) to get your Pagies. I also count Kartos' mine cart challenges as mini-games. Some of them are really easy and some require you to do them over and over until you've learned the entire course.
In some of the mini-games you need to collect a certain number of objects. If you get hit you'll lose some of those objects. In a couple of mini-games you can get hit after you've crossed the finish line, making you potentially lose the mini-game even if you had collected enough objects. This is extremely poorly designed.
- Unresponsive controls. Going back to the fact that you "slide around" after moving, and that you need to "turn around" before you can go in any given direction - sometimes the game requires you to turn on a dime and act really fast. Even though you really can't. You need to "know" certain things will happen and react before they happen, wich usually means you'll die or fail a few times before you can complete a certain mini-game or beat a boss.
- Few worlds. Five worlds with 25 "main" collectibles is way too few. I'd much rather have seen eight smaller worlds with 10 or 15 collectibles.
- Backtracking. Many collectibles or puzzles require you to first learn abilities from later levels to complete. Having to go back three or four times just to pick up a few stray Pagies didn't add much positive to my experience.
- Abilities progression. The "currency" you use to buy abilities were never hard to come by. I always had enough to buy everything at once.

Overall a fun game, possibly the best Star Wars game I've played. The gun play isn't really the best, but aside from one level taking away your lightsaber, who would use a blaster in a game like this anyway? The best part in my opinion is definitely the lightsaber combat, and while it takes some time to get used to and has a bit of a learning curve, if you can master your saber, nothing will stand in your way.
However, as much as I enjoy Jedi Academy, certain issues became more clear the longer I played. I undertand you're supposed to be given harder missions as you rank up as a Jedi, but most of the difficulty seems to come down to extreme artificial difficulty, often reaching points where it can take five to ten minutes to put a Sith down, all the while they can put you down with one hit. As annoying as this can get, it only gets worse when Sith that only attack with the Force are introduced; holding you in place with Force Grip while their friends continue to attack, completely obscuring your vision with Force Lightning while a Dual Saber user and a Double-Bladed Saber user run through the arcing lightning, or just being damn annoying be constantly using Force Push or Pull on you, sometimes leading to an uncontrollable death via falling down a bottomless pit. Speaking of Force using Sith enemies, it often seems like enemies have infinite Force usage, and I'll admit that the constants streams on Force Drain and Lightning while being Force Gripped from someone using a long lasting Force Rage has often tempted me to cheat my way through by giving myself infinite Force. Luckily I've been able to keep myself from doing so, and I hope I can continue to do so since I'm so close to finishing the game.
Aside from certain enemies being a nuisance, my second biggest complaint has to be the controls. When the work, they work well, but when they don't, a simple action can often lead to an unfair death. Along with one-hit kills, a majority of my deaths have been from my character doing an unnecessary backflip into a ravine when I just want him to jump on a Sith, wall running into a bottomless pit, performing a ground attack or back stab when I'm just trying to attack the guy in front of me, or wasting my Force by using a long range Force Drain despite being right in the enemy's face, giving me less health than I needed and usually dying to a stray blaster shot. Furthermore, since I often find myself fumbling around on my keyboard during frantic situations and deactivating my lightsaber, pulling out a blaster, or accidentally using a different Force Power than the one I wanted, I would probably recommend playing this game with a controller if possible.
All in all, despite the major annoyances I'm having with this game, whenever I get into the flow of combat and everything goes my way, I have a lot of fun cutting down one enemy after the next, which is why I recommend playing Jedi Knight - Jedi Academy.

I've been playing Prison Architect for about 30 hours per alpha release for the latest few versions that came out before the final release came out. An early access game that not ONLY has relesed new versions on schedule for a long time, and now actually has reached version 1.0, is, sadly, something to celebrate on Steam.
Aside from the fact that the devs have used the Early Access platform the way it was meant to be used and that should be commended, it's also a pretty damned good managment game. Prison managment has been done before, but not for a long time, and never well, and it's a change of pace from the usual town managment sims. Now your "population" is the enemy, as well as your source of income.
The number of systems that works togheter to form the complete simulation is very impressive, and even a small change can shatter a very stable system. For example. I had a prison with 750 prisoners, running very smoothly. Then a gang leader arrived on the bus one morning and started organizing the red gang, one of the three gangs in my prison. I had never had a gang leader before so I let him work for a bit before sending him to my supermax facility, so I could experience how running a prison with an organized gang was like. In supermax he lost his temper, and ended up in solitary. This angered his gang enough that they started a riot. A couple of hours later when the dust settled and the riot police left there were 54 dead, over 60 injured, and 200 prisoners who were up for solitary for their actions during the riot. The rioting prisoners broke into protective custody, where snitches and former policemen who ended up in prison are kept, and killed half of the protected prisoners. I was put on notice, and risked ending up as a prisoner in my own prison. Luckily my lawyer got me out of that... A prison is a delicate system, and care needs to be taken when introducing anything new.
There is now added a story mode, to work as a guide for new players, and an escape mode, where you get to play as a prisoner, as well, but I still feel that the sandbox mode is the meat of the game. You learn some new tricks each time you build a new prison, and as you can sell your old prison for an extra cashboost in the startup phase of your next one, you will get more and more funds for each prison you build.
My only problem with the game is that it starts to lag when your prison grows too big, depending on how good your computer is. I first start to notice it at 750 prisoners and roughly 350 staff, so at just over 1000 individual characters present in the same prison, but my computer is pretty damned good. I know that a lot of people can't even get 500 prisoners to work well.
tl:dr
Damned good simulator/managment game. Buy it, play it, profit. A bit unforgiving if you make a mistake though, but that's the way in a prison.

Having played this game for over thirty hours at the time of writing this review I feel confident enough to review it now.
I picked up the Euro Truck Simulator 2 Deluxe Bundle at the recommendation of a friend. I paid about £30 something at the time and got a bunch of rubbish games with it that I played for about seven seconds before uninstalling. However this game was worth the £30 alone.
Euro Truck Simulator is a super basic game. You drive a truck from point A to point B, that's really all there is to it. But don't let that put you off. You still need think about how to turn corners without crushing your cargo, when to indicate, etc. It's pretty realistic. Also, if you go too fast you can tip your truck which I have done a couple of times...
It has full controller and racing wheel support and soon I plan on getting a racing wheel to enjoy this game to the fullest.
The unintended side-effect of this game is how relaxing it is. Cruising down the motorway in a truck, listening to the real radio stations provided to you in-game. It's a great game to unwind with. But be warned. Longer journeys can take a very long time to complete and there is a real genuine risk of falling asleep and having your truck crash during the few seconds your eyes were closed. My tip? Don't bother with the long distance hauls unless you're very very awake and alert.
Apart from that though, I give this an easy 10/10. Especially with all the DLC currently available.

So I'll say upfront that I'm writing this review after playing this game for 9 straight hours. Not to be a Quizmaster Quinn, but gotta love that "playing a dating sim for several hours straight to avoid anxiety", am I right? Right guys? Right? (oh god, i'm so sad--)
Anyways, Dream Daddy is a great game with a fantastic sense of humor. Several times during my playthrough I found myself literally laughing out loud, struck by the acute comedic timing that is difficult to do over a mostly text-based medium. The characters are all fantastic, even the side characters, and there were moments that were surprisingly touching. The story, though mostly light, contains scenes that can really resonate with a diverse audience; from characters that seriously feel real. The dialogue never sounds fake--it's all very natural, even (and I would argue, Especially) the dad jokes.
There were small technical issues, but I only ran into them when I gave in to save-scumming (something that is sort of hard to resist in these types of games, if you're like me.) If you saved during a scene, and then decided that you wanted to change an answer that you selected--loading the scene often times resulted in the music track that was previously playing over it being completely silent. The music would start up again, but only after it transitioned into a new scene (or, more specifically, a new song.) This could be irritating, if only because I couldn't see a way to circumvent it unless you saved often, and didn't mind going back far enough that you could restart the full scene. The only other issue I ran into besides that one was that once, after reloading a scene, a character sprite that had been on the screen in an earlier scene showed up over the top of the character sprite of the person that I was currently speaking with. This lasted until, basically, the "end of the day". (It was Joseph's creepy little twins as well, which.... was an Experience.)
All that having been said, the game is still incredibly charming and the few bugs that I encountered weren't enough to ruin that for me. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys dating sims, cute music, endearing characters, and/or Very Good Dad Jokes. Happy Dad-ing!

I know I haven't played much of this game, but it was enough for me to get the impressions I needed. So, on with the review:
The premise is great. Something that feels like Starfox, but with a great original spin to it. The cutscenes got me pumped up, the HUD caught my attention (specially the 3D mini-map). Then came the info dump at the start of the tutorial.
When you first hop into the game, you are greeted with not only one, but three (maybe more, I kinda lost track) windows with info thrown at your face. They explained how the HUD and the controls worked. I do believe it is important for games to have tutorials or ways to have the player learn the game without running for outside help, but throwing a info dump at their faces is NOT the best way. It might confuse them even more.
I had problems with the resolution and window sizes, because this is one of those games that needs you to restart the game for changes to apply, and every time you restart it you're greeted with a long cutscene (skippable, at least) and a kind of long loading screen. Now thanks to those resolution problems, I could /barely/ read the tutorial text dump. I actually had to squint my eyes once or twice.
After you go through all the windows that vomit information onto you and expects you to swallow it, you're tasked with killing a pirate, to get used to the controls. And that's precisely the nail in this game's coffin for me: the controls.
They're incredibly counter-intuitive and confusing. The right and left movements through the keyboard are fine, but up and down are inverted, maybe for realism, which I think is a double-edged sword. The mouse controls are really sensitive, I couldn't keep the ship in a steady, linear flight with them. It would take me /ages/ to track the enemy ship down once it made a turn and got out of the screen, just because how confusing the controls and the envoirnment were. I also had no idea if I was hitting the pirate ship when I shot at it, because the actual bar that tells you that is so god damn subtle and tiny.
After all that, I was tasked to fly to the planet that was in the background while I was hopelessly dancing in circles with my pirate, and I realized after a small text dialogue from the characters that that was it. That was the base tutorial. You were supposed to go to the next mission knowing everything there needs to know about the controls and the HUD, and I knew almost nothing about them. So I closed and unninstalled the game practically instantly.
It has a lot of problems. If you're a fast learner, you might be able to finish this tutorial with ease, so in this case, that's great, go you. But for people who need comprehensive tutorials, like me, the info dump and the counter-intuitive controls ruins the game. I wouldn't personally play it ever again. But if you think you can handle it, be my guest.

This is a must-play for fans of interesting narratives and experiences that challenge what a game should be. Yes, the majority of the time you are going to be playing a console-style checkpoint-based linear shooter where you walk through beautifully-rendered warzones mowing down waves of enemies. The shallow gameplay and gratuitous violence is exactly the reason i personally don't tend to enjoy this style of game. But what makes Spec Ops interesting is that instead of letting the player come to that conclusion on his own, it pushes the main character into situations where you, as a player, are forced to consider how messed up it really is. There are strong parallels with Apocalypse Now, especially in the great music and over-the-top violent imagery, but i ultimately found myself more reminded of The Stanley Parable, another game that makes you think about why we, as players, play the games we do. The highlight of the whole experience is an insanely good "hallucination" toward the end that just punches you in the face with meta, especially if you have played the whole game in one sitting (highly recommended). Very, very clever.

I wish I didn't have to rate this game too negatively, as there are some really neat aspects to it that I like. Cover works well for the most part, the endless hunting and hoarding of weapons and ammunition, and the overall atmosphere is spectacular. My problem with it is that the gameplay itself is rather bland, much more like the old quicktime event games than any sort of real simulator. You move forward a bit, stumble into a trap, find the right place to stand/crouch/cover behind, then click your button when the enemies head pops up.  Wait, you weren't supposed to stand there, so you die, respawn, try again, this time stand over there behind that box, no wait, that is not the magic spot either! Die respawn, try a different spot.  The bullets also dont feel very satisfying, you dont get that seratonin inducing impression upon impact, they feel more like instant tranquilizing darts then hunks of hurtling lead.
If you dont mind extremely linear gameplay (this game practically runs on  a monorail), with oodles of trial and error type set pieces, there is 'an experience' to be had with this, however I prefer at least a little more complex gameplay, even from such a simple shooter. If you're in that same category as myself, best look elsewhere.

At the moment I can't recommend this, but I do have hope for the future.
This is a colony builder in a similar vein to games like Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress, Spacebase DF-9, and so on-- in particular, it seems to take a lot of inspiration from Rimworld. And although there are technical issues (crashes, pathfinding, etc), there's a fair bit of content to explore.
The reason I don't like it is it's very much a 'race against the clock (and diminshing resources)' game. Life-essential processes aren't self sustainable until the very late endgame, meaning you're constantly depleting limited and non-renewable resources to keep your colony going. For example, early game you use both algae and water to produce oxygen and scrub carbon dioxide. Algae is finite (can only be consumed), water is finite until endgame. Polluted water, produced from midgame CO2 scrubbing as well as bathrooms/showers and so on, cannot be effectively cleaned until you can meet the tech and large energy requirements to near-boil the water and cool it again as filtration units are actually a breeding ground for germs But by this time, you'll have tapped the steam geyser for unlimited water. And so on.
If you want a Rimworld-esque colony building game with a race-against-the-clock theme, then I would recommend this title, but not for the average player.

Yooka-Laylee is an inconsistent game, but overall, it manages to successfully capture the feel of the Banjo-Kazooie series.  It certainly fills the niche it set out to--just don't expect much iteration on 1998's gameplay, for better or for worse.
The
worlds are sizeable and well-stocked with content, though the concept of expanding a world seems like a strange mechanic.  If possible, you might as well expand a world before entering it for the first time.
The minigames and puzzles are sometimes repetitive, though for the most part, there's enough variety.  Few are interesting enough to replay for fun, however, and some are uninspired duds.  Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts suffered from this kind of by-the-numbers challenge design.  There are a few difficulty spikes at certain challenges or boss battles, but most are not hard.  The main punishments for failure are the long transition times and having to replay easy segments before getting back to the difficult parts.
I found that the puzzle mechanics weren't always as intuitive as I felt they should have been.  It can be hard to differentiate between glass and ice, for example, and you are sometimes left trying all your moves to see which one causes an interaction.
The character designs are great, for the most part.  Form usually follows function, so you can tell that some thought was put into them.  The dialogue did not strike me as particularly noteworthy, however.  Like most Rare games, it does not take itself very seriously and often breaks the fourth wall.
New moves are unlocked in each world, so if you want to collect everything, you will have to backtrack.  I know some people found this frustrating, but I was mentally prepared.  A certain move that you acquire near the end of the game--
--seems unnecessary, and harms the platforming gameplay.  Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie only allowed it in limited circumstances, which I think is the way to go (if it even has to be included at all).
The controls are tight enough when simply running around, but they become slippery when using any other form of locomotion (by design).  Combat is terrible (as it was in the other Banjo-Kazooie games), but the environments are so interesting and pretty that there is still excellent plaforming to be had.  Some areas reminded me a bit of Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts' hub world, which was the best part of that game.
I should mention that I encountered two different bugs where I was unable to control Yooka in some way.  Nothing a reload couldn't fix, though!
All in all, I'm satisfied with the quality of Playtonic's first game, and I'm looking forward to a sequel that will be able to build on its foundation.  Collectathons may have died 15 years ago, but the simple joy of obtaining an item is timeless.

Yooka-Laylee is a game desperately in need of a sequel. It is a solid 8/10 game; I enjoyed my time with it very much. However, my demand for its sequel comes not from my wanting to see more of the original, but rather from my desire to see its flaws fixed. To provide some context: Banjo-Tooie is my absolute favourite game of all time. I replay Tooie about once a year. To get a pseudo third entry to the Banjo-Kazooie series after 17 years felt like a godsend. For me to only award an 8 to a game that should have been absolutely cherished by me should be very telling of how absolutely grating the game can be at times, and why I can't in good faith hold it in the same regard as Kazooie and Tooie before it.
Yooka-Laylee comes very close to getting it right. Had the game had more professional supervision, more development time, and more areas tested before release, it might have been able to rival its spiritual predecessors. As it stands, Yooka-Laylee is simply 'good.' I'll first expand on what it does right, and explain why I still recommend the game to collectathon fans.
My first several hours with Yooka-Laylee were blissful. As I explored Shipwreck Creek and Tribalstack Tropics, the charm and worldbuiling that made the originals so great were still in tact. Quills were strategically leading me around the world, the NPCs I discovered were varied and engaging, Pagies were a blast to find, and I was absolutely struck by the aesthetic and music (I'd like to briefly point out here that Kirkhope totally delivers on this soundtrack. It does a great job of recapturing Rare's unique sound while simultaneously setting Yooka's world up as its own). The writing is also reminiscent of the studio's style and made me smirk and laugh many times, although the repetition of fourth-wall jokes did become a bit tiresome. The characters' grunts and groans that they make as they stumble through their dialogue is also a staple. While many find it grating, I would have been upset to see it go. However, I understand other peoples' complaints and would suggest a no-grunt option in the menu.
Reviewers who chastise the game for being similar to Banjo baffle me. What an ignorant and ridiculous claim. There hasn't been a main-series Banjo game in 17 years. The appeal of a collectathon is exploration. I replay Tooie every year; I have been CRAVING new levels to hunt in. Playtonic promised to fill the void left in my and many other fans' hearts by staying true to a genre that's been pretty bone-dry for almost two decades, and they should be rewarded for keeping their promises and sticking by their niche as opposed to generalizing their audience.
Yooka's level design is more similar to that of Tooie's than Kazooie's. Fans of the series will know that that means favouring larger, open worlds as opposed to more compact, filled areas. This pleases me greatly, but I understand why the difference in level design tends to split the fanbase. What Yooka-Laylee doesn't borrow from Tooie, though, is its distribution of Jiggies/Pagies. Tooie's open worlds were accompanied by 10 Jiggies that often required completing multi-layered tasks that felt rewarding. Yooka instead features 25 Pagies in each world, meaning that many are just strewn about the level, often just lying around or blocked off by a simple platforming challenge. It hardly rivals the scope of Tooie's quests, and when a Pagie
held captive by a larger-scale task, it feels worthless, considering you could have gotten 3x the result by simply jumping through some hoops or pounding some switches. I think trimming the fat would help the game greatly here.
Also sorely not returning from Tooie are Warp Pads. In Tooie, these were used as in-world fast-travel points. They helped cut down on backtracking without making movement feel overpowered. This sort of feature is all but nonexistent in Yooka-Laylee (perhaps most perplexingly in the hub world) making re-entering worlds to collect new Pagies a chore, especially when every world for some reason starts you on the other side of a huge gap.
The levels also, sadly, decline in quality, with my glowingly-reviewed Tribalstack Tropics being the best by a mile, while Worlds 4 and 5 were much more of a drain. For some reason, Tribalstack is the only world that is outdoors and brightly lit. The engine certainly looks best when the vibrant colours of the Rare characters and environments are allowed to shine brightly, but they shy away from that after World 1.
The game's infamous camera problems weren't the deal-breaker for me that everyone else seems to claim they are. It was flawed, sure, but it only reared its head a few times during my playthrough. It wasn't the worst part of the game.
Many of the quests that can be trimmed are quite a slog, too. Things like pushing a giant golf ball around in a physics engine or trying to get the flying controls to cooperate can be hair-pulling when you have to try at a challenge potentially dozens of times. So many challenges span several minutes too, so a reduction in both time and difficulty would have made a lot of the challenges more bearable. These challenges are not the game's worst, however...
Yooka-Laylee, in trying to keep tradition with Banjo-Kazooie's various minigames, includes two new characters, Kartos and Rextro, who visit the player in each world to invite them to minigame challenges. I have to say, I actually quite like both of these characters. Kartos and Rextro are both pretty funny in dialogue, and their designs are cool.
However, I've never wanted to end my miserable life more than when playing the awful, awful Kartos and Rextro games. Kartos is the lesser of two evils here, but both provided me with enough reason to quit the majority of their challenges. They're unfun. They're unpolished. They're unresponsive. They're unclear. They're aggravating. They're 1000% too long. They are flat out unacceptable and insulting. Kartos and Rextro's combined effort have guaranteed that I will NEVER 100% this game because I will NEVER again subject myself to the bogus challenges that they put forward. Every single game feels like an intern followed a basic Unity tutorial, made something that technically qualified as functional, and submitted it without changes. The removal of Kartos and Rextro would bump my review of Yooka-Laylee up to a 9. While mostly optional, a large appeal of collectathons is collecting
, so this game's ability to stifle my desire to 100% my first Banjo game in 17 years is mind-blowing. If you buy this game, avoid these two characters at all costs. It truly is a great game otherwise.
A large contributing factor to the levels' decline in quality is the game's tendency to reuse its characters. I'm not talking about Kartos and Rextro, but rather the hoards of non-main NPCs that will reappear in EVERY level. It really does become quite boring, and it makes the character parade at the end look pathetic.
Yooka-Laylee is a very good game that should have been a perfect one. Marred by poor design choices, a lack of testing, unfinished worlds, and half-hearted challenges, it fails to reach the heights that Kazooie and Tooie did 17+ years ago. I wasn't expecting it to trump my childhood nostalgia, but I had hoped for a better show than this -- even if it did, at first, really impress. Because of this, I would love to see a Tooka-Laylee. I want to see these flaws fixed. The perfect collectathon is in here. When it's good, it's fantastic. But there is simply too much clutter and too many cut corners. This game sparked a 17-year-old nostalgic fire in me, but then let it die. I want to see it recapture that for the whole game.
And despite my harsh critiques... I have faith. My true Banjo successor has to be out there, and the day that I play it will be magical.

This game is good, janky but good. I had a great time collecting and exploring! I loved all the music, levels, and abilities I learned. Expanding the worlds was a little weird at first but I got to where I looked forward to seeing how the levels looked. I LOVED the jingle that plays when you collect a pagie. I do wish the game had more worlds though. Expanding them is cool, but there is one major flaw with that. There are WAY too many things to collect in each world. Now, I don't say that as a bad thing, I encourage collecting tons of arbitrary items. However collecting the same pagies from the same characters over and over were disappointing, I looked forward to finding new stuff, not the exact same ones over and over. If they had a few more worlds and spread out the collectibles it would be a much smoother experience. Collecting the pagies and ghost writers from exploring the levels caught that Banjo-Kazooie vibe on the nose! I just like the movement and exploration so much that I was able to push back the negative aspects of the game. Now for the bad. The Rextro mini games are absolutely awful, and by far my least favorite  and I'd say probably the worst parts of the game. They stopped me from getting all of the pagies because of how unfun and long they were.If these were games were optional bonuses for finding Rextro's play coin I wouldn't have minded. The fact that you have to find a coin and then play each one at least twice to get all the pagies is frustrating. Kartos was not fun either. If the mine cart levels were in, say half of the levels, I would have liked them more. I wish the game had some more features as well. Pause music, enemy variety, and just the use of the unity engine. The thing with unity is that objects don't have a specific amount of weight, thus making everything seem like it was light as feather which does not feel good. It just makes it feel like nothing is really there, and other than Yooka & Laylee  nothing feels as if it's there. Also character variety is a big aspect that this game is missing. You'll run into the same characters over and over and over. That's fine in some levels but not the in every single level. They have some unique characters to each world but it's like a group of them. In Glitterglaze Glacier, the second world, there are nothing but snowmen, but they have different hats. Same in world three, four, and five. You'll meet a bunch of the same character model but in a different hat and they talk different. I know if they released this game in the fall or the winter quarters it would be so much better. The enemies are also a huge disappointment. I remember tons of unique enemies in all of the rare n64 games. In this game there's a world variant of the basic monster which is thematically nice, but then they copy and paste the same five enemy type in each level. Thus making some of the levels feel empty or barren. I wish they included some more background elements. Like fish in the water. bugs crawling around, etc. If they included some more of those the world would feel more alive instead of kind of boring. They need a lot more polish to make this a must buy, but if you love either Banjo-tooie or Donkey Kong 64 then I highly recommend it! If you're skeptical then maybe hold off until a sale. I know this review seems pretty negative, and I listed more complaints and improvements than praise but there is a truly fun game in here. I enjoyed the time I played, and I would think about it as I would about it after I got done playing it. It's a lot of fun! Hopefully if this game gets a sequel of some sort that it will be much bigger in scope. I know that the team at Playtonic are able to make a true follow up to Banjo-Kazooie.

Garfield Kart is a revolutionary racing experience. It encapsulates everything that modern racing games strive to be, and quite appropiately leaves its so called "peers" in the dust. No racing game that exists in the world today, or any that will ever exist, will be able to rival the unparalleled experience that is Garfield Kart. As Solomon is to mankind; so is Garfield Kart to the racing game genre.
From the moment I opened the game, I was overwhelmed by the vibrant array of graphical ingenuity. For a moment, I stared at my computer in awe. It was as if the screen had vanished, and I was instead looking through a window to another world. A better world. The world of Garfield Kart. The meticulous attention to detail impressed me beyond measure. Never before have my eyes beheld a game with graphics so incredible.
I was especially surprised by it, because I had put the graphics on their lowest possible setting. I didn't dare try to turn the settings up, lest I risk being struck blind by the glorious luster.
But don't be mistaken, Garfield Kart is not all flash and shine. The gameplay is flawless and smooth, just like the graphics. Few games have a HUD that is worth noting, but Garfield Kart's is innovative beyond measure. I lack the words to expound upon that any further, because the conceptual genius behind it has rendered me speechless.
And the controls! The controls function so naturally that it's as if you are physically driving the cart. This only enhances the experience further, adding to the illusion that you are the character behind the wheel.
To conclude, Garfield Kart is a transcendant approach to the racing game genre. In a single game, the devlopers have accomplished more than most game developers will accomplish in a lifetime. I feel so much gratitude and admiration to these brave folk, because they have shaken up the entire gaming industry in a way that no one could've possibly anticipated.
And so, finally, to answer the question that was originally posed.
Yes. I heartily recommend Garfield Kart.

I was really hyped for this game when it was announced, and truthfully I can't really say it was worth the wait. Dream Daddy is by no means a bad game, just a little disappointing. Personally it feels a little awkward to get to know someone for a few days and then enter a "relationship" with them. It's a lot more understandable for the character Craig since the Player Character and him have history together, but from what I can tell everyone else is someone you're meeting for the first time. As much as I wished that's how it worked, I really don't think it works like that in real life. There we're also a few bugs that kind of... bugged me. Hugo's/Mat's glasses popped in and out whenever they felt like it, a few characters would remain on screen after leaving, and the "Approval Hearts" would sometimes pop up away from the character. But as I said this is by no means a bad game, the game itself is really cute and it was a blast getting to know all of these characters. The dialogue was a real joy to read through and it was really fun making a "Dadsona". The sound and music design were pretty good and nothing really sounded too out of place. The approval/disapproval system was well done as well, you could easily the effects of your decisions on the main Daddy characters, which will help you achieve the best rating possible and thus the best ending possible for each character, it eliminates the need to continuously replay the same character over and over again to see if the choices you made were the "right" ones, which is one of my major gripes about some dating-sims. If you made the "wrong" choice, you can load up the previous auto save before you made the choice if you so desire. Finally, the puns. Oh my, the amount of dad-puns. They're just so bad, and I know they're bad but I can't help but giggle whenever one appears, they have that odd charm to them where you know their bad, they are bad, but they're so bad they're actually good. Anyways the overall experience was enjoyable, just a little light on content as some games in this genre can have character routes potentially lasting up to a few weeks.
TL;DR-ish VERSION
Pros:
-Really cute and hilarious dialogue
-Good "approval/disapproval" system, you could easily tell whether you did something a character disliked/liked/really liked
-A good father-daughter simulator, can either be an amazing or okay dad depending on your choices
-THE CREATORS WEREN'T KIDDING WITH THE DAD PUNS THERE WERE SO MANY OH MY
Cons:
-Story could've possibly been longer, every character only has a "3-day" route, doesn't really feel like a dating-sim for certain "dates" or the majority of bonding is stated instead of shown
-Somewhat frustrating/uninteresting mini-games
-A few bugs that BUGGED me, will probably be fixed the future so not a big deal (Hugo's/Mat's glasses kept popping up then disappearing, and certain characters remained on screen even after they left)
Rating: 7.5/10

Well, I got everything, and every achivewment, and now I can make this Review.  So, let's run it down!
First off, Yooka-Layee was a fun, and very inviting experience to say the least. The game had awesome music and brought me a lot of job playing. I had those classic vibes the whole way here, and will look forward to the sequel they winked at the whole game. Now....
PROS
-Collectables!  This really nailed the classic feeling of eyes on the details, and checking all surroundings. Had fun getting all the collebtables and it was worth it!
-Yooka-Layee make a a fun duo, and I got a good amount of laughs between the dialogues from the many chraracters. Layee is the star in my book.
-Sound is fun, and nothing wrong with it. Well timed, and no issues there.
-Music is outstanding! Grant is a legend in the work, and he still had that magic!
-Controls work well enough
-Lighting. Well lit in the game, the moods were set well for the music pieces.
CONS
-Camera. Yeah, let's talk about this. This camera needs a little more tweaking. At times, it would throw me a loop and give me issues. While not game breaking, it needs fixing.
-Lack of map.  This was an issue I felt needed to be addressed at times. I put a  good amount of time into finding everything, but what would of make it nice would of be a minimap to help aid me on getting around and finding things. World 4 was a good example to why I could of used one.
Overall, it's not a perfect game, but it's sharp and polished very nicely. I can't wait for Yooka-Layee 2, and HIGHLY RECOMMEND this to play!

Yooka Laylee is a 3D platformer that's in the same vein as Banjo Kazooie, Conker's Bad Fur Day, Super Mario 64, Gex etc. This review isn't going to be as long as my normal reviews though. If you loved playing those types of games, then you should definitely add this one to your collection.  I read critic reviews bashing the game for various reasons but what I think they fail to realize that this game is made for a specific niche of gamers. Gamers who already know what it means to play around in the old 3D Platformer genre and know what controls and game mechanics to expect, both the good and the bad. I grew up with a Nintendo 64 and played Banjo Kazooie again just last year and I can say that Yooka Laylee, though not as good as Banjo Kazooie (that game was lightning in a bottle anyway), is still a good 3D platformer.
If you're dying to play this immediately then buy it at full price. I can't guarantee that you won't be dissapointed but I can only draw from my own experience.  Otherwise wait a few months for a sale if you're on the fence about it.

This game feels like it wants to give you a lesson on the reality of war, like the developers were sick of the way other ''war games'' romanticise honour and battle, and how easy killing is - and yet you kill 40 people out of a helicopter, or jump off of extremely high buildings and survive, get set on fire numerous times, mow through enemies like they're grass.  This just gives you that feeling of "Nothing can really happen to you", which makes you stop caring. Now, this would be fine, other video games are like this too, but there is one difference: the characters.
I couldn't care about any of them because they seemed to have the personalities of cardboard cut-outs, there is nearly no work at all put into establishing characters, and here lies my problem with the game. None of the characters are humanized, we don't care about them, so when the game shows us terrible things happening to them, trying to make us sympathize with them, it just doesn't work. With a set of outstanding characters, this could have been a fantastic game, but sadly, it feels like the writers were so caught up in their ideas for the plot, they forgot to make the characters likeable and/or memorable - a big problem for a game which is supposed to be driven by its characters.

When I first got this game, I was hoping so much, that it would be pretty much just like Virtual Pool 3, but with better graphics. Essentially, that's pretty much what I got! At first, I wasn't sure if I liked the "feel" of it as much, but once I'd played a good few games, I find I do like it a lot! The only bad things I have to say about it (and it's not even that bad) is that there is a slight difference in the movement of the cue stick between single player, and multiplayer. I'm not sure if it's just my pc or not, but for me, single player feels very 1:1 in terms of how much I expect the cue stick to move in relation to how much (and quickly) I move the mouse. In multiplayer for me, it feels like there is a very very slight delay between me moving the mouse, and it moving the cue. When I say very very slight, I really mean it. It's easily the kind of thing you can get used to, and after playing several games, I barely even notice it myself, unless I actually jump from playing single player, straight in to an online game.
The only other disappointing thing, is that it doesn't have Snooker. If it did, this would be the penultimate pool game! Certainly not a deal breaker though! If you like pool games, or are a fan of the Virtual Pool series, you won't regret purchasing this at all. I've played many many games online with a friend of mine (usually several matches a day!) and we both get great enjoyment from doing so! As you can see from my playtime, I've already spent a significant amount of time playing this, and it's only going to grow further!
Trick shots are hard to master, but once you get your head around how to do jump shots and curve shots, whole new ways of playing become apparent, and you truly start to feel like a master!
The single player is challenging and fun, and having mini goals in each round keeps you coming back for more, since usually completing those goals, leads to unlocking new locations, balls, decals and cues.
At it's current price of $1.49, you'd be crazy not to grab a copy! I think I payed $3 or $5 for it at the time of purchase, but I would say that even if it was $10-$15, it's still worth every cent!

Jedi Academy, while not quite as good as its predecessor Jedi Outcast in my opinion, is a fantastic game. The lightsaber combat and gun-play is excellent just like Outcast, and there are a lot more lightsaber duels with dark jedi. You won't find better lightsaber duels in any Star Wars games outside Outcast and Academy. The biggest change Jedi Academy brings to the series is player choice. You start the game with character creation, which is definitely shallow by today's standards, but is adequate for an action adventure game in my opinion. You can choose your race, gender, clothing, and lightsaber. Continuing the trend, there are three chapters in the game and in each chapter you can play the selection of missions in the order you choose. Before each mission you can choose a loadout of weapons (which granted you will hardly use because lightsabers), and a new force power. The game also has two alternate endings based on whether you choose the light or the dark side. Most people will probably prefer this game to Jedi Outcast because of these factors, personally I prefer Outcast because of its more linear approach, but both games are among the best Star Wars games in existence.

Max Payne is your everyday New York cop. That is until one day, his loving wife and newborn daughter are murdered by three drug addicts. The drug addicts were using the "V" drug, a hostile and dangerous drug, which is getting bigger and bigger in New York City. After the dead of his wife and daughter, Max becomes an undercover DEA agent, working on the "V" drug case. Three years later, the city of New York finds itself in the biggest snow storm in history, and the "V" drug rempant the city. Max gets a tip from another DEA agent. An old friend of Max, knows something about this "V" drug. Finally meeting each other, his old friend Alex Balder is shot right before Max's eyes. Now, Max is framed for the murder of his friend, and is more than determined to break the "V" case.
Max Payne is known for it's great bullet time, and its smooth third person action gameplay. The basic gameplay is actually pretty easy to master. There are three parts in the game, every part has around seven to nine chapters. In every high detailed chapter you mostly walk through the chapter, killing every enemy in your path. Even though this sounds easy, Max Payne is a fairly difficult game. Which will take the average gamer around 9 hours to complete the main story. Max Payne is iconic for it's amazing bullet time, your stamina meter slowly fills up, which will allow you to dive or run in slow motion, easily picking off enemies.
The first Max Payne in this amazing trilogy is a joy to play. Some people might back away from it because of its outdated graphics. The amazing and complicated story is a very fun ride, while the great gameplay really takes the cake. For any fans of great third person gameplay with an amazing story, here you have a great game for your collection.

Max Payne really is quite the video game. It is one of those video games that makes us question what a video game truly is. Almost all the cutscenes are done in a graphic novel style literally going from one page to the next after the charecters have spoken. It is very interesting and unique to the point where I wanted to play just to get to the next scene sort of like how I would want to play MGS games just to get to the next scene. However unlike MGS the gameplay is extremely unique. It is a third person shooter that places Max in the middle of the screen with a crosshair in the very center of the screen. Most people who play this game rave about how fun it is to use the bullet time effect to take out enemies. I agree that it is extremely fun and sometimes difficult to do. You use quick saves in the game which you NEED TO USE unless you are a god at the game then you will not be getting through that many levels without dying. Ofcourse there is an autosave feature but it is pathetic how often it is used. With quicksaves you will find yourself saving before a fight then going into the fight and most likely dying in which you will rethink everything like where you aimed, how you entered the area or what gun you used.
Let me just put it this way. I was up late exausted playing this game just desperatley wanting to get to the next scene.
I think the only bad things about the game (gameplay wise) really are the underpowered weapons or not knowing where to go or what to do at times.
Now the bad things about the game in general that are not really related to the gameplay is how Max just all of a sudden becomes a mass murderer after his family is killed. Max never talks about how hard it is to shoot and kill people just to get to the person responsible for the murder. There is also quite a lot of blood and very sexual things in the game but I think that is to be expected when the game is advertised as a Noir story.
Overall this game is fantastic and if you are not bothered by anything that I have mentioned in the last two paragraphs you are crazy not to be playing this game as soon as humanly possible (Unless you are one of those unfortunate enough to have a computer that will not start this game up due to the direct X 8 requirment)

One of my favorite games of all time. Max Payne is a shooter way ahead of it's time that takes you through a long, dark, well written adventure.
Each level is long with lot's of work and detail put into it. You have a slow-motion meter and you can watch each bullet hit its target in your firefights and every item in this game reacts differently to bullets and shotgun shells(Televison sets explode with electricity, walls spark and spit out debris, metal clunks and sparks, fire hyrdrants emit foam and the list goes on!) making for some EXTREMELY satisfying gunplay.
Plenty of humor and detail thrown into the game, if you wait before confronting certain enemies, they'll have different (and oftentimes, hilarious) scripted conversations that are worth listening to. As the sh** hits the fan later on in the game, the enemies and levels get crazier and more menacing all the way to the final level taking place in the heavily guarded and delightfully long and huge(very funny) Aesir Corporation building.

This was a good game.  In terms of nostalgia, it hit a bullseye.  In terms of gameplay, it was mostly good but needed a bit of work.  Due to the fact that I don't want to spoil anything, I'm not going to get into any major details.  Instead I'll just give a few pros and cons and something that doesn't fit into either category.
Pros:
-Beautiful world design.  The scenery is amazing, the worlds are expansive but just the right size so exploration doesn't feel tedious.
-Amazing soundtrack.  The legendary composers from the Banjo games have created yet another wonderful soundtrack.
-Dialogue.  The conversations in the game were witty and extremely reminiscent of the Banjo games.  Considering the fact that those games greatly influenced my sense of humor, I'm a huge fan of the dialogue in this game.
-Controls.  The controls feel very intuitive and are tight enough that I can do the platforming without getting frustrated.  The only downside is the transformations (mentioned later).
Cons:
-Rextro's arcade machines.  Even if you beat the high score the 1st time, you still had to play the machine a 2nd time to get a pagie for beating the high score.  By far the worst part of the game in my opinion.
-Enemy diversity.  There's almost none.  I'm not sure if it was just due to time or financial constraints, but apart from bosses, the enemies in each world are just reskins of hub world enemies.
-Transformation controls.  The snowplow was a pain to manuever, the helicopter felt sluggish, and the plant had a slight movement delay after jumping which really threw me off.
-The puzzles.  For the most part, the puzzles were decent, but rather simple.  They gave you plenty of room for error, which I disliked because I like the exhilaration that comes from not knowing if you'll beat the clock.
Another "issue" I'd like to address is the camera.  I've read reviews that the camera controlled poorly, but I haven't run into any major issues with it apart from when it switches from free camera controls to forced perspective, but if you know where it switches it's easy to transition.  Little things like the camera getting stuck on geometry or shaking while in enclosed areas is pretty much par for the course in games with a 3rd person perspective.  To me, the camera did not take away from the gameplay at all.
Overall, the game is pretty average.  Apart from the Rextro games (mostly just world 5's because I kept screwing up and it was an autos roller), I enjoyed the game the whole time I was playing it.  Looking back, I see now that it had many flaws, but while I was playing I didn't even notice.  I'd definitely recommend playing this if you like the collectathon genre of games, but don't expect it to be another Banjo game.

Garfield Kart has cute cartoon graphics, Good sound samples and music that fits the theme.  The game might be a generic arcade kart racer, but it is true to the Garfield theme with all the main characters from the Garfield cartoon and lots of Lasagne thrown in.  The animation is smooth and the controls are smooth.  Mouse cursor is used for menu navigation and either keyboard controls or X-Box 360 controller can be used for game input.  There are several tracks and the player can choose either Garfield or Jon to race initially.
Garfield Kart is fun to play and is a family friendly game which is aimed at younger audience but will appeal to players of all ages depending on their taste.  A great addition to any steam user's library of games that can be played when there is not enough time to play more time consuming titles.  A typical race should take only about ten to fifteen minutes.
There is a tutorial which automatically runs when a new character is created, and it will only allow you to exit once you show that you have mastered the controls and game mechanics.
All in all a competent arcade Kart racer well worth getting especially if you like the Garfield franchise or are looking for something with a different theme to Sonic or Mario.  Looking elsewhere I can solidly recommend F1 Stars Racing.

It is an excellent old game and has aged very well. Released in 2003 but the modding community is still very active. Even though the single player game is short, it is very enjoyable to play with it's fun combat and different level designs. It gets harder into the game as you fight lightsaber users.
Once you have complete the single player (or you do not have to), download MovieBattles 2. It is what the game now is all about as the vanilla multiplayer is dead.
MovieBattles 2 is loads better with better modded maps throughout the StarWars saga. Now with the enhanced combat system is even more enjoyable to play for both shooting and lightsaber combats. More characters to play as from clone troopers, Darth Maul, wookies and even more in multiplayer deathmatch games. Do you like fighting others with lightsabers? Join in a duel server and challenge other jedis or siths in a lightsaber duel and beat each other over countless of hours!
Overall this game is fantastic to play only with MovieBattles 2 as the vanilla game has aged and is dead. I really recommend this game to either StarWars fan or a non fan after a huge disappointment over the release of Battlefront game. Jedi Academy is the real and the best StarWars game out there.

I've been a fan of the Grumps for about two years now, and it's exciting to see that they/their friends have made a game.
That being said, this game is far from perfect.
First off, the voice acting. It's not bad, since dating sims tend to not have a heavy focus on spoken dialogue, but I went in expecting a bit more than grunts and the occasional 'Bro'. I followed this game on Twitter, and voice actor Matt Mercer displayed interest in the game. One of the creators (Vernon Shaw, specifically) said that he could be a DLC dad. While this isn't that much of an issue, if the DLC claim is legitimate, I am not willing to spend any amount of money just to hear the voice of Jesse McCree do dad grunts.
Second off, walls of text and minor grammar/punctuation errors. I understand that dating sims need enough background so the player can fully understand what they're doing, but there is a difference between providing background in readable chunks and dialogue and providing background in paragraph after paragraph. HuniePop and Hatoful Boyfriend did this well; it chunked what plot it had into readable boxes with an appropriate amount of text. Dream Daddy's dialogue formatting is a wall of text that can be difficult to read. While minor grammar and punctuation errors are to be expected, the frequency in which they show up is irritating and distracted me from what I was doing.
Third off, the character creator was a bit underwhelming compared to the rest of the art in the game. That didn't really impact anything, just figured I should point it out. Very nice that they included a transgender option, though.
Finally, it takes a decent length of time to get into the game's plot. For example, about thirty minutes in, I had hardly gotten to the barbecue scene where you can start dating people. Introductions to the characters and their quirks are important, but it should happen gradually rather than all at once in a too-convenient location.
Now, the positives.
Characters are lively, exaggerated, but in a good way that makes the player giggle at their chosen dad's sense of humor. The kids, from what I have seen so far, are also great and I very much enjoy seeing them onscreen with their eye-rolling and 'Ugh,
's.
Dialogue, while not brilliant or particularly astounding, alternates between funny and heartfelt and it works well. Amanda's conversations with the player and interactions with other characters stand out.
The character design is well-done; again, it makes the characters come alive despite limited facial expressions. HuniePop had a bad case of same-face and basic emotions* (for an example, think Fire Emblem Awakening's support Avatars and their decent but lacking emotions), while Dream Daddy's characters are more unique and more expressive (think Kid Icarus Uprising's conversations between Pit and Palutena on the bottom screen and their expressions).
The story/plot itself is a bit cliche, but it's a dating game. I'm not expecting a sweeping tale of romance and chivalry, here. I will say, though, that the dates (speaking only from the Robert route) tend to be better than the general storyline.
Additionally, a statement for all those looking for sexually pleasurable material in this game: you may find it in another game, but you will not find it in this game. This is not HuniePop, you will not receive raunchy pictures, see dirty scenes, or do anything that's more than implied to be sexy.
All in all, Dream Daddy is decent. The delays built hype that underwhelmed me, but it's not terrible. Paying fifteen dollars for it isn't really all that worth it. It's a good Summer Sale/Sale game that the player can enjoy despite some of the problems. 7/10, would play again.
*And yes, I am aware HuniePop is not supposed to be a game where you care about who you're getting with. It was the best example for me to use because 1) I have 19 hours logged in it and 2) Using Hatoful Boyfriend's pigeon stock photos as an example of a lack of emotion shown in a character's face felt cheap.

This game gets so much right about what makes a Hitman game great and then proceeds to crap all over it. I've been a fan of Hitman since the very first game and played (and purchased on different platforms) more hours of Blood Money than I could even guess. I was really hoping that this game would be a return to form for the franchise, and from some of the things I've seen and done in the game I honestly believe that it could have been.
I don't absolutely hate the episodic release, I wish it would have been a full form Hitman game but this gives me some incentive to really flesh out and explore each level. Honestly there seems to be a lot to do in the main Paris mission that we have available, and that really bodes well for each subsequent level we get next.
Now on to why I wouldn't recommend this game in it's current form. I've got a pretty beefy PC rig that should be absolutely able to run this game at 60fps on at least high settings. The entire first "tutorial" mission was initially unplayable due to what seemed to be a problem with shadow mapping, causing the screen to be almost completely blacked out by blown out shadows. After resetting the game multiple times it finally randomly decided to start working. After getting through the tutorial stage I was able to get into the real meat of the game in the Paris level. This time a lighting issue (that I still haven't been able to fix, regardless of what settings are changed) made the game look like absolute garbage with flickering lights and overblown shadows. As long as I wasn't in an exterior environment it seemed to function fine.
Finally to put a stellar cherry on top of this turd sunday I was just about to complete my first Silent Assassin run of the Paris mission when I get this text popup onscreen stating that I was disconnected from the server. In some bizarre choice of DRM the game needs to be online, I assume for the leaderboard to function correctly. One would think that the best option in that situation would be for your game to go into "offline" mode, nope it just kicks you back to the main menu. I will add that the game has an offline mode that I will now be utilizing.
There is great potential here, and honestly it seems like there's many things that IO Interactive could fix. I think this speaks to a larger issue with games in the last five to ten years, the mentality that "hey we could just patch it" if things aren't working. I understand the idea behind releasing patches for obscure bugs/glitches that weren't picked up during testing, but for the game to be nearly unplayable at times is (to me) unnacceptable. For many developers patching seems to have become a crutch. In short, I would wait until a few episodes have been released along with (hopefully) a few patches as well. If you're a fan of Hitman I know you'll recognize the potential this game has, but I still couldn't recommend it as it currently stands. I give it 3 crow suits out of 600 rubber duckies (review scores are pointless).

I was quite disappointed with this game. I was expecting it to be more or less like Blood Money, but with the Absolution style game mechancis and graphics. However, in it's current state, there are a lot of problems and I wouldn't recommend buying it at all.
Cons(-):
- Always Online
- If your machine was just good enough that you could run Absolution on Ultra high settings, you can run this with everything on minimum and it will still lag
- The "Modular" release format leaves this game with a serious lack of content at the time of release; this is pretty much the same thing that happened with 'Elite Dangerous' (i.e. it was released to meet a deadline, when it was obviously not developed enough to be ready for release)
- It feels like the game was based off of the blood money rather than absolution as it's backbone; clues to be found in some glitches from blood money like how sometimes dragging a body would not work
- Running the same mission over and over in different ways is very repetitive; at the moment, there is no variety in missions (there are literally just the tutorials, and one single map! Is this a joke?). Blood money had a lot more content than this. So did all the other hitman games. I would rather play the old ones than this.
Pros(+):
- Honestly, I have no pros to post. As a huge fan of the hitman series up until this point, I am seriously disappointed.
Conclusion:
If you have a machine that can run this on max settings, and you want a good game at similar price point, get 'The Division' instead. Unless they release like 10 more levels in the upcoming patches, this is not worth it at all.
EDIT: Updating my review for the release of the Sapienza portion of the game. IMO if they genuinely only plan to release one more map after this, then that's an absolutely disgusting lack of content. Having been a fan of all previous hitman games, this one is just bad.
However performance-wise, the game performs better on this level than on Paris for some reason. Playable FPS is possible on semi-decent machines if you overclock the GPU (still, you shouldn't have to) but it's still doesn't have the look or feel of absolution. Yes, they spent lots of time making the maps big. But 3 maps does not a good game make and playing the same map over and over in 100 different fashions is just not good. Waiting for the 3rd release, but after the first elusive target and Sapienza, I would still DEFINITELY not recommend this game to anyone under any cirucumstance.

Secondly it is your choice if you want to wait until the game is complete and the full release is out at end of this year but if you want to play now you can do it. The choice is yours.
2. You have to be online. Firstly you not have to. You can play off line. Yes for the full experience you have to play online. This is clearly a copyright protection. An off line single player game 100 times more likely being stolen than an online multiplayer game. Why, because if you go online the server won't let you use a pirate copy. If you think it is not your problem thank again. Do you think that anyone will invest millions in a game which going to be stolen on the first day after the release. I also believe that most of the gamers on Steam always online anyway.
3. Hardware demands. Yes new AAA titles can be demanding. In my case I play 1080p ultra on a three years old radeon 7950 graphics card and I get 30-35 fps. It is not 60, but playable especially because this is not a fast paced game.
Non of these points are about the actual game play. Which is really good. Most of the negative reviews are even admitting this.
This is a great game. If you don't my the episodic release buy it now if not wait for until fully released.
