I'm very much in two minds about Dream Daddy.
On the one hand, the story is excellent, even though I was worried about the minigames, they didn't turn out too bad, and the feels were very real.
On the other hand, I feel the game is more of a visual novel with dating elements, rather than an actual dating simulator. Not to say that's a bad thing.
As a visual novel, the game is excellent. The writing is full of feeling and is humorous. The most important character (your daughter) is well developed, and I grew quite attached to the daddies as well. And even if it isn't necessarily the truth, it at least feels like your choices have different consequences. I wholly recommend this game as a visual novel.
As a dating simulator, the game was subpar at best. Granted, at time of writing, I've only completed the Brian dates, and made it partially through Robert's. If the other daddies make me change my mind, I will take this review down. But I sincerely doubt that. See, there is a maximum of 3 dates per daddy. Even with the best storytelling in the world, I sincerely doubt anyone could write a compelling romantic narrative in only 3 parts. And while the story with Brian was great, it was lacking. I was left wanting so much more.
So if you're like me and waiting for a good mainsteam gay dating simulator, then you're not in luck. Dream Daddy, despite being an excellent game, is not that dating simulator you're looking for. But, if you're looking for a compelling narrative about a single dad and his daughter, and there are dating elements, then I would heatily recommend the game.
TL;DR: Dream Daddy: A Dad Dating Simulator is bad. Dream Daddy: A Dad Simulator is good.

I can't recommend this game, I simply can't. I tried very hard to enjoy it and love it, but the further I got into the game, the harder it became to play.
- The art style clash
The art for the datable dads, the background, and the player's dad are all VASTLY different, and it's noticable most when actually playing the game. The dads you can date are hyper realistic and detailed, where the backgrounds are bland, flat, too bright and unrealistic. The player dad is something you'd expect to see as a forum avatar. My dad's hair wasn't even colored in all the way, which left a very ugly white outline between the line and the color.
- "Voice acting?"
The game is described as being voiced, which to me means I won't have to sit through walls of text with nothing but music to listen to. Unfortunately, this game isn't voiced, it's grunted, with every character having about a dozen or so grunts, groans, moans, and sighs that consist of their "voices." Most of the time you'll get a dad saying "Dude" when the text reads anything but that. It clashes with the story, and it really shouldn't have been there in the first place. Either fully voice act the game as I'm sure we expected, or don't claim it to be voice acted and have there be no grunting. The middle ground we got was lack luster at best.
- Boring
The story is hardly compelling at all. There are moments of charm, like the interactions you have with your daughter, but otherwise you're stuck with bland text that never ends. Even character dialogue switches from "nervous dad trying to fit in" to "alien who is trying to fit in." Through the two hours I put into the game, it took about five or six different sessions because I just couldn't justify sitting down to listen to grown men (and my daughter) grunt while being harassed by the never ending text.
- Bethesda choices
When you're prompted with a choice (however rare it is), they all feel like they'll lead to the same end most of the time. It's like the classic example from Fallout 4. No (Yes), Sarcastic (Yes), Hesitant (Yes), Yes (Yes). Very rarely did I think my choices matter, and I was often rewarded with arbitrary clouds of hearts or blackness (I suppose that's my favor with that person when dating them, but why does my daughter do the same thing?).  Even though it's a story-based game, I would have liked some sort of explanation of what was going on, rather than fumbling to try and find a meaning.
- Pointless "dates"
I went for "dates" with Robert to only find that he ignored me for the entire day, then I was rewarded with points, skills, and a score? I didn't do anything with him, and I somehow got a C rank? If this is supposed to be a joke, they should try a little harder, because with all the flourish and offical looks of it, it seemed like it was supposed to be how I actually progressed in the game.
EDIT: In the comments I have been made aware that this is the natural function of the game, but I believe it still echoes my earlier point of "some sort of explanation of what was going on, rather than fumbling to try and find a meaning."
- Cost
This game was fifteen dollars, and I can't for the life of me see why. Especially when the promised features are more like flops, I couldn't justify paying ten dollars for the game, much less the asking price of fifteen. At seven I would perhaps consider it, but it's just unrealistic as it stands.
I have put in my request for a refund and I honestly couldn't recommend this game to anyone, especially with the current market of competitors.

First off, I'd like to say that I won't talk about graphics and game physics, because obiviously they're pretty bad compared to games nowdays, I'll review this game as if I played it back then when it came out(Which unfortunately, I didn't).
Pros:
+Excellent level design - there's no set objective you need to follow, no markers or pointers that lead you exactly to where you need to go, you gotta figure out all of that on your own with hints that the level designers put it in to give you some kind of direction. I often find myself in a serious need for painkillers(the health pickups), and it feels so good to find some in a secret place. You don't really see these kind of games anymore.
+High quality voice acting(especially the narration and cutscenes, which I'll talk about later) - nothing much to say here, just that the first time I heard the narration, it was so good that I thought it was recoreded about  2-3 years ago.
+The gameplay - I've never played the game before untill now, so I didn't know what to excpect from a game this old, and I have to say that I genuinely enjoy the gameplay. Of course, the animations are a bit clanky, but it still feels good, the weapon variety, the shooting, the bullet time, everything.
+The comic book-ish cutscenes - I really love the way the story is told, instead of  advanced animations with crazy effects, each cutscene is a comic book "page", beautifully drawn and narrated.
+The story - I haven't finished the game yet(I don't think I'm even close, only 5 hours in), but so far the story is quite good, right at the beginning the game throws at you some powerful and sad scenes. My expectations are high, I'll update this section when I finish the game.
Cons:
-Illogical enemy spawnings - the enemy spawnings are pretty weird in the game, most of them are activated by you reaching a certain point, but sometimes after you clear an area, and later need to backtrack, enemies spawn from no-where(of course not in front of your eyes), no doors openings or anything.
-Bugged sounds, but it can be fixed anyway.
Overall, I can easily recommend this game to anyone, don't be afraid of the old age, it plays perfectly fine, and anyone can really enjoy it.

Don't let the inital lack of sound fool you (Google the sound patch for it and it'll all be fine), this game is timeless. Having just recently started getting into video game franchises, I decided to give Max Payne a try (it was bundled with Max Payne 2 for only a few bucks!).

Due to my being accustomed to third person shooters like Uncharted, it was definitely jarring going into the game and realising there's no cover and the enemies have no propensity for self-preservation. And Max is
easy to kill (meaning in the gameplay, not in the storyline). This made things extremely interesting and fast paced. The AI could be dumb a lot, but I mean AI wasn't what it was now. Nevertheless, these elements made for very actiony gameplay. Although the game is set in the 90s, the atmosphere, the vehicles and the dress of some of the characters made it all seem like a proper film noir. The storyline is intricate and very entertaining and the graphic novel scenes are very well-voiced (for the most part).
And of course, I can't do this without mentioning bullet time. Springing forward or sideways in slow motion to take on your enemies is
satisfying. Best of all, the bullets are all rendered, even shot from your shotgun, meaning it's not just hitscan and you can see the bullets  land. It's really cool.
All in all, the game is cheap and very much worth it, even after all these years.

I found Call of Duty Black Ops II to be my favorite in the series to date. The single player campaign is okay but has what you'd expect from a normal Call of Duty campaign on rails, cut scenes, etc. I found multiplayer to be fun and enjoyalbe despite very few changes from previous Call of Duty's multiplayer modes. The "Pick 10" system is my favorite addition. Instead of requiring the player to have a grenade for instance they can remove it and spend a point on another category. Wild cards also add additional customization to the multiplayer loadout by allowing the player to have two primary weapons or two perks in the same category. Of course the players are required to sacrifice something else in return to use the wildcards so it maintains balance. On the zombies side of things I found the zombies to be just as fun as the multiplayer. Each of the base maps were very well made for long rounds of survival with each map requiring different strategies. The DLC maps are definitely worth a look at too. They add a story to these maps and make new challenges for the players. For instance the DLC map "Die Rise" has perks randomly dispersed among elevators throughout the map instead of having them in stationary places. Overall if you are buying this for multiplayer, zombies, or both it is definitely worth it. If you are buying this for the single player campaign only, I would find a better way to spend your way. But for those players who want multiplayer and zombies, this game gives you a good value for your money!

Here's a review for Quarter Life 5. To make the mix:
1) Grind the oats in a food processor until they're chopped fine, but not a powder.
2) Put the flour, oats, and all other dry ingredients into a mixer with a paddle. Mix on slow speed, and drizzle the vegetable oil into the bowl slowly while the mixer is running.
3) Store in an airtight container for up to two weeks at room temperature, or indefinitely in the refrigerator or freezer.
To make pancakes:
1) Whisk together 1 cup of mix, 1 cup of buttermilk (a combination of half plain yogurt and half milk also will do), and 1 large egg. Don't worry if it seems thin at first: the oats will soak up the milk, and the mix will thicken a bit as it stands. Let the batter stand for at least 20 minutes before cooking.
2) Heat a lightly greased griddle to 350°F (or medium to medium-hot will do).
3) Drop the batter onto it in 1/4-cupfuls to make a 4" diameter pancake.
4) When the edges look dry and bubbles come to the surface without breaking (after about 2 minutes, if your griddle is the correct temperature), turn the pancake over to finish cooking on the second side, which will take about 2 minutes.
5) Serve pancakes immediately, or stack and hold in a warm oven.
Cooking Note:
If you don't have buttermilk in the house, try the yogurt and milk combination first; if you happen to have buttermilk powder, try this: In place of the buttermilk, add 1/4 cup buttermilk powder to 1 cup of dry mix, then stir in 1 cup water and 1 large egg. The results won't be as magnificent as using liquid buttermilk, but you'll still have very tasty pancakes.
Variation:
Add 1 tablespoon orange juice to the dry mix along with the buttermilk. We've found that the acidity and sweetness of the orange juice helps mellow the tannic taste some people perceive in whole wheat flour; while the pancakes won't have any orange flavor, they may taste slightly milder to you, if you're not a fan of whole wheat flour (but still want to get more whole grains into your diet).

Super Meat Boy is a crazy jump & run game, where you can slide, jump and die a lot! The story is crazy but told in a nice way. The best thing is: the levels are made in a really smooth way. If you can figure out the special way to beat it, you "fly" through it and think: WTF? That is POSSIBLE? o.O
You feel the game is made for consoles, but that's not too distracting, you can play it very well with the keyboard. The menus are a little bit fiddly.
This game is a must have for everyone.

Fiendishly difficult for all the right reasons, Super Meat Boy offers a genuine challenge without ever feeling unfair. The controls are solid, the levels are varied and interesting, and the near-instant respawns result in a fluid gameplay experience despite countless inevitable deaths.

All the game icons are presented simultaneously. That's a bad design. They should be rendered visible gradually in a step-by-step manner. When introduced, they should blink to draw the player's attention to it.

Was immensely put off by stuttering of *prerendered cutscenes* before even beginning.
Video footage was choppy and sporadic. Not renders and 3D models--prerendered video. That is immensely disconcerting, especially considering I'm well above recommended specs with a 1070gtx. (Seems to be happening to EVERY 1070 user as well.) Whatever though, I'd excuse that if the game itself ran fine.
However, something as simple as making any mundane graphics changes requires restarting the game. Even something as making a small quality change. That's pretty inexcusable if there's no pre-launcher to set your graphics settings.
If you play in windowed mode and try to move your window around, but instead rescale it, instead of auto-adjusting your aspect ratio, it stretches the screen--so you can wind up with squashed or stretched imagery.
These are inexcusably poor optimizations before even starting the game. Even the worst ports I've played have avoided doing this. They're almost enough to make me drop the game before even starting it.
Went to play it anyway, muscling through to force the game to display correctly.
The game itself meanwhile has a very VERY poor tutorial system that freezes the game to drop pop-ups on you whenever you so much as mouse over a UI element you haven't touched yet. The first few moments of the campaign involve flying for a while to reach a planet--you could easily just have passive popups come up to explain things WHILE traveling so the player doesn't waste time. Or, better yet, just use tooltips that appear to the side instead of entire dialogs that freeze all interaction until they're read.
It's a bit contradictory that people say the game doesn't 'hold your hand' despite having an obnoxious tutorial system like that.
Not to mention the UI is incredibly gaudy and is overall a poor user experience. Some of the interfaces don't have a close button--you're expected to click escape instead SOMETIMES. Other times there actually is a button to close the interface. So you don't know if you need to look for a button to close a dialog or hit a key instead, which sometimes can result in you doing something you don't want, such as hiring or firing an officer. (And actions like these often don't have a confirmation dialog as a failsafe.)
All these little issues added up and prevented me from wanting to even attempt to enjoy the game itself. The diehard fanboyism that acknowledges these issues but opts to excuse them is also a major turnoff.
I don't think a lot of diehard fans of this game or the devs understand just how important the opening moments of a game are. Having played Elite: Dangerous quite a bit, I had been looking forward to playing the game as something slightly more tactical, but it does everything in its power to make the opening bits as rough and dry as possible.
Oh well. It was free. I'd be mad if I had paid for it.

A revolutionary game in the form of a distilled platformer for the ADD generation. Not only with its challenge level and precise control does it define what difficulty should really rely on in a game (player skill, not lives-based punishment), but Super Meat Boy also manages to revitalize old school platforming notions of perseverance, muscle memory, concentration, and practice to almost zen-like levels (if you're willing to commit). Respawn times are also virtually nonexistent, giving you little chance to grieve over your last death.
By helping put a spotlight on many other interesting games via unlockable characters, SMB has increased its replay value ten-fold and helped put a much-needed spotlight on the indie games movement. The indie development model is also celebrated here, with increased emphasis on discounts and endless content (level editor, user-created level portals).
There are bosses to beat and an ending to achieve in Super Meat Boy, but it is hardly the destination of the game, something that is evidenced by the journey of 300+ timed and leaderboard-enhanced levels of pure platforming bliss that Team Meat clearly put two years of blood, sweat, and tears into. Ah, my old friend. Looking a little older, but no worse for wear.
Seriously, this review can be summed up as: BUY NAO!!!
Besides some initial trouble in starting up the game on a Windows 7 HP (fixed with this
, and some graphics hiccups, this game has more than held up well since the last time I played it approx. 5 or 6 years ago. I've played the Dark Forces series since the first game, though I've only beaten the first and this one. This game optimizes the story and gameplay of the previous titles in my opinion, mainly because you start off with a lightsaber but also because the pacing is simply better. The combat is more or less copy+pasted from Outcast, but instead of just being thrown into the mix, you're given an adequately progressive series of missions that, for me, feel tailored to the experience level you should have by the time you reach each one. Note that you receive several missions per chapter, and most are more or less around the same level of difficulty, but some are more unique and require different playstyles to complete.
Combat is pretty well optimized, again IMO, for close quarters lightsaber combat. You may think fighting a few blaster-wielding enemies is laughably easy as you one-shot three of them in a row, up until you take a quick glance at your health and shields and realize you need to rethink your decisions. You can clear a room of 5 stormtroopers just to find yourself at 25 HP with 0 shields if you don't pay attention. Then a crimson lightsaber pops up in your peripheral and you find yourself weighing your options.
Which brings me to what is without a doubt this game's main draw: lightsaber combat. You'll probably see a few reviews complaining about the one-shot kill ability of it, and while I don't deny it, no review I've read so far has appropriately described it. Every lightsaber battle has felt absolutely rewarding, up to the the multiple "Knight-level" ones you find mid-to-late game. You have just enough offense and defense to hold your own and wear down your opponent, but you can be taken down quickly if you don't take a tactical approach and exploit openings while keeping your distance. It truly hits the right balance of challenge and intuition that many other Star Wars games lack. In short, you want a Jedi Knight/Sith Simulator, you've got one.
The only complaint I might have with the end-game/climax. The story is for the most part one of the few I've seen that is most reminiscent of the original trilogy's themes - simple-yet-somehow-deep, cliches and deus ex machina abound yet still engaging. The last chapter of the game, however, gets.....what I can only describe as weirdly campy. I'm a person that likes campy when it's done in the right way, but I was kinda turned off by these particular developments. It's like Episode 1 Phantom Menace Jar Jar Binks in Episode 2 Attack of the Clones campy - imagine his godawful dialogue from the first movie in all the Geonosis scenes. Well, it's probably not as bad as that, but it can be pretty distracting at moments and takes away a little from an otherwise amazing game.
WARNING: SPOILERS (And I haven't written enough reviews to know how to black out text). As can be expected from a Star Wars game, towards the end you're faced with a choice between the Light or Dark Side. The choice changes the story up to a point, though you still go to the same locations regardless. The Dark Side choice is harder as you have to fight more enemies, though in my experience it ends up being more fun. However, the campy bits show up in either choice. If you choose Dark Side, your character.........starts yelling. Like, Hayden Chistensen-style yelling, though luckily the voice actor is leagues above him in deliverance, so the questionable dialogue is bearable and even entertaining at points. If you can take Christian Bale's Batman in stride, it shouldn't be a big deal, just be prepared for a sudden character change.
In the Light Side portion, the campiness is far worse but doesn't really show until the tail-end of the game, in the 2nd half of a 2-part boss fight. I can't really explain this without SPOILERS: you fight Marka Ragnos. I'm an Old Republic nerd with a Sith fetish and a love of Tales of the Jedi, so his portrayal really made my♥♥♥♥♥itch. Even if you haven't touched a bit of Expanded Universe media, you might find the final boss on the wrong side of cartoonish. When I say that, I mean Scooby Doo villian level cartoonish, complete with "meddling kids" type lines. The dialogue made him sound like he belonged in the Adam West-era Batman. The bad guys can be pretty cliche even up to that point, throughout the whole series if we're being honest, but Ragnos really takes the cake. It kinda feels like the developers just rushed through the last chapter and needed a quick gimmick for each choice section to stand out. If you don't take the game too seriously these bits shouldn't bother you, but they can take away from the immersion for the scenes they're in.
Still, it probably says a lot about the game that I can remember it in this detail after half a decade. As of writing this review, I've only played a few missions in the Steam version and it already fits like a glove. Actually it plays better than many of the contempary games I've tried out in the past year. All in all, more than worth the price tag by far. BUY NAO 10/10

I felt that I needed enough play time to play this game to give it a proper review. I do believe that 12 hours is more than enough with this particular game.
First things first, this game is a pretty good game and is pretty fun for a casual type of game and simulator. It really has ups and downs, but I'd say more downs than ups because the 'simulator' part of this game isn't realistic enough. If you're American as I am, I didn't think there would be much difference in driving within each country, which there isn't.
With the settings, you may as well want to use the km/h speed limits simply because the only thing that changes is your own speedometer whereas all signs and such do not change to your standards.
Another thing about this game that is not so good, which is the worst thing about it, is the AI. The AI is horrible when it comes to driving alongside them on the roads and interstates. On the interstate, when the speed limit suggests that you drive at a certain speed, all other cars will drive probably over 20 km/h over that you're driving and the speed limit. And if you try to go that fast, you will immidiately get fined for too much money. Another thing that really upset me about this game that deals with the AI, is getting in small wrecks. When you get hit by a car that is NOT your fault, you will get fined for way too much money and causing you to lose experience that you earned. There have been too many times where I was making a turn, using my blinker and a car speeding trying to pull ahead of me and hitting me from the side or back. I got fined for getting hit when it was completely not my fault. The game also breaks standard traffic laws, such as turning at a green light. There have been a couple times where the light just turned green and the cars on the opposite side of the road turned while I was trying to go straight. I'm pretty sure that is not how traffic works. If the light is green, straightaways go first THEN turning lanes.
Again, this is a pretty decent game but the AI is really stupid and doesn't abide by traffic rules. I do suggest this game, however I do not suggest buying it at the full price because it's not worth it.

I'll just start off by saying I love this game. For all its faults and flaws, it is undoubtably a hell of a lot of fun. It's an open world, with so much going on that you're never short of anything to do. The story is decent, if nothing spectacular, but in getting away from that and forging a career for your captain, that's where the best of this game lies. You can do so much, from being a miner, to a pirate to playing Dora the space explorer to a mercenary. Hell, you can be all of those at once. I've clocked up a full day of play time on this game and feel I've only scratched the surface of what it has to offer.
Pros:
- Open world with many options to do things
- Good leveling, balance and progression (most of the time)
- Easy to use controls
- SO MUCH TO DO!!!!
- Decent graphics and a good selection of ships that both look and play in different styles
- Easy to make money and progress, without it ever being too easy or too grind-y
- Did I mention there's a lot you can do in this game?
- The difficulty curve is well sorted and always gives you a sense of achivement without ever making anything too hard
Cons
- UI can be a bit of a faff and it's easy to miss important things in combat until it's too late
- Tutorial leaves a lot out and you have to figure quite a bit out as you go along (Not a problem so much as a downside to the large amount of content and devs clearly trying to avoid a bloated and OTT tutorial, just be aware you have to use your brain and think outside the box and read through the controls and manual sometimes)
- Not a great game if you want something on rails that will hold your hand
- Sometimes you spend 5 to 10 minutes sitting around as your ship flies from point to point
- Occasionally has an air that it could have been even better than it is
In short a very good space sim that was everything I've always wanted a space sim to be. It manages to balance a good deal of content against lots of options without ever being bloated. It draws together all the core stuff you'd expect in a space sim into a very good package, and it keeps me coming back for more!

While there are certainly some areas open to criticism, at its core the new Hitman is a great addition to the franchise.
The style and feel of the gameplay return to the characteristics that made Blood Money so great. While the new Hitman isn't as stunning graphically as some other titles available today, it is nevertheless a very good looking game. The Paris level looks great, and is fun and challenging.
By design HItman levels are highly replayable, given the variety of Challenges, Contracts, and Escallation modes (and expected Elusive Targets) encouraging further exploration, experimentation, and creative strategies to take down any number of potential targets. If you enjoy the replaly factor, as I do, then the episodic release schedule may work for you. But if not, then you may prefer to wait until the whole "season" has been released.
The continuous online requirement can be aggravating at times if your internet connection gets interrupted even briefly during a playthough, as you are immediately booted out to the menus.   Although the game can technically be played offline, it's greatly limited, with no advancement in points or experience, no contracts, and no access to saves made while online. The developers say this is a necessary condition for the "live" aspects of the game. So like it or not it looks like this is here to stay.
Some people have complained of poor optimization and bad framerates, however, I haven't encountered any serious problems with this. I'm sure there's room for improvement, but for me the gameplay has been quite smooth already.
In any event, while it's not perfect, the new Hitman is definitely one I'd recommend getting.

There's absolutely no excuse and no reason to make this game episodic other than being lazy and wanting to cash in before the game is finished. I love to support early access games, but that's really something meant for indie game devs who need financial support.
The game itself isn't bad, here are the pros:
+ Fun gameplay (physics, AI, variety of options)
+ Good graphics
+ The Paris map is huge (currently the only available full level)
+ It gives the feeling of Blood Money.
+ It's Hitman
However, the game also has serious and minor flaws:
- Performance issues (low fps with decent GPU)
- Pay in advance and only play one level per month (Completely ruins the story)
- No option to buy and modify weapons (I'm not sure if this feature will come at all)
- 3 different missions on one map
- Lacks variety of weapons
- There's absolutely not enough blood for a game like Hitman
I'm a Hitman fan, but I do not recommend this game yet. It has to offer all levels and more weapons before I can recommend it.

In a single word Hitman can be summed up as "bland".  Nearly ever aspect of the game is bland, boring, uninspired, and unimpressive despite how nice the trailers leading up to release were.  The game fails to deliver pretty much everywhere.
The gameplay just doesn't have "it".  That feeling past Hitman games have had, it lacks.  As a veteran who's played every single game since the original back on my old Windows Millenium PC I can't believe just how lackluster it feels to be a Hitman.
There are tons of reported DRM, "Online Always" and save game issues that have plagued the release, but to be honest none of that has affected me at all.  I've never had a game interupted, nor have I been disconnected.  So when you factor that into the equation this game should be relatively good as major publishers have stated right?  Wrong.
The game's gameplay itself is extremely basic.  While the previous Hitman installment lacked variety, and assassination targets largely because it's adopted a linear story mission based world, it nailed the gameplay mechanics perfectly.  In the previous hitman game the controls, and gameplay were rock solid.  Weapons felt great, player movement was spot on, and you generally felt like you were Agent 47.
In this new release I don't feel like 47.  In fact it feels more like a bad Hitman knock off.  The gameplay feels watered down.  Player movement and animations feel dated, and it's a big step backwards for the series.  The gunplay is abyssmal.  Never in the history of Hitman has shooting your signature pistol felt so underwhelming.   The typical methods of killing your targets are there, guns, poison, explosions, and a few unique ones.  But now that the missions are so large they are actually a drawback for the series.
The Paris mission is quite large, and there are many of conversations to be heard which open new ways to kill your targets. But it takes time, a lot of time in fact.  You can spend hours on a single mission, but after the hit is done I never got that old satisfying feeling.  It's marred by technical issues, poor AI, watered down gameplay, and just doesn't feel good.
The soundtrack is fine, but for whatever reason the game starts if off way too loud.  I think that's to hide the fact that enemy AI doesn't pick up on sound cue's well, or at all.  The sound bars all end at 20, and I had to put the sound down to 4 before it was acceptable.  I want to hear footsteps, doors closing, and everything else that I would imagine an assassin would.  I can't see an assassin of 47's calibre walking around with earbuds on...
Graphics are good.  A downgrade from the previous Hitman, but still good enough maxed out to be pretty.  The game makes a poor choice of locking Textures on Low as if you're too stupid to tweak settings yourself.  You can do some in game, but I've seen others state that with less then 2gb of Vram on your GPU you cannot put textures on Medium or High which is silly.  The previous Hitman title didn't do this, so why now?
I found the tutorial to be pretty frustrating.  Big dump tips and tricks to help you succeed, and very poor controls from the get go.  Unfortunately the game locks the Key Binding outside of the ingame menu, so you have to quit in order to change the controls then go back and see what you like.  Overall the controls suck.
In the end you get a highly diluted Hitman game.  There are tons of challenges that aim to improve the replay value, but personally I would have wanted more missions from the start.  With completion of the Paris mission you're left with more or less nothing.  If the gameplay mechanics were spot on then maybe I could see the replay value, but when the gameplay isn't good you're not going to be coming back for much.
Episodic Hitman is bad on many levels, and here's why.  In previous Hitmans if you didn't like a level or had a hard time on it you could go in guns blazing, get the kill and continue on.  Here, you can't do that because there's nothing to continue on to.  Personally I found the Paris mission to be horrible.  Unappealing on the eyes, boring characters, and no reason to replay.  It's the type of mission I would complete and never replay.  As a first impression this game leaves a dirty taste in your mouth.
Another issue is the lack of 47's previous bullet proof self.  In past games he could absorb quite a bit of damage, so if you decided to guns blazing you could succeed.  Here that's no longer the case.  2-3 bullets and you are done.  The games blood is also a downgrade.  Kills used to be colorful, and there would be more blood.  Instead here it's limited as if it was made for a younger crowd.  This is not the Hitman game I want.
As a longtime Hitman player this is a series low.  The fact you have to wait weeks to get another taste on another level just boggles the mind.  If the initial impression was amazing we would put up with some crappy follow up levels, but the initial impression here is full of failure.  If this is the end of the Hitman series it's a damn shame, but at this point it's not hard to see someone else come along and do it much better.
Overall 4/10.  Back to the drawing board.

As I said in the Conquest of Elysium 3 review, in spite of being a strategy and open-world game fan, I've just never been able to enjoy the 4X genre.  All of the promise of customizing your civilization to suit your own fantasy gives way to cold calculations and optimization strategies, and all the exploration is just for finding more resources to exploit.  Worse, by the end game, 4X games are just bogged down in micromanagement to maintain your war machine.  It's just as the armies of my enemies are broken and victory is assured that I find myself entirely bored of the game and unwilling to bother completing it.
Dominions manages to be something of a split between a 4X and... well, the best I can come up with is a deck-building style of game.  Compared to a game like Civilization, where all cultures are basically the same except for a couple unique units and one bonus or two, Dominions pits a stand-in for ancient Greece, led by Zeus or Athena or Aphrodite or some other Greek god with hoplites and such up against a stand-in for ancient Egypt filled with lizard-people and led by a dracolich against R'Lyeh, an entirely subaqueous civilization of D&D aboleths and Lovecraftian horrors.
Although the game definitely pushes you to optimize your god, the game's god-creation system is also probably its best and most interesting feature.  You can be anything from an obvious stand-in for mythic deities like Thor or Kali or Quetzcoatl to some of the monsters of myth, like Tiamat or a gorgon or a straight-up demon from Hell, to a stone statue or fountain that pours the blood of virgins and demands blood sacrifice through taking possession of mortals, to just some jerk human Caeser of Rome claiming he's God-Emperor of Mankind, and out to make that claim real.  Deities can craft and wear magical items based upon their magical powers, and in deity creation, you can set their magical talents (I.E. standard fire/water/air/earth, but also "death" (necromancy), "astral" ('pure' magic stuff like counterspells and magic resistance), "nature" ("druid" magic like growing plants or barkskin or regeneration or summoning fairies), and "blood" (murder slaves for magical power - based upon Aztec blood sacrifice).  Beyond this, there is dominion power (higher means your religion evangelizes more successfully) and "scales", which are an alignment with different factors that affect your lands.  ("Order" gives income bonuses and reduces random events, while "Turmoil" gives penalties and increased randomness. You gain more points to spend on other things taking Turmoil scales, so "Order" is always better.)
In spite of the fact that you can play as a fountain of blood that demands blood sacrifices so that you can twist the souls of your followers into horrible abominations to throw at your enemies or a straight-up angel with a flaming sword set up to bless her followers with peace and prosperity, there isn't any real acknowledgement of morality in this game (beyond "might makes right"), and there is no real sense of whether any particular cultures or peoples you conquer have any particular opinions of your religion, outside of a randomized chance of revolt (which seems to have more to do with your "misfortune" scale than anything to do with how you reign, other than pillaging the land to take slaves for blood sacrifices.)
Gameplay is basically "stack mashing", where you pile up a giant glob of units and lob it at the enemy and hope for the best.  This doesn't mean it lacks strategy, however. Unlike many games like this, it actually simulates the battle. This is outside your direct control, although you can set a very basic script of actions for your units, like "attack archers" or "attack rearmost", or script up to 5 specific spells for casters, so that you can tell a gish to cast stoneskin and quicken before rushing the enemy in melee.  Combat is fairly deep, with some units having light or heavy armor, weapons having bonuses against shields (which boost dodge chance rather than armor), morale and terror attacks being common, elemental attacks, and effects on the battlefield from dominion scales all taking place, there is a lot of strategy in battle.
Combat is somewhere between an RPG and a traditional RTS.  Units gain experience and leaders can gain special abilities, but they can also gain permanent injuries.  Leaders can also be given magical items you forge to greatly improve their combat performance, and can gain permanent (as long as they live) improvements to their magic-casting capabilities.  On the other hand, death is super-cheap in this game, and you basically just churn out units as fast as your castles can muster them to throw into the meatgrinder.  Common infantry units, in particular, tend to die by the dozens even in victory (and there's tons of friendly fire in this game, since friendly archers tend to aim at enemies in melee, and have poor aim).
Empire management is massively streamlined to the point of practically nonexistent compared to most 4X games.  The only thing you build are castles (which dramatically increase how many units you can build), temples (which spread your religion - "Dominion" is the area where your religion is dominant), and laboratories (which let you transfer magic items). None of these need to be unlocked through research, so what you see at the start is what you get (although high-level magic can let you magically create castles where you otherwise couldn't, such as underwater if you are a land-based civ).
Those who love empire management in Civilization or even Total War may be disappointed in being "dumbed down to just combat", but there's something to reccomend it in the fact that, once you're up to "steamrolling" power levels, you can just stop caring and steamroll away instead of having an ever-more-complex empire to manage as you attain more lands. In this sense, this balance between a 4X and RTS actually appeals to me more than either those those genres do on their own.
That said, I do have to warn prospective players that there ARE things that need a form of micromanagement:  Leaders (like wizards and army generals) default to "defend province/castle", but that's basically the order of last resort because it's never useful.  If you have wizards you want researching magic any time you're not making magic items, then you have to remember to babysit the wizard's tower to make sure anyone who just finished a magic item goes back to research.  Remember where the priest searching for holy sites is, and give new search or move orders every turn.  As with a 4X, this starts to become somewhat tedious the larger your empire, and the more laboratories with wizards to manage you have to keep track of, although it's thankfully not as terrible as constantly managing a build queue since you tend to have relatively few major centers to check.
Like with "defend" as a default, I also get annoyed with how the game has a lot of bad default options, forcing a lot of constantly needing to click the same commands.  Army management suffers from this frequently.  The UI could be brushed up in just plain telling me how many soldiers I have total in a province, rather than making me add it up per leader.  (Sure, there's consumed supply, but some troops don't eat, giants eat more than humans, and units that provide supply subtract from supply consumed rather than add to total supply, making that a false image for many circumstances. I might have 500 troops but only see 200 supply consumed.)  This leads to it being rather difficult to tell just HOW strong a very large army actually is.
In all, it's far from the best strategy game I've played, but it's a very interesting one, and on sale, it's definitely worth picking up just to see what it does differently from other strategy games.  (Especially since its sequels are more expensive, but better-polished games, buying this on sale makes for a good way to test the series out on the cheap.)

I  own Dominions 3 and 4. Started playing Dominions 3, few monts later Dom 4 came out - moved to it.
Now I'm playing Dominions 3 and enormousely enjoying it. Less spells, less magical items than in Dom 4 - somehow even more fun.
Why I like Dominions:
1. Very interesting fantasy setting (not just elfes and other copies of Tolkien imagination) with Valkiries, armoured gorillas, ghouls, giants, chariots, eagle-men, bat-men, spider riders, raptor riders, fiery salamanders, armoured or undead elephants, giant ants, tiny dragonflies, barechested warriors, tritons with amber armour, hydras, halfblind cyclopes, nagas, twoheaded giants, liches, krakens, dragons, mechanical dragons, trolls, tengu, ghosts, lamias, jaguars, werejaguars, powerfull but insane gods, mages of various kinds,assasins, shark knights, Vikings with glamour, Aztects with flying ability and many, many more...
2. Ingenious balancing of nations. Other games do balancing + variety this way: one side gets a sword and shield the other axe and a shield. Dominions does it like this: one side gets a sword and a shield the other gets a catapult and a sharpened stick :-)    and it works!
3. No researching of buildings, basically there are only 3 buildings you can build in a province: castle, magical reaserch lab  and a temple. Less hasle with buildings and a refreshing change from the industry standard.
4. Spells, spells, spells :-) starting from minor ones like fire flies (weak and available with no reaserch) to fire storm (burns everything on the battlefield that does not have full fire protection, requires a lot of reaserch and a powerfull fire mage).
5. IT'S DIFFRENT.
6. Challenging single player even after hundreds of hours of play.
7. Great and athmosferic music.
8. The battle set up: give orders to commanders, mages and units before battle; later during the battle you just watch how your orders interplay with orders given by your oponent: surprises guaranteed, especially in multiplayer battles. Many a time I was watching biting the nails, seeing how my main force was pummeling the enemy but my oponents flanking party was going for my commander - battle of Gaugamela all over again.
9. Great community - higher IQ average than the many other games out there :-)
10. Small developer firm with dedicated staff. Basically like Creative Assembly before they were bought with Total War series by Sega. Upgrades are free and regular, game works like a clock on day one, patches fix some mechanics you never even new existed, developers behave on forums like your friends: nice, profesional, informative and surprisingly patient towards the odd troll or idiot :-)
11. Depth. 3 eras with circa 20 nations in each one, every nation has different soldiers (is hydra a soldier?) and commanders, some very usfull, some meh and some ridiculosly usless until that day when you find a use for them :-)    Hundreds of spells that can be divided in 3 categories: battlefield spells that have effect on a particular battle (relevant mage has to be present), rituals used on strategical map (for example ritual that summons wywern or mechanical men that you can use in later battles) and global rituals that have a major effect on the strategical map and the battles (for example global ritual that calls darkness and gives penalty to all units in battle that don't have the special ability darkvision). Hundreds of magical items (dwarven hammer is so  much better in Dom 3 than in Dom 4).
12. The distinction between strategical map and tactical map and how both are working.
13. The ideas inherent to the game and seen nowhere else e.g.:
A. units get tired on battlefield and that makes possible for an army of pitchfork fielding peasants to overwhelm a small group of knights (even though initially the knights cut them in heaps) IF (very big if) there is enough of the peasants.
B. bless effect that changes sacred units into even stronger ones and you can choose the bless effect at the start of the game.
C. Dominion which is like the population strenght of faith in you, the Pretender God. Has effect on how many sacred units you can buy, how strong some global rituals are and on morale of your troops. Also as you are pretending to be a God (one of many) in the game, the added benefit is that no fundamentalist muslim can play the game :-)
D. the way afflictions affect the units - especially extremal cases when you see a unit that is blind, cripled, weakened, with a chest wound and battle fright but still on the battle rooster.
Could go on and on but 13 is my lucky number so...

A game of master strategy... Played for about 10 hours straight and I barely scatched the surface of this game.

This is a very enjoyable fantasy strategy-sim. It's plays very similar to a Total War series game, but with a more hands off approach to the battles (you don't directly control units, but you can give them pre battle formations and priorities, like telling your cavalry to wait a turn before going to attack the enemies archer units).
There is kind of a big lack of explaination for a lot of things in the game itself, so you'll have to refer to the manual or the wiki, but I figured out 95% of it on my own. One example is the game lets you give magic gems (that are a resource for casting global spells and making magic items) to your commanders, but it doesn't explain anywhere ingame the benefits of doing that. Turns out it improves their magic casting abilities of the associated gem/magic type by 1 level for having the gem equiped. But some characters also generate magic gems for you and they get put in their inventory until you retrieve them.
It took me about 4-5 games to explore how the various mechanics work, like how faith spreads, how you research magic, how building good armies and giving them the right orders to increase their effectivness. Experiment and read the ingame hints about the things that are described and it's easy enough to catch on.

If you don't have dominions 4 and don't plan on waiting for that to go on sale, this is still a solid entry to the strategy genre.  There are quite a few ui improvements absent from 3 as opposed to 4, and the win conditions are more simplistic, but you still won't find a better strategy pick if you're willing to overlook the old-looking graphics.
Also, as I understand it, the multiplayer scene has moved on from 3 to 4, so it may be better for playing alone.

My critiques:
-The storyline can be pretty short since you only go on three dates with your chosen daddy, HOWEVER you can go on dates with multiple dads and make the story longer, and the game has great replay value.
-*SPOILER* The story and writing got a bit jumbled, sometimes it would act as if i had met Robert when I did not meet him the night before. My character mentions Mary flirting with other men even when I had not seen her do that. I think there was a time where my character mentioned "your dad" to Amanda when I had chosen the "wife" option. So I found the writing to be a little confusing at times.
-The minigames where kind of confusing at times since there isn't really any directions, for example I didn't really know what i was supposed to be doing in the concert minigame and the radio fixing minigame.
-The sound seemed a little funky to me at times, specifically Hugo sounded like his voice was recorded with like different equipment or something? Maybe that is just my headphones or something though.
-*SPOILER* The inclusion of "bad" endings and "good" endings is great, keeps the game replayable. However, I am a bit unsure if getting the "pinup" pic means you got the good ending or not? With Joseph I seemed to have gotten a bad ending (He dumps me and goes back to his wife) and yet I got his picture. I guess the unsureness keeps people playing to see how many endings there are, but maybe a definite number or how many endings there are would be nice.
-The difference in style between your Dadsona and the actual game art irks me a bit. I understand that the character creation can't be as detailed as the art of the game, but I have to admit it's a little strange to me seeing my character in the corner looking  different from the style of the dads.
Overall, I have enjoyed the game thus far and will continue to enjoy it. This game actually makes me smile and laugh and the addition of the Grumps voiceacting is just icing on the cake. Congratulations to the Dream Daddy team on making a great game!

Yooka-Laylee is a fun callback to 90s gaming, and a satire on modern gaming. Dispite the game feeling like an old classic, it is still very fun to experience. The game starts really easy and simple to get you interested without scaring you away, but as the game procedes, the dificulty increases exponentially. This difficulty is not necessarily fair by modern standards in video games, but it's fair enough that the completion of these difficult challenges is very satisfying. I enjoyed over 40 hours of this game, and I am not a completionist. There is enough veriety and challenge in this game to entertain you for a very long time. If you enjoy games like Banjo-Kazooie, Super Mario 64, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, then you'll probably enjoy this game. If you have never been fond of the 3d platforming genre, obviously you aren't going to suddenly like this one.

I'm happy to see a good-mix of reviews on this, but I'm also saddened by the amount of negativity. Nostalgia goggles can make you picture things way better than they actually are, Banjo Kazooie/Tooie had flaws to. Were they amazing games? Yes. But they also had flaws. I occassionally  died from being at a wrong angle. I drowned in Clanker's Cavern god knows how many times because 3D platformers switch camera views when you swim into them, and I'm still, to this day, thrown off by that. Before you critizise the developers, remember that this is a fan-sponsered game. There might have been design choices that are somewhat questionable sometimes, but they met their shipping date, delivered a quality, non-broken game, in a quicker time then other projects I have supported that stiill have yet to come out, such as Spaceventure. This is exactly what you think it is, and maybe more than that. Instead of including a bunch of bite-sized, quick to beat levels, they included massive worlds. Is there flaws? of course. Because people designed this, and after 1,000,000 hours looking at the same batch of code, you tend to forget "hey..if this camera goes out right here it might be hard to see this boss for the average player..." First boss annoyed the living heck out of me, as it's hard for all the wrong reasons, but did I not play the level for about 3 1/2 hours before even encountering the boss? That's the beauty of this game. Remember how you wished the Pirate Level from banjo Kazooie, and Tooie for that matter were bigger? That's were the mechanic of expanding the levels comes in. As a kid, I used gameshark codes to get to the hidden levels in kazooie, just to see a little more of the game. For the abilitiy of the developers to be like, okay, You've seen everything there is in the level, but what, what if that locked door at the top of the tower you can unlock, and it's a whole dungeon, but a different perspective, called Icymetric Palace( har har har). That's another thing, the comedy was lambasted on professional reviews. It's like making fun of a pixar movie's comedy, of course it's obvious, it was designed around kids with adults getting a light chuckle. You can turn into the world's ugliest flower in the first level, but the plants in the level now think you are literally "hot stuff" and if you spray pollen on them, they remark"isn't it a little early for that kind of thing?" Or you meet a mine cart, named Kartos, who Yooka remarks" let me guess, you're the God of Ore?"  If that doesn't make you smile, don't buy this game. You are so far gone from the kid you used to be, life has hit you and you are to cynical to enjoy something like this without looking at it through a microscope. Is it stupid decicions sometimes? Of course, like there's quite a few times where you don't know what move to use. Remember in Kazooie? Had the context sensitive buttons that would trigger the move needed for that area, and if you came to an area without knowing the move, it' be greyed out so you knew you couldn't do this puzzle yet? Yeah, nothing like that here. I'm not saying that was the best way to do it either, but at least I knew what specifically I needed for what sections. Also, they built a bunch of platforms in the side of rocks, just so you can get up to things an alternative way. Is it quick? No, but it's one of the very few games where it felt like actual exploration, not just " go here, do this, you have to" (See: The Stanley Parable)
Yooka-Laylee is the game that feels like it came out as a kid but you didn't have the system it came out on. It's colorful, unique, and far from boring. Flawed? Yes. but buy the heck out of this game, because if you want a game where the developers  can just make what they WANT instead of simply what is EXPECTED, than this needs to be successful. For it to not be a fan-feedback to an extreme degree, it needs to be successful. Psychonauts expanded what a platformer could be a lot more than this did 15 years ago. However, Psychonauts was also originally a failure, which is why the second game was crowdfunded. If you don't support this genre, it will die, and Candy Crush will be all your kids ever get to experience.

If you don't know, this game is a pretty good 3d platformer with some pretty harsh weak points in gameplay. The main two weak points being
A) Controls are either tight and polished or (by design) sloppy and frustrating.  The latter is found when walking on ice, when flying, when using almost any of the game's transformations, most of the arcade games, and a few other places as well.
B) Plenty of use of plain-old outdated gameplay mechanics.  Bosses (each about a 4-5 minute battle) go on about 2-3 minutes too long.  Minecart sections aren't any different than what you'd find in the Donkey Kong Country series on the SNES, save for being able to shoot a projectile forward.
And what both A and B have in common is that they're just not fun.
This is another game I wish Steam would implement a "meh" button for reviews - if I had to grade this game, I'd give it a 6/10 because only about 60% of the content is actually fun to play.  And that 60% is really fun, but the other 40% is just so dated and unfun that it really makes it hard to recommend this game.
That said, I hope Playtonic takes all of the critisim of this game to heart and makes an fantastic Yooka-Laylee 2.

The game as I have played is still in Early Access. It's a simulator type game where you give characters called 'Dupes' tasks, such as building or digging, etc in an effort to survive inside an underground area/asteroid. You must manage to gather or grow food for your Dupes and also ensure that they have enough oxygen to breathe by harnessing plants or science.
Keeping your people alive is a major drive in the game. I have found that once you reach a point in the game where everything is now managable you can continue by building or put the game away for a time. The Developer, Klei, has a fantastic schedule set in place where content updates are published every 6 weeks. This is better than other titles they have had where there would be no news or information available and several years would go by before the games status was updated.
Once new content is published you can continue to play your previous game, but starting a new games is what I find the most entertaining (mixed with anxiety as my people are struggling to breathe and are starving).
I highly recommend this as it is simpler and easier to play for a few minutes than other sims I have played.

This game seems simple at first, but can grow very challenging if you don't pay attention to what you're doing. Very fun, but don't be suprised if you lose several hours to playing without noticing.

This game has a certain je-ne-sais-quoi. It just pulls you in with its cuteness, and the need to constantly problem-solve to get your base back to normal.
You'l be off working on a way to boil water to clean germs from it, when all of a sudden your main base's temperature has risen by a couple degrees, killing plants responsible for your main food supply! Then, while fixing temperature you realize your supply of clean water has run out, so you frantically explore to look for that ever-elusive water gyzer. But the water coming out of the gyzer is hot! which makes your base heat up again, bringing you back to where you started.
As this game expands and adds new mechanics the different ways to tackle these problems is mind boggling. It's really fun to try to optimize your little machines that you build, all the while making sure your base doesn't get overrun by noxious gasses, germs, or bodily fluids leaking from poorly maintained toilets.
I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who likes problem solving games. At times it can get hectic, but the pause button lets you think things through before you act.
The only real issue I have with the game is how your minions seems to prioritize new orders over old orders. So sometimes you give build orders, and then go on building new stuff in other parts of them map, and find that hours later those things still haven't been built! It's a bit frustrating to manually have to prioritize orders just based on when they were given.

At this early point (100 hours as of this writing), I've grown a fleet of mercenaries, a strong boarding crew, and after developing strategies, stuffed my garage with ships that I can't even use yet.  There's nothing quite like flying into an ongoing space battle, capturing a weakened ship, and getting the heck out of Dodge before anyone's the wiser. And there is so much more to explore.  I'm barely out of the "beginner" areas of the starmap.
The UI could use some work, and the multiple view options are a little overkill for me, but it's something I can work with.  I do wish there was a better ship monitor that would show effects/status/problems easier.
Anyway, it's a good game that is huge and open, which makes it hard for some. I recommend it for those wanting to run around space, doing space related things.

This is going to be a though nut to crack, I recommend the game but it has a lot of flaws. At the same time I'm really enjoying it and in the end that is what probably counts the most.
First, lets get this straight, the amount of detail that went into this game is phenomenal. The animations, the environment and the sound effects are all top notch. No complaints there.
Even though the graphics are great, there isn't much variety in them. I get that it all takes place in this desolate post-apocalyptic world, but everything looks the same. Enter a new area on the map and behold! everything is brown and gray and there is lots of sand. Sure, the main colours shift slightly between areas and you get a bit more mountains or some other landmarks, but it still looks basically the same. Don't expect to be wowed by the scenery, this is no Fallout or Skyrim world which is lush with variation. Areas are mostly empty, there is one stronghold in each where there is some livery, but it ends there. In the stronghold there is mainly only one contact to interact with. Sure the map is littered with small and bigger camps, but the purpose is to wipe out everybody living there (resulting in even less life). And again, sadly, camps are basically the same. Made up out of old scrap parts of planes, boats, cars or rocks, ofcourse they differ in size and layout but it all looks very dull. This being despite the fact that it is all very well made and probably has the best graphics quality of any game I've played so far.
Every now and then a contact pops up on the map you can have a small interaction with, they will give you information, a quest or some money and are gone after that. Yes, it's a sad place to live in.
The sound is very well done. The cars make weird sounds and their engines sound nothing like the real thing, but they are very satisfying, and just like in real life you get a kick out of driving your car through a tunnel and letting it roar, awesome! Same with explosions, crashes, bone breaking during fights, you name it! Turn up the volume when playing this game, it probably does more to immerse you then the graphics can.
Mad Max itself as a playable character is somewhat of a problem too. His capabilities feel very limited. The best way to describe this is with his jumps, it's complete rubbish. My 6 year old can jump better then him. He's this though guy, but you can't jump over a small 30cm stone because...? This is just an example, but you get this feeling a lot when playing and exploring.
Still there is enough to do in the game to keep you busy, you have a main story line, there are small quests. You have to upgrade Max's gear, his abilities, build out your car, find resources to pay for all these upgrades, do races, clear up mine fields, collect relics, destroy bosses, destroy convoys, collect ornaments, go sniping, collect cars, fly balloons, and so on and so on...
Although some of these things seems pointless. For example, you can upgrade strongholds so that each time you enter them your gas tank will be filled up. But what is the point for doing this for each stronghold? You can fast travel between them freely, so if you've done one of them, there is no point in upgrading the others (except for achievements). Fast travel only works for your main car, which is silly because some things require the use of other cars (like clearing mine fields) and then fast travel doesn't work resulting in long tiresome drives across whole or multiple areas. It's these small quirks, which there are multiple off, throughout the game that really prevent this title to truly shine.
The difficulty of the game is also strange, for me it's becoming easier as progress is being made. At start with no upgrades and a very basic car and Max, it is difficult to survive even the most basic encounter. Destroying a convoy takes a long time, clearing out a camp is dangerous and deadly. With upgraded gear, a convoy is a matter of a few minutes at most, walking into a camp you feel like a terminator (most of the time).
Like i said at the start of my review, I'm really enjoying this title, even despite all the shortcomings it has. I'm not really sure why that is, but there is something that makes me go back to it. If you like driving around, ramming and slamming other cars and kicking and punching people in the face a lot, you might forgive all the mentioned (and more) shortcomings of this game and enjoy it just as much as I do.

Voted YES because it is a good game, BUT consider investing later on in the release cycle if you want to get more 'bang for your buck' straight away.
The game strays away from the constrained, highly story-driven experience brought by Absaloution and instead goes back to the grassroots Sandbox experience offered by Blood Money, with some of the good stuff Absaloution introduced as well, such as the Instinct View, albeit highly nerfed to remove a lot of the OP abilities.
Currently, there's only one real mission to play, which is pretty dissapointing, especially after you complete the Tutorial levels, get your appetite wet with the Showstopper mission, and then have nothing to do other than replay those levels while trying to complete the challenges or exploring other options within the level.  This complements the return to a sandbox gameplay design quite well as different (and sometimes fun & gimmicky) things to interact with in the environment can change up the experience completely.  The encouragement to seek out different ways to complete the mission and rewarding the player for doing so adds replay value, which is CRUCIAL given the way in which they have decided to release content.
I can see this game having a lot of potential.  If Square Enix are smart, they will use this release schedule to their advantage by studying customer feedback and tailoring future content releases around it.  So maybe progressive release of content is not such a bad thing.  If the current content sets the bar for the rest of the game, I can comfortably say that my £30 investment was worthwhile.

Origins puts forth the greatest story telling the Arkham series has seen yet, and while it doesn't deviate greatly from the foundation City nearly perfected, it does offer an interesting look into the character's early crime fighting career. The campaign is meaty. I put more than 20 hours into it myself and still left quite a bit of the side missions untouched. On top of that and the challenge maps, you'll find an asymmetric multiplayer mode-a series' first.
If you're a fan of the Arkham games, this should be a no brainer. It's more of what you love.

Origins was nearly guaranteed to be a best selling game judging by the two prior games in the series. It's important to remember, however, that the game is made by a different developer, and worst of all: It shows. While Arkham Origins' storyline and characters are amazing, including the new "younger" cast of voices for some characters, the mechanics themselves are querky. For once you are limited to grappeling to certain areas only while soaring through the skies of Gotham, and random glitchy occurences will also have you performing flips in the air, going through objects, or best of all punching someone twenty feet away as the game teleports you to the nearest enemy regardless of distance during your combos. Putting aside these imperfections, however, the storyline is progressively exciting with great twists for any fan of the lore. Surprise appearances by various personalities are also a treat, but nothing beats watching Batman's struggles as he learns to mature over the course of this game with the help of Alfred as he realizes he cannot be the sole savior of a city when its filled with villians he could never have imagined.

Is it good? Yes. I've laughed and I've teared up while playing this game. It's lighthearted overall, but touches on some serious themes. "Lol you're a dad and you date dads" is a funny gimmick, but it follows through on the premise. Characters talk about getting older, times changing, and trying to do your best as a parent and a person that comes from a very sincere place. It's also inclusive in an understated way. You have the flexibility to determine a lot of things for yourself about your dadsona (though do note the character has a lot of personality in internal monologues that you do not get to change, you're going to be a pun-loving dork who was in a ska band and had wild college roommate adventures with Craig no matter what). An earlier build the devs streamed showed the player character having been married to a woman before, but the final release allows you to choose the gender of their previous spouse, which was a pleasant surprise. Your character's daughter is also a delight.
Gushing aside, the game does have some unpolished edges I've noticed so far. Several lines crop up that assumed I'd made choices I had not, and Hugo's voice clips seem to have been recorded on a really crappy microphone or something. The character builder is a little rough. I wasn't expecting anything robust by any means, but the art style doesn't quite match the rest of the game and your character portrait is probably going to look kind of weird no matter what you do. I've also noticed some slight halos on the character images (and poorly filled pixels in my dadsona's image.)
But I would still recommend this game on the strength of its writing, and how much fun I have had so far. I don't even generally like dating simulators, but here I am. Try it. Get to know some handsome dads. Cry a little bit about how much you love your daughter.

This game is probley my fav nostalgic game from my child hood, this game is problely the closest thing you can ever get to feeling like an actual jedi. I have always said that if they were to remake any star wars game it should be this one, although that will never happen. I am even more happy that this game still has an active community despite its age.
However despite my love for star wars and this game espically, I must point out that it isn't perfect. So I will go over the pros and cons.
Pros:
The lightsaber fighting is amazing and feels rewarding, the addition of using blasters and mines/thermal detonators also allows you to take down enemy too far for you to reach with force powers or your light saber.
The voice acting is realtivly well done for its time with a few hicupps here and there.
The story line and missions are fun and addctive and kept me playing well after I told myself I was done.
Creating you own character has always been a feature in games that I love, it allows you to immerse your self in the world by having you be your character, despite the limited choices the customisation is a nice touch.
Cons:
The ai can be really really stupid and un balanced at times. The normal enemys die in one hit from your lightsaber which is fair enough, and the other jedi you fight is fun as well, but when you start to get to the point when you are facing down multiple jedi at once, and even more so with the harder enemy being able to have a one shot mechanic, it gets very frustrating. But dont fear, most cases you can run past those enemy as they wait for you to come to them while you just proced to the next area while they just go about their bussiness or run into the enviroment hazards and kill themselves.
The force powers are really unbalanced, using force pull and push is fun, but is redundent when you can just force lighting everything to death which even at max level takes very little force power and does insane damage and knockback, which leaves you going "Well I guess I will just use force lighting all the time then" which undermines your other force powers which is disapointing.
Now with this game being released in 2003 the graphics are pretty crappy, but thats just a fact of time, but I can understand people not wanting to play a game with out dated graphics, me personally the game was good enough for me to ignore it since it added to the nostalga, but if that bothers you it might turn you off this game.
Now I must make aware that these are things I had expirenced in single player, in multiplayer I did not encounter as many of the problems i did in single player, which is good, as multiplayer is fun and enjoyable with skill being a high factor in it.
Overall if you are a fan of starwars you will most likely like this game. The multiplayer is fun as well as the single player, despite what ever happens this will always be one of my most fav games.

Max Payne is, in some ways, a very unique game, and in many other ways it is just another third person shooter.
It really depends on how you look at it. Stylistically, Max Payne is very engaging simply because you don't really see a lot of video games in a 'Noir'-kind of setting; I really have never played a game that is anything like Max Payne! If Noir is your thing and you love yourself some of those 'bloody revenge' stories in which one guy shoots his way through Mafia goons, you will probably not be disappointed by Max Payne...
... That is, if you are sure that you can handle old-school shooters. For someone like me, this game aged very well actually, since I do not mind these older shooting mechanics which simply involve you evading fire rather than covering from it. It's a very simplistic game in that sense; don't expect any sort of depth. That's not a fault of the game, but I have talked to players who could not get into the game because they thought these mechanics lacked the intricacies of newer shooting games, like cover-mechanics and upgradable weapons. Not to mention, death is inevitable in Max Payne, mostly because Max can die in just a few gunshots (it's 'realistic' that way) and because he does not regenerate health on his own, so expect to be overwhelmed by enemies more often than not. Some may call it frustrating, but I call it challenging!
Players who grew up playing games that force you to constantly quick save, quick load and just abuse the terrain to get cheap shots at enemies will enjoy this game no matter what, I would say. There isn't any variation in gameplay, all you do is search for ammo and health, and then shoot bad guys - Nothing more, nothing less. Either way, Max Payne is a classic.
