I'll start of by arguing against some of the things mentioned by reviewers of this game:
This game has gotten some flak for its camera problems and although most of that was fixed with the release day patch it was something I still heard people talk about after the game launched. First off, I would like to say that I never played original N64 3D platformers when I was a kid. My first 3D platformers were probably Spyro the Dragon and later the Ratchet & Clank and Jak & Dexter series. These games always had slight camera issues especially in small rooms and Yooka-Laylee is not an exception to this. Although the annoyance that can come from this can impact your enjoyment, for me it never did enough to keep me from playing and enjoying the game.
Another thing I would like to adress the bugs and performance problems complaints. I haven't encountered many. During my whole playthrough I think I encountered two or three times that my animation stuck after performing an action, but this was usually fixed within two seconds by just doing another action. I have not had any performance problems and my computer is so old I think toasters have better hardware. But aside my lack of these problems, these problems seemed to be larger on consoles resulting in a lot of negative reviews (especially from pre-release reviews). However, why is this game slammed because of performance problems while other (AAA-)games get a free pass on problems like these in reviews? Yes, performance problems are part of the game and if these are big enough they should impact the review, but to those reviewers I would say to also do it on other games. Don't slam this game for something you don't see as a problems in other games.

About the game itself:
I loved this game from when I started playing until I finished collecting every last little piece of collectable stuff hidden away in the expansive worlds. The worlds in Yooka-Laylee work like this: you unlock a world (jungle/ ice/ marsh/ casino/ space) in the hub-world by using a type of currency called pagies, after that you can use more pagies to upgrade the world, adding new areas and things to do. The way I played it was to go through the normal words to get all the abilities as soon as I could and then expanded all the words to go treasure hunting. This is in my eyes the best way to play as you can collect everything you need in the normal worlds to unlock all worlds and all abilities, so when I expanded the worlds I could do everything in them instead of later on having to come back because I couldn't get something because I didn't have an ability yet. However, one of the last abilities you unlock is the ability to fly. This makes a lot of the platforming that you would normally have to do to get something obsolete and thus making it a lot easier to collect everything than it should've been, taking away any challenge. On the one hand this is nice, on the other you can see it as an oversight of the developers.
One thing that annoyed me a little bit is the transformations. In every world you can find one Mollycool, a collectible resembling an atom, that allows the scientist to transform you into something that's useful in the world. However, in some worlds, you can only do one small thing with it, in others it's used for a lot of things. Why not make this a little more even across the worlds?
The aesthetic of this game is gorgeous. From the worlds to the character designs. From the music to the animations. The dialog can be cheesy with the A-O-A-O-U-A grunting of the characters which you may find amusing, annoying, amusingly annoying, or annoyingly amusing, just like in the old Banjo-Kazooie games. At first the game kind of keeps the fourth wall intact, sometimes scraping it a bit, but after a while all pretence is thrown out of the window. This 'we-know-we-are-a-game-lol" mentality combined with the obvious corporate badguy, might be a bit on the nose and especially nearing the end I noticed I lost interest in the dialog and story.
The gameplay itself I found really enjoyable, there are tons of challenges to complete and collectibles to find. The challenges are diverse and can be quitte tricky to complete. The abilities obtained are varied (even though some are only used a handful of times) and improve the difficulties of the puzzles. Every world has a boss fight which all need there own ways to be defeated. Although some (especially the first world boss) can be frustrating, it is very satisfying to defeat them and claim the prize. All these challenges let the worlds feel fresh and for me it really made me want to find all the challenges and complete them. Same with the collectibles, I wanted to find all of them even though I'm normally not a completionist. But this game made me WANT to find everything, complete everything, conquer everything.
In summary, this game has flaws and will probably not be for everyone, however I loved this game and just would have liked more worlds to explore and more challenges to overcome. I hope this game can give way to a new market for 3D platformers, a genre I thought had mostly died years ago.

I legitimately hate this game. Playtonic ought to hang their heads in shame for launching such a lucklustre successor to the great Banjo-Kazooie series.
Not only does Yooka-Laylee ignore everything from the lessons of modern game design we have learned since the late 90s, it fails to get even the simplest things Banjo-Kazooie did right 20 years ago. It then has the audacity to poke fun at newer, better games.
A terrible camera, uninspiring and lifeless levels, infuriating mini-games, boss fights which were clearly rushed through development, a completely forgettable cast beyond the titular characters and unresponsive controls leave Yooka-Laylee as nothing more than another failed Kickstarter attempt. Yooka-Laylee will be remembered along with Mighty No. 9 as one of the greatest examples of Kickstarter failures.
Yooka-Laylee is riddled with far too many moments that will leave you scratching your head asking "Why would you do this? Why would you ever put this in a video game?" Save yourself your money and many hours of frustration. Do not buy this game.

(First off, this review has nothing to do with the drama involving our beloved JonTron as I feel it should not impact anyone's impression of the game itself.)
This game is definitely targeted towards a specific niche. If collectathons are your thing, if you remember the N64 fondly, if you have a tolerance for less than optimal controls, well Yooka Laylee is for you. Let's get the cons out of the way first. The camera can be rather restrictive at times and during certain instances it is nothing short of an obstacle. The controls are also rather floaty and on M+K you will have a hard time navigating smaller platforms. Early on the dialogue is rather tedious to slog through and during the quiz segments, rather than skipping the dialogue it will just select the first answer if you button mash.
That being said, I feel this is a worthy successor of the Rare heritage, especially for a first entry into the ip. One of the most common complaints is the camera. Sure, it's a pain at times, but it's negligible in most cases. I mean, back in the B&K days we had one analog stick to work with so by comparison this is a cakewalk. Although slow at times, the dialogue is littered with witty banter and one liners. I should definitely make clear that playing with a controller vs. M&K is like night and day. The controls, being floaty as they are, benefit from being able to throttle your movement with an analogue stick. With a Keyboard, you're either floored or not moving at all.
This game isn't perfect by any means. If you have a taste for the nostalgic and a working controller, this game holds hours of fun and a wellspring of charm. Great for a more casual session.

I don't understand the mitigated reviews on this game.  It is wonderful.
This is the only space pilot game I know of that doesn't require 4 hands with 8 fingers each for all the controls.  The control scheme itself is pure genius and enough to count as an innovative, never-seen-before feature.
I won't describe it in detail, I will only say it works really well and all you need are a few keys on your keyboard and a mouse.
Preferrably a mouse with more than 2 buttons, but any decent gaming mouse in 2017 has at least 7 buttons counting pressing down the mouse wheel.  But you won't need them all, either.
Anyway, on to the game itself... This is a space-sim action-rpg. I know, right? How many games fit into that category?  Either way, this is another way this game innovates and has its unique flavor.
The campaign is engaging, and there are characters you can relate to.  There are multiple factions, some of which have their own territory, some don't.  You can't be friends with everyone, so yeah, you'll be choosing sides and living (and dying) by those choices.
The atmosphere, sound effects and music, graphics, are all immersive and just right.
Frankly, I don't know what more people could possibly want out of a space-sim action-rpg game.
I'll take off 1 point for the universe not being as interactive as I would like, and I'm really picky.
So 9/10 for this gem!  Worth every penny!

The story line itself is lethargic and not very engaging and the voice acting does not help. Super Meat Boy is a crazy jump & run game, where you can slide, jump and die a lot! The story is crazy but told in a nice way. The best thing is: the levels are made in a really smooth way. If you can figure out the special way to beat it, you "fly" through it and think: WTF? That is POSSIBLE? o.O

Fiendishly difficult for all the right reasons, Super Meat Boy offers a genuine challenge without ever feeling unfair. The controls are solid, the levels are varied and interesting, and the near-instant respawns result in a fluid gameplay experience despite countless inevitable deaths.
Upon successfully finishing a level, the player is treated to a parallel replay of every previous attempt, a brilliant feature that really serves to strengthen the sense of achievement.
I've rarely had this much fun with a game, and count it as one of my all-time favourites.

A revolutionary game in the form of a distilled platformer for the ADD generation. Not only with its challenge level and precise control does it define what difficulty should really rely on in a game (player skill, not lives-based punishment), but Super Meat Boy also manages to revitalize old school platforming notions of perseverance, muscle memory, concentration, and practice to almost zen-like levels (if you're willing to commit). Respawn times are also virtually nonexistent, giving you little chance to grieve over your last death.
By helping put a spotlight on many other interesting games via unlockable characters, SMB has increased its replay value ten-fold and helped put a much-needed spotlight on the indie games movement. The indie development model is also celebrated here, with increased emphasis on discounts and endless content (level editor, user-created level portals).
There are bosses to beat and an ending to achieve in Super Meat Boy, but it is hardly the destination of the game, something that is evidenced by the journey of 300+ timed and leaderboard-enhanced levels of pure platforming bliss that Team Meat clearly put two years of blood, sweat, and tears into. Although Dominions 4 kinda makes Dom3 obsolete, for a cheaper price you can get essentially the same intricately complex game. It's not pretty and it's UI is at best painful, but it's still easily the best "4X" game ever developed for die-hard fans of the genre. Cons:
- The worst flaw of this game is that most of the cryptic game mechanics cannot be accessed in game and you have to rely on google search to find out. For example, while researching the "construction" school of magic, you are given no clue on what you can craft from it. Even after researching the spell, you have no idea what you can craft because many of the craftable items are not visible because the mage you select do not have the required paths in magic.
When summoning a monster, you have no idea what stat and abilities that monster will have and will need to trial and error to find out. To make an informed decision in a strategy game like this you really need detail info that the game does not provide. Is a summoning a giant turtle better or a sea serpent? Who knows? Just toss a coin to decide!
- Really dated graphics
- No control over the actual battle itself. You really need good understanding of the games' mechanics (which are cryptic and inaccessible) to script your troops to do combos and perform desirably.
Pros
- Huge variety of customizations.
You can design your avatar, a pretender god in multiple ways that will drastically affect your game. Your god might be good at combat, single handedly defeating whole armies, support your faction by providing various faction wide bonus or give your troops powerful buffs in battle. The possibilities are endless.
Not only can you customize your avatar, you can customize your heroes by giving them various crafted artifacts while a variety of effects. The kind of artifacts that you can create are limited by your god's and your mages' power in the different schools of magic, so careful planning is needed.
- The game mechanics is excellent once you grasps the basics. The the variety of tactics and combos that can be pulled off are almost limitless.
- Many factions to choose from that play very differently from one another. The lore of the game is refreshingly different from standard fantasies.

I am the type of gamer who loves complexity and choice over graphics.  With that in mind, this is one of the best civilization type games I have ever played. Its similar to the old 'Master of Magic' but WAY beefed up.  Random world generation, different elemental magics, different races, hundreds... thousands?  of different units. Each with their own stats page, armors, weapons, etc.  Cast global enchantments, combat spells, or ritual spells. immensly complex magic item forging system, massive spell books, great hero and levelling systems. Endless opportunities with the right Pretender God, using the right spells. Like I said, the graphics are... basic, but it's the content I am focused on. If you like civilization, Master of Magic, and Dwarf Fortress, sign up.

Dominions 3: The Awakening (and I imagine all other Dominion games as well) promises much but - aside tons of statistics and sprites - delivers a little.
You choose a god, well a sprite for your god and go through pages and pages of descriptions and statistics while doing it. It's fun if you're into details like I am but the ingame version of my God wasn't nearly as exciting.
You start from the rather ugly map that consists most of the gameplay. There's your starting grid where you click recruit troops to... recruit troops. Then you assign these said troops under commanders which are like better troops than 'just troops'. You can choose the actions they take in battle... wait, oh, that's it! The problem is that you don't play any part in the combat itself. You move to a grid containing enemies and the combat auto-resolves to show you the outcome as a text-file or you can choose to watch the sprites go at it. It's fun for a couple times but you just start to slowly wish you could do more. But no, that's it.
Next turn begins and you recruit more troops and set the ones you recruited last turn to move and capture more grids until you find your opponents. There's endless amounts of content here if you enjoy reading a novel of statistics but besides that there's no much to do. You might argue that there's a deeper level to the games strategy and there might be, I would've died to boredom if I tried to find out.
I'm deeply dissapointed that there's also a fourth instalment of the series and by the looks of it's store page nothing has changed. It's just an add-on for Dominions 3 with now even more statistics to play around! Yay.

Is it good? Yes. I've laughed and I've teared up while playing this game. It's lighthearted overall, but touches on some serious themes. "Lol you're a dad and you date dads" is a funny gimmick, but it follows through on the premise. Characters talk about getting older, times changing, and trying to do your best as a parent and a person that comes from a very sincere place. It's also inclusive in an understated way. You have the flexibility to determine a lot of things for yourself about your dadsona (though do note the character has a lot of personality in internal monologues that you do not get to change, you're going to be a pun-loving dork who was in a ska band and had wild college roommate adventures with Craig no matter what). An earlier build the devs streamed showed the player character having been married to a woman before, but the final release allows you to choose the gender of their previous spouse, which was a pleasant surprise. Your character's daughter is also a delight.
Gushing aside, the game does have some unpolished edges I've noticed so far. Several lines crop up that assumed I'd made choices I had not, and Hugo's voice clips seem to have been recorded on a really crappy microphone or something. The character builder is a little rough. I wasn't expecting anything robust by any means, but the art style doesn't quite match the rest of the game and your character portrait is probably going to look kind of weird no matter what you do. I've also noticed some slight halos on the character images (and poorly filled pixels in my dadsona's image.)
But I would still recommend this game on the strength of its writing, and how much fun I have had so far. I don't even generally like dating simulators, but here I am. Try it. Get to know some handsome dads. Cry a little bit about how much you love your daughter.

When I heard about Dream Daddy, I was very excited. As I'm sure is the same for many people within the queer community, a dating game that's based around queer relationships that doesn't appear to use abuse or dub-con as vehicles to get to "romance" is an exciting prospect. There are so few games that show queer relationships in a positive light and to see one being made within the semi-mainstream is uplifting.
It is probably this mindset that's made me disappointed in Dream Daddy; I was very hopeful about the game and excited about it. I was looking forward to a deep, meaningful game that explored romantic relationships between two men in a respectful light. While playing, I desperately wanted to like it. Unfortunately, I do not.
Forewarning: I have played no previous dating games before so if there are certain points here that are basically found across the board in dating games and are pretty much native to the game type, then I had no clue.
review below contains certain spoilers. Not major plot points, but endings and gameplay are referenced, as well as the overall design of the game. Major spoilers are hidden within spoiler tags, but general set-ups are not.
While playing the game, your central hub is a "DadBook" where you get to click on the icons of the various characters and scroll through their likes, dislikes, turn-ons, etc. While I was scrolling, the images were jittery and at times appeared to glitch out, becoming very disorienting. It happened a lot, almost every time I attempted to click the scroll bar to scroll through information.
Similarly, throughout the gameplay itself, certain avatars appeared to freeze, pop-up before they were prompted, disappear, etc.
This relates more so I believe to my own expectations than the game itself, but is perhaps my biggest hang up on me not liking the game. To some people, the dad humor and jokes might be amusing despite their cringey-ness or maybe because of it but for me, it was just cringey. There's a section within Damien's route where you accidentally happen upon some fanfiction mixed up in all the old books within the library and was just cringey instead of entertaining. I'm sure that for some it was laughable but for me it was a severe "meh" factor.
And perhaps that's just my humor. I didn't find the dad jokes that funny. I rapidly clicked through the scene where you dance in poor dad fashion within Joseph’s route without actually reading because I found it not in the least entertaining and actually tedious. The constant stream of "bro" within Craig's route I felt cut into any of the emotional scenes and building of character. I've watched plenty of Game Grumps before, my favorite being their Blood Borne playthrough so I came in expecting a certain level of humor that I felt wasn't delivered.
For a $15 game, I expected a certain amount of play time. I simply didn't get it. I don't know if dating games are usually this short but I felt like for what I paid, this game is very short. For each of the seven dads, you get to go on 3 dates with him. The last date is the date that will get you to an ending and as such, you really can go through around 2 with each dad before you have to commit and subsequently lose your progress with the others (unless you save and go back). To me, that's not a lot of playtime or even enough time for storytelling when it comes to those characters.
by suggestion, I'd like to mention that I did click rather rapidly through at least one scene. Even so, the scene itself was shockingly short, with very few exchanges between you and the actual dad and very few choices to make in the first place.
I also feel as though the game isn't really re-playable. You go through a route. If you do well, congrats! If you don't, bummer. But I'm not very motivated (and maybe this related to my personal taste) to go back and replay over and over and over again to get a "good" ending because I simply don't feel connected to the characters which leads into my next point.
In a word, I feel like the stories are rushed. Three dates to get to know someone? The dates don't feel that long, either, something that you can rapidly click through. Hell, within my 2.7 hours of playing, I managed to complete 1 route entirely, start the 3rd date on one (more on why I didn't finish that later), get 2 done on one, and 1 done on 2 others. It doesn't feel like there's enough time realistically to connect with these characters.
The route that I finished, Craig's route, also had a somewhat jarring way of wrapping things up.
It doesn't feel like a conclusion and honestly, given how it appeared to be ending it was a surprise twist that was, well, a surprise.
The route that I almost finished but did not was Joseph's. It felt like I was playing a totally different person within this route; easily flustered, in love very quickly, debating the ethicacy of being in love with a married man, etc. etc. It was different from the bro-y, college-story telling individual I was in Craig's route. This might relate to the limited choices and attitude you can have as a dating game but all the same, it felt like there was a severe dissonance between personalities when it came to different routes. It didn't feel like the same uniform person throughout.
Furthermore, the gameplay is interlaced with your daughter and her troubles. Now, this is not a
thing, at all. If anything, I found the interactions that I had with my daughter to be the most uplifting and powerful ones. However, they don't feel linked to the entire story. I feel like it would have been better to somehow mention your own attempts at dating, or feelings about moving on from your former S.O with your daughter, and in turn maybe at least reference your daughter struggling, in broad terms, with her own troubles growing up. It feels like two different stories running parallel to each other rather than just two aspects of life that could potentially be occurring at the same time and be tied together.
The reason why I didn't finish Joseph's route was because of the damn mini-game. When it comes to the mini-games, we need far better instructions or help to figure out what the hell we're supposed to be doing in the first place. I had a conversation with a friend about the gargoyle mini-game in Damien's route, where they didn't even realize you could flip the pieces, as it only appeared possible to turn them. In Joseph's mini-game, you're somehow supposed to make a broken radio work again, but there's no arrows, no instructions, no indication of how. There's a few visual prompts of sparks flying when you hover an item over a certain area, but it still doesn't help much because dropping an item doesn't even drop it in that spot.
It's incredibly frustrating and disheartening and I feel could have been better designed to give users a better sense of what to actually do.

Before I sing praise for such a rarity of a game that you don't normally see in today's modern gaming world, I need to get a little salty, because I have a pretty hefty plate of beef here. I did find the game enjoyable to an extent, but there's just some things that have been nagging at me throughout my entire playthrough.
First off, If you're a Macintosh user (like myself) who eagerly anticipated this game's release after so long then you've likely encountered an enormous problem with the framerate. Yooka-Laylee performs very poorly on this computer platform, and because of the bad optimization you may find it impossible to do certain missions or mini-games, even on the lowest possible graphic setting. In fact I have observed that the "fastest" setting in the game is barely that; there are still vast amounts of bloom effects and reflections being rendered, just less intense than in the higher quality settings. I was barely able to scrape by the world 4 boss, for example, because instead of the challenge being in the attack patterns of the boss, the real difficulty came from fighting with a consistent 20 FPS throughout the entire battle. I honestly have little faith that the devs will actually come around and optimize the Mac version since it's obviously not the biggest demographic for this game, but the least they can do (if they don't end up making hard fixes) is make the display settings more in-depth, for example being able to enable and disable effects (like bloom and shaders) separately. This game honestly doesn't need to look this high-end to begin with anyway, because the art style and cartoonish graphics already give it a huge amount of personality that easily makes it stick out.
Now with that out of the way, Yooka-Laylee is a charming and whimsical 3D platformer that aimed to bring back the atmosphere of platformers from the N64 era of gaming, and I would say it mostly succeeded! The worlds are vast and colorful, and the characters are very memorable. The power-ups are extremely helpful while also not being too game-breaking, and the main game has a great progression throughout. I especially love the theming of each world; each of the five worlds presented give a distinct and unique feel that easily have their own experience to go with them.
Now I do mean what I say in that Yooka-Laylee follows the formula of Banjo-Kazooie down to a science. Unfortunately what that also means is that it borrows from the bad aspects just as much as the good ones. For every fun pagie there is to collect there's two or three unenjoyable ones. And it isn't necessarily because of how the buddy duo of this game control, but allow me to elaborate: For platforming and getting around the controls for the duo are par none and very fluent, but it's when the games stops doing that does it become a headache to deal with. There's Rextro's arcade games which have very uncomfortable and often slippery controls that command unreasonable dexterity to merely complete, let alone beat the high score of. Kartos's kart missions are also very annoying to control, mainly because of the speed boost and brake mechanics which are a feat and a half to time correctly; this could have been a lot more tolerable by just passing the tracks, but when you add in collecting an unreasonable amount of gems before crossing the finish line it's just an extra layer of frustration. I do, however, enjoy the pagie missions where you're exploring a piece of the map that you haven't been to before, which does add a sense of progression throughout each of the worlds. I guarantee there's at least one significant point of interest on every corner of the map, which is a great way to motivate players to explore more.
Overall though Yooka-Layle is a borderline solid game. In a way it's like a bowl of Lucky Charms cereal; there's a lot of crude, bland and unappealing contents within the product, but scattered throughout are genuinely good, "marshmallow" bits that are always a fun time. Yooka-Laylee is a good game, but there's just so many weird parts in it that keep it from being a fantastic game. It's great to see a reimagining of a classic Banjo-Kazooie platformer, but what I think wasn't considered is that when you're trying to do something like this you shouldn't also be bringing back the more frustrating parts of those games as well. Focus on the good aspects, but also learn what didn't work too.

This game has a whole new set of characters and worlds yet it still has that strong Banjo-Kazooie feel from the music to the characters and the atmosphere. It includes the more simple, small worlds but for those who want more to do and explore, you're able to expand the worlds. Including this option in the game is beneficial to a wider range of people.
The characters, in my opinion, still have that same feel but are maybe a little more lacking. Of course they can't be made to identically match those of the Banjo series otherwise they wouldn't be unique or new, and there are still a few groan-inducing puns (the first ones that come to mind are
) as well as some rude remarks from Laylee to resemble Kazooie a bit with Yooka getting after her the way Banjo did, but it feels as if the characters perhaps aren't as full. There's also not much of a wide variety of baddies. The main one is just a varient depending on which world you're in. There are a few other baddies as well, at least 4 I can think of off the top of my head, but they're all a bit difficult or impossible, at least to my experiences, to defeat. One of them requires a temporary projectile that needs to be sought out and doesn't last a very long period of time.
When I initially started playing I thought that 5 worlds wasn't a very large amount and I might be able to zoom through the game. That's where the expansion of the worlds comes into play; instead of having more worlds, it extends the current worlds and opens up more possibilities for tasks to complete or things to collect. I feel like it makes up for the possibly considered small amount of worlds. I've seen some complaints about the worlds feeling too big and confusing which I suppose I can understand some people might have difficulty with, especially those who put such a short amount of time into the game and were quick to be critical of it because it's not exactly like Banjo-Kazooie or any other Rare game from the N64 era.
Once you've explored the worlds a little more, it's actually not that difficult to navigate. The trickiest one for me so far is the third world, but I haven't spent too much time there. I know the first world and how to get around really easily, and the second world as well for the most part. Those are the only two I've 100% completed so far. I haven't spent much time in the other worlds yet, seeing as I'm not that far into the game. I jumped ahead to the fifth world to look around because its theme is a favourite of mine. Unexpanded, that world is a pretty fair size and not challenging to get around at all.
There are definitely some more difficult tasks to complete in this game. I think the best part about it is that not absolutely everything is necessary to be collected in order to proceed further. They took some of the more challenging aspects of the Banjo-Kazooie/Tooie games (like the Canary Mary race, specifically the one in Cloud Cuckooland) and included them but with more of a twist to make them their own. I personally prefer to have these types of challenges because otherwise it feels like a straight-forward collectathon with not really too much of a challenge.
The soundtrack definitely reminds me of the N64 era of music which is surely a bonus for myself, possibly others as well who loved the older games. I found that the first level especially had that sort of vibe. Along with the music, the graphics are absolutely beautiful. The graphics of the characters are well done and the scenery is incredibly visually appealing.
Generally,
I greatly enjoy the fact that there is no lives system in this game so I can die as many times as I want to without worrying about being sent back to the hub world or even the entrance to the world I'm in, unless I haven't been inside any other structure. This is a very small point of the game but I often find myself thinking how grateful I am to not have to worry about losing all my lives then having to start over and travel back to where I was.
My only large complaint so far in the approximate 40 hours I've put into the game is the camera controls and character movement. The camera tends to be postitioned at awkward angles sometimes that makes it more difficult to maneuver. In terms of character controls, I find it a bit slippery sometimes, as if the character doesn't have too much control. It's not particularly the smoothest. Although, once I started to play the game a bit more, I was able to grow accustomed to them.
All in all, there are some pros and cons to this game. The cons don't make me disappointed as it has some people, nor does it give me any incentive to stop playing this game altogether. I wish that some of those aspects could be improved but overall the game is a lot of fun and it's interesting to explore. I haven't fully finished it yet so my opinion may change by the time I've completed all the worlds and the final boss but at the moment it's a game I would recommend to people, despite some of the flaws this game has.
I understand that Yooka-Laylee might not have lived up to everyone's expectations, especially considering the high standards that were set by the N64 era of games, but based on what the team had, they were still able to put together a fairly well designed game.

This is going to be a though nut to crack, I recommend the game but it has a lot of flaws. At the same time I'm really enjoying it and in the end that is what probably counts the most.
First, lets get this straight, the amount of detail that went into this game is phenomenal. The animations, the environment and the sound effects are all top notch. No complaints there.
Even though the graphics are great, there isn't much variety in them. I get that it all takes place in this desolate post-apocalyptic world, but everything looks the same. Enter a new area on the map and behold! everything is brown and gray and there is lots of sand. Sure, the main colours shift slightly between areas and you get a bit more mountains or some other landmarks, but it still looks basically the same. Don't expect to be wowed by the scenery, this is no Fallout or Skyrim world which is lush with variation. Areas are mostly empty, there is one stronghold in each where there is some livery, but it ends there. In the stronghold there is mainly only one contact to interact with. Sure the map is littered with small and bigger camps, but the purpose is to wipe out everybody living there (resulting in even less life). And again, sadly, camps are basically the same. Made up out of old scrap parts of planes, boats, cars or rocks, ofcourse they differ in size and layout but it all looks very dull. This being despite the fact that it is all very well made and probably has the best graphics quality of any game I've played so far.
Every now and then a contact pops up on the map you can have a small interaction with, they will give you information, a quest or some money and are gone after that. Yes, it's a sad place to live in.
The sound is very well done. The cars make weird sounds and their engines sound nothing like the real thing, but they are very satisfying, and just like in real life you get a kick out of driving your car through a tunnel and letting it roar, awesome! Same with explosions, crashes, bone breaking during fights, you name it! Turn up the volume when playing this game, it probably does more to immerse you then the graphics can.
Mad Max itself as a playable character is somewhat of a problem too. His capabilities feel very limited. The best way to describe this is with his jumps, it's complete rubbish. My 6 year old can jump better then him. He's this though guy, but you can't jump over a small 30cm stone because...? This is just an example, but you get this feeling a lot when playing and exploring.
Still there is enough to do in the game to keep you busy, you have a main story line, there are small quests. You have to upgrade Max's gear, his abilities, build out your car, find resources to pay for all these upgrades, do races, clear up mine fields, collect relics, destroy bosses, destroy convoys, collect ornaments, go sniping, collect cars, fly balloons, and so on and so on...
Although some of these things seems pointless. For example, you can upgrade strongholds so that each time you enter them your gas tank will be filled up. But what is the point for doing this for each stronghold? You can fast travel between them freely, so if you've done one of them, there is no point in upgrading the others (except for achievements). Fast travel only works for your main car, which is silly because some things require the use of other cars (like clearing mine fields) and then fast travel doesn't work resulting in long tiresome drives across whole or multiple areas. It's these small quirks, which there are multiple off, throughout the game that really prevent this title to truly shine.
The difficulty of the game is also strange, for me it's becoming easier as progress is being made. At start with no upgrades and a very basic car and Max, it is difficult to survive even the most basic encounter. Destroying a convoy takes a long time, clearing out a camp is dangerous and deadly. With upgraded gear, a convoy is a matter of a few minutes at most, walking into a camp you feel like a terminator (most of the time).
Like i said at the start of my review, I'm really enjoying this title, even despite all the shortcomings it has. I'm not really sure why that is, but there is something that makes me go back to it. If you like driving around, ramming and slamming other cars and kicking and punching people in the face a lot, you might forgive all the mentioned (and more) shortcomings of this game and enjoy it just as much as I do.

--UPDATE--  Starpoint Gemini Warlords has entered the beta stage of Early Acces.  If you haven't already bought SG2, I would recommend skipping right over to SGW instead.  It directly addresses the issues found in  SG2  and offers fleet building and management while retaining the things that were great about SG2.  SG2 is still a worthwhile purchase if you have money to spare, but comparing the two, SGW is definitely a step up - including the ability to hotswap between KB/M controls and an XB1 Controller.
It's a pretty good game.  I feel that SG2 is deep enough to be interesting, but not so deep that it becomes a chore to play.  It is very RPG-like in that regard.  This isn't what I would consider a "super-complex" simulator, but the gameplay elements are more reflective of mainstream game design.  This is not X3: Albion Prelude (a great choice if you're looking for an extremely long-term 4x/space simulator game, btw.  I highly recommend X3AP, too.).  You don't need to spend hours on end just learning the game to enjoy it, but it is still a deep enough system that you can do what you want with it.  "Easy to learn, difficult to master", is I guess, as close to the truth as possible.
There are a large number of ships to be purchased and each has a number of components that can be swapped out.  The individual components can be upgraded with a variety of stat bonuses.  Crew members can be hired who will also provide different stat bonuses.  You can choose a character class at the beginning of the game that will give different abilities, and that character will gain levels as you play.  NPC wingmen can also be hired.
I like it because it is all the things I enjoy from EVE Online, but as a single-player game, with all the single-player elements I would expect.  There is an optional story-line campaign that can be played or ignored at your leisure.  I'd recommend starting the game in Campaign Mode, not Free Roam.  The only difference between the two modes is the lack of story-line missions in Free Roam as far as I can see.  Free Roam in SG2 is like playing Skyrim without the story missions.
The game is very flexible in terms of how it can be controlled.  I've seen people say that the controls are bad, but I got used to them quickly.  Once I got used to switching between control styles with the press of a couple of buttons it became a very fuid experience.  You can take manual control of ship-to-ship combat or allow the game to do the bulk of the work depending on your mood with the press of a few buttons.
You can switch between multiple camera perspectives, mouse vs keyboard turning, and/or lock the camera to your turrets or follow your ship with the press of a few buttons.  This dynamically changes the gameplay ranging from playing the game like a 1st person space flight shooter to a 3rd person EVE Online style point-and-click system complete with the wheel-menu auto-pilot system.  There is even the EVE Online style auto-targetting system that allows you to tell your ship's turrets to automatically fire at hostile targets in range with the press of a button.  Manually aiming and shooting will increase your rate of fire and damage potential, but your ability to hit the target is based solely on your aiming skills.  Auto-targetting slows down your rate of fire, but hitting targets is based on your ships numerical statistics.
The game also randomly generates side-missions, which are the standard faire ("go here, pick up this, scan that, kill something, deliver this" etc, etc.).  I can't really complain about that, though.  They're optional and I don't know what I would have done differently.  They're short and sweet and appropriately rewarding.  It's something to do and it keeps the money flowing in!
Choosing missions is a simple process.  You open up the Starmap and click on the icon to bring up the mission description and click accept (or the "OK" button to close the window if you don't want to do it).  These missions tell you the recommended level, what needs to be done, and the reward for accomplishing it.  The game also allows you to click anywhere on the map and select a "Go to" option from the pop-up menu.  This will set your ship on auto-pilot and take you to the location.  Just keep an eye on the screen for long distances.  Unlike EVE Online, objects in space are actually solid and running into an asteroid or space-station isn't going to do your ship any favors.
Graphically, it looks really great on max-settings.  It is slightly stylized, so it should age well as time goes on.  And holy crap, the customization for the ships is great.  Other games would charge micro-transaction fees for what you're allowed to do with your ship customization in this game.  You can change the name, the color of the name, the logo, the color of the logo, the paint color, the "glossiness" of the paint (to the point of making your ship look like a mirror, if you want).  Flying around in the USS SrFrogg23 with a neon-red logo and Skull & Crossbones Pirate logo with reflective black paint that you can see the surrounding stars on is pretty cool!
The game's performance on my computer has been great.  I haven't noticed any frame-rate drops, even when there's a lot going on on the screen.  There is a slight hiccup when travelling from one "sector" of the map to another (the hexagonal sections of the Starmap), but I think that's probably textures being loaded.  Not a big deal considering the game doesn't use any load screens or "instances" to separate locations.  The whole map is "open-world" so everything is connected.
If I have any complaints about this game it is the voice-acting and music placement.  The voice-acting is passable, but not great.  I really wish the devs had put the ship's voice through a few filters to give her a more synthetic sound.  I guess she's supposed to be a helmsman or something, but she constantly provides updates using the same sound-bytes and it just doesn't sound natural for a human being to provide the exact same dialog in the exact same tone for the same situations over and over and over again.  That's something I can look passed, but I think it would have been easier to accept as a player coming from an on-board A.I. system.
The music is also really nice when I'm out flying about, but docking (Anchoring) at stations has music that seems extremely out of place.  It's epic, and it's ok for a title-screen, but it gets really loud and obnoxious when I'm browsing through a station's selection of ships and component upgrades...  The station music wore out its welcome extremely fast.
The game also has controller support.  It's passable, too, but not customizable in any way that I would like.  I recommend playing with a keyboard and mouse to get the most out of the game, at least until you know all the icons and abilities by heart, but that may just be a matter of preference.  Mousing over abilities and ship commands with the mouse will show a tool-tip that tells you what the button does.  Using gamepad controls, on the other hand, doesn't provide a tool-tip.
TL;DR:  It's a good Space-based RPG that takes older, more complex space simulator games and gives them a more modern/mainstream feel.  It is easy to get into and provides a lot of gameplay flexibility.  I have only minor gripes.

BLUF:  This game's pretty awesome, if you can get past the ancient graphics and focus on the creative/imaginative aspects.
I loved the game.  Yes, it is complex, but I think the complexities are actually exagerated.  It's basically raise armies, research spells, invade provinces, collect gold, etc.  But somehow I find it 20x more engrossing than any other "4x" game (which I don't think it quite is).  There are little quirks, like that it is turn-based, but then all the movement happens at once for everyone, seasons affect gold income, but they also affect how many mushrooms grow in the forest for your witches to collect, and it's all these quirks and the plethora of races to play that make the game world feel alive.  I love how you are slowly introduced to the lore; it never feels like a chore to read it to get into the game, you just pick up some of it as your priests randomly summon some ultra-powerful seraphim that then randomly gets itself killed by wandering around the map.
Sure, there's certain techniques that are pretty powerful, and certain races in certain ages are far stronger than others, but it's a game you can learn, and like life not everything has to be balanced.  It's fun to learn, fun to play, and fun to experiment with.  Enjoy, especially if it's on sale (though I get all my games on sale :)).  Also, check out Conquest of Elysium.  Same developers, also very interesting game, and generally much cheaper.

Ambitious and with a fresh look at US-Middle Eastern conflict, this game could have been something awesome if the designers did their job.  The game assigns you objectives without telling you, leaving you to die endlessly without ever knowing what you were supposed to do to progress the story.  Weapons are portrayed horrifyingly inaccurately - if you're going to use real life forces and real life weapons, get the capacities right.  Remember Mass Effect 3's signature screw up, the "omnikey"?  This game's controls are so wonky and counterintuitive, I find myself wishing for the omnikey.  Now, I'll admit, there seems to be a common belief that failure is fun - but that's not the only way to play games, and if you are going to design a game only to appeal to those who enjoy failure, you're doing it wrong.  Spec Ops: The Line is a classic example of why shooters have a limited appeal even as gaming becomes mainstream.  Teenagers and the unemployed may have the time to fail every checkpoint over and over, but it's been decades since those were the primary demographics playing games.  Don't pay full price for this - it isn't worth it.  For $5, I can see it being money well spent, assuming you actually enjoy frustration.

I picked up the Euro Truck Simulator 2 Deluxe Bundle at the recommendation of a friend. I paid about £30 something at the time and got a bunch of rubbish games with it that I played for about seven seconds before uninstalling. However this game was worth the £30 alone.
Euro Truck Simulator is a super basic game. You drive a truck from point A to point B, that's really all there is to it. But don't let that put you off. You still need think about how to turn corners without crushing your cargo, when to indicate, etc. It's pretty realistic. I haven't played many Hitman titles over the years so I'll be judging this one primarily on it's own merit. First off, it runs smoothly with the occasional freeze. Once or twice that nearly cost me a mission but usually it was fine. The game looks great. And it feels immersive and really like an assassin game should feel. Plenty of ways to kill your targets and the world in which they operate works without your presence. They keep doing their thing even if you aren't there to eavesdrop or interrupt their schemes. I get a steady framerate (gtx 970) and use high settings. Sometimes when the load is especially heavy the game freezes up and then continues like nothing happened. Never crashing or anything weird like that. It's far from perfect but ok.
I purchased the intro pack. And after trying it out I know I will buy the rest of the game. But this allowed me to try it out and feel around it. I don't know when I'll buy considering the current selection of missions is few. Though the game challenges you to repeat the same missions over and over again in different ways which actually works. It's fun to experiment in this game. And rarely does the game punish unjustly for your attempts at freeform assassination. You can't go in guns blazin but that isn't unfair or wrong. This is the wrong game if that is what you want from your gaming experience.
Always online DRM is really annoying for people with unstable connection or living in more rural parts. I have a great connection and wasn't annoyed. Which mean that during my brief time with the game (will update if needed) their servers worked well. But I understand that people have a problem with this. It's just not justifiable for a single player game with some minor online features.
Triple A games cost a lot. And this game is obviously no exception. So it might annoy people to sell a not finished product at full price. I agree. That's why if you want to try it you should buy the intro pack first. I don't recommend anyone who just want to see if this is any good to buy the full game. But I felt I really got something out of the 13 euros I spent on the intro pack. It was fun. It felt modern and good.

This is going to be a though nut to crack, I recommend the game but it has a lot of flaws. At the same time I'm really enjoying it and in the end that is what probably counts the most.
First, lets get this straight, the amount of detail that went into this game is phenomenal. The animations, the environment and the sound effects are all top notch. No complaints there.
Even though the graphics are great, there isn't much variety in them. I get that it all takes place in this desolate post-apocalyptic world, but everything looks the same. Enter a new area on the map and behold! everything is brown and gray and there is lots of sand. Sure, the main colours shift slightly between areas and you get a bit more mountains or some other landmarks, but it still looks basically the same. Don't expect to be wowed by the scenery, this is no Fallout or Skyrim world which is lush with variation. Areas are mostly empty, there is one stronghold in each where there is some livery, but it ends there. In the stronghold there is mainly only one contact to interact with. Sure the map is littered with small and bigger camps, but the purpose is to wipe out everybody living there (resulting in even less life). And again, sadly, camps are basically the same. Made up out of old scrap parts of planes, boats, cars or rocks, ofcourse they differ in size and layout but it all looks very dull. This being despite the fact that it is all very well made and probably has the best graphics quality of any game I've played so far.
Every now and then a contact pops up on the map you can have a small interaction with, they will give you information, a quest or some money and are gone after that. Yes, it's a sad place to live in.
The sound is very well done. The cars make weird sounds and their engines sound nothing like the real thing, but they are very satisfying, and just like in real life you get a kick out of driving your car through a tunnel and letting it roar, awesome! Same with explosions, crashes, bone breaking during fights, you name it! Turn up the volume when playing this game, it probably does more to immerse you then the graphics can.
Mad Max itself as a playable character is somewhat of a problem too. His capabilities feel very limited. The best way to describe this is with his jumps, it's complete rubbish. My 6 year old can jump better then him. He's this though guy, but you can't jump over a small 30cm stone because...? This is just an example, but you get this feeling a lot when playing and exploring.
Still there is enough to do in the game to keep you busy, you have a main story line, there are small quests. You have to upgrade Max's gear, his abilities, build out your car, find resources to pay for all these upgrades, do races, clear up mine fields, collect relics, destroy bosses, destroy convoys, collect ornaments, go sniping, collect cars, fly balloons, and so on and so on...
Although some of these things seems pointless. For example, you can upgrade strongholds so that each time you enter them your gas tank will be filled up. But what is the point for doing this for each stronghold? You can fast travel between them freely, so if you've done one of them, there is no point in upgrading the others (except for achievements). Fast travel only works for your main car, which is silly because some things require the use of other cars (like clearing mine fields) and then fast travel doesn't work resulting in long tiresome drives across whole or multiple areas. It's these small quirks, which there are multiple off, throughout the game that really prevent this title to truly shine.
The difficulty of the game is also strange, for me it's becoming easier as progress is being made. At start with no upgrades and a very basic car and Max, it is difficult to survive even the most basic encounter. Destroying a convoy takes a long time, clearing out a camp is dangerous and deadly. With upgraded gear, a convoy is a matter of a few minutes at most, walking into a camp you feel like a terminator (most of the time).
Like i said at the start of my review, I'm really enjoying this title, even despite all the shortcomings it has. I'm not really sure why that is, but there is something that makes me go back to it. If you like driving around, ramming and slamming other cars and kicking and punching people in the face a lot, you might forgive all the mentioned (and more) shortcomings of this game and enjoy it just as much as I do.

I never thought that anyone would make a dating sim for people like me. Queer men, trans men, something not focused on abuse or titillation for straight fans. I've played my fair share of male-oriented dating sims and they tend to be dark, gritty, and full of assault.
But not Dream Daddy. You're a single father trying to support his daughter, who finds love in a new town. The eligible partners are also dads, most of whom single, widowers, or divorced. The  main focus is building relationships, helping one another, helping your children, and living a happy life.
Character creation lets you play a cis or trans man with no shame or awkwardness. You can choose whether your partner was a man or a woman, and whether or not your daughter is adopted or born to you. There are many outfit options, many look options, to the point I was able to genuinely make myself for my first playthrough.
Some of the minigames are very difficult, but not anger-inducingly so. The music is beautiful, the art is incredible, and the story brought me to tears several times.
Dream Daddy was worth the wait. Thank you to the whole team - I needed this. We needed this. It's perfect.

I really wanted to like this game... honestly, I did. I waited with everyone else, refreshing incessantly while we waited for what seemed like the inevitable "see you on Wednesday" tweets. I played just over an hour of this game, and I just can't. Yes, it's possible that it gets better, but as it stands, there is absolutely nothing that pulls me into this game. 10 minutes felt like 40, and I can't make myself want to play any more. The "voice acting" is nothing to write home about, half of the time the various grunts and snippets they say don't fit the scene at all, and Hugo's vocals sound like they were recorded inside of a tin can. Daisy is ridiculously pixellated against what is otherwise really awesome imagery, and the bubbly noise that accompanies the text as it scrolls merrily along the text box makes my skin crawl (which is admittedly an odd issue of mine and mine alone, and not one I think a lot of people would care about).
I like that the game is inclusive AF, and it's customizable (though in a perfect world there would be more options... the lip options were all kind of hideous, but I guess that's what beards are for). I know it's supposed to be a bit satirical, and "hyuck hyuck, bad dad jokes", but it feels a bit like they tried too hard in the wrong places. I also couldn't care less about any of the characters - I wanted to like Brian but the first interaction with him made me hate him, and Mat is literally just Wyatt from 6teen all grown up (although maybe that's just my Canadian showing), and the only possible way I could see Joseph working out is if you turn your character into a homewrecker.
Again, full disclosure, I could only stand an hour of it, and that hour felt very much like a generic dating sim. Maybe I'll take a look at it again when it goes on sale, but for now I think I'll be requesting a refund.

When I was 18. 18 years old, I saw for the first time in my life. I saw an image of clarity. What was it called? Garfield. The story here is of a man, a plain man. He is Jon, but he is more than that. I will get to this later, but first let us say that he’s Jon, a plain man. And then there is a cat. Garfield. This is the nature of the world, here. When I see the world, the politics, the future, the. the satellites in space, and. the people who put them there. You can look at everything as a man and a cat. two beings, in harmony and at war. So, this strip I saw; this man, Jon, and the cat, Garfield, you see. Yes. hmm. It is about everything. This. little comic is, oh, lo and behold. not so little anymore. So yes, when I was 18, I saw this comic. and it hit me all at once, its power. I clipped it, and every day, I looked at it, and I said “Okay. let me look at this here. What is this doing to me? Why is this so powerful?” Jon Arbuckle, he sits here, legs crossed. comfortable in his home, and he reads his newspaper. The news of the world, perhaps. and then he extends his fingers lightly, delicately. he taps his fingers on an end table, and he feels for something. What is it? It is something he needs, but it is not there. And then he looks up, slightly cockeyed, and he thinks. His newspaper’s in his lap now, and he thinks this. Now where could my pipe be? This. I always come to this, because I was a young man. I’m older now, and I still don’t have the secrets, the answers, so this question still rings true, Jon looks up and he thinks. Now where could my pipe be? And then it happens.
You see it, you see. it’s almost like divine intervention, suddenly it is there, and it overpowers you. A cat is smoking a pipe. It is the man’s pipe, it’s Jon’s pipe, but the cat. this cat, Garfield, is smoking the pipe. and from afar, and someplace near, but not clear. near but not clear. The man calls out. Jon calls out, he is shocked. “Garfield!” he shouts. Garfield. The cat’s name. But, let’s take a step back. let us examine this from all sides, all perspectives. and when I first came across this comic strip, I was at my father’s house. a newspaper had arrived, and I picked it up for him, and brought it inside. I organized its sections for him and then, yes, the comic strip section fell out from somewhere in the middle, and landed on the kitchen floor. And that curiously plain man. I did not know, at the time, that his name was Jon. This strip, you see, had no mention of this man’s name, and I’d never seen it before. But I had these clues; Jim Davis, Garfield. And then I saw more, I spotted the tiny copyright mark in the upper left corner. Copyright 1978 to. what is this? Copyright belongs to a. PAWS Incorporated. I use the local library and mail services to track down the information I was looking for.
Jim Davis, a cartoonist, had created a comic strip about a cat, Garfield. and a man, Jon Arbuckle. Well, from that point on, I made sure I read the Garfield comic strips, though as I read each one, as each day passed. the strips seemed to resonate with me less and less. I sent letters to PAWS Incorporated, long letters, pages upon pages. asking if Mister Jim Davis could somehow publish just the one comic, over and over again. “It would be meditative,” I wrote, “the strength of that.” Could you imagine? But. no response. The strips lost their power, and eventually I stopped reading, but. I did not want my perceptions diluted, so I vowed to read the pipe strip over and over again. That is what I call it, “The Pipe Strip.” The Pipe Strip. Everything about it is perfect. I can only describe it as a miracle creation, something came together. the elements aligned. It is like the comets, the cosmic orchestra that is up there over your head. The immense, enormous void is working all for one thing, to tell you one thing. Gas and rock, and purity, and nothing. I will say this. When I see the pipe strip. and I mean every single time I look at the lines, the colors, the shapes that make up the three panel comic. I see perfection. Do I find perfection in many things? Some things, I would say. Some things are perfect. and this is one of them. I can look at the little tuft of hair on Jon Arbuckle’s head. it is the perfect shade. The purple pipe in Garfield’s mouth. How could a mere mortal even MAKE this? I have a theory, about Jim Davis. After copious research and, yes, of course, now we have the internet, and this information is all readily available, but. Jim Davis, he used his life experiences to influence his comic. Like I mentioned before, none of them seem to have the weight of the pipe strip. But you have to wonder about the man who is able to even, just once, create the perfect form, a literally flawless execution of art, brilliance!
Just as in a ward. I think there is a spiritual element at work. I’ve seen my share of bad times and. when you have something. The lavender chair, the brown end table, the salmon-colored wall, the fore’s green carpeting, Garfield is hunched, perched. perhaps with the pipe stuck firmly between his jowls. Since it has drawn so much attention, i have played it recently to see what was new offline ( internet issues). For some reason it didnt show how much i played recently and my total is incorrect because i got the spacebuttplug ( tsar) and restarted a few times, played some of the story. so since you all are reading it, let me elaborate further,
What i noticed that has changed, Gravity field of wormholes, wormholes are now working, some balancing stuff, same ship enemies dont go down as fast and use their abilities.
Gameplay: The central game mechanic is the combat and trade system which are very tight, trade is simple but at times exploitable thanks to licenses and some close stations that are close by, no big deal though you can only get a few millions at most each run. Camera views, weapon systems etc were good but for the love of all that is space worthy why not include a database for weapons and enhancements like you did with trading? This might seem minor to you but it is infuritating to go to wiki ( which also turns the game to windowed so i have to restart) while same thing exists for trade. Gameplay is very solid which is why it got my hopes up. Those are pros mostly, cons would be mostly with presentation.
Story: I must say i mainly played freeroam but when i did try story mode. Something about main character put me off. It might have been choosen one wibe i got from the start (son of an admiral and all that) not to mention his accent was strange. The voice acting was done by professionals this time i see but the ghost from starcraft 2 telling me where to go felt funny, love his accent and voice.
Those are fine, what kind of broke it with me was that missions were presented through text that was in a box and UI designers would know, the things in small boxes should be small because for some reason we are not inclined to read all that. Nice flavor text on bouties though. 2 major problems with freeroam story, repetitive missions ( transport X to Y, or go here kill all that moves, very little flavor to it but if the surrounding fluff is good, that is all you need, world of warcraft did it. lots of games had repetitive missions that did not feel repetitive, Why? Answer in presentation )reputation that do not even feel like you are progressing, easier to read reputation bar and actually meaningful reputation would be nice.  I will explain the biggest problem that is connected to this in presentation. By meaningful some contact from faction representatives contacting you for special missions and thanking you for your help, you can go nuts from there. As it stands now. the only faction i know is trinity coz they have a weird space station.
Presentation: Here is the place where i loved it and hated at the same time. Graphics are some of the best i have seen, sounds are great ( computer voice being modable is good too), ship designs are hit and miss but even the ones that are bad have something good about them such as tsar the spacebuttplug, it is pretty funny how it looks but is still intimidating. Tutorial is a bit annoying but the game is complex so its fine, takes practice but not as bad as many other games ( elite dangerous comes to mind, which i quit because 4D parallel parking in a flying box is not my fun)  The problem is, the real problem is despite all those great gameplay, the space is made lifeless, it would have been so easy just to add some flavor fluff like in rebel galaxy, visit a bar, with people, get some place specific music and visuals. Officers are nothing but stat sticks. In fact let me explain the crux of the problem by drawing comparison from world of warcraft and harry protter:
In harry potter, wands are used for spell casting but are such a big deal and visible in the story that you know what they are and they make the universe feel complete.
In WoW: They are stat sticks, something you forget you had and just use for stats exactly like officers here, wasted potential.
That is why it is so painful to engage in all that space combat again and again, the space feel lifeless, like you are the only living thing in the galaxy. I understand your main thing was the gameplay and combat, i get it but you need to support it with other things. This could have been mount and blade in space easily. Why did mount and blade succeeded? Because outside of its outstanding combat ( just like this game), it had decent world building, there were lords who acted based on whats going on in the world, lords and ladies who talked, npc's who you would see face to face, so what if they had literally 2 lines of dialogue, it was still an improvement over a text box, It is even more painful when you see these gorgeous graphics but all this dead space. The only reason i considered rebel galaxy superior because it had this world building, world still felt shallow but it felt like a world, not a combat simulator.
Remember why No Man's Sky failed? Trillions of planets that all felt same and lifeless? Here it is the same thing but here is is painful because it can be fixed so easily. As a side note: combat is meh compared to other RPG games, in space simulator genre, its pretty good ( but can you make the boarding a bit more interactive? Its a space sim not pokemon) I hope this wall of text explains your worries, again i played before and after writing this review  ( after since the reactions) I think it could be great but you need to work on the world building, it is simply inexcusable with such talent you guys got.

I'm enjoying the game quite a bit because the graphics and core gameplay are enjoyable.  There's also a relaxed atmosphere to the game - I don't feel pressured into "grinding in order to get to the good part".  The story is decent and there's plenty of "flavor text",  galactic "news", and loads of other ships flying around that altogether make the game world feel alive.  The GUI is well-designed and easily accessable with the mouse - I don't even bother using the hotkeys 90% of the time.  This also means that learning to play the game does not require memorizing a bunch of hotkeys!
The random mission system is better than average compared to other games in this genre.  Also, progression happens at whatever pace you choose - you can sit near a station and shoot asteroids in relative safety for small rewards, or you can do the level-adjusted missions for a modest reward at minimal risk, or you can rush straight to the hostile sectors and do missions 30 levels higher than your own.  Or you can skip the missions entirely and capture ships, selling them for massive profits if you have the skill to pull it off.
On the negative side, the game's ambient music lacks variety, so it gets annoying quickly.  Also, the ship's computer sometimes repeats warnings more frequently than necessary, which is especially annoying if the shields repeatedly drop due to EMP effects.  These problems are simply fixed by adjusting the volume settings.  I recommend listening to some space ambient music on youtube/spotify/whatever.
I bought the game and DLC ("gold pack"), and I feel like I got my money's worth.

Overall, I think this is a pretty fun game...just not worth the $40 they want for the game + DLC.  Given that it's been released for several years now, and apparently, is still full of bugs/missing mechanics that the dev's were promising would be fixed years ago, I don't think I'll be buying anything else by this company.
The Titan DLC was rather dissapointing, it was more of a God mode than additional content...once you're in a Titan, just hit fire at will, and a few seconds later, even fleets of carriers are goners...and there's only 2 enemy titans as opponents, once you've captured/destroyed them, you're pretty much invincible.
Also, voiceovers frequently failed, the game would occasionally crash for no apparent reason, and planets/bases only stocking 1-3 of consumables is frankly annoying and ridiculous, particularly when it comes to those used for salvaging/mining.
One thing I found particularly annoying, is that on the context menu, there is a button labled Follow.  None of the in-game tutorials mention this button, and as far I can tell, it remains greyed out no matter what you have selected...and does not work to let you follow any of your escort targets, or enemies, or anything else.  Nor does it work to tell hired mercs to "follow" you...apparently, it is one more vestige of over-ambitious devs that gave up on the game to move on to something else.
I will mention that I have not tried any of the mods for the game, but as it stands by itself, it is definitely a product that did not live up to its potential.
...and the reputation system? Really? 1 kind of good vs. evil rep with all those factions? and if you go outlaw...its hilarious...once you can land on an outlaw planet, failing to smuggle on that planet moves your rep more towards outlaw(just like failing to smuggle on "good" planets), making outlaw factions(including that planet) more friendly...lol.
I mean, how hard would it REALLY have been to include a reputation number for each faction?
Don't get me wrong, I did find that game enjoyable overall...but there was so many constant things that made me feel like I was playing a beta instead of a game that had been released more than 3 years ago...

I'm a fan of space games. The problem with them has been for years that there's no depth to trading or interesting story to delve into. Quests in this one are all either mail carrier types or combat based. The fighting is fairly uninteresting as well.
On the plus side, the graphics are very good and I loved the scenery. The game does have a very large area to explore if that is yoru thing, but as I mentioned above, it gets very monotonous quickly due to lack of depth.
The other big flaw is that the only real way in this game to make money is by capturing ships. You can trade or just do missions, but it would take an awful grind to get enough money to change ships which seems like a balance flaw to me.
Even on sale, I'm going to actually suggest you skip this one. No, there doesn't seem to be much better out there, but I would say you are better off never playing than to waste time on such a shallow game.

Alright so full disclosure to start with since this game has needless controversy surrounding it.
I was a backer of the kickstarter: basic level, just enough to secure a copy of the game.
I played both banjos back on n64 and also played them recently to prepare myself for Yooka.
Where do I begin here... I've seen so many complaints about the game, many counteracting each other, I'll try to break these down the best I can. The first complaints I saw really were regarding the camera saying it made the game almost unplayable so as I played I made to sure to note any place I have severe trouble with the camera and... gotta say for the most part, what camera problems are people talking about?
I noted only two major instances where I struggled with the camera, the first being at the bottom of the ramp where the world 1 boss is, it would flip my viewing angle alot due to trying to auto correct. The other being when flying and getting too close to a wall in a tight space. In general though the camera performed very well and intelligently, are people just parroting what people said about the prerelease copies and not actually playing the game? Thats what it feels like to me.
Also to the people who say the camera is horrible compared to Banjo-Kazooie/Tooie, seriously go back and take a more recent play of it I beg you. The camera in those games are absolutely terrible. Comparitively Yooka's camera is a vast improvement.
Another major complaint is one I slightly do agree on, the collectables and how they are placed, though only slightly. Some of the collectables are placed in annoying "one shot" places where if you miss them you gotta go through the whole mini section again to try for them. This was most noted for me with quill feathers on the slides of the Casino worlds.
It later becomes trivial once you aquire flight in the 5th world but I still gotta say it was a tiny bit of design flaw if you assume someone is playing spoiler free, if they didn't know flight was comming they'd keep going at those over and over. While this isn't a huge flaw, it is one
none the less.
The last major complaint is a weird one, cause half of people are saying it captures the classic feel too well thus being full of flaws, and the other half saying it fails to capture the feelings at all being too modernized. where as my experiences were... in the middle.
The game gave me alot of classic feelings but updated as well, updated largely where needed and left alone in others. I had a great nostolgic experience while enjoying many modern features and upgrades. To me, Yooka strikes an almost perfect balance between nostolgia and modernization.
Nobody wants a completely nostolgic game, even if they say they do, they don't realize what that'd imply. So Yooka updates what needed to be updated but it also doesn't go so far that the game is unrecognizable from what it was trying to capture, It really to me is a perfect balance.
In the end it was a game made not just for Banjo fans, but collectathons in general and I feel it does an amazing job. If you don't like exploration style collectathons you wont probably like this game, but for those that do. This game really did an amazing job all things considered. Though I do advise you to not bother doing a world completely till you get flight, it will save you time and frustration.
