Pool Nation is one of the most polished indie games of 2013- the animations are shiny and smooth, the gameplay is responsive and the physics are realistic. You won't find yourself screaming at this game for bouncing your balls in the wrong direction, or glitching out and dropping your cue ball through the table. With eleven game modes including tournaments, online play, and single-player endurance mode; as well as a slew of collectables to unlock, Pool Nation has no shortage of goodies to keep gameplay fresh.
The single player component revolves primarily around tournaments where you take on AI challengers of ever increasing difficulty. Each match has an associated list of challenges, and completing them unlocks a variety of cosmetic changes like cues and balls. Standard games like 9 ball are present along with more interesting options like Golf, which challenges you to put specific balls into specific pockets. There’s also a time attack style mode, where balls spawn on the table and you have to sink as many as possible in the time limit. There are Free Play, Versus, and Online modes present too, but I had a hard time finding anyone to challenge online.
Pool Nation is a great looking game that features bright and shiny graphics that makes each game, literally, feel new and different. There are some good themes on the game's soundtrack, and though the game's controls look difficult to use, they aren't difficult to learn. There are also options that can be easily turned on or off to give players assists in a game including arrows that point at the next balls that need to be hit or arrows that show where a ball will travel when hit. All of these features combine to make an excellent presentation for Pool Nation.
But is it fun? In short stints I definitely enjoyed playing the game, but it isn’t the type of thing I’d want to play for hours at a time. Having said that, I think Pool Nation is the kind of experience that would be a hit at a house party. If you’ve been searching far and wide for a Billiards simulator, and don’t have room for an actual table, Pool Nation is probably the solution. The physics are solid, the controls allow for extreme fine tuning of shots, and everything looks super shiny. A few more game types would be welcome, but for $10 Pool Nation is the gold standard in the category.

Combat is a bit arcade-y which is kind of nice for people who seek to score high. Additional multipliers for not being hit, varying your attacks, I can see the draw to the challenge modes that further this goal. The shock gauntlets kind of cheese the difficulty by being able to override shields and foes that typically have to be stunned, so it feels like a bit of depth is lost once you have those. Perhaps alieviated when played on a higher difficulty. I just played on normal.
The stealth sections or room clears didn't gel with me. Particularly because I guess I was not great at them. Clearly them silently seems to require extensive patience since any stealth take down typically results in the enemies finding the body and them all being near each other until you wait for them to spread out again. Plus it's easy enough to just to knock out who you want and then retreat to the rafters and repeat.
Story is forgettable. Joker is bad. Other villians. Yes. Cool.
No real interesting variations to the boss fights. Just lots of enemy hoards or sneaking around. For the most part.
People who seek collectables and enjoy filling bars will find plenty to do. Clearing optional villian based objectives or performing combat challenges. I'd enjoyed clearing the map and the Most Wanted but Enigma Trophies are too numerous and same-y for me to drop the time required to gather those up. I can see the draw, though.

In my quest to find the funnest open world game this one kinda flew under my radar.  Can't really blame me since just recently I upgraded and am able to play games like this now.
Simply put this game is absolutely fantastic in everyway.  The car mechanics are the best I've seen in any game making someone like me who doesn't care about cars fall in love with it.  This is something that would have ruined the game entirely if it sucked.  But its flawless.  Just driving around the wasteland is a blast!  But combat with enemy cars is even more so!
On foot combat is just as fun if not a bit easy.  When I started playing I thought it would be similar to Batman or Shadow of Mordor but its not.  You're not nearly as fluid in your attacks.  Its just punch and bone smashing and shotgun to the face brutality.  Which is awesome in a different way.
The open world is gigantic and not a dull section to be found.  Which says a lot when its a desert wasteland that at first glance all looks the same but no.  Plenty of locations to search for scrap.  There is no shortage of exploration here even the optional collectables are fun to find!
The only area this game falls flat is the story.  Just upgrade car to fight bad guy.  Haven't finished it yet but I don't care.  The game is just an excuse to be a badass in the Mad Max world.  Much like how Shadow of Mordor is an excuse to kill orcs.
I cannot find a single thing to complain about here.  This is just pure post apocolyptic fun and I cannot reccomend this game enough.  If you like open world... If you like cars.  If you like beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of scumbags this game is for you.

Overall, I think this game is adorable. It has a story that it set out to tell for the seven different dateable dad characters (happening in tangent to a plot with your daughter as she gets closer to the end of her High School career), and it did very well to tell that story. The art is well-done, the humor is on point without being overly stupid.
As a queer trans man, I like the simple, but meaningful depth there was put into the game not only to include the ability to play as a trans dad, but also having the open (but again, simple!) option of having a past relationship with a man or a woman (who is Amanda's other father or mother). No great attention is paid to these details, and they don't add or detract anything to the game, but the fact that care was taken to include them was a nice nod to the fanbase this game seemed to appeal to.
It took me about ~2 hours to do one playthrough (admittedly, I wasn't speed-running, but actively talking about my experience with others, so it was a little slow), but I imagine that most people would want to romance all of the options at some point. For the worth of the game, I think 15 is just a smidge too high, especially since I would have loved a lot more depth given to each of the dads, but it's otherwise a fair price for a simple, memorable game that is by far one of the better and more genuine dating sims I've played in years.

Dwarf Fortress in global strategies genre. Thousands (literary) of units, hundreds of spells, tens of nations, infinite number of [winning] strategies. Really, the scope of what you can do in this game is astonishing.
The only real problem with this game is getting through a steep learning curve - manual for this game is 300 pages, it's highly recommended to read it (and you'd certainly refer to it time to time) and even manual doesn't cover all the things there are in the game.

Many turn based games try to blend high strategy with RPG elements but they fall short when compared to Dominions.  With such a dizzying array of nations, units, spells and commanders coupled with a massive number of player made maps and an engine that provides real strategic play, dominions contains an eternity of replay value for those who can grasp its juicy offerings.

I enjoy this game but for once I would like a diplomatic system added to future dominions and maybe a kingdom based on vampires and undead since you won't base on race but this game to me gets an 8 out of 10 mainly thanks to the gameplay and the fun you can have.

If you aren't sure - find the demo, which blocks technology progress at something like level 5.  This game has a very long (but not too steep) learning curve.  I'm just now beginning to read the manual that goes along with it.
So what do you want from a game?
If you want a way to spend your time which is compelling: maybe sitting in front of the computer looking at the game itself and going through some grand strategy plan, or it might be reading the book that will gently unfold "every byte in the game" for you.  If this sounds like fun (and it is!) then trust me, you won't regret buying this game.
Every "square" on the board begins at the start of the game as neutral (except for starting cities).  As armies conquer squares, they contribute to your economy, but they are also then easily conquered unless you station vast defending armies (which you're rather use for conquering new squares).  So it eventually becomes a land-grab game that I still haven't quite gotten my head around.  It's quite difficult.
The depth in the game is an insane amount of content.  Every time I play I'll discover some new item I didn't know could be forged.  I'm sure there are people who know all this stuff, but it's quite something discovering new items or spells and the possibility of new strategies as a result.
There are also placement and timing strategies to look at.
And afflictions.  I LOVE that heroes in the game can have afflictions!
Religion plays a big role adding flavor to the game and I still haven't quite grasped the historical references other than resemblences to myth.  It's almost alien almost familiar - I like how they did it.
Dominions 3 also seems to be designed to play multiplayer by e-mail, so all moves by all players are concurrent (rather than taking turns) - this is one of the few turn-based games I'm aware of which uses concurrent moves - which is why battles are auto-resolved (they have to be).  Even though battles are auto-resolved, as already mentioned, there are troop placement and timing strategies which will make a huge difference in battle outcomes (guaranteeing that troops arive at the front line all at the same time becomes a consideration).
[EDIT]
Cons:
The game does have a downside, which is the lack of automating some very repetitive tasks, such as what actions you always want a specific unit to use.  My impression is that the game designers are really good at designing gameplay and background, but horrible at designing "workflow", which are repetitive tasks that eventually wear down the player.  In it's defense, the game seems to be designed for multiplayer via e-mail - where you might make a few moves a day and games could go on for a very long time - rather than single player versus AI where you're making several moves every few minutes.

Note: This review only reflects single player. Some of the concerns should be equally valid in multiplayer tho.
Pro:
- lots of nations and spells to play with
Contra:
- no upgrade path except for magic, you start and end the game with the exact same troops
- larger empires are micromanagement nightmares (commander limits, picking up scattered units, managing troop supplies for fronline armies etc on a 45 province map is already horrible)
- tedious mopping up of beaten opponents (hopefully you didnt pick low dominion while trying to assault a water fortress with Shamblers ...)
- hands off battles
- almost non existent province development
And just as a side note there isnt really a steep learning curve, its just that you have to memorize spells and units or you will be looking up those all the time. Games like Chess and Go can offer a deep strategic experience without overboarding rule complexity. Dominions while initially fun becomes tedious and boring very quickly.

I'm not sure how to review this one. There are some issues that I have with it that are just hallmarks of past space sims. So if you hate typical downsides of space sims, then this game doesn't really break that barrier. If you're not a fan of classic space sims, then this game doesn't deliver much outside of that. But first off, I got this game when it was 80% off 2 years after it released. I got it primarily to scratch that never-ending itch of playing a worthwile space sim while waiting for Star Citizen to be a more complete game. My review is about the base game with its base story missions and content.
The main campaign is a revenge story of a son wanting justice for his dad's murder, but like past sci-fi games it quickly evolves into you saving the whole world or in this case a solar system. Cliched, I know, but I won't spoil it. The story likely took me about 8 hours to complete which I expected for a game like this. Like previous space sims before it, it allows you to do whatever you want and start any mission you want after the initial mission without an artificial lock like you need to be level X to do mission Y. Personally, I like that in open world games. There are supposedly 13 non-story mission types that are randomly generated on the map, but depending on your ship these missions can range anywhere from super easy or downright impossible. That was my first problem with this game. The randomly-created missions support the grindiness aspect of the game, and the rewards often feel lackluster even after progressing so far into the game. When you've done one ferry mission or security mission, you've done them all. There's no variation in each mission type. Just a difference in NPC ship difficulty. That's where problem 2 comes in.
You can mine asteroids, crystals, and pockets of gas in certain sectors of the map that will reward you depending on the market value and how big your cargo hold can take. After getting the ship with the most cargo capacity and mining said sectors, the tediusness and grindiness settles in quick. If you like that aspect of space sims, where grinding = bigger and better ship then this is right up your alley. If not, then look elsewhere. Personally, after ~50 some hours of mining, salvaging, bounty hunting, raiding commercial ships and stations, escorting/protecting/rescuing NPCs and scanning space anomalies, I feel like this game scratched that itch. I can't say I enjoyed the whole grind experience, but I did feel satisfaction upon earning one of the best ships in the game. Once you get past the tedium and set up a ship goal, hours did fly for me by working up the reputation and credits to earn it. If you expect not to grind for a better ship, then expect to mod the game or not get the game at all.
The leveling system is typical with missions giving you x amount of credits and experience points. You use these points to level up different abilities for one of three chosen classes (commander, gunner, engineer) that activate in-game to give your ship better stats momentarily like faster speed, more weapon damage, faster shield regeneration, etc. The reputation system is binary where doing missions for X faction will yield Y rep points and -Y rep for the opposing faction. You can side with "bad" factions, stay lawful/chaotic neutral, or side with "good" factions. I chose to be lawful good throughout the game, like a good boy scout that I try to be irl. Siding with either faction will either open or close certain planets and stations which will lock you out of a certain achievement if you're not neutral. It's a lot harder to stay neutral because the story doesn't let you choose outcomes and there aren't enough non-story missions that will help keep you neutral. So what's my problem with this? The leveling system on top of the grindy non-story missions really does show how tedius this game can get. It doesn't really get better once you reach your ship goal. I'm still left with the same missions and rewards that don't scale as much as I wanted it to.
You'd think that once you're Commander Badass with a Dreadnought, fighter ships you can deploy and merc ships you can hire, that you'd be making bank by melting everything in sight with your plasma cannons. Nope. I still have to mine/salvage/scan/trade ad infinitum to make serious money. Having a bigger ship does help with not dying every 10 minutes or so from seemingly random incursions with other giant ships, often multiple giant ships to contend with. That's another problem I have with this game. NPC ships that scale from a trivial threat to impossible come out of nowhere at random times. Even when you're technically in safe sectors of space, NPCs that are against your faction (which to me is every bad guy in the game) will spawn or decloak out of nowhere and proceed to tear you a new one very early in the game, until you have one of the best ships then you can go toe to toe with one of them. If dying repeatedly due to random incursions regardless of where you are in the map isn't your thing, then that's a big problem. I get it, space is dangerous and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s can be anywhere in the vast emptiness of space. But if I'm 10 seconds away from the good guys Navy fleet, you'd think that pirates and marauders wouldn't go that close and tear you a new one. If/when I create a chaotic evil character save, I will update this review to reflect my experience being on the other side of the law.
One aspect I failed to use in this game before this review are mods from the Steam workshop. They range from quality of life mods (better loot, more damage, faster speed) to custom assets in game (ships, stations, missions, etc.) to total conversions, so fellow Star Trek fans will be able to scratch that itch.
I'd like to say that after ~60 hours of playing this game, I will recommend it to fans of classic space sims with the caveat that there is a space sim grind to it and that it doesn't hold your hand. If you're looking for a revolutionary game that breaks the typical downsides of space sims, then please look elsewhere. If you know that you want to scratch that classic space sim itch with the understanding of the problems that I've explained above, then I do recommend this game to you.

Whether it be with a knife, a chandelier, or rat poison, assassinating any target assigned to the latest Agent 47 is a tremendous amount of fun. As a game and a concept, the newest Hitman is fantastic and offers a great sandbox stealth experience. But looking past just the game, and instead at the choice to make this game episodic, it brings up the question of whether or not this game has enough to play.
Before I answer that, I want to go into how the actual game was. As with most games, the first thing I notice is the art style of the game, and the graphics presentation. Though a few textures here and there looked slightly muddied, overall the graphics and art are great. There was clearly a lot of effort put into making the world you enter as detailed and immersive as possible, effectively making you feel like you really are at a fashion show in Paris, or a military hangar in the 70’s. While going about my business and killing people, I also noticed that I had not and still haven’t run into any bugs. IO Interactive did a great Job with the release of this episode. They made sure the game had a great presentation and, in my experience, no bugs to hinder the mission.
Yet another great part of Hitman is the sandbox stealth gameplay. Usually in stealth games I tend to get a little frustrated, but because Hitman has so many ways to take out a target, I was on my toes but having fun the entire time. If I choose to, I can pretend to be anything from a waiter to a fashion model. Disguises are also a big part of the game. They can get you into new areas that are otherwise inaccessible, and if you hit a new speed bump, there are always other people wearing outfits that you can take. Along with many disguises is many weapons. There are a plethora of ways to approach a situation and kill a target. I could spike their drink, drown them in a toilet, or even blow them up. Plus as you move through areas and eaves drop on conversations, opportunities will come up. These allow for new possible ways of killing a target. All of these elements allowed me to adapt to a situation and play the way I wanted to, giving the feeling of an almost life like or dynamic world. I also experimented with these systems multiple times out of pure curiosity. I would keep replaying the Paris mission to see how many ways I could assassinate my target, or how effectively. I even tried just dropping stealth completely and starting a firefight with an assault rifle.
However, as much fun as Hitman is, there is only so many times you can play the same tutorial and Paris mission until you just want to move on. I wanted so bad to be able to play another huge mission in another city, but it isn’t there. Sure, additions like Contracts, where you are assigned a new target in the Paris mission, are being patched in. But that’s another hour at best of gameplay. I played for five hours myself and was done. That is including any replayed missions and story cutscenes, which are probably the one weak point of the actual game. There isn’t much story at all right now, but once again, that is the problem with this episodic system. I was left wondering what is happening in this new Agent 47 story, and wanting more gameplay.
Another problem with the decisions made for this game, other than the episodic system, is the online aspect. If you are online, as you complete challenges in the Paris mission, you are allowed to prepare yourself for the mission again with tools like snipers or different starting points. However, if you are not online, you are not able to use any of these new tools and must keep playing with the starting items. This makes no sense to me in a single player game, and should really be taken out.
The online and episodic systems given to Hitman are really the only things holding it back at the moment. The game itself is fantastic, the world is detailed and immersive, the gameplay is great, and the missions definitely have a lot of replay value. I think Hitman will be much better once everything is released. Perhaps by then, the story will be much better, and there will be more than one actual mission to play. Until there is more to the game I would wait to pick it up. As fun as it is, and it is exceedingly fun, you will most likely be done the day you buy it.

Quickie review - having jumped into this game a for a li'l bit,  I must say from the start that I enjoy it LOADS better than Hitman: Absolution.  This game does alot of things right, but it does have its drawbacks.
Starting with the bad:  I haven't had any server issues and personaly I don't find "always online" single-player games to be any different from ones you can play offline, but I feel as if I should note that this game does require an internet connection regardless, since I have seen alot of complaints about it.  Now, the biggest drawback I've found in this game is optimization.  I have a pretty good build, but it does stutter from time to time, and overall just needs more work on the technical end.  More than a few times I've had to close out the game and restart it, which can be pretty frustrating.
However, the reason I recommend this game DESPITE the technical issues has to do with the way the game actually plays.  First thing: It's gorgeous.  Not in the way many games have been in the past, with super high-rez textures and that stuff, but rather in terms of the lighting (it looks realistic AF) and the animations (also realistic AF).  This brings me to my next point.  The game plays like a movie.  You know how people always say the Uncharted series is like playing an Indiana Jones movie?  Well, I'd say this Hitman game is like playing a James Bond movie, but with more murder.  The story (so far) isn't by any means revolutionary, but the way it is presented to you is truly masterful.  After the tutorials, it leaves so much open to personal choice concerning how to approach situations that I can't imagine 100%ing this one.
In the end, I'd say if you're iffy on this game, drop the $15 for the intro pack.  There's plenty to do there, and you certainly get your money's worth.  Personally, I cannot wait for future updates, hopefully including some optimization tweaks, but more than anything new (big) content.

Here's the deal guys, this games critique is very valid. Does that make HITMAN a bad game? Well, it has all the hallmarks of a negligent studio for marketing, but the core still seems to be valid so I would say no.
This version brings back all the old glory we used to love in the hitman series. You decide how things are done and have free reign of the place. Overall the controls aren't that bad, and everything seems to feel pretty fluid. The level design is pretty legit, and just on a few play throughs, I've only less than a quarter of the level. Sound design is immersive, and doesn't pull you out of the game, and characters react to you in a more realistic fashion. The graphics are actually pretty good even though they are locked at low -_-. I also have to mention the menu design is gorgeous. Really dig the art design.
I'll put it this way I think it was worth 15$, but that's all it's worth at this point.
Many people are complaining about DRM and having to be online or you get booted off while this only happened to me once I can absolutely agree with the hate. It's a single player game, this shouldn't be required. They obviously want to stop piracy, but it seems like there trying too hard. SE are you guys that broke that not only do you need to release in episodes to keep the project going, but you wasted money on some buggy DRM?
The Episodic release really pushed me away from hitman, I think it's a trend growing in the industry that absolutely shouldn't be. It worked with the walking dead, and that's where it should have stayed. It's not like the story of this game is so gripping you can wait for another portion. I mean for that matter there really is no story so far. There's a narrative, but nothing that's deep enough to warrant episodes. There basically releasing a game in pieces because they failed to finish it on budget, and on time. If this isn't the case I highly suggest you guys review your model. As it sits you got 15$ out of me, and you would've gotten the full 60$ had it been a full release. I'm not sure if I really want the rest, I kinda got the hitman hype outa me at this point.
The FPS lag is real, although my computer really didn't have trouble with it. Keep in mind I did have to turn it down from ultra to high, though, and it seemed to work. I'm also significantly over the recommended hardware requirements. It ran alright, but there were serious lag spikes in certain places. Definitely not that optimized. Also, the locked graphics thing was kind of a joke. I feel like you think were children when things like this are done. What's the point in putting graphics settings if you just going to dictate them anyways?
I had fun with it, and I guess there's more good than bad to a degree, but the bad is so blatant in your face it's hard to overlook it. I have to give this a thumbs down, simply as a sign of protest with what the AAA community tries to pull on its customer base. If this was not in episodes I would overlook much of the cons, but it all adds up to one stinky pile of sadness.
If you are on the fence, though, I do recommend you to buy the intro pack. Play the game for a bit, and leave a review. I only hope SE listens to its fan base and fixes some of this. If they do I will buy the full game and change my rating, but like most AAA titles the player base is ignored. If that's the case I will make sure they don't get anymore of my $$.

I'm not a huge fan of Banjo-Kazooie, but I do love games with collectibles.  Donkey Kong 64 and Mario 64 were my favorites.  If you like collecting all the things in this genre of game, I think you will enjoy this game too.  It took me about 38 hours to 100% this game playing with a keyboard and looking up where the last two pagies were after looking everywhere for them.  This game is not perfect, but it definitely captures the best of what this genre of game once was.
World sizes are just right.  There are a number of reviews saying the worlds are too small or too big.  This probably means the worlds’ sizes are just right.  I did not begin to get bored with with a world until I was down to the last few pagies/quills to find.  You can add the pagies you find to a world’s book to make the level larger.
Engaging Boss fights.  The boss fights have simple mechanics but require a little practice to master.  Once you figure out the movement patterns and what you need to do to damage the bosses, they become fairly easy.
Fun dialogue and voices.  The voices I thought were entertaining but I can see them being annoying if the sound is too loud.  Take a moment to turn down the sound effects a tad in the game menu if necessary.
New puzzles and mechanics in every world.  Some of the shape changing mechanics were only useful for collecting one or two pagies.  Wish they were used a little more.
Camera issue. In a couple levels, the camera locks in place in an attempt to make the area play like a side scrolling platformer.  The camera is at a little bit of an angle causing Yooka and Laylee to move away from or towards the camera a bit when walking left or right.  This made jumping between platforms in these sections a bit of a pain. Keep in mind, I payed using the keyboard.
Key bind issue.  The game seems to be lacking a key binding for the B action when using a keyboard.  Luckily B is only used to answer NO on yes/no screens.  You can press escape to imitate a “No” response.  This opens the main menu effectively backing out of the yes/no screen.  This does not work when interacting with Kartos and Dr Puzz.
Arcade mini games.  I liked the kartos racing game, the controls were a little odd however and difficult with the keyboard.  Would have liked to see more courses.  The other arcade games were a little dull.  Up-N-Nova was especially annoying, just a fancy flappy bird game.  I liked the Rocket Barrel levels in Donkey Kong Country Returns better.
The Flappy Flight ability allows you to fly.  This allows you to completely avoid some of the platforming puzzle mechanics you would normally have to complete to collect some of the pagies.
One bug I ran into. Do not use the Sonars Splosion to break the mushrooms on the underwater platform covering the Mollycool.  This will break all the mushrooms at the same time and the platform will not be triggered to float to the surface.  If you do, you will need to completely leave the world and re-enter to reset the mushrooms.

Once I encounter a bug that prevents me from reaching 100%, even if I'm at like 60%, I have no desire to get to 99% if that makes sense. As soon as I encountered a bug that would prevent me from getting to 100%, I lost all desire to continue. Hopefully there will be a patch to address these issues, but until then, I can't recommend the game. If these things get fixed, I will amend my review.
Edit: The bug that was preventing me from moving forward to 100%, needed a couple of extra tries to complete. but was eventually doable. I'm not 100% yet, but i'm confident the Devs are working hard to fix any bugs in the game as they reached out to me about this particular problem. I've been excited about this game for a while now and I am very happy that my excitement wasn't disappointed in any way!
This is a very different kind of Dating Simulator which makes games like HunyPop look incredibly bland and superficial.
Most people expect nothing else from Dating Sims but stereotypical characters, a whole lot of awkward and unrealistic flirting, bribing of your 'crushes' with gifts and nice things to say which eventually lead to the main character getting into the oversexualized girl's panties.
Good Lordy I am glad to say that Dream Daddy is anything but that.
Your Dadsona (which you are free to create at the beginning of the game) actually has a whole lot of personality and flaws. He's a single father of an 18 years old daughter moving into a new neighborhood full of other Dads to socialize with. Dates actually help you to get to know the other characters and let me tell you, I am having difficulties to decide which one my Dadsona's gonna hook up with!
They're all very interesting characters and each has his own charme.
Here some other things that I really like about the game:
+ The dialogue is very well written and doesn't feel forced and/or unnatural.
+ The art is amazing and especially the characters look incredible
+ A lot of inclusion
+ Very supportive of Dads taking care the kids rather than the mom
+ No oversexualization of anyone
+ The voice acting adds to it and is especially fun if you're familiar with the Game Grumps
+ Fun little minigames
The only thing that bothers me is the music. Sometimes it gets a little repetitive and can get on my nerves, but this is anything but a dealbreaker for me. I can deal with that.
Definitely a must-buy if you're into games that include cleverly written fun dialogue, charming characters in a heartwarming story that helps you relax and take your mind off things.

Dream Daddy is a wholesome, well written and engaging visual novel/dating sim. It's well worth what it costs. The characters are all unique and likeable and interesting. The writing is also very witty at times. The artwork is vibrant and colorful. Each of the dating paths are very unique and charming.
*NOTE* It's important to note that Dream Daddy is a PC, PG kind of game. It a family-friendly affair meant for a much broader audience, so much of the dating is toned down.  It reads and is presented like a family-friendly TV show. This is not a bad thing, it's good to see a gay dating sim that can appeal to a wider audience. There are Mature/explicit dating sims out there and then there are games like this, which are much more PG. Variety is the spice of life and Dream Daddy will appeal to a much wider demographic.
Dream Daddy at it's core is about family and the love of that family, moreso then the love of the two daddies. It's full of love and wholesome dialogue.
Still, some may go into this expecting a hardcore gay dating sim. This is not that. If you want a more explicit/mature gay dating sim, check out Coming Out On Top.  (Great mature/explicit dating sim).
If you want a wholesome dating sim filled with heart that just happens to be between dads. Dream daddy is perfect.

I highly recommend this game to any strategy enthusiasts or fans of mythology out there. I'll go ahead and get the (tiny) amount of bad out of the way - the game has an unusual user interface, and selection of units can be especially tedious sometimes. With that detail out of the way, I only have good to say about Dominions 3. The writing in the game is top-notch, and very detailed. You often have to play multiple races to get a fuller picture of the history, but it's rich and satisfying once you put it together. The Tuatha and the Fomorian Giants are a good example. The game plays in a standard fashion with territories and movement, much like other turn-based games. However, to locate the useful goodies in a territory, you'll have to cultivate a few powerful mages, to find hidden sites that can provide mana gems, unique units for recruitment, or unique effects once unearthed. You'll need them (and magi once again) for the forging of magical items to equip your agents, priests, mages, generals, and your Pretender God. But the true meat of the game is in spreading your dominion (aka faith) across the map. It is the source of your power, and since it can flow into enemy territoy, it can also hamper their efforts to withstand your (inevitable) attack. Be sure to build lots of temples in your own honor! Put those puny mortal mages to work researching powerful magic that can affect the whole world. Turn day to perpetual night, bring on and endless winter, kill someone anywhere in the world, dispach the flying monkeys! Last Pretender God standing wins the prize - true Godhood. Sounds simple, right? Think again. It's a deep and complex game, and can be quite the challenge at times. So join in the fun, weave your own epic tale! Smash vampires with giants, ♥♥♥♥♥ queens (yes, its a real pretender) with a midget masher, run from Cthulu! It's all in there, and waiting for you!

Since all the other recent reviews were so negative I avoided this until it was 80%-off.
If you can get it at that price then I certainly recommend it but that doesn't make liars of the other reviewers - at full price it is too buggy, limited and awkward (when you start) to recommend.
Bugs (under Win 10) - rare crashes to desktop after 10+ hours continuous play, not-at-all-rare and repeatable loss of accepted (but not completed) missions on loading a game.
Limited - like most space games it's deliver this there, do this there, kill that there.  Get money and experience for a bigger ship so you can do the same missions against bigger enemies.
Awkward - the context-menu takes a bit of getting used to and there can be a LOT going on at some points so you need to practice to keep up with everything.  This is especially true when boarding ships in the middle of an ongoing battle, but then capturing three or four ships in a single engagement is unusual and earns mega-credits.  Seriously, play it right and you can buy a ship, use it to capture enemies in a battle and immediately afford the next bigger ship.  Practice does pay off though and after a few hours it all feels pretty straightforward.
Bigger, longer battles really bring out the awesome in this game.  It might not be Eve level but it has Elite beaten!  I have seen groups of 4 factions fighting each other (with me generally mixing it in the middle ^^) with reinforcements spawing/arriving for battles of 20-30 or so ships at a time, lasting 20 minutes and leaving more 'derelict's than I cared to name.  That's nice, because you can drift around after the battles and loot all those dead ships for all sorts of goodies.  Naturally,  you have to be in a pretty substantial ship yourself if you're going to survive such an event.
Broadly, it starts grindy and confusing, quickly gets interesting and gets better the longer you play.  Until 'been there, done that' sets in (in free roam).

Jedi Academy is the last of the "Legacy" Jedi Knight games before Force Unleashed came out and bummed all JK fans out. Jedi Acedemy is (Predictably) the best looking of the JK games and the smoothest in terms of control and capabilities. You start out and right away have missions in any order you wish. The missions are of good variety and interesting. There are some that are (in part) on rails or guided, but for the most part, there is a lot of freedom to handle the levels how you wish.  Use a lightsaber or guns. Use force powers or no.  Use light force powers, dark, or the combination.
Pros:
-There is very much still an active multiplayer scene.
- Lots of mods and built- in support for them if thats your thing
- Multiplayer options include bots.
- Pretty good level design, good sense of power and flexibility.
- It is fun. A lot of fun.
If there are any cons, it would be the following:
- There are some force powers that were in older games (like force jump) that are not here.
- There are some moments where they just HAD to squeeze in nostaglia for the sake of nostalgia. It is fun at first, but gets kind of annoying after a while. It doesnt happen too often though.
- The levels are generally a BIT smaller than say Jedi Knight, but a lot more is going on, so I guess thats to be expected.
- There is no lightsaber in first person like in JK.

Sift the combined flours and cinnamon into a large bowl. Stir in the sugar and make a well in the centre. Yooka-Laylee is a 3rd person platformer from the same people who created Banjo-Kazooie. The game consists of exploring open levels collecting items though contained platforming challenges, puzzles, and secrets to learn new moves and unlock more worlds. The controls feel tight and while Yooka-Laylee's move kit might not bring a whole lot of new items into the genre, it does a good job of using the moves it provides. I only got into a couple of tiffs with the camera over 12 hours of playtime, and I never felt like it detracted from the experience. The artstyle feels coherent, colorful, and aesthetically pleasing. The level designs felt good, with plenty of room for roaming around looking for secrets.
The difficulty curve isn't as notorious as some popular platformers, but the game can be unforgiving in select parts, especially the boss fights. The pacing can also slow a bit with a few poorly placed unskippable cutscenes, the worst offenders which take place right in the middle of said boss fights. The writing didn't create an interesting narrative (I don't think it was really intended to), but there is some good humor in the dialogue.
For better/worse, the game sticks very close to the Banjo-Kazooie formula and I wish they had taken a few more bolder steps distinguishing the game from its predecessors. They executed the forumla well however, and I enjoyed my time playing it.

TLDR PRE-CONCLUSION:
Yooka-Laylee is a colorful, whimsical game that fits in well with the standard of mascot platformers of old.  Unfortunately, it has elements that may or may not bring the whole affair down depending on the type of person you are.
If you're just looking to have fun, enjoy the cuteness, and finish the game as fast as possible -- 8/10.
If you feel compelled to find everything, collect everything, and do everything there is -- 7/10.
WHAT I LIKED
The Visual Design -- In all honesty, I never played Banjo-Kazooie, which is the biggest source of "parent DNA" for this game, so I don't really see it through nostalgia glasses.  That said, I found a lot of things about the design appealing.  The bright colors and bouncy, squishy features, like the best of Rare games of old (as one would expect).  The soft, cartoony designs of the major characters, complete with a memorable two-color asthetic for all of them.  It all combines into something that is appealing and endearing in a kid-friendly way, like the best cartoons with a wide-ages appeal.
The Music -- Now, after having finished the game, I still find myself mentally replaying some of the music that played and replayed over my adventures, proving that it has a bit of an earworm quality to it.  It transitions easily from happy-fun medlies of bright spring days in butterfly-ful fields, and then goes into brassy, powerful overtures that would make good theme songs for the best cartoon villains.
The Sound Design -- One of the things you can do in the game is eat butterflies to regain health by snatching them up with Yooka's long chameleon tongue.  The little yelp they make when you do so made me grin every single time, and I would find myself eating butterflies when I didn't need to, just to hear that sound.  This copious level of cute applies to so many of the sounds in this game.  Every squeak, skwonk, and grunt of exertion as Yooka and Laylee jump, bounce, fly, and roll around the levels is pleasant and adorable.  Every enemy has a clear and defined noise that lets you identify them without seeing them.  Levels have environmental touches to their sounds which are great.
The Level Design -- Each level is quite large, with plenty to see and do.  The fact that you can go back and expand them with Pagies makes it more fun, because you can wheel around in them for a while, change the level, and dive back in to marvel at what's different, which is sometimes pretty extreme.  Levels can vary from twisty areas full of hazards to vast, wide-open spaces full of towering details far above the ground.  Always, there are caves and nooks to find that lead you to smaller, self-contained areas of challenge and exploration.  Exploration is heavily rewarded, in fact, as you can often find hidden items in obscure places.  If you find yourself getting overwhelmed or that the level is wearing out its welcome, the beauty for the more casual player is that you can skip a great deal of them, as you like.  For the most part, you don't need to collect anywhere near the full amount of Pagies per level in order to progress through the game.
Also of note, the transformations can be a fair bit of fun, and usually apply to a small enough scope of the entire level to not be overbearing, but . . . (read on).
WHAT I DIDN'T LIKE SO MUCH
The Visual Design -- Specifically, the camera.  For the most part, hitting the auto-snap button will keep the camera wrangled well enough, or even keep it behind you for more precise driving, but there are sections where the camera will snap to a set position without warning, and this can be jarring.  One of the cardinal sins of this design is that if you're going to steal the camera, keep the character moving in the same direction until they let go of the stick, regardless of which way they're pushing.  If I'm pushing forward and suddenly the camera snaps in front of me, I don't want to then turn around and go back the way I came, leading to annoying bouts of back-and-forth as you try to wrap your head around it, and the camera keeps snapping to and fro.
The Sound Design -- Like I said before, I've never played Banjo-Kazooie, so this particular brand of vocal utterance often hits me as teeth-grating.  The whole repetitive-grunty-noises to represent the dialogue they're supposed to be saying can be humorous the first few times (and it's a creative way to not have to record a lot of voice lines), but after hours and hours, it can drive you nuts.  A lot of the time, you can quick-skip your way through dialogue exchanges, so it's not so bad, but there are numerous places where you can't skip, and have to just endure.  Some characters, like the titular two, aren't so bad, but characters like Capital B make you want to drive nails into your ears after a while.
The Level Design -- It is super easy to get lost in some of these levels.  Getting turned around, not being able to remember which cave entrance lead to which area, areas that are hard to navigate and easy to fall off of.  It's not all roses.
The area-transitions, complete with fade-out and slide whistle, are overwhelming.  There are SO MANY of them.  A particular zone in the Glitterglaze Glacier world is just the worst for this, because it happens between every room.
Some of the minigames and event-fights are excrutiating, with obtuse implementation, slidey and unresponsive controls, or just lackluster gameplay.  Some of the transformations count toward this, with you having to navigate touchy areas with a form that slides all over the place, and even a boss fight later on that it's hard to avoid getting hit during because of the controls.
A lot of this is mitigated by the fact that, for the casual player, you can avoid most of this.  Even the boss fights.  The amount of Pagies you need to open up new worlds, expand them, and then move on is quite small.  In the end, you only need about 2/3 of the total Pagies to even face the final boss, and those are the easy ones to get.  So anything that annoys you, you can most likely just skip.
For those like me, though, that are obessively compelled to ferret out every last thing in this game, though, this leads me to my last negative point . . .
Collecting Everything -- Most of the problems Yooka-Laylee has are based around wanting to collect everything.  Granted, excusing poor design by saying "you can skip it" isn't really great, but when you have to play a particularly bad section over and over and over again for a single Pagie because it's the last thing in the world, and you have to have that nice, round number, it can drive you up the wall.
There is a particular powerup you can get that supposedly tells you when you are near "rare things" in the level, which helps you find those last few Quills or errant Pagies in a level.  But it's kind of a lie, because it doens't help you find EVERYTHING rare.  Want to find that last health or energy powerup?  Want to find the Ghost Writers?  Want to find the Play Coin or the Mollycool?  Tough luck!  Those don't count, I guess.  And some of the levels (I'm looking at you, Moodymaze Marsh) are so full of nooks and crannies and hard to reach spots you might never see.
There are artificial attempts to pad things out, such as in two spots where you don't have to find just one Pagie, you have to find a handful of pieces to make a single Pagie.  There are challenges you can only overcome by using your acquired abilities in ways you had no idea they could be used, as the game doesn't teach you how, and you have to find out through your own flailing experimentations.  And all of this with the endless backtracking, including the hub world that takes quite a bit of time to traverse, relatively.
If you're the type of person who can find everything without looking up a single thing in a guide, I salute you.
At any rate, I did enjoy the game, and would like to see a sequel, but it's not without its faults.  Especially if you're OCD about 100%.

Taking over from Rocksteady for the third game, WB Games Montréal tries to reach the heights of the first two Arkham games with an interestingg origin story of the Dark Knight. But can they live deliver and live up on the expectations? It's around two years after Bruce has put on the mask for the first time, so he still supposed to be a newbie at his outings at night. This Batman, however can act and look like a beginner but his moves tell us otherwise.
When it comes to gameplay Origins is almost a clone to Arkham City. The combos, special moves and counters look and feel like the same. There are time when you feel the new team tried to innovate here and there, but those, like countering enemies, aren't decisive enough. On the other hand any game would be delighted to have a combat system like Arkham City, so in the matter of fact the gameplay still works perfectly. It's just that the innovation is missing, which is the game's greatest flaw. There are new gadgets, but even those are sometimes carbon copies of the missing ones, for example the Glue Grenade which has the exact same effect as the Freeze Grenade in Arkham City.
One thing you can certainly be hyped for in the game is its story. The game delivers from that perspective putting in front of you a greatly crafted, interesting story which is furthermore amplified by the cast. The Joker, Bane, Black Mask star in the game but others have their important roles as well. It's a tale that is on par with the comic books. And one more word about the cast; even though the Batman's and Joker's voices has been replaced most of the time you won't notice any major difference as Roger Craig Smith and Troy Baker both make hard effort to genuinely impersonate those two epic characters.
So, yes 8 assassins are after you on Christmas Eve to kill you even though you aren't as big player in Gotham as you'll become. Interestingly not all of them get the same amount of space. One thing the games does very well are the boss fights. In the first two games there weren't any really challenging and grand boss fights as we had hoped for (except Poison Ivy), but in this game almost every boss has its differently paced fight. There is a different strategy to beating every one of them. This keeps the games varied and you'll always look forward to the next boss. While beating up assassins and progressing in the story there is the moment when you suddenly realize that "this is THE time". The time when those two will meet...for the first time...and you are about to witness it all. It's a thing the creators weren't allowed to screw up. It had to be epic. And it is. The time when Joker reflects on his first meeting with Batman is just unbelievably awesome.
Arkham Origins is a really good looking game but there is very little innovation over Arkham City. It's not the best looking game of 2013, but looks great enough to hold up with the competition. Mainly the character models are those that stand out. Batman, Joker, Bane and all of the major characters look detailed. On the audio front it isn't as strong as City. Simply the prominent melodies aren't there that support you as the predator of the night. It's a bit of a disappointment.
After you finish the main campaign, which shouldn't take longer than 8 hours, you can do the side-quests Arkham City style. The overall content here is somewhat less than in the second game, but you can easily squeeze out 20 hours by searching every inch of Gotham for data packs and tags on wall. What is very discouraging that WB Montréal didn't have the balls to bring some innovation where they really could have. And those are the side quests, which are again mostly copies of those in Arkham City. There you had to look for phones by the time the counter hit zero, here you have to race to bombs. Before you had to collect question marks, here you have to pick up data packs. The names and locations are changed, but most of the work you have to do remained the same. If this wasn't a Batman game everybody would call it a rip-off. Crime scene investigations are the one that stands out. Those are really new and fun, but it's not groundbreaking. We appreciate the effort though. When you're finished you can fight in the familiar challenge mode or the new multiplayer.
Batman: Arkham Origins is a super game that took everything that made Arkham Origins a stellar title and kept all of them. However, they played it very safe introducing only a handful innovation none of which is strong enough to hold out. The side-quests are a real disappointment. When you are like Arkham City you are great, but after playing that game for 40 hours it's not enough just to be like it. Fans will appreciate the story, but everything else (missions, quests, places, etc.) is something we have seen already. And this is why the game will divide fans and players.
Rating: 85/100; Replay Value: 3/5; To Beat: 8 hours (main campaign), 20+ hours (with collectibles); Played on: normal.

Whether it be with a knife, a chandelier, or rat poison, assassinating any target assigned to the latest Agent 47 is a tremendous amount of fun. As a game and a concept, the newest Hitman is fantastic and offers a great sandbox stealth experience. But looking past just the game, and instead at the choice to make this game episodic, it brings up the question of whether or not this game has enough to play.
Before I answer that, I want to go into how the actual game was. As with most games, the first thing I notice is the art style of the game, and the graphics presentation. Though a few textures here and there looked slightly muddied, overall the graphics and art are great. There was clearly a lot of effort put into making the world you enter as detailed and immersive as possible, effectively making you feel like you really are at a fashion show in Paris, or a military hangar in the 70’s. While going about my business and killing people, I also noticed that I had not and still haven’t run into any bugs. IO Interactive did a great Job with the release of this episode. They made sure the game had a great presentation and, in my experience, no bugs to hinder the mission.
Yet another great part of Hitman is the sandbox stealth gameplay. Usually in stealth games I tend to get a little frustrated, but because Hitman has so many ways to take out a target, I was on my toes but having fun the entire time. If I choose to, I can pretend to be anything from a waiter to a fashion model. Disguises are also a big part of the game. They can get you into new areas that are otherwise inaccessible, and if you hit a new speed bump, there are always other people wearing outfits that you can take. Along with many disguises is many weapons. There are a plethora of ways to approach a situation and kill a target. I could spike their drink, drown them in a toilet, or even blow them up. Plus as you move through areas and eaves drop on conversations, opportunities will come up. These allow for new possible ways of killing a target. All of these elements allowed me to adapt to a situation and play the way I wanted to, giving the feeling of an almost life like or dynamic world. I also experimented with these systems multiple times out of pure curiosity. I would keep replaying the Paris mission to see how many ways I could assassinate my target, or how effectively. I even tried just dropping stealth completely and starting a firefight with an assault rifle.
However, as much fun as Hitman is, there is only so many times you can play the same tutorial and Paris mission until you just want to move on. I wanted so bad to be able to play another huge mission in another city, but it isn’t there. Sure, additions like Contracts, where you are assigned a new target in the Paris mission, are being patched in. But that’s another hour at best of gameplay. I played for five hours myself and was done. That is including any replayed missions and story cutscenes, which are probably the one weak point of the actual game. There isn’t much story at all right now, but once again, that is the problem with this episodic system. I was left wondering what is happening in this new Agent 47 story, and wanting more gameplay.
Another problem with the decisions made for this game, other than the episodic system, is the online aspect. If you are online, as you complete challenges in the Paris mission, you are allowed to prepare yourself for the mission again with tools like snipers or different starting points. However, if you are not online, you are not able to use any of these new tools and must keep playing with the starting items. This makes no sense to me in a single player game, and should really be taken out.
The online and episodic systems given to Hitman are really the only things holding it back at the moment. Quickie review - having jumped into this game a for a li'l bit,  I must say from the start that I enjoy it LOADS better than Hitman: Absolution.  This game does alot of things right, but it does have its drawbacks.
Starting with the bad:  I haven't had any server issues and personaly I don't find "always online" single-player games to be any different from ones you can play offline, but I feel as if I should note that this game does require an internet connection regardless, since I have seen alot of complaints about it.  Now, the biggest drawback I've found in this game is optimization.  I have a pretty good build, but it does stutter from time to time, and overall just needs more work on the technical end.  More than a few times I've had to close out the game and restart it, which can be pretty frustrating.
However, the reason I recommend this game DESPITE the technical issues has to do with the way the game actually plays.  First thing: It's gorgeous.  Not in the way many games have been in the past, with super high-rez textures and that stuff, but rather in terms of the lighting (it looks realistic AF) and the animations (also realistic AF).  This brings me to my next point.  The game plays like a movie.  You know how people always say the Uncharted series is like playing an Indiana Jones movie?  Well, I'd say this Hitman game is like playing a James Bond movie, but with more murder.  The story (so far) isn't by any means revolutionary, but the way it is presented to you is truly masterful.  After the tutorials, it leaves so much open to personal choice concerning how to approach situations that I can't imagine 100%ing this one.
In the end, I'd say if you're iffy on this game, drop the $15 for the intro pack.  There's plenty to do there, and you certainly get your money's worth.  Personally, I cannot wait for future updates, hopefully including some optimization tweaks, but more than anything new (big) content.

Here's the deal guys, this games critique is very valid. Does that make HITMAN a bad game? Well, it has all the hallmarks of a negligent studio for marketing, but the core still seems to be valid so I would say no.
This version brings back all the old glory we used to love in the hitman series. You decide how things are done and have free reign of the place. Overall the controls aren't that bad, and everything seems to feel pretty fluid. The level design is pretty legit, and just on a few play throughs, I've only less than a quarter of the level. Sound design is immersive, and doesn't pull you out of the game, and characters react to you in a more realistic fashion. The graphics are actually pretty good even though they are locked at low -_-. I also have to mention the menu design is gorgeous. Really dig the art design.
I'll put it this way I think it was worth 15$, but that's all it's worth at this point.
Many people are complaining about DRM and having to be online or you get booted off while this only happened to me once I can absolutely agree with the hate. It's a single player game, this shouldn't be required. They obviously want to stop piracy, but it seems like there trying too hard. SE are you guys that broke that not only do you need to release in episodes to keep the project going, but you wasted money on some buggy DRM?
The Episodic release really pushed me away from hitman, I think it's a trend growing in the industry that absolutely shouldn't be. It worked with the walking dead, and that's where it should have stayed. It's not like the story of this game is so gripping you can wait for another portion. I mean for that matter there really is no story so far. There's a narrative, but nothing that's deep enough to warrant episodes. There basically releasing a game in pieces because they failed to finish it on budget, and on time. If this isn't the case I highly suggest you guys review your model. As it sits you got 15$ out of me, and you would've gotten the full 60$ had it been a full release. I'm not sure if I really want the rest, I kinda got the hitman hype outa me at this point.
The FPS lag is real, although my computer really didn't have trouble with it. Keep in mind I did have to turn it down from ultra to high, though, and it seemed to work. I'm also significantly over the recommended hardware requirements. It ran alright, but there were serious lag spikes in certain places. Definitely not that optimized. Also, the locked graphics thing was kind of a joke. I feel like you think were children when things like this are done. What's the point in putting graphics settings if you just going to dictate them anyways?
I had fun with it, and I guess there's more good than bad to a degree, but the bad is so blatant in your face it's hard to overlook it. I have to give this a thumbs down, simply as a sign of protest with what the AAA community tries to pull on its customer base. If this was not in episodes I would overlook much of the cons, but it all adds up to one stinky pile of sadness.
If you are on the fence, though, I do recommend you to buy the intro pack. Play the game for a bit, and leave a review. I only hope SE listens to its fan base and fixes some of this. If they do I will buy the full game and change my rating, but like most AAA titles the player base is ignored. If that's the case I will make sure they don't get anymore of my $$.
It's Hitman, big worlds and bigger things to happen. It's episodic, everything else doesn't matter.

I was not a fan of this game.  I normally don't play this kind of genre, but I was swayed by the reviews.  However, I found the game to be pretty tedious, and not fun or clever.  It had humor, but G rated humor you'd see in kids cartoons.  The "combat"  consists of you moving a small square around a 2 inch arena, and memorizing which squares to touch or avoid.  Also, you have to choose between several actions that aren't logical, but totally determine how the combat goes.  I basically just followed the online guidebooks because otherwise it was very tedious to spend 30 minutes dying against an enemy several times before discovering you apparently have to hug this enemy three times in a row, instead of fleeing, surrendering, fighting, etc.  I suspect everyone does the same thing, as for such a small game, the online guidebooks are very popular.
Also, a large portion of your time will be spent reading text scroll across the screen, as the story plays out.  I ended up finishing the game out of spite, and then had to sit through like a 20 minute ending scene that was horribly slow and boring.
So if you love the original zelda type games, you might like this, but if you like games that are after 1987, this might not be for you.

Dominions 3 stands as one of my favorite strategy games of all time. It's not really that similar to anything else; the combat is all automatic, and your main job (as a god) is to manage your empire, build armies, build forts, research and cast spells, and plan out where your armies will go.
The graphics are sufficient for the job they do, and there's a plethora of addtional mods and maps and what not available for it.
All told, i quite recommend it to any fans of strategy who are looking for something a little different.
